title: Split out the website from the rest into a separate project, squash repository size down.
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 62)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 18, 2009 at 15:18 UTC

Between a bunch of now useless checkins of lombok-patcher.jar, and the website data 
(including the video!) and 10MB worth of tools.jar and 15MB worth of eclipse jars, a fresh clone 
of the repo is now weighing in at 100MB.

We should split out the website into a separate project, remove the commits of lombok-
patcher.jar, and move the downloads of the eclipse plugins into ant installDeps, as, if you HAVE 
an eclipse (v3.5, I guess), installDeps can just plunder them from your local eclipse installation 
and save you a big download.

Of course, that'll mess with published history, so everyone would basically have to toss their 
clone and re-clone from scratch!

See 'git rebase --help', under the heading "RECOVERING FROM UPSTREAM REBASE".

To pull changes in, you'd have to do "git pull --rebase", which won't work if there are local 
changes or merges.

body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 70)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 04, 2009 at 21:21 UTC

We're probably going to either come up with a defaults system, or have a separate constructor annotation to 
force it. For now, to be consistent in applying the lombok rule (lombok does not generate a method if you 
already have one with the same name, regardless of parameters), this will remain a wontfix. Rest assured we're 
not entirely happy with the status quo :P

:bust_in_silhouette: **jpyeron**   :clock8: Nov 04, 2010 at 12:50 UTC

Would have to say, that constructors are not methods, and this area would be a justifiable exception to the pattern. The static method hack would not be advisable because it would break many reflection based instantiations.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Nov 04, 2010 at 16:36 UTC

Lombok 0.9.3 which has been out a while now adds @ RequiredArgsConstructor, @ AllArgsConstructor, and @ NoArgsConstructor. The presence of any one (or multiple, they don't exclude each other) of these annotations forces lombok to generate them, even if you have your own. That's the fix for this problem.
_End of migration_

title: @Data with arrays generates FindBugs violation
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 77)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **jacek99**   :clock8: Dec 04, 2009 at 16:54 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Create a @ Data POJO with a String[] field (e.g. private String[] services;) 2. Run the FindBugs maven plugin against the code 3. Findbugs generates a warning on the generated code: "may expose internal representation by returning" your array MALICIOUS_CODE EI_EXPOSE_REP The FindBugs glossary describes this as: EI: May expose internal representation by returning reference to mutable object (EI_EXPOSE_REP) Returning a reference to a mutable object value stored in one of the object's fields exposes the internal representation of the object. If instances are accessed by untrusted code, and unchecked changes to the mutable object would compromise security or other important properties, you will need to do something different. Returning a new copy of the object is better approach in many situations. What is the expected output? What do you see instead? No FindBugs warnings What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? 0.9.0, on Ubuntu 9.04 with JDK 6 Please provide any additional information below. Found this after adding the Findbugs maven plugin to our pom.xml

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 04, 2009 at 20:12 UTC

The only way to fix this is to duplicate the array.

Which is not a good solution - it's somewhat surprising that this will in fact happen, and for consistency we 
should then duplicate ALL mutable fields. But we can't. For two reasons:

(1) we have no idea which types are mutable and which types are immutable; mutability is not part of java's 
type system.

(2) Even if we did know, there's no general way to duplicate an object. clone() usually doesn't work.

So, good point, but we can't fix it, at least not without adding a heap of complexity into how lombok works.

:bust_in_silhouette: **mclauss77**   :clock8: Jul 01, 2013 at 13:30 UTC

This problem also adds for other situations, e.g. Date types.
What about a specific annotation to get lombok provide a clone-based implementation? That might be generic enough...

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 01, 2013 at 16:08 UTC

This will remain WontFix - this academicy model of thinking just doesn't fly in java. Array data is usually very large, so just duplicating it is crazy, especially as, in the vast majority of circumstances, that duplication is completely pointless as nobody _actually_ messes with the data. More generally, if this is an issue you should not just duplicate the array*, you should change the API of the object so that it is no longer possible to just ask for the array data. For example, change to a list implementation, and wrap things in guava's ImmutableList. Telling lombok to clone isn't good enough. When should lombok clone?
- When the object is provided during object creation / calling of the set method.
- When the object is returned via a getter.

Cloning for both produces a huge amount of garbage collection cruft and in general results in ridiculous performance penalties. Again, this is working on the general basis that your mutable objects are large, but they tend to be.

For java.util.Date objects, the right solution is to not use date and instead roll with jodatime's date representations, or 'long', because those are both immutable. The solution is not to clone the incoming j.u.Date object on both edges of the set/get process. That's crazy. The solution for arraydata is to make it ImmutableList, and to actually _USE_ the ImmutableList type in your data, or, alternatively, to accept in constructor/setter any list, but to have the field type be immutablelist. This makes it clear for those doing a get() call that the returned list is immutable.

*) You can't just create a single public copy or even cache this copy, because if you did, then 2 different codebases that both call getX() can see each other's modifications.

It's hugely impractical to try and automate this with lombok. Even if it was possible (and note that the feature page for this would be many tens of pages long to cover all the hairy details!), it's clearly no longer boilerplate.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 01, 2015 at 23:22 UTC

We stand by the advice that you should just in general tell findbugs to not warn on this, but a feature was just added to tell findbugs not to warn on anything that lombok generates. See:

issue #737
_End of migration_

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 19, 2010 at 20:01 UTC

Issue #181 has been merged into this issue.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 19, 2010 at 20:14 UTC

We've now added this to lombok 0.9.3 (Burrowing Whale). We still have to update the site documentation, but, in short:

@ NoArgsConstructor
@ RequiredArgsConstructor(access=AccessLevel.PROTECTED, staticName="of")
@ AllArgsConstructor

will generate no args constructor (and error out if that's not possible due to final fields), required args constructor (all final fields and all fields with constraints such as @ NonNull - this is what @ Data does by default), and a constructor for ALL fields. You can choose the access level (public by default) for any of them, and you can turn any of them into a static constructor via the staticName annotation argument.

You can play with this feature by installing the edge release of Burrowing Whale, available here:

https://projectlombok.org/download-edge.html

title: When running netbeans on a JVM1.5, lombok stops netbeans from starting.
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 82)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 09, 2009 at 11:12 UTC

See http://groups.google.com/group/project-lombok/browse_thread/thread/cb4a96bd843ab366

solutions:

Figure out exactly why netbeans fails to start, catch that problem, and render some sort of dialog 
box instead and disable lombok.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 12, 2009 at 13:31 UTC

The difference in javacs between 1.5 and 1.6 is enormous. Backporting lombok would be a lot of work.

JVM1.5 is end-of-lifed, and there's no good reason to run netbeans on a 1.5 JVM. Solved in commit 
d9d7fe80637e3d543ca193730f5b8a4e4dbc6a5a by detecting the situation, disabling lombok, and, once 
netbeans has been fully loaded, showing an error box explaining the problem.

NB: This issue has never been in a non-beta/HEAD version of lombok. It was found in a 0.9.2 beta.
_End of migration_

title: AnnotationValues.getProbableFQTypes does not work for class literals not on CP
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 88)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **petr.jiricka**   :clock8: Dec 16, 2009 at 19:57 UTC

I have an annotation that uses a Class parameter, so it is used like this:
@ MyAnnotation(forClass=some.pkg.MyClass.class)

In the Javac handler for this annotation, I call
annotation.getProbableFQType("forClass")

However, this does not work, as the implementation calls
Class.forName("some.pkg.MyClass"), and this class is not on Javac's
classpath (it is part of the user code being compiled).

I am attaching a patch that fixes this problem for me - though I am not a
Javac expert so I don't know if this is the correct patch. 

(It also fixes one other minor problem that the compiled source's package
is not correctly populated if the package name is just one level without
any dots.)
:bust_in_silhouette: **petr.jiricka**   :clock8: Dec 16, 2009 at 19:57 UTC [:link: patch1.txt](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/6153646924581208426/patch1.txt)

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 17, 2009 at 11:59 UTC

Thanks for the patch, it showed me this is a bit more involve than I at first thought when I read the issue report.

The biggest problem I have with your (very nicely designed) setup of letting each concrete implementation of lombok (eclipse, and javac) set up the job of arriving at an FQN will 
invariably result in only two possible scenarios:

1) We specify exactly what FQN resolution should do, and we enforce that each implementation does no less, but also _no more_ than this.

2) We don't specify exactly, or we are lax about enforcing it, and the inevitable result is that compiling code on eclipse is going to give you a different result compared to compiling 
with javac. This is not an acceptable scenario.

Thus, we must go with the first scenario, but therein lies a problem. Javac is fairly nicely designed and uses round-based compiling consistently, and will thus give you excellent 
resolution. Eclipse doesn't do this; at the phase lombok (currently) runs in eclipse, resolution just isn't available. Therefore, speccing that FQN resolution should do what the javac-
specific implementation in your patch does means a massive amount of work on eclipse to completely change how and where lombok plugs into the eclipse architecture. We actually 
want to go there, because having resolution available allows for some awesome transformations, but it's a lot of work and we're not ready to do this yet.

I'll make sure that when we do go there, that getProbableFQTypes is rewritten. It'll also be renamed; there's no more 'probable' about it once resolution is available to us. You won't 
get the probable type, you'll get _the type_, properly resolved.

Thus, unfortunately, I can't accept your patch. However, I can rejigger how it works.

Separate from that there's the bugfix to "package foo;" which I did accept, and it's in the master branch on git now as 61b054d78784f27be5420474af4ccb047e1668cc.

 How's this:

Instead of trying to use Class.forName, which admittedly is not a particularly good idea, how about this more complex but more powerful algorithm:
1. Walk through the type hierarchy in the local file. If you have a field in an inner class annotated with "v=OuterName.Foo.class", we'll get that right and stick the local Compilation 
   Unit's package in front, and return that. So, "package.OuterName.Foo" would be returned.
2. Walk through the import statements. Any non-star match is returned. Thus, if you write v=Foo.class and your source file includes "import bar.baz.Foo;", we'll return bar.baz.Foo.
3. for any star import (code presumes there's an import java.lang.\* at the end of your import declarations), _IF_ it starts with "java.", we'll use Class.forName. Such a class should be 
   available to the compiler classloader.
4. If all these strategies failed, and the type name includes no dot, stick the CU's package name in front, and return that (so v=Bar.class, where we have no idea what Bar is referring 
   to, if it occurs in a file with "package x.y", we return "x.y.Bar". It's also possible this class is imported via a star import, but then, that's why its called "probable" - this is a 
   guesstimate, not an infallible algorithm.
5. If the type name does include a dot, and the type name DOES NOT start with a titlecase or uppercase character, we presume this is a fully qualified name, and we return it 
   verbatim. If the first character IS titlecase or uppercase (ex: Foo.Bar.Baz), then we presume this is a reference to a nested class in a sibling class (a class in the same package) and we 
   use the same strategy as ﹟4: We prefix this type with the local CU's package name and return that.

This ISNT the proper java resolution algorithm. There are edge cases where the proper resolution gives you a different class than this hack, but the only ways I can think of that this 
is not going to work is if you either star-import non-java stuff, or if you throw the conventions to the wind and start your package names with capitals or your class names with 
lowercase letters.

This concept is now in the master branch (though not tested very well): 31d7d8ec92314e4e571d95d8a71e1e981004ae29

It's not as good as using the true resolution, but I think it'll do until we upgrade lombok to run with full resolution support.

:bust_in_silhouette: **petr.jiricka**   :clock8: Dec 17, 2009 at 13:07 UTC

Thanks for a quick fix - I will test it.

I did not look into the Eclipse support area at all, and I did not know type
resolution was not possible there.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 17, 2009 at 16:33 UTC

If eclipse just ceased to exist overnight, lombok could do a lot more than it does now. Eclipse's internal AST and 
compilation code is a disaster. It's unfortunate in the extreme eclipse doesn't just dump the entire JDT core and 
swap it over to a javac based solution. NetBeans proves that this can work rather well.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 21, 2009 at 13:33 UTC

I don't think we're going to implement it like that. That would be the same as
inserting an instanceof check. Is suppose for Hybernate, we need a entirely different

We cannot fix this; the rules for equals and hashCode are fundamentally incompatible with hibernate proxies.

For your information, we were talking about annotation processors and not the buit-in

- Built-in support during compilation (provided by java)
- Runtime inspection, used for instance by JEE
- class-file processors that run stand alone, used for instance by findbugs
- Annotation Processors that create files during compilation

The first three ones have had good support since java 1.5, when annotations were
added. For the annotation processor to work, you had to use the apt tool for
compilation (instead of javac). Since java 1.6, they slightly changed the API and put
the apt code int javac.

title: Delombok should generate Javadoc comments
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 97)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **vit6ak**   :clock8: Jan 08, 2010 at 18:44 UTC

Hello,
I've found that Delombok does not generate any Javadoc comment.
I'm not sure wherher it is feature or bug so I'm not sure wherher I'm
writing a bug report or feature request.
I think that delombok should generate javadoc comments for e.g.:
- constructors (@ throws NullPointerException and @ param)
- getters and setters
- equals ("... if foo, bar and baz are equal")

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 08, 2010 at 19:17 UTC

I'm fairly sure Roel thinks the same way, which would mean this won't get addressed, but I'll wait for his 
feedback before marking this as WontFix:

Trying to stick javadoc on everything is seriously misguided; often the name of the method and the 
parameters are by themselves all the documentation you could ever want. Any further documenting of the 
obvious only results in repeating yourself and headaches whenever you change things. Comments cannot be 
unit tested.

Lombok generates the obvious, which almost by definition means that any javadoc would be superfluous.

There isn't even any need to javadoc the nonnull behaviour; a @ NonNull annotation will take care of that, and 
the annotation is copied to the arguments to the setter and the constructor (if it isn't, that _would_ be a 
lombok bug). Not all @ NonNull annotations in the wild are @ Documented, but most are, but, er, not ours. 
Fixed that right away, it's in commit 9c07a465c1976140a11c1bee78af485a1c907f63 and will be in 0.9.3.

At any rate it's not a bug, but a feature. It is not written anywhere that all public API needs javadoc.

Roel: WontFix?

:bust_in_silhouette: **vit6ak**   :clock8: Jan 08, 2010 at 19:24 UTC

Well, it is sometimes useful to add some extra info about the field.

@ Documented at Lombok's @ NonNull is not same as @ throws, but I'm a bit conservative
about JavaDoc.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 08, 2010 at 19:29 UTC

If some constructor parameter is documented to be @ NonNull I would expect an NPE to occur at some point, 
sooner or later, when I ignore it. Yes, lombok will in fact throw the NPE immediately, but if we document that 
we might as well document a thousand other things. It's not out of the ordinary and therefore does not 
deserve explicit mention in documentation.

A lot of the arguments against stating the obvious in the documentation aren't valid for lombok-generated 
stuff; it's NOT much of a maintainance nightmare, it doesn't waste precious programmer time, and it's not a 
violation of DRY. So, this boat hasn't quite sailed yet. I'll take it up with Roel on our next lombok hacking 
session.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jan 13, 2010 at 13:33 UTC

I do want to investigate this before writing it off.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 13, 2010 at 22:28 UTC

We've talked about this and we're going to add this feature.

Design:

javadoc of the field is parsed; anything in <setter>TEXT HERE</setter> is copied only to the setter. Anything 
in <getter></getter> goes to the getter, and anything not in those specific tags (top-level only!) is added to 
both. Any @ param statements are presumed to go to only the setter, and @ return will go to the getter. If they 
are missing, we'll generate a default message for them. If the field has javadoc, but no text at all for a getter 
or setter, we'll generate a standard story ("Sets the foo of the bar"). Finally, if the field is @ NonNull annotated, 
we'll add a @ throws line for the setter. We'll add no other notes; the @ Documented nature of the @ NonNull 
annotation you're using will have to take care of any further documentation needs.

Any @ param lines as well as any @ throws for NonNull annotated fields will also be put in the javadoc for a 
generated setter, but the exact body of the generated constructor javadoc is something we still have to think 
about.

NB: If there's no javadoc on the field, we won't generate any on the getters/setters either. I doubt anyone is 
going to be able to change our minds on this. However, adding the following javadoc: /*\* */ to your field, will 
generate a completely boilerplate getter and setter javadoc, so this isn't a big problem in our eyes.

:bust_in_silhouette: **stefatwork**   :clock8: Jan 14, 2010 at 09:50 UTC

The syntax looks nice and flexible! 
But considering we're in the lombok context, some people might complain about the use
of @ param and @ return which could cause their IDE to display warning messages.
Perhaps a more proprietary syntax for those two (<setter-param>, <getter-return>)
could avoid such things?

Just an idea...

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jan 14, 2010 at 16:14 UTC

Lombok would "remove" the javadoc from the field. So your IDE won't hava any problem
with it. Maybe we should consider adding a <field></field> combo to allow the user to
specify the javadoc for the field though.

:bust_in_silhouette: **vit6ak**   :clock8: Jan 16, 2010 at 17:42 UTC

Well, there are also constructors that are similar to setters. I think
that @ param can be copied to constructor and notes for setters can
also be copied.

Tried Lombok in my company, but we have abandoned it due to the the lack of support for generating Javadoc.

title: Ability to Set Dirty Bit in Setters
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 104)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **machineghost**   :clock8: Feb 18, 2010 at 01:49 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. None; it's a feature request In our codebase (and I would imagine in many others as well), we have a simple pattern that we use for any class that is going to be serialized to the database. When a setter is called, in addition to setting the field, we also set a "dirty" field to true. That way, when we call the method to commit the object to the database, it can check whether anything actually changed since it was first instantiated, and if not it can save the trouble of a DB hit. Unfortunately there doesn't seem to be any way to reproduce this using Lombok. It would be nice if there was some way to pass @ Data/@ Setter either the name of a dirty field to set, or an anonymous class with a method to be invoked for all setters, or _something_ that so that you could get "dirty = true;" included in all of your auto-generated setters. I realize of course that the whole idea of Lombok is to account for the common scenarios, not the uncommon ones (you just make custom setters for those), but because this applies to every setter method in any class that wants to track whether it has changed since instantiation, I hope you will at least consider this feature request.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 18, 2010 at 03:05 UTC

Well, you nailed it. It's not even remotely close to a common enough case to warrant putting into @ Setter / 
@ Data. The problem boils down to this: If this is good enough for lombok, then I can name at least 5 features, 
and imagine about 50 others, that also make sense. However, if lombok @ Setter/@ Data actually supported all 
50, it would be far more difficult to use vs. what it is now.

We see the solution to issues like these to eventually be to either write your own plugin (which is still somewhat 
complex today).
_End of migration_

title: Hibernate proxies cause problems with equals method's direct property access.
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 110)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Mar 22, 2010 at 18:19 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Use @ EqualsAndHashCode on a Hibernate POJO. 2. Generate a query that returns a proxy object but doesn't initialize it. 3. Call equals() method on the POJO and pass in the uninitialized hibernate proxy. What is the expected output? What do you see instead? Since no methods are actually called on the proxy object, it remains uninitialized. All references in the uninitialized proxy are null. What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? Lombok 0.9.2. Hibernate 3.3.2 GA with JavaAssist bytecode generator. Please provide any additional information below. The simplest (and possibly most convenient) solution would be to add a flag to @ EqualsAndHashCode like: boolean useAccessors() = false; If true, Lombok would use generated (if applicable) or user-specified accessors when accessing properties in equals() (and hashCode(), though I only mention it because this single annotation generates both). Code like (attached) java.txt would end up generating (attached) lombok.txt.
:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Mar 22, 2010 at 18:19 UTC [:link: java.txt](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/-5552770960492633010/java.txt)
:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Mar 22, 2010 at 18:19 UTC [:link: lombok.txt](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/-3995775212881931117/lombok.txt)

:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Mar 22, 2010 at 18:20 UTC

Forgot to put "useAccessors=true" in the @ EqualsAndHashCode annotation, but you get
the idea.  Thanks!

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Mar 22, 2010 at 19:41 UTC

Actually, equality (and thus, hashCodes) for JPA/Hibernate proxies is a hairy issue. For example, hitting each field 
via getX(), and then calling .equals() on each field (which we do; objects are equal if all fields are equal to each 
other, which requires another equals call per non-primitive field), which would in turn hit all its fields with getX() 
and call equals on all of them, can and usually will result in 1 equals call querying half your entire database.

We've met this need by allowing you write @ EqualsAndHashCode(of="foo"), where foo should be some simple 
suitable field such as unid.

:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Mar 22, 2010 at 20:05 UTC

The example I posted actually satisfies the criteria you specified (write
@ EqualsAndHashCode(of="foo") where foo should be a simple field) but could STILL
trigger the issue with the uninitialized proxy, if this proxy is an argument to
equals().  Thus there is absolutely no safe way to use @ EqualsAndHashCode with
Hibernate POJOs.  EVER.  Even with properties of type int, char, etc. (they don't get
initialized either until a non-PK accessor or other method is called).  Unless you
disable bytecode-assisted optimization in Hibernate (which I don't think is possible
anymore), or take absolute care that all your objects are initialized if you think
they're going to end up in a collection on which you call contains(), or some other
method.

The hashCode portion of the annotation doesn't suffer from the uninitialized proxy
problem, because hashCode() is an overridable method invoked on its members and will
automatically trigger proxy initialization before any private properties are directly
read.

Now my opinion is if I'm taking time enough to use "of={ <property list>... }", then
I'm knowledgeable enough about the underlying database relationships, and thus I
should be responsible for worrying about database hits.  If I end up with more than
just a few database hits while calling equals(), I need a smack in the head for my
design or laziness.  Lombok shouldn't be responsible for this.

Even without Hibernate, can I make a valid case for a property that needs to be
mucked about with in the accessors?  e.g. (attached) MyClass.java.

Note there's no "myProp" property, but it looks like there is to other callers since
getProp and setProp are there.  Now this is sounding more like a JavaBeans kind of
problem set, but where I found the lombok annotations so convenient in this case I
thought I'd ask.  At the very least, is it possible to have a standalone @ HashCode
annotation, since it doesn't trigger the same issue with Hibernate proxy objects? 
Then I can just write my equals() method and be done with that part of it.
:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Mar 22, 2010 at 20:05 UTC [:link: MyClass.java](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/8587407368903364958/MyClass.java)

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Mar 23, 2010 at 06:46 UTC

Hibernate POJOs are _always_ annotated with @ Entity, no?

It would be a rather sizable injection of 'magic', but how about this:

We'll switch to calling the get methods if there's an @ Entity annotation?

The alternative is that we simply always use getX() instead of X; the performance impact is negligible as the 
JVM inlines such calls if the object is involved in an oft-run piece of code.

:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Mar 23, 2010 at 16:54 UTC

I like your note about the performance impact.  I think you'd have a better
understanding of any other side effects that might occur while using accessors
instead of direct property accesses.  Essentially you'd be accepting the JavaBeans
way of referring to properties (so that you can have "virtual" properties that don't
actually exist as a concrete private property).

@ Entity is only used when annotations are used to map Hibernate POJOs.  XML mapping
files are still supported, and provide the same mapping abilities (though
non-standardized at least as far as JSRs are concerned), and don't necessitate adding
a whole slew of JARs to your project for annotation mapping support.

Or we could rally Orasun to add true property support a la C﹟. :)

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Mar 24, 2010 at 23:14 UTC

Oh, yeah, Orasun is going to get right on that lickety split :)

So, the concensus is for Roel and I to sit down and figure out if there's any big (negative) impact to rerouting the 
equals/hashCode calls to use the getters instead of direct field access, yeah?

Can anyone help us along and point out some issues with going the getter route? Any performance issues 
preferably stated in the form of a profiler report. In my experience, reasoning about JVM performance never 
works very well.

:bust_in_silhouette: **mwanji**   :clock8: Mar 25, 2010 at 15:36 UTC

In a hand-written equals(), I use getters, too, which seems to be the recommended way 
of avoiding problems with proxies. Any performance issue is going to come from 
possibly triggering DB queries.

And you'd have to exclude getId() to be able to compare a saved object to an unsaved 
one. Though it's a best-practice, I never find myself mixing saved and transient 
instances in collections or directly comparing them. So I'm not sure what the default 
behaviour should be. If you _do_ compare IDs and at least one is set, then that might 
be sufficient.

:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Mar 25, 2010 at 15:51 UTC

I use getters as well, but usually only for the argument (e.g. 'return
this.employeeName.equals( o.getEmployeeName() )), but that's getting a little
pedantic.  Essentially you're guaranteed that "this" is properly initialized, because
you're in a non-static method.

In any case, I make sure the object graph traversed by the equals() method only goes
so deep.  Occasionally I'll use the primary key for the equals contract, because
there's no clearly-defined business key enforced by the database, or because it would
take 4-5 traversals (effectively e.g.
this.getParent().getOtherParent().getAnotherParent().getName(), which could cause 3
database fetches) to actually return a result.

:bust_in_silhouette: **mwanji**   :clock8: Mar 25, 2010 at 16:04 UTC

"I use getters as well, but usually only for the argument"

I guess that works because the proxies implement an equals() that delegates to the 
wrapped object?

"this.getParent().getOtherParent().getAnotherParent().getName()"

Does that really happen? I was thinking more along the lines of 
this.getOtherEntity().equals(that.getOtherEntity()), which might trigger any number 
of queries. Should @ ManyToOne and @ OneToMany relationships be eliminated by default? 
(I'm not even sure Lombok can resolve that kind of thing)

:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Mar 25, 2010 at 16:26 UTC

> this.getParent().getOtherParent().getAnotherParent().getName()

That was just an example.  In reality it would be exactly like your example
(this.getOtherEntity().equals( o.getOtherEntity() ).  I have a database design now
where the natural id is a combination of two foreign keys.  Those two foreign tables'
natural ids are each a single string column.  But for the first entity:

  equals( Object o ) {
    return this.getFirstEntity().equals( o.getFirstEntity() )
      && this.getSecondEntity().equals( o.getSecondEntity() )
  }

So each of those two calls to equals() would cause two separate database hits (4
total) if all 4 properties are uninitialized proxies.  The first two database hits
occur for each equals() call, and the second two would only occur if those equals()
methods themselves use getter calls.

That's why I'm a little confused about this stuff, especially as to how responsible
Lombok should be for this, because I don't really think I take advantage of natural
keys.  I never call equals(), hashCode() or even compare() on a transient (no-PK)
entity, so what's the problem with using the IDs (which are always initialized) in
@ EqualsAndHashCode?  Opinions?

:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Mar 25, 2010 at 16:28 UTC

This issue report is turning into a Hibernate issue report, but I just wanted to add
one more thing--maybe as a temporary workaround, we could simply declare, in the
mapping file, that any foreign key entities involved in the natural id be fetched
eagerly, so they'll never be uninitialized proxies.

:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Apr 01, 2010 at 20:40 UTC

Proxies don't initialize the primary key either.  Unless lombok's equals()
implementation will use the argument's accessors, @ EqualsAndHashCode can never be
used with Hibernate POJOs.

title: @Getter should generate get() for Atomic*** objects
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 113)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Apr 02, 2010 at 21:59 UTC

We can't do this because there's clearly no end in sight for it. There's an infinite amount of wrapper-ish classes 
out there, and even if somehow we could add a feature to unwrap every wrapper, the notion that AtomicInteger 
is truly a wrapper is dubious; after all, it also adds the atomic nature to it.

Nevertheless, thanks for the feedback. I'll chalk this down as a request for making extending lombok simpler :)

:bust_in_silhouette: **jacek99**   :clock8: Apr 02, 2010 at 22:21 UTC

Well, yes, but the Atomic**\* objects are usually transparent to the caller. They
expect to get an Integer in this case (that's what the calling code wants). The
Atomic part of it is because the instance has to handle concurrency while updating
it,but that should be hidden when retrieving the value by external classes.

It makes all the calling code litered with

someComponent.getMyInteger().get();

vs. just

someComponent.getMyInteger()

Maybe we could add some option to @ Getter to activate this on demand (e.g. 

@ Getter(wrapperMethod="get") private AtomicInteger myInteger;

Could be a generic solution for anything.
_End of migration_

title: Project Lombok annotations do not compile under Ant4Eclipse
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 114)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **gmcnaughton**   :clock8: Apr 05, 2010 at 03:36 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Create a new Eclipse project 2. Add lombok.jar 3. Write code using Lombok annotations (like @ Getter) 4. Verify that the code compiles under Eclipse 5. Verify that the code compiles under javac 6. Attempt to compile the code via an Ant4Eclipse ant task (<buildJdtProject>) What is the expected output? What do you see instead? The @ Getter code compiles under Eclipse and javac, but the annotations are ignored when Ant4Eclipse tries to compile it. The getters are not generated, even though lombok.jar is in the classpath and 'import lombok.Getter' does not cause complaints. What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? Using Project Lombok v0.9.2 with Ant4Eclipse 1.0.0.M2, compiling on Win2k under JDK 1.6.0_17. Please provide any additional information below. Here's a sample Eclipse project that demonstrates the problem! http://www.whitelite.net/LombokTest.zip Ant4Eclipse substitutes its own compiler wrapper (org.ant4eclipse.ant.jdt.ecj.JDTCompilerAdapter) when calling the <javac>, so presumably that is causing the issue somehow. I reported the problem on the Ant4Eclipse forums too: http://www.ant4eclipse.org/node/105 I'd love to use both of these libraries together! Hopefully it isn't an architectural limitation of either project.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Apr 06, 2010 at 01:48 UTC

lombok is compatible with both ecj and javac, and I'll eat my shoes if Ant4Eclipse doesn't use one of those two 
to perform the actual compilation. If lombok.jar is on the classpath when Ant4Eclipse calls on javac/ecj to 
compile the code, _and_ it does NOT disable annotation processors, _AND_ it compiles for 1.6, then it should 
either (A) work, or (B) confuse lombok into thinking its being run the wrong way in eclipse which will result in 
a compiler error explaining this. That would be a lombok bug, but one we could easily fix.

We'll need some more information to analyze exactly what's happening here:

 1) What's the project's target/source set to? 1.6+ for both?
 2) Do you happen to see any errors related to agents, plugins, or lombok itself, before you get the compiler 
errors resulting from lombok never running on your code?

As a workaround you can use delombok until we clear this up: 
https://projectlombok.org/features/delombok.html

:bust_in_silhouette: **flusinak@spambog.de**   :clock8: May 06, 2010 at 12:51 UTC

Please note the following issue on that:

   http://www.javakontor.org:8080/jira/browse/AE-190

Even though the Eclipse Java Compiler is used the annotation processor cannot be
setup as the compiler relies on it's own batch compiler type ('Main') thus the
eclipse java compiler requires some changes 8-(
You can close this issue without any problem.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 06, 2010 at 13:48 UTC

Thanks for finding this. Do you think we can help in any way to get this fixed in
either AntForEclipse or Eclipse?

:bust_in_silhouette: **flusinak@spambog.de**   :clock8: May 06, 2010 at 14:10 UTC

It's just an old relict in the Eclipse java compiler. They do provide a way to make
the compiler available for other and they even provide possibilities to capture
errors/warnings etc. 
But the contained batch annotation processor does not reflect this. The api allows to
pass any kind of object but they assume their own 'Main' class used to launch the
compiler in their context. So it's an inconsistency within the api of the eclipse
java compiler.
Nevertheless Ant4Eclipse does not depend on the eclipse java compiler. I will
probably write an adapter so the java compiler will be capable to be initialised with
the settings from eclipse. Unfortunately that will take some time and can't be done
in an instant.

From the 'lombok' perspective there's nothing to be done as it's just used by the
first user who encountered this annotation related issue.

Btw. lombok is a nice tool and I will definitely contribute my own code (I've got a
similar project internally used as I didn't knew about lombok before).

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 19, 2010 at 15:10 UTC

Closed per request

title: @Data shouldn't try to override final hashCode and equals
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 120)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **joseph.pachod**   :clock8: May 07, 2010 at 09:07 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1.make hashCode and equals final in a superclass 2.in a class extending it, put @ Data on top 3.see the compiler getting all red What is the expected output? What do you see instead? I would assume it to be normal for Lombok not to try to override final equals and hashCode. Currently it tries, fails and put an error.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 07, 2010 at 11:21 UTC

You're right, that should be the case. However, currently Lombok does not have access
to the superclass, since that would require resolution. For now, there is no good
workaround available.

:bust_in_silhouette: **joseph.pachod**   :clock8: May 07, 2010 at 11:45 UTC

thanks for the return :)

is there a known work around, instead than just removing the final keyword ?

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 07, 2010 at 12:35 UTC

No really. You could use @ Getter and @ Setter for all fields and @ ToString on the
class. But then you still have to generate the constructor. We are working on a new
version of Lombok with resolution, but that will take a while. Possibly, we could
release a patch for the current version that allows you to disable the generation of
equals and hashcode. I'll have to talk about this with Reinier.

:bust_in_silhouette: **joseph.pachod**   :clock8: May 07, 2010 at 13:50 UTC

that would be great, thanks a lot

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: May 07, 2010 at 15:56 UTC

I think adding something like @ Data(skipEqualsAndHashCode=true) is going too far into the DSL route - the 
problem where @ Data, @ Getter, @ Setter and the other property annotations gain an endlessly growing army of 
switches and settings to customize them into whatever you want. The bad thing about that is that you're 
layering almost a new programming language on top of java which already works fine, so probably in the end 
its better to not add this kind of complexity and instead let people write their somewhat more complicated 
data classes the old way.

If however we do go the DSL route because its still a significant savings in boilerplate, then we definitely 
should not just add whatever comes up. Instead we should sit down, write down a bunch of use cases that 
lombok currently doesn't handle well, and then figure out the simplest possible thing that could possibly work 
that'll let lombok handle well as many of those use cases as we can manage.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 10, 2010 at 07:54 UTC

I was thinking that if you use @ EqualsAndHashCode(of="") we could just not create an
equals and hashcode method. So no new flags.

:bust_in_silhouette: **joseph.pachod**   :clock8: May 18, 2010 at 12:03 UTC

hi

Having been speaking of this issue recently, we came to some other way to "resolve"
it. Indeed, currently, the need for @ Data not overriding equals and hashcode is
present because @ Data is very convenient and doing without it is painful. 

Indeed, @ Data provides @ Getter and @ Setter on a class level, whereas without @ Data
one has to provide @ Getter/@ Setter on a per field level... 

so, providing each convenience of @ Data on a class level would make it easier to skip
it when it's not possible to use it, reducing the need for some DSL or convention
like @ EqualsAndHashCode(of=""). I esp. think of the construction enhancement feature
of @ Data, which currently has no corresponding annotation that I know of.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 17, 2010 at 04:56 UTC

Now that issue #202 implements @ Getter and @ Setter on entire types, this is far less of a problem; you can pick-n-mix what you want from @ Data. We'll tackle constructor generation in a similar fashion later on.

:bust_in_silhouette: **joseph.pachod**   :clock8: Jul 17, 2010 at 07:14 UTC

great, thanks!

the sooner it's released, the better :)
_End of migration_

title: Lombok in javac messes with enum annotation methods with defaults.
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 121)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **google-auth-21ov9@codesmell.de**   :clock8: May 10, 2010 at 16:08 UTC As soon as lombok.jar is in the classpath when compiling, i get a spooky behaviour when building with maven: What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Have these example classes in src/main/java @ Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @ Target(ElementType.TYPE) public @ interface ComponentPermission { String value(); ``` ActionType type() default ActionType.RENDER; ``` } and public enum ActionType { RENDER, ENABLE; } right next to each other. 1. Compiles in Eclipse (with or without lombok) and maven. 2. add lombok dependency to pom, and mvn clean compile and face: ComponentPermission.java:[19,40] incompatible types found : com.softculture.services.authorization.wicket.ActionType required: com.softculture.services.authorization.wicket.ActionType What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? lombok 0.92, jdk1.6u20/32, eclipse 3.5, maven 2.1.0, maven-compile-plugin up to 2.3 (does not matter) problem is reproduceable with simple javac. fails with lombok.jar included in classpath, passes otherwise.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: May 12, 2010 at 11:10 UTC

This is a javac bug that lombok makes more likely to occur. The fix is even more of a headscratcher - write out in 
full the package name of one of them:

ActionType type() default full.package.ActionType.RENDER;

We'll fix this most likely when we tackle resolution as this seems to be related to somehow causing javac to 
maintain more than one symbol table.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 18, 2010 at 17:22 UTC

Issue #200 has been merged into this issue.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 06, 2011 at 19:28 UTC

This bug is _still_ here and we really should look into fixing it.

:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Jun 16, 2011 at 07:59 UTC

See: http://netbeans.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=193952﹟c4

I stumbled over it too, adding the CleaningAnnotationProcessor fixed it.
the question is whether this should just be documented or lombok should include CleaningAnnotationProcessor and CleaningAnnotationProcessorImpl.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 16, 2011 at 08:07 UTC

Good question. This problem will go away on its own eventually (as javac 1.7 is adopted). I'm marginally in favour of adding it to lombok, though lombok cannot as far as I can tell ensure it ends up running last. Nevertheless, lombok stripping the default attribution out too early is far less likely to actually cause a problem than not doing so, hence why I'm in favour.

Roel?

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jun 16, 2011 at 08:58 UTC

So basically the code checks if the compiler contains the bug once, and if so it calls the (package) private static method JavacProcessingEnvironment.cleanTrees(JCTree[]) with all the methods in all compiled classes.

http://bugs.sun.com/bugdatabase/view_bug.do?bug_id=6512707 stats that it is fixed in java7 and openjdk6 b16.

I'm on the fence.
- It not OUR bug; any processor would trigger the bug
- Then again, we might be the only one, so our users experience this bug
- We want to be the first Annotation Processor, so other processors get access to our generated code

I propose to document this behavior, make it googleable, and link to or provide a separate jar containing the code from the netbeans site. We might want to modify that code to also do a test to see if our environment is actually a JavacProcessingEnvironment (instanceof check) and make sure it works in Eclipse (as in, does nothing, no Exceptions)

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jun 16, 2011 at 08:59 UTC

What would happen if we're not the last processor, but call cleanTrees anyway? Will it break other code?

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 16, 2011 at 09:04 UTC

As Jan Lahoda explicitly said in the netbeans bug report that CAP should preferably be run last, I'm guessing it'll break any other AP that runs after us that tries to inspect the default value of any @ interface.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Dec 19, 2011 at 20:58 UTC

Issue #392 has been merged into this issue.

:bust_in_silhouette: **askoning**   :clock8: Apr 13, 2012 at 13:47 UTC

Issue #429 has been merged into this issue.
_End of migration_
I think lombok no longer has this bug. Even if it does, pretty sure time and bugfixes in other tools have made this bug moot.

title: Add @ConstructorProperties to generated constructor
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 122)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **jonathancrosmer@hotmail.com**   :clock8: May 19, 2010 at 14:46 UTC

@ ConstructorProperties is a new annotation in Java 6.
http://java.sun.com/javase/6/docs/api/java/beans/ConstructorProperties.html

The most obvious use of this annotation is that it enables XmlEncoder
to automatically encode immutable POJOs as XML (normally, XmlEncoder
can't encode immutable objects without special handling). 

The constructor generated by @ Data should automatically add this
annotation.  For example,

@ Data
class Point { private final int x, y; }

...becomes...

class Point {
    @ ConstructorProperties({"x", "y"})
    public Point(int x, int y) {
    ...
}

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 20, 2010 at 08:47 UTC

Thanks, Jonathan, for submitting this feature request. Looks like a great addition to 
Lombok to me.
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 20, 2010 at 08:48 UTC

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 19, 2010 at 21:50 UTC

We've added this feature to 0.9.3 (Burrowing Whale)!

There's still the issue that such a file won't compile on java 1.5, as @ ConstructorProperties is new in java 1.6. It can be suppressed with @ RequiredArgsConstructor(suppressConstructorProperties=true), though we've already deprecated that feature as we intend to remove it once 1.5 fades into the limelight.

Done in commit 5c6fe62a854ef6c98920bc90e71664238a7b2f84

Leaving this issue open until we update the web docs

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 20, 2010 at 05:43 UTC

Docs have been updated in aaf8547d91a540334419f2faebb897b327d535d8
_End of migration_

title: delombok does not create compilable code for Exercise<T> from DataExample
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 140)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **anthony@whitford.com**   :clock8: Aug 12, 2010 at 06:36 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Run delombok against the DataExample class found here: https://projectlombok.org/features/Data.html 2. Attempt to compile the delombok'd java code and you will get a compilation error: DataExample.java:[23,16] incompatible types found : T required: T I would seem that there is a syntax error with this: private <T>Exercise(final String name, final T value) { this.name = name; this.value = value; } I must admit that I don't understand why the compiler is complaining (Found T, Required T makes me wonder if the compiler is buggy, but...) I'm using Lombok 0.9.3 and Javac 1.6.0_21 on Windows 7.
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Aug 13, 2010 at 02:05 UTC

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Aug 13, 2010 at 02:07 UTC

Ugh, this is a javac bug. We've tackled a few, but we must have missed this one. We rely on javac to turn one of its own ASTs back into a compilable source file, and it doesn't always get this right. It looks like its injecting an erroneous type variable into the compiler.

In case you are wondering, what's happening here is that the class has a type var named 'T', and the 'value' field is of this type 'T'. The constructor has its own type var, also named 'T' which is shadowing the classes T. You haven't seen this because this is an extremely obscure java feature nobody ever uses (constructors with their own type vars). the value parameter is of this shadowed T. The complaint will be on the "this.value = value;" line. The field (left of =) is of the class's T, whereas the parameter (right of =) is of the constructor's T. These Ts are completely unrelated, and thus they aren't compatible, though in the error message this isn't clear, as they are both named T.

The mistake is in javac emitting that <T> in the first place, which it should not be doing.

We're planning on ditching javac for this part of delombok in the next release, which would resolve this problem. But if we don't, we'll definitely patch the printer. Thanks for spotting it!

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Aug 14, 2010 at 02:05 UTC

Fixed in commit 2043399d3916cf5c1b34b9552394f25d58068008
_End of migration_

title: delombok is overzealous with adding java.lang.SuppressWarnings("all")
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 141)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **anthony@whitford.com**   :clock8: Aug 12, 2010 at 06:49 UTC

Take an example like https://projectlombok.org/features/Data.html and run it through delombok.  You will notice that every method has a java.lang.SuppressWarnings("all") annotation.  But why?  If I remove them, I get no such warnings, so I'm thinking that they are superfluous.

I would prefer to only see such annotation if it is truly necessary.

I am using Lombok 0.9.3 on Windows 7 using javac 1.6.0_21.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Aug 13, 2010 at 02:13 UTC

There is no way for us to determine if a @ SuppressWarnings is needed or not. Littering @ SuppressWarnings around everything lombok does is a new feature of lombok 0.9.3, and I admit we hadn't quite thought it through for delombok. I'll talk to Roel and see if we can cook up a scheme to reduce our use of it in delombok. Possibly warnings are acceptable in delombok's case. (We do it because we have no idea what warnings a user has set up, and getting warnings on phantom lines you can't even see is a bad thing. In delombok, you CAN see the lines).

Some obscure things which may cause a warning:
- some folks are crazy enough to consider ANY shadowing of ANY kind worthy of a warning. This means our setters generate warnings, because the setters we generate use the same name as the field for the parameter, and then assign it with this.x = x.
- some editors consider even checking for null on a field that couldn't possibly be null and/or is marked with @ NonNull as a warning. Nevertheless we always check it in equals and hashCode, because throwing an exception in either method is a big no-no, and the actual timewaste is negligible, as the JVM has to nullcheck anyway, and if hotspot can eliminate it, it'll also eliminate the branching code we generate.
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 09, 2011 at 19:30 UTC
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 06, 2011 at 19:15 UTC

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 06, 2011 at 19:17 UTC

Most likely we'll give a command line option for delombok to run in 'pretty' mode, where we prioritize readability over correctness. This mode is for when you're moving away from lombok, i.e. it'll be looked at by human eyes and modified by human hands.

The normal mode will continue to emphasize correctness, for use in passthrough mode for i.e. javadoc and pmd and such.

title: @toString may be protected from inadvertent use on recursive objects
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 145)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **francois.marot**   :clock8: Aug 26, 2010 at 07:49 UTC Running the provided file will give an exemple of a StackOverflowError inferred by the use of @ toString on to Objects having a circular dependency upon each other. My point is that @ toString is so easy to use that we could add some checks to prevent the 'thoughtless' developper to make this mistake. A specific parameter for the annotation could be created to use the original "full-speed but risky" anotation. What is the expected output? What do you see instead? The observed output is the expected one, a crash ! ;) What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? Eclipse 3.6 / Ubuntu 8.04 / java 1.6.0_14 (but this is not important as this 'Issue' is more a change request than an abnormal behaviour) Please provide any additional information below. Possible solution: A possible solution would be to change the @ toString annotation to add a default check to see wether or not an object has already been displayed. Objects already used could be kept in ThreadLocal. For specific cases where the user knows what he is doing, we could add a 'check' parameter to the @ toString annotation. Thus, a @ toString(check=false) would use the full-speed version with no check at all.
:bust_in_silhouette: **francois.marot**   :clock8: Aug 26, 2010 at 07:49 UTC [:link: Container.java](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/8719146595516870289/Container.java)

:bust_in_silhouette: **francois.marot**   :clock8: Aug 26, 2010 at 07:51 UTC

priority should be set to "low" ;)

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Sep 03, 2010 at 12:00 UTC

Lombok's goal is to reduce or eliminate boilerplate, i.e. things that are both commonly done and tedious. This is certainly very tedious, but it isn't common.

I can't come up with any solution that is fully transparent and a leak-less abstraction. Using a ThreadLocal adds a field that's visible in the overview, or, if we use a service in the lombok package to manage remembering references, that would mean there's a runtime dependency on lombok when using toString which we don't want.

This system would also be unreliable; if one of your lists or arrays contains itself, you still get the stack overflow. We'd have to take over toString() duties of lists and arrays entirely, not something we want to do, and in fact not something we _CAN_ do if the type in question is not ArrayList or LinkedList but some other list instance. So, at best the extra field buys you some luck. It doesn't guarantee anything. Not worth it.
_End of migration_

title: @Getter Boolean isWorking produces isWorking() instead of getIsWorking()
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 148)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Sep 07, 2010 at 11:53 UTC

Heh, by centralizing the detection of booleans, this part got updated too.

I'm guessing you'd rather see that the method is indeed called isWorking(), and that we should update the documentation. Am I missing a good reason to go with getIsWorking() instead?

:bust_in_silhouette: **bobthule**   :clock8: Sep 07, 2010 at 15:57 UTC

One reason to go with getIsWorking() is to keep the code it generates compatible with the code that Eclipse generates-- which would make switching easier for already existing code.

:bust_in_silhouette: **jcpeters**   :clock8: Dec 08, 2010 at 19:31 UTC

If the field name starts with "is" and then an uppercase letter (or effective word boundary equivalent), I think the getter should start with "get".

In any event, the text on the GetterSetter page should be updated to reflect what actually happens today.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 09, 2010 at 06:31 UTC

So, 'foo' becomes 'isFoo()', but 'isFoo' becomes 'getIsFoo()'? That makes no sense at all to me.

it's a shame the beanspec had to be so convoluted in regards to boolean handling, but the notion that eclipse doesn't scan java.lang.Boolean as boolean gives away that this is uncharted territory for not just lombok, which makes me feel better.

I'm getting the sense this is one of those coinflip moments: It really doesn't matter what we do, we'll piss off half the community and make the other half happy (and by happy coincidence, actually 95% won't care, this is such a corner case). As lombok currently already does the prefix thing I'm tempted to stick with it and update the docs to match actual behaviour.

Though, that opens the door to a second issue: We already give 'get', 'is' and 'has' special treatment. If you know that, principle of least surprise dictates 'can' should be in that list of prefixes too. It isn't now. Still tempted to stick with what we do now just because that gives the least backwards compatibility headaches, even if its not the most consistent treatment, and not what the docs currently say.

:bust_in_silhouette: **bobthule**   :clock8: Dec 09, 2010 at 13:19 UTC

I don't think it is just Eclipse, but it is also NetBeans, Hibernate, and other code generation tools that work different than how Lombok works currently.  Also, I think following the bean spec yields boolean isFoo() and Boolean getIsFoo().  As far as least surprise goes, it would be nice if Lombok was consistent with those.

Also, a Boolean is not a boolean.  A Boolean is an Object, and "least surprise" says that all Objects should be treated the same.   The exception to the "least surprise" should only be for primitive booleans. I know the line between boolean and Boolean is a bit blurred these days because of auto-boxing, but a boolean is still different than Boolean.

http://netbeans.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=160531

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 09, 2010 at 13:23 UTC

Do you have a link to the relevant part of the beans spec? If it is non-ambiguous on this + the fact that everyone else apparently rolls with getIs, would be compelling evidence.

I assume the name becomes getIsFoo() for no special reason, just applying the standard 'get in front, titlecase first char of field name' algorithm to a field named 'isFoo'.

What does netbeans and company do when you write 'isFoo' as a field? isIsFoo()?

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 09, 2010 at 13:26 UTC

Er, whoops, that link IS the proof. Still interested in what netbeans does for:

private boolean isFoo;

Roel: I guess we'll break backwards compatibility and remove boolean treatment for Booleans?

NB: Le sigh. Another crazy corner case that's going to make eliminating primitives from java (the language) needlessly difficult.

:bust_in_silhouette: **bobthule**   :clock8: Dec 09, 2010 at 15:25 UTC

Ah, maybe we can find a happy solution: implement the getter both ways.  The spec says that is allowed:  "This “is<PropertyName>” method may be provided instead of a “get<PropertyName>” method, or it may be provided in addition to a “get<PropertyName>” method." (section 8.3.2 of JavaBeans 1.01-A)

As for the example "boolean isFoo;"-- I can't say for Netbeans, but Eclipse generates isFoo() and setFoo(), and for "Boolean isBar;", Eclipse generates getIsBar() and setIsBar().  There is nothing in the spec that says that you can't assume the property name for "Boolean isBar;" is "bar"-- if that was the case, then the required methods would be getBar() and setBar().  Because getBar() does not do a great job of showing that it is a BOOL property, it seems that assuming the property name is "isBar" might  be preferred.

The JavaBeans spec don't specify any tie between the field name and the property name-- so I suppose Eclipse takes the liberty of assuming that when you have a field boolean isFoo, that you really want a property name of "foo", but when you have a field Boolean isBar, that you really want a property name of "isBar".  Things get muddy when you try to cover every option.  I mapped out every option below, but I suggest maybe just include the "required by spec" and "optional by spec".  It wouldn't hurt to include some of the other methods if they really appeal to you.

/////
boolean foo; // assume property name "foo"
void setFoo(boolean b); // required by spec
boolean isFoo();  // required by spec if getFoo() is not implemented.  If this and getFoo() both are implemented, APIs should prefer to call this method.
boolean getFoo(); // required by spec if isFoo() is not implemented.
/////
Boolean bar; // assume property name "bar"
void setBar(Boolean b); // required by spec
Boolean getBar(); //required by spec
Boolean isBar(); // not mentioned in spec
/////
boolean isWorking; // assume property name "working"
void setWorking(boolean b);  // required by spec
boolean isWorking();  // required by spec if getWorking() is not implemented.  If this and getWorking() both are implemented, APIs should prefer to call this method.
boolean getWorking();  // required by spec if isWorking() is not implemented.
// Also, to be interchangeable with "Boolean isWorking;", the following would methods would be needed that assume a property name of "isWorking":
void setIsWorking(boolean b);  // not mentioned in spec
boolean getIsWorking();  // not mentioned in spec
/////
Boolean isNotWorking; // assume property name "isNotWorking"
void setIsNotWorking(Boolean b);  // required by spec
Boolean getIsNotWorking();  // required by spec
Boolean isIsNotWorking(); // not mentioned in spec
// Also, to be interchangeable with "boolean isNotWorking;", the following would methods would be needed that assume a property name of "notWorking":
void setNotWorking(Boolean b);  // not mentioned in spec
Boolean isNotWorking(); // not mentioned in spec
/////

https://cds.sun.com/is-bin/INTERSHOP.enfinity/WFS/CDS-CDS_Developer-Site/en_US/-/USD/ViewProductDetail-Start?ProductRef=7224-javabeans-1.01-fr-spec-oth-JSpec@ CDS-CDS_Developer

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 03, 2011 at 16:34 UTC

Great work, bob. Thanks. The problem with your last one (adding 'setIsWorking and 'setWorking' both) is that this effectively creates 2 properties, one named 'isWorking' and the other named 'working'. That's a bit much. Other than that, the answer seems clear:

(A) Boolean is like any other object - we strip 'get' off the front if the field name is getX, with X being a non-lowercase letter, otherwise we make no changes, and the getter name is formed by prefixing with 'get' and titlecasing the (stripped) field name if the (stripped) field name starts with a lowercase letter.

(B) for booleans we do something similar, except 'is', and 'has', in addition to 'get', count as field name prefixes that will be stripped out. The getter name is generated by prefixing the title-cased stripped field name with 'is' instead of 'get'.

This is mostly similar to what happens in lombok today. The changes:

A) Booleans lose their special treatment. They get prefixed with 'is' today.

B) a field named 'isFoo' currently gives 'setIsFoo' for setter. We'll be changing that to 'setFoo'.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 28, 2011 at 18:49 UTC

To commenter ﹟10 (lpin...@ gmail.com): That doesn't sound related to this problem, or in fact to anything lombok did. As ComboBox is not a Boolean nor a boolean, getIs and setIs are generated as usual.

This will be fixed before 0.10 is out the door as this is a backwards incompatible change (admittedly in rare circumstances) which means we need to do a major version bump. Might as well take care of it with this one.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 07, 2011 at 20:40 UTC

Fixed in c98cec7d2ddceddcc0f127185912be4f826a6caa and 30b63deaff82128ca8c3e7b59884b4fc2caf929c

Will be in 0.10.0 final.

lpin...@ gmail.com: This should also fix your problem.
_End of migration_

title: Wrapping toString with try-catch block
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 149)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **yonatan.graber**   :clock8: Sep 07, 2010 at 15:04 UTC

When using an ORM object that was lombokated (such as hibernate @ Entity objects), if a fatal exception is thrown (exception that closes the database connection) and one of the fields that are required for the toString() generated by lomobok is set to be lazy loading, a JDBCException is thrown ("closed connection") instead of the original exception - which makes it almost impossible to track the real bug. (since the exception is thrown out of the entity's toString method)
Catching those kind of exceptions using try-catch block will allow to see the original exception. In case of an exception within the toString code, the toString code can return a "toString exception thrown"+message value.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Sep 29, 2010 at 16:25 UTC

I'm not sure what you'd like us to do here. toString calls getWhatever(), and this in turn will result in the JDBCException. What exception would it be hiding?

:bust_in_silhouette: **yonatan.graber**   :clock8: Oct 10, 2010 at 09:06 UTC

Attached a (very simplified) example. 
In the example, if two concurrent users will call BusinessLogic.do() simultaneously, the BusinessLogic.doPersist() will throw a UserException, but when the do() method will try to log that exception, because "user" is a JPA proxy object with closed connection, a JDBCException will be thrown, and it will be almost impossible to track down the root of that exception.

I know that this sample looks artificial, but I did encounter similar scenario in "real life", and it took me several hours to find the cause of the JDBCException.
:bust_in_silhouette: **yonatan.graber**   :clock8: Oct 10, 2010 at 09:06 UTC [:link: example.java](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/7078303812226144953/example.java)

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 12, 2010 at 09:58 UTC

I still don't understand what you'd like Lombok to do instead.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 06, 2011 at 19:05 UTC

Rereading this issue, what you want us to do is update our toString to return a string containing the text: "Hey, I can't give you a meaningful toString because this exception occurred" (probably a bit more professional than that). That's not a bad idea.

I think we'll go with catch Exception and not catch Throwable, but if we do go with catch Throwable, OOMEs should be thrown onwards.

:bust_in_silhouette: **askoning**   :clock8: Oct 09, 2013 at 10:40 UTC

Issue #622 has been merged into this issue.
_End of migration_

I'm hesitant to add this, as we'd generate a ton of code to your toString (every single call gets its own try/catch wrapping, inflating every get call to a 5-liner), and this is a rare scenario. Given that we have so many other things to work on and this rarely comes up, let's not do it after all.

title: Class reference comparison fails in equals() when exactly one object is a proxied object
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 152)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Oct 09, 2010 at 21:29 UTC

It looks like using getters and setters for property access in the equals() method wasn't enough to play nicely with proxied objects :(.  It seems that the following clause fails in the lombok-generated equals method when one object is a proxy and the other isn't:

  if (o.getClass() != this.getClass()) return false;

Personally I use "if ( !( o instanceof ThisClass ) ) return false;" but I don't know the arguments for using class reference comparisons in the equals method.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 12, 2010 at 09:56 UTC

We can't fix this because that style of equals/class check is not compatible with the equals contract. The solutions are extremely complicated and involve generation of "canBeEquals" methods. In general you need a concept of whether extension is being used as an implementation detail (in which case equality is possible, and the instanceof check is right), or if it is being used to add state, in which case the objects should never be equal.

The real problem here is the leaky abstraction of JPA, which is using extension as an implementation detail, which is something you shouldn't be doing.

We've yet to hear of a suggestion that's worth the complication for @ Data itself. Possibly we may release a JPA-specific variant of @ Data that takes care of this.

The argument goes like this:

Imagine I have a ColouredList, extending ArrayList. It simply adds a colour, which you can set and get. Things would be very weird if a red empty ColouredList is equal to a blue empty ColouredList, so let's posit that those would not be equal.

Whoops, we broke the equality contract, at least, if we use the instanceof check.

emptyArrayList.equals(emptyRedList) would be true (redList is an instanceof ArrayList, and when treating it as an arraylist its equal to an empty one).

emptyArrayList.equals(emptyBlueList) is also true.

Then by the equals contract, which says equality is reflexive, transitive, and symmetric, we must conclude that:

emptyRedList.equals(emptyBlueList) MUST be true. And yet it isn't: Voila, equals contract broken.

By using the .getClass() style comparison, this problem does not occur; emptyArrayList.equals(emptyRedList) returns false, and thus we are free to include the colour of a list in its equivalence code.

:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Oct 12, 2010 at 17:13 UTC

I dunno if I see any problem with emptyRedList.equals( emptyBlueList ) being true, and vice-versa, though maybe it's just that analogies are never perfect :).

Would it be possible to remove/suppress the warning that occurs when @ EqualsAndHashCode is used but equals() is still implemented by the dev:

"Not generating equals(Object other): A method with that name already exists"

I can still make use of the hashCode method, which saves me a lot of work.

On a somewhat related note, I'd be interested to see how other JPA providers fare with this issue (i.e. whether or not this is a Hibernate-specific thing).  I know Eclipselink uses a completely different (non-javassist/non-cglib) method to proxy the entity objects.

Thanks for the detailed response!

:bust_in_silhouette: **silvaran**   :clock8: Oct 12, 2010 at 19:13 UTC

It turns out that copypasta and some rudimentary learning of the JDT and Sun compiler tools took less time than re-writing equals() methods for 120 POJOs.  I added useInstanceOf to @ EqualsAndHashCode (default false) and would be more than happy to submit a patch if you're interested.  Looking at the stuff you've built tells me it wouldn't take you too long to whip up a better solution though.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Nov 30, 2010 at 16:32 UTC

This will be in Burning Emu (0.10) and was announced to some fanfare at Devoxx :)

The current preview release of 0.10 already has this feature - we generate a canEquals() method because this is how scala does it, and being compatible with other JVM stuff is always a  bonus. proxy classes work "out of the box" now - you don't need to do a thing.
_End of migration_

title: Add lazy init support (@LazyInit)
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 153)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Oct 21, 2010 at 16:13 UTC

Hi Peter, great suggestion.

I would really like to remove all that boilerplate! We would have to look at the appropriate syntax and all the possible corner cases. 

The holder pattern would only work for static fields, and I'm not convinced that that's where we can gain the most. I mean, the holder pattern is already very compact and does not add a lot of complexity. 

For instance fields on the other hand I think we can really make things a lot better. About thread safety: we should make it thread safe. Maybe that adds a bit overhead, but you are doing lazy instantiation for good reason: creation costs either a lot of memory or a lot of time. So adding code to make it thread safe would relatively be cheap. Double checked locking would provide an acceptable solution, but requires us to make the field volatile. Furthermore, it needs to have a synchronized block, and typically uses the this-reference for that. I am afraid that if we use the this-reference we might cause undebugable deadlocks. So I suggest to use a custom lock object per instance. 

Other things to consider:
- How does it work together with @ Data, @ Getter, @ Setter, @ Synchronized? I would expect lazy instantiated fields not to be able to be set. 
- How about serializable classes? Do they need special handling during either serialization or deserialization?

:bust_in_silhouette: **peter.fichtner**   :clock8: Oct 22, 2010 at 17:58 UTC

> I would really like to remove all that boilerplate! 

Beside the boilerplate aspect it will prevent NPEs: Considering you'll code a lazy-initialized field, you (and every programmer maintaining the code) have to consider that the field is lazy-initialized and access it using the method, if someone will not the code probbly will raise a NPE. The @ LazyInit annotation will prevent this because all field accesses will be redirected using the lazInit-method, btw: To get this pattern work correctly the field has to be private, what will AnnotationProcessor do if the field is non-private? Throw an exception? 
Perhaps it would be sensible to add an attribute to the Annotation to switch off the synchroization stuff (default is threadsafe), e.g. @ LazyInit(threadsafe=false)

> For instance fields on the other hand I think we can really make things a lot better. About thread safety: we should make it thread safe. Maybe that adds a bit overhead, but you are doing lazy instantiation for good reason: creation costs either a lot of memory or a lot of time. So adding code to make it thread safe would relatively be cheap. Double checked locking would provide an acceptable solution, but requires us to make the field volatile. Furthermore, it needs to have a synchronized block, and typically uses the this-reference for that. I am afraid that if we use the this-reference we might cause undebugable deadlocks. So I suggest to use a custom lock object per instance. 

I agree: A private per instance lock object has to be generated

> Other things to consider:
> - How does it work together with @ Data, @ Getter, @ Setter, @ Synchronized? I would expect lazy instantiated fields not to be able to be set. 

As from user's view there should be no difference for lazy-/non-lazy-initalized fields. 
@ Data public class Foo {
  @ LazyInit List<Person> ps1 = new ArrayList<Person>();
  List<Person> ps2 = new ArrayList<Person>();
}

For both attributes getters and setters should be generated, I'd prefer another attribute on @ LazyInit to turn this off: 
@ LazyInit(createGetter=false, createSetter, false), default is generating the getter/setter. 

I thing existing @ Synchronized annotated fields are not affected by generated code as the rest of the code will work as it worked before and the new code is just the replacement for the field access (which is internally synchronized if not turned off). 
- How about serializable classes? Do they need special handling during either serialization or deserialization?

I think the generated code will not break serialization and work as expected. 

I would be happy if this will be integrated into lombok, any discussion is welcome. 

Thanks! 
Peter

:bust_in_silhouette: **peter.fichtner**   :clock8: Nov 20, 2010 at 15:09 UTC

Was a nice demonstration yesterday at devoxx :-)
Thanks for that.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 31, 2010 at 21:26 UTC

Thanks, peter. As you saw, we've added this in a slightly different form: @ Getter(lazy=true). It'll be part of the 0.10.0-Burning Emu release.
_End of migration_

title: Lombok does not work on JDK7
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 161)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **lahoda**   :clock8: Nov 19, 2010 at 09:06 UTC

## Using a recent (custom build) JDK7, Lombok does not work for me. Consider this class:

@ lombok.Data
class Test {
    private int foo;

## }

## Using a "stable older release" from projectlombok.org:

$ javac -classpath lombok.jar -source 1.5 Test.java
error: operator ^ cannot be applied to Object,Test

## 1 error

## using the 0.10.0-BETA1 from projectlombok.org:

$ javac -classpath lombok-0.10.0-BETA1.jar -source 1.5 Test.java
error: operator ^ cannot be applied to Object,Test

## 1 error

The problem is that lombok still uses the JCTree.{PLUS, ....} compile-time constants, whose value gets copied to the actual place of use. These constants change from time to time in javac, though, which lombok does not handle properly.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Nov 19, 2010 at 09:19 UTC

We've moved this to the top of our list. We have a patch contributed by Team netbeans (I believe Petr Jiricka, I'll check after we give our Lombok presentation at Devoxx) to use some fancy reflection footwork to immunize lombok against order changes in enum-like lists.

Nevermind, that was your patch :)
