Lombok or some eclipse code delivers an invalid AST (where some of the AST nodes' scope variables are still null), but this doesn't cause any problems right away. Then, later, when some worker is fired up to do some analysis on the AST, it crashes with the above 2 stack traces. We do think we figured out a point in lombok where, if this bug is going to happen, we'll be called, and we can figure out that it'll happen. title: Overriding of Object#equals with EqualsAndHashCode fails when another method "equals" exists.
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 165)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **Pepijn.Kokke**   :clock8: Nov 23, 2010 at 15:46 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Create a method signature SomeType﹟equals(SomeType) 2. Use @ EqualsAndHashCode to override Object﹟equals What is the expected output? A working implementation of Object﹟equals(Object). What do you see instead? An error, stating that "!" is not implemented for SomeType. What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? The latest stable version, 0.9.3. Please provide any additional information below. The error stems from the testing of the superclass or any properties that also match the interface SomeType. It's an obscure one, but it's there. The bug can easily be fixed by inserting a cast to Object, thus ensuring that the method overridden from Object﹟equals(Object) will be called, i.e. if (! this.property.equals((Object) other.property)).

:bust_in_silhouette: **Pepijn.Kokke**   :clock8: Nov 23, 2010 at 16:05 UTC

I should add that the method SomeType﹟equals(SomeType) is defined in a subclass of the class in which the error occurs, as not implementing equals when any other method is named "equals" is documented behaviour, and generates a compiler warning.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Nov 27, 2010 at 18:30 UTC

That makes sense. Will do!

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 31, 2010 at 21:17 UTC

Fixed in 49100b43c084f6774d43d93eee98440253965047 and will be in 0.10.0 (Burning Emu).

In the website doc about @ ToString ( https://projectlombok.org/features/ToString.html ) there is written:
@ ToString(excludes="id")

This should be:
@ ToString(exclude="id")

title: In some (rare) cases @Delegate produces NPE in Eclipse Error Log
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 171)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Dec 03, 2010 at 15:00 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? Toy around with @ Delegate transformation. What is the expected output? What do you see instead? clean Error Log What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? HEAD after aligning PatchDelegate with the standard infrastructure (since commit e308909def27a6940792) Please provide any additional information below. In PatchDelegate you do something like: CompilationUnitDeclaration cud = ... EclipseAST astNode = TransformEclipseAST.getAST(cud); EclipseNode typeNode = astNode.get(decl); Where in some rare cases 'typeNode' is null due to an incomplete AST. This lines did the trick for me: if (typeNode == null) { astNode.top().rebuild(); typeNode = astNode.get(decl); } Pretty sure they don't belong in each Patch though. (currently I put them in all 3 transformations I have in my fork that need resolve) Anyways if you've already stumbled over this issue, sorry for the inconvenience.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Dec 31, 2010 at 21:11 UTC

Fixed in fb1d6c0f0dfafcd889cac8906246803349c353f2 and will be in 0.10.0 Burning Emu.

I can't actually test this because I can't seem to get the NPE you're talking about. Nevertheless, the getAST() method on TransformEclipseAST now takes a boolean named 'force'. Update your own plugins to call this with 'true', and you can remove that workaround.

The way we've written PatchDelegate and PatchVal will be revisited in a future release to make the process more plugin-friendly and a bit less hacky. We'll revisit how whether each post-resolve handler needs to force-rebuild, or if it only needs to be done once, then.
_End of migration_

title: onMethod for RequiredArgsConstructor
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 172)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **peter.fichtner**   :clock8: Dec 06, 2010 at 12:41 UTC

I'd like to use Dependency Injection (DI) with Lombock and would like to use a final field which is supplied by a constructor. 

Instead of typing
@ Setter(onMethod = @ Inject)
private final Field field;

I'd like to use
@ RequiredArgsConstructor(onConstructor = @ Inject)
public class Example {
    private final Field field;

I think this would be useful in general since it's not possible at the moment to deprecate a lombok generated constructor. 

Regards Peter

:bust_in_silhouette: **grootjans**   :clock8: Dec 18, 2010 at 14:09 UTC

We're not sure if we're going to add this issue to burning emu (0.10), but it does sound logical to add this option to the constructor annotations.

It is however possible to deprecate a method or constructor within lombok at this moment, but you need to code it by hand.

checkLegality was added so that adding the annotation to i.e. an interface, or _explicitly_ to a method, gets flagged down. title: Lombok annotation processor causes javac failure when downstream annotation processors are invoked
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 176)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **neildo**   :clock8: Dec 28, 2010 at 20:50 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Create a project that uses lombok with another annotation processor. I used the SPI annotation processor. Make sure lombok processor runs first. 2. Compile project using javac. What is the expected output? What do you see instead? During compilation the following error is thrown: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Not supported: lombok/dummy/ForceNewRound0.java from at com.sun.tools.javac.util.DefaultFileManager.isSameFile(DefaultFileManager.java:928) at lombok.javac.apt.InterceptingJavaFileManager.isSameFile(InterceptingJavaFileManager.java:116) at com.sun.tools.javac.processing.JavacFiler.checkFileReopening(JavacFiler.java:488) at com.sun.tools.javac.processing.JavacFiler.getResource(JavacFiler.java:439) at org.mangosdk.spi.processor.ServiceFileInitializer.initialData(ServiceFileInitializer.java:45) at org.mangosdk.spi.processor.Collector.getService(Collector.java:47) at org.mangosdk.spi.processor.SpiProcessor.register(SpiProcessor.java:280) at org.mangosdk.spi.processor.SpiProcessor.handleElement(SpiProcessor.java:159) at org.mangosdk.spi.processor.SpiProcessor.handleAnnotations(SpiProcessor.java:140) at org.mangosdk.spi.processor.SpiProcessor.process(SpiProcessor.java:105) at com.sun.tools.javac.processing.JavacProcessingEnvironment.callProcessor(JavacProcessingEnvironment.java:625) at com.sun.tools.javac.processing.JavacProcessingEnvironment.discoverAndRunProcs(JavacProcessingEnvironment.java:554) at com.sun.tools.javac.processing.JavacProcessingEnvironment.doProcessing(JavacProcessingEnvironment.java:699) at com.sun.tools.javac.main.JavaCompiler.processAnnotations(JavaCompiler.java:981) at com.sun.tools.javac.main.JavaCompiler.compile(JavaCompiler.java:727) at com.sun.tools.javac.main.Main.compile(Main.java:353) at com.sun.tools.javac.main.Main.compile(Main.java:279) at com.sun.tools.javac.main.Main.compile(Main.java:270) at com.sun.tools.javac.Main.compile(Main.java:87) What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? lombok.0.10.0-BETA2 Please provide any additional information below. I tracked this down an issue with DefaultFileManager where it requires all JavaFileObject instances to implement BaseJavaFileObject. The DummyFileObject that lombok creates implements JavaFileObject but not BaseJavaFileObject. In the failure above, isSameFile gets called with mixed arguments of type BaseJavaFileObject and DummyFileObject. I hacked together a fix locally by overriding the isSameFile method to intercept calls where one of the arguments is a DummyFileObject and return false if the other is not the same DummyFileObject. I've attached a maven project that reproduce this. If you try to use this, you'll need to install lombok, spi and eclipse jdt-core into your maven repo.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 19, 2011 at 02:07 UTC

Still can't reproduce, but I think I figured this out.

in LombokFileObjects.java, we detect whether we're on JAVAC6 or JAVAC7 by doing a Class.forName sweep of the affected class (due to a package rename, we need to detect the difference). You're using javac 7, but by stuffing javac6 on the classpath, we erroneously detect that we're in javac 6. We wrap the File Object in a javac6 based BaseFileObject, which javac 7 promptly chokes on because that's not what it was expecting.

The basic problem here is that our "are we in javac 6 or in javac 7" detector is flawed; it thinks we're in both and it defaults to javac 6.

All that would make perfect sense except on your system javac -version appears to be returning 1.6.0_22 and not 1.7 something.

Still, us making the wrong wrapper is the only possible explanation I can see (well, that, or you're using a pre-RC1 lombok).

Let's check a few things:

(A) Is the class com.sun.tools.javac.file.BaseFileObject, or com.sun.tools.javac.util.BaseFileObject (difference is the package name of the last package) in the javac.jar you're putting on the classpath, or both?

(B) Find the tools.jar that 'javac' ends up invoking. Which of the BaseFileObject classes is in that jar?

My theory is that the answer for A is c.s.t.j.util.BFO and for B it's c.s.t.j.file.BFO. That would explain it (though that would not explain why a javac 6 has a bunch of javac 7 code in it, or why my javac which is newer than yours and also of the 1.6 variety does not!)

Downgrading priority for now.

:bust_in_silhouette: **osa8aso**   :clock8: Jul 19, 2011 at 15:51 UTC

> My theory is that the answer for A is c.s.t.j.util.BFO and for B it's
> c.s.t.j.file.BFO. That would explain it

You're absolutely right: my javac's tools.jar contains com.sun.tools.javac.file.BaseFileObject, and javac.jar which I put on classpath (and which was obtained from https://projectlombok.org/ivyrepo/) contains com.sun.tools.javac.util.BaseFileObject. 

> (though that would not explain why a javac 6 has a bunch of javac 7 code in it,
> or why my javac which is newer than yours and also of the 1.6 variety does not!)

This is easy to explain, actually. I'm using Ubuntu Linux, and it provides OpenJDK 6: 
$ which javac
/usr/lib/jvm/java-6-openjdk/bin/javac
$ jar tvf /usr/lib/jvm/java-6-openjdk/lib/tools.jar | grep BaseFileObject
  3616 Sat Jun 11 05:52:44 CDT 2011 com/sun/tools/javac/file/BaseFileObject.class

However, OpenJDK's JDK 6 is not identical to "real" JDK 6, as explained here: http://openjdk.java.net/projects/jdk6
Quote: "After considering the alternatives, OpenJDK 7 build 20 was chosen as the basis of a backward branch to create OpenJDK 6 by removing from the OpenJDK 7 sources changes inappropriate for a Java SE 6 implementation."

That's why your "javac 6 or javac 7" detector gets confused.

What are my options then? I has to use OpenJDK anyway, so I either revert back to lombok 0.9.3 (which works fine in my case), or find a way to use on classpath a javac.jar which corresponds to the JDK being used. The latter is not so easy I believe :(

title: toString printing in a better formatted way
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 183)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **Coffy.Sk**   :clock8: Jan 21, 2011 at 15:50 UTC

I didn't find feature request mentioned in the forum post http://groups.google.com/group/project-lombok/browse_thread/thread/5ef8d6e248af3061 so I create it now.

How could be done? e.g @ lombok.ToString(format=multiline) ?

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 21, 2011 at 17:41 UTC

Accepted at medium because its really not that hard to do. I like putting some items on the roster that don't rate "rocket science" :)

Roel, RJ: Are there any problems (other than spending the time adding it) here? Does it pass the value-per-complexity threshold? I'm pretty solidly on the side of: Yes, it does - but maybe I'm overlooking either the utility or this, or the complications.

The output would look something like:

Person:\n
  super: (whatever)\n
  name: Joey Bloggs\n
  Age: 16\n

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jan 31, 2011 at 22:10 UTC

Well, there is the "problem" of the super-call returning multiple lines. If we would want to do the right thing, we should detect a multiline super.toString() and multiline toString of any of the fields and adjust the indenting. That would mean lost of code, but then again, we're generating it. Personally, I've never used it. But I'm not against it. 

It might just be as simple as a replace("\n", "  \n"), probably with a negative lookahead for just trailing whitespace.

:bust_in_silhouette: **hazendaz**   :clock8: Oct 08, 2011 at 21:03 UTC

I'm new to lombok and would like to see this as well.  What would also be nice for using new line is that the overall fields line up such as follows (ie values line up rather than field names)...

SampleBean(
      field=value 
     field2=value
    field21=value
   field210=value 
  bigfield1=value)

This is a little different than the suggested output but makes it much easier to read when glancing over large amounts of log files generated with the toString() considering we know the field names and are really only concerned on the field values.  For the sake of difference, maybe an additional flag to determine how the output will result.

Also, side note, I think the lombok documentation needs a little updating.  The toString() vanilla java shows use of string concatenation still.  When I saw this I almost immediately wrote off lombok but verified the generated code seeing that stringbuilder was used.  This might save others time when they see the documentation matches the generated code especially when the sample shows inefficient code results which actually is not the case.  Otherwise, I'm extremely excited to start using this!

:bust_in_silhouette: **hazendaz**   :clock8: Oct 13, 2011 at 00:26 UTC

My prior note about the lombok generated toString() generating inefficient code turns out to be true.  I had used dj java decompiler to see what was actually generated but that appears to clean up inefficient code.  If I use delombok or jd-gui, I end up with inefficient code.  Is there any work being done to create the toString() using stringbuffer or stringbuilder rather than string concatenation?  To the original post, simply writing our own toString() resolves all issues but that still means I have lots of boilerplate code that is unnecessary.

:bust_in_silhouette: **hartmut.benz**   :clock8: Dec 16, 2011 at 08:13 UTC

I really like the output and flexibility of apache commons ToStringBuilder. Perhaps lombok could make use of that (code/example) when doing the toString?
My computer science teacher was pretty strong on 'do not re-invent the wheel' ;-)

:bust_in_silhouette: **MichaelPiefel**   :clock8: Jun 05, 2012 at 06:00 UTC

An answer to hazen...: Sorry to be rude, but since you accused Lombok’s authors of writing inefficient code (while mentioning the synchronized StringBuffer!), I cannot resist. I would recommend you actually profile the code, and then wonder and learn that String concatenation is not necessarily slow. The Java compiler will detect the pattern and use whatever method is fast – like using the StringBuilder. Lombok’s toString() is as fast as can be.

:bust_in_silhouette: **hazendaz**   :clock8: Jun 21, 2012 at 03:50 UTC

MichaelPiefel...I mentioned one inefficient piece of code (maybe the wrong wording) and my great "excitement" for this project as well as a suggested enhancement for a different toString output look and feel.  My posts mentioned both stringBuilder and stringBuffer.  I know stringBuffer is synchronized, doesn't everyone?  Both provide better performance in most cases over concatenation when jvm cannot determine before runtime the value of the data in order to enhance it.  Obviously there is debate over that but there are plenty of stack trace posts showing exactly how to set tests up to prove it and the results are consistent.  I in no way was even remotely discounting any of the developers behind lombok.  Lombok is a great project and reduced our boilerplate code quite considerably.  I realize the guys creating this are off the charts in java knowledge as they are doing amazing things very deep in undocumented code.  No ones code is perfect including my own.  For now, we are using apache commons lang 3 to solve our toString needs using reflection.  Yes, I know that is an issue as well which is why I keep checking back here.  I'd much rather prefer a solution that builds out the code as best possible before I ever drop the code on any box to run.  However, for now, I get the look and feel I need as well as use slf4j/logback in order to not incur the cost of toString unless we are actually logging it.

:bust_in_silhouette: **maia@lucidfox.org**   :clock8: Jun 04, 2013 at 08:11 UTC

Concatenation is only inefficient if used iteratively, progressively adding to a gradually growing string.

Since the compiler in fact implements concatenation using StringBuilder, there is no performance penalty for using multiple concatenations in a single statement. It is converted to a single StringBuilder object. Furthermore, the compiler typically generates more efficient bytecode with concatenation than with manual StringBuilder calls.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jun 04, 2013 at 11:34 UTC

@ hazendaz: Can you provide some numbers to show that lombok's implementation is a lot slower or uses more memory that alternative implementations?

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Nov 20, 2013 at 01:55 UTC

@ hazendaz: I checked and okayed our current implementation back then and I double checked again to be sure but:
- If you write a string of concatenated constants, then javac will compile it down to StringBuilder usage. It wasn't dj-java 'cleaning up' inefficient code, it is dj-java correctly rendering the exact contents of the produced class files. Feel free to check this yourself by running javap -c on produced sources. Let me rephrase this so that it is crystal clear: There is NO DIFFERENCE in the produced class file if you hand-write a StringBuilder constructor + a bunch of append calls vs just blithely concatenating strings as we do. Except the concatenated strings read much nicer when delomboked, and leave the choice up to javac which is always better than anything we can hardcode, thus our code is totally, 100%, more correct. Which is why we'll stick to it.
- Making life unnecessarily hard (and unreadable) for ourselves by using StringBuilder anyway just because this looks better to your misguided performance needs is not something we're ever going to agree to. We'll explain why the code we generate is better and we'll bust some common misguided performance myths (such as 'don't concatenate strings') while we're at it, though.
- In general, complaining about performance without a profiler report is not something we're ever going to accept. The JVM is a very complicated piece of machinery. You are utterly incapable of guessing the first thing about the performance characteristic of pretty much anything. That's okay. Neither can we. Neither can the core JVM engineers, even. Too complicated. The answer is simple: ALWAYS write your code so that it is flexible and readable. NEVER let imagined performance concerns of any sort dictate how you write code. ALWAYS use a profiler to handle performance issues. NEVER trust your gut instinct. The only 2 allowed exceptions to these rules are (A) Algorithmic Complexity (for large sets, quicksort is much faster than bubblesort. No profiler required to figure that one out), and (B) known tight loops such as a blit loop in a graphics driver. But that's only half of an exception, you really should still profile here.

Quotes from your comments which we've checked to ensure they are incorrect:

> Both [Referring to StringBuilder/Buffer] provide better performance in most cases over concatenation when jvm cannot determine before runtime the value of the data in order to enhance it.

This is false. If the concatenation is in 'single expression form', javac will optimize the whole thing into StringBuilder automatically. You don't need to concat just constants, even concatting a mix of constants and variable references (the way we do in toString generation) gets turned into StringBuilder-using bytecode.

>  Obviously there is debate over that but there are plenty of stack trace posts showing exactly how to set tests up to prove it and the results are consistent.

I assume you meant stack overflow? At any rate, no, javac has worked like this since at least 1.6, and as that is the first version of javac that lombok works on, digging further back is irrelevant.

> For now, we are using apache commons lang 3 to solve our toString needs using reflection. 

While complaining about performance without a profiler report is always a very silly thing to do, if we MUST resort to what is technically, micro-benchmarky, very slow, then, well, you nailed it. Reflection is quite slow. Using apache commons lang 3 for toString instead of lombok for performance reasons is completely backwards. If you're using commons-lang's toString for other reasons (outlining on = for example), that's okay. We find most of the apache commons libraries utter disasters, API-wise, and an excellent example of how NOT to write generalized APIs. So, if apache allows something, our kneejerk reaction is generally to do the opposite anyway. Guava is a fine example of conservative API that is very well considered before release.

Your request for toString's output to align things on the equals sign is something worth considering, but very low on the priority totempole. It's a little weird so probably requires a special setting (such as a parameter on @ ToString), and we do not introduce additional parameters to annotations lightly, because if we were to acquiesce to all such requests easily, soon @ Data and co would have 50+ parameters, and hopefully you agree with us that this situation is much worse than what we have now.

Issue remains open for the original feature request (newlines option). However, the enchantment request for either using StringBuilder or aligning on equal sign will not be done, and push requests to add these features will not be accepted.
_End of migration_

body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 187)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **benjamin.j.mccann**   :clock8: Jan 29, 2011 at 03:26 UTC

ASM should not be included in the lombok jar, but instead it should be required that clients include both ASM and lombok on their classpath.  Because ASM is included I get all types of errors when I include the ASM jar in my project myself. title: Conditional logging
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 193)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Feb 13, 2011 at 22:31 UTC

@ Log could shave some CPU cycles by checking if the logging infrastructure already knows that the selected logging level will simply be ignored.

:bust_in_silhouette: **lorenooliveira**   :clock8: Aug 22, 2013 at 13:08 UTC

Any plans for starting the work on this? This will be a very interesting feature of lombok.
_End of migration_
Is this feature dead or still somewhere in the pipeline?

I think log frameworks have caught up with this - by allowing you to shove your log outputs in `() -> ...` form.

There is a 'fix' available but both obvious strategies seem like non-starters:

* Lombok could attempt to detect any and all calls to your preferred logger and automatically and silently add an `if`, e.g. find `log.warn("foo {}", a, ex);` anywhere and silently change that to `if (log.isWarnEnabled()) log.warn("foo {}", a, ex);`, but, that's _very_ hairy indeed: The mere inclusion of lombok on the classpath would do this? We should probably say that we do this only if you use one of lombok's `@Log` annotations. Even then, that's quite drastic, and raises the question: Is e.g. generating that `if` for severe error levels even worth doing? But it also feels weird that lombok's spec says something like: "all calls at warn or less severe will get the check, but error and up do not".
* Instead lombok could introduce its own `lombok.LOG.warn` method which is then turned into `if (log.isWarnEnabled()) log.warn...` and even silently introduces a logger variable (i.e. you never need to even add `@Slf4j` or whatnot to your class again, it just happens automatically, logger picked via `lombok.config`).

That second option sounds like a __much__ nicer API to me. Now you can just... log... where-ever you want, and lombok just takes care of it for you, making the logger static field appear just-in-time and adding the `if` guard as a bonus. But now lombok is in the 'business' of being a log frontend, and part of the issues is that not all log frontends are the same. For example, `Flogger` and `Slf4j` are quite different on the front-end. Lombok would be in the business of writing a log frontend.

I'm game, but it's a big project. That's why there hasn't been any attempt yet: It's a bit daunting.

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **verszou**   :clock8: Feb 19, 2011 at 12:12 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Run installer on Mac OS X Snow Leopard 2. Look at list of the IDE that the installer suggests What is the expected output? What do you see instead? And when I tried to point the installer to the Eclipse.app manually it claims that it is not a recognized IDE. What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? This was done with 0.9.3 on Mac OS X Snow Leopard running on an iMac. Please provide any additional information below. I ran the same version on my Linux box and there it correctly identified my Eclipse installation, as well as the Netbeans one. On my Mac I went into the application directory itself, copyied the Lombok.jar file there and added the lines to Eclipse.ini, and with this manual installation it works ok, so the problem seems to be in the way the installer searches for Eclipse installations. Perhaps it looks for the unix executable, which is hidden two levels down below the Eclipse.app?

:bust_in_silhouette: **benjamin.j.mccann**   :clock8: Mar 23, 2011 at 23:17 UTC

I can confirm I also encountered this issue.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Mar 24, 2011 at 10:48 UTC

This isn't a case of "Oops, we accidentally forgot OS X" - I own a mac :)

Here's the general procedure of how we look for Eclipse on macs.

First, the automatic detection algo:

It'll check all files in both /Applications and your user home dir for either of 2 conditions:

(A) It contains a directory named "Eclipse.app" (Mac apps are, at the file system level, directories and not files).

(B) It contains a directory that contains "eclipse", case insensitive, anywhere in its name, and this directory contains a directory named "Eclipse.app".

If the auto-detector finds a hit, OR you manually specify one via the button, then the following algorithm determines if its actually a legit eclipse install that lombok's installer can work with. If it's not, then the entry won't appear on the list (so its entirely possible that the autodetector does find eclipse on your system, but its then discarded as an invalid location):

(A) It checks for "eclipse.app" in the found directory. named like that. That's a mistake, though out-of-the-box Macs are configured as a case-insensitive file system. Might this be the issue? This is something I'll fix either way. This part is only done if you specified a directory instead of Eclipse.app itself. (Though, this IS how the auto-detector always feeds its guesses to the location validator).

(B) If eclipse.app isn't there, it looks for eclipse.ini in that directory. (The true goal of the validator is to locate the eclipse.ini file, as that's what lombok has to edit).

(C) If the passed location is a file, it either has to be eclipse.app or eclipse.ini (this time case insensitive).

If the found location was eclipse.app, it'll go from there to the ini file by checking if eclipse.ini is a sibling (i.e. in the same dir as) the found eclipse executable. If it can't find eclipse.ini there, it'll look for "dir-of-executable/Eclipse.app/Contents/MacOS/eclipse.ini".

 If neither strategy works, the location is abandoned as invalid.

Finally, if the pointed-at app is a softlink, it'll follow it a few times and reruns the algorithm, with a limit in case you've got an endless loop in your softlinks.

Can you guys check your eclipse installs and run through this process by hand? If not, could you provide me with the following info:

 (A) fully qualified path of your Eclipse.app file
 (B) fully qualified path of your eclipse.ini file
 (C) Your OS version
 (D) Eclipse's version

For eclipse.ini, you may have to delve into Eclipse.app to find it. Easiest way to do so is from the command line, otherwise, right-click on Eclipse.app and select 'show package contents'.

Thanks!

(A) /Users/kentdamgaard/Applications/eclipse/eclipse_jee
(B) /Users/kentdamgaard/Applications/eclipse/eclipse_jee/Eclipse.app/Contents/MacOS
(C) OS X 10.6.6
(D) Eclipse Java EE IDE for Web Developers.

Version: Helios Service Release 2

title: Generate object comparison implementation (implement Comparable<T>)
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 208)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **rodion.moiseev**   :clock8: May 05, 2011 at 03:03 UTC

Automated generation of Comparable<T>﹟compareTo(T) would be a great addition to a @ Data-annotated class, or by itself using @ Comparable annotation.

Proposed specification (the intuitive part):
- Class T marked with @ Comparable by default implements Comparable bound to T and implements compareTo(T), taking into account all non-inherited instance fields in the order of declaration.
- Changing comparison order and/or excluding fields can be done by explicitly specifying comparable fields in the desired order using @ Comparable({"field1","field2", ...}). Although, not very refactoring-friendly.

Tricky parts:
- Due to a generics restriction, class T who's super class S already implements compareTo(S) legally can only be comparable to type S, which means it cannot implement Comparable<T> or compareTo(T). If you can trick javac around the problem it would be great. When, delomboking, however, you'll need some ugly casting.
- If super class is not comparable it could be useful to both, ignore it completely, or use available getters in the order declared. Although the latter could introduce weird bugs, so should not be recommended.
- For non-comparable fields, they should be ignored with a warning. To hide the warning the user would have to either make all fields implement Comparable, or explicitly exclude those fields in the @ Comparable({"field1", "field2", ...}) annotation.

There are probably couple of more corner cases that make it difficult to implement this cleanly, but even implementing the bare minimum I believe would be very useful!

Regards

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 06, 2011 at 18:21 UTC

Comparable is not the right name for this because it would clash with java.util.Comparable. The problem with a superclass that already has Comparable<Super> means we can never add this to @ Data directly, it'd have to be a separate annotation. I'm not particularly bothered by this problem if its a separate annotation (You'll get errors and the fix is: You can't create a hierarchy of comparables. This is basically already screwed beyond all recognition in java anyway. Lombok can't really fix this!)

I'm more concerned about interaction with superclasses in general. Just like it would make no sense at all to generate an equals() method involving only the fields of the superclass (though we do let you get away with that right now, but you have to be explicit about it) - it's much harder to figure out what to do here. Optimally we call on super's implementation of comparable to sort this out, but you can't have a stack of inherited compareTo methods.

For non-comparable fields, I'd far prefer an error. I'd find it rather strange that behaviour changes directly when you make changes in comparability of your fields' types.

I doubt we'll ever add this to lombok. It shouldn't be too difficult to generate a Compara_tor_ implementation, and you don't even need lombok shenanigans to do so - a simple annotation processor is enough.

We might even adopt such a tool into lombok if it already existed and sees some use.

:bust_in_silhouette: **rodion.moiseev**   :clock8: Jun 11, 2011 at 02:06 UTC

Thanks for the reply. With regard to naming, how about @ CompareTo (as in @ ToString)? I would agree with you for the most part with regard to interaction with super classes. If the super class already implements Comparable it's probably for the best to prohibit the usage of @ CompareTo annotation in the subclass. Effective Java also recommends using composition over inheritance in such case.

For non-comparable fields, you're right, an error is probably the best. 

I don't know exactly the kind of vision that drives this project, but I believe that generating compareTo has all of the advantages implementing getters, setters, equals, etc has. I don't know of any simple annotation processor to do the job, and I doubt many other Java do. Implementing one myself is not an easy task, as you say. So in the end I will end up using source-code generation or CompareToBuilder(in apache commons), which has all the disadvantages of source-code generation of getters, setters, equals, etc. 

The cool thing about Lombok is it's intuitive interface: you add @ ToString and it gives you toString(), you add @ Getter and it gives you a getter. I feel it's only natural to add @ CompareTo and see a compareTo() in your class. Let me know what you think.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 11, 2011 at 05:00 UTC

Checking superclass is not really feasible; running processors at a point in time where we can resolve (i.e. ask questions such as "what methods are in my superclass") is very tricky. So far only @ Delegate and val get this treatment because they can't work without it.

I agree but this is so far down the list of 'want to haves' that I doubt we'll _ever_ get to it. Now a patch of some sort, that would make it in, no problem.

:bust_in_silhouette: **rodion.moiseev**   :clock8: Jun 11, 2011 at 05:30 UTC

Thanks. I see, seems like removing any support for super-classes is probably the best option for compareTo() support.

From my personal experience with Lombok, as a user of Lombok in production environment, it would definitely help having compareTo(). We have lots of immutable data objects, and introducing Lombok has removed ALL code from class definitions, except compareTo()s which as still dangling around (leaves me wondering: why, oh why?). So in my personal opinion, support for compareTo() should be as natural as the one for other features (personally, I would even prefer it to 'val'). I don't understand why would you treat it as a 'want to have'. 

Anyway, I think Lombok is one of the best things that happened to Java, and I am very much looking forward to seeing more boiler-plate disappearing. 

PS. I didn't know there is support for @ Delegate, I'll definitely check it out.
_End of migration_
This issue is closed, but there's a newer discussion (but no progress) in #512.

The problem is, that the jdt.core classes and lombok are not in the same classloader. When lombok is used as agent it's loaded by the AppClassLoader, as you can see, and not by the OSGI ClassLoader. That's why it doesn't have access to the jdt.core classes.

But you gave me the right clue. It works when using 
-Xbootclasspath/p:lombok-edge.jar;org.eclipse.jdt.core-3.6.2.v_A76_R36x.jar

In some places lombok patches the classloader to be able to access the jdt.core classes. Is this also possible for this scenario? It would be better not to have jdt.core on the bootclasspath.

title: canEqual misses @Override
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 213)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **peter.fichtner**   :clock8: May 31, 2011 at 10:55 UTC

When annotating a class with @ EqualsAndHashCode that extends a class already containing a canEqual method (e.g. when super class also annotated with @ EqualsAndHashCode) the compiler complains the missing @ Override annotation at the overridden canEqual method. 

Solution: All generated overridden canEqual methods should be annotated with @ Override

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: May 31, 2011 at 15:04 UTC

We can't know whether or not we're overriding an existing method. I guess you've got your eclipse configured to consider this an error? We add the appropriate @ SuppressWarnings annotation.

I don't foresee a way to solve this problem anytime in the near future.

:bust_in_silhouette: **peter.fichtner**   :clock8: May 31, 2011 at 15:42 UTC

That's right, the compiler is configured to complain about missing @ Override annotations. And this is exactly my problem: I'd like to use this compiler feature but the lombok generated code isn't suitable. 

I understand that you can't see inside the compile progress that the method is overridden but when accounting lombok as a tool that generates the boilerplate for me I would expected that lombok would generate the same code that I would write and this code would contain the method with an @ Override annotation set. 

Otherwise I would have to turn off the compiler feature of warning me about missing @ Override annotations just because of this problem.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 31, 2011 at 15:50 UTC

As Reinier stated, we do add the SuppressWarnings annotation. So as long as you have the compiler Errors and Warnings settings set to issue a warning for missing @ Override annotations, you're still in the clear: You will get the warnings in the rest of your code, but not on lombok-generated code. However, if you've set the Errors and Warnings level to ERROR, there's not a lot we can do.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 31, 2011 at 15:50 UTC

Right now that is. Possibly we can check the superclass in the future...

:bust_in_silhouette: **peter.fichtner**   :clock8: May 31, 2011 at 18:05 UTC

Roel, thanks for your reply, 
I could not find any @ SuppressWarnings in the bytecode. I then took a look into java.lang.SuppressWarnings and it has a source retention policy (of course) since it's a hint for the compiler. 
Of course the solution for me is to use my previous compiler settings and add the @ SuppressWarnings annotation to the classes the compiler complains at the moment. 

But is it useful that you add this annotation to the bytecode?

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jun 01, 2011 at 07:33 UTC

We can't. Since the Retention of @ Override is set to RetentionPolicy.SOURCE, we cannot put it in the bytecode.

:bust_in_silhouette: **peter.fichtner**   :clock8: Jun 01, 2011 at 08:12 UTC

Yes, I did saw this too. I fear that this issue can't be fixed since you can't add @ Override nor @ SuppressWarnings to the bytecode. 
The question is: Why does  the eclipse compiler complain missing @ Override annos? It should not be able to see the mentioned methods since they do not exist in sourcecode. 

Perhaps this is a hen/egg problem!?

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jun 01, 2011 at 08:58 UTC

Lombok will make Eclipse "see" the methods even if they don't show up in the source code. The thing I don't understand is why "the eclipse compiler complains". Can you tell me what your project properties and workspace preferences are for the following items?
- Java Compiler / Errors/Warnings / Enable project specific settings (project properties only)
- Java Compiler / Errors/Warnings / Annotations / Missing '@ Override' annotation
- Java Compiler / Errors/Warnings / Annotations / Enable '@ SuppressWarnings'
- Java Compiler / Errors/Warnings / Annotations / Suppress optional errors with '@ SuppressWarnings'
- Java Compiler / Errors/Warnings / Treat optional errors like fatal compiler errors

:bust_in_silhouette: **peter.fichtner**   :clock8: Jun 01, 2011 at 19:14 UTC

We are using project specific settings (but identical for all projects): 
- Java Compiler / Errors/Warnings / Annotations / Missing '@ Override' annotation
  used to be "error" but is reduced to "warnings" since otherwise the metioned class won't compile
- Java Compiler / Errors/Warnings / Annotations / Enable '@ SuppressWarnings'
  [X] checked
- Java Compiler / Errors/Warnings / Annotations / Suppress optional errors with '@ SuppressWarnings'
  [ ] unchecked
- Java Compiler / Errors/Warnings / Treat optional errors like fatal compiler errors
  [X] checked

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 03, 2011 at 17:29 UTC

Its the last one: treat warnings like errors, perhaps.
_End of migration_

title: Missing @Override when using @Delegate
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 214)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **peter.fichtner**   :clock8: May 31, 2011 at 14:26 UTC

When using @ Delegate the generated delegate methods misses @ Override (which should be used on overriden methods when using JDK 5 and on overridden and implemented methods when using JDK 6). 

Solution: Add @ Override to each overridden/implemented method

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jun 01, 2011 at 07:36 UTC

That would probably be hard. Currently, we don't look at the superclass, not the implemented interfaces. And it is valid to delegate to a field with interface X without implementing X. But we do generate @ SuppressWarnings("all") to the generated methods, so you shouldn't get any warnings.
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 06, 2011 at 18:13 UTC
_End of migration_

title: Eclipse can not resolve class dependency with classes that uses @Synchronized
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 217)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **andreas.muenstermann@web.de**   :clock8: Jun 08, 2011 at 11:12 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. create a class A with a method annotated with @ Synchronized 2. create another class B within the same package that refers to the first class A 3. The eclipse IDE will mark the reference with "cannot resolve class B" What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? Lombok 0.9.3 Eclipse Helios SR2 Please provide any additional information below.

:bust_in_silhouette: **grootjans**   :clock8: Jun 08, 2011 at 18:16 UTC

I was able to reproduce this both with the 0.9.3 and the edge release. A few important things to note;
- doesn't happen in the default package
- the error doesn't appear in the problem overview, only in the class file view itself.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 13, 2011 at 20:37 UTC

Well, this is some voodoo:

If there are 10 annotations in a source file, this problem goes away. Generated annotations count, so just @ Data even with no fields is enough, as is @ ToString + @ EqualsAndHashCode (2 annotations right there + the @ Synchronized, then 3 methods with @ Override and @ SuppressWarnings, and 1 with just @ SuppressWarnings, adds up to exactly 10). The annotations don't need to be valid or even exist; as long as the parser recognizes them as an annotation, it counts.

Yes. Huh?!????

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 13, 2011 at 21:04 UTC

Adding fields is actually very very tricky; the positions have to be set to 0 or -1 (very carefully, some later math done by eclipse has to add up to exactly 0). However, this appears to be messing with the ability of eclipse to find the package statement, thus resulting in a type not found error as it thinks the type is named just "A" (default package) and not "foo.A" - also explaining why this error does not occur when all involved classes are in the default package.

There is no short-term solution to this problem that we can see. Changing the positions to anything else causes the dreaded 'second AST' to attempt to reparse the field which will obviously fail as its not actually there. The long-term fix is to hook into that reparse, and prevent it if we detect that the field is generated. I recall we've done this before for other handlers, but @ Synchronized is by far the least-used and 0.10.0 is about half a year late, so pushed back to 0.10.1

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 21, 2011 at 14:13 UTC

Might this be caused by something similar to issue #114?
:bust_in_silhouette: **grootjans**   :clock8: Jul 18, 2011 at 21:46 UTC

:bust_in_silhouette: **andreas.muenstermann@web.de**   :clock8: Jul 19, 2011 at 07:12 UTC

Is there any update to this issue? When can we expect a bug fix?

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 19, 2011 at 16:31 UTC

Lets work around this by removing the suppress warnings annotation in 0.10.0 and add a more thorough fix in 0.10.1.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 25, 2011 at 18:24 UTC

Worked around as promised; now @ Synchronized does not produce a @ SuppressWarnings annotation on the $LOCK/$lock field. We'll revisit this issue once we figure out how to add those safely to fields without causing half of the eclipse features to break. Done in dfca0e4cbdf761bcb119dc2b5bd1598e455d6d09 and will be rolled out in 0.10.0-RC2.

Going to keep this issue open on low priority.

:bust_in_silhouette: **tomkedem**   :clock8: Feb 07, 2014 at 14:24 UTC

Hey, it's been two and a half years. Will you get to it someday?
I'm more interested in the application of this solution for issue #637.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Feb 07, 2014 at 15:33 UTC

title: Annotation to wrap exceptions
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 227)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **grootjans**   :clock8: Jul 18, 2011 at 17:47 UTC

I expect you are talking about checked exceptions here (as your referring to them as 'imposed').

I'm not sure I can empathize with your situation, as I don't have a readily available example. Perhaps you can give us a more concrete one. Usually, lombok will only adept features that have a clear intent (I think this one satisfies this) and a number of real-world examples.

Also, you could use @ SneakyThrows to take away situations in which your absolutely not interested in the checked Exceptions your api is imposing on you:
https://projectlombok.org/features/SneakyThrows.html

:bust_in_silhouette: **gbierner**   :clock8: Jul 18, 2011 at 18:33 UTC

Yep, checked exceptions.  As an example, how about the Externalizable interface?  You're only allowed IOException in the writeExternal method, but maybe your implementation needs to handle a FooException.  Right now, your only choices are to eat the exception, wrap it in an IOException, or wrap it in an unchecked exception.  In the latter two cases, it would be nice to avoid the boilerplate.

There are other cases where there is no throws clause at all (eg Runnable.run) where it would be nice to use an annotation to wrap with an unchecked exception.  Also, these examples are from the Java API, but I see a lot more of them when using 3rd party libraries or even the code within a project when you're trying to avoid methods that throw an annoyingly large number of exceptions.

Re @ SneakyThrows, while that seems useful, it doesn't seem a substitute for the cases listed here.

:bust_in_silhouette: **daniel.yokomizo**   :clock8: Jul 18, 2011 at 20:03 UTC

It should not wrap Error either.

:bust_in_silhouette: **gbierner**   :clock8: Jul 18, 2011 at 20:11 UTC

r.spilker, that sounds good to me.  A good idea to use initCause instead of new.   Thanks for considering it!

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jan 23, 2014 at 22:38 UTC

I still think it is a good idea, but it hasn't happened yet and there too much too to and so little time. So I'm marking this as WontFix. It is comes up again in the Google Groups, we might reconsider.

:bust_in_silhouette: **grootjans**   :clock8: Jul 18, 2011 at 18:41 UTC

When compiling stuff that uses onmethod with javac, an error message is printed to the console, but the final number of errors is zero. Turns out javac will print errors to the console even if annotation processors that are yet to be run might invalidate those error messages. This is a known javac bug, fixed in javac 7, which will apparently not be back-ported. It's kind of a big deal but there's absolutely nothing we can do about it.

Unfortunately this phantom error is rather noticable in Netbeans. The classes with the errors do actually compile (assuming you've turned "compile on save" on).

We've looked at fixing this but there's simply nothing we can do. The error is already there before lombok even runs. Hopefully this problem goes away in a future netbeans due to using an updated javac without this bug - or we figure out a way to scrub an already reported error out of the list.

title: @Synchronized on a field should make the getters/setters synchronized (as generated by @Data/@Getter/@Setter)
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 235)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 13, 2011 at 12:13 UTC

See https://groups.google.com/forum/?hl=en﹟!topic/project-lombok/jLjl6Lwpjxw

We still need to decide if this is worth doing or not.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jan 24, 2014 at 10:32 UTC

I'm still on the fence... what about equals and hashCode? I mean: having thread safe mutable state is a bit harder than making the getters and setters synchronized.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 27, 2014 at 02:03 UTC

equals and hashCode actually use the getters. And we cache the results. In that sense all it really would take is to just treat @ Synchronized on the field as a sign to inject synchronized blocks into the generated getter and setter, and the constructor isn't relevant. Even builder and wither aren't an actual issue. We might have to disallow 'doNotUseGetters', but, on the other hand, threadsafe is rarely relevant for equals and hashCode.

The obvious downside is that this will VERY rarely be used and it just gives those clueless about how to do proper thread safety yet another gun to shoot themselves in the foot with.

But, java has already given them 7 bazookas, 12 uzis, 18 AK-47s, and a magnum .44 as cherry on top to pull this off with, so if we give em a pea shooter I don't think we're really making it worse.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jan 27, 2014 at 09:15 UTC

Well, I understand what you're saying, but I think people might expect that one lock is aquired for all the synchronized fields used in the equals, hashCode and toString to make sure the invariants are respected.

Furthermore, the getters and setters we generate will not touch the internal state of the objects involved, but equals, hashCode and toString probably will, potentially leading to hard to find race conditions, including deadlocks and infinite loops.

I'm okay with annotating a method with @ Synchronized because the user explicitly thought about the synchronization protocol.

So given the potential problems AND the fact that is is probably rarely used, even combined with the fact that we'd like to promote immutable shared state I'd like to mark this issue as WontFix.

Agreed?

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 27, 2014 at 13:31 UTC

Agreed
_End of migration_

Long story short, I assume that lombok generates an equals method you did not expect.
But maybe I'm assuming wrong. Make sure to check the feature example. If you need another implementation you can't use @ EAHC, but be advised that lombok pretty much offers the text-book implementation of equals.

:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Jul 15, 2011 at 07:50 UTC

I think I finally understand want you are trying to achieve.
You are using @ Data on your subclass but you don't want an equals() method at all or, if need be, an equals() method that just calls super.equals().

I'm afraid thats not the intention of @ EqualsAndHashCode.

As a solution you could:

[A] Override equals() yourself, as you did in your initial report

or

[B] Replace @ Data with @ RequiredArgsConstructor @ Getter @ Setter since @ Data is shorthand for @ RequiredArgsConstructor, @ Getter, @ Setter and @ EqualsAndHashCode

And if I'm still on the wrong track a small example would be really appreciated.

:bust_in_silhouette: **dsuepke**   :clock8: Jul 19, 2011 at 07:05 UTC

Thanks for you remarks, that was helpful. I will just include the equals method to stop @ Data from adding further checks. Intuitively I'd say that if I say "callSuper=true" there should be no need to provide the method, but that's certainly not a big deal.

The equals contract should be mutually true, as both instances will always be of the type ParentEntity, thus the id check should work.

https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/commit/8c61bb0990a861ef481e2b9034b4c36df09e1061

excludes=Types has been added to counteract this. Once we figure out how to

title: Delombok file to another package causes incorrect reference if 'val' refers to a nested non-public class
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 247)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **maartenhoedjes**   :clock8: Aug 03, 2011 at 12:25 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Create a testClass with a nested class nestedClass which is not public. 2. Use the following code somewhere in targetClass: val variable = new nestedClass(); 3. Delombok the file to another file What is the expected output? final src-delomboked.testClass.nestedClass = new nestedClass(); What do you see instead? final src.testClass.nestedClass = new nestedClass(); And I get the error: nestedClass is not visible. What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? Lombok 0.10 on Windows XP Please provide any additional information below. Might be a feature.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Aug 03, 2011 at 12:52 UTC

Can you please attach a complete source file?

:bust_in_silhouette: **maartenhoedjes**   :clock8: Aug 03, 2011 at 13:48 UTC

I have the impression this might not be a bug, but a difference in philosophy.

It ties into something else which is an issue to us: that the package declaration is not updated to the folder to which the delomboked is copied. (So 'package src;' is not updated to 'package src-delomboked;'.) I think there are good reasons not to do this, because most of the time users would probably like to replace the original file with the delomboked file and they do not want the package declaration to change.

My problem is analogous to this, but just a little bit more complex: whenever you use a 'local type' such as newClass, it would suit my needs better if delombok should take this into account and update the reference, and in the new file not refer to the original nestedClass.

I have attached an original and delomboked file for reference.

:bust_in_silhouette: **maartenhoedjes**   :clock8: Aug 03, 2011 at 13:48 UTC

[:link: delombok-val-issue.rar](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/2470002000/delombok-val-issue.rar)

:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Aug 03, 2011 at 16:52 UTC

Yeah it's no bug. And there is nothing philosophical about it either.
First of all in your example "src" is package rather than a source-folder.
Delombok leaves the project structure intact, so it does not touch package names.

I would advise you to redesign your project structure. Read this advise:

"You should arrange source files in a directory tree that reflects their package tree. For example, if you keep all your source files in C:\workspace, the source code for com.mysoft.mypack.MyClass should be in C:\workspace\com\mysoft\mypack\MyClass.java." - [1](http://download.oracle.com/javase/6/docs/technotes/tools/windows/javac.html)

You could also follow the maven standard directory layout [2](http://maven.apache.org/guides/introduction/introduction-to-the-standard-directory-layout.html)
:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Aug 03, 2011 at 17:15 UTC

:bust_in_silhouette: **maartenhoedjes**   :clock8: Aug 03, 2011 at 18:09 UTC

I see what you mean. I guess it's an error in our project setup. We copy delomboked files from one package into another. It might be better to copy the files from one project into the other, so they can have the same package structure.

Thanks for the clarification.
_End of migration_

title: Output directory is incorrect for non-Windows
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 249)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **anthony@whitford.com**   :clock8: Aug 08, 2011 at 04:25 UTC

From a non-Windows machine (Mac OS X or Linux Ubuntu, for example), run something like:

$ java -jar lombok.jar delombok /Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/src/main/lombok/ -d /Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/target/generated-sources/delombok

Then, list the file in the output directory:

$ ls -l /Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/target/generated-sources/delombok

In my example, I have a source code file:  /Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/src/main/lombok/org/projectlombok/test/DataExample.java
Since I specified the source path to be /Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/src/main/lombok/, I am expecting the generated files to be:
/Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/target/generated-sources/delombok/org/projectlombok/test/DataExample.java
Alas, what I see instead is:
/Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/target/generated-sources/delombok/Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/src/main/lombok/org/projectlombok/test/DataExample.java

I have seen this problem with 0.10.RC1 through 0.10.RC3 -- but only on non-Windows (Mac and Ubuntu).  Windows works as expected.

Consider the following debug from Delombok.createFileWriter:

inBase       : /Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/src/main/lombok
inBase.toURI : file:/Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/src/main/lombok/
file         : /Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/src/main/lombok/org/projectlombok/test/DataExample.java
relative     : /Users/anthony/Documents/lombok.maven/test-maven-lombok/src/main/lombok/org/projectlombok/test/DataExample.java

You can see that "relative" is not properly being transformed to be "relative."  I would expect it to become:
    org/projectlombok/test/DataExample.java

It would seem that the URI being generated for the last argument from this line:
            else rawWriter = createFileWriter(output, baseMap.get(unit), unit.sourcefile.toUri());
is lacking the "file:/" prefix, so the relativize is not working…

I can resolve this problem by changing this line:

```
URI relative = inBase.toURI().relativize(file);
```

to:

```
    URI base = inBase.toURI();
    URI relative = base.relativize(base.resolve(file));
```

Note that I'm running into this problem during testing of the new lombok-maven-plugin.  I am using Java 6 update 26 on Mac OSX Lion.  Thanks for your help.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Aug 08, 2011 at 20:04 UTC

Fixed in d00576e30774eac3d93bd14a7ef1600b0a7cbbfa and will be in 0.10.0. Implemented just like you suggested and attributed to you in the commit.

title: Make generated source code for equals static code analysis friendly
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 250)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Aug 08, 2011 at 19:41 UTC

About the converting the if one-liners to blocks; will do, but not in 0.10.0. About everything else: we add SuppressWarnings("all"). PMD should respect that.

In fact, _any_ inclusion of anything lombok does in any code metric is silly, however @ SuppressWarnings("all") and the idea 'this is generated code' don't overlap perfectly. There's unfortunately no @ java.lang.Generated (yet). Nevertheless, in PMD's case it is a tool that creates warnings for your code and therefore it is very obvious to us that we've done all we should do here.

To be specific, we will not clean up the code generated by lombok just to satisfy style checker rules, for a very simple reason: Everybody has their own rules, and conflicts are likely, where we simply can't make everybody happy.

Accepted only for if-blocks.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Lord.Quackstar**   :clock8: Aug 09, 2011 at 03:28 UTC

Just curious: Why would you run PMD on the generated source instead of the real source?

:bust_in_silhouette: **anthony@whitford.com**   :clock8: Aug 19, 2011 at 04:30 UTC

Because then you end up with lots of other issues.  For example, if you are using @ Data to generate getters and setters, PMD will complain that fields are unreferenced (because it does not see the public getField and setField).

:bust_in_silhouette: **anthony@whitford.com**   :clock8: Sep 22, 2013 at 04:50 UTC

I discovered a nice workaround for PMD 5, and documented it in my blog:  http://anthonywhitford.blogspot.com/2013/09/suppressing-pmd-alerts-for-lombok.html
_End of migration_

Just so you know, you will get the same error without using lombok.
lombok translates your small example into this:

public class Test {
    private static final org.slf4j.Logger log = org.slf4j.LoggerFactory.getLogger(Test.class);

```
int org;
```

}

There is just nothing we can do about it.

A solution would be to add import statements for "Logger" and "LoggerFactory" instead of using fully qualified names.
Let's assume we were to that. If the user has his own "Logger" or "LoggerFactory" types and wants to use them in his code, we would force him to fully qualify these names.

I think both scenarios (this issue and the one I described just now) are rare corner cases and each "solution" would have its downsides, so I say let's stick to how it works right now.

But thanks for the good find.

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Aug 10, 2011 at 10:08 UTC

One reason is that com.sun.tools.javac.parser.Scanner$Factory got replaced by com.sun.tools.javac.parser.ScannerFactory. So we need two factories for the CommentCollectingScanner. The next thing I can imagine is the PrettyCommentPrinter failing.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Aug 15, 2011 at 20:52 UTC

With Philipp's sleuthing work putting us on the right path, delombok now appears to fully work with java 1.7, including the only new AST type node (JCTypeUnion, used in catch (Ex1 | Ex2 e) { ... }.

This work is spread across commits:

c996e8749db4cf049401e961dba1b72ea5d1b85d
f7ec1e33ed4db5f31d288dd7d2c909b83b2d418f
d8d47c687d7ec22e481cf10782f1f889485c39fa-82b14a30893d509e055ed06d1576c5e16d397995

because a number of logistical changes have been introduced to accomodate this; mostly we now compile against a bunch of stubs of javac internals instead of against javac itself directly. These stubs are explicitly excluded from the lombok.jar we build, and thus the build process has changed a bit.

title: force @Cleanup  (wishlist)
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 261)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **amanic**   :clock8: Aug 17, 2011 at 07:52 UTC

In the @ Cleanup documentation fineprint you say that that any exceptions during cleanup can hide application exceptions.
In some cases this can be a serious problem.

It will be nice if you can tell lombok to print or log exceptions that happen during cleanup. I think cleanup is a courtesy call i.e. you try and if it fails tuff, don't annoy me. 

I'm thinking @ Cleanup can automatically log the cleanup exceptions
if one of the new @ Slf4j, @ Log4j etc. are present. Otherwise print to system out?

Maybe @ Cleanup shoult take a parameter to be able to force it. eg.
@ Cleanup("log")
@ Cleanup("print")
@ Cleanup("ignore")
@ Cleanup("throw")

:bust_in_silhouette: **amanic**   :clock8: Aug 17, 2011 at 08:23 UTC

I see the default value is already taken. So it can be a normal annotation param eg.:
@ Cleanup(onError="log")
@ Cleanup(onError="print")
@ Cleanup(onError="ignore")
@ Cleanup(onError="throw")

:bust_in_silhouette: **amanic**   :clock8: Aug 17, 2011 at 14:39 UTC

It is a pity that this isn't possible :(
I'd think sneakyTrowing the real exception that was thrown is much better than hiding it. In the absence of a perfect solution, isn't this better?
The user can then actually have a chance to catch the right exception, 
he would just need to check for the RealException of if it is a sneaky throw containing a RealException.

:bust_in_silhouette: **amanic**   :clock8: Aug 25, 2011 at 20:33 UTC

Matt Fowles mentioned on the mailinglist:

ARM in Java7 does clever things with adding associated exceptions into a parent exception (if there is one).  It would be nice if @ Cleanup did the same thing.  Using the new Throwable.addSuppressedException [if available]

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Sep 20, 2011 at 18:33 UTC

I'll try and keep this brief and clear:

We CANNOT reproduce the ARM behaviour of attaching the exception thrown by the cleanup method (if any) to the originally thrown exception (if any). It's just not possible without reams and reams of code to do static analysis, which is beyond the scope of lombok.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Sep 20, 2011 at 18:36 UTC

To OP: A cleanup operation is _CRUCIAL_, it's not a nice-to-have. For example, if you open a FileOutputStream, make a bunch of write() calls which all work out fine, and then finally call close(), and that one throws an IOException? Guess what: Nothing was written at all, all those write calls were just going into a buffer.

The idea that a close call is a courtesy is indeed true for read-only resources. However, practically speaking, InputStream.close() simply doesn't fail. Ever. I know the signature says it throws an IOException, but as far as I'm concerned you could sneakythrow that thing, it just doesn't happen. So, we're talking entirely a hypothetical here: Resources where closing is nice-to-have don't _actually_ throw any exceptions. If an exception is really thrown, it'll be a mutable resource, and the exception signals that any number of previous operations actually failed, but it took the implied 'flush' of closing the resource to figure that out.

:bust_in_silhouette: **amanic**   :clock8: Sep 20, 2011 at 21:12 UTC

Fair enough guys thanks for looking at this.
I was hoping though that if there was any chance of hiding any exceptions to at least log them or print them out somewhere to at least give developers a fighting chance to fix the root cause.
_End of migration_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **jwnimmer@jaybridge.com**   :clock8: Aug 25, 2011 at 18:59 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Open my project of ~20kloc Java with eclipse + lombok: 2. Edit, run, save, etc. as usual. 3. After 30-60 minutes, everything becomes unusually slow (3-15+ seconds to save, intelli-sense, compile, ...) due to GC pauses. The 1GB heap size of the eclipse JVM is full and a force-GC only reclaims a couple percent, soon to be used up again. What is the expected output? What do you see instead? No performance degradation over time, memory use scales with the size of the project, not how long my IDE is open. What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? - Running on Ubuntu 10.04. - Lombok v0.10.0 "Burning Emu" (August 19th, 2011). - Eclipse Version: 3.7.0, Build id: I20110613-1736 - +FindBugs 1.3.9.20090821 - +Subclipse 1.6.18 and related dependencies. Please provide any additional information below. Unfortunately, I cannot share the source code for the project. I can post the eclipse settings and preferences if that is helpful. I have several save actions enabled, including auto-formatting. FindBugs is also set to run incrementally on every save. I've taken a heap dump and used eclipse MemoryAnalyzer. The Leak Suspects report says: The classloader "lombok.patcher.equinox.EquinoxClassLoader @ 0x69f24ec0" occupies 741,208,216 (92.32%) bytes. Within that classloader, there are: 140 MiB of org.eclipse.jdt.internal.compiler.lookup.LookupEnvironment 70 MiB of org.eclipse.jdt.internal.compiler.ClassFile 67 MiB of org.eclipse.jdt.internal.compiler.lookup.BinaryTypeBinding 65 MiB of org.eclipse.jdt.internal.compiler.lookup.SourceTypeBinding 61 MiB of org.eclipse.jdt.internal.compiler.ast.CompilationUnitDeclaration ... etc ... This is fairly straightforward to reproduce for me (happens regularly) but does need at least 15 minutes of use to see a substantial increase in live heap use. I'm going to bisect across my plug-ins and settings to find the minimum sufficient setup to reproduce this, but it will take me a little while. If anyone has ideas on other diagnostic tools or settings to explore to help narrow this down, I'm open to suggestions.

title: Javac incorrect output
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 266)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **mplushnikov**   :clock8: Aug 30, 2011 at 12:31 UTC

I'm working on lombok plugin for IntelliJ and have some issues with lombock (tested with last version 0.10.0) :

IntelliJ is not able to finish compilation of "lomboked" files, and produce errors like: "MyClass.class not found"

The cause of problem is that lombok annotation processor added to the IntelliJ Idea javac classpath is producing incorrect console output. (IntelliJ reads output of the javac compiler and interpet some of the producing lines).

Example:

Have a look at javac output for a small empty test class "Main.java" without lombok.jar in classpath:
D:\javac de\plushnikov\lombok\Main.java -verbose
[parsing started de\plushnikov\lombok\Main.java]
[parsing completed 13ms]
[search path for source files: .]
[search path for class files: .....]
[loading java\lang\Object.class(java\lang:Object.class)]
[loading java\lang\String.class(java\lang:String.class)]
[checking de.plushnikov.lombok.Main]
[wrote de\plushnikov\lombok\Main.class]
[total 112ms]

Now the same class and lombok.jar in classpath: D:\javac de\plushnikov\lombok\Main.java -verbose -cp lombok-0.10.0.jar
[parsing started de\plushnikov\lombok\Main.java]
[parsing completed 14ms]
[search path for source files: ......]
[loading java\lang\Object.class(java\lang:Object.class)]
[loading java\lang\String.class(java\lang:String.class)]
Round 1:
        input files: {de.plushnikov.lombok.Main}
        annotations: []
        last round: false
Processor lombok.core.AnnotationProcessor matches [] and returns false.
[parsing started lombok/dummy/ForceNewRound0.java]
[parsing completed 0ms]
[loading java\lang\Object.class(java\lang:Object.class)]
[loading java\lang\String.class(java\lang:String.class)]
Round 2:
        input files: {}
        annotations: []
        last round: false
Processor lombok.core.AnnotationProcessor matches [] and returns false.
Round 3:
        input files: {}
        annotations: []
        last round: true
[loading java\lang\Object.class(java\lang:Object.class)]
[loading java\lang\String.class(java\lang:String.class)]
[checking de.plushnikov.lombok.Main]
[wrote Main.class]
[total 223ms]

Compare the lines starting with "[wrote ":
You can see the difference:
[wrote de\plushnikov\lombok\Main.class]
and
[wrote Main.class]

Solution:

There is a small problem with current implementation of lombok wrappers for com.sun.tools.javac.util.BaseFileObject.

The classes Javac6BaseFileObjectWrapper, Javac7BaseFileObjectWrapper and InterceptingJavaFileObject have to override default toString() method and delegate it to the "delegate.toString()" method of the wrapped object.

title: @EqualsAndHashCode generating Unecessary casts
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 272)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **peter.fichtner**   :clock8: Sep 07, 2011 at 16:08 UTC

We have set eclipse's compiler setting of "unecessary cast" to error. After migrating from lombok 0.10.0-beta2 to the released version all classes annotated with @ Data and/or @ EqualsAndHashCode do have compile errors telling that there are unecessary casts from fields' types to Object. 

Can you please remove the generation of these unecessary casts to java.lang.Object like it used to be in 0.10.0-beta2? 
I am sure there is no need for these casts. 

Thanks

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Sep 20, 2011 at 19:10 UTC

There is actually a need for those casts. Seriously.

We used to call equals of Object type fields just with .equals(otherRef). However, there are classes out there, no matter how dumb this may seem, which have an equals(Object) method but also an equals(SelfType) method. That's what the casts are for.

In just about every case the cast is indeed useless, but we can't know that (generating code in such a way that we already know structural information about other classes is far more difficult than being able to do so without that knowledge).

A general piece of advice: You should NEVER tell eclipse to error on ANYTHING. There's no real point to this; you just make your own life hard because code that seems buggy can't even be run to test something completely different. Instead, set just about everything to warning, and make a policy that you should never check in anything with warnings on a branch that's looked at by multiple people.

We avoid this and many other problems by adding a @ SuppressWarnings("all"), which conveniently sidesteps this issue, but @ SuppressWarnings doesn't help if you've configured your eclipse to treat things which are at best warnings (such as unnecessary casts) to errors.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Sep 29, 2011 at 06:32 UTC

I thought, _for sure_, i updated this to a low priority 'will fix if we get to it', but I guess I didn't. Doing it now.

I'm not sure we can make it work though; we have create a separate Object-typed variable for EACH field in the class, as canEqual(Object) needs to be called, but that isn't in java.lang.Object. That'd be a heck of a lot of overhead.

Developers checking in warnings just means you need to crack the whip more. You DO NOT check in warnings, period. (unless it's a workstore personal branch). As I said before, lombok WILL do things that will run afoul of some of your settings, it's inevitable. This one is fixable, but they won't all be, and some will be mutually exclusive (big company X has settings such that we need to write it some way to avoid errors, but big company Y will error on that and needs the code to be generated differently, in a way that X would error out on).

:bust_in_silhouette: **simioni.eduardo**   :clock8: Feb 12, 2013 at 15:41 UTC

I'm trying lombok (0.11.6) for the first time and I have run into this limitation, like Peter, I'm not going to change my project's compiler settings and allow developers to check in code with warnings.

You are creating a tool to help people write better and cleaner code and sacrificing its usage to cover a stupid corner case that only really bad codebases can have. It doesn't make sense to me.

I have a suggestion tough, you can add a parameter to @ EqualsAndHashCode, something like @ EqualsAndHashCode(imNotStupidEnoughToOverloadEquals=true).
Then you don't need to know anything in advance about the code.

Does that sound like something you could be adding in the near future?

Thanks.

:bust_in_silhouette: **simioni.eduardo**   :clock8: Feb 12, 2013 at 15:48 UTC

Sorry about to the double message, but thinking again, I believe that the correct behavior should be the default behavior. Then with @ EqualsAndHashCode(imStupidAndILikeOverloadingEquals=true) you would fallback to current implementation.
_End of migration_

@simioni.eduardo let's say lombok added that setting. Take it to its logical conclusion. `@EqualsAndHashCode` would have, literally, 90 different parameters. Obviously a crazy plan.

Reconsidering it, and given how this is never ever going to bubble to the top of the pile, along with various other issues (such as how this is not gonna play well with valhalla), I'm just gonna call time of death on this issue.

Besides, since this issue was opened we've adopted a policy that any linter tool that gets annoyed by lombok code is to be fixed by instructing the linter to stop linting generated code. If the linter doesn't let you do that, file a bug report with the linter. It's perhaps a bit 'kicking the can down the road', but, honestly, linting generated code of any stripe is a silly notion.

Note that lombok can (and does) generate annotations that indicate the method is generated. Various linter tools CAN be configured (and you can tell lombok to add annotations, too).

What do you see instead? The enum constructor body should remain empty. Instead, it gets "super();" added, and therefore fails to compile. What version of the product are you using? Lombok version: 0.10.1-EDGE 2011-09-20 18:50 UTC" java version "1.6.0_20" OpenJDK Runtime Environment (IcedTea6 1.9.9) (6b20-1.9.9-0ubuntu1~10.04.2) OpenJDK Server VM (build 19.0-b09, mixed mode) Ubuntu Lucid (10.04).
