:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 03, 2011 at 17:01 UTC

Well, that is obscure. the RHS of the val assignment has to be an anonymous inner class, which has to be in the same source file, AND there needs to be an enum with an explicit constructor, AND val needs to be involved. However did you find that?

I also have no idea why javac is stuffing superfluous super calls in there.

:bust_in_silhouette: **jwnimmer@jaybridge.com**   :clock8: Oct 03, 2011 at 17:48 UTC

We run "delombok + test-compile" as part of our regression build, so one morning I wake up to find that for some reason, a 12kLOC package wasn't passing anymore.  It only took me a minute to isolate which changeset was the issue, but then took me a couple hours to distill the subsystem down to a failing test case that I was able to share.  As you note, the failure conditions are fascinating and random.

Thanks to everyone @ projectlombok for your great work, it's a great tool to use.

:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Oct 03, 2011 at 20:50 UTC

I found the culprit in javac6.jar:
com.sun.tools.javac.comp.Attr.visitMethodDef(JCTree$JCMethodDecl) line: 661
but I'm pretty sure we can't do anything here. Seems like a 'simple' javac bug to me, since the enum check is just missing.
Let me check javac7.jar real quick.

:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Oct 03, 2011 at 20:59 UTC

Same bug is present in javac7.jar.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 10, 2011 at 17:40 UTC

I don't think this is java bug, just a misfeature, as in, ugly code.

My guess is: This obscure corner of Attr space isn't reentrant. In pseudocode, this code (line 661 of Attr) does:

for all constructors:

_IF_ there's at least 1 statement and that statement is a this or super call:

Check if explicit super/this calls are legal here and if not, error.

_OTHERWISE_, generate an (implicit) super call and DO NOT report any errors.

Running that snippet twice will first generate the implicit constructor... and then error out.

Going to investigate if/how we can fix this now.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 10, 2011 at 17:58 UTC

Given the OPs slightly more elaborate example, apparently an attr call triggered in file A.java will cause a super() call to be inserted overzealously in B.java. So, either:

(A) every time we call any attr we delve through the _ENTIRE_ sourcebase and filter out any created implicit super calls, which is clearly not a reasonable option, or

(B) we copy/paste all 5000+ lines of Attr so we can emulate its behaviour. Also not reasonable, or

(C) we patch Attr, from javac, which we don't normally do either.

So... exactly how much is this bug worth to us? From here it looks like fixing it is many man-days of work, and a considerable future maintainance burden.

title: In latest version (0.10.1) @Data is incompatible with Spring's @NotNull
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 287)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **francois.marot**   :clock8: Oct 13, 2011 at 08:21 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. anotate a class with @ Data 2. add Spring's @ NotNull annotation on a private member ( import org.springmodules.validation.bean.conf.loader.annotation.handler.NotNull ) 3. Eclipse will complain (java error), underlining the @ Data in red with the error: "The annotation @ NotNull is disallowed for this location" What is the expected output? What do you see instead? everything should be fine What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? Eclipse indigo up to date Lombok 0.10.1 spring-modules-validation-0.8-sources.jar Please provide any additional information below. Lombok 0.10.0 does not have this error so it was introduced in Lombok 0.10.1 I imagine that Lombok expects all @ NotNull annotations to be its own and that a more precise check on the whole @ NotNull annotation class+package would solve the problem but I may be wrong as I didn't look at the sources.

:bust_in_silhouette: **steven.dick.1972**   :clock8: Oct 14, 2011 at 07:59 UTC

I'm using the javax validation API (with hibernate validator 4.2.0 final) and Eclipse is fine, but javac running from ANT complains about the @ NotNull when using Lombok 0.10.1 - downgrading to Lombok 0.10.0 resolves the problem.

:bust_in_silhouette: **graham.berks**   :clock8: Oct 17, 2011 at 09:40 UTC

Any update to the use of javax validation API ? Bit of a stopper from us to upgrade this.

Thanks

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Oct 17, 2011 at 09:57 UTC

We will discuss this tonight during our weekly Lombok development meeting

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 17, 2011 at 17:20 UTC

We've looked at version 0.8 of spring modules, here:

http://java.net/projects/springmodules/sources/svn/show/tags/release-0_8/projects/validation/src/java/org/springmodules/validation/bean/conf/loader?rev=2110

And as you can see, there's no 'annotation' package. We have no idea where its from, in fact; googling around doesn't give us much.

As far as we know, for years and years now, the right annotation for this stuff is javax.validation.constraints.NotNull and not spring's own variant.

Spring's own variant seems to only be legal on fields, whereas a recent version of javax.validation.constraints.NotNull is valid on fields, methods, and parameters - everything we need it to be legal on.

We suggest you switch versions. Otherwise, can you point us at the sources of this NotNull annotation so we can learn a little more about it? We could try to hardcode an exception for that annotation, but without any trace of that annotation other than this bugreport we're a bit hesitant to do so.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 17, 2011 at 17:20 UTC

Stephen, Graham:

When we look at the javadoc for javax.validation.constraints.NotNull here:

http://download.oracle.com/javaee/6/api/javax/validation/constraints/NotNull.html

It looks like there should be no problem; it's legal everywhere we need it to be legal. When I check the javaEE 5 docs, there is no javax.validation at all, so it seems to be new in javaEE 6.

What error message are you getting? What version are you on? The same caveat applies: We can hardcode an exception but before we do so we need to know what's going on.

:bust_in_silhouette: **graham.berks**   :clock8: Oct 18, 2011 at 07:33 UTC

Attached a small example, error can be seen with

mvn compile 

gives

Test.java:[8,1] annotation type not applicable to this kind of declaration

Appears to me that Lombok should not be getting involved but some error in processing is causing @ NotNull to be processed.

Thanks

:bust_in_silhouette: **graham.berks**   :clock8: Oct 18, 2011 at 07:33 UTC

[:link: Lombok-Bug.zip](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/2870008000/Lombok-Bug.zip)

:bust_in_silhouette: **graham.berks**   :clock8: Oct 19, 2011 at 07:11 UTC

As i'm not including Lombok's @ NotNull via an import statement I would assume it shoouldn't be processing the @ NotNull.

That assumption correct ?

:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Oct 19, 2011 at 20:55 UTC

Any annotation that matches the pattern ^(?:notnull|nonnull)$ will be processed by @ Data.

:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Oct 19, 2011 at 21:22 UTC

Issue #364 has been merged into this issue.

:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Oct 19, 2011 at 21:29 UTC

Only affects javac and works if the @ NotNull annotation is applicable to local variable declarations(so ElementType.LOCAL_VARIABLE), which I find particular strange.

:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Oct 19, 2011 at 21:47 UTC

As for the Spring @ NotNull annotation, it is only allowed on fields and methods(so ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.FIELD). This means it shouldn't qualify for an annotation @ Data should process.

The question is how should we handle these cases?

:bust_in_silhouette: **graham.berks**   :clock8: Oct 20, 2011 at 07:45 UTC

To me it would seem dangerous to process annotations without an explicit call to use it. ie. an import statement.

:bust_in_silhouette: **graham.berks**   :clock8: Oct 21, 2011 at 07:35 UTC

Perhaps the change should be backed out until a solution is available. We are having numerous issues with eclipse and would like to narrow down any issues and get the change to remove the memory leak with @ Delegate. Though I don't really know if this is causing us any real impact.

:bust_in_silhouette: **dsuepke**   :clock8: Oct 24, 2011 at 08:22 UTC

Getting the same problem with javax.validation.constraints.NotNull, making it necessary to fall back to the previous version of Lombok. A quick fix would be greatly appreciated.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 25, 2011 at 13:02 UTC

We've stumbled on this issue before, and at that time I 'fixed' it by just not treating @ NotNull (Any kind of @ NotNull, from any package) special. I forgot to update the documentation and I also didn't document the code. Philipp recently noticed the discrepancy in the docs, and added it back in.

Seems like this is still the best option as we've never actually heard any complaints about _not_ having @ NotNull trigger lombok's usually non-null processing.

We'll push a new version out the door with the fix soon. That would be version 0.10.2

 Fixed in commit 782daa49979c35cd93139b3cfbc98eafe346f790 (and this time I did update the docs and add a comment explaining why NotNull isn't in the list).

:bust_in_silhouette: **dsuepke**   :clock8: Oct 25, 2011 at 17:32 UTC

Great, many thanks :)

:bust_in_silhouette: **graham.berks**   :clock8: Oct 25, 2011 at 17:59 UTC

Fab, thanks

:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Oct 26, 2011 at 06:48 UTC

title: Feature request: abbreviated package names
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 290)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **jwnimmer@jaybridge.com**   :clock8: Oct 18, 2011 at 19:14 UTC

It would be nice if lombok provided a way to abbreviate package names, so that classes with a duplicate name but in different packages could more easily be used together.

For example, say I have code that uses both com.google.common.base.Predicate and org.apache.commons.collections.Predicate.  I can only import one of them, so the other class name must be spelled out long-form every time.

Ideally, I would like to be able to say "google.Predicate" or "apache.Predicate" and then have lombok rewrite that into the full package name.  I expect to have to write down a "google => com.google.common.base" or "google.Predicate => com.google.common.base.Predicate" annotation rule somewhere for lombok to know what to do.  Given that teams should probably strive to use the same abbreviations from one file to the next anyway, an annotation on a package-info.java file seems like a good way to specify the abbreviation mappings, which could them be used within all code in that package.

This problem is really a failing of the Java language's "import" syntax (no "namespace aliasing" or "import as", but it does cause the occasional headache and seems worth thinking about a fix for, at least.

Note that at runtime, I still do want the full (com.google...) name to be used, so the various jar-repacking techniques aren't the right fix here.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 25, 2011 at 07:12 UTC

Looking for config info such as these package shorthand mappings anywhere but the source file itself is extremely problematic. It can be done, but the last time we introduced features that did this is over a year ago and we're still cleaning up bugs related to how  complicated things get when we look outside of source.

I'm fairly sure we don't want that burden for this feature, so it would have to be local to each file, and then I'm not sure how much boilerplate you really save.

Let's revisit this when we have a config framework in place, preferably one project-wide.

:bust_in_silhouette: **grootjans**   :clock8: Nov 07, 2011 at 21:28 UTC

We think this might be a nice feature, so we proposed an initial syntax on the forums:
http://groups.google.com/group/project-lombok/t/db9ff859978d710f

We still have to hash out the syntax, and see if we can really make this work in javac and Eclipse.

:bust_in_silhouette: **askoning**   :clock8: Oct 07, 2013 at 17:22 UTC

Issue #619 has been merged into this issue.
_End of migration_
Any news on this feature? I would love to see this in lombok!

@cardil 
I'm afraid, with
```
static alias EmployeeView = org.example.view.model.Employee.class;
```
the compiler would abort before even calling Lombok (the parser would complain). It'd probably have to look like
```
@alias interface EmployeeView extends org.example.view.model.Employee.class {}
```
so that it comes through.

However, for naming consistency, I'd suggest not to support anything on the class level.

---

@rzwitserloot 

> Let's revisit this when we have a config framework in place, preferably one project-wide.

Now we do. I'd suggest a simple syntax like
```
typeAliases+=EmployeeView->org.example.view.model.Employee
typeAliases+=base.Predicate->com.google.common.base.Predicate
```
which would make Lombok unconditionally replace all occurrences. No resolution and no complicated logic. This can lead to naming conflicts, but let's say, it's user's responsibility to choose a globally usable shortcut.

> I will not use it as it is dangerous.

IMHO, it's not dangerous at all, when used sparingly and properly reviewed. I'd only use it for classes having a name conflicting with something else or legacy classes like
```
awt.List = java.awt.List
obsol.JulDate = java.util.Date
obsol.SqlDate = java.sql.Date
```
and forbid myself ever importing them. This would be actually safer than the current state.

---

Your use case is clearly different. Actually, I try hard to avoid having two equally named classes in my projects - I use a lot of class nesting and funny prefixes/suffixes, but I can see why you do not.

> You want to have those aliases private, used only in parts of the code that meets with similar domains - that is only in Mappers.

- Actually, `lombok.config` applies to a whole subdirectory, i.e., to a package and its subpackages. This may be local enough for you.
- I guess, any top-level definition in *.java can only be applied to the current file only as inspecting other files is rather impossible.
- For the start, I'd forbid nesting alias definitions as it's probably rarely needed.

> It will be limited to non final classes and interfaces.

Not necessarily..... the parser doesn't care and maybe Lombok can do its job before it blows. It can probably do the replacement and remove the alias declaration.

---

The remaining problem is the implementation..... more precisely, an implementer is needed. I hope, the project maintainers (not me) say what they think about the syntax and whether a PR is welcome (I'm pretty busy and hacking Lombok is hard).

Oracle implementing your JEP would be best.

We know that naming your fields with a prefix character is a reasonably accepted approach to splitting your variable namespace into local and global(field) variables (as far as people go in accepting each others Hungarian-esque notations.)

That said, we are not going to introduce heuristics to determine what the accepted field name would be. title: "Cannot override the final method" on @Getter
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 297)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **dsuepke**   :clock8: Nov 07, 2011 at 16:20 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Have a class extend another class with a final getXYZ() method 2. Annotate the extending class with @ Getter or @ Data What is the expected output? What do you see instead? Class cannot compile because of "Cannot override the final method from XYZ" error. Expecting Lombok to recognize the final or to provide and to provide an exclude for @ Getter or ignore that attribute What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? Lombok 0.10.0-RC3 Eclipse Indigo Linux Java 1.6

:bust_in_silhouette: **grootjans**   :clock8: Nov 07, 2011 at 18:58 UTC

Lombok isn't going to second-guess the fact that your super-class has a getter. You say @ Getter... we make it!. There is, however, an exclude mechanism. With the following code you should be hunky-dory:

@ Getter
public class Foo extends Bar {
    int abc; // will have getter.
    @ Getter(AccessLevel.NONE) int xyz; // won't.
}

:bust_in_silhouette: **dsuepke**   :clock8: Nov 07, 2011 at 19:01 UTC

If I have the @ Getter annotation on an attribute I'd understand, but with an annotated class, especially @ Data, a compile error shouldn't happen in my opinion. Well, without the alternative I guess I'll be setting the AccessLevel.

Thanks for Lombok in any case :).

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Nov 07, 2011 at 21:28 UTC

We rather seriously dislike compiler features that try to guess your intent based on vague hints. What you're asking for is effectively that lombok reasons like this:

Oh, hey, look. Parent class has a final name that conflicts with the getter that I would normally make here. **_I guess the author intended for me not to generate it then!**_

That stuff in the stars? I don't like it. It's almost as likely that the programmer wasn't aware of the final method and will get very confused. That confusion will take quite a while to clear up, but an explicit error takes all of 5 seconds, so if the chance of accident (i.e. that the author did NOT know the parent has the getter name locked out like that) is very low, it's _STILL_ a bad idea to introduce it, as the penalty for a false positive is so much lower than the penalty for a false negative.
_End of migration_

title: @InheritConstructors to inherit constructors (especially useful for Exception classes)
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 302)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **pe.fips**   :clock8: Nov 24, 2011 at 06:56 UTC

I would rather suggest we finally add @ Data(callSuper=true), see issue #92.
So you would also get @ Required/@ All/@ NoArgsConstructor(callSuper=true).

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Nov 28, 2011 at 18:33 UTC

TLDR: Cool, will do eventually, but very complicated.

Good idea, but requiring resolution of any sort makes for extremely complicated features that require loads of point-patching in eclipse to fix strange bugs that pop up. We have 2 resolution-dependent features (@ Delegate and val) and we spent months getting those to work right.

So, eventually, we'll get around to it, but don't expect this feature any time soon.

Also, we need to do some resolving of our own to work it out when generics are involved, i.e. if you inherit constructors and you are 'class Foo extends Bar<String>', we need to replace all the occurences of 'T' or whatever type param is used in Bar, with 'String'. Then of course you can also write 'class Foo extends Bar', which will net you a generics warning, but what do we do then? We'd have to resolve the 'T' down to the bound and use that for lack of a better choice. A third option is to just say: Nuhuh, not going to work with generics, but I think usage of generics is common enough that that's not a good idea.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Mar 18, 2013 at 20:24 UTC

Issue #528 has been merged into this issue.

:bust_in_silhouette: **askoning**   :clock8: Apr 02, 2013 at 17:37 UTC

Issue #541 has been merged into this issue.
_End of migration_
+1 I hate the boilerplate of rewriting constructors. It would be a great, simple addition.

+1 
Exceptions are a great example of the case, where Builder is unable to do the job.
What's the current state on this?
+1. I use @Delegate all the time, it encourages a nice maintainable pattern for runtime wrapping. Similarly if @InheritConstructors was implemented it would encourage extension when appropriate.

A low hanging fruit might be an @ExceptionConstructors annotation that would add the five constructors that Exceptions usually have. I think that would cover 95% of peoples needs (also mine) and doesn't require any sophisticated introspection.

There's also a discussion on this topic (`@ExceptionConstructors`) in the lombok forums: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/project-lombok/x1DdJvG-PKc

My impression is that the lombok maintainers like the idea, but do not have it very high on their priority list. So if someone wants to take it, you should post in that thread and go for it.

Is there any way to address this, [@Data call super](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/29740078/how-to-call-super-constructor-in-lombok), I have a project which have a bunch of classes that inherit classes down the line, and it would be much helpful, if we can have this feature in lombok.

I had to delete a big batch of useless '+1' comments. Feature requests aren't a popularity contest, and github has a feature to add an emoji thumbs-up, my dear commenters. Please use those; not that it'll help solve the problem that this feature is extremely complicated.

> this feature is extremely complicated.

Could the idea be borrowed from `groovy.transform.InheritConstructors` annotation ?

+1
We have a lot of classes with multiple constructors which needs to inherited by child classes for better user experience. Ability to recreate all constructors from super class would be very useful not only from Exceptions.

+1
Would be very helpful esp. for exceptions.

In advance, if the class contains any final fields, those fields should be automatically added to the constructor arguments.

Furthermore, you could provide a `@Exception(inheritedFrom=<super>.class, inheritConstructors=true|false)` to get exceptions more comfortable.

Example:
``` java
@Exception(inheritedFrom=IOException.class)
public class MyCustomException {}
```

@Manfred73 What doesn't work? It works for me. Adding another constructor, calling `this()`, using other constructors, etc. Is this an IDE issue? Does maven compile work? Eclipse has to be updated manually https://projectlombok.org/setup/eclipse

@ Manfred73 Or, possibly, an older lombok in eclipse with a newer lombok on the classpath - `@StandardException` would be available, but the lombok installed in their eclipse has no idea what it is. Could you do me a favour and file a separate issue if this doesn't explain it? I don't think a bug in `@StandardException` issue is related to this issue.

I'm using Intellij idea with latest lombok plugin (bundled 212.5284.40) and lombok maven dependency 1.18.22.

The problem I have is that I can't access the default constructors that are generated by lombok in the ResourceNotFoundException class that is annotated with @StandardException when I add another constructor myself. If I remove the `public ResourceNotFoundException(@NotNull Long id)` constructor, it works fine.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13829887/139040919-a01e54dc-5835-4d19-b561-9383ad94743b.png)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13829887/139041371-7a57be5f-6b16-44f1-896a-909868fc9254.png)

Generated by lombok (cannot access the generated constructors):
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13829887/139051287-2aad8c93-47f4-418d-b0f1-00f0a19d9a8e.png)

@Manfred73 The intellij plugin probably does not support `@StandardException` yet. You can file a feature request (though there probably already is one, make sure to search first) over at [their issue tracker](https://github.com/mplushnikov/lombok-intellij-plugin/issues) - it's a separate project, with a different core maintainer.

@rzwitserloot yes, I guess it's probably the plugin in Intellij that's doesn't play well. I'll check the issue tracker. It seems it does recognize @StandardException as long as you don't add any custom constructors to your Exception.

I would also like to have a `@InheritConstructors` annotation. I see the value not just for exception classes. For example, if I need to extend `ArrayList` to add a single custom method, the code would be ugly having to redefine all the constructors to keep the features of the underlying class.

I veto this proposal. The OP's snippet is an anti-pattern. You should never swallow exceptions like that.

It _SEEMS_ like its a good idea to just ignore the exceptions that fall out of someInputStream.close(), but, there's no need to do that, because inputstreams do not actually throw any exceptions when you close them. That's just a major brainfart on the part of the API designers of java.io.

title: Enable field initializations to reference fields set by @RequiredArgsConstructor
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 314)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Dec 19, 2011 at 21:20 UTC

First of all, in java the initialization happens in declaration order. Without lombok, you would also have to write the constructor yourself. I would say that this scenario is not common enough. That said, you can already get the desired behavior by adding (lazy=true) to the second @ Getter :-) This does cost you some extra memory though.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jun 11, 2012 at 07:46 UTC

Actually, I could have used this twice in the last four classes. I strongly prefer direct field initialization and whenever I make a field dependent on a constructor argument (e.g. variable buffer size instead of fixed) I need to move code (it's just one line but without refactoring support in eclipse it's boring).

But there's one reason related to lombok. There's no way to inject any code (except for null-checks and one day also for copying) into a lombok-generated constructor. So in one case I had to replace the generated constructor by my own.

A possibility to move the initialization code into the constructor would have helped.  So would the lazy getter, but what I have is actually a private variable needing no getter at all (sure, I could use "@ Getter(value=AccessLevel.PRIVATE, lazy=true)" and encapsulate the field access, but this is too much boilerplate for me).

Maybe there should be a special annotation @ AfterConstructor (or maybe @ InConstructor) denoting that the java standard construction order gets modified. So the rule would be something like
- unannotated field initializers in declaration order
- constructor
- annotated field initializers in declaration order

The only thing needed would be to move the initializers into the constructor. Actually into all constructors, no matter if generated or not.
_End of migration_

Does there already exist a solution to this?

In my case a private non-final field needs to be initialized to the value of a final field initialized via @RequiredArgsConstructor. Since the field in question is not final, the solution with the lazy @Getter is not possible. Currently I only see the solution to write the constructor myself.

Disclaimer: Not a Lombok team member answering.

> Does there already exist a solution to this?

No. You might be able to refactor and replace the non-final variable by a method or have a special getter replacing the initial dummy value by the value of the final field. Sometimes, such tricks work well, sometimes they don't.

Implementing this in Lombok is pretty difficult and there's a lot of work with new Java versions now.
In that case I will use a workaround. Thank for the feedback though :)

:bust_in_silhouette: **JasonWest08**   :clock8: Oct 07, 2014 at 18:52 UTC

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 29, 2015 at 21:06 UTC

Team lombok recommends http://www.joda.org/joda-beans/ for property stuff, not the actual official JDK-shipped property stuff, which is an epic fiasco.

The most egregious horror of that API is the firePropertySupport aspect.

This fires a bunch of listeners as part of the set call, which is such an offense to the entire concept of the thread model that the mind boggles that any code written based on this will ever work quite right (freezing GUIs, infinite loops, race conditions, memory leaks, it's all likely with this insult of an API).

We don't intend to support it, ever.

We _WOULD_ like to add property support some day, probably by relying on joda.beans as the underlying library, with lombok generating the appropriate boilerplate.

if that support ever includes property change support, it'll take the form of a fairly complex ordeal using a separate executor pool to handle the actual firing of event handlers.

Essentially, Roel and I know enough about how one should do this to know that the java beans / PropertyChangeSupport implementation is about as far away from the right way as one could possibly get, but not quite enough to come up with a proper implementation ourselves, which is not helping the odds that we'll ever cook something up. The existence of joda beans has brought the odds of us ever doing something nice for properties way up though, so there's that. The fact that joda.beans lacks property change support speaks volumes, of course.

It's a shame so much traffic (and pull requests, our favourite!) has been dedicated to this issue, but it does show that there's a fair amount of demand. I suggest that future endeavours focus on integrating with joda.beans or look to it for inspiration.
_End of migration_

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 06, 2012 at 06:31 UTC

If eclipse is running on a 1.6 VM, we should be able to use lombok.patcher's hook-into-self trick to live-patch eclipse during the initialization of our plugin. That way, lombok can just be an eclipse plugin, no messing with eclipse.ini needed. Of course, on 1.5 VMs we either have to tell users to run the installer, or we run the installer from inside eclipse (and, presumably, we rewrite it to SWT. Well, next time somebody sticks something stupid in a final release, I've got a punishment all worked out :P)

This would also be a fine springboard for eclipse-specific features like 'show delomboked result' and perhaps even lombok-specific refactors/quickfixes (replace setters/getters with @ Getter, turn an entire class into a @ Data class, add sneakythrows, etc).

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 06, 2012 at 06:32 UTC

See also http://dev.eclipse.org/mhonarc/lists/eclipse.org-committers/msg00870.html

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 19, 2012 at 13:52 UTC

According to Peter Mucha, eclipse plugins can add/remove JVM arguments as part of their install/uninstall scripts, and eclipse will automatically force a reboot of eclipse if you do this. He's built a demo plugin and has managed to make this work, which means an eclipse plugin will take the place of the lombok installer.

This seems like a great idea - but should it take priority over other features or IntelliJ support?

Think that the fact of installing a plugin to get it working is yet a problem. Programmers are not always "advanced users" of IDE's. My possibilities to get accepted my recommendation of lombok to be used in my company (+/- 1000 programmers) depends on this kind of facility

:bust_in_silhouette: **ogierke@pivotal.io**   :clock8: Apr 01, 2015 at 11:42 UTC

Hi all, any interest to revive this one? The rather awkward installation procedure seems to be the ﹟1 reason why people refrain from using it. I just spoke to the maintainers of STS and they'd be eager to add a Lombok Eclipse Plugin to their welcome dashboard which would make the installation a one-click issue. We could even think about shipping it out of the box with the default installation.

Any chance we can get a Eclipse 4.5 compatible plugin/updatesite hosted somewhere?
_End of migration_

This would also make make it so that Lombok can automatically be added to an Eclipse Installation by Eclipse Installer (Oomph) configuration i think (and potentially synced to all Eclipse installations of a user).

Adding the vm arguments during plugin installation should be possible using p2 touchpoints in the p2.inf, see https://help.eclipse.org/neon/topic/org.eclipse.platform.doc.isv/guide/p2_actions_touchpoints.html?cp=2_0_20_1_3 and 
Seems someone got this to work already: https://github.com/adangel/custom-eclipse/blob/cb895947e620f3b502fd0c27a790071489b64f72/lombok/META-INF/p2.inf

In our organisation we automatically distribute Eclipse using Oomph.
The custom installer provided by Lombok does not quite fit into the workflow.
To solve this I created a p2 repository.
This enables us, and every other eclipse user out there, to install the Lombok Agent into eclipse using standard installer mechanisms.
I created a pull request here: #2371
Here is the p2 repository which was created with the sources of the pull request:
https://jordiboehmelopez.github.io/lombok-eclipse/
The PR is in (well, it's been rewritten a bit, but the functionality is in), but the docs still need an update. We'll use this issue to track progress on that.

Yes, the problem is that if you turn warnings into errors, you can't suppress them using @ SuppressWarnings. We have no solution for that. We strongly believe that you should treat warnings as if they are errors, but not by telling eclipse to do so. That also has other side-effects: For instance, the debugger will fail to do hot code replacement if you have an error, so debugging becomes much harder.

title: Update 'ant test' with separate java6 and java7 targets.
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 330)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 23, 2012 at 19:04 UTC

Running 'ant test' with a JVM1.7 hosting the ant doesn't work, because the javac we use (straight from our own dependencies) will then complain that it doesn't understand the java/lang/Object.class from the bootclasspath because its a version that's too new... thus all tests fail.

I believe the right answer is that we host the rt.jars of both 1.6 and 1.7 someplace, import them via ivy or otherwise, and use javac's -bootclasspath argument (and -source and -target) to then have 2 tests:

test 6:
- Host VM is either 1.6 or 1.7, shouldn't matter.
- our javac6 uses -source/-target/-bootclasspath pointing at 1.6.

test 7:
- Host VM is probably only 1.7 (assuming javac uses MethodHandle or other new goodies in 1.7 somewhere)
- our javac7 uses -s/-t/-b pointing at 1.7.

We could also do more tests (1.7 javac with 1.6) -s-t-b but I'm not sure that's useful. Maybe define these tests put skip them by default.

:bust_in_silhouette: **askoning**   :clock8: Jul 26, 2013 at 22:25 UTC

I think that this one can be closed, as the ant script since a while allows of setting the target environment.

title: @Getter(lazy=true) does not work with byte/short/float fields and values that are initialized with a constant.
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 345)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 14, 2012 at 00:14 UTC

This is the stupidest bug report ever, because this is only an issue with constants, and why the heck would you want to @ Getter(lazy=true) on a constant?

Anyway, this:

private byte test = 1;

is fine, but throw a @ Getter(lazy=true) in there and it'll fail to compile, complaining that AtomicReference<Byte>(int) does not exist. Indeed it doesn't; only AtomicReference<Byte>(Byte) exists, and there's no type coercion+boxing path that leads from int to Byte.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 14, 2012 at 00:15 UTC

Wont fix anytime this century because it's actually relatively difficult to do so and as stated in the report this will never happen in real life.

Note that we might revisit the way we generate lazy constructors, and there's a chance this bug will end up solving itself when we do.

title: @Getter and @Setter on a Date
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 347)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Feb 16, 2012 at 15:05 UTC

We know that this is a problem, but the problem is not just for Date; it is a problem with all mutable objects. We have no concrete plans to address this.
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Mar 19, 2012 at 20:17 UTC

:bust_in_silhouette: **alexej.kubarev**   :clock8: Oct 19, 2014 at 19:01 UTC

Would it be possible to add an annotation to make sure the clone is being used in setters & builder methods?

We could, for instance annotate fields that cause problems with findbugs with @ UseClone and then methods generated by @ Getter, @ Setter, @ Data and @ Builder would use a clone in generated implementations? Is this not a good way of doing it?

:bust_in_silhouette: **eli@eflee.us**   :clock8: Dec 14, 2014 at 23:36 UTC

Please implement something like @ clone

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 01, 2015 at 23:23 UTC

Commenting in a 'WontFix' doesn't do much. We can't just implement clone, it's very hard to do, and it's a really bad programming model, and we don't want to give you a tool that is almost always used badly.

You can tell findbugs to stop generating issues on lombok generated code now though. See:

issue #737
_End of migration_

Guys I understand your point with regarding to not being able to support ALL mutable fields,
but dates are a very common use-case, and not having support for date fields in many cases just makes Lombok not usable for creating class builders, and adds a burden of adding special getters and setters just for Date fields.

Please reconsider having a special treatment for dates, or for the very least allow registering a global clone-factory for certain types. e.g. 

@CloneFactory(class = java.util.Date, factory = MyDateCloner.class)

If you don't make a defensive copy of all mutable instance fields (like Date), then you don't have an immutable object!!! This also holds true for @Value which sells itself as an "easy way" to create immutable objects. So, users think they have immutability based on the documentation, but that may not be true. Very dangerous and misleading behavior for such a widely used API.

What do you see instead? Expect that the java file compiles properly and the bar variable is inferred to be an Integer. Instead, we get a stack trace with a NullPointerException: error: Lombok visitor handler class lombok.javac.handlers.HandleVal failed: java.lang.NullPointerException java.lang.NullPointerException at com.sun.tools.javac.comp.Check$Validator.visitTypeApply(Check.java:761) at com.sun.tools.javac.tree.JCTree$JCTypeApply.accept(JCTree.java:1697) at com.sun.tools.javac.comp.Check.validate(Check.java:732) ... :bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Apr 11, 2012 at 23:21 UTC

Hypothesis:

When we encounter a 'val', we need to do something calling 'attr'ing the entire block that contains the val statement. This basically assigns types to each expression in it. In order to 'attr', javac needs to have a table with names in them; otherwise it wouldn't know what "new MyOwnClass();" meant.

The problem is this: When annotation processors (and thus, lombok) are called by javac, javac has done the minimum necessary work to make the public API of annotation processors work. This involves creating the aforementioned symbol table (because you can ask for i.e. the method members of a type), but NOT the attr stuff (because that's for statements inside a method, and you can't get to statements with the public annotation API. Lombok actually can, but that's the hacky part of what lombok does). That's why we 'fake' attr by creating a copy of the method or initializer block and then calling attr on that.

The problem is that we made the assumption that javac _FULLY_ fills in the symbol table.

Now we get to the actual hypothesis:

Our hypothesis is that javac only fills in those symbols which it must to support the public annotations API. When you have a local class declaration (these come in 3 variants: An anonymous inner class on a field declaration, an anonymous inner class in a block, and a method local class), then there is NO WAY for a user of the public annotations api to get there, and thus javac decides NOT to create a symbol for the methods in such a class (and possibly not for the class itself either).

This means the method that we end up wanting to 'attr' does not have a symbol. No symbol means 'attr' cannot work.

In practice we could just start the 'attr' process from the deepest node that DOES have a symbol (which would be the field itself), but this doesn't work; maybe we can make that work but I somewhat doubt it. If we dig 'deeper', down to the compareTo method in the TestVal example, we've moved into territory that's invisible with the public annotation API, and therefore there are no symbols here, and therefore we can't attr here.

We don't know of an easy solution to this dilemma. Presumably it'll be one of the following two strategies:
- Create symbols, possibly first copy the tree and then create symbols for the copy (and then restore the symbol table somehow; these things are cached unfortunately). Then we attr the compareTo method as normal.
- Figure out how to make the 'attr this copy of the entire field declaration, anonymous inner class declaration and all' work 'better'. Right now it does not attr the generics on the field and the anonymous inner class declaration but it does need them later on, resulting in the NPE.

I have significantly more faith in option 2. Also, option 2 is effectively how it works now, but, when generics are on the anonymous inner class, this will fail. The fail condition should be easy to explain:

_ANY_ use of 'val' _ANYWHERE_ in _ANY_ local class, if the local class has generics, will fail with an NPE.

NB: It is trivial to generate an error on the usage of 'val' with some sort of message saying that, unfortunately, we can't support val inside type parameterized local classes.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Eric6iese**   :clock8: Jun 01, 2012 at 14:50 UTC

Hi,

I ran into this issue in my ant build on a regular basis. I love using comparators, functions, predicates and that stuff from time to time... Solving the issue is easy after the second time, but it was real pain in the first build, and it had lessened my trust in the val feature.

It's not that i restrain from using it now - far from it! However, i am concerned that other people who start to use val could get frustrated pretty fast by this, since there is no clue at all in the compiler output where the problem occured, and why.

I would make a suggestion for this one: Is there a way for lombok to find out that it is in a hidden inner class? If so, could it just emit an error and tell the user that val does not work here, much like in traditional for-loops?

That is a step back, but it might help until a real solution to this compiler dilemma is out. And this is really an edge case were I don't care if I can't use val for now.

When compiling an @ Data class that contains float fields under GWT, compilation fails with:

The method floatToIntBits(float) is undefined for the type Float

I suggest changing the data to Float.valueOf(var).hashCode(). It's slower but more portable.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Apr 23, 2012 at 18:33 UTC

I am reluctant to create Float objects, and Double objects for that matter, in the hashCode implementation. On Java 7 Hotspot, they might be optimized and removed, but I rather not depend on that. In general, allocation in hashCode leads to surprises. Futhermore, on Android this might be an unacceptable expensive operation. 

As far as we can tell there is an implementation if Float﹟floatToIntBits available in GWT: http://code.google.com/p/google-web-toolkit/source/browse/trunk/user/super/com/google/gwt/emul/java/lang/Float.java﹟102 

Are you using the latest version of GWT?

:bust_in_silhouette: **inetperson**   :clock8: Apr 23, 2012 at 20:01 UTC

That's in SVN trunk, not in GWT 2.4. I assume that code will be integrated in GWT 2.5, whenever it's released.

The "good" news is that I cannot find Float﹟floatToIntBits in the 2.4 source, so presumably this is going to be new in the 2.5 and then your troubles are over. title: Two thoughts on equals
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 366)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **k.tinnefeld**   :clock8: Apr 21, 2012 at 20:08 UTC

What version of the product are you using? On what operating system?

0.11.0 on Windows 7 64 Bit

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Apr 23, 2012 at 19:04 UTC

2nd point: We can't call canEqual without first casting; canEqual is not a method that java.lang.Object has. The way canEqual works, calling this.canEqual(o) doesn't do anything useful, the whole point of the call is to ask the other object.

As to point ﹟1: it is a good idea to only call the getter on the this object only once and store the result in a local variable. There is no need to also call the call to the other object since it will only be called once anyway, albeit on two different locations.

For the naming of the local variable: we can just use one simple name like "object" and use it for all the fields containing an object reference.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Apr 23, 2012 at 19:06 UTC

We should also call the getter in hashCode only once as well.

:bust_in_silhouette: **k.tinnefeld**   :clock8: Apr 24, 2012 at 20:13 UTC

Sure, forget about 2nd.

We should also call the getter once in LONG.equals. I chose "field" over "object" as field name, though.

The attachment does the javac changes, didn't look into the eclipse code too deep yet.
:bust_in_silhouette: **k.tinnefeld**   :clock8: Apr 24, 2012 at 20:13 UTC [:link: lombok-#366-javac.patch](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/3660004000/lombok-#366-javac.patch)

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Apr 25, 2012 at 08:57 UTC

Thanks for dedicating the time to create a patch. In the mean time we've been working on this issue as well. To prevent double work, next time please contact us through the issue if you plan to create a patch.

In our implementation we've modified the following:
- Always use a local variable if we read a value twice, even for fields (Android currently cannot optimize field access)
- Create the local variable just before its use instead of on top of the hashCode method (smaller stack-size)
- Better naming for the local variables ($fieldName in hashCode, this$fieldName and other$fieldName in equals)
- No longer need to cast to java.lang.Object in equals (since the local variable is alreadt of type Object)
- Updated all test cases to reflect the changes above.

If you plan to create a patch in the future, which is highly appreciated, please clone the github repository, and add your name to the AUTHORS file as well. That way we can also ensure we don't run into legal problems in the future. And we can give feedback before integrating it into Lombok.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Apr 25, 2012 at 08:58 UTC

We still need to work on the Eclipse implementation, so the source is not yet pushed to github.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Apr 29, 2012 at 21:59 UTC

Fixed in 25def866b50860715ee7c315c678b8c3d1ba9b56

title: RFE: lombok.Cleanup quietly
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 388)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **Sam.Halliday**   :clock8: Jun 29, 2012 at 17:34 UTC

It would be great if there were a "quiet" option to @ Cleanup which essentially did the same as Guava's Closeables﹟closeQuietly

http://docs.guava-libraries.googlecode.com/git-history/release/javadoc/com/google/common/io/Closeables.html﹟closeQuietly(java.io.Closeable)

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jul 02, 2012 at 19:31 UTC

If you read the documentation, you'll notice that the correct way to use this feature from guava is by using a boolean variable to detect if an exception has occurred in the try-block. We're planning to handle that case in issue #457.

Perhaps you are talking about a very common misunderstanding of the close() method: it is NOT okay to chuck any IOException that falls out of a call to a close() method. There are two scenarios:

A) You are writing data, i.e. to a Writer or OutputStream. These are allowed to cache writes, which means you can only be sure that data is written when you close it. Throwing any IOException away from calling close() on a writable resource is a severe code bug. You should NEVER ignore IOException in such a case.

B) You are reading data. Here it does indeed feel a bit wonky that you have to deal with IOException falling out of a close call. One could argue (and I'd be right there along with you!) that InputStream and Reader's close() method never should have thrown IOException in the first place. However, in practice, they just don't. If for whatever reason you find it annoying to have to deal with it, there's @ SneakyThrow(IOException.class). The close() is almost always coupled with the read() operation which also throws exceptions (which DO make sense), so just stick your close call in along with the reads and it'll all work out.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jul 02, 2012 at 21:18 UTC

Issue #380 has been merged into this issue.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Sam.Halliday**   :clock8: Jul 04, 2012 at 21:39 UTC

lombok-pg is looking at implementing this, which will be a good testbed [1]

My use case is exactly as r.spilker has described: to ignore IOException when reading but let the IOException remain when writing. (BTW, in NetBeans the current @ Cleanup works even if the method doesn't throw IOException - a bug in itself because the IOException will be thrown unchecked at runtime.)

[1] https://github.com/peichhorn/lombok-pg/issues/92

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **BigMichi1**   :clock8: Jul 06, 2012 at 08:29 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. annotate Class with @ Data(staticConstructor = "of") 2. no Cstatic Constructor generated named of() 3. verify with delombok on the anotated class What is the expected output? What do you see instead? Constructor should be created like mentioned in doc What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? 0.11.2 Please provide any additional information below.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jul 16, 2012 at 11:21 UTC

Could be related to issue #469

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 16, 2012 at 21:19 UTC

Not related to issue #469.

The problem is simple: When an explicit constructor annotation is present (i.e. @ NoArgsConstructor), @ Data just offloads all responsibilities to that parameter. Your code is buggy: You should use:

@ Data
@ NoArgsConstructor(staticName="of")

instead of:

@ Data(staticConstructor="of")
@ NoArgsConstructor

Note that your confusion is entirely justified, as lombok silently ignores you. We've added a feature to @ Data that it will warn you that your 'staticConstructor' is going to do absolutely nothing in this scenario.

This will be in 0.11.4, which will be released soon.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 16, 2012 at 22:21 UTC

https://projectlombok.org/download-edge.html

title: Reducing gap between Lombok-javac model and the original source code while in the NetBeans editor
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 393)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **lahoda**   :clock8: Jul 10, 2012 at 14:22 UTC

Filling this because of NetBeans bug:
http://netbeans.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=215078

The problem is that a lot of IDE features are misbehaving w.r.t content of methods marked with @ Synchronized (and similarly @ SneakyThrows and @ Cleanup (on local variables, of course)). The example in the bug talks about unused imports, which basically ignores content of the @ Synchronized methods, but the problem is not limited to this one feature or to that annotation.

The immediate cause is that when a synthetic tree node wraps existing tree nodes, the IDE considers all children of such "synthetic" tree node to be synthetic (holds for all standard javac trees, to the best of my knowledge). The high level problem for the @ Synchronized  is that the model (standard javac trees) is very different from the actual code in the source code.

I think that in general the javac trees and the source code should be as similar as possible, at least as long as the (NetBeans) Java language support is expected to handle the Lombok source code. Adding a synthetic tree into a list usually does not cause big problems (several problems related to this were workarounded in NetBeans and there were related changes in Lombok as well, IIRC), but wrapping trees that correspond to part of an actual source code with a synthetic tree does cause problems. The only solution I see in NetBeans would be for each feature to second-guess what the lombok-adjusted trees mean in the source code, which is defeating the purpose of reusing Java language support for Lombok sources, IMO.

I think that ideally the javac model when running inside the NetBeans editor should be made more similar to what is written in the source code, to make it easier to consume by the NetBeans Java language support.

I am attaching a patch that shows what I mean for:
-@ Synchronized: as this only changes semantics, nothing needs to be done when in the NB editor, and the model will match the source code exactly.
-@ Cleanup: similar to @ Synchronized, except that NB might produce warning about not closed resource, but that might be resolved in NB if needed
-@ SneakyThrows: this one was hard and the solution is quite hacky. The solution I sketched in the patch is to add a synthetic "throws $$undefined" clause, and prevent the error that is produced for the unresolvable identifier (the hack with the Log.recorded).

The patch does not contain any tests - I will see if I can find time to create some.

As a side note, looking at the extensions methods, I am not sure if that can be supported in the NetBeans IDE. But the current version seems to produce uncompilable trees for javac, so I cannot say much about that.
:bust_in_silhouette: **lahoda**   :clock8: Jul 10, 2012 at 14:22 UTC [:link: nb-215078.diff](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/3930000000/nb-215078.diff)

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 10, 2012 at 22:55 UTC

Looking at the diff, why go through the effort of making $$undefined and then hacking the error out of the reporter? Wouldn't it be easier to take each of the sneakythrown types and just throw them on the 'throws' typeline _JUST_ for the javac run that isn't background compilation but is an IDE?

Also, the $$undefined option would seem to me like it means NO exceptions, of ANY kind, will flag a compiler error. If I write @ SneakyThrows(IOException.class) and my method throws SQLException, then the line that throws this SQLException should be flagged with a 'catch or declare in throws clause' compiler error, and I don't think that will happen with this hack.

By adding each sneakily thrown item verbatim (as in, a direct clone of the AST Node used in the @ SneakyThrows annotation, with 'java.lang.Throwable' for the default option of including none in the annotation), there's no need to hack the error log.

I'm guessing calling code will erroneously error with 'you need to handle [sneakily thrown exception here]' in the IDE, which is why you have to resort to using $$undefined. In that case, maybe this is the 'best effort' solution.

Other than the @ SneakyThrows solution this looks great, so I committed the fixes for cleanup and synchronized:

https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/commit/6bf2b9299d2f1bcc00b8a0f253aae8fd4fcb6baa

as we'll be releasing an 0.11.4 very soon to solve a memory leak issue on eclipse this will be out soon.

:bust_in_silhouette: **lahoda**   :clock8: Jul 13, 2012 at 11:37 UTC

Thanks a lot for adding the support for @ Synchronized and @ Cleanup.

I forgot about @ SneakyThrows(exception). I was considering simply amending the throws clause with Throwable (or alike), but it has exactly the problem you mentioned. I was considering a few more options as well, but unfortunately the hack in the patch is the best I was able to think up.

Following up on comment ﹟7, Roel is absolutely right. The issue was the weakhashmap introduced in 37cbe2d3f9cd8737b46b6bfb263277f7b7cd7861.

I've attached a patch with a different solution for Issue #449, that avoids using a weakhashmap.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 22, 2012 at 05:22 UTC

Ah, yes, we added a weakhashmap to keep track of getX() methods we have generated to handle @ Getter(lazy=true). We should probably have paid a little more attention to this; it is notoriously easy to introduce leaks when you resort to such blunt tools.

In regards to the patch: This patch has two problems as far as I can tell: It is overly reliant on our implementation for @ Getter, which will at some point be improved somewhat. It also cannot tell the difference between Boolean and boolean (and Boolean does not 'count' for isX() treatment, so it is important to be able to tell the difference).

I've gone a different route: Instead of creating a weak hashmap linking the FieldDeclaration to a GetterMethod instance, I've turned it into a WeakHashSet. If a FieldDeclaration is in there, then it is a lowercase b boolean regardless of its actual type. (It's still a map because there's no such thing as a WeakHashSet, but the value is now always a dummy marker object).

As far as I know the only way WeakHashMap goes wrong is if the value holds a ref somehow to the key. GetterMethod contains a TypeReference, I'm guessing somewhere in its innards that holds a ref to the parent CompilationUnitDeclaration, and that in turn contains the FieldDeclaration.

It's been checked into master as https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/commit/34055fcdff786c9b809ce1a08c1c9218968ebc7d

I've pushed out an edge release at https://projectlombok.org/download-edge.html - so if anyone can give this a try and report back if this solves the problem, that'd be great. Thanks, and great work on doing the hard part, which is finding what's leaking.

title: Log: Respect the java conventions
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 400)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **sebastien.lepage.pro**   :clock8: Jul 14, 2012 at 09:26 UTC

I read that the log variable is "log" while it's a static final variable, using checkstyle,it generates some errors because the java conventions want this kind of variable write like "LOG" in upper case. Could you do that?

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jul 16, 2012 at 11:18 UTC

Actually, `log` IS following the naming conventions. The conventions[1] state 'The names of variables declared class constants and of ANSI constants should be all uppercase with words separated by underscores ("_").'

So, we agree that constants should be in uppercase. We also agree on the fact that constants should be static and final.

We disagree on the definition of what a constant is. In my opinion, a constant is immutable. And the loggers are not immutable by any definition. The simplest example is that the level of the logger can be changed during the run of the program, and this is observable from the program by calling for instance isDebugEnabled(). If the Logger was truly immutable, said method would always return the same value during one program run. But it isn't. Therefore the Logger is not immutable, so `log` is not a constant and should be written in lowercase. 

```
[1] See http://www.oracle.com/technetwork/java/javase/documentation/codeconventions-135099.html﹟367
```

title: @FieldDefaults takes away template autocomplete options.
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 411)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Sep 03, 2012 at 19:31 UTC

@ FieldDefaults(makeFinal=true)
public class Test {
    ma(fire auto-complete dialog here)
}

This is due to 'ma' being parsed as a CompletionOnFieldType node which is a subtype of FieldDeclaration, thus, its modifiers are changed to add final to it. However, the eclipse code that adds templates to the auto-complete list requires that no modifiers have been set, in order to let something like 'final ma(fire auto-complete dialog here)' NOT show the main option which in that case wouldn't be appropriate.

The fix is to not change any field object except actual FieldDeclarations.

Thanks to Marius Kruger for spotting this one. Forum thread: https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=﹟!topic/project-lombok/jUqMKjHpTxs

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Sep 03, 2012 at 19:36 UTC

Fixed, as per the submission's suggestion.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 30, 2012 at 00:09 UTC

Now officially released in lombok v0.11.6.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Oct 22, 2012 at 16:11 UTC

The linked issue suggests that the problem is caused by using a dollar sign in identifier names. I don't know if and how we should solve that.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Oct 22, 2012 at 16:12 UTC

IIRC, the dollar signs were introduced in @ EqualsAndHashcode recently.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Oct 29, 2012 at 22:22 UTC

We used to make 2 calls to .getX(), once to check if it was null, the second time to call either .equals or .hashCode, depending on what we are generating.

As an optimization move, we now call .getX() only once and store the result in a temporary variable.

This variable name includes a $ to avoid shadowing and such. Evidently, this $ is something the GWT compiler chokes on.

It is indeed related to bug https://code.google.com/p/google-web-toolkit/issues/detail?id=5475 - which is still in state 'new'.

We are not currently planning to make lombok's generated code be crappier just to work around a GWT bug. If GWT has a reasonable explanation for why their compiler randomly chokes on $ in variable names, feel free to re-open this issue (or if you can't, file another one, and we'll take care of it).

variables starting with $ are some gwt internal javascript variables as far as I understand.

title: Add capability to add marker annotations to constructor created by @RequiredArgsConstructor

:bust_in_silhouette: **oliver.gierke@me.com**   :clock8: Oct 31, 2012 at 19:33 UTC

> Your example would compile and work, but would only be useful to for so-called normal annotations or marker annotations.

That's what the ticket asks for explicitly :). I am not looking for an end-to-end annotation generation mechanism but a solution to the 80% use case to design components for dependency injection (@ Inject and @ Autowired being the most prominent examples). So I'd be perfectly fine with a solution with exactly this scope.

A different approach to a more general way might be to allow the Lombok annotations to be used as a meta-annotations such as:

@ Autowired
@ RequiredArgsConstructor
@ Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@ Retention(RUNTIME)
public @ interface WithAutowiredConstructor { … }

used like this:

@ WithAutowiredConstructor
class MyComponent {

}

This would also allow to capture repeated setups of other Lombok annotations to be captured in one place:

@ Getter
@ Setter(access = AccessLevel.PACKAGE)
@ ToString
public @ interface ValueObject { … }

used like:

@ ValueObject
class MyValueObject { … }

It's pretty much like a more configurable way of implementing @ Data and scenarios where you find yourself repeating a custom setup all over the place. If you think that's a reasonable idea I might extract it into a separate ticket. Besides that, simple support for marker annotations would be highly appreciated :).

title: @Slf4j and possibly other log annotations should use an uppercase variable.
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 425)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **derickf**   :clock8: Oct 30, 2012 at 18:13 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Use at @ Slf4j What is the expected output? What do you see instead? The variable to use is log rather than LOG or LOGGER. This is generally Java convention. What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? 0.11.4 Please provide any additional information below. This should apply to other loggers as well.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Oct 30, 2012 at 23:18 UTC

According to the guidelines, uppercase field names are meant for constants. Not all static final fields are constants though. Constants should be immutable. Loggers are not immutable. One of the reasons they are not is the fact that the current level can be changed during the lifetime and that that is observable from the program. That's the reason why we chose to make is a lowercase field.

Makes sense, thanks for the feedback.

title: the setter method got letter case error...
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 431)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **awanabe**   :clock8: Nov 24, 2012 at 09:07 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. define a bean with format "aBxxx", that means the first letter is lowercase, the second letter is uppercase. 2. use lombok setter annotation. 3. the auto set method will be setABxxx() 4. but the spring know the set method is setaBxxx(). so the bean can not be injected. What is the expected output? What do you see instead? What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? lombo 0.10.8 Please provide any additional information below.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Mar 11, 2013 at 19:55 UTC

According to the bean spec, spring is in error, so you should probably file this with them.

Actually, the bean spec says that, to maintain all-caps properties, the rule is:

If both the first and second letter of the camelcased (i.e. from setter/getter method name) property name are uppercase, then DO NOT lowercase the first letter to arrive at the property name.

If you take that to its logical conclusion with capitalizing, which the beanspec never actually talks about, and for which there is no method in Introspector, then in your example:

capitalize("aBoo") would seemingly have to become getABoo(), but then if you were to decapitalize this, then according to the very same beanspec, you end up with 'ABoo' as property name. That means the  beanspec's own rules aren't idempotent; taking any property name, capitalizing it, and decapitalizing it does not necessary result in the original string.

I'm guessing spring figured out this screwup in the spec and 'fixed it' by basically not changing the casing of anything if the second letter is a capital.

However, we are of the opinion that this alternate rule ("If the second letter is a capital, then, whether capitalizing or decapitalizing, don't change anything") is just crazy and not at all logical. It's also a spring invention (I can see why they did it, but, still, an invention).

Basically, the bean spec is broken in this regard and lombok and spring have chosen different tactics to solve the discrepancy.

We could try and be more compatible with spring, but then we'd be breaking backwards compatibility. Not to mention we're joining this train into crazytown.

If you can find anything from official oracle spec that shows this silly behaviour is in fact what you are supposed to do we'll re-open this issue. Also, if there are other major tools that work the same way and lombok is really the only exception, that too would be reason to re-open this issue.
_End of migration_

nodes.body:

The Getter and Setter annotations should have an optional String parameter, which when set alters the name of the generated method. This would be really useful for example on a project I am working on where the interfaces I have to implement are getXXX (boolean) hasXXX (boolean) etc etc etc.
I was surprised to see such a feature didn't already exist.

:bust_in_silhouette: **brinkmann.michael**   :clock8: Dec 04, 2012 at 08:31 UTC

But that's not a defect, it is a feature-request.
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Dec 04, 2012 at 08:58 UTC

:bust_in_silhouette: **the.md5encryption**   :clock8: Dec 04, 2012 at 23:03 UTC

Couldn't see the button. Why do you even use this over Github?

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Mar 11, 2013 at 21:12 UTC

@ the.md5encryption(Comment ﹟3): Because 'this' is much more awesome and does not require logging in. We manage the tagging, so that wasn't your problem.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Mar 11, 2013 at 21:19 UTC

The 'default' parameter position is already taken up by AccessLevel, i.e. it's @ Getter(AccessLevel.PROTECTED), so we can't change that to @ Getter("hasFoo"). We could do something like @ Getter(name="hasFoo") which is fair enough as a feature request I suppose, but this is actually an extremely complicated change:

A LOT of our code has to go out and look for existing getters/setters. For instance, @ EqualsAndHashCode (and thus @ Data, @ Value, etc) use getters if they exist. It would be very strange if @ EqualsAndHashCode can't find the getters generated by lombok itself, so we have to complicate that code by checking which name the getter was generated as.

So, technically, yeah, if we had infinite time, we'd implement this feature. But we don't.

A push request would be accepted, but we'd hold this one to an extremely high standard. It would need everything:
- Both a javac and an ecj implementation.
- Tests (ecj and javac!)
- Documentation updates
- Javadoc updates to the relevant annotations.
