title: Use a sane multiplier in @EqualsAndHashCode
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 625)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jan 09, 2014 at 16:09 UTC

For whatever crazy reason, Java uses in many places the "proven multiplier" 31 in the hashCode computation. This leads to more collisions than necessary, partly because of the unfortunate number, but mainly because of re-using this number in different places.

My attached example shows collisions due to using 31 in String, List, and lombok-generated hashCode. For the 256 generated objects, there are only 64 unique hashes. If lombok used a better multiplier, this number would increase to 144.

Here, nearly any odd number would do. Using 31 is one of the few bad choices.
:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jan 09, 2014 at 16:09 UTC [:link: LombokHashCodeDemo.java](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/6250000000/LombokHashCodeDemo.java)

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 09, 2014 at 20:27 UTC

Such a shame that THIS issue isn't itself a prime number, or I would have used that.  Should have waited until 631 ;P

There are some caveats to just changing the implementation on a dime, but, you made your case quite well and we gotta go through this pain at some point, right?

Crossing my fingers that this won't break stuff, I've committed to a randomly chosen shortish prime number (277 is the lucky winner). While I was there, I also updated the primes used to stuff booleans into hashCode (they, too, were directly copied from Effective Java, which is where the '31' comes from and probably explains why its use is so widespread). Instead of 1231 and 1237, now we use 2591 and 2609.

I don't think there's a need to spin out an edge release for this update, but, we'll release soon, so, coming to a maven repo near you soon :P

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jan 15, 2014 at 21:26 UTC

This fix is now part of the latest official release. 1.12.4 was just pushed for download and to maven central.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jan 15, 2014 at 23:23 UTC

Surprisingly, there's a tiny speed penalty for using such a "huge" multiplier as 227. This penalty is 1-2% in the case of integer pair (which is I guess the maximum as it minimizes the other computations). I'd bet that in any realistic scenario, this is more than offset by the reduction of hash collisions, but I'd suggest to change the multiplier again to avoid this penalty.

An amd86 CPU can encode an immediate operand in a single byte if it fits, otherwise it uses as many bytes as the instruction works with. Since the byte is signed, 227 doesn't fit in, so four bytes instead of one get used, which may make the instruction fetch to a bottleneck. I was curious if this can be actually measured in Java, and it looks like it can and the results are fairly consistent:
https://microbenchmarks.appspot.com/runs/9237a1d7-6836-441e-ab77-7f4ab218b8b7﹟r:scenario.benchmarkSpec.parameters.seed,scenario.benchmarkSpec.parameters.use227

I'd suggest to use the biggest prime fitting in a signed byte, i.e., 113.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jan 15, 2014 at 23:23 UTC [:link: LombokHashCodeBenchmark.java](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/6250003000/LombokHashCodeBenchmark.java)

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jan 19, 2014 at 20:53 UTC

We now chose, using pseudo random selection, 59 for the PRIME and 79 and 97 for boolean true and false. It is available in the edge release: https://projectlombok.org/download-edge.html
_End of migration_

title: @Getter/@Setter broken with 2014/01/09 Lombok edge release and javac
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 626)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **steven676**   :clock8: Jan 13, 2014 at 23:41 UTC

When trying to compile the following class file with javac (Oracle JDK 7u45, OpenJDK 6u27 as shipped by Debian, and OpenJDK 7u45) and the current (2014/01/09) edge release of Lombok:

import lombok.Getter;

public class Foo {
    @ Getter
    private int foo;
    @ Getter
    private int bar;
}

the compiler complains that Getter cannot be found:

src/Foo.java:4: error: cannot find symbol
    @ Getter
     ^
  symbol:   class Getter
  location: class Foo
src/Foo.java:4: error: cannot find symbol
    @ Getter
     ^
  symbol:   class Getter
  location: class Foo
1 error

Removing one of the @ Getter annotations allows the code to compile.

The same happens with @ Setter in place of @ Getter.  There's also some dependence on the order the annotations are specified:

```
@ Getter @ Setter
private int foo;
@ Getter
private int bar;
```

fails, while

```
@ Setter @ Getter
private int foo;
@ Getter
private int bar;
```

works.

All these examples work fine in 1.12.2 and in an older edge release (I _think_ built from commit 83b7e77 based on the date and the description, though I can't be sure).  I'd bisect, but for some reason the downloads in the build process don't work over my current cellular network link.

fix: https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/commit/ae4864ebc3974b17a512849e7018556c4a3d1935

Refactors run on the org.eclipse.dom variant of the AST, and not the one lombok primarily works with (the internal). The dom variant has a flag called 'ORIGINAL', set on almost every node (in the 'typeAndFlags' field). The refactor scripts won't consider non-ORIGINAL nodes as places to generate code for / into.

The relevant block when using @ SneakyThrows is the (generated) braces that go with the generated 'try' statement. This block IS in the org.eclipse.dom variant, but does NOT have the ORIGINAL flag set. That seems to be the problem (it's possible that further problems will ensue when we fix this).

This bug has now been reduced to: Why is that ORIGINAL flag not set? Should we use patches to force-set it, or is there something simpler we can do to set this flag? Should we even set this flag (in many ways, it is enticing to treat generated code as not original), in which case we should patch org.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.dom.RewriteEventStore﹟isNewNode(ASTNode node) to always return 'false' is ASTNode is generated. That is a dom-style ASTNode, which has a generated $isGenerated field).

It would be simpler just to return the value that is assigned to the local variable, directly. " it is like writing : Object obj = xxx; return obj; It's more logic (and need less RAM) to write : return xxx; This is with Lombok version 1.12.x, but i suppose it is the same with older version

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jan 31, 2014 at 14:09 UTC

I'm pretty sure that it is NOT true that more RAM is being used. Also, what is the code it is complaining about?

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Feb 02, 2014 at 00:26 UTC

Yes, when the interpreter calls the method, the stack needs 4 more bytes. When the method returns, you get them back. So your program needs _up to_ 4 more bytes (it can't be more as the method calls nothing, no recursion).

That said, the size of generated bytecode might matter a bit and so might the interpreted speed.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Feb 04, 2014 at 22:02 UTC

I don't know what to do with this issue. There are several parts:

1) We might be able to generate different code to please Findbugs in this scenario. We need to know what Findbugs is complaining about. The test code is not specific about that. Please tell us it it is the getter, setter, equals, hashcode, constructor or toString and don't make us do all that work as well. We don't have findbugs installed, so make please make it easy for us to find the root cause.

2) We probably won't be able to please all compilers, lint tools, Eclipse preferences etc. regarding code style and potential problems. If there is a real problem in our code, we'll fix it. But we do generate code that has to always work. In general it is better to somehow convince the tooling not to look at generated code, or make them lombok aware. For PMD, some initiatives have been taken, but nothing publicly available yet.

3) We might be able to generate @ Generated annotations in the class files to help tooling to skip generated code. Since that also makes bigger class files (I personally couldn't care less), I can imagine a command line parameter for the compiler and have a separate compilation for lint tool processing. We already have delombok formatter switches to generate different source files for different "target audiences". Lint tools might be one of them.

Any suggestions?

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Feb 04, 2014 at 22:06 UTC

4) Some code is not strictly generated. It would be hard to specify how tools should handle that code. @ Getter generates an entire method, but @ Cleanup moves the rest of the statements in the same block into the try-block of a generated try-statement and generates a finally block. It is not possibly to place an annotation on a try-statement. And the try-block is not generated.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 06, 2014 at 19:52 UTC

We have 2 bits of lombok policy that are pertinent to this issue:

1) We CANNOT address style / code checker complaints on generated code. There are a bazillion ways to configure these things, and there are mutually exclusive ways to configure these. Therefore, it is literally impossible for us to make code that everyone is happy with unless we start adding hundreds of nitty gritty configuration directives. The only right answer is to make such style checkers ignore generated code, and we'll do whatever we can to enable that. For now, that means @ SuppressWarnings. This may also mean adding @ Generated. See Issue #658 on further discussion on @ Generated.

2) We do not accept performance-related issues with generated code unless you can prove an actual, real-life performance issue based on for example a profiler report. 4 extra bytes in non-hotspotted code is completely irrelevant, and hotspot will twist your code into something completely different.

title: @Value + declared no-args constructor => generates nothing
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 638)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **gregoire.neuville**   :clock8: Feb 07, 2014 at 21:43 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Add @ Value to a class with at least one final field 2. Add a default (no arguments) constructor to the class 3. Observe (using javap) that no constructor with one or more parameters has been generated What is the expected output? What do you see instead? Expected is a constructor with as many parameters as the number of final fields in the class ; but as soon as a no-args constructor is explicitly declared, nothing as such is generated. What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? Lombok 1.12.4 on Linux amd64 (debian and archlinux) Please provide any additional information below.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 10, 2014 at 19:18 UTC

That is intentional. If you DONT want that constructor, how else would you do it (well, you'd recreate the entire constructor, with all those arguments, and make it private, presumably)? On the flipside, if you DO want the generated constructor, all you need to do is add @ AllArgsConstructor, which is no big deal.

I did notice the documentation does not reflect that this is the intent, so we'll update that.

Separately from the above design reason, there's also a pragmatic reason: We can't identify a constructor as being the same signature as the one we would have otherwise generated, because we can't introspect types like that in the phase where we have to generate these constructors. So, we'd have to hack it: Either just count arguments (but, varargs exist...), or try to match types based on literal equivalency (thus, if you use java.lang.String, written just like that, in your field, but just 'String' in your constructor, we wouldn't identify it right), or try to match against the import list, knowing that this won't work right if you have naming conflicts in the same package, because we can't look at your classpath in this phase.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 10, 2014 at 19:23 UTC

Documentation updated in the git repo; next version will also roll out these updates to projectlombok.org.

:bust_in_silhouette: **gregoire.neuville**   :clock8: Feb 10, 2014 at 20:14 UTC

Hi,

I'm not sure I understand your nicely offered explanation. How could a hand written no-args constructor be confused with a generated multi- (one or more) -args constructor ? Why can't you just ignore - at 'generation time' - a constructor bearing no arguments, since @ Value is intended to produce a constructor with at least one argument ?

Maybe the documentation you just added will answer those questions ?

Thanks again,

G.N

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Feb 10, 2014 at 20:31 UTC

I don't think the documentation will be much help.

We agree that it is easy to detect the no-args constructor.

Reinier tried to explain that it is very hard/impossible to check if a constructor is an exact match for the AllArgsConstructor. So we cannot just say: we will always generate the AllArgsConstructor, even if you have written constructors yourself, unless is is an exact match.

The reason for this is that we don't have type resolution available. We don't know if List is java.util.List or java.awt.List, let alone that ArrayList or Collection might be a valid substitute, depending on the direction. And then there is auto-boxing/unboxing and varargs making things more fun.

We could count the parameters, but then varargs are still a problem. 

We could count the parameters and count varargs as anything from 0 to infinity.

We could make an exception for the no-args constructor.

Or we say: whenever you write a constructor yourself, lombok won't generate the AllArgsConstructor for Value nor the RequiredArgsConstructor for Data unless you explicitly tell it to by adding @ AllArgsConstructor to your type.

We chose this, because it is consistent and easy to explain. It is also consistent with @ Getter, @ Setter etc.

I hope you understand.

:bust_in_silhouette: **gregoire.neuville**   :clock8: Feb 10, 2014 at 21:50 UTC

Ok, I get it. Thank you very much and sorry for the false alarm.

G.N

title: Add @Validator.
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 639)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 10, 2014 at 19:42 UTC

Any method with @ Validator is called right before returning from any generated constructor and any generated setter.

A warning is not emitted if lombok never generates a call to it; eclipse / your IDE will take care of it if it's private and you don't call it yourself, and it's rather ugly to try and hack support for that, as it'd be a cross-cutting concern.

@ Validator has no parameters. You can't suppress lombok's generation of a call to this method in all generated setters and all generated constructors (if you want to skip validation, it's no longer boilerplate).

Multiple methods can have @ Validator on it; they'll all be called in declaration order.

The @ Validator method may have a return type, but the returned value is ignored. The idea is to accept the object's state, or, to throw an exception. @ Validator methods must not have any arguments, and must not be static. otherwise, any combination of keywords is fine.

Any throws clauses on validator method(s) are copied to all generated code (whether they are  checked or not). Lexically identical exceptions are not copied (though note that java.io.IOException and IOException are not lexically identical even though they refer to the same type. Fortunately, declaring the same exception a bunch of times on the same method is actually legal java code).

:bust_in_silhouette: **smarencik**   :clock8: Nov 22, 2014 at 19:32 UTC

For constructor it has sence but I don't understand how about setters. If I need validation for setter then I write setter manually.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Nov 25, 2014 at 22:02 UTC

Simple; whenever you set 1 of the many fields of your object, they are ALL validated again. This is highly efficient: If you're messing with validation at all then clearly this is not your super-tight inner loop that actually cares about performance at the CPU cycle level, at any other level, validation is free, and this way you waste no code or time trying to specify which code validates what, and also gives you trivial access to cross-field validation (where the validity of one field depends on the contents of another, so setting either should retrigger that particular part of the validation. Easier to just trigger it all everytime).

:bust_in_silhouette: **marco.servetto**   :clock8: Nov 26, 2014 at 00:42 UTC

> whenever you set 1 of the many fields of your object, they are ALL validated again.
> Yes, I like your philosophy. I think this is the way to go
_End of migration_

title: @Builder and @Data(staticConstructor = "of") omits generation of static constructor
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 657)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Mar 26, 2014 at 19:05 UTC

Technical Analysis of problem:

This is a 'bug' in the spec. The way @ XArgsConstructor works, is that any @ XArgsConstructor takes precedence over any 'implicit' constructor generating annotation (such as @ Data, @ Value, or @ Builder), and @ Builder takes precedence over @ Data and @ Value.

The way this works is that @ Data, for example, invokes the Constructor-making code to do its thing, which will in turn check for the presence of a 'higher precedence' constructor-generating construct, and if present, just returns without doing anything, knowing that the higher precedence construct will take care of it.

The problem with this model is that staticConstructor = "of" will then be summarily ignored. You can see the same thing with this code:

@ Data(staticConstructor = "of")
@ RequiredArgsConstructor
public class Foo {
    private final String x;
}

That won't get you an 'of' method either.

Bug marked as valid, we're going to discuss how to address this issue.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Mar 26, 2014 at 19:13 UTC

Okay, we have decided to solve this problem this way:

While @ Data's constructor-generating aspect will remain implicit (meaning: Does nothing if a higher precedence constructor-generating construct is also present), the staticConstructor aspect of it will become explicit. Meaning: Regardless of any other higher-precedence construct, the 'of' static constructor will be generated, and will assume the constructor that @ Data would have generated if not pre-empted by a higher precedence construct, is present.

Thus:

@ Data(staticConstructor = "of")

will produce a private constructor of all required fields and a public static 'of' method that wraps around that constructor.

@ Data(staticConstructor = "of")
@ RequiredArgsConstructor

will produce a **public** constructor of all required fields and a public static 'of' method that wraps around that constructor.

@ Data(staticConstructor = "of")
@ RequiredArgsConstructor(staticConstructor = "of")

will produce a compile time error, as that produces 2 'of' methods with the same signature.

@ Data(staticConstructor = "of")
@ AllArgsConstructor

will produce a compile time error due to the generated 'of' method calling a non-existent constructor unless the @ AllArgsConstructor ends up producing a constructor that signature-matches what @ RequiredArgsConstructor would have generated (or an explicitly typed constructor that matches what @ RAC would have generated is written in this source file).

@ Data(staticConstructor = "of")
@ Builder

As Builder is a higher-precedence constructor-generating construct that creates @ AllArgsConstructor, the same applies as above: This will not work unless @ AAC produces the same constructor as @ RAC. You can explicitly add @ RAC if you want an 'of' method with that signature, or if you wanted an 'of' method for the constructor that @ Builder is going to make, you'd write:

@ Data
@ Builder
@ AllArgsConstructor(staticConstructor = "of")

We won't fix this right now, but we'll fix it soon.

:bust_in_silhouette: **joseph.gregory**   :clock8: Mar 28, 2014 at 14:43 UTC

How about support for both @ Data and @ Builder ? It's causing the same sort of problems: only the all-args constructor is generated (unless I explicitly add both @ NoArgsConstructor AND @ AllArgsConstructor)
_End of migration_
It looks like the same applies to `@Value`. I wonder if it's worth adding that to the description (instead of creating a new issue).

title: @Builder clobbers initial field values
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 668)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **jeacott1**   :clock8: Apr 16, 2014 at 01:29 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? imagine some class: @ Data @ Builder public class MyComponent{ private String someString; private int value=1; } ... MyComponent myComponent= MyComponent.builder().someString("fish").build(); What is the expected output? What do you see instead? expected: Assert.equal(myComponent.getValue(),1) actual: Assert.equal(myComponent.getValue(),0) What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? Lombok 1.12.6, win7 Please provide any additional information below. really nice feature, hope this glitch gets fixed.

:bust_in_silhouette: **cbeams**   :clock8: Apr 22, 2014 at 12:32 UTC

I just ran into this bug as well (independent of my possibly-related report at Issue #707). Took quite a while to pinpoint that this was the problem.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Apr 24, 2014 at 19:21 UTC

Given that Lombok creates a new object by invoking the AllArgsConstructor, I don't find it surprising at all. It's rather a problem of Java which executes all initializers prior to the constructor (which renders the non-static initializers useless 99% of time).

I can imagine three possible behaviors:
- the current one (ignored initializers)
- initializers always taking precedence (so the builder ignores initialized values)
- values explicitly set in builder taking precedence over initializers

I guess what's requested is the last variant. For this the builder should keep track of variables which have been set. This is simple (a single bit per variable would do), but the builder could not invoke any current Lombok-generated constructor as the constructor must decide to set a field or not. It also doesn't generalize to the general use of builder as "argument list builder".

There are two simpler alternatives:
- Magically copy the object initializers to the builder.
- Implement "toBuilder" requested in issue #635 and use `new MyComponent().toBuilder().someString("fish").build();`. This sounds rather error-prone.

Other slightly related issues: 610, 571.

:bust_in_silhouette: **jeacott1**   :clock8: Apr 24, 2014 at 23:31 UTC

I'm not sure how the internals are working, and maybe this is a really dumb suggestion, but if the problem is starting with the AllArgsConstructor, isn't it possible for Lombok to start with the noArgs constructor instead for this feature (or as suggested a toBuilder() option on whatever constructor the developer chooses), and move on from there?

For me, I'd prefer if this feature maintained normal Java rules, whereby non static initialisers are honoured. I think its likely to save many hours of headscratching.

:bust_in_silhouette: **shawn.tuatara**   :clock8: Jul 02, 2014 at 22:39 UTC

I ran into this same issue. I was under the assumption that the builder would initialize the object with a noArgs constructor and then call the setters for the specific fields that had been assigned while building.
_End of migration_

+1
`@Builder` should carry values from original fields to respective ones in builder class

> I ran into this same issue. I was under the assumption that the builder would initialize the object with a noArgs constructor and then call the setters for the specific fields that had been assigned while building.

A builder is typically used for immutable objects, so the `@AllArgsConstructor` is the way to go.

---

> `@Builder` should carry values from original fields to respective ones in builder class

This may not be always possible, e.g., for something like

```
int x = aProtectedMethodOfASuperclass();
```

I guess, such funny things are pretty rare.

---

As `@Builder(toBuilder = true)` has been implemented, my above workaround should work:

```
new MyComponent().toBuilder().someString("fish").build();
```

To make fool-proof, define

```
public Builder builder() {
    return new MyComponent().toBuilder();
}
```

in the containing class instead of letting Lombok generate it.

title: @Builder should require invoking methods associated with final fields
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 672)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Apr 29, 2014 at 20:44 UTC

I don't agree that final implies that you must set a value.

:bust_in_silhouette: **cbeams**   :clock8: Apr 30, 2014 at 06:11 UTC

The final keyword, when applied to a field in vanilla Java certainly implies (nay, enforces) that a value must be assigned, whether at declaration or construction time. That value may be null, but a value is in any case required.

I'm sure you know all this perfectly well, but I wonder: how do you rationalize changing the semantics of 'final' when a builder is involved? Currently, @ Builder sets any final field value to null on your behalf if you do not otherwise explicitly call its corresponding builder method. This creates a situation where as a user of the builder I'm left wondering: did I call all the right methods? And of course I don't know unless I look very closely at which fields are declared final; I'm simply left waiting for an NPE to inform me of my mistakes.

Currently Lombok's @ Builder support encourages incomplete construction of instances because it does not enforce final semantics as they are commonly understood. Hopefully a better approach can be developed, but in the meantime, I've moved away from @ Builder and back to static factory methods.

Thanks for your consideration.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: May 27, 2014 at 19:18 UTC

Not valid: Builder has 2 intentional design concepts:

(A) it is a builder for a static method call / constructor call and NOT a type (Putting @ Builder on a type is shorthand for @ AllArgsConstructor and having @ Builder on that constructor). The notion of a 'final field' versus a 'non-final field' does not exist at this level, so Builder cannot possibly cater to it. We don't really want to treat @ Builder on a type as any different vs. @ Builder on a constructor.

(B) To simplify matters, we have chosen not to make a difference between nullbits (null / 0 / '\0' / false / 0L / 0D / 0F) and 'never set'. So, .someBuilderMethod(null) is not detectable.

I guess what you want is that if someone calls .field2(null), that that's okay, but if they forget to explicitly call .field2() with something (even null), that .build() should throw an exception. Well, we have explicitly chosen for this to be impossible in order to simplify matters.

If you do want @ Builder to fail in your example, you should put @ NonNull on that field. That does mean that it'll still fail even if you add .field2(null) to the build() chain.

:bust_in_silhouette: **kevin.peter.wong**   :clock8: Feb 13, 2015 at 16:06 UTC

+1 on ﹟2 comment. 

The semantics of the implementation of Builder are not even consistent with that of other annotations in this library, e.g., @ Data. @ Data adds a parameter to the constructor for each final field. Why would @ Builder not also add a parameter to the builder() method for each final field? Defaulting unassigned final fields to null is not sensible; the consensus and direction of the community is away from null values (introduction of java.util.Optional in Java 8 as evidence). Why would the behavior default to an antipattern? 

For a class X, "new X()" and "X.builder().build()" serve the exact same purpose: construct an X. So, if @ Data responds to a final field with "new X(someFinalField)", similarly @ Builder should respond with "X.builder(someFinalField).build()". 

I love this library, but I can't use @ Builder as it is, since it would expose me to incompletely initialized instances. Consider a refactoring where a final field is added. Hopefully the WontFix status of this can be overturned, or a new feature can be added, e.g., @ SafeBuilder.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Feb 13, 2015 at 20:57 UTC

> Why would @ Builder not also add a parameter to the builder() method for each final field?

This would mean that a typical builder use would look like `X.builder(a, b, c, d, e, f).build()` as many objects have final fields only.

But as an optional feature, I guess I could love it.

Regarding ﹟4 (A):

> The notion of a 'final field' versus a 'non-final field' does not exist at this level, so Builder cannot possibly cater to it.

That's not actually true. Some arguments are required, others are not. A static method has no relation to fields, so it gets no requirements from them. There's no contradiction, it's just a special case.

Fields may be required, because of being `final` or `@ Nonnull`. The latter is well possible for methods, too, so you could let `@ Builder String static someMethod(@ Nonnull A a, B b)` produce a builder with one required argument.

Again, this could be a nice option.

Regarding ﹟4 (B): I guess that builder could simply forbid setting a `@ Nonnull` field to `null`. While the field gets initialized with `null`, setting it to `null` explicitly is most probably a mistake, and detecting this mistake early could be helpful. For this you don't have to additionally keep track of anything.

:bust_in_silhouette: **kevin.peter.wong**   :clock8: Feb 13, 2015 at 21:09 UTC

Regarding ﹟6 part 1, a builder isn't much use for a class with all final fields; in that case a constructor with params for the fields is enough. Builders add value when constructing objects with optional fields. So, I don't think this argument holds water.

:bust_in_silhouette: **chris@ethergit.com**   :clock8: Feb 14, 2015 at 16:40 UTC

> a builder isn't much use for a class with all final fields

This is true given the current implementation (and its disregard for final semantics), but it is the point of this issue to consider changing that situation.

> in that case a constructor with params for the fields is enough. Builders add value when constructing objects with optional fields.

I see the situation differently. It is sometimes the case that one is dealing with a value class that should be immutable and therefore should have all fields marked final. Sometimes these types have many fields and those fields are often of the same time (e.g. String, int, etc). This makes constructor-based instantiation problematic because the only way to distinguish the fields is by positioning.

The real problem here is that Java does not have named constructor parameters. That is what I actually want. I use Lombok's @ Builder as a way to achieve what named ctor params would give me if they existed, but doing so comes at the cost of abandoning the assignment guarantees that are normally enforced by marking a field final. So there's a really unfortunate catch-22 here.

Perhaps a variant of the ﹟build method could be provided--one that checks that final fields have indeed been assigned? This would perhaps be something similar to the @ SafeBuilder suggestion above, but would not necessitate the introduction of an altogether new annotation.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Feb 24, 2015 at 21:15 UTC

I don't think there's anything wrong with the current Builder. It's just that its flexibility allows many different use cases and some of them demand even more flexibility in order to really make sense.

> This is true given the current implementation (and its disregard for final semantics)

Actually, it's just a part of the final semantics. Using a constructor, you must assign all final fields explicitly, but that's a sort of Java internal detail.

It's a good practice to make all fields final whenever possible. But this doesn't make a field _logically_ required. You can write a static factory method providing some defaults. Also using a builder, some final fields can live happily with their default values. That's a feature, not a bug.

So an option like finalFieldsAreRequired=true makes sense.

> Perhaps a variant of the ﹟build method could be provided--one that checks that final fields have indeed been assigned?

This question in general is undecidable as a builder is an object which may be passed around at will, so all you can get is a runtime check (which would require keeping track of assigned fields).

I can also imagine a warning "Field b hasn't been assigned" in the common case `builder.a("a").c("c").build()`. It's rather hacky (too specialized), but for your use case (named constructor parameters replacement), it makes sense.

> Perhaps a variant of the ﹟build method could be provided--one that checks that final fields have indeed been assigned?

This would give you the flexibility but also a chance to forget to use the checking variant. IMHO too bad. I'd go for `@ Builder(finalFieldsAreRequired=true)` instead. Still, there could be something like `builder.a("a").c("c").buildIgnoringUnassignedFields()` if you want the flexibility.
_End of migration_

@Maaartinus If a PR were to be submitted for this, would it be considered?

I think it's reasonable to at least have a `finalFieldsAreRequired` parameter to the `@Builder` annotation (defaulting to `false` for backwards compatibility), which would:
- introduce a boolean field in the builder class for each final field of the target class called `<field>Set`
- set this boolean to true whenever a `<field>()` method in the builder is called for a final field of the target object
- check in the `build()` method that all these booleans have been set to `true` before actually creating the target object instance, or throwing an `IllegalArgumentException` if one or more fields have not been set (possibly indicating in the error message which fields these are)

I think this provides full backwards compatibility with how `@Builder` currently works, while introducing stronger checks for objects with final fields, aligning to the checks the Java does in the constructor of a class with final fields.

title: The video player on the website is broken
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 676)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **prof7bit**   :clock8: May 06, 2014 at 20:00 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. (K)Ubuntu 12.04 2. Firefox 29 3. Flash installed and working 4. All html5 video formats supported and working 5. Visit https://projectlombok.org/ ﹟ What is the expected output? I can watch the video after pressing play button ﹟ What do you see instead? There are at least 2 players on top of each other (in z-direction), one of the players starts playing immediately (I can hear the sound) but its hidden in the background while the topmost player which is the only one visible is paused. If I press the play button then the topmost player starts playing too and I hear the audio of 2 players playing at the same time. This is the main entry page of this project, the very first thing one gets to see when linked to this project and its completely broken. There are many examples on the web of how to properly embed a video in html, I suggest using one of these proven html snippets that are known to work on all platforms and in all corner cases instead of trying to reinvent the wheel, getting it wrong and producing such a horrible first impression on the _landing_ page of the project.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 07, 2014 at 08:06 UTC

Thank you for the feedback. 

Your comment about reinventing the wheel doesn't help getting this fixed. When we created the website, the wheels you're referring to didn't exist, and we were one of the first to feature a video on the main page that worked on all browsers including iPhone and Android.

So if you have a pull request using state of the art wheels, we're happy to pull it. You can also give us some pointers on what to use.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 07, 2014 at 23:24 UTC

The website is pretty simple. We use the video tag as supported by Chrome, Firefox and Safari with several source elements. For Internet Explorer we use some object elements. Those should be skipped in other browsers. 

We did find one closing object tag too many and removed it. 

Did that fix your problem? We couldn't reproduce it.

:bust_in_silhouette: **prof7bit**   :clock8: May 08, 2014 at 10:46 UTC

its the 

<object width="800" height="500" type="video/quicktime" data="videos/lombok.mp4">

which is beginning to autoplay immediately if in firefox the preference "media.gstreamer.enabled" is set to true which is the default in current versions of firefox and is required anyways to be able to handle the non-free (h264) formats for the <video> tag. It autostarts despite the "autoplay=false" which seems to be completely ignored.

If I remove this <object type="video/quicktime"> element then the page behaves normally.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 21, 2014 at 20:04 UTC

I've removed all quicktime references from the page. Also tried to make the <object> and </object> tags more symmetric. Since I cannot reproduce the problem, I hope it's fixed. It will be available online when we release the next version of lombok.
_End of migration_

title: Incorrectly generated equals() for @Nonnull field causes findbugs errors
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 681)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 26, 2014 at 09:08 UTC

Yes, they do make sense. The fact that the field is annotated doesn't mean it can never be null. There's always reflection and deserialization.

We're looking at a way to tell findbugs not to check generated code (issue #658) but that's not going to be trivial since findbugs operates on bytecode, IIRC.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 26, 2014 at 09:09 UTC

Plus the nullcheck is free on most platforms.

:bust_in_silhouette: **jaragreat**   :clock8: May 26, 2014 at 09:30 UTC

Agree with: The fact that the field is annotated doesn't mean it can never be null.
As programmer I am aware it can be null, but if I put this annotation what it means for lombok is: "expect this field not to be null and does not check this in equals". Check if this field is null (in equals) is same as throw NPE from equals while reflection and deserialization do the bad things. It is mostly matter of taste how to deal with null value in annotated field, is this official opinion of lombok team? Thank you and best regards.

:bust_in_silhouette: **jaragreat**   :clock8: May 26, 2014 at 09:42 UTC

Just one more note, if findbug mark it as issue ignore this and use @ javax.annotation.Generated annotation is not always the best practice. Generated code is not bug-free.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: May 26, 2014 at 10:09 UTC

We've talked about this in the past and the conclusion was that throwing a NPE in equals or hashcode is worse than always generating a null check.

But basically we agree that we should not take reflection or serialization too much into account.

On the other hand, the annotation doesn't force the programmer to do the null check before assigning a value. Even though findbugs might warn you, not everyone uses findbugs.

So even without using reflection and deserialization, the value might be assigned null in handwritten code.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 01, 2015 at 23:26 UTC

You can now tell lombok to tell findbugs to ignore all code it generates. See this issue:

issue #737

@ jaragreat: The solution to 'lombok might generate buggy code' is obviously not to bother end users with it, but to file a bug report with lombok. It would be ridiculous to fill up every findbugs+lombok-using programmer with a horde of irrelevant warnings.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Mar 24, 2015 at 20:58 UTC

Issue #821 has been merged into this issue.
_End of migration_

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jun 03, 2014 at 22:30 UTC

This is NOT fixed at all, we merely hid the problem. The issue is that we try to find, as a sibling file to your source file, the file 'lombok.config', and there are some fancy scenarios where this doesn't work. So far we know of at least these 3:
- In javac, with some as yet unknown scenario probably involving maven.
- In eclipse, with a 'virtual file' that is simply being tossed through the parser for some source arithmatic. For example when refactoring or save actions or scala plugin stuff.
- In eclipse/rational rose, with the 'jazz' sourcecontrol system, where files aren't officially hosted on disk at all, but instead at URL 'sourcecontrol://jazz/etc', which we don't know how to resolve.

The quick and dirty non-fix for all of these scenarios is to just not look for lombok.config at all but this is _NOT A SOLUTION_: The lombok config system is here to stay and we can't just randomly decide it's too hard to find it and stop there. However, that is exactly what the edge release currently does - hence, not a fix.

We're currently looking into how to detect these scenarios, and, optimally, figure out how to still find lombok.config. This is an extremely difficult task because for a lot of the above scenarios, we do not have a system to reproduce, and it takes a lot of effort to create it (example: Installing rational whatsit with jazz and all that, well, that's a lot of work, obviously). So, it'll be slow going and require a lot of feedback.

We're calling it a night for now. Progress on our research is on public branch:

https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/tree/configResolutionInEclipse

In the mean time we have the rather acute problem that 1.14.0 is causing tons of show-stopping problems, so most likely we'll push a release out the door soon that'll catch these issues and instead post a warning in the eclipse log imploring the user to get back to us.

title: @EqualsAndHashcode for implementation for parametrized fields must be able to detect if generic parameters are arrays and use deepEquals for them.
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 685)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **illya.kokshenev**   :clock8: Jun 01, 2014 at 01:18 UTC [:link: LombokTest.java](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/6850000000/LombokTest.java)

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 01, 2014 at 08:15 UTC

No, we will not implement this. The general idea that you need some deepEquals variant instead of an equals variant is true for any number of types. For arrays we can both (A) detect that we need an alternate equals and (B) we can call an already existing alternate equals implementation, but for many other types we can't do that.

We don't want to create a maybe-yes-maybe-no kind of situation here, so the rules are simplified considerably: The equals() we generate is shallow. Yes, it fails for arrays.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 01, 2014 at 08:33 UTC

Hmm, reviving this; we seem to use deepEquals on arrays when they are explicit and not 'hidden' by a generics parameter.

:bust_in_silhouette: **illya.kokshenev**   :clock8: Jun 01, 2014 at 16:09 UTC

Yes, that's what I'm talking about. Note, that it's not even about shallow vs deep - the Object.equals() currently used for generic fields which is only a reference level comparison. Array.equals() is shallow, and Array.deepEquals() is what one would normally expect to be used by default.

I know that arrays in Java have many complications, and using them all the time is not really a the best pattern. So, I guess, array usage for generics is quite rare.
Since putting Array.deepEquals() for all generics may slow down the whole thing, my proposal would be to add some annotation parameter such as 

@ EqualsAndHashCode(checkForArraysAndUseDeepEquals="genericField1,genericField2")

Then, anyone would be able to control its own implementation.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jun 02, 2014 at 02:13 UTC

I'm completely unsure about what's best. Indeed, it's not only about shallow vs deep, it's also about actual vs. declared type.

The `Item` from the example above is (except for the missing methods) just like a `singletonList`. But two lists both created as

Collections.singletonList(new int[]{0});

are not equal. So why should Lombok do it differently? Maybe it should, but probably not by default.

> @ EqualsAndHashCode(checkForArraysAndUseDeepEquals="genericField1,genericField2")

I guess, specifying fields should be better done by annotations. I wonder if there's someone out there, who wants neither `equals`, nor `Arrays.deepEquals`, but `Arrays.equals`?

:bust_in_silhouette: **illya.kokshenev**   :clock8: Jun 02, 2014 at 02:57 UTC

Well, I understand the nature of your doubt: apparently "deep" comparison pattern (A.equals(B) iff A.field1.equals(B.field1) && A.field2.equals(B.field2) ...) breaks for arrays because of their own .equals() implementation, and not because of the pattern itself. 

I have no idea why Java decided to treat arrays in the way so different to standard collections:  ArrayList<T>.equals() is perfectly deep, i.e calls T.equals(). Someone could say "just do not use arrays", but I'd prefer just to be able to decide which equals() method to use. 

Another point, trying to answer your doubt:

> So why should Lombok do it differently? 
> is: why should Lombok do it differently (for generics), if it already does it (calls Arrays.deepEquals()) for non-generic array types?

In my case, I had to implement a kind of a generic caching mechanism for domain objects that relied on Tuple<A,B> structure, implemented with just a copule lines with lombok. It worked fine until the moment I used Tuple<int[],...>, so it stopped caching and started to leak memory. I had to de-lombok it and provide changes to the code, but before that I had to debug by entire project to find out what happened: other non-generic classes implemented with lombok worked as expected...

So, I guess, default behavior must be the same everywhere. But to make it comfortable, I strongly suggest to include some adjustment mechanisms (class annotation, or field annotation, whatever) for controlling equals() method. And, of course, good documentation would save us all ;)

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jun 03, 2014 at 04:11 UTC

> is: why should Lombok do it differently (for generics), if it already does it (calls Arrays.deepEquals()) for non-generic array types?

It's not about generics, it's about what you're declared in the class itself. Maybe it should do no special handling for arrays at all - hardly any classes do. This is not a proposal (I personally don't care).

The problem you encountered with `Tuple<A,B>` is exactly the same problem you'd have with Guava's Cache or any HashMap. They just don't care. The array semantics is strange, but not useless. As arrays are mutable, someone might want to differentiate between different instances with the same content. Actually, using the identity relation is the only way to make it work if you change the content of the key array while it's in use.

> So, I guess, default behavior must be the same everywhere.

It is, based on the _declared_ type. You get an element-wise comparison IFF you declared the field as an array. Using the _actual_ type may be better or worse, but it's not per se more consistent.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jun 03, 2014 at 16:03 UTC

I guess there are more options that just the array handling. For example, I'd love an alternative computation for embedded enums, as their hashCode is non-deterministic and I'd like a reproducible behavior across JVM runs.

But too many options may kill the feature, so I'd like to see a possibility to specify a method which handles individual fields. Something like

boolean equal(Object a, Object b);
int hash(Object a);

But there are many obstacles:
- Java has no method literals.
- There's no interface in JDK you could use.
- Lombok can provide none as it'd be a runtime dependency.
- Anyway, you have no object, so the methods must be static.

This makes the universal solution

@ EqualsAndHashCode.DelegateTo(MyEquivalence.class)

with @ Target(ElementType.TYPE, Element.Field) a bit ugly: MyEquivalence must have the two above methods and they must be static.

:bust_in_silhouette: **r.spilker**   :clock8: Jun 03, 2014 at 20:43 UTC

We won't fix this. We've thought about it quite a bit and here's why we decided it is a bad idea to try and address this:

1) Lombok is a boilerplate buster. Not a framework for trying to address the considerable inherent complexity of hierarchical type hierarchies and a runtime where a couple of classes have known broken implementations of same.

2) Is should be generally known that generics and arrays don't mix. Therefore the case with a field of type T is no different from a field of type Object as far as we are concerned. 

3) We're not going to do this for fields with type Object:

3a) To implement it correctly, we'd have to throw literally tens to hundreds of lines into your equals method! We have to check if 'this.x' is (A) not null and then (B) .getClass().isArray() is true, then (C) 'other.x' is also not null and (D) is also .getClass().isArray() AND (E) .isComponentType() are either both the same primitive or both an object type, and if all that is true, we can generate Arrays.equals() with a bunch of casts (casts dependent on types). If that isn't true, we either return 'false' immediately, or, we have to revert to normal object.equals code. We have to do that for every field and we cannot rely on a static method that abstracts all this work away. We are quite literally looking at an equals method with pages upon pages of output from lombok if you have lots of Object or generic fields. The answer is just plain old no to this: We can't produce reams of incomprehensible stuff to cater to this corneriest of corner cases in everything we do. There's delombok to think about at the very least.

3b) We could resort to the hack of wrapping both 'this.x' and 'other.x' in an Object[] of size 1 and then calling .deepEquals on those (or even recycling that object array for every field comparison) but now we're creating extra objects and we now have to explain this code, because anybody looking over lombok's shoulder with delombok or just on the features page is going to look at that and immediately spit out their coffee. That's a concern that we're more than willing to handwave away, but not to address this tiny corner case.

3c) Arrays.(deep)Equals is expensive. For large arrays, by many orders of magnitude. While equals(), especially as lombok generates it, can not be relied upon to be fast, it can be a bit surprising that 2 huge arrays in a place where you didn't at first expect them results in really really slow code (and all the hoops we jump through to either check all that reflective stuff or abuse .deepEquals by wrapping in a container array won't help either). If your field types are explicitly arrays, it's more visual. Again this isn't a showstopper argument, but it doesn't help.

4) Big one: What we do is exactly what eclipse does. I don't know about other IDEs, though.

5) Where does it end? Arrays aren't the only special case. AtomicReference doesn't even try to do the tiniest effort here: It doesn't override equals/hashCode at all (identity equality only; they are .equals() if they are == equals). So, do we pick up the slack here and automatically unwrap the referent from AtomicReferences and go through the whole array shebang? What if you have an array of AtomicReference[]? What if it's AtomicReference[][][]? Or what about List<int[]>? The point of this exercise is: There's _ALWAYS_ a scenario you can think of where lombok's generated equals method isn't "perfect", so fixing this just means we move the line. It doesn't mean we get rid of it; that is an impossible task. The line, as we have drawn it now, is easy to explain, easy to generate code for, and matches what eclipse does. It's totally arbitrary, but we like where it's at right now.

 We'd then have to explain that we jump through that hoop and slow down their equals() calls (which can actually be performance sensitive sometimes due to being used in sets/maps)
_End of migration_

title: Random javac compilation error:  Cannot use 'val' here
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 694)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **rtiernay**   :clock8: Jun 13, 2014 at 18:14 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. git clone https://github.com/icgc-dcc/dcc.git 2. git checkout 5df0ba29beb8779fa75ae28c55aff40cbb5c2cb3 3. mvn clean package -am -pl dcc-etl/dcc-etl-indexer -DskipTests You may need to repeat 3. multiple times to observe the error What is the expected output? What do you see instead? I expect the build to complete successfully, but see the following output instead: ERROR] Failed to execute goal org.apache.maven.plugins:maven-compiler-plugin:3.1:compile (default-compile) on project dcc-etl-indexer: Compilation failure [ERROR] dcc/dcc-etl/dcc-etl-indexer/src/main/java/org/icgc/dcc/etl/indexer/document/core/DocumentProcessor.java:[121,9] Cannot use 'val' here because initializer expression does not have a representable type: Type cannot be resolved Please provide any additional information below. I have given access to my private github repo to one of the core developers (rzwitserloot) who has confirmed that this occurs randomly. Using Lombok 1.12.6 mvn -v Apache Maven 3.2.1 (ea8b2b07643dbb1b84b6d16e1f08391b666bc1e9; 2014-02-14T12:37:52-05:00) Maven home: /usr/local/Cellar/maven/3.2.1/libexec Java version: 1.7.0_55, vendor: Oracle Corporation Java home: /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/jdk1.7.0_55.jdk/Contents/Home/jre Default locale: en_US, platform encoding: UTF-8 OS name: "mac os x", version: "10.9.2", arch: "x86_64", family: "mac"

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jun 28, 2014 at 22:52 UTC

After _A LOT_ of searching and trying things, it looks like this is caused by the following:

1) The order in which source files are processed is semi-random, probably because a map with undefined order is in the process somewhere, and it sorts on memory position which is non-deterministic.

2) You use val x = new Foo() {} syntax someplace (as in, the RHS of a val-typed local variable declaration is or contains an anonymous inner class literal), _AND_ this is evaluated BEFORE Foo itself. In this case, all usage of 'val' in Foo will cause errors.

We're not 100% sure if that really is it, but so far it looks like it is. In the original sources, the relevant line is:

 dcc/dcc-etl/dcc-etl-indexer/src/main/java/org/icgc/dcc/etl/indexer/document/schema/ForwardSchemaGenerator.java:115 (method: createProcessor), which uses 'val' along with an anonymous inner class literal of DocumentProcessor on the right hand side. The actual errors which usually (but not always) occur, occur during val usage of DocumentProcessor.

So far, on successful runs, DocumentProcessor is done first and ForwardSchemaGenerator later, and on failing runs, it's the reverse. 'unvalling' the assignment on line 115 so far has resulted in 10 successful runs and no failures, so seems like bingo.

We're going to try and 'fix' this by eliminating the anonymous inner class aspect of any RHS expression and then attribing it, and if that does not work, we're probably going to declare any usage of AICLs in the RHS as invalid. Note that our preferred solution does mean that this:

val x = new Object() { public int someNewMethodThatDoesntOverrideAnything() { return 5; }}.someNewMethodThatDoesntOverrideAnything();

would NOT be equivalent to 'final int x = ...' even though it should be, but we'll assume that the above is pretty much never used by any java programmers ever. So, that particular bit being broken is fine in my book, I think.

:bust_in_silhouette: **rtiernay**   :clock8: Jul 07, 2014 at 14:00 UTC

Thanks again

title: Builder name conflict should be reported
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 695)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jun 14, 2014 at 02:24 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Create two methods returning the same type and annotate them both with @ Builder. What is the expected output? What do you see instead? An error should be reported as the same builder class is used for both methods. Instead of this, one of the methods gets called in builder().build() and the other gets silently ignored. Please provide any additional information below. This happens whenever two @ Builder annotations lead to the same class name for whatever reason (e.g., annotate both the class and a constructor, or two different constructors, or assign conflicting names explicitly). The problem may get undetected for a while, as the created Builder accumulates the fields for the arguments of both methods and produces the correct type for both. A similar problem exists for the method builder().
_End of migration_

Accepted. Should fix three things:

* If two or more builder methods are generated with the same name, error out (usually `builder()`).
* Same for `toBuilder`.
* If two or more builder classes with the same name would be generated, error out.

Whilst we should optimally fix this, it's a little bit complicated to 'see' the effect of the 'other' builder and I think the messup is fairly self evident. Let's just let it go and avoid the code complexity.

title: Consider allowing some annotations on Builder class
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 696)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jun 14, 2014 at 15:18 UTC

On the Builder class many (all?) Lombok annotations are forbidden. Sure, most of them don't make any sense, but some do.

Currently, @ Builder supports just the most straightforward way of building the argument list for a constructor (or a static method). Sometimes a bit more is need, e.g., inspection of the Builder fields (there were many similar requests in issue #89).

I could imagine also allowing @ Setter so that the builder can be also a valid bean (this leads to having both x(1) and setX(1), but who cares, when this is what the user explicitly requested?).

Allowing @ AllArgsConstructor could help those who'd like to convert an object into its builder (easier workaround for issue #635).

All the above needs nothing but removing the classes from HandlerUtil.INVALID_ON_BUILDERS and writing some tests (which I could do).

Possibly also @ ToString(includeFieldNames=false) may make sense, but this would require more work.

All this said, I'm specially interested in @ Getter.

:bust_in_silhouette: **jorn86**   :clock8: Aug 05, 2014 at 12:17 UTC

+1, this would help me with extending @ Builder-generated functionality

:bust_in_silhouette: **stefan.baur@namics.com**   :clock8: Apr 07, 2015 at 16:16 UTC

It would be nice if you could tell the builder the use the getters/setters instead of the fields directly. 
Also, it would be great to tell the Builder the target Class to generate the Builder for. 

Using this, you can generate a Builder for a Class that comes from a Framework.

Example: 
@ Builder(forClass = org.thymeleaf.Configuration.class, builderClassName = "ThConfigBuilder",builderMethodName = "thBuilder")
public class BuilderTest {
}
_End of migration_
Adding support for `@ToString(includeFieldNames=false)` to Builder would be great
@rzwitserloot, would you consider a PR that adds `onBuilderClass` to `@Builder`? I have a working concept, just need to polish a few things and add some documentation.

@mthmulders Yeah, that sounds like a good addition. I'm leaving this open for the `onBuilderClass` request.

Let's not allow `@Setter` and co. on Builder. Don't use em as beans. I can't foresee the impact having to support that idea in future updates is going to have.
@mthmulders Is `onBuilderClass` a good idea when we can add an empty `public static class Builder {}` and annotate it? It's more readable and doesn't depend on the `@__` hack.

@Maaartinus It saves you boiler plate code, and as far as I'm concerned, that's one of the main features of project Lombok. Explicitly writing the `XBuilder` class for the sole reason to put an annotation on it feels redundant to me.

@mthmulders Sure, but there may be other reasons why you need to write the class (making it package-protected or adding some other stuff). With this annotation parameter, you can save about ten characters, but when you later need to create the builder class, you actually wasted about ten characters. I'm not really opposed to the idea, it's just that it gives me a choice I don't like.

Maybe I don't understand your concern correctly, @Maaartinus, but if it's a choice you don't like then you're free to pick the other option? You could still write your `XBuilder` by hand and modify it the way you like?

@mthmulders I'd prefer not to be able to pick (unless the options bring a lot of value). I hate [TMTOWTDI][1], but it may be just me. Just don't let you stop by it.

[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/There's_more_than_one_way_to_do_it

Update: I'm not planning to work on the `onBuilderClass` annotation. It turns out that #1180 actually saves most of the Jackson-related boilerplate: manually defining and annotating it with `@JsonPOJOBuilder`.

title: onMethod=@__() breaks in JDK1.8.0_05
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 700)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Jul 01, 2014 at 19:56 UTC

Okay, this is a JDK bug, and not something we can ever fix with lombok, because lombok is never even initialized (unless we want to do something really drastic and cheese it by registering as a charset provider or some such).

We now need to try and explain to oracle that they ballsed this up. The general trick will be to write an entire small system to show how they've broken their own spec, and to push oracle towards solving it 'the right way' (as in, that we can continue to 'ab'use @ __):

Write an annotation processor which produces an annotation type, which takes as parameter another annotation type. Then have a source file that has @ AnnGeneratedByAP(@ ExistingAnnotation) somewhere in it, and which, if processed by the annotation processor, results in generating the type 'AnnGeneratedByAP' with as content 'ExistingAnnotation value();', thus making the whole thing legit.

This WILL work on 1.8.0-ea and 1.7.0, but will fail on 1.8.0_05, and yet no specs are being broken and no private API is being accessed.

There is in any case not a thing we can do other than report this bug. As such this issue will be broken on all lombok releases until sun fixes it, and then it'll be fixed for all lombok releases (or broken permanently). I'll keep this bug on file as a central point to coordinate sending this bug report to oracle giftwrapped. So far our experience with trying to talk to oracle more directly on these matters is somewhere between deplorable and downright rude, so it'll be a little while before we muster up the stamina to jump into this cesspool yet again.

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **fabrice.daugan**   :clock8: Jul 18, 2014 at 11:01 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Create a class with a single "String name" field 2. Add @ EqualsAndHashCode(of = "name") to this class In this case, the generated code contains useless variable assignment since it is immediatly returned after in the hasCode() function. Returning directly the hashcode value would be more efficient. Since this function is very often used (hibernate caches, Map,...), I see there a very simple way to improve the performances.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jul 21, 2014 at 17:00 UTC

> Since this function is very often used (hibernate caches, Map,...), I see there a very simple way to improve the performances.

In fact so simple, that the JIT sees it, too. Which means, it optimizes it away, which means, there's no reason for doing it manually (or in Lombok).

Maybe for something like Dalvik, which is not as good in optimizing, it might make sense, although I wonder if there can be any speedup demonstrated in a benchmark.

:bust_in_silhouette: **fabrice.daugan**   :clock8: Jul 22, 2014 at 11:27 UTC

I have to accept the JIT aguments since I've created a serious benchmark (attached Java class) to check hashCode computation times confirming your assumptions.
Bellow the results (null and not null average times, ms) : 
Lombok : 293-336
Manual : 291-338

Indeed, the computation times are close(<1%), at least on Windows Oracle SE 8.
It would be interresting to run this benchmark on other VM as you've suggested.

:bust_in_silhouette: **fabrice.daugan**   :clock8: Jul 22, 2014 at 11:29 UTC [:link: LombokSingleHashBench.java](https://projectlombok.org/googlecode-issue-attachments/7090005000/LombokSingleHashBench.java)

title: Constructor annotations ignore annotations on fields
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 710)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **jorn86**   :clock8: Jul 21, 2014 at 13:30 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Have a class with @ AllArgsConstructor or @ RequiredArgsConstructor 2. Have a final, uninitialized field in that class, so it will be included in the generated constructor 3. On the field, have an annotation that is allowed on both fields and parameters, for example @ MyJavaxInjectQualifier What is the expected output? What do you see instead? Expected: constructor with annotation on the parameter Actual: constructor with the parameter, but without annotation What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? Lombox 1.14.2, Eclipse Kepler, Windows 7 Please provide any additional information below. This should be obvious from the example, but when I'm generating a constructor for a Guice-created class, I'd like the qualifier annotation to be preserved in the constructor.
_End of migration_

+1 (I wish GitHub would have a vote feature)

Other valid use case: @Nullable

+1
I think this breaks null analysis in IDEs because the generated constructor/getters/setters do not have the nullable/notnull annotations from the fields.
This would also be useful for Jackson-compatible immutable DTOs that have all-final fields annotated with `@JsonProperty("fieldName")`, where the constructor parameters also need the annotation

@lc-nyovchev Lombok is mainly for POJOs, not for dependency targets

Besides, if you want thread safe code, write explicit constructor with final fields. The value of copying field level annotations will be useful(in the loose sense of the word) w.r.t POJO validation (plus what @Felk mentioned), not dependency targets

Instead of writing this ugly mess
```java
@RequiredArgsConstructor(onConstructor = @__({@Autowired}), copyInstanceVarAnnotations = true)
```
to get what we want for dependency targets, simple java constructor in spring world is both safe, explcit &  far superior option

In the next release, it is possible to configure what annotation types should be copied from the field to the parameters. It is already available in the [edge release](https://projectlombok.org/download-edge). Feedback is welcome.

Works great!  This is going to make guice + lombok very slick.

One issue I'm having is figuring out how to add an inner class annotation to lombok.config?  I've tried mypackage.MyClass$MyInnerAnnotation but no dice?

> @benjaminjbachman
> 
> > I've tried mypackage.MyClass$MyInnerAnnotation but no dice?
> 
> Haven't you tried `mypackage.MyClass.MyInnerAnnotation`? No idea, if it works, but that's what I'd try.

I did try that too; did not work.

> @rspilker can you give an example how to achieve that in the latest edge release?
> Assuming I have a class like this:
> @AllArgsConstructor
> class A{
> @qualifier
> 
> what is the configuration I should make to have @qualifier on the generated constructor's parameter.

Make a lombok.config file with 

`lombok.copyableAnnotations += mypackage.qualifier` where mypackage.qualifier is the full class name.
@benjaminjbachman Thanks it works.

> One issue I'm having is figuring out how to add an inner class annotation to lombok.config? I've tried mypackage.MyClass$MyInnerAnnotation but no dice?

@rspilker any thoughts on this issue?  is this a bug or am I doing the config wrong?

I suggest closing the ticket as it is possible now to achieve everything we ever wanted:

https://ath3nd.wordpress.com/2018/12/13/spring-lombok-or-injection-just-became-a-bit-easier-part-2-of-2/

Thanks a bunch for the great implementation @rspilker !

Wrote a small project to demonstrate it working:
https://github.com/lc-nyovchev/lombok-spring-qualifier

@zachofalltrades The problem now is that we end up in a combinatory explosion of options.

It's like a noodleshop ordering menu:

* Would you like us to remove the annotation from the field, or keep it there? Trivial example for removal: Your case, any annotation whose `@Target` list doesn't include `FIELD`. 3 choices: No, Yes - but only if lombok generates anything, and Aggressively Yes - lombok should delete this annotation even if lombok ends up not generating anything.
* Would you like us to copy the annotation to the setter parameter (likely cases: Any annotation whose targets include TYPE_USE or PARAMETER but not METHOD), or copy it to the setter method itself (likely cases: Any annotation whose targets include METHOD), or not copy it at all to setters? 3 choices.
* Would you like us to copy the annotation to the relevant argument to any generated constructors, or not? 2 choices.
* Would you like us to copy the annotation to generated getters, or not? 2 choices.
* Would you like us to copy the annotation to the generated wither's parameter, or to the generated wither itself (on the method), or to nothing. Let's assume that _if_ you want copying to occur in the first place, that you then want the same choice (between: Don't / to the param / to the method) as for the setter, so, 2 choices.
* 
No 'path' of choices is on its face idiotic, therefore nothing can be eliminated, thus we simply multiply: `3*3*2*2*2` is __72 different configurations__.

How in the blazes do we make that accessible to lombok users? The only feasible option appears to be to actually list out all these options, and thus end up with either in lombok.config:

```
lombok.copyableAnnotations = com.foo.MyAnnotation(mode = ON_PARAM, setters = true, withers = true, getters = true, constructorParams = false, deleteFromField = AGGRESSIVE)
```

Or something like:

```
@AnnotationCopyingBehaviour(target = com.foo.MyAnnotation.class, mode = CopyingMode.ON_PARAM, toSetters = true, toWithers = true, toGetters = true, toConstructorParams = false, deleteMode = DeleteMode.AGGRESSIVE)
```

Which is a ton of text, and thus rather awkward for a boilerplate busting tool, and in any case can you imagine the documentation for this feature? It'd be a joke.

Hence __we just cannot do this__, or at least, I'm making a decision here, and we won't. I get your current needs, but once you take the millions of lombok user's individual needs, toss em in a bag, and have a look and see how you can cater to all of them, hopefully you see why I have to ignore this.

Our solution is very different: We cater to the community. As in, we hardcode into lombok all commonly used annotations and register in lombok source code what the right behaviours are. And yes, that system may need some extension to really really support all 72 cases.

We keep the current `copyableAnnotations` system but its intent is effectively for TYPE_USE style things like `@NonNull` where the idea is that if you want it copied at all, it's always to the param, and to spam it (copy it everywhere relevant and keep it on the field as well).

This gives a lot of advantages:

* Lombok just works out of the box for everything we hardcoded.
* For the stuff we didn't hardcode, I'm pretty sure the top hit in that list of 72, by a large margin, is 'copy to setter param, getter method, wither param, and constructor param, and do not delete from field', and we do cater to this via `copyableAnnotations`.
* We do not need to document the combinatory explosion. Just explaining all this is on its own a herculean task, and would be quite a mismatch: We'd be tossing 5 pages worth of docs at something that the user probably thought was really simple. In my experience, the messenger is shot _all the time_ in such scenarios. Lombok will be blamed for making something simple needlessly complicated (erroneously; it's not simple, but many folks don't know that and don't want to accept it, because in their world, most of those 72 cases seem silly).
* We do not need to build half of a programming language in `lombok.config` to let you specify which of the combinatory explosion you want.

Hence, that's the plan.

It does mean we need to make it simpler to send Pull Requests. This is on its own also quite complicated, as we don't know every library out there. Given we don't have infinite time to go check 'your work', and I think maven central and other projects have thoroughly showed that just blanket accepting all contributions leads to a crap ecosystem, how do we 'judge' whether a PR correctly identified which of the 72 is right? How do we 'judge' a conflict where we get 2 issues that indicate conflicting answers?

To solve _that_, I think we instigate the following process:

* If you want the lombok hardcoded list to include your annotation, it _must_ be for a maven-hosted dependency, and open source (I'm not avidly anti-closed-source or anything, but there's simply no way for us to judge or test closed source stuff), __and the PR must be sent or endorsed by the project owners__.
* Hence, you'd have to ask the project owners to create or at least endorse your PR, otherwise we simply can't accept it.
* This absolves us of becoming arbiters. We can just tell anybody who feels the setting is wrong: Well, the project owners disagree with you, so get lost. Or rather, talk to the project owners and convince them to tell us that they messed up and a different setting is now required. We can then also aggressively redirect everybody to the project owners to go yell at them for breaking backwards compatibility (as any change in which of the 72 is, naturally, backwards incompatible). It also significantly increases the odds that the first take ends up being the right one.

I expect few takers on this, so I'm not rating the priority of making it easy to write those PRs as particularly highly. Hence, I'm just closing this. Maybe we'll get around to it someday. But a well written take (so, includes tests and documentation, and updates all relevant parts of lombok, both ecj and javac side, to use a single frameworky thing to navigate through that sea of 72 choices), if sent as a PR, would be accepted.

@rzwitserloot you have given a wonderful explanation of the complexity that would be involved in making `lombok.copyableAnnotations` fully configurable. 

Thank you. 

I am not so foolish as to think that it would have been easy to set up configurable behavior for `copyableAnnotations`, and I do not begrudge your decision to shield the community from something that could easily have led into a quagmire. 

The very last thing I said was that "It might be easier to satisfy this use case with a new and specific lombok annotation that could be applied to a field, and would designate annotation(s) to be moved to constructor arguments." I will try to do some homework on the subject and see if I can come up with a more specific proposal in a new feature request (or PR) -- or I will simply resign myself to being happy about the volume of boilerplate code that lombok has already saved me from writing over the years and find some other new ways to avoid work.

title: Delombok a single annotation
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 711)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **snekse**   :clock8: Jul 23, 2014 at 15:20 UTC

With the @ Delegate annotation being moved back to Experimental, it seems like it would be useful to have a flag option in Delombok to remove just the annotations that I specify.

e.g.
delombok -a Delegate,SneakyThrows

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Feb 08, 2015 at 21:02 UTC

I can see why you'd possibly want that, but we're not going to build this. We don't foresee any main-package feature ever moving into experimental. Delegate was a unique case (it was added before we came up with the 'experimental' concept).
_End of migration_

`val` migration is certainly useful, yes. But I think we need to do something else for that - if delombok makes modifications it might various parts of your file a little bit (not in a syntactically relevant way, of course).

For `val` specifically we could write something that leaves everything bit-for-bit intact, replacing _just_ `val`.

Or possibly even simpler, just replace `val` with `final var` and be done with it, which is probably the simplest thing to do here (and if you want to move away from `val` but stick with JDK8, maybe we just say you can't do that).

A 'dumb' `sed` script can do it, more or less, but it'd be nice if only specifically `lombok.val` usage is replaced and not any mention of `val` anywhere in a java file. That's not quite safe.

> There are other use cases as well such as retroactively banning @SneakyThrows from the organization

That sounds like a mistake. Nothing about why `@ST` has been introduced changed.

> possibly combined with an inplace argument to update the source rather than a target.

Boy, the scope creep, I can _smell_ it from here.

A `val` replacement script, that makes sense to me. The rest not so much.

Good to hear we agree at least on the `val` migration; would you want track that as a separate issue?

Or are you suggesting users apply that themselves with `sed`, without further changes to Lombok?

Well, the `sed` thing is hard to do correctly, in the sense that you don't want `String x = "Please select a different val"` to be turned into `String x = "Please select a different final var"`, but writing a sed script to do it correctly is tricky, especially considering that `int val = 5;` is legal java and definitely should not become `int final var = 5;`.

I think a separate issue is in order, specifically for a `java -jar lombok.jar valToVar` command (Possibly it makes more sense to make this a 'mode' of the delombok tool instead, we'll think about it).
Perfect; want me to create a new issue? Or are you planning to add some implementation details already yourself?
Go ahead :)
Perfect, thanks; details here: https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/3207
