title: Fix @Cleanup
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 799)_

nodes.body: _End of migration_

I don't know when this issue was written, or when the lombok docs were last updated, but ever since try-with-resources, Java has offered **suppressed exceptions**.

It's all explained here: http://www.oracle.com/technetwork/articles/java/trywithresources-401775.html#nb2

I think `@Cleanup` should work the same way as try-with-resources.

Thanks. People seem to forget about suppressed exceptions. Regarding the implementation, I'm fine with reflection, but you can't put `close` in the body because it will be skipped by `return`. The article I linked to shows Oracle's implementation.

The article contains an interesting point:

> It also advises not to [throw inside `close()`] any exception that should not be suppressed, with `java.lang.InterruptedException` being the best example. 

Might we improve over try-with-resources by not suppressing InterruptedExceptions?

Looks correct. I understand where you're coming from with keeping the behavior consistent. But that warning from _Oracle_ that you shouldn't use try-with-resources together with certain close methods which throw certain kinds of exceptions gave me pause.

Here's my take on it:

Ultimately, it doesn't _really_ matter which exception is suppressed. Both have been thrown. Both have been declared. Both might be handled by an upstream exception handler. And it's highly unlikely those upstream handlers are complex enough to have special behavior for when both are thrown at the same time. What I think should happen is that the **worse** exception should get priority. Ie, we should go up the call stack as much as possible. Therefore, I would not suppress `Error`s, as well as `InterruptedException` (since it's a rare exception that's usually associated these days with forceful cancellation of tasks and should be treated as a non-recoverable Error.)

Ideally, you could actually determine which exception is handled furthest up the stack. Perhaps some magic with proxies?

@einar-saukas  You forgot to throw `$t`.

@almson

> What I think should happen is that the **worse** exception should get priority

This is an interesting point, but very subjective. And it'd hardly ever get used. How often it happens that
- some exception gets thrown in the body
- some _different and more important_ exception gets thrown when closing
- there are _different_ handlers for the two exceptions

and the handlers do really different things and everything works fine only when your approach gets used?

>  you could actually determine which exception is handled furthest up the stack.

I'm afraid, it's not possible at all. Moreover, you'd have to consider exception wrapping, too.

I'm sure, it's not possible for Lombok. It works in a place, where it's hard to find out the fully qualified class name (search for "resolution") and this is a few orders of magnitudes harder.

> Ultimately, it doesn't really matter which exception is suppressed.

I disagree. By convention, the original exception (the "cause") should be kept, and the following exception (the "consequence") should be supressed.

According to the Oracle article you mentioned yourself: "Developers lose significant time debugging when a main exception is masked by a further exception being thrown while closing a resource."

> Both have been thrown. Both have been declared. Both might be handled by an upstream exception handler. And it's highly unlikely those upstream handlers are complex enough to have special behavior for when both are thrown at the same time. What I think should happen is that the worse exception should get priority. Ie, we should go up the call stack as much as possible. Therefore, I would not suppress Errors, as well as InterruptedException (since it's a rare exception that's usually associated these days with forceful cancellation of tasks and should be treated as a non-recoverable Error.)

You are suggesting to keep the "most important" exception, instead of keeping the causal exception. The problem is, exceptions don't have priority, thus the concept of "most important" exception is subjective. You propose that Error should be more important than InterruptedException, which should be more important than other exceptions. According to the same logic, one could except that RuntimeException should be also more important than other exceptions, which should be more important than other throwables. Also a RuntimeErrorException should be more important than a RuntimeException, and so on...

Again, there's also the problem that your proposal would make @Cleanup behaviour more complex, inconsistent, non-intuitive, and differ from try-with-resources.

> Ideally, you could actually determine which exception is handled furthest up the stack. Perhaps some magic with proxies?

Are you suggesting that the same routine using @Cleanup should throw errors in different ways depending on the rest of the program using it? It would become impractical to write proper test cases or even reuse libraries reliably.

> @einar-saukas You forgot to throw $t.

No, there's no need.

The first catch block already rethrows t, nobody else catches it again.

Your example goes directly against the article you mentioned yourself, namely:

> The specification for auto-closeable classes [...] also advises not to declare any exception that should not be suppressed, with java.lang.InterruptedException being the best example. 

Although special treatment could be convenient for certain situations as your example, it would make @Cleanup harder to use, and inconsistent with try-with-resources. Thus it's not worth it.

IMHO the only acceptable way to prioritize certain exceptions would be declaring them explicitly as an optional list, such as:

```
@Cleanup(precedence={ InterruptedException.class, RuntimeException.class })
InputStream in = new FileInputStream(args[0]);
```

In this example, if both main block and close block both throw exceptions, then close exception will be still suppressed by default, except if close throws InterruptedException but main block doesn't, or if close throws RuntimeException but main block doesn't throw either InterruptedException or RuntimeException.

I think the explicit prioritization is better than nothing. Note that because @Cleanup allows calling methods other than AutoCloseable.close, the called method might not obey the AutoCloseable.close contract which (as you point out) "forbids" InterruptedException. (Actually, the javadoc "strongly advises" not to throw it... does that count as being a contract?)

I propose calling the parameter "dontSuppress".

Ping!

Current "small print" documentation for @ Cleanup still contains the following remark:

"The authors of lombok do not currently know of a feasible way to implement this scheme, but if java updates allow it, or we find a way, we'll fix it.".

However a way was found over 2 years ago, but it hasn't been fixed yet. Was it forgotten?

I came here while looking for a discussion on a variant @Cleanup specific for AutoCloseable types. Above, it was remarked that try-with-resources makes @Cleanup obsolete. I disagree: @Cleanup brings a lot of legibility which is particularly useful when writing small unit tests. I think it would be great to have some kind of @AutoClose as an improved @Cleanup for Java 7 AutoCloseables.

Please align @Cleanup with try-with-resources! Actually, just emit try-with-resources. (Why would someone use this? Because try-with-resources requires annoying indentation.) Or, idk, delete it.

Java 1-7 have lost nearly all vendor support. New versions of Lombok shouldn't cater to them!

Even after Java 1.7, annotation @cleanup still has the advantage of working with any existing class, while try-with-resources only works with classes that implement AutoCloseable.

Although I don't recommend using it until it's fixed to behave exactly like try-with-resources as described above...
@einar-saukas What kind of class has close but isn't AutoCloseable? That's a bit of an abomination.

> @einar-saukas What kind of class has close but isn't AutoCloseable?

Older libraries.

Annotation @Cleanup works even for a method to close resources that's not called "close".

_EDIT_: See org.eclipse.swt.widgets.Widget.dispose()

title: @Getter custom method name
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 801)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **mibac138**   :clock8: Mar 21, 2015 at 13:35 UTC

I think it would be great if we could in @ Getter pass argument which will be methods name. For example: @ Getter(name="isTrue") or @ Getter(name="isRunning")

:bust_in_silhouette: **mibac138**   :clock8: Mar 21, 2015 at 13:36 UTC

For @ Setter it would be good too I think.
_End of migration_
Any progress on this?

Any progress on this? One motivation would be customization of getter/setter names for field names starting with underscore. In my case, I need setter named `setIF()` for field `protected String _if;`. I do not want to rename the field (it was generated from XSD and Dozer relies on the name for mapping). CXF/JAXB generates seter `setIF()`, also Dozer seems to be relying on such getter/setter name. Customization of getter/setter name in Lombok would be the most elegant and easy-to-read solution.
Yep, will be nice to have this imlemented

Regarding underscores: you can add them as field prefix in `lombok.config`:

```
lombok.accessors.prefix += _
```

The would remove them from the getter/setter names,

Nice try, however, it's getting even worse: "Not generating getter/setter for this field: It does not fit your @Accessors prefix list".
![2016-09-27 17_58_57-spring - jrfo_src_main_java_com_ibm_sk_jrfo_ws_nice_dto_zs_trvervxo java - sprin](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/3438246/18881582/2e89f7ca-84dc-11e6-88c1-7d2c5b678ded.png)

I too would like to be able to set custom names or characters to ignore. In my example, I would like getter/setter names to ignore the `_`  on variables.

I'd like `private String _username;` to generate `getUserName()`, not `get_userName()`
Would be a nice feature

@dslivka @blindgoat please take a look at `@Accessors` annotation. It has two targets: type and field. So you can use it for a specific field. Just add `@Accessors(prefix = {"_"})` to your `_id` / `_username` field.

#### Another possible use-case

Boolean properties don't always follow the same scheme — even within the same class. For example:

  - It is ok to have `isEnabled` and `setEnabled` methods for boolean property `enabled` of class `Control`; or `isVisible` and `setVisible` methods for boolean property `visible` of class `Control`.
  - But it is **not** ok to have `isAdministrator` and `setAdministrator` methods for property `isAdministrator` of class `Person`; or `isRoot` and `setRoot` for property `isRoot` of class `Node`.
    Method names `setAdministrator` and `setRoot` suggest that a parameter is reference to another object (e.g. `setAdministrator(Person administrator)`, `setRoot(Node root)`), not boolean.
    As for me, it is reasonable to retain full method names (`getIsXxx` and `setIsXxx`) even for boolean properties when `xxx` is not an adjective-or-participle, but is a noun (so that method name `setXxx` would wrongly suggest that it sets reference to another object, while it actually sets boolean flag).

And the problem is hardened by the fact that both schemes could be used within the same project and even within the same class (even the same class `Node` may have `boolean isRoot` (`getIsRoot`, `setIsRoot`), `Node root` (`getRoot`, `setRoot`) and `boolean enabled` (`isEnabled`, `setEnabled`)).

<sub>P.S.: Another possible solution for the problem described in this comment might be not to remove `is` from field names. I.e. if field name is `visible` → let it be `isVisible`/`setVisible` (unless `lombok.getter.noIsPrefix` is set to true, of course), if field name is `isAdministrator` → let it be `getIsAdministrator`/`setIsAdministrator` (not `isAdministrator`/`setAdministrator`; regardless to the `lombok.getter.noIsPrefix` setting). But, I suppose, it would be too incompatible change.</sub>

#### Resume

In fact, current getter/setter name generation scheme is non-ideal. And whatever we will change it to, it would be non-ideal either. Allowing custom getter/setter names would make lives of those-who-struggle-from-current-glitches (e.g. from #757) easier.
I feel this issue is appropriately addressed in lombok right now with `@Accessors`.

@rzwitserloot, surely not.

1. <s>`@Accessors` sets style **per-class**. But, as I described above, one class may use different schemes.</s> _Sorry, I was wrong in this point; never-the-less the two other points are true._

2. `@Accessors` can specify what prefixes to **remove**. But what is the most awaited (at least by me) is a possibility to **keep** prefix in certain cases.

3. `@Accessors` is limited (non-flexible).

Sometimes `is` is just wrong for booleans. E.g. `private boolean continueExecution` would become `isContinueExecution()` when in reality I'd want it to be `shouldContinueExecution()`. I can work around this by implementing the getter/setter myself, but I'd much rather do `@Getter(prefix = "should")` or similar on the field.

Please correct me if this is already possible on a per-field basis.

@JoshMcCullough It's not possible and there are IMHO only three sane choices for a getter name (all three are supported):
- If you have to follow the Javabeans crapification, use "is".
- If you want to have a machine-friendly system, use "get".
- If you want to have short names, use no prefix.

Using anything else adds some semantics to where it IMHO does not belong to. A variable called "continueExecution" should be always called just that (possible with a semantic-less prefix), not "shouldContinueExecution" nor "mustContinueExecution" nor "willContinueExecution". IMHO applying grammar or making it sound better is much less important than consistency - one day, you may need to make some tool understand your conventions. Sometimes it leads to misleading names, like "getReady", but then I'd just call my variable "isReady" and the name of the getter "getIsReady" can't mean anything but "get isReady". YMMV.

*That's just my personal opinion.* I'm not in charge of the project, but I guess it won't get implemented because of [these reasons](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/wiki/LOMBOK-CONCEPT:-What-does-it-take-to-become-a-lombok-feature%3F#overgrowth-of-annotation-parameters).
@Maaartinus Fair point, in this example `continueExecution` is fine as the field _and_ getter, with a reasonably named `setContinueExecution` to go with it.

@Maaartinus, you somehow miss very important thing: if you call you variable `isReady`, its getter and setter would be (in Lombok 1.18.8) `isReady` and `setReady`, not `getIsReady` and `setIsReady`. There is no straightforward way for you to create `getIsReady` and `setIsReady` methods. That's what all this thread is about.

@o-pikozh It's you who is missing thing:

https://projectlombok.org/features/GetterSetter
> `lombok.getter.noIsPrefix = [true | false] (default: false)`
If set to true, getters generated for boolean fields will use the get prefix instead of the defaultis prefix, and any generated code that calls getters, such as `@ToString`, will also use get instead of is

It's somewhat hidden... and probably not much used. IIRC it was me, who added this feature (but I'm not sure anymore) as I hate the default.

@Maaartinus, AFAIK, in that case it would be `getReady` and `setReady`, but not `getIsReady` and `setIsReady`.

(And I am not even talking about the fact that it's global setting, not field-wide and not even class-wide.)

> @o-pikozh It's you who is missing thing:
> 
> https://projectlombok.org/features/GetterSetter
> 
> > `lombok.getter.noIsPrefix = [true | false] (default: false)`
> > If set to true, getters generated for boolean fields will use the get prefix instead of the defaultis prefix, and any generated code that calls getters, such as `@ToString`, will also use get instead of is
> 
> It's somewhat hidden... and probably not much used. IIRC it was me, who added this feature (but I'm not sure anymore) as I hate the default.

@o-pikozh AFAIK, it must be `getIsReady` and `setIsReady`, at least that's how I always wanted it and how I (believe I) implemented it. Anything else would be a nonsense - either you want to stick with the crapification or you want some system.

I've just checked it and it works like I wrote. I had to check as I'm using
```
lombok.accessors.fluent=true
lombok.accessors.chain=true
```
which makes it irrelevant.

> And I am not even talking about the fact that it's global setting, not field-wide and not even class-wide.

Do you want talking it? I doubt it, as the only IMHO plausible reason for this setting is that you want a systematical naming. This makes per-field or per class settings useless as they'd spread even more chaos than the crapification.

@Maaartinus, you're right, it's `getIsReady` and `setIsReady` in `lombok.getter.noIsPrefix = true` mode. At least, documentation then is misleading, because it states _"will use the `get` prefix **instead** of the default `is` prefix"_ (and says nothing about fixing the prefix of setter).

The `lombok.getter.noIsPrefix` flag really makes lombok more usable, though it still looks somewhat counter-intuitive for me.

@o-pikozh Agreed that the name isn't very good (I originally proposed `consequentBoolean`, but this wasn't good either), but this train has departed long ago.

However, anyone can improve the documentation, just clone the repo, edit `website/templates/features/GetterSetter.html` and submit a PR. I guess, the `isReady` example would be useful, but I'm afraid that more than a single sentence won't be welcome (other features don't get long explanations either and it's pretty long already). Note that I'm just guessing; I'm not in charge of the project.

@Maaartinus, anyone can improve the code as well, the same as documentation (but that doesn't mean we can't discuss current state).

What bothers me the most in the current default behavior is not what exactly prefix is added, but the fact that **existing prefixes are removed**. I.e. I don't care too much whether `enabled` field creates `getEnabled/setEnabled` methods or `isEnabled/setEnabled` methods, but I expect `isEnabled` field to create `getIsEnabled/setIsEnabled` methods (or at least `isIsEnabled/setIsEnabled` methods) -- not `isEnabled`/`setEnabled`. I.e. I dislike the fact that, by default, `is` prefix is removed (then, of course, it's re-added in getter, but setter gets just `set`), and for years I was looking for a flag that will allow lombok not to remove `is`. And, of course, I seen `lombok.getter.noIsPrefix`, but from documentation it looked that it would just turn `isEnabled` into the `getEnabled` and nothing more (thus just changing a weird behavior into even more weird one), so I never tried it. What documentation, IMHO, should say about `lombok.getter.noIsPrefix` in the first order is that it **prevents removing `is` prefix from the field name** (so `isEnabled` field creates `xxxIsEnabled/yyyIsEnabled` methods, not `xxxEnabled/yyyEnabled`), and only in the second order that it changes the prefix adder to boolean field getters from `is` to `get`.

> anyone can improve the code as well

@o-pikozh Sure, but just changing the name won't be any improvement, even if the new name was perfect (because of compatibility). I proposed you (and everyone else) to improve the docs as a starting point. I fully agree about what you wrote about the brain-damaged prefix removal; that's one reason why I say "javabeans crapification". I also agree that "noIsPrefix" says nothing about the removal prevention. As changing the feature name improbably gets approved, I'd suggest you to PR the docs.

title: Lombok does not work on eclipse-mars (verifier errors)
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 802)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Mar 31, 2015 at 00:14 UTC

Try to edit any java file in eclipse mars with lombok installed, and eclipse will blow up with a verifier error.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Mar 31, 2015 at 00:19 UTC

The problem is that eclipse has (finally!) distributed their code compiled with -target 1.6; up to luna, eclipse's class files were compiled for -target 1.5.

The class verifier has different rules; in particular, 'stack frames' aren't required (or legal as far as I know) in 1.5 class files, but they are in 1.6.

We rewrite some of eclipse's classes using ASM, and we ask ASM to give us the luxury recalculate frames treatment. Unfortunately, this doesn't work, and cannot be made to work, because we don't know the class hierarchy of all of eclipse's classes beforehand.

The solution is to manually manage the frames. There is only one patch script that appears (we just looked at code for now, haven't tested this theory yet) to require frame calculation, and we can avoid it by generating a new method. We also have some other ideas to obviate the need for it.

Once we've solved that problem we can run ASM in 'do not automagically calculate frames anymore' mode, and then this problem should go away.

NB: MAXS is another automagic luxury feature and we'll still need that. However, from what we understand of the class verifier and how ASM works, this will not be a problem.

NB2: This is a theory, as yet untested if this is the actual cause of the problem.

:bust_in_silhouette: **reinierz**   :clock8: Apr 05, 2015 at 02:22 UTC

Current master should have this problem all fixed, including a change in how save actions are handled which broke format-on-save, a bug we previously fixed.

We'll get a fix out the door soonish; mars is nearing stable and I'm kinda itching to start using it myself because it looks like they did some major work on the stability of auto-complete and the like in lambdas.

Thanks!

title: Add @Logger(factory=MyLoggerFactory.class)
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 808)_

nodes.body: _End of migration_

I'm actually surprised nobody else upvoted this feature. It would be quite useful when you write a wrapper around SLF4J or any other logger, to have business-oriented log methods (e.g. you create a logger method `sensitiveOperation(BusinessContext context, User user, OperationEnum operation)`, or to use `Supplier<String>` for SLF4J.
The statement "when you write a wrapper around SLF4J" doesn't really make sense since it is a facade. It is already a very extendable system.

@rspilker It does. While SLF4J is a facade, it's purpose is to interact with logback and other loggers. IMHO placing another facade over it makes sense. Especially, `logger.sensitiveOperation(BusinessContext context, User user, OperationEnum operation)` won't ever compile for `logger.getClass() == org.slf4j.Logger.class`. That said, I know I don't know much about SLF4J yet, but I'm thinking about a facade, too.

I exactly need the same feature as e.g. SLF4J does not support Java 8 specific features like the Supplier functional interface that makes lazy log evaluation much easier, e.g.

```
Logger.error(java.util.function.Supplier<String>)
```

Hi @rzwitserloot I'm not sure I understand why you closed this issue?

The only reason why it would be useful to configure it in the Java annotation is so users create their own annotations (e.g. `@MyAmazingLogger`) which would configure the generic `@CustomLogger` a certain way, and that way each application may create several overrides of `@CustomLogger` (maybe one for perf, one for business, one for tech, etc).
And for each the field name could be different.

sorry to comment on a closed issue, but I have the same requirements like:
```
@Slf4j(loggerClass= MyLogger.class)
public class MyClass
```
or the param is a loggerFactory

Becasue sometimes we really can not use the default one.

We have the same kind of requirement. We have a wrapped logger from ESAPI for Log4J. It would be nice to be able to use an annotation like ``` @ESAPILog4J```. However that is a lot less flexible than being able to use ```@CustomLogger(loggerClass=ESAPILogger.class)``` or ```@CustomLogger(factory=ESAPILogger.class)``` which is like the original request.

1) Presumably, you have a lot of calls to create a specific logger. So you don't want to do a lot of configuration in each annotation, otherwise you would be better of just creating the logger yourself. So you want some configuration, probably in `lombok.config`.

2) This configuration should specify the fully qualified name of the type of the field, The fully qualified name of the logger factory, The name of the factory method. And possibly if the factory method needs a String parameter or a class parameter. But if the other ones are configurable, you could create a static method anywhere to do any conversion.

@rspilker Yes, I agree it could be handled someplace like ```lombok.config```. I am just looking for a means of providing a custom logger regardless of the more intimate details. If we are in agreement on the idea for a custom logger, the details of configuration should match the existing mechanisms as much as possible, or use a mechanism in place for that specific logger. The ESAPI configuration handles the configuration of the logger in this case.

If someone wants to pick this up, we would accept pull requests. Before starting on this, please contact me and/or Reinier on how to approach this.

Typically we start with a design, using before and after code. We can move those designs to the tests directory afterwards.

It does not need to be in lombok.extern, since there should not be any external libraries involved.

Currently, I think `@lombok.CustomLog` would be a good name.

Regarding parameters for the factory, I think an enum can be used:
- String
- Type
- None
I need this feature, too.

Hi all.

I also need this feature.
Basically I came to it when our application became clusterized. It has several instances deployed in the same tomcat and we would like to distinguish which line is written by which instance.

Let's assume we have class MyClass that writes some data into log on line 70. Usually we would see something like
```
[INFO] MyClass:70 - data
[INFO] MyClass:70 - data
[INFO] MyClass:70 - data
[INFO] MyClass:70 - data
```
From this log it is not possible to understand which node created which line. I have an id of every node in the cluster and what I want is to write some prefix with this id like
```
[INFO] [node:1] MyClass:70 - data
[INFO] [node:2] MyClass:70 - data
[INFO] [node:1] MyClass:70 - data
[INFO] [node:2] MyClass:70 - data
```
I can achieve it easily by custom slf4j logger wrapper like this:
```
public class NodeAwareLoggerWrapper implements Logger {

    private final int nodeId;
    private final Logger wrappedLogger;

    public NodeAwareLoggerWrapper(int nodeId, Logger wrappedLogger) {...}
}
```
but it requires manual logger creation because it is not possible with lombok annotation.
It would be really nice to have a custom logger extension in lombok.
@Diarsid have you considered https://logback.qos.ch/manual/mdc.html ?

What do you see instead? there should be a method isFoo as there is when the field has type boolean instead there will be a getFoo method with return type Boolean What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? 1.16.2 on OS X 10.10.3 Please provide any additional information below. Boolean and boolean should be treated the same for the getter method.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: May 15, 2015 at 12:35 UTC

> Boolean and boolean should be treated the same for the getter method.

This makes sense, but unfortunately the Java bean spec does not.
See issue #382, comment 3

:bust_in_silhouette: **alex.weirig@technolink.lu**   :clock8: May 19, 2015 at 07:06 UTC

How about leaving the default behaviour compliant with the bean spec but offering an option to treat Boolean as boolean. This would be a win-win situation as I guess that most developers will use "is getters" even for Boolean fields.

There is already an option to no generate the is methods
lombok.getter.noIsPrefix = [true | false](default: false)
If set to true, getters generated for boolean fields will use the get prefix instead of the defaultis prefix, and any generated code that calls getters, such as @ ToString, will also use get instead of is

eg
lombok.getter.isForBoolean = [true|false](default: false)

Alex

I just ran into this issue.

Running from IntelliJ using the "Run" command on the Spring Boot Application results in the bytecode not being manipulated. When using lombok with my project the @ NonNull annotation I had created was being subsumed by the annotation processing in lombok instead of being handled by my own code. This is because lombok uses a regex of the simple class name instead of the class and package together. title: The generated equals and hashCode methods disagree
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 821)_

nodes.body: :bust_in_silhouette: **copolii**   :clock8: Jun 04, 2015 at 23:17 UTC What steps will reproduce the problem? 1. Consider the 'StringWrapper' class below 2. Instantiate two instances of StringWrapper: new StringWrapper ("") and new StringWrapper () or new StringWrapper (null) 3. As expected, the equals method correctly determines that the instance with an empty string does not equal the one(s) with null 4. The hashCode method, however does not agree with the above and will generate '59' for all 3 mentioned instances What is the expected output? new StringWrapper ("").hashCode() != new StringWrapper ().hashCode() new StringWrapper ("").hashCode() != new StringWrapper (null).hashCode() What do you see instead? new StringWrapper ("").hashCode() == new StringWrapper ().hashCode() new StringWrapper ("").hashCode() == new StringWrapper (null).hashCode() What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? Lombok-1.16.2 on Windows JDK 1.8_u45 According to https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/api/java/lang/Object.html﹟hashCode(): - If two objects are equal according to the equals(Object) method, then calling the hashCode method on each of the two objects must produce the same integer result. - It is not required that if two objects are unequal according to the equals(java.lang.Object) method, then calling the hashCode method on each of the two objects must produce distinct integer results. However, the programmer should be aware that producing distinct integer results for unequal objects may improve the performance of hash tables. @ AllArgsConstructor @ NoArgsConstructor @ EqualsAndHashCode @ ToString public class StringWrapper { @ Getter String string; }

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jun 06, 2015 at 10:14 UTC

It's not a bug, though it might be worth changing. See an analogous discussion at
https://github.com/google/guava/issues/2037

Note also that such things are pretty common, e.g., the hashcodes of all these three strings equal 3587: "ps", "qT", "r5". And there are 560 such 3-way collisions among alphanumeric strings of length 2.

PS: You're wrong concerning `new StringWrapper()` and `new StringWrapper(null)` as they ARE equal (not "==", just "equals").

:bust_in_silhouette: **copolii**   :clock8: Jun 06, 2015 at 17:48 UTC

I should have been more clear:
1- Yes, it's not a requirement, but more of a recommendation (for improved hash table performance)
2- In ﹟2 above, I have an OR between 'new StringWrapper ()' and 'new StringWrapper(null)' meaning either one. I didn't mean the two shouldn't be equal. I meant 'new StringWrapper("")' should not be equal to either of the two (which are equal to each other).
_End of migration_

This isn't a bug; it's perfectly fine for 2 non-equal objects to generate an equal hashCode (it's also trivial to prove it must be this way; it is possible to have more than 2^32 distinct different objects of the same type, and yet there are only 2^32 hashCodes, thus...)

Sure, it'd be better if you had fewer collisions but what you're asking is that lombok ditches string's hashCode impl and instead writes its own string hashcode impl that has fewer collisions.

Presumably putting it that way makes it clear that it's absolutely out of the question.

title: @Nonnull causes errors in Findbugs
body: _Migrated from Google Code (issue 836)_

nodes.body:
:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jul 08, 2015 at 11:40 UTC

The check is not really redundant as there may be a way to make the fields null (e.g. reflection). The real problem is Findbugs checking generated code. Use

lombok.extern.findbugs.addSuppressFBWarnings=true

in lombok.config to stop it.

:bust_in_silhouette: **piotr.kubowicz**   :clock8: Jul 08, 2015 at 12:09 UTC

@ Value creates final fields, so a correct code using reflection should not modify them. I don't think that writing a code that expects final fields to change after initialization is reasonable - it's a bit paranoid. If someone broke into the data and changed nonnull fields to null, failing toString() is the smallest problem you will get, as the whole system reasonably expects the fields to be non null.

Lombok promises to generate code that is as good as written by hand. No one sane would write nullchecks of nonnull final fields, so Lombok is overzealous in this case.

The real problem is that Lombok requires hacking Findbugs configuration to successfully build a hello-world-style project. My opinion is that good products work out of the box and don't require working around their own known shortcomings. It's really frustrating to be required to google for a problem appearing in your 'hello world'.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jul 12, 2015 at 17:02 UTC

Lombok has no way to ensure that the fields are really `@ Nonnull`. It's not only Unsafe, reflection and all kinds of serialization, it's people writing their own constructors, calling methods before the constructor finishes and whatever.

> No one sane would write nullchecks of nonnull final fields

Am I insane? I'd probably omit them, but only because of their benefit not being up to with their cost. The cost is 1. effort (better spend on more important parts), 2.
readability (which doesn't matter in generated code), 3. runtime (zero as the JVM has to check it anyway and it's smart enough to collapse the checks). So there's a non-zero benefit and zero cost in generated code.

Just put a breakpoint in a constructor and look at `this`. `toString` gets called and without a null check, it throws and you see nothing.

> The real problem is that Lombok requires hacking Findbugs configuration...

If you wrote

"The real problem is that Findbugs requires hacking Lombok configuration to successfully build a hello-world-style project.",

it'd be accurate (It's Lombok configuration, what I wrote about. Put it in the project root and you're done)

:bust_in_silhouette: **piotr.kubowicz**   :clock8: Jul 12, 2015 at 18:59 UTC

But why do all people using Lombok and Findbugs need to make hacks to have their "hello world" working? Just don't be lazy and generate better code, period. This will fix anything.

Are you sure that Findbugs or even the compiler won't catch using uninitialized final fields? I would be surprised. Using debugger does not count, as you observe code in an invalid state. Just don't do it. Plus, we are talking about equals() and hashCode(), not about toString().

Lombok promises to generate good quality code, similar to hand-written. If Findbugs considers something a bug, just don't try to be smarter than it and don't do this.

:bust_in_silhouette: **Maaartinus**   :clock8: Jul 13, 2015 at 13:31 UTC

Concerning laziness, just do it and offer a patch (speak to the Lombok authors first; I am not an author).

Concerning what's better, I strongly prefer the current code.

Concerning smartness, why do you think that Findbugs is smarter? Smarter than who?

> Are you sure that Findbugs or even the compiler won't catch using uninitialized final fields?

The compiler? That's a nonsense. It allows no uninitialized final fields but can do nothing about seeing them before they get assigned.

Findbugs? What about people not using it?
_End of migration_

I don't care about `hello world`. People that do typically have switched to another language already.

It's trivial to add `lombok.extern.findbugs.addSuppressFBWarnings=true` to `lombok.config`

We prefer to use the same code in `@Value` as in a plain `@EqualsAndHashcode` and `@Data`

nodes.body:
Pretty sure github kinda ruined your formatting there :/ – prefix it all with 4 spaces and it should format as code.

Pulling this off would require tossing the .toString() result of the composite fields through something like .replace("\n", "  \n") to fix indents. That gets a little hairy for the final newline, and we can't rely on calling methods to format things nicely (lombok is a compile-time only dependency). This one is gonna be tough.
Caught in umbrella #1297.

title: Version 1.16 doesn't properly construct @Data

nodes.body:
I have the same problem. Versions 1.14.\* works fine, with 1.16.\* I cannot compile my project

Apache Maven 3.3.3 (NON-CANONICAL_2015-04-29T11:04:34_root; 2015-04-29T10:04:34+02:00)
Maven home: /opt/maven
Java version: 1.8.0_51, vendor: Oracle Corporation
Java home: /usr/lib/jvm/java-8-jdk/jre
Default locale: pl_PL, platform encoding: UTF-8
OS name: "linux", version: "4.1.2-2-arch", arch: "amd64", family: "unix"

I'm also having trouble with this problem. I can't upgrade Lombok to anything >= 1.16.0.

I suspect this has something to do with a combination of class annotations being used, but I can't seem to find an order that works. There are a number of messages about this on the mailing list, so this is not an isolated problem.
It might be worth mentioning that the affected classes for me are all subclasses of another class using lombok annotations. Maybe it's not ensuring that parent classes are processed before children?

Yeah, I'm pretty sure the problem is with subclasses. It appears all the errors I'm getting are in subclasses of something, and it looks like _nothing_ works in a subclass. @NoArgsConstructor, @Data, and access to the constructors and getters/setters that should have been present in the parent class all don't work.
I'm having this issue with @Value objects, no subclasses involved.

Update: My issue was a maven 3 issue.  Apparently, the way that lombok & maven interact changed at in 1.16.x of lombok.  I had to add a new flag to the maven compiler plugin configuration:  
`<forceJavacCompilerUse>true</forceJavacCompilerUse>`

That's fixed the problem for me as well. Here's the relevant doc page for maven-compiler-plugin:
https://maven.apache.org/plugins/maven-compiler-plugin/compile-mojo.html#forceJavacCompilerUse

And here's the description of that option:
Since: 3.0
compiler can now use javax.tools if available in your current jdk, you can disable this feature using -Dmaven.compiler.forceJavacCompilerUse=true or in the plugin configuration
Default value is: false.
User property is: maven.compiler.forceJavacCompilerUse.

Is it possible to detect when this setting is not enabled and throw some meaningful error? There's no way I was ever going to guess this was the fix. I also probably wasn't going to try downgrading Maven to 2.x series.

Thanks @jkwatson  for finding this!

I found this by noting that everything worked great in my IDE, but not in maven. Hence, it had to be something maven related. I decompiled the class files that maven had generated and noted that there were none of the lombok methods present. Then, it was just a matter of googling for maven annotation processing, and voila!  Glad it helped, @elreydetodo!
This fixed my issues with 1.16.x also. Thanks!

I had the same issue with maven 3 and lombok 1.16.x but simply updating maven-compiler-plugin to 3.3 (from 2.3.2 which does not support forceJavacCompilerUse) fixed it for me (no need for forceJavacCompilerUser, maybe because I'm still using Java 6?)

I'm still having the issue with Maven 3.3.3, Java 1.8.0_60, Lombok 1.16.6 and maven-compiler-plugin 3.3.

```
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>3.3</version>
    <configuration>
        <source>1.8</source>
        <target>1.8</target>
        <showWarnings>true</showWarnings>
        <showDeprecation>true</showDeprecation>
        <forceJavacCompilerUse>true</forceJavacCompilerUse>
        <compilerArgs>
            <arg>-Xlint</arg>
            <arg>-proc:none</arg>
        </compilerArgs>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
```

No setters and getters are generated when I use @Data on a class.
My bad - without <arg>-proc:none</arg> everything works just fine...

title: Add NullConstructor

nodes.body:
Good idea. Implemented here: https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/tree/force

the biggest issue is the name of the parameter. setFinalFieldsToNull is very long and misleading (ther'es also false and 0 for primitives for example). But 'force' is perhaps not quite enough either. Any ideas?
Great! For the naming I agree. Maybe the use case then: proxySubclassAllowed=true. A bit long but explicit.
Maybe `force(With)DefaultValues` or `setFinalFieldsToDefault(s)`? But IMHO `force` is good enough as there's nothing else what could be forced.
maybe defaults, but yes force is good enough once you met it once.
Closed in commit fd1d18a29957fc1999b7dd5725641662ad3bd887 which will be in v1.16.6

```
.target(new MethodTarget("org.eclipse.jdt.internal.formatter.DefaultCodeFormatter", "formatCompilationUnit"))
```

title: @Getter(lazy=true) causes unchecked cast warning
body: The Lombok-generated code from @Getter(lazy=true) contains a cast from Object to the field's type, which causes an unchecked cast warning when compiling with -Xlint:all.

nodes.body:
There's not a lot we can do here.

We do put two annotations on the method to let the compiler know it shouldn't emit warnings:
- `@java.lang.SuppressWarnings("all")`
- `@javax.annotation.Generated("lombok")`

The code is fine. Yes, the cast might be unsafe, but the code makes sure it isn't.

Is SuppressWarnings definitely being added correctly?

I'm ~~not setting any special lint options~~ using `-Xlint:all -Xlint:-processing` and `warning: [unchecked] unchecked cast` is showing up for any use of `@Getter(lazy=true)`.

For what it's worth, here's the workaround we settled on, which gets rid of the warnings.

```
@Getter(lazy = true, onMethod = @__({@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")}))
```

@rspilker According to the [duplicate thread](rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/994), adding the "unchecked" token to "all" helps, and it should be rather easy for Lombok to do this. Should I give it a try? Or would you?

There's a minor complication: For primitives, the "unchecked" token produces a warning in eclipse.

@rspilker One wrinkle that makes this a bit more problematic: the `onMethod` workaround suggested in this thread currently causes an exception in Checkstyle when using the `SuppressWarningsFilter`, per checkstyle/checkstyle#7522.

Just to get it on the record: Whomever designed how `@SuppressWarnings` works should be flogged. What an omnibomb of a disaster. There are no specs, everybody does their own thing, and `"all"` means so many things... except "all". There is in fact no actual "all" at all. Aaaargh 🤢 💥 

Adding "unchecked" helps, yeah. We'll get on that; good point by @Maaartinus that we do need to check if the type is primitive in which case, don't (we already do this, I think; we have to use a different AtomicX if the field is primitive already, and whilst we can't do resolution, primitives are hardcoded concepts we can trivially check for – not complicated in either case).

> There's a minor complication: For primitives, the "unchecked" token produces a warning in eclipse.

Can't reproduce. We actually cast e.g. `(java.lang.Long)`, letting auto-unboxing do the final step, so hopefully you meant this comment as a more general observation and not specifically for what `@Getter(lazy=true)` does.
Live in 1.18.12.

> Although, Netbeans with nb-javac doesn't complain, so it must be a bug in javac I suppose.

I am leaning towards the opposite conclusion: this must be a bug in Lombok. I've only ever seen this bug when using Lombok. If this was a bug in javac, someone would have produced a testcase without the use of Lombok. Thus far, this does not seem to be the case.

nb-javac uses the JDK9 compiler so you're right that it's possible javac's behavior changed between JDK8 and JDK9. One way to find out is to download JDK9 and try to compile this testcase from the command-line.

This is a duplicate of many, many bug reports. However, lombok cannot fix this.

See:
https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/wiki/LOMBOK-CONCEPT:-Resolution
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/47674264/static-import-not-working-in-lombok-builder-in-intellij

I just ran into this, and it took quite some time to debug. When I have a failure, the last thing I suspect is a bug in my toolchain. Instead, I spend a lot of cycles looking for anything _I_ may have done wrong (did I put an unprintable character in there? Did I do some wrong capitalization, maybe of a file name? Did I this, did I that??). Imo, the build tools should be as rock-solid as possible.

If Lombok cannot fix this, it should require the `static` modifier in the code, or at _least_ emit a warning from its IDE plugins. Adding `static` is an easy workaround, doesn't add much text, and removes the possibility of hitting this bug.

And this _is_ a bug. The docs say:

> _All_ members of a utility class are automatically marked as `static`. Even fields and inner classes.

That's not true, because they don't work exactly as `static` members, in that they can't be static-imported.

Just spent my own afternoon dealing with this. Frankly, figured it out mostly by luck (because the static method errors were first in the list).

I'm totally ok with the notion that Lombok can't handle this, but **please** put it into the documentation and/or Javadoc on the annotation, in big, bold letters. I understand this is an experimental feature, but if this annotation combined with a standard Java feature makes the compiler go haywaire, it should be officially mentioned.
Duplicate of #2044

title: @Accessors defaults chain to true, it should be false
body: When my class has `@Accessors(fluent = true)`, setters return `this`. I have to force it with `@Accessors(fluent = true, chain = false)`.

nodes.body:
Why do you say that it should be false? Is there a viable reason to this?  
When setting `fluent = true` you're practically leaving the road of old-established accessor-naming (prefixing with 'set').  
In my experience, when I encounter classes like that, I infer they support chaining as well...

Some do, some don't. I always check because I've seen a bunch that don't work that way. I don't think that you should change the default value of a property based on the setting from another property. I know there are some that do that, and it's caused me problems in the past (`@Builder` makes the constructor private). I would rather I have to explicitly enable chaining when I want it rather than remember to turn it off everywhere.

More importantly, I can't find anywhere in the changelog where behavior changed. I've been using lombok and the `@Accessors` for 2 years and it didn't default to chain until recently. If that's the way that the project decides to do it, that's fine, but it needs to be documented as an intentional change.

title: @cleanup - multiple method calls
body:
Hi

It would be nice if  'cleanup' would be able to accept an array of values, representing a sequence of cleanup methods - which will be then executed in order.

Example:
@ cleanup(["disconnect","close"])

nodes.body:
It's not (just) about the time. We don't see this pattern a lot so we do not consider it boilerplate. 

Even though the existing code would still work, it is not strictly backwards compatible in the binary. 

It is similar to changing `void foo(String)` to `void foo(String...)`. All code calling `foo(String)` will still compile and on the surface behave the same, but under the hood, now an array is created and a different method is invoked. The method `void foo(String)` is not in the bytecode. This leads to unexpected binary incompatibilities.

title: @EqualsAndHashCode - redundant null check on @Nonnull attributes
body:
When a class has attributes with annotation javax.annotation.@Nonnull, and has annotation @EqualsAndHashCode, the generated code checks if the value is null.
And Sonar notifies about redundant null check:

```
Redundant nullcheck of $attr1, which is known to be non-null in org.example.Test.hashCode()
Redundant nullcheck of $attr1, which is known to be non-null in org.example.Test.equals()
```

Can you skip this check if attribute is annotated with @NonNull?

nodes.body:
The java universe (core libraries + all code ever written) simply doesn't work that way. `@NonNull` is a suggestion. It's not a guarantee. Even if some slice of code can be statically analysed to ensure that non-nullness is guaranteed, _WE_ (lombok) isn't going to do it, those checks are very complex and rather expensive. Even if we or the IDE can guarantee that it can't happen, adding or removing the nullcheck silently depending on what you do with your code doesn't really sound like a 'win'.

That's a long way to say: The right thing to do with generated code especially, is to do the safe thing, even if the safe thing is thought to be overkill.

So, we have no intention of 'fixing' this. Our general policy on such things is as follows:

It's generated code. Don't worry. It knows better than your linters and code checkers. Configure your code checkers to not look at lombok code. We generate a `@Generated` annotation on all the methods we generate (including `equals` and `hashCode`), so you might want to file a bug with sonar that they should NOT ignore that annotation (this is exactly what it's for). This is only an option for source-level code checkers (the `@Generated` annotation, in an apparent momentary lapse of all reason and judgement, was marked as retentionlevel = source. Yeah. D'oh. Not our fault.

We can also generate the findbugs annotation, but you have to enable that via the config system:

```
lombok.extern.findbugs.addSuppressFBWarnings = true
```

If some other annotation is needed to do this, er, I guess we could add it. Please give us all the necessary details (mostly: The javadoc of said annotation, and where one would download the dependency jar containing this annotation) and we'll consider it.

title: Subclassing @Value objects
body:
Apologies if this has been discussed before, but I didn't find any issues here or anything in the google group.

I understand the caveats when subclassing value objects (cf. _Boch: Effective Java_ as well ass [VALJOs](http://blog.joda.org/2014/03/valjos-value-java-objects.html)), but making `@Value` annotated pojos completely `final` is quite restrictive.

Say you have a `Point` class and a `ColoredPoint` subclass. An instance of one can never be equal to an instance of the other, but still both are valid value objects. `@Value` makes the `Point` class `final`, so `ColoredPoint` can not be a subclass of `Point`, the `ColoredPoint` needs to duplicate the complete code of `Point`. The rationale for this is that a subclass must never change the behavior of the superclass, which is especially important with regard to constructing and `equals`.

But it would be possible to allow new methods in the subclass to add functionality without breaking the consistency of the parent. E.g. the `ColoredPoint` could add the color property (i.e. getters and setters) to the parent `Point` class, without changing anything of the `Point` class.

To make sure this never happens, _all methods_ of a `@Value` class must be made final (except for the methods `equals`, `hashCode`, and `toString`). But the superclass itself doesn't have to be `final`. Of course, subclasses would break consistency, if they didn't call `equals` of the superclass, but I'd say this is extremely stupid in any case.

Can it be because of retention policy of NotNull annotation?

No, the problem is that you marked it as `provided`. Lombok is a compile-time only dependency. Recently I've seen a post about someone providing a gradle example. I might be able to find it and add the documentation to the project lombok website.

> No, the problem is that you marked it as provided. Lombok is a compile-time only dependency. 

AFAIK while plain `compile` means "needed to compile and run`,`providedCompile`means "needed to compile, but when run, someone else will provide it or whatever". So a compile-time only dependency should indeed use`providedCompile`.

A very good reason against `RetentionPolicy.SOURCE` are class file analysis based checkers. The presence of unknown annotations (`RUNTIME`) is specified to be fine, and all the OP gets is a warning. I'd bet that spring is just too curious and precautious.
> Failed to class-load type while reading annotation metadata. **This is a non-fatal error**, but certain annotation metadata may be unavailable.

The general policy on annotations, as applied by javac itself and countless tools, is that an annotation that is not available on the classpath is ignored. One should not whine about this. This goes doubly for class-level retention.

In other words, we consider this a spring bug, being a bit overzealous in reporting this non-fatal error. We will not be addressing this.

Small followup: this also causes a similar issue in OSGi environments because bnd will add Import-Package directives for lombok because it detects this annotation in the class file. I suppose this is probably a bnd issue if that's the case.

title: In Java 8 and above @Log (and friends) should be allowed on interfaces
body: @Log annotations should be allowed on Java 8 and above as interfaces can have static and default methods.

nodes.body:
Actually, thinking about it some more; we'd have to make the field public, and we'd have to ignore attempts to make it non-static, as all fields in interfaces are public, static, and final. More generally, the 'intent' of a field in an interface is for it to be a constant, and a logger isn't semantically speaking a constant.

The upshot is that you'd have to generate the logger elsewhere (for example, an inner class, which has to be public too, but the members in _THAT_ don't have to be), or for the default impl to be a wrapper around an implementation that lives elsewhere. Either way, lombok can't just allow @Log and co on interfaces.

Couple things:
- How is one supposed to log in interface declared methods (default and static)?
- In java 9 private static fields will be allowed on interfaces.
- Can you give an example of when one would attempt to make an interface logger non-static?

title: Enforce `@NonNull` on method return and locals

nodes.body:
So, you want lombok to silently inject: if (result != null) throw new NullPointerException("Erm, what do we put here then?");? I'm not sure that's particularly useful; presumably your method is going to blow up all by itself soon. Well, it might not. Still, there's a pretty big difference between `@NonNull` on a param and on your internal code (that is, a local var or the return type): Params can always be null, at any time, due to changes in code or because other libraries etc call you with weird values. But, what you set your own locals to, and what you return, that's within your control.

Your IDE should just generate the warnings; the right move is NOT to generate an actual at-runtime check. Runtime checks are of dubious value here; you really want static code analysis.

We have 3 options here:

(A) Disallow the use of `@NonNull` on methods / method return types and local variables because we have no intent on generating any code for this.
(B) Carry on as normal: Acknowledge that `@NonNull` also has a documentary purpose and might be a part of your IDE's/analyser's configuration of static code analysis. It's got a retention policy of 'class' for this reason.
(C) Write an analyser. Because if we don't do the same deep and resolution-requiring analysis that IDEs do, **then your static analyser is going to whine about the lombok-generated null check!**. Presumably, anything marked `@NonNull` is usually already determinable as never null by analysis, so you'd run into that, let's say 80%+ of all the stuff you marked.

C is impossible. A is backwards incompatible. B is the choice we're going with.

Yes, but what about cases where I get a property from a bean and just want to validate it's non-nullness?

I don't like `Objects.nonNull` because it throws `NullPointerException` when really I want `IllegalArgumentException` plus the name of the field/variable, which Lombok's `@NonNull` provides.

See [this gist](https://gist.github.com/mbjelac/faee5b754558f2243bf550989b85c75c) for an example test which I would like to pass.

One approach I've used before on similar situations is to have a small utility method to check my post-conditionss/ constraints.  Something like ...

    <code ...>
    assertExitConstraints(
        (result    != null),
        (counter <  MAX_TRIES),
    );

Where the helper method `assertExitConstraints( boolean... )` throws the Exception you want to see.  In my case I have a Constraint Error.  It would also be possible to pass the type of exception or exception(s) as parameters if that were desirable.

Personally, if the error was in the parameters that is when I expect an: `IllegalArgumentException`.  Not on the return value.  It sounds like the null check we're discussing is a proxy for not validating the input constraints / pre-conditions.  For that  case I use the same pattern wth `assertEntryConstraints(...)`.

I find these most useful in Spock specifications  and JUnit tests.

Ah, I was falsely assuming that Lombok preferrably used it's own utility methods for things like this, but `Objects.requireNonNull` is just perfekt for this.

> (that's a good thing, as activating the checks afterwards is a bit risky). 

TBH. I would rather have my production throw errors on me than search for data inconsistencies. But I believe that to be dependant upon personal preference, and of course the project's context.

Null is far more complex than this; I'm done trying to explain the garbage fire that is nullity annotations and null checks in general on an issue per issue basis because it is taking up tons of time. I regret that I can't get into it more, but these kinds of issues shall remain closed, and any debate on why or how lombok can be of use can be held in person at conferences or if you're anywhere around Delft, The Netherlands, contact us and we'll meet. Make sure you free up an  hour or 3 on your calendar, because it is _that_ complex.

What's left for me to say is: Oh, I have thought about this. Lots of time spent thinking about it, in fact. It's not this simple, this won't work well. I may be wrong, but going a few rounds on an issue tracker is not an acceptable use of time.
Sorry, I was very much unaware of the deep implications of my question and apologize for it. It won't Happen again. I might take you up on your offer though, when in the netherlands again.

title: As a User I want to be able to use @CopyConstructor annotation to get rid of the boilerplate code

nodes.body:
I think that is a very useful feature; would love seeing that :)  
It would only take some concern as to whether it would shallow or deep, and how to control that.

I'll also cast a vote for an annotation to create a copy constructor.  In my typical use-cases, I'd say that I use a deep copy greater than 90% of the time, so that seems like a sensible default (to me).

+1

This could help avoid some stupid hand-coding bugs.
@rspilker Any benefit in builder here? `@Data` classes are mutable and can be considered as builders themselves (if copy constructor is available).

@rspilker Sorry, didn't know there is already existing `@Builder` functionality )
Cool! It's a way to go!
I assume the `@Builder(toBuilder = true)` trick only creates shallow copies of collections?
Please stop posting +1 comments, and use the thumbs-up button under the original post.
Do you accept PRs? Would love to look at this.

Before you start working on a pull request, we first need to figure out how to handle deep copies. Also, we need to find out why people would like to create a copy at all. In my experience, having Immutable objects is gaining more traction. For shallow copies we already have the toBuilder trick. What gap would adding CopyConstructor fill?

Deep copying is very complicated and personally I don't think it's Lombok's job to do this.

The common technique is to serialize and deserialize using object streams because most object graphs are too complicated. You lose transient data this way. No reason for Lombok to do this for you, there are tools like Apache commons that can do it.

The other way is to traverse the object graph recursively and copy each object in the graph. It's like recursively annotating a shallow copy constructor. Here you'll have to take care of collections since they require to deep copy their elements. Since not all classes in the JDK permit this functionality, I don't think it'll be possible.

I agree with Maaartinus to implement a shallow copy constructor.
Please stop with the +1 comments. It notifies subscribers and creates noise. Use a thumbs up emoji on the top post instead.
As an alternative, maybe @Builder or @CopyConstructure chaining is possible - make deep copy for member fields that are also annotated with @CopyConstructor

As a matter of preference I like what [Immutables](https://immutables.github.io/immutable.html) does..

`
ImmutableValue.builder()
    .from(otherValue) // merges attribute value into builder
    .addBuz("b")
    .build();
`
For the second time, stop commenting with +1 and thumbs up the top comments instead. You're creating a lot of noise for nothing.

@omega09 

> But it's marked with `@NoCopier` so I though just don't copy.

I see, it was a stupid name. Indeed, the object won't get copied at all, just a reference to it, so `@ReferenceCopier` might be better. For what you understood, maybe `@CopyConstructor.Exclude` could be a good name.

> `// no annotation - no copy`

That's very error-prone. Moreover, it makes the `@CopyConstructor` copy nothing by default!

> What if I annotate User owner with `DEPTH_ONE`? Generate `owner = new User(cart.owner);`? 

I guess so. If there's such an annotation.

> Doesn't this make sense mostly for collections?

Yes.

> Are the DEPTH_ONE classes supporting their own copy constructors?

Lombok should handle classes it knows (JDK + Guava) perfectly. For others, it should have a simple default strategy like call their copy constructor and let the user handle it, if it doesn't compile. When the compile-time error is obvious, then it's fine. If it should lead to cryptic error, then giving up immediately with a sane message asking the user to provide their copier is better.

> If this can be done then a full deep copy can be done by recursively applying depth one copy

I don't think so: You'd lose the object identity and any circle would lead to an infinite graph. IMHO the real full deep copy is grossly overrated, so far I had no single use for it.

> the details need to be *really* ironed out.

Indeed. That's why [I wrote][1] that the shallow constructor should be done first and independently. Anything beyond that is orders of magnitude more complicated; even understanding what it should do is hard. IMHO it's impossible to do anything useful (beyond the shallow copy) without letting the user specify their own helper methods (and I see things like `@Copy(value=DEPTH_ONE)` just like shortcuts for the common cases).

Maybe we should write a copier using an ordinary annotation processor (which is much simpler) or look if someone already did. Or do it using reflection, which is even easier. Then we'd have a reference implementation to play with.

[1]: https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/908#issuecomment-267043654

@omega09 
IIUYC `shallow` on a field means copy the reference but not the object. That's confusing as the "shallowness" for the whole object means "reference" for the fields. Similarly for depth 1. I'd call it differently:
- `@CopyConstructor.Exclude`: leave it as is, probably null
- `@CopyConstructor.Reference`: copy the reference to the old object
- `@CopyConstructor.Copy`: 
  - for *known* immutables (`String`, Guava immutables like `ImmutableSet`, ...), copy the reference
  - for other *known* collections and maps, create a new one as a shallow copy (i.e., referring to the same objects as the old one)
  - for other *known* classes, do what's needed (`Date.clone` or alike)
  - for anything else, invoke their copy constructor, which may or may not compile
- `@CopyConstructor.Copy(MyCopyingHelper.class)`: invoke `MyCopyingHelper.copy(thisField)`, which may or may not compile, just like `@ExtensionMethod`

On the whole class, I see three possibilities:
- `@CopyConstructor`: a shallow copy, using `@CopyConstructor.Reference` on fields by default
- `@CopyConstructor(DEPTH_1)`: a depth 1 copy, using `@CopyConstructor.Copy` on fields by default
- `@CopyConstructor(MyCopyingHelper.class)`: a user-defined constructor, using `@CopyConstructor.Copy(MyCopyingHelper.class)` on fields by default

> Don't think we can check is a field is a collection in Lombok

Agreed. I'd only check for known classes according to their declared type.

@Maaartinus 

Alright, I'll fork something this weekend.
Why is this still open? It's very useful feature indeed.

@balajeetm You mean why it's not implemented? It needs to be finished and then a PR need to get reviewed. I more or less forgot about it since I posted the initial implementation. The previous post's "Copy behavior" section contains some questions that need to be answered.
@omega09 - Can you make summary of questions open regarding this cool feature?
What about a parameter to control whether to call the `@CopyConstructor` of the superclass (instead of calling `super()`)? This would allow for copying fields from superclasses.

I just tried the Builder and it's not working properly, see also: https://github.com/peichhorn/lombok-pg/issues/78 - it is not considering inherited attributes, which means it's basically unusable for me (want a replacement for clone()). So I would also prefer a dedicated @CopyConstructor, along with option to set visibility to private.

Making a deep clone is not possible: There is no general way to clone objects; you need to know what you're dealing with. Integer, String, etc are immutable and a deep clone should just copy the reference, though sometimes for exotic reasons you really do want to deep clone an immutable in which case you need custom code.

arrays and such need special treatment to clone. You can't just go around and call clone() on things; clone() generally makes shallow clones, and once you commit to making a deep clone, that should be turtles all the way down.

Thus, the only feasible thing we can add is a shallow clone, and toBuilder already suffices for that use case.

We will not add this; please don't waste your time with PRs or further discussion.

toBuilder is not usable if there is a hierarchy of objects.

Am I missing something?

Yes.

Of course you can use toBuilder with a hierarchy, just make sure everything
in the hierarchy has builders / toBuilder and you can do nested builder
calls:

Given a toplevel object with an List as as inner field, which contains leaf
nodes created by a method named createLeaf():

TopLevel newtopLevel = topLevel.toBuilder()
        .innerField(topLevel.getInnerField().stream()
                .map(t -> t.toBuilder()
                        .leaf(createLeaf(t))
                        .build())
                .collect(Collectors.toList()))
        .build();

The only time that you get in trouble with this pattern if there are
backwards references to the top level object, and even that has solutions.
(if not terribly pretty ones, but no uglier than if you do this the
conventional way.)

Not honoring your initializer expresssion is no bug: When you look at the generated constructor (e.g. in the "members" view), you can see

```
 BuilderInitialization(String, List<String>)
```

Feature Request: add configuration key lombok.toString.includeClassName
body:
It could be useful sometimes to prevent displaying the class name and the parentheses in the string produced by the Lombok generated 'toString' method.

This could be done using a new configuration key:

```
lombok.toString.includeClassName [true|false] (default: true)
```

Here are some examples of the expected result:
1. `ClassName1(field1=value1, field2=ClassName2(field1=value1, field2=value2), field3=value3)`
2. `field1=value1, field2=ClassName2(field1=value1, field2=value2), field3=value3`
3. `field1=value1, field2=(field1=value1, field2=value2), field3=value3`

| Example | ClassName1 | ClassName2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | true | true |
| 2 | true | false |
| 3 | false | false |

nodes.body:
Your third example is incorrect: it added parenthesis. The correct rendering should have been:
3. `field1=value1, field2=field1=value1, field2=value2, field3=value3`
Removing the parenthesis is, in my opinion, a bad idea. 

The (generated) toString is for debugging purposes only. I can see some value in not adding the class name. However, I don't think a configuration key is the best place here, since then all toStrings in at least a package, will not show the class name resulting in confusing strings. However, adding a field to the `@ToString` might just have enough value: `@ToString(className=false)`

I perfectly agree with you about using a field instead of a key. Actually I thought it was equivalent when I looked at an example of it in the online documentation. So yes for field, not a key.

About the parenthesis question now, the third example can't be incorrect since it is a feature request, not a description of reality (I will edit my message to make it clearer).

So if I try to explain the idea behind these examples, a think the main point is that `ClassName2` (child class) does not output itself any parenthesis around its fields: it is `ClassName1` (parent class) that produces them in the case `includeClassName` is `false` for `ClassName2`.

I admit, this may greatly complicate `@ToString` algorithm, but personally I find it useful and elegant.
Caught in umbrella #1297.

title: Ability to apply ExtensionMethod project wide
body:
I asked about this before here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/project-lombok/4NGp9Rzr6aM
Figured we should have an open issue for the request.

Requesting ability to enable ExtensionMethod across an entire folder using the lombok.config file, to be able to apply it to an entire package and configure it.

Would greatly improve the use of this feature as I can not realistically see us adding the annotation to every class created, but would love to be able to extend API's we are using.

nodes.body: Agreed. This was the whole inspiration for the [lombok configuration system](https://projectlombok.org/features/configuration.html). We're still working on it.
@rspilker Any update on where this lands priority wise? I really believe this would be lombok's #1 feature once this is done.

> I really believe this would be lombok's #1 feature once this is done.

I agree with @aikar as well

I can imagine how expensive would it be to check for "unknown" method that might be extensions. Specially if we're walking through all classes in a given directory (and sub-directories). I wonder if changing the mechanics on how we define extension methods would relief the burden it imposes and make it easier to be implemented.

@miere 
> I can imagine how expensive would it be to check for "unknown" method that might be extensions. Specially if we're walking through all classes in a given directory (and sub-directories). I wonder if changing the mechanics on how we define extension methods would relief the burden it imposes and make it easier to be implemented.

I don't know. With extensions defined project-wide, I guess that scanning the extension classes only once per compilation should be possible. Thereafter, two `HashMap` lookups should do:

- the first hash map lookup by name returns a map to be used in the next step
- the second hash map lookup by receiver type returns the class defining the extension method

This goes as follows:

- The first step eliminates all methods not named as an extension method. This is a sure and simple speed up.
- The second step uses the receiver type directly. When there's no value for it, a test like in [this line](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/master/src/core/lombok/javac/handlers/HandleExtensionMethod.java#L186) gets done and the result gets stored back. When no extension method applies, a sentinel value gets used.

I may be wrong with it all as I know too little about the compiler internals. If I'm right, it could be way faster than what gets done now and that independently of the number of extension methods.

@rzwitserloot Could you comment on it? I guess, the idea of storing all method names should apply to the current code, too. Something like
```
/* Set<String> */ extensionNames = extensions.stream()
    .flatMap(e -> e.extensionMethods.stream().map(m -> m.name))
    .collect(Collectors.toSet());
```
in the `ExtensionMethodReplaceVisitor` constructor and a check like
```
if (!extensionNames.contains(methodName)) return;
```
in `handleMethodCall` could save most of the effort for a majority of methods, couldn't it?

It'll have a significant impact.

We are focussing on different high-impact features right now; see the ones marked as 'next milestone'.

I prototyped this for javac to check out the performance impact during compilation. It seems like it takes 10%-20% more time to complete compilation. I also added an additional name and parameter count check to skip reslution, without these it is really slow.
bump.  any updates on this?  Even a partial solution like being able to inherit `@ExtensionMethod` from a base class would help.

No updates on this; for headline features, meta annotations is currently ahead in the queue, and ExtensionMethod needs a whole bunch of love in the first place.

There's also the topic of generics. On the one hand, doing something like this is amazing:

```java
public static String join(List<? extends CharSequence> listOfStrings, String separator) { ... }
```

That would mean any `List<String>` or `List<StringBuilder>` or whatnot just has a `join(', ')` method, but other lists simply don't have it.

On the other hand it complicates matters.

Keeping the issue open because whilst it's got a very long list of caveats (really high costs), the potential benefits of this are similarly sky high.

title: @Delegate doesn't work well with varargs
body:
Lombok 1.16.6

When @Delegate is used to delegate methods with Varargs params, the parameter is changed into an array:

``` java
public void myMethod(String param1, Object... otherParams) {
    // Code
}
```

is changed into

``` java
public void myMethod(String param1, Object[] otherParams) {
    this.delegate.myMethod(param1, otherParams)
}
```

This results in the following code not compiling:

``` java
myObject.myMethod("Test", "myParam");
```

Error message will be something like

```
Error:(XX) java: no suitable method found for myMethod(java.lang.String,java.lang.String)
    method MyObject.myMethod(java.lang.String,java.lang.Object[]) is not applicable
        (argument mismatch; java.lang.String cannot be converted to java.lang.Object[]))
```

nodes.body: Will be in 1.16.8

title: Use FindBugs-compatible @SuppressWarnings on generated methods
body:
Lombok annotates generated methods with `@java.lang.SuppressWarnings("all")` to try to get rid of lint warnings. The `"all"` suppression is specific to the Eclipse compiler and is ignored by javac. If I run `delombok` and change the generated code to use `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` instead, the unchecked cast warnings on `@Getter(lazy=true)` generated methods go away.

It would be great if Lombok could generate both annotations. The `"unchecked"` suppression is defined by the Java language spec so it ought to work on any compiler.

nodes.body:
```
$ javac -version
java 1.8.0_60
$ javac -X
  ...
  -Xlint:{all,auxiliaryclass,
          cast,classfile,
          deprecation,dep-ann,divzero,
          empty,
          fallthrough,finally,
          options,overloads,overrides,
          path,processing,
          rawtypes,
          serial,static,
          try,
          unchecked,
          varargs,
          -auxiliaryclass,
          -cast,-classfile,
          -deprecation,-dep-ann,-divzero,
          -empty,
          -fallthrough,-finally,
          -options,-overloads,-overrides,
          -path,-processing,
          -rawtypes,
          -serial,-static,
          -try,
          -unchecked,
          -varargs,
          none} Enable or disable specific warnings
  ...
$ 
```

Thanks; my analysis of the problem was wrong. It turns out the unchecked cast warning is coming from FindBugs, not from `javac`. FindBugs is what is ignoring the `"all"` suppression, and it's also not paying attention to the `@Generated` annotation.

While that's arguably a FindBugs bug, Lombok could switch to `"unchecked"` and still achieve the desired goal of suppressing the unchecked warning. Hopefully the Lombok developers will consider doing it.

It's not easy to generate the minimal suppression for each type of code, especially since different tools have slightly different implementations of their analysis and resolution, leading to different conclusions. Also, if we always generate `unchecked` you might get a warning on the `@SuppressWarnings` that it isn't necessary to suppress it since it wouldn't occur.

All in all, we always at least also need to add "all". That says it all.

Did you see on the [configuration system page](https://projectlombok.org/features/configuration.html) that you can instruct Lombok to also generate `@SuppressFBWarnings` using `lombok.extern.findbugs.addSuppressFBWarnings = true` so Findbugs will not emit warnings for generated code?
