title: Any reason why we can't have an OptionalGetter annotation?

nodes.body:
Just to throw in a couple more arguments for adding this feature:
- Optional getter is not against Optional design - see Stuart Marks Optional talk [at 55:06](https://youtu.be/Ej0sss6cq14?t=55m6s)
- any kind of argument against using Optional because of boxing or performance considerations is invalid as the goal is to make Optional a value type in the future (same talk at [47:10](https://youtu.be/Ej0sss6cq14?t=47m10s)) => performance is a moving target but today's workarounds are tomorrow's technical debt (if you don't add this feature).
- Guava recommends using java.util.Optional instead of Guava provided one - [source](https://google.github.io/guava/releases/22.0/api/docs/com/google/common/base/Optional.html)

> `@NonNull` just affects generated constructors/getters, right?

Right. And you're right: Without generating a constructor, the field may be `null` even when annotated `@NonNull`. Forbidding to set it to `null` explicitly might make sense.

> it might be easier to implement this feature instead as `@Getter(optional=True)`

I guess so. This precludes the possibility to generate also a normal getter, but having two getters would be pretty strange anyway. I wouldn't call the argument just `optional`, but rather `useOptional` or alike (as the getter isn't really optional).

A nicer possibility could be to use `@UseOptionalGetters` as a modifier, possibly on class level, or even a configuration, similar like `@Accessors` works.
In case of modifier at type level, it would be nice if bean validation annotations were also supported (@NotNull).
:+1: for an optional getters configuration.

If you add this, I will dance at your wedding.

+1

I think this feature (as previously said `@Getter(optional = true)` or something similar) would be a very desirable feature for Lombok, letting the user to decide if work with Optionals or not.

Lombok already provides mechanisms to indicate which fields are nullable so I see this one a very viable feature.

Why not just make the field itself Optional?

This is an unnecessarily limited view. The `Optional` interface follows monadic laws (comparable to `Maybe` in Haskell and the like) and the above sentence is the exact purpose of such data structures when it comes to return types: representing something that can either be present or absent, and providing a standardised (i.e. common) way of safely interacting with it.

`Optional` shouldn’t be used as field type, there is no doubt in that. And it’s certainly a bad practice to use it for method input parameters either. So it’s either of:

```java
// We might or might not find it:
Optional<Something> findSomethingById(@NonNull String id);

// We can guarantee at compile-time that it will always be there:

```

interface. As far as I can tell not even Hibernate really needs it anymore
for simple applications.

Given that Serializable feels like old deprecated nonsense I do not see the
point of not using Optional wherever you can, either. There is nothing
wrong with Optional<> fields per sé. Frameworks nowadays usually support
this just fine. Jackson does. JPA does. Hibernate sorta can but doesn't
(yet). So what is the reason that using this thing for fields is
discouraged?

Seriously: Why? People aren't discouraging the use of Collection<>, List<>
or Set<> either, so why is Optional<> any different?

Well, I don't get the problem with introducing Optional getter either. 

Let's make it clear: optional is for API designers, so:
1. Optional should not be used as an argument, thus declaring field as Optional  does not make any sense. Optional is NOT for replacing null, so if one wants to set "no value" then null should be passed. API designer dictates if nulls are allowed or not, not you as a user.

2. Declaring a field as an Optional is asking for a trouble. Try anything that requires serialization into string, like converting to/from JSON representation and it will become clear what pain it is. That's because Optional was NOT designed to store value.

3. Optional however WAS designed for APIs. It exists to indicate to the user that returned value MAY not exist. This means that is perfectly fine to have: Optional<String> getSomePossiblyOptionalProperty(). Consider a case of driver class often recalled. API may specify that some property of driver Optional<Cache> getCache(). That's how user knows that cache may or may not be present and should handle the situation properly. It is much easier to make a mistake and ignore possible null if it would only be Cache getCache().

Summarizing I don't see any cons for Getter(optional = true), only pros.

Please reconsider @rzwitserloot .

1. "should not be used" - says who? And more importantly, *why*? I haven't
seen a single good reason to accept nulls anywhere, whereas I've seen lots
of reasons to not do so. The only good reason against Optional I've heard
so far is the serializable interface, which I consider a misdesigned
malfeature. And if you really need that there's still Vavr's alternative
version of this.
2. Serialisation into string works fine. Jackson does it without any
problems, just make sure you have the dependencies right and put a default
in. And if it *doesn't* - that's a bug in the serialisation framework, not
the use of Optional.
3. That distinction between use in an API and regular use is therefore
entirely artificial personal preference.

Summarizing: just make your field Optional<> and you will actually get all
the benefits of compile-time null check enforcement, instead of asking for
a workaround for something that doesn't make sense in the first place.

Summarizing:
1. Yes, getters (and other methods returning value) should return Optional if it is possible that there is no value. If calculate(arg1, arg2) cannot calculate something and there is no reason for exception the return value should be Optional as well.
2. No, Optional should not be used as parameter - we have found no just cause to do this, every argument is against using Optional this way.
3. Optional actually could be used as field. Potential problem are serializations of any kind (Java serialization, JSON, Hibernate etc.). If that is not the case, then actually we found no good reason for not using Optional as field - use it or not, it is a matter of taste.

BUT, regarding Lombok features:
Making field Optional when getter AND setter are required does not solve the problem of missing Optional Getter, as in this case Setter would be bad (see point no. 2 above). Also Builder should be considered with Optional fields so no strange methods were created.

This is why this issue is still valid and justified and I advocate reopen and accept :-)

I don't think it makes sense to argue here about how someone should use `Optional`. The fact is, there are multiple different opinions, with large groups behind each. For example, talk to anyone with a Scala background that is doing Java, and they will tell you that `Optional` should be used as much as possible in place of nulls everywhere, because that's exactly how Scala uses it with its equivalent `Option` type. Now whether they are right or wrong is beside the point, people with this opinion exist, and they form a significantly sized portion of the lombok user community, and would benefit from better support for `Optional` in lombok. As an example of such a community, the Java APIs for Play Framework, Lagom and Akka all make strong use of `Optional` in fields and as method parameters, and all three of those frameworks recommend using lombok for immutable Java classes. These are large communities that have this opinion, it's not a fringe view.

So the question is, is the use of `Optional` something that lombok itself should have an opinion on? I don't see why it should. Providing better support for `Optional` fields won't have any negative impacts on people whose opinion it is that you shouldn't use `Optional` fields, because they're not going to use `Optional` fields and so they'll never see that support. But it will certainly help those whose opinion it is that you can/should. And it doesn't seem to be a feature that would have a very high cost to implement or require significant refactoring in lombok. So why hold out on this portion of your users?

title: Hashcode generation: enum ordinal option?

nodes.body: I did just run across [Improve @Tolerate, so it really works with @EqualsAndHashCode](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/pull/52) which doesn't give me much hope that this'll be a popular proposal. I do think there's value in deterministic hashcodes as the non-determinism of enums have bitten us more than once. However, it is perhaps more niche than I'd thought.

Right now we just call the hashCode and equals method on all reference type variable. This is something we can determine compile time. We do that by excluding all built-in types and arrays, and what remains is an Object. Unfortunately, we are currently unable to use resolution to inspect the concrete type of a reference field. So we don't know if it is an enum.

We could determine it in the generated code at runtime, but that would impact the performance of all hashCode implementations.

Also, if you have a collection's hashCode method or Array.deepHashCode, those will still use the enum's built-in hashCode. 

I think this is something for the JDK to solve.
Fair enough. Thanks for the time! :)

title: @Value is not experimental, but it implies @FieldDefaults which is?
body:
I have a class with a package-private static field which must remain package-private.
Then I annotate my class with @Value, and Lombok turns my package-private static field into a private static field, so everything breaks.
So, I have to use @Data instead, which is not what I *really* wanted.

I suppose, the problem can be worded as follows: @Value is not marked as "experimental", but it implies @FieldDefaults, which *is* experimental, so in light of that, shouldn't @Value also be marked as "experimental"?  (Either that, or can @Value please not mess with my static fields?)

nodes.body:
A workaround would be to add `@Getter(access=PACKAGE)` and/or  `@Setter(access=PACKAGE)` to the static field. Surely better than using `@Data`. You could also use all needed parts of `@Value` separately.

Sure, that's just a workaround (I'm not a project maintainer, just trying to help).

First of all, it does not _imply_ `@FieldDefaults`, but is equivalent to it.

We still think that `@FieldDefaults` could be experimental as a stand-alone feature. However, `@NonFinal` and `@PackagePrivate` should not be in experimental. Also, I think it is a bug if it touches static fields.
I've created issue #1254 to skip static fields.

title: @Value and @FieldDefaults should skip static fields
body:
`@Value` and `@FieldDefaults` add the private and final modifiers to the fields if possible. This behavior is influenced by `@NonFinal` and `@PackagePrivate`.

For instance fields, this makes sense. But for package private static non-final fields, this is an unexpected side-effect of adding `@Value`

nodes.body: Would it be possible to add optional support for static fields in @FieldDefaults?

I'm just upgrading my Lombok JAR from 1.16.10 to 1.16.16 and this "correction" just killed all my projects.

My very simple use case is to put `@UtilityClass` and `@FieldDefaults(makeFinal = true, level = AccessLevel.PUBLIC)` to get a class to store my constants.

Now, everything is broken in all my projects and it makes Lombock useless for that kind of configuration.
I go back to do everything manualy.

Another simple use case : on my "POJO beans" (ex : `@Entity @Data` serializable classes), I use `@FieldDefaults(level = AccessLevel.PRIVATE)`, as certainly almost everybody using Lombok.
Now I have to manually write that `serialVersionUID` is private.

But, in fact, I use it in a "lombok.config" file to have it by default on the entire project. So I have to search for all my static fields and manually make them private where needed...

It looks like 2 little things (combined with my previous post), but in the big company I'm working for, because all the newly (last 2 years) created applications (at least a dozen) use a parent Maven dependency configuration including Lombok, that king of modification causes a not so little work to do when updating...

title: EqualsAndHashCode work with BigDecimal ?
body:
Is it possible using compareTo rather than equals to compare BigDecimal ?

Now, I have to create a specific method equals for BigDecimal objects and add all of them in exclude of @EqualsAndHashCode.

I found some discussion about that problem :
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/36625347/how-to-make-lomboks-equalsandhashcode-work-with-bigdecimal
http://tech.transferwise.com/fun-with-bigdecimal/
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/project-lombok/BigDecimal|sort:relevance/project-lombok/oRdyHiecgWE/GHLLhL8FYdIJ

Maybe just an option in annotation @EqualsAndHashCode for switching between equals and compareTo for some kind of classes...

nodes.body:
Unfortunately, this is not possible. Also, if you put them in an array or collection, that also wouldn't work.

We are looking into a system to provide method for specific fields, but we're not there yet.
Oh, by the way, beware that if the equals returns `true`, the hashCodes should also be the same. How would you do that?

I don't think this issue should be closed.

It would be great to be able to provide a specific equals method for given fields. Probably like the OP, I have a deep structure with a few `Big Decimal` here and there and it fails equals if one `BigDecimal` field is `1` and the other one `1.0`
I'd also vote for reopening this issue

Is this issue going to be fixed anytime in future? Because equals generated by lombok isn't very useful in case we have some fields of BigDecimal. That would be great if this equal check on BigDecimal replaced by compareTo.

@nihadibrahimli I don't think that anything should or can be changed as the current behavior is the most correct possible. But now, there's a workaround, working exactly as [described years ago](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/1260#issuecomment-268114093).
Why not Lombok generates exactly how it is explained by @Maaartinus? Ok, maybe with some options on the annotation `@EqualsAndHashCode(bigDecimalMessAvoided=true)` ?

Just guessing:
1) It extends the annotation with a parameter that more than 99% of the Lombok users will never need. It could lead to confusion for users, and increases the maintenance costs for the Lombok team.

2) There is an easy workaround. Even better, this workaround _makes it clearly visible_ that you deviate from the regular `equals`, which makes it (imo) an even better solution than an additional parameter.

If you're using BigDecimal in your POJO you'll want correctly generated HC&E methods that ignores scale. That should be more that 99% of developers. When adding new BigDecimal attribute you need to make extra work and is actually more work than when not using Lombok(2 extra annotations and an extra method when on manually will be 2 lines - one in equals, one in hashCode). 
OK, I agree it's not clearly that standard HC&E rules does not apply but developer should be aware of this when using BigDecimal.

> Use @EqualsAndHashCode.Include, solves all your problems and also [...]

You forgot about the engineering notation. `stripTrailingZeros()` does not help with `BigDecimal("1E+2") != BigDecimal("100")`.

@wacker No I did not. That you think 1E+2 is 'equals' to 100 is your choice. As I keep saying, 'equality' has different definitions. If you want such values to be equal to each other, .. .`@EqualsAndHashCode.Include` still solves all your problems; just write a method that compares the way you want.

Suppose one has the outlandish requirement to care specifically about arithmetic equality. The usual way is `x.compareTo(y) == 0`. How would you suggest implementing this using `@EqualsAndHashCode.Include` considering the above?

As mentioned before, `stripTrailingZeros()` does _not_ put a BigDecimal into a universal form for arithmetic comparisons when mixed exponential notations are used.

You could, of course, try to take that into account as well:

```java
return number.stripTrailingZeros().toPlainString();
```

But is this complete?

And even if it is: Why should the use of Lombok comparisons force you to carry the load of all these transformations, also potentially creating big strings as part of the process when on the other hand there is a perfectly suited `compareTo` functionality? Lombok should make it somehow possible to use it.

I showed how lombok can be extended to allow such a thing, but that's a lot to add for this _one_ edge case. It sounds like a better plan to point at BigDecimal and state that it's not quite fit for purpose. OpenJDK should fix this and add a `.normalize()` method of some stripe. A lot of the inner workings of `compareTo` could be made public. It just isn't.

BigDecimal is sort of a built-in, so it carries _a lot_ of clout. Just not quite enough to introduce an annotation _just_ to configure how BD's supposed to act in equality operations.

That clout does cut both ways. The BigDecimal authors think you are wrong and do not implement their `equals` the way you want. Given that they wrote it, I defer to their expertise on this, and therefore I'll join them: Apparently, you're doing it wrong. What you really want isn't what the BD team defines as 'equality'. You want something else, which in basis means it is no longer boilerplate.

However, offering a way to provide a comparing function (vs a method that 'transforms' any value and then lombok compares the post-transform values, which is what you can do right now) would be useful in general, and would make this edge case a lot easier. I'm open to at least a design (I find it a bit annoying as to how one would specify that a given method is to be used for comparison operations. Naming that method identical to the field just feels wrong, naming the field in the annotation requires 'stringly typing' which we do not like at all, and you can't stick method refs in annotations, so that leaves us at a bit of a dead end. We could make you put a class reference (legal in annotations) someplace and then document that the named class is _required_ to implement Function<T, T, Boolean> or BiPredicate or whatever the most logical functional interface in `j.u.function` would be. Except now we're forced into always instantiating that thing, and documenting all this is a nightmare.

Hence, a low-priority feature at this point, not a bug fix.

Apparently I was wrong, at least I can no longer reproduce the problem. When `stripTrailingZeros()` is applied _to both sides_, `equals()` and `hashCode()` work as expected, also when applied to mixed exponential notations:

```java
new BigDecimal("1E+2").stripTrailingZeros().equals(new BigDecimal("100").stripTrailingZeros()); //true
new BigDecimal("1E+2").stripTrailingZeros().hashCode() == new BigDecimal("100").stripTrailingZeros().hashCode(); //also true
```

Sorry for the confusion. `stripTrailingZeros()` does indeed appear to be a "normalizing" transformation, as you assumed.
Awesome.

title: @EqualsAndHashCode(unsupported) wanted

nodes.body: I think it would be good to make the methods final, to prevent subclasses to override the methods with an actual implementation and get into trouble with the equals contract.

That's wrong. You class is a subclass of `Object` and there's nothing about `equals` being optional. You're also making `equals` non-reflexive, which isn't allowed either. Moreover, it gets often used in tests.

Anyone is free to put any object in a collection, at least in Java.

Doing nothing seems to be the right thing as then the inherited identity based `equals` gets called and that's probably just right.

Maaartinus,
Let me explain me this more to you. I come across lots of code when I do reviewing for performance. One of the things that strike me is that equals and hashCode are most of the time not implemented. They are just implemented when something breaks and they find that. Usually in dev or test and sometimes this leads to serious production problems which can be very expensive.
When I confront them, the answer usually is that they don't want to code stuff that is not needed, because the methods are not used. And in fact, I find that a valid argument, unneeded code is waste. 

However, then the objects are not prepared for normal use with collections and this can easily lead to production problems. The equals and hashCode methods of Object typically make no sense, identity checking is different from equality checking. Hence, the solution to throw the unsupportedexception in case the object is not intended to be used in a collection. You get fail-fast instead of unintended behavior.

Of course Lombok make equals and hashCode much easier to deal with. However, for the classes which you intentionally don't want to use in a collection and not have equals called on, you still have think about how to specify it, e.g. have excludes, deal with super; and unneeded code gets generated.

I think the non-reflexity, as with other aspects of the equals contract, only needs to hold when it is supported. Unsupported means no contract, no support.

However, you get into trouble when you define unsupported on the super level and want to override that to an actual implementation in the sub class, like:
(case 1)
aSub.equals(aSuper); // returns false (or possible true if instanceof is used)
aSuper.equals(aSub); // throws unsupported exception
So, this is not symmetric.

(case 2)
And also the simpler case with Dog not supporting equals and Cat supporting it:
aCat.equals(aDog); // returns false
aDog.equals(aCat); // throws unsupported exception
is not symmetric.

I think case 1 should be made impossible by making the methods final.
And case 2 is a matter of getting a fail-fast with the conclusion: equals/hashCode should be implemented, a programming error. Equals contract should be fixed.

> One of the things that strike me is that equals and hashCode are most of the time not implemented. They are just implemented when something breaks and they find that.

I've never heard about something like that. When you write just a couple of unit tests (which you really should), there will be some `assertEquals` there and then you'll need it.

> equals... you still have think about how to specify it

Sure, but for me it's an important part of designing the class. I think about equality, so that I better understand what I'm doing. Usually, it's trivial (identity-based equals works for most classes, my entities compare nothing their ID, my value classes compare everything (except for cached fields, if any), etc.).

> I think the non-reflexity, as with other aspects of the equals contract, only needs to hold when it is supported. Unsupported means no contract, no support.

In a sense, I agree. Unsupported means you *are already* violating the contract, so you may happily continue violating it.

I'm not in charge of Lombok, but the authors will most probably have the same doubts. Wouldn't logging (`@EqualsAndHashCode(log=true)`) be good enough for you? It's feature idea which may be more usable and violates no contract.

The problem with `log` is that you would also need to configure the logging system/field.

We're not going to make it easy to break the general contract.

The only thing that I can imagine is that we add a flag to use the object's identity (`System.identityHashCode()` and `other == this`) but we have no concrete plans to add this.

> The problem with `log` is that you would also need to configure the logging system/field.

You could require an additional `@Log` annotation or configuration (IMHO a log configuration would be better than having multiple log annotations, anyway). I personally don't care.

title: @Value - suppressing @Getter?
body:
After scouring the [Lombok feature-list](https://projectlombok.org/features/index.html) and in particular the documentation for the [Getter/Setter](https://projectlombok.org/features/GetterSetter.html) and [`@Value`](https://projectlombok.org/features/Value.html) annotations I have not been able to find any setting that suppresses the code generated by `@Getter`.

> In practice, @Value is shorthand for: final @ToString @EqualsAndHashCode @AllArgsConstructor @FieldDefaults(makeFinal = true, level = AccessLevel.PRIVATE) @Getter

This is important as I do not want to leak references to objects that are themselves mutable.

Effective Java references this type of issue in "Item 39: Make defensive copies when needed". It seems that [`@Wither`](https://projectlombok.org/features/experimental/Wither.html) could partly solve this issue by making actual defensive copies but I want to avoid leaking attributes what so ever, regardless of them being mutable.

While it is possible to roll one's own [`@Value`](https://projectlombok.org/features/Value.html) annotation that omits the [`@Getter`](https://projectlombok.org/features/GetterSetter.html) I would, of course, prefer not to as that would add unwarranted complexity to the codebase if such a setting already exists.

If this feature does not yet exist, I think it would be a good addition to the `@Value` annotation.

nodes.body:
There's no setting, but you can add `@Getter(access=NONE)` and it has priority over the default used by `@Value`, even when used on the class level (field level annotation are even stronger).

> This is important as I do not want to leak references to objects that are themselves mutable.

Composing an immutable object from mutable components is usually hard and usually, the best solution is to avoid them (e.g. by using `javax.time` instead of all the obsolete crap). Wrapping (a defensive copy of) them comes next. If you really have to use them directly, then `@Getter` should surpressed, but so should be `@Wither` as it makes no copy of the field, it only makes a modified shallow copy of `this` object.

Your example doesn't compile: `Implicit super constructor Bar() is undefined. Must explicitly invoke another constructor`.

But if it did, you'd be right. Lombok knows nothing about inherited fields and there's currently no solution for this. The problem happens already with the `@AllArgsConstructor`.

There's not even a good workaround. I just avoid inheriting from classes containing fields. Sometimes, it's a pain, but usually still much better than doing everything manually.

Sorry for not checking code, I was sure it's OK, but `@AllArgsConstructor` requires empty constructor in parent class, which I forgot to add.

This issue is very discouraging to me because I still have to create a ton of `withSomething` boilerplate, and avoiding the extension of model classes makes impossible to implement desired app design... Much hope it will be resolved...

> Sorry for not checking code, I was sure it's OK, but `@AllArgsConstructor` requires empty constructor in parent class, which I forgot to add.

That's another expression of the impossibility to access the parent class. If Lombok could access it, then it could find the non-empty constructor and call it. Note that for `final` fields (i.e., those `@Wither` is meant for) there can be no useful empty constructor.

> Much hope it will be resolved...

I don't know the problem exactly (I'm just someone having contributed some small piece), but IIUIC information about other classes is not available at the time Lombok does its job. The problem is called "resolution" and blocks also other useful features.
Hey thank you @hunter-t . Your tip saved my day.

@jose-jurado Note that `@Accessors(chain = true)` does not but provide the chaining syntax possibility. The `@Setter` still modifies an existing object, while the `@Wither` returns a new object without changing the old one. Sometimes, it doesn't matter, sometimes, you need the former, sometimes, the latter.

title: Implicit @RequiredArgsConstructor on @Data will be removed when using @NoArgsConstructor

nodes.body: This is by design: any explicit constructor - which includes constructors from other Lombok annotations - will cause `@Data` to not generate others.

The bug wouldn't it be that it creates a default constructor with your non null string attribute ?
What default value your attribute would have ?

You'd have to set it before it's useful, but that holds for all fields. Note that `@NonNull` only prevents you from _setting_ a null value, its initial value doesn't matter.

`@NoArgsConstructor`  in combination with a `final` field will cause a compilation error as Java itself will not allow this field to remain non-initialised. But that's not the case here.

May I please reopen this issue. Please let me explain why:

In a standard hibernate java application every managed entity needs a NoArgsConstructor, so that the container can create entity classes. So the example given at the top is quite common. For another reference that states the same problem, see for example this stack overflow question: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/37671467/lombok-requiredargsconstructor-not-working

The most common case actually _IS_ that one needs automatically generated getters, setters, a NoArgsConstructor **and** a RequiredArgsConstructor.

**So I'd like to suggest that this should be the default behaviour of the @Data annotation, becasue it is the most common scenario.**   

Why and where would any additional constructors ever hurt?  Lombok should create them. This is the behaviour that IMHO most users would expect.

If NoArgConstructor works, then RequiredArgsConstructor does nothing more.
If there is a change to be made maybe remove the first because the second does the same job on the same class.

Maybe you meant the AllArgsConstructor

> Why and where would any additional constructors ever hurt?

When your object grow and get new attributes, all the calls to the full constructor must be reworked again.

I have to upvote what  @Doogiemuc said. This is a fairly common scenario. Off course, you can solve all by having just the NoArgsConstructor and calling all setters, but this is error prone and its fairly common to have both constructors since Spring Boot Mappers use the parameter constructors by default, while JPA demands a constructor without any argument. 

The natural usage should be use @Data and include even more constructors with the constructor calls (No/All args). So, please consider reopening this issue, or at least, insert a parameter in @Data to insert both constructors.

If @Data provided both required and noargs by default, Spring Boot implementation with Lombok would become incredibly elegant.

title: Add change detection on @Setter

title: @Builder not preserve default value of field

nodes.body:
I can think of a work-around:
1. change the index field to be of type Integer
2. implement your own AllArgsConstructor (it will be called by the builder).
3. If the index parameter passed in to your customer AllArgsConstructor is null, assign it to its default value in the constructor.

I suggest adding an optional build strategy to `@Builder`: `constructor`(default), `field`, `property`.

- Call the current behaviour: `constructor`, that implies building through a `@AllArgsConstructor`. 
- `field` strategy builds via assigning fields directly, thus implies a `@NoArgsConstructor`.
- `property` strategy builds via `@Setter`s and also implies `@NoArgsConstructor`
This intentional behavior. We're away it's perhaps somewhat unexpected, and in general some way to specify defaults would be nice. We haven't figured out a nice way to make it happen.

title: @SafeCall annotation on local variables as an analogue of the Safe Navigation operator in Groovy (?.)
body:
Hi @rspilker. 
Java language doesn't have ?. operator for safe calling methods of class as in Groovy or Kotlin languages. 
It is impossible to compile code like this: 
`String version = computer?.getSoundcard()?.getUSB()?.getVersion();`
But I'm trying to make some analogue using annotation.
 `@SafeCall String version = computer.getSoundcard().getUSB().getVersion();`
Example of code transformation: [source code](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bulgakovalexander/lombok/feature/safeCall/test/transform/resource/before/SafeNullVal.java), [code after delombok](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bulgakovalexander/lombok/feature/safeCall/test/transform/resource/after-delombok/SafeNullVal.java).
Currently the feature is under development, but I hope to finish it.
What do you think about this feature? Would you like to include it in Lombok project?
 [Link to working branch](https://github.com/bulgakovalexander/lombok/tree/feature/safeCall)

nodes.body:
Long time ago, I started a [lengthy discussion][1] with Reinier and others. There's no real conclusion there, but there's an analysis of tons of corner cases.

In the meantime, I don't believe, it's as useful as I thought initially. IMHO the real problem is the lack of a null-safe type system. Having a nice way to write null-safe expressions doesn't help with the places where I forget to use it. So I'm avoiding nulls everywhere and the possible use cases for the null-safe expressions get avoided, too.

[1]: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/project-lombok/2c9Txx8SKGc/Ab_6OwClFPcJ

Did some more thinking about the onNull() approach and it's as hairy as it was when we discussed it two years ago.

However, mixing the work @bulgakovalexander has done so far with the sneaky trick of generating LetExpr and letting javac figure out, that's promising. Eclipse unfortunately doesn't seem to have anything like it (weirdly enough, there's a 'fake' AST node for JSR/RET shenanigans – SubRoutineStatement. whaaaaaa?), so, yet another dead end.

The onNull() stuff seems so complex I'm rather tempted to just accept `@SafeCall` as a perennial _experimental_ feature with the note that it can't make it out of the experimental package; it's a placeholder until we truly nail it via onNull.

Okay, how about this rule:

Given:

Lombok.onNull(A.B(ARGSLIST1).C.D(), defaultValue), where:

ARGSLIST1 is any (even 0) amount of comma separated expressions and we're just going to copy all of those verbatim so they can contain whatever, and A, B, C, and D are all single-word identifiers, then the following rules apply:

1. If the content of the first arg to the onNull method doesn't fit this, it's an error, for example, Lombok.onNull(a + b, 5) is not legal.

2. It desugars to: Optional.ofNullable(A).flatMap(x -> Optional.ofNullable(x.B(ARGSLIST1))).flatMap(x -> Optional.ofNullable(x.C)).flatMap(x -> Optional.ofNullable(x.D())).orElse(defaultValue).

Given that it desugars to a single expression we can use these in constructor super calls, field initializers, and all the other places making statements is very hard to get right.

It's going to utterly fail if you try some stunt like: onNull(java.lang.String.CASE_INSENSITIVE), but that makes no sense in the first place: packages cannot be null, and static invocations/references to static fields can't NPE, so that's just weird and I'm okay with lombok trying to desugar that and producing WTF code that produces vague compiler errors (because we can't tell those are packages/types instead of potentially null variables/fields/parameters).

Every '.' in the chain is guarded, but any null-derefs in any argumentlists won't be, but I think that's fine and probably even desired behaviour (if you want to guard those too, well, toss an onNull around that; we can write it to support recursion like that).


There's no need to postprocess at the bytecode level and it does therefore delombok fine, although the delombed result does look like some seriously ugly crazy code. Still, it would work fine. It would be slower than you'd expect, but lambdas can in theory be fast so hopefully future JVM releases fix that. It wouldn't work in java7 or below, and crucially that means android is excluded, but I think this is the way forward.

About the 'it desugars to ugly tripe' problem: Oh you don't know the half of it. We'd have to sneakythrow-guard ALL the intermediate method invocations, given that flatMap takes a function and those can't throw checked exceptions. Still, we CAN do that:

    .flatMap(x -> {try{return Optional.ofNullable(x.A(ARGSLIST1));}catch(Throwable t){throw Lombok.sneakyThrow(t);})

Thoughts?

LGTM except may for the package confusion being slightly worse as it can be also something like
```
onNull(com.mypackage.Myclass.ANullableStaticMethod())
```
or
```
onNull(com.mypackage.Myclass.someStaticField.someMember.someSubmember)
```
which are legitimate uses, but I don't care as there's maybe one FQN in thousand files of mine.

---

> Every '.' in the chain is guarded, but any null-derefs in any argumentlists won't be

Agreed! For "full null-safety", catching the NPE would be the way to go (if someone thought it was a good idea).

> It would be slower than you'd expect

This may be a problem for some performance-obsessed users. I could imagine generating a faster code in the places where locals are allowed, but this is more work and can be done later (or never). Relying on JVM improvements is OK.

Errr, good point. That does mean this:

onNull(SomeType.staticMethod().whatever()) will not actually work, and we can't tell without throwing resolution into the mix. We can try our own resolution, but let's not. To go into some detail:

We could scan for fields, local var names, and parameters, that's easy enough. This doesn't sound like a good solution; inherited fields from your supertype (and statically imported fields/constants) won't be picked up, and it'll be _silent_ – the nullguard simply won't be applied. Which scares me, so let's not go there.

We can also go back to the rule that only method calls are null-guarded, with field accesses (which look equivalent to packages and typerefs) being copied over verbatim without null-guarding. Fields aren't exactly popular, but that is still a bit surprising and it'll be silent.

Blindly applying denulling, thus breaking with syntax errors if types or packages are involved, at least isn't silent, and in theory we can 'fix it' later if we find a good, fast, reliable way to hook into the resolution.

It's a shame that converting it to optional chains with lambdas will make it run very slowly until tier 2/3 compilation, where it will hopefully get inlined.

What about your work with LiveInjector and redefining classes in the compiler at runtime? Would it be possible to define a class for a new safe navigation AST node `?.` rather than being limited to what is already present?

It's not currently used in lombok other than for the experimental (broken?) global checked exception disabling - did you find it was too fragile?

@nallar The LiveInjector is a really dirty hack that we prefer not to dig into without putting a lot more thought into it. It would probably also be quite a thing to try to introduce into the lombok plugins for MS VisualStudio and IntelliJ which also makes us rather hesitant to go down that path.

Hi, IMHO the SafeCall would be a very interesting feature.
I would love to see it, any update on this item?

title: Something with annotation values that use a constant instead of a literal

nodes.body:
I think this qualifies as the most exotic thing ever in the entire world. How did you find this bug? I'm... flabbergasted.

To wit:

* If you put `@FieldDefaults(makeFinal=true)` on a class, then static fields are _skipped_ – they won't be made final.
* If you put the above _and_ `@UtilityClass` on a class, then you do end up with a `static` and `final` field even if you started out with a non-static, non-final one. This is a bug in lombok, but not a particularly important one.
* Given the above bug, you end up twisting something like `String foo = "hello";` into `static final String foo = "hello";` but in a way that javac, at least, does NOT mark it as a compile-time constant. This is generally not relevant.
* ... unless you then try to use a ref to that field in an annotation. Then it matters.

> If you put the above and `@UtilityClass` on a class, then you do end up with a static and final field even if you started out with a non-static, non-final one. This is a bug in lombok, but not a particularly important one.

I don't think so. IIUYC your fix makes combining `@UtilityClass` and `@FieldDefaults(makeFinal = true)` pointless as the latter will *never* do anything. Therefore, the old execution order was actually the right one, making the combined annotations to a constant definition tool. :)

Not that I'd care...
FieldDefaults is not intended to _ever_ turn static things final. If the two now combine to do nothing useful, at best that means lombok should warn you that what you're doing isn't useful.
How do we create a Lombok annotated class of public static constants, without the repetitious `public static final` modifiers?
