title: WrappedThrows

nodes.body:
The cool thing about `@SneakyThrows` is that it just... throws it.

Here we have to wrap, which raises the issue of: Kay, but, WHAT should we wrap? Presumably, there's no sense wrapping something that needn't actually be wrapped.

That'd be:

* RuntimeException
* Error
* anything that is declared in the closest method scope's 'throws' line
* anything that is declared in any catch block associated with any encompassing try.

Therefore, we'd have to generate an instanceof for all of that.

We can do that, of course. It's boilerplate hidden from view, who cares that it might turn into quite the unwieldy list. Also, presumably, if you're using `@WrappedThrows`, you aren't catching a whole host of explicitly listed exception types.

I like it. Not too high on the todolist though, I think; it's a bit exotic.

Rethrow RuntimeException is generally a bad coding practice.
What about args like: `@WrappedThrows(catch = {IOException.class}, value = {MyCustomNonRuntimeException.class})` or `@WrappedThrows(MyCustomNonRuntimeException.class)` which will catch any non-runtime exception on the catch block

Also I think @SneakyThrows is a bad coding practice ^^ This idea is better, but not likely to be used: How often would you use this in a real project? Not really often, I think.

You can say things like 'throwing RuntimeException is a bad coding practice', but that doesn't make it true.

Facts are required. An appeal to authority also, generally, does not apply unless it's one heck of an authority.

Defaulting to RuntimeException is fine until such convincing argumentation is provided.


The notion of being able to specify exactly WHAT the exception should be wrapped into, that's a fine idea.

Given the confusion, I don't think it's a good idea to name either one 'value'. That is, `@WrappedThrows(SomeExType.class)` simply won't be legal. We'll force you to specify catch= and wrapWith= or something similar. catch= will default to Throwable.class, wrapWith will default to RuntimeException.

I guess, I'd like to use configuration for specifying the wrapping exception. It could be something allowing things like `e.rethrowIfCausedBy(IOException.class)` or whatever. I guess, I'd always use the same exception. Defaulting to `RuntimeException` sounds good.

Regarding the wrapped exception, I guess, catching everything what has to be caught is a good default and would make me happy >90% of time. So writing just `@WrappedThrows` without any arguments would be the favorite usage.

> `@SneakyThrows` is so useful that it's worth the risk (with periodic grep-audits for mistakes)

I'd suggest to write a test loading all *your* classes and scanning the methods for the annotation. I do this for similar reasons and it works perfectly and fast (initially, I used `ClassPath` from Guava, but that's too slow as there's much more stuff on the class path than my code; so I scan a directory or a JAR file instead).

> but I'd love to use `@WrapThrows` instead.

I was too afraid to use `@SneakyThrows` as the undeclared exception could sneak though some third party code meant to catch *everything*. Lacking `@WrappedThrows`, I wrap everything manually and that's rather boring.

> I'm perfectly content with `RuntimeException` as the wrapper.

Me too.
It is fairly common for transaction-processing libs to commit on checked exceptions??? That sounds _INSANE_ to me, I must be missing something.

[Insane but true](https://docs.spring.io/spring/docs/4.2.x/spring-framework-reference/html/transaction.html#transaction-declarative-rolling-back):

> *In its default configuration, the Spring Framework’s transaction infrastructure code only marks a transaction for rollback in the case of runtime, unchecked exceptions; that is, when the thrown exception is an instance or subclass of RuntimeException. ( Errors will also - by default - result in a rollback). Checked exceptions that are thrown from a transactional method do not result in rollback in the default configuration.*

It seems to be configurable (in a wonderful XML), however, it may not work if Spring relies on the method signature specifying no checked exceptions.

Okay. My head asplodes. It's a cliche, but, what were they smoking?

I'm having a hard time catering to clear boneheadedness like this. Surely there is a sane explanation, but I may have to insist I get it before we introduce any lombok features that attempt to cater to this (so far, to me anyway) crazy default.

Fortunately, I do see the point in wrapping exceptions, but not to cater to crazy spring defaults, just, for general purposes, and in passing it would help out the spring db users a bit.

Still struggling with the ideas of syntax and how we need to avoid attempting to catch anything for wrapping when you catch it yourself; the feature sounds quite a bit more complicated than `@SneakyThrows`, weirdly.

> Okay. My head asplodes. It's a cliche, but, what were they smoking?

Not sure, but I guess I should try it, too.

> Still struggling with the ideas of syntax

See [my above comment](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/1289#issuecomment-575785079). Basically three optional arguments:
- `catching() default {Exception.class}` - what's not there won't get touched
- `passing() default {RuntimeException.class}` - what's there will be rethrown
- `throwing() default RuntimeException.class` - the wrapping exception class

The real default should be configurable. It doesn't support the possibility of throwing different exceptions based on what gets caught, but that's IMHO not necessary.

> and how we need to avoid attempting to catch anything for wrapping when you catch it yourself

I see, you wrote "anything that is declared in any catch block associated with any encompassing try.", but I can't see why. When the user catches something, then it's the same as if they didn't throw it, so it doesn't matter for the resulting code, does it? *I don't think we have to ever look at the wrapped code at all.*

The most basic usage would just
- catch and rethrow all declared exceptions plus `RuntimeException` in the first clause
- catch and wrap `Exception` in the second clause
- do not touch `Error`.

For me and for the poor Spring users, it'd be enough. It could happen that it doesn't compile, but only if the original method doesn't compile either (or it declares `throws Exception`, but then the wrapping is pretty pointless).

For the general usage, see the above comment.

> the feature sounds quite a bit more complicated than `@SneakyThrows`, weirdly.

I must be missing something.

Good point. And if someone catches, say, IOException, in the catch block rethrows it, and they have annotated the method with `@WrapExceptions, then, presumably, they still wanna wrap that.

You're not missing something – you're right, there is no need to introspect the body, but I thought we did, and that's why I said it seemed complex. Rejoice! This shouldn't be too difficult :)

Sorry about missing out on all the commentary since January, not sure why Github only notified me now.

As a historical note the "runtime exceptions rollback, checked exceptions commit" rule dates back at least to the EJB spec of the late 90s (checked exceptions were considered "application exceptions" - an intentional part of control flow). It's weird but seems like just one more bit of downstream inanity caused by checked exceptions.

IMHO (emphasis on the H, since someone else is doing the work):

I'd make the first pass at this wrapper as simple as possible, no configuration options to start. Always wrap with RuntimeException, always wrap every checked exception that isn't declared. The reasoning is:

 * Anyone who wants alternative behavior can always use a try/catch block instead.
 * You can always add other options later after this feature gets some real-world use.
 * This is the easiest thing to implement.

Cover the most likely use case, get some real world experience, then build configuration options for the pain points (if they exist). My WAG is that the only real configuration anyone will want is a global config flag for "use this wrapper exception instead" but even that might not be necessary.

Keeping it simple is always a good idea but I'm not sure if we would restrict this feature to much by doing so. Adding some parameters and create some dynamic code is not that hard.

Right now I still try to figure out how the generated code should look like. The example I added in my last comment will also show an error if we try to catch an exception that cannot be thrown or was catched earlier...
Any word on this? As simplified at the end of this discussion, I'd use it.
Would be good to have it!

@stickfigure @Maaartinus I think you two appear to be the primary folks who want this and who have some idea about what it should look like. Pinging you two in case you're thinking of solutions I've missed!

@rzwitserloot I appreciate the long response. Some things that come to mind:

1) You seem to be far too nice! I personally have little problem telling people that demand features to bugger off, but I guess this is your call to make.

2) I think throwing any kind of checked exception out of `@Rethrows` (or whatever) is a nonstarter for all the reasons you point out. If someone wants checked exceptions, they can use `@SneakyThrows` (or use try/catch). I see no value in supporting that use case, and would refer any demands for it to point 1.

3) I think you are vastly underestimating the appeal of throwing runtime exceptions. I can't tell you how many times I see catch/throw new RuntimeException(e) littered across codebases.

It seems like this conversation can be roughly summarized:

Me: "We need a way of rethrowing checked exceptions as runtime exceptions"
You: "This won't work because of [...problems...] wrapping with checked exceptions"
Me: "But the whole point of this feature is to avoid throwing checked exceptions!?"

We have two camps, "Checked Exceptions Are Good" and "Checked Exceptions Are Bad". The later camp has pretty thoroughly routed the former camp at this point. C# abandoned checked exceptions. Newer JVM languages like Kotlin and Scala have completely abandoned checked exceptions. It's not niche.

This `@Rethrows` feature is proposed specifically to make life easier for the "Checked Exceptions Are Bad" camp, which I will hazard a guess is a majority of Java platform programmers these days. It doesn't need broader appeal. @cchudant clearly falls into the "checked-good" camp and is not the target audience.

Regarding Spring - just wanted to mention that the runtime vs checked transaction rollback convention (and thus problem with `@SneakyThrows`) exists not just in Spring but also in Guice Persist and in old school EJB persistence. It isn't just a Spring issue.

FWIW I'm willing to do the work and submit a PR for this. If you're still hard veto, is there some way of making this an optional third-party add-on to lombok? If so could you point me at an example?

I too appreciate how much @rzwitserloot has obviously thought about this, and was not sure I was going to comment because of how strongly held the conclusions of the post seemed, but FWIW @stickfigure summarized in words my own thinking (when I read the original post) better than I would be able to write down.

> The later camp has pretty thoroughly routed the former camp at this point. C# abandoned checked exceptions. Newer JVM languages like Kotlin and Scala have completely abandoned checked exceptions. It's not niche.

And yet there's all sorts of noise about returning `Result<Err, V>` style things, which is a crappy reinvention of checked exceptions, and a lot of traffic about moving things into the typing system (such as nullity). Checked exceptions is moving alternate method exits into the typing system. The fact that scala which _loves_ to insult java by stating its typing system is primitive, decided to ditch checked exceptions means that the authors either have their heads up their behinds, or they owe us an explanation. Where's the paper showing that _despite_ strongly held beliefs that moving things into the typing system is fantastic, checked exceptions are so incredibly bad, it was worth going against their own strongly held principles?

You see why 'but scala!' does not convince me at all. I think scala as a language is a mistake on almost every level. In fact, a low-key way to convince me that X is a good idea is to tell me: "Scala did the opposite!". Not "Scala also did it". "Kotlin did X!" or "C# did x!" also has zero net effect on convincing me X is a good idea (but it does, at least, not suggest that X is a _bad_ idea, whereas I do get that sense if you told me that "Scala did X", so that's improvement, maybe?)

At any rate, even if what you say is true, it doesn't matter. Java has checked exceptions. I'm sticking with my veto, the fact that you're convinced checked exceptions are 'dead' doesn't mean every java user is in that camp.

The use case of wishing to wrap one checked exception into another is __not__ pointless in the slightest; that's apparently simply a code style you don't use / don't like. We can't just eliminate it here, unfortunately.

Trivial example:

```java
public void saveGame() throws SaveSystemException {
 // some implementation that saves into the DB
}
```

The 'signature' of this method (including the javadoc) is about saving games. That's it. It says what it does, not how it does it. The signature also acknowledges that saving may run into various kinds of failures, hence, it lists an exception that this method may throw. Let's say it's checked. You should then be wrapping the SQLExceptions that occur at the DB layer into SaveSystemExceptions. That's.. how the system is supposed to work. And many style guides, books, and libraries do exactly that. The fact that even more libraries don't do this and that many have tired of it doesn't change this.

It's a classic situation of 2 significantly different code styles, where some hypothetical lombok feature caters quite nicely to one crowd, and utterly befuddles the other. __We veto those__. Sorry, I know that sucks if you're in the crowd that loves the feature. I know why you proposed it. It'd work if we name it`@RethrowsForPeopleWhoThinkCheckedExceptionSuck`, but that isn't an appropriate name for obvious reasons.

This feature would be called `@Rethrows` and has stapled to it this pseudo-restriction that it doesn't work well or has seemingly bizarre behaviour _unless_ you solely wrap in runtime exceptions. This makes eminent sense to you. It would seem nuts to people in the other camp.

>  exists not just in Spring but also in Guice Persist and in old school EJB persistence. It isn't just a Spring issue.

Get me written promises by the spring, guice persist, and EJB team that they categorically agree this behaviour is idiotic but that they feel locked out due to backwards compatibility needs and I'll reconsider.

If they aren't willing to say that, then this argument doesn't make sense. The core maintainers of these libraries need to be written off as idiots in order to establish that this feature is so crucial, lombok needs to come up with a solution to unfuck those libraries. That... doesn't seem right. Your 'camp' is on the opposite of where the spring+guicepersist+EJB-persistence folks live, and I'm pretty sure they're much larger.

> I'm willing to do the work and submit a PR for this.

That definitely helps, but without satisfactory answers to how it works, we'd be forced to turn PRs down, and as it stands, I think that satisfactory answers are impossible to provide.

> is there some way of making this an optional third-party add-on to lombok?

Due to various complications in loaders (Specifically, eclipse OSGi-equinox, and java's module system), you can't simply add a second jar to the compilation class path with lombok extensions. We wish that would be possible (a lot of lombok is written with registries of handlers in mind, with some facilities to interact with other handlers without being dependent on their APIs even - because we want that to be possible), but so far we haven't been able to deliver on nice ways to integrate with jigsaw/equinox and keep that 'just add a jar' ability intact. Thus, right now, to extend lombok, you have to fork it.

@sergmain Your feature request boils down to: "Can you write a lombok feature that is custom designed for my specific company". It's a fine highlight: If many companies handroll bizarro solutions like this, and a proposed feature request is not capable of catering to most such setups, the feature request isn't useful.

But, in case that was a specific: "Hey, would you mind writing this specific thing", the answer is obviously no.

It's not code anybody would ever write by hand, but that's far less of a problem than my concerns. I do worry about linter tools going ape on this, but I can't recall anything that would specifically set off a linter.

We're heading to:

* We add the wrap-into exception to your throws clause list unless it is already there, unless it is specifically `RuntimeException`, given that this is clearly an indication the author wants to forget about it.
* We catch any Exception and then do a lot of instanceof checks on it: If it's RuntimeException, we throw it onwards unmolested (possibly we do that with a separate catch instead. We could).
* We then instanceof against ALL types listed in the `throws` clause (including the wrap-into type, as we added it). For each, we cast-and-throw the exception unmolested.
* Finally, if none of the `instanceof` if cases triggered, we wrap. We don't copy the message, we use `initCause` to init the cause. We demand the wrap-to type has a no-args constructor, and operate without checking this assumption (so, you'd get a compiler error if you try to use this feature and wrap into a throwable type that doesn't have a noargs).
* Message is, at least for now, not configurable.
* For now we have no facility to add more than one rethrows config to any given method. You can list any number of exception types in the 'from' and you're free to omit it entirely (in which case we act as if you wrote `from = Exception.class`). You must pick exactly one exception type to wrap to; it is not an optional annotation parameter.
* We check if you include j.l.Error or j.l.Throwable in your `from` list. If you include these, we just generate an error and do nothing. It gets too complicated, and it seems like a bizarre style choice to try to wrap those.
* We check if you attempt to pick Error or Throwable as 'wrap-to' and error out, doing nothing. The reason is - I don't want to write `catch (Throwable)`, but those instanceof checks can compile-fail if you try to e.g. do:

```java
catch (Exception e) {
  if (e instanceof SomeError) {}
```

So if non-Exception throwables are involved anywhere, it all just falls apart. We can't know if some type is _not_ an Exception subtype (I guess we could attempt to do a convention scan and see if the types end in `Error`, but maybe we shouldn't do that), but we can at least detect specifically `j.l.Error` and `j.l.Throwable` being used in wrap-from or wrap-to and throw in the towel immediately.

My fear is that we build all this and linters go ape on the result. I was also fearing performance complaints ("There is a completely pointless `instanceof` check in the generated code that cannot fire!"), but now I'm rethinking that concern. Is someone really going to complain about a _performance issue in a catch block_? Exceptions are rather well known as being pretty bad for performance, so you should not be using them for control flow in a tight loop in the first place.

It wouldn't solve @sergmain 's need to rewrite the message, but I think their setup is made up (no standard in common use whatsoever), and the topic of messages can probably be delayed for later - I don't think any of what we decide here is going to get in the way of future plans to do stuff with the messages. I can see explicitly calling out in the docs that we reserve the right to mess with messages.

Should we 'launch' with "copy the message from the cause"? I'm open to that idea, though given that the causal chain ought to be logged, that's just duplicating the same string over and over, no?

>  and initCause only as a fall-back when a single-arg-constructor cannot be found, as e.g.

We can't do that. We have no way to list the constructors available, at least, not without forcing rounds and adding a whole boatload of maintenance burden. Not an option. Given that it's not an option, that's why I want the initCause: That works for more types.

UncheckedIOException is voodoo magic, but it does throw a wrench in the gears. We could detect it, perhaps. Or we ditch the initCause plan and say, after all, that you can only wrap-to throwable types that have a `MyThrowable(Throwable cause)` constructor. But, something as common as `NumberFormatException` simply doesn't have that constructor, so this is all very disappointing.

We could:

* Default to `new X(cause)`, and write a separate hardcoded list into the lombok sources with known exception types that require `initCause` instead; NumberFormatException would be on this list.
* Default to `new X(); x.initCause()`, and write a separate hardcoded list with known exception types that must go via constructor instead. `UncheckedIOEx` would be on that list.
* Same as above and also add lombok.config keys to allow you to add additional exception types to the 'do it the other way' list.
* ... and that lombok.config goes a lot further and lets you configure calling `new X(cause.getMessage(), cause)`, or even a static method so that you can write your own code for how to 'map' one exception into another.
* Treat `UncheckedIOException` as a precedence-setting item: initCause is used normally, unless the wrap-to type's simple name begins with Unchecked, in which case we use the `new X(cause)` constructor.

I'm tempted to go with option 2. In other words, initCause but add awareness of UncheckedIOException specifically.

> I like the "copy the message from the cause" approach (despite the duplication) but wonder how you'd like to do it (without reflection), as there's no public Throwable.setMessage() method.

We'd call `new X(cause.getMessage(); x.initCause(cause);` - in other words, require that the wrap-to type has a constructor that takes 1 string. This is _far_ more common than a constructor that takes 1 cause, so I'm willing to accept that as a precondition (with the caveat that we have a hardcoded list of known types where we know we have to change things. UncheckedIOEx would be on there: Oh, for that one, just call `new UncheckedIOException(cause.getMessage(), cause)` and leave it at that.

I'd prefer option 4 as it offers wide flexibility for all sorts of cases, yet I'd be happy with a start with option 2, as configuration options could be something to add later on. Option 5 feels rather nay to me, as it introduces name-magic, and is probably prone to cause trouble in the future if later iterations want to refine the feature by e.g. adding config-options ...

> I still think you're all overthinking this. I'll make one last plea.

I think you should be able to get exactly what you want using the current state of discussion, by the following syntax:
```java
@WrappedThrows(from=Exception.class, to=RuntimeException.class)
```

Reasonable defaults for `from`/`to` would be nice, but as @rzwitserloot on Jan 30, 2022 feared maintenance burden because expecting too many issues about "throwing RuntimeException is bad", that has been vetoed (at least the "`to`"-part  :-P ... we could maybe convince him to have the `from`  default to something like `Exception.class`?!?).

@stickfigure wrote:

> There are two discrete camps in the Java world, "use checked exceptions" and "don't use checked exceptions". @rzwitserloot, you are obviously in the former camp, yet you added @SneakyThrows to lombok so I'm a bit puzzled about your motivations.

I disagree that there are camps like this. I'm in the 'ecosystem' camp: A programming language's utility and expressive power derive primarily from the ecosystem: What libraries are available, what tutorials, how many folks on the planet use this language, and what style is popular? You should follow in the footsteps of what the ecosystem does and where the ecosystem appears to be going unless you are willing to accept a significant amount of complication and therefore have extremely good reasons to deviate.

Checked exceptions exist and are widely used by the ecosystem, therefore, no matter how much you think they suck, you can't stick your head in the sand.

If SneakyThrows comes across as an enabler for 'head in the sand', then that's unfortunate. That's not what it is for, and if you try to use it that way, you're not going to have a good time. After all:

```
@SneakyThrows(IOException.class)
public String readFileFullyAsUtf8(Path path) {
  ...
}
```

> It has a couple quirks that make it imperfect

The inability for callers to catch a sneakythrown checked exception is a little more than 'a quirk'.


is a horrible idea: Callers __cannot__ catch those `IOException`s, except by catching all exceptions, and doing an `instanceof` + cast (or the new patterned instanceof). Javac won't let you write ` try { readFileFullyAsUtf8(..); } catch (IOException e) {}`.


So, why does SneakyThrows exist?

Sometimes a checked exception is thrown but is either not 'expectable' or not 'handleable'. For example, the IOException that is declared when you write `new String(someByteArr, "UTF-8")` is not 'expectable'. The JVM spec guarantees UTF-8 support. The catch code I'd have to write here is crazy. What do I put in the catch block? `throw new InternalError("UTF-8 is missing: Your JVM is corrupt");`? If doing that is the right idea, I need to wrap every line of java code in a try/catch in case `String.class` has been removed from your JVM distro or what not, that's clearly not right. The vast majority of checked exceptions aren't like that, but in rare case they are. And that's annoying. "Not expectable" means: "I read the documentation and I believe I understand it. I cannot fathom any realistic scenario in which this exception could ever be thrown. Hence, if it IS thrown, I do not actually understand what is happening". That's quite a significant definition, and most checked exceptions don't fall under it.

Similarly, sometimes I write code and a checked exception is declared. I know it can happen, but there's absolutely nothing I can do about this. "Just aggressively asplode the stack until you get to the entrypoint and it will catch all throwables and abort / log / reset accordingly" is as good as anything else. For example, say I'm writing a command line tool to do some DB interaction. All SQLExceptions likely fall in this camp at that point: Print stack trace, terminate process - that's the best possible action at that point. Plan A in such cases is to just add `throws SQLException` to all relevant signatures, but due to rules about not adding new checked exceptions when you override, that is not always possible.

In those 2 cases (not handleable / not expectable), it'd be really nice if you just ignore them (not expectable), or throw them without declaring it (not handleable). SneakyThrows deals with both.

> Yes, Java has checked exceptions, but there is a large and growing body of people who don't use them.

Says you. But, even if true, I don't care. There may well be a large and growing body of people who `write_their_variables_like_so` and I wouldn't care about them either. I need to believe that 'their camp' is going to take over and become the new normal, and given that `java.*` itself uses lots of checked exceptions, that is never going to happen. That body of people who 'do not use them' are aware that they're off the reservation and that the rest of the ecosystem disagrees with them. If they do not understand that, they're just wrong.

> `@SneakyThrows` targets the "don't use checked exceptions" crowd.

Very much the opposite, as explained above.

> Since 95% of the users of @WrappedThrows will be the "don't use checked exceptions" camp

A wild claim with absolutely no backing.

I think you're living in your own little world. More power to you, if it works for you, that's great, and don't fix what isn't broken.

But it's quite a different thing if you conclude that therefore everybody who doesn't live in your little world is wrong, and that lombok should actively proselytise for it.

We can debate who is in a bigger bubble but I don't think anyone can argue that try/catch exception/throw runtimeexception is not an *incredibly* common pattern in Java code. I've never seen a java codebase that wasn't littered with them. Anyone know how to get a count of this pattern via some sort of structural search of github?

The Java stdlib is incredibly inconsistent when it comes to checked vs runtime exceptions. You seem to be making the argument for that - why does `String(byte[], String)` throw a checked `UnsupportedOperationException` whereas `Integer.parse(String)` throws an unchecked `NumberFormatException`? Your argument for `@SneakyThrows` is exactly the same as mine: Other programmers misuse checked exceptions and we need a convenient escape. The only difference is how broadly we interpret the word "misuse".

Every argument you just made for `@SneakyThrows` applies to `@WrappedThrows`. The only ergonomic difference is that instead of catching an Exception and calling instanceof, you catch RuntimeException and call instanceof the cause. In practice we usually let these exceptions bubble up to a broad exception handler that doesn't care what the types are. `@SneakyThrows` is great but it has a hidden footgun because several popular database frameworks have behavioral differences when checked vs unchecked exceptions are thrown across an aspect boundary. So here we are.

I'd rather Lombok not proselytize at all; it should simply cut out boilerplate for patterns people already use. Programmers already heavily use "wrap checked exceptions" as a pattern, and lombok already enables equivalent behavior - slightly imperfectly. I'm simply asking for this existing feature to be made less dangerous.

> I don't think anyone can argue that try/catch exception/throw runtimeexception is not an incredibly common pattern in Java code.

I'll argue. That is not an _incredibly common pattern in Java code_. If it was, specifically, then you should be advocating for `@WrapAllCheckedExceptionsAsRuntimeException` instead, because that sidesteps the problem of 'folks who do not live in your bubble will misunderstand what it does'.

> I've never seen a java codebase that wasn't littered with them.

Can you cut this out, please? You're not going to convince me that you are aware of a world outside your bubble by continuing to explain how much you live in your bubble. You're a programmer with technical chops, surely you can use that analytical power on your own argument and realize in incredibly fruitless it is here.

> The Java stdlib is incredibly inconsistent when it comes to checked vs runtime exceptions.

Absolutely. That only further highlights how picking any particular bubble and building a feature such that it makes sense _only_ to those who live inside it is a really daft thing to do. The basis (how exceptions are designed and used in `java.*`) leads to a varied view. Bubblethink bad, especially here.

I've discussed it with @rspilker and the technical solution proposed above does not work. I'll try to gather my thoughts and explain why it won't work in the weekend. Consider this issue as hopeless for a few months at least, I'm not particularly hopeful a technical solution exists.

I'm also putting a moratorium on any further discussion on feature scope. I appreciate the insights, @stickfigure. But it's ran its course. Let's focus on implementation from here on out.

Problem:

UncheckedIOException is just a disaster. It doesn't have a no-args, but that's not the worst of it: It specifically requires an IOException. That means e.g. `@Wrapped(from = GeneralSecurityException.class, to = UncheckedIOException.class)` simply __cannot__ be made to work, but I fear that folks are going to write it, and will not understand the compiler error that falls out. We can't write code that detects this situation and warns or acts accordingly; lombok cannot know that e.g. `@Wrapped(from = FileNotFoundException.class, to = UncheckedIOException.class)` __is__ sensible code. We do not have resolution ; which is required to know that FNFEx is a subtype of IOEx.

In essence, the underlying issue here is that no specifications about the nature of the constructors of an exception type exist, but folks think that `@Wrap(this in that)` should be possible. This indicates that users (me included) simply do not understand that there's a semantic definition that needs to be adhered to first. Hence, we can't just make up a definition and stick it in our docs: Your average java programmer wouldn't know they need to look at them for guidance on semantics of the target exception type. This is one of those 'folks do not understand how complex it really is' issues, and that leads to confusion.

Problem:

Imagine `@WrappedThrows(from = Exception.class, to = RuntimeException.class)`.

What does this mean?

What it literally says is that all RuntimeExceptions (given that they are also Exceptions), should be wrapped in.. RuntimeException. However, that's a rather silly thing to want to do so I simply do not accept. I think the above is something many folks will want to write (testify, @stickfigure !), which goes a long way towards explaining why I keep running into problems translating this feature request into an actual implementation plan.

In essence:

* The general idea of "I wish to take all CHECKED exceptions thrown in the body of this method and rethrow them as this RuntimeException type" is something I imagine many java programmers want to do.
* ... and most programmers will think the above line accomplishes this.
* ... but that's not actually what it means. This feature is therefore too confusing to release, if it works this way.
* conclusion: It should not work this way.

Thus, a dilemma. Do we take the above code and do what we _think_ people want (namely: Do NOT wrap RuntimeException in itself), or do we take the above code and do what it says, even though we think it's probably not what they wanted?

I'm __vetoing__ the latter. If the community / @rspilker wants to veto the former we need a rather significant redesign of all this.

One way out is to say in the docs that we __never__ wrap something in its own type or a supertype.

But, this gets us to...

Problem:

Imagine `@WrappedThrows(from = Exception.class, to = MyCustomEx.class)`.

Note that, due to lack of resolution, we have no idea if MyCustomEx is checked or not.

What does this mean, in regards to RuntimeExceptions?

* Given the comment immediately preceding this one, even though the text literally appears to say: "Wrap everything that is an Exception into MyCustomEx", we add our standard caveat: Any exceptions that are MyCustomEx are not wrapped and just thrown.
* But what about RuntimeException? I can completely understand, especially in light of the fact that the argument 'just do what the line says' is a dead end (see previous comment as to why I just do not accept that view - it's simply not what was intended) - that the intent of the programmer who wrote that line is that they want to wrap all _CHECKED_ exceptions. Not RuntimeExceptions. Whether MyCustomEx is checked or not is immaterial.
* ... but I  can also understand that the intent was to wrap everything that is an Exception and is not a MyCustomEx (so, including RuntimeExceptions), into MyCustomEx. I see how one would interpret the line that way, and I see how one would have such a need.

Thus, the feature proposal, if it works this way, __is dead__. We do not release features where two incompatible understandings of a line exist where both understandings are reasonable.

But we have a way out - we KNOW the type hierarchy of RuntimeEx. We can detect if you list `RuntimeException`, `Exception`, or even `Throwable` and act accordingly.

One way out is that we add `@WrapChecked(MyCustomException.class)`, which specifically covers: "All Exceptions, except RuntimeExceptions and MyCustomExceptions, will be wrapped".

Now we still have the use-case of: I wish to wrap all exceptions, even runtime exceptions, into this custom type. If we allow it via `@Wrap(from = Exception.class, to = MyCustomEx.class)`, we run into the problem that this will likely be interpreted as / the intent of the author was '... but not RuntimeExceptions', but they don't know that they should be using `@WrapChecked` for that instead. So, I don't want to accept that code and error out instead. But what if the intent specifically is: No, I do want to wrap RuntimeExceptions.

I guess we can allow it if you write: `@Wrap(from = {Exception.class, RuntimeException.class}, to = MyCustomEx.class)`. Because now the intent of the author is clear, and anybody reading this code has more than enough to figure out both intent and effect. But it's ugly as all get out: It seems on its face crazy to do this, given that `Exception` already covers `RuntimeException`. I don't like `@WrapAll` either - I don't think the `All` does the job here (the job being: Convey that the tricky decision is whether RuntimeExceptions are included or not). `@WrapCheckedAndUnchecked` would work, but what a mouthful.

We're paying for the sins of crappy design here. `Exception` as a type should have been sealed, and the only 2 subtypes of it should have been `java.lang.UncheckedException` and `java.lang.CheckedException`, and then we wouldn't have any of these problems.

Yes, it's a bummer that there is no CheckedException base class.

I don't think anyone wants double wrapping. `@WrappedThrows(from = Exception.class, to = RuntimeException.class)` should not wrap RuntimeException in RuntimeException. I also don't think the name matters too much. It's not like `@SneakyThrows` really explains it, you just have to learn what it does.

You're right, the problem is `@WrappedThrows(from = Exception.class, to = MyCustomRuntimeException.class)`. Does the programmer want a regular RuntimeException thrown as-is or just the checked exceptions? It's plausible to want either, though in practice I think the common case is "leave runtimes alone". `@WrapChecked` would be fine.

Another option is something like `@WrappedThrows(from = Exception.class, to = MyCustomRuntimeException.class, wrapRuntime = false)` (with a default of false). A bit weird if you say something like from=IOException.class.

Speaking as a user, I really just want `@WrapChecked` with defaults from=Exception.class to=RuntimeException.class. Maybe sometimes a different to= exception. Other situations are not so common that typing the try/catch out longhand is onerous.

I wish I could figure out how to do some sort of structural search to check the frequency of these patterns across all of github. It seems like sourcegraph should be able to do something like that, but I'm not seeing it.

I agree with `UncheckedIOException` being a disaster ... yet I can't imagine what kind of error message would actually pop up, and if this would be totally confusing or more or less understandable. If we had some kind of "option 4" from https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/1289#issuecomment-1104020602 we could actually work around such cases by configuring `new UncheckedIOException(new IOException(cause))`, yet I don't really would like to have such code as *default*... but if anyone wants to configure it somehow, I'd be okay with it.

Regarding the other "bears" -- how about something like
```java
@Wrap(from = {Exception1.class, ...}, to = MyWrapperEx.class, dontWrap = {RuntimeException.class, Error.class})
```
with some reasonable default for `dontWrap` (e.g. like in this example). [I wondered about naming this `except` but maybe this might be confusing...]

Thus the user would get total control of what to wrap and what not to wrap if needed, and even making it somewhat more explicit that there are things that don't get wrapped. Yet: depending on the defaults it could make "regular" usage quite compact:

```java
@Wrap(from = {Exception1.class, ...})
```

given defaults: `to = RuntimeException.class` and `dontWrap = {RuntimeException.class, Error.class}`.

With other defaults it might differ a bit, of course.

> yet I can't imagine what kind of error message would actually pop up

The same thing that pops up if you manually write:

```java
NumberFormatException e = null;
throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
```

Which is simply: 
```
/tmp/QuickJava.java:10: error: incompatible types: NumberFormatException cannot be converted to IOException
throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
                               ^
```

But the problem is, the line this error will point at, and the little caret, will be in a befuddling place (we have some control about where, but its limited. Best case scenario:

```
/tmp/QuickJava.java:10: error: incompatible types: NumberFormatException cannot be converted to IOException
@Wrap(from = NumberFormatException.class, to = UncheckedIOException.class)
                                               ^
```

But I don't think we can get there. Instead we have to do some hacky dance to cast the exception to IOException and things will just be very very ugly. As I said, disaster.

@dstango wrote:

> ```java
> @Wrap(from = {Exception1.class, ...}, to = MyWrapperEx.class, dontWrap = {RuntimeException.class, Error.class})
> ```

This doesn't work, I think.

## The linter problem

The code we generate cannot be marked as generated. When we generate an entire method, we can easily mark it, and then we can handwave away linter issues as: "Hey, the method is marked in whichever way you please that a linter tool needs to skip it, if your linter tool does not do that and is not capable of being configured to do that, go file bugs with them".

But we don't, here. We simply wrap your method body in a try block with a bunch of catches. Therefore, we need to figure out how to generate code that:

* Compiles. This is trickier than it sounds, e.g. `catch (IOException e) { if (e instanceof RuntimeException) ...;}` __is a compiler error__, you can't write `a instanceof T` where `T` is not a supertype of whatever the type of expression `a` is, that's a compiler error.
* Doesn't fall afoul of commonly used linter tools with commonly used settings. This requires a study. I'm not going to do this study, but without it this feature request cannot be accepted.
* Does what we want the annotation to mean, and without requiring resolution.

## It won't work

```java
@Wrap(from = IOException.class. to = MyWrapperEx.class)
```

This therefore has `dontWrap = RuntimeException.class` associated with and the entire block is on its face silly: The `dontWrap` clause is nonsense, given that `IOException` cannot possibly be a RuntimeException. But lombok cannot know this. Therefore, you must now write code that checks for the impossible. If a linter tool does not complain about it, that is merely indicative that the linter tool isn't advanced as it could be, as the entire task itself is silly on first principles. Nevertheless, we may be able to dance around all of them, somehow. Now we 'merely' face the fact that if you delombok this seemingly simple statement it looks incredibly ugly and bizarre.

```java
@Wrap(from = Exception.class, to = MyWrapperEx.class, dontWrap = {})
```

Random Jane Q. JavaCoder looks at that line and is to understand that this means: Wrap all exceptions, even runtimeexceptions?

Ugh. I don't like it. Hence why I'd far rather have `@WrapChecked` and `@WrapAll` which always apply to all exceptions (there is no `from`), and `@Wrap` which just errors out if you attempt to stow `Exception.class`, `Error.class`, or `Throwable.class` in the from list.

> But the problem is, the line this error will point at, and the little caret, will be in a befuddling place (we have some control about where, but its limited. Best case scenario:
> ```
> /tmp/QuickJava.java:10: error: incompatible types: NumberFormatException cannot be converted to IOException
> @Wrap(from = NumberFormatException.class, to = UncheckedIOException.class)
>                                                ^
> ```
> But I don't think we can get there. Instead we have to do some hacky dance to cast the exception to IOException and things will just be very very ugly. As I said, disaster.

I'd be happy with such an error message, even if it's simply pointing to the start of the line. I agree dancing around IOException is really ugly. "Option 4" could be a way, but even an error message is totally acceptable IMHO.

Let's see about the other things you bring up ...

> @dstango wrote:
> 
> > ```java
> > @Wrap(from = {Exception1.class, ...}, to = MyWrapperEx.class, dontWrap = {RuntimeException.class, Error.class})
> > ```
> 
> (...) Therefore, we need to figure out how to generate code that:
> * Compiles. This is trickier than it sounds, e.g. `catch (IOException e) { if (e instanceof RuntimeException) ...;}` **is a compiler error**, you can't write `a instanceof T` where `T` is not a supertype of whatever the type of expression `a` is, that's a compiler error.

I wouldn't put the `dontWrap`-Part into the `from`-part, but e.g.

```java
@Wrap(from = {Exception1.class, ...}, to = MyWrapperEx.class, dontWrap = {RuntimeException.class, Error.class})
public void foo() throws MyWrapperEx, IOException {
  if (cond) throw new IOException();
  if (foobar) throw new MyWrapperEx();
}

// becomes:

public void foo() throws MyWrapperEx, IOException {
  try {
    if (cond) throw new IOException();
    if (foobar) throw new MyWrapperEx();
  } catch (RuntimeException | Error e) {                 // everything listed in dontWrap
    throw e;
  } catch (Exception1 e) {                               // everything in from
    if (e instanceof MyWrapperEx) throw (MyWrapperEx) e; // line repeats for everything in from
    MyWrapperEx $w = new MyWrapperEx();
    $w.initCause(e);
    throw $w;
  }
}
```

> * Doesn't fall afoul of commonly used linter tools with commonly used settings. This requires a study. I'm not going to do this study, but without it this feature request cannot be accepted.

Linter tools will probably complain about the `if (e instanceof MyWrapperEx)`-part as bad style. 
What kind of study would suffice your needs? I could offer to try out code like the above and some variations you specify with the SonarLint-eclipse-plugin, and report what kind of result I get. Please specify some criteria/examples, and I'll give it a go.

> * Does what we want the annotation to mean, and without requiring resolution.

I don't see a problem with that in the pattern above. If I understood "resolution without extra rounds" correctly, we don't need any resolution with the pattern above. Please specify if you see something that won't work.

> ## It won't work
> ```java
> @Wrap(from = IOException.class. to = MyWrapperEx.class)
> ```
> 
> This therefore has `dontWrap = RuntimeException.class` associated with and the entire block is on its face silly: The `dontWrap` clause is nonsense, given that `IOException` cannot possibly be a RuntimeException. But lombok cannot know this. Therefore, you must now write code that checks for the impossible. If a linter tool does not complain about it, that is merely indicative that the linter tool isn't advanced as it could be, as the entire task itself is silly on first principles. Nevertheless, we may be able to dance around all of them, somehow. 

I don't see this problem in the template above any more.

> Now we 'merely' face the fact that if you delombok this seemingly simple statement it looks incredibly ugly and bizarre.

Yeah, it probably looks somewhat ugly, but for generated code I'd accept it. Can't judge if it's bizarre, though ;-) ...

> ```java
> @Wrap(from = Exception.class, to = MyWrapperEx.class, dontWrap = {})
> ```
> 
> Random Jane Q. JavaCoder looks at that line and is to understand that this means: Wrap all exceptions, even runtimeexceptions?

Actually: yes, I would agree with Jane Q, and I don't see a problem in this: if someone is a big fan of his/her own exception class, and wants to code it like this, let them have their way ;-).

> Ugh. I don't like it. Hence why I'd far rather have `@WrapChecked` and `@WrapAll` which always apply to all exceptions (there is no `from`), and `@Wrap` which just errors out if you attempt to stow `Exception.class`, `Error.class`, or `Throwable.class` in the from list.

If you would prefer to have three new annotations for various scenarios, it would also be possible. After taking part in the discussion it's hard for me to imagine if Jane or James Q. might find three distinct annotations or one with parameters easier to grasp. I know usual clean code recommendations would prefer a minimal set of arguments, yet I'm not sure about the tradeoffs it might involve. I personally would prefer one annotation, as it offers wide flexibility yet might be handy enough for the "regular case" of wrapping some checked exception into some unchecked exception, and I don't have to learn when to use which of the three annotations. But I won't lead heated discussions about getting it my way ;-). In the end the only chance is to win over you maintainers to a way you're willing to support, because it looks like a workable and reasonable way to go.

> ```
> @Wrap(from = Exception.class, to = MyWrapperEx.class, dontWrap = {})
> ```

If I read something like this I would check why `dontWrap` is empty. But without this attribute I expect that it wraps all `Exception`s including `RuntimeException`s. Someone else might expect something different so it is not directly clear what the annotation does. This is something we should address because it will confuse at least some users. Multiple annotations might help but it also might be hard to spot the difference between them as long as you don't know all of them.

>Compiles. This is trickier than it sounds, e.g. catch (IOException e) { if (e instanceof RuntimeException) ...;} is a compiler error, you can't write a instanceof T where T is not a supertype of whatever the type of expression a is, that's a compiler error.

We can use `Class.isAssignableFrom` instead of `instanceof` to solve this.

@Rawi01 wrote:

> This is something we should address because it will confuse at least some users. Multiple annotations might help but it also might be hard to spot the difference between them as long as you don't know all of them.

If multiple annotations aren't a good idea:

There's `@Wrap(from =, to =, wrapUnchecked = true/false)` with the rule:

* If `from` specifically lists `Throwable.class` or `Exception.class`, then it is an error if you don't have an explicit `wrapUnchecked` value in the annotation. This cannot be fulfilled or opted out of using `lombok.config`.
* If the `from` does not list those, that it is an error if you __do__ have an explicit `wrapUnchecked` value in the annotation.

Invalid annotations produce an error explaining the problem and don't do anything else. That should get us closer.

> We can use Class.isAssignableFrom instead of instanceof to solve this.

I fear linters who are not as easily tricked as `javac`. It's also distasteful and a maintenance burden (even if linters don't trigger on this today, they may well tomorrow) - if lombok generates code no sane person would ever write because an obviously superior alternative is available (but that we cannot generate without resolution, hence, we don't), that's bad.

```

INFO: Elapsed time: 6.225s, Critical Path: 3.03s
```

I'm not totally clear what the new processing round error refers to - I had a look at the source code and it looks like it tries to create a temporary file somewhere and fails when that file creation fails. Is that more or less correct?

That is correct. Lombok needs multiple processor rounds to do its job. That is uncommon for annotation processors and no API exists for this. But if a new source file is generated, a new round will be triggered.

Are you sure the edge release is being used by all those projects? Can you explain how I can test this using Bazel myself?

I am reasonably sure the edge release is being used by all of those projects. Each project has a list of deps that are specified like so:

```bzl
java_library(
    name = "spinaltap-client",
    deps = [
       ...
        "//third_party/plugins:org.projectlombok_lombok",
       ...
    ],
    srcs = glob(["src/main/java/**/*.java"]),
)
```

In `//third_party/plugins`, we have the following:

```bzl
java_library(
    name = "org.projectlombok_lombok",
    exports = ["//third_party:org.projectlombok_lombok"],
    exported_plugins = [":lombok_plugin"],
)

java_plugin(
    name = "lombok_plugin",
    processor_class = "lombok.launch.AnnotationProcessorHider$AnnotationProcessor",
    deps = ["//third_party:org.projectlombok_lombok"],
)
```

This, in turn, points to `//third_party:org.projectlombok_lombok`, which looks like the following:

```bzl
java_import(
    name = "org.projectlombok_lombok",
    jars = [
        "jars/lombok-edge.jar"
        # "jars/org.projectlombok/lombok/1.16.8/2ce9de13f277ec1600e7e04231477e3e5f59d317/lombok-1.16.8.jar"
    ],
)
```

This would be built using a command like `bazel build //projects/spinaltap/spinaltap-client/... --strategy=Javac=local`

Lombok v1.16.14 will ship with a potential fix, which... we can't test. It appears to be a race condition where 2 separate threads both try to load the same class simultaneously and this causes us to try to load it twice which doesn't work. The hopeful fix is to catch this error and just try to return the evidently already loaded classes verbatim. Whether that actually fixes the problem..... well, it was already exotic before this fix, but if we get no more bug reports on this, let's close it.

Let's say if nobody fills a bugreport for lombok v1.16.14 or higher on this topic between now and 2017-07-01, let's consider it fixed.

title: ExtensionMethod to the stable APIs
body:
Hi!

Could you please move ExtensionMethods out of Experimental section to the stable APIs? :)

It's a brilliant feature and will motivate IDE plugin developers to support it ASAP (i.e. https://github.com/mplushnikov/lombok-intellij-plugin/issues/21 )


Thanks!

nodes.body:
My review of "Experimental because" section:

> High-impact on code style

People got used to the extension methods thanks to Groovy, Kotlin, Scala and other alternative JVM languages. 

> Really would like to ship with utility methods to expand common classes, but so far lombok doesn't have a good distribution method for such runtime dependencies

Since Lombok is a syntax sugar library, IMO it's better to let other developers produce their libraries focused on this feature. There are many extension-ready libraries like Apache Commons as well.

> Affects quite a bit of eclipse, and auto-complete e.d. do not work yet in netbeans

So far many Lombok features were supported after they made their way to non-experimental status. For instance, IDEA plugin is waiting for this feature to become non-experimental

> Should @ExtensionMethod be legal on methods? Should it be legal on packages?

I definitely see scoped use-cases for it, if it's doable without huge implementation changes - IMO it's a good addition to the feature. Also, it will allow to gradually add them, on a per-method basis. At the same time, package annotation will help to use them in a code base where you have multiple classes in the same file. Both :+1: from me.

Agreed, it's a great feature and it works pretty well. I'd personally prefer to use it without any annotations, just *configure* the whole project to use one or more extending classes (as this helps to keep the style consistent). But that's a different story. I'm all for promoting `@ExtensionMethod`.

It's a great idea to move it out of experimental :)

Of the scopes of `@ExtensionMethod` discussed here the per-project scope is the most appealing to me because I would like to have project-wide extensions for Strings, Collections, Streams, Optional, and even for primitives.

@tlinkowski I was using Groovy where extension methods are global (well... I'm a committer actually :D ), I was using Kotlin where your have to import your extension method.

And I must say that import-based approach is better.

It's much easier to review such code, to avoid conflicts (you can select which method to use, in Groovy, for instance, it's classpath-dependent)

I don't mind if global extension methods will be supported later in Lombok, but right now I want them "as is" because global version is questionable, but current is strong and usable enough.

> It's much easier to review such code, to avoid conflicts

@bsideup You're probably using tons of them. I'm much more conservative and use only a couple of them. This precludes conflicts and implies my desire for global definition. I guess that people more used to other JVM languages are less conservative and that we can agree on supporting both in the long run.
Hi @bsideup and @rzwitserloot! :) Is it still planned to mark ExtensionMethods as stable API?

title: @ToString formatting 'language'.

nodes.body: This issue also supercedes #256 #529 #1211

I don't think hideNulls (#256 #529 #1211) should be covered (only) by pattern. The pattern is for formatting while hideNulls is for filtering content. Also it would be over-complicated to write a pattern just to say "hide nulls". Please keep the boolean flag separated from the pattern.

a separate boolean flag for hideNulls is very useful.
- This is the most wanted feature about ToString annotation
- It's much easier to use for client
- It's much easier to implement

It's disappointing to not have even a reply. Lombok made Java great again, please continue to improve it.
Please reopen one of the hideNulls issue ! Or explain why this unrealistic issue supercedes the easy-to-implement really-useful *hideNulls* issue) !

> It's disappointing to not have even a reply.

I'm not a project owner, but my answer may be better than nothing.

---

Lombok doesn't support traits. There's `@Delegate` and `@ExtensionMethod`. The latter could help. It add s no methods, but let's you write `yourObject.toJson()`.

> `@ToString(delegate=toJson)`

This could be a nice feature. It may be better to allow placing `@ToString` (or `@ToString.Delegate`) on a method (avoiding stringly-typed arguments). This obviously won't work with `@ExtensionMethod`.

But maybe you can define an `@ExtensionMethod` for `toString()` directly? No idea if it takes precedence over an inherited method (I guess so, as lombok knows nothing about inheritance).

> And this is my suggestion as to how to solve the toString() formatting issue discussed here: in an imperative, instead of a declarative way.

This is similar in spirit to my proposal #1393.

In my opinion, merging 'skipNulls' feature requests into this issue is misleading.
Having boolean flag should be sufficient, checking for nulls before on fields directly should be enough.

I guess this subroutine has to be rewritten to use StringBuilder.append
https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/master/src/core/lombok/javac/handlers/HandleToString.java#L141
And insert maker.If that checks for nulls before appending each field, or something along these lines
EDIT:
@rzwitserloot , I see you already came to the same conclusion 4 years ago:
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/project-lombok/9on7mFH3z34/Y9HvIJxn0JAJ
Any progress on this issue?

> * Print classname, fully qualified classname, or nothing.

I think it would be useful to choose a custom class name to be printed out as well.  I view this as being analogous to the member-level annotation `@ToString.Include(name = "nameToUse")`.

In my current use case, I have a private inner class that implements a public interface, and I'd rather my debugging logs not contain `ReallyLongOuterClassName.KindOfLongInnerClassName` whenever I'm logging that particular class.

We explicitly cover this in our various presentations as one of those issues where many are adamant that juuuust one more straw on this particular camel's back is all that you need to be happy, but surely all that does is open the door to the next batch. If null needs to be skipped, why not sentinel blank values? How do we identify those, etc, etc, etc.

There is no progress on this issue because there is no design that is suitable, and we (@rspilker and I) have little hope that a suitable design even exists.

We do not believe 'just add hideNulls' is the correct 80/20 balance.

@wheredevel 

> Why isn't it good enough?

- It solves just one problem: You already have an implementation and want to call it.

- It doesn't save much: You write `@ToString(delegate = Printer.class)` instead of `public String toString() {return Printer.toString(this);}` plus some formatting.

IMHO it's not bad, but it solves none of the other problems (just look at the links above) of people having no method to delegate to.

Disclaimer: I'm not a project owner.

@Maaartinus ,

My workaround is good enough for me.
In my opinion, `@ToString(delegate=Printer.class)` is just a short for defining interface, mixin, and delegate. This is where Lombok shines: reducing the boilerplate code.  

I see my workaround as a solution design, which @rzwitserloot said is missing.  

To me, it solves many, if not all, the issues people mentioned related to `toString()` fine-tuning.  
As I already sugested, the delegated Printer could utilize the power of libraries such as Jackson to drive how fields are marshaled during the delegate `toString()` - giving all the power to the developer to modify `toString()` behavior, including the choice of the "fine-printing" library.

@wheredevel As maaartinus said, your workaround is not good enough because it saves virtually no boilerplate at all. `@ToString(delegate = Printer.class)`? This is not a win, at all, over a one-liner toString impl.

> If null needs to be skipped, why not sentinel blank values?

Who asked for filtering sentinel blank values? I didn't see any mention in the related issues.
In Java "null" is a pretty specific value and still commonly used (despite Optional, that's another debate!). On the opposite sentinel values are an edge case, there's no clear definition of it (and I totally agree we don't want to open that door).

> There is no progress on this issue because there is no design that is suitable, and we (@rspilker and I) have little hope that a suitable design even exists.

Probably because this ticket is trying to solve too many problems at the same time. I repeat some issues linked here should have stay separated (like "hide nulls" which is not about formatting).

> We do not believe 'just add hideNulls' is the correct 80/20 balance.

not 80/20 regarding formatting? sure. But hiding nulls is a common need, without it Lombok ToString is kind of useless because most real-life objects have too many properties, making the output too verbose (especially combined with associations). I think anybody using Lombok on an enterprise project will face this issue. We end up rewriting all the toString() manually. We see less and less value in Lombok...

It's disappointing to see no solution in years. A not-perfect-solution is still better than no solution at all. You could flag it "experimental" so you could change it later.

@rzwitserloot,

> @wheredevel As maaartinus said, your workaround is not good enough because it saves virtually no boilerplate at all. `@ToString(delegate = Printer.class)`? This is not a win, at all, over a one-liner toString impl.

I agree it's not a big code line saver. I can always opt for either overriding the `toString()` OR (usually, more useful solution to me) using interface to define the behavior to be modified, class implementing the desired behavior, and mixin to inject the modification into the existing classes.  
That's where Lombok's `@Delegate` does particularly great job.  
So, in this context, it's very troubling to me to read the following:
> Current status: negative - Currently we feel this feature will not move out of experimental status anytime soon, and support for this feature may be dropped if future versions of javac or ecj make it difficult to continue to maintain the feature.
Source: [@Delegate](https://projectlombok.org/features/experimental/Delegate)

I always say that with Lombok and a Dependency Injection (i.e. Spring) I don't need to remember patterns - I can always make up the required ones from basic building blocks. `@Delegate` is central to that practice.

Please restrict further issue debate on either a solid plan on how to end up at a design that covers a bunch of feasible use cases in an easy to understand way. Refrain from 'but I just want X' or 'this is disappointing'. Sure. I'm disappointed too. It doesn't change my belief that it's better not to have the feature at all, than to 'eh, whatever good enough it' with an ill-thought through feature we have to then support forever.

Note that we can't stick half of ToString in experimental and the other half outside of it, either. Or at least, we don't want to.

> We see less and less value in Lombok...

Is this like a threat? Add this feature or else we will stop using it?

I understand that if lombok cannot deliver something you need, that makes it less valuable to you. But you don't need to keep whining on and on about it. This feels disrespectful: I'm weighing your needs against the needs of all the other lombok users, and I have arrived at a decision which you are disappointed with.

**I'm putting this thread on freeze for 3 weeks. Only comments with serious proposals will be allowed, and the rest will be _deleted_. If you wish to debate the policy of how we don't want to slap-dash a bunch of arbitrary features into lombok on an as-requested basis, by all means hold it, but not in this issue, maybe the forum is the right channel for such a debate. If you wish to chime in that you want more from toString but without a serious attempt at a complete proposal, please don't.**

FREEZE ENDS: 2020-03-01.

A possible generic solution, is to pass an optional filter to `@ToString` annotation that takes a String and returns a String and that would post-process the string returned by lombok.

 Evidently this is not the fastest implementation, but I don't see this as a block, since `toString` is intended chiefly as a debugging tool, and in theory anything can be done via postprocessing (admittedly somethings would be harder than others).

As a concrete example, the following filter can be passed to remove null values from the output. The credit for this idea belongs to https://stackoverflow.com/questions/54604701/how-to-skip-null-field-with-lombok-tostring/59323411#59323411

``` java
/**
 * Removes the null values from String generated through the @ToString annotation.
 * For example:
 * - replaces:  AddressEntity(id=null, adrType=null, adrStreet=null, adrStreetNum=null, adrComplement=null, adrPoBox=null, adrNip=null, adrCity=city, adrCountry=null, adrNameCorresp=nameCorresp, adrSexCorresp=null, adrSource=null, adrSelectionReason=null, validityBegin=null, validityEnd=null, lastModification=null, dataQuality=null)
 * - by:        AddressEntity(adrCity=city, adrNameCorresp=nameCorresp)
 * Note: does not support tricky attribute content such as "when, x=null, it fails".
 * @param lombokToString a String generated by Lombok's @ToString method
 * @return a string without null values
 */
public static String removeToStringNullValues(String lombokToString) {
    //Pattern
    return lombokToString != null ? lombokToString
            .replaceAll("(?<=(, |\\())[^\\s(]+?=null(?:, )?", "")
            .replaceFirst(", \\)$", ")") : null;
}
```

The work around I am currently using to remove nulls in my actual implementations is to do a static import of the function above and explicitly call it every time I want a non-null representation of objects. This is evidently an issue if objects of this kind are printed or logged in many places, which is why having a way of passing a filter to the `@ToString` annotation would be very nice.

This is error-prone (as the Lombok-generated strings are not escaped) and slow (you could do better with some static final `Pattern`, but still slow). Maybe filtering with a `BiPrecidate` (if such a thing exists) taking the field name and value could be the way to go (but there's the problem with primitive values).

There have been many related proposals, with many of them pretty good, but none of them really good enough. The project maintainers want to keep Lombok small, so it looks like none passes anytime soon.

If you really need the flexibility, I'd suggest to switch to reflection. It most probably will be faster than the string manipulation and it'll be much more flexible. You only write
```
@Override public String toString() {return MyReflector.toString(this);}
```
and can do everything with little effort.

If speed is really at premium, then you could switch to an annotation processor instead. It's much more work (but only once; no per class work) and doesn't give you access to private members, but it's full-speed.

@jmoraleda  wrote:

> A possible generic solution, is to pass an optional filter to @ToString annotation that takes a String and returns a String and that would post-process the string returned by lombok.

Vetoed; this is a dead-end idea. The toString output of lombok involves invoking toString()s on objects of all sorts of types, and in general toString output doesn't fully any spec (that's sort of the point), and even where it does, rarely in a 'this is easily parsable by code' way.

For example, your 'find `x = null` and strip it' plan can be trivially asploded into making a complete hash of the string output if one of the string fields includes the construction `"this is a string with, oooh=null, how mean"` - and your filter will ruin that. No filter that isn't incredibly complicated can address this.

title: Operator overloading

nodes.body:
Adding new operators: Impossible; lombok does not get a go until after the source has been syntactically parsed, and '===' isn't legal java.

Adding operator overloading as a concept: No. Both Roel and I think that the programming community at large has conclusively proved they are not grown up enough to be trusted with that power. Not happening.

Adding operator overloading for BI/BD specifically: Sure. That sounds awesome. If someone sends us a patch request that adds this, we'd accept it.

indexing overloading for maps and lists: No. How often have you called list.set() in your code? How about list.get()? If the answer is 'like once a year', you're doing it right. Not worth the mental overload. map.get() is used often enough, but, you should really be using .getOrDefault instead.
Get on map and also put is pretty common, right?

I suspect that most uses of `put` are actually to initialize a collection; eventually, collection literals should put a stop to that. (Many implementations of the collections API already offer helper methods for this sort of thing.)

I'm curious about a special case of operator overloading, namely `compareTo`, which is interesting because (1) it is defined by an interface, `Comparator<T>`, which allows types to opt-in to defining their own unique natural ordering; (2) direct calls to `compareTo` are much harder to interpret/write correctly than the theoretical overloaded equivalent using inequality operators; (3) unlike `equals`, inequality operator overloading can be implemented in terms of existing Java operators (whereas `equals` would require something like `===` as `==` is reserved for reference equality).

Maybe only add certain operators for different classes. E.g.  for Classes which extend 
Number only +,-,/,== (== would also be OK in this case) etc.
 and for
Collection only []
So you could at least prevent the "misuse" of OO a bit. 

Btw: Did you ever try to write an emulator, implement a Matrix/Complex or Unsigned Number Class  in Java? You will see that OO would be a great feature, so you can implement such stuff with more ease.

This is a Implementation of OO https://github.com/amelentev/java-oo

title: Parallelization Annotations
body:
As you know, sometimes a method is not fast enough or you want to parallelize a certain bit of Code. But setting up the parallelization of e.g. loops can be quite the hassle and can not only add a lot of boilerplate code, but also make it difficult to read the Code. 

So I'd like to see a Annotation, which adds all that boilerplate Code to parallelize a piece of Code. 

A Annotation could look something like this:
`@Parallelize ("OPTIONS")
`
With no options the Annotation would "create a Thread" (in reality you would use a ThreadPool) everytime a Method is called.

And with a Option  e.g. 
`@Parallelize (options = "for label" )
` 
only that loop marked with LABEL will get parallelized. 

As you can also annotate Block statements, parallelization of any Code would be possible.:
`label:{
//code to parallelize ...
}
`

nodes.body: This functionality has already been provided by Spring with @Async annotation : https://spring.io/guides/gs/async-method/

title: Lombok and the JSR process
body:
I found the following message from a few years ago:

> Re: [project lombok] Why not request a JSR to include it in Java SE?
> 
> We've tried to get far less ambitious changes into java, and I'm holding back when I say that the experience has been "disappointing".
> 
> Our most recent 2 attempts:
> 
> * Allow 'any annotation' as a valid option for annotation fields. This lets us enable onMethod, onConstructor, and onParam properly. This was shot down under the motto: "Looks like you put in all the effort we usually ask for" (including patches to both the JLS and javac, and a lengthy discussion on the effects), but there is 'no time'. Note that the 2 persons involved in this part of java, Joe Darcy and Alex Buckley, created an entirely different annotation-related feature a few months later, so I can only conclude that either Not-Invented-Here syndrome is involved, or, anything that isn't directly requested by other departments in oracle is simply not important.
> 
> * Show how that other proposal (multiple annotations of the same type on a single member) is ill thought through and is clearly being rushed, with a spec half-baked. I've been informed my comments are not welcome, and that there is at this point no time (heh, that sounds familiar) to fix things. Note that right now the spec is being changed anyway due to comments from the JavaEE lead that originally asked for this feature. Yet again that 'no time' things seems to be a convenient excuse, but, then, I don't know how things are run inside oracle. That is a big part of the problem - opaqueness.
> 
> You can see why, personally, I've given up. The process to add things to java is too opaque and the effort required to satisfy requirements is far too large knowing that so far we've been turned down every time. If I had a reasonable guarantee that, if the spec is near perfect, the patches to javac are bug free, and there are no outstanding issues, that it would happen, I'd put in the effort.
> 
> I get the strong feeling that if no project lead within Oracle personally cares, your odds of getting anything into java is pretty much nil, but no Oracle project lead is going to go public with support in case things backfire.
> 
>  --Reinier Zwitserloot

Now that a few years have passed, I had two follow-up questions:

1. Is your overall impression of the JSR process (or the JEP process) still the same?
2. Has Oracle ever considered any features (e.g. declarative macros or some sort of Annotation Processing 2.0 proposal) that would reduce the overall amount of hackery needed to implement Lombok?

title: Create @Decorate annotation to make decoration painless

nodes.body:
It already exists, but is still experimental. it is called [@Delegate](https://projectlombok.org/features/experimental/Delegate.html).

The reasons it is still experimental:
- It need resolution, and that's still brittle
- The java compiler needs to determine all field and method signatures at the same time, and that's before resolution is possible. However, for this to work properly, the fields need to be resolved before the methods can be created.

For now, we got it working for most use cases.

I also don't think that the `@Override` annotation should be missing, see e.g., [this test](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/aa2f4424a78b962edf0b7e0ef551a82c5822619a/test/transform/resource/after-delombok/EqualsAndHashCode.java#L7). Isn't a different class the culprit rather than the one you put `@EqualsAndHashCode` on?

The message doesn't speak about missing `@Override` annotation on an overriding method; it complains about a missing method. This all should work (I'm using Lombok with Hibernate, too; they both do some magic, but their magic paths don't conflict as Lombok is long done when Hibernate starts).

Hello, sorry for such a long answer. It was probably something with IDEA as currently everything is ok.
Thanks for your explanation!

Closing this ticket as irrelevant.
