title: @EqualsAndHashcode violates symmetricity rule for polymorphic classes if not all classes use Lombok

nodes.body:
The suggested change would fix one problem, but introduce another. There are plenty of valid use cases for instances of different classes being equal to each other.

While searching for a more inclusive solution, it would be good to amend the documentation of EqualsAndHashCode to indicate that, in addition to overriding canEqual if writing your own equals method, you should also consider overriding it if you plan on subclassing with classes which cannot be equal to instances of the original class.

@irobertson I think that making objects of different classes being equals is a bad idea and a bad practice. It is almost always simply buggy. If it is done intentionally, this is a sloppy programming style.

It would be nice if lombok generates an `equals` methods that never makes the object equals to something else from another class. If the user wants it to be considered equals to something else from another class, then he/she is free to write the `equals` method for that by hand and take the burden and the risks of that decision for himself/herself.

> `y.quals(x)` does not return true, so `x.equals(y)` is not allowed to return true. But it does return true!

@ewirch Wrong! `x.equals(y)` does not return false, so `y.equals(x)` is not allowed to return false. Does the superclass have to obey the contract of a subclass or the other way round?

> `canEqual()` is a mere workaround not a solution to this problem.

The sole problem is the broken `Y#equals`. `X` was perfectly fine before that. The purpose of `canEqual()` is not the solve the non-problem, but rather to allow both behaviors: allow or disallow subclass equality. The generated `canEqual` allows it and subclasses have to follow. You could have provided your own `canEqual`.

> Default implementation of `@EqualsAndHashCode` should use `getClass() == other.getClass()`.

This would be better for maybe half of the uses, while breaking the other half and losing the current flexibility.

---

> While searching for a more inclusive solution

@irobertson Maybe add a *warning on non-final classes* which define no `canEqual`? To keep it concise, add a `subclassesCanEqual` parameter as a shortcut? Final classes are fine and for the others we have
- `subclassesCanEqual=false`, no `canEqual` defined → 
    generate `canEqual` testing `getClass() == other.getClass()`
- `subclassesCanEqual=true`, no `canEqual` defined →
    generate `canEqual` like before
- no `subclassesCanEqual` set, but `canEqual` defined →
   let's hope you know what you're doing
- anything else →
  a warning

---

> I think that making objects of different classes being equals is a bad idea

@victorwss Tell everyone using dynamic proxies (e.g., Hibernate users).

> ....

If the user :rofl: *does not want* :rofl: it to be considered equals to something else from another class, then he/she is free to write the equals method for that by hand and take the burden and the risks of that decision for himself/herself.  

There were quite a few discussions about `this.class == that.class` vs. `that instanceof ThisClass` and IIRC both camps were about the same size. AFAIK `canEqual` is the only solution satisfying both.

title: @Factory - new annotation -  proposal - to automatically produce a factory class.

nodes.body: Any progress?

I'm just a contributor and not speaking for the dev team, but I don't think this feature will ever make it into Lombok.
The reason is that it requires resolution, and that will make it very hard to implement and create a high maintenance burden. When Lombok runs, you simply cannot get info about subclasses, and there is no such thing as "currently compiled sources", because the compilation is not yet finished.

You have to think of "no resolution" as if you cannot inspect anything of a referenced class. You don't know any methods or constructors of that class, you even cannot say if the class exists at all. All this is processed at a later stage of the compiler, and it's to late for Lombok then.

This means that everything you have to generate must be computable using only lexical/syntactical information from the annotated class. So you not only have to annotate the class name, but also the method name or constructor and all its parameters. This would create the most ugly Lombok annotation ever, and you would simply move the reduced lines to the annotation.

Of course you could return a builder, but this is usually not what a factory does, and it requires the referenced class to have one, which you cannot know. And as the name of the `builder()` can be customised, you have provide that parameter too.

> @janrieke :
> You have to think of "no resolution" as if you cannot inspect anything of a referenced class. You don't know any methods or constructors of that class, you even cannot say if the class exists at all. All this is processed at a later stage of the compiler, and it's to late for Lombok then.
> ...

Absolutely fine with me.  
Generating a constructor method, by template, for each enlisted subclass requires "no resolution" at all!!!  
See my comment above for an example: https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/1408#issuecomment-439678883

BTW: The generated code you propose is not an example of the factory pattern as described by the GoF. Typically you have an interface as return type, because you want to allow to redefine which class to instantiate. Including this would further increase the annotations parameters.

> @janrieke :
> BTW: The generated code you propose is not an example of the factory pattern as described by the GoF. Typically you have an interface as return type, because you want to allow to redefine which class to instantiate. Including this would further increase the annotations parameters.

I don't know if anyone would ever want it to become a fully-blown GoF.  
I'm seeing ```@Factory``` annotation as simply: "Add here constructor methods for enlisted subclasses of the annotated class."  
This simple feature is very important in virtually all projects I do.

Out of curiosity: Why exactly do you use this pattern so much? What is the
value of that pattern?

> @randakar:

Regarding the "value"
--------
As my example above shows:  
```java
------------------------
public class Example {

 public static void main() {
  //
  // Autobots
  //
  Autobot optimus = Autobot.optimus().build();
  Autobot bumblebee = Autobot.bumblebee().build();
  //
  // Decepticons
  //
  Decepticon megatron = Decepticon.megatron().build();
  Decepticon soundwave = Decepticon.soundwave().build();
  //
  // Transformers
  //
  Transformer[] transformers = {
    Transformer.optimus().build(),
    Transformer.bumblebee().build(),
    Transformer.megatron().build(),
    Transformer.soundwave().build(),
  //
  //...
  //
 }
}
```

In other words:
1) make a discovery of a "contract" implementors as easy as possible at the codding time.
2) hide details of their construction

Note: 2 - is of less importance than 1, but nice to have.

Regarding the frequency of use
--------
I can't reveal details of my projects, of course.  
But, empirically, every project has Interfaces and their implementations, right?

As an example, let's say, I have a ```BinaryExpression``` (abstract class) and plenty of its subclasses: ```Addition```, ```Subtraction```, ```Multiplication```, ```Division```, ```Modulo```, etc. etc.   
So, ideally, I'd like my IDE to auto-suggest this:  
```java
BinaryExpression.
                 addition()
                 subtraction()
                 multiplication()
                 division()
                 modulo()
                 ...
```
And, it would be silly of me to expect it would auto-suggest this:
```java
new 
    ??????
```
(...actually why not?!?!)  
```java
new BinaryExpression
    Addition
    Subtraction
    Multiplication
    Division
    Modulo
    ...
```

Another example, from the apps world.   
Let's say, I have a ```Controller``` (interface) and its implementors: ```UserController```, ```DataController```, etc.. And also ```Service``` (interfaces) and its implementors: ```UserService```, ```DataService```, etc.  
Now if I'm in the Spring world - great! I can both instantiate and tie controllers and services together.  
Otherwise I would have to do that myself. Than the Factory approach would be of help, of course.

Now, as for "value" Point 1 above - I would really love the package auto-scanning for implementors of interest.  
But, as the discussion above goes, it's a tougher task for Lombok team: https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/1408#issuecomment-439678883 .  
So I'm fine with manually maintaining this implementors list. 
For now... :)

Right.
Well, I get why you find that useful. But I think that once you know the
name of the class you want to instantiate the usefulness of this kinda ends.
You're right. The IDE should be able to discover implementers of an
interface somehow. And honestly, doing it with inheritance? That kind of
sucks, if only because usually inheritance is the wrong tool for the job.
(almost always, in fact. There are a few narrow cases where it's better
than interfaces or delegate objects, but not many).

title: Can't use bothNoArgsConstructor and AllArgsConstructor for empty objects

nodes.body: In addition to this you cannot use the `@AllArgsConstructor` and `@RequiredArgsConstructor` if every field is marked with Lombok's `@NonNull`. This creates two constructors that conflict which both take all the args.

For my case, I use mustache template and since I cannot be sure there will be field in classes, I added both @NoArgsConstructor and @AllArgsConstructor but then I also get Constructor already define error.

Few suggestions in preference order:

1. The annotation AllArgsConstructor can have a parameter to specify if the no argument constructor must be added (includeNoArgs= true) defaulted to false.
2. The annotation AllArgsConstructor can avoid creating no argument constructor if the class is annotated with NoArgsConstructor
3. The annotation AllArgsConstructor must not generate the no argument constructor since there is an annotation for that.
4. The annotation AllArgsConstructor can generate a warning if there is no field to use and do not generate no arguments constructor. 

Let me know which one you prefer and I may help...

No comments in 6 years... ? Anyone at the office?

Hmm, I kinda like how the `@XArgsConstructor` annotations are simple in that they _always_ generate. But, I do see your point about how that's a problem if you template your code together.

I don't like `includeNoArgs`, that doesn't make much sense. `@NoArgsConstructor` already exists.

We get a ton of feature requests, we don't write answers on them if we don't have a clear internal idea of whether we'd think that's a good idea or not.

I think the way forward is for any of the `@XArgsConstructor` annotations to check if a constructor already exists with the precise signature, _and_ if that constructor is lombok-generated. If yes, just silently do nothing.

That would also tackle `@AllArgs` and `@ReqArgs` conflicting with each other if every field is `final`/`@NonNull`.

This isn't as easy as I thought; when applying the same logic to `@RequiredArgsConstructor @AllArgsConstructor` overlapping, we do need to check every parameter type first. It's not enough that 'a constructor' exists that lombok made, it needs to be the exact one lombok is about to make, which is only trivial for the 'zero arguments' case.

It's not exactly rocket science either, but too complicated to add last-minute before a release. Diverting this to next.

title: Failing to calculate the hashCode with bidirectional references

nodes.body:
I'd expect a `StackOverflowException`. However, I can't recall *any* `hashCode` implementation suited for cyclic structures. It's surely doable, but there's a cost as you have to keep track of all already visited objects (somewhere in a `ThreadLocal<IdentityHashMap<Object, Object>>`).

It still blows whenever you do something like `List l = new ArrayList(); l.add(l); myThing.add(l); myThing.hashCode();`.

So I'm afraid, the workaround is the (only sane) solution.

This is definitely a problem. I'm delegating to a rather complex type (Clojure's `APersistentMap`) and it fails to add delegate methods for supertypes of supertypes, such as `Associative` (superinterface to `IPersistentMap`). Here's the problem class: https://github.com/tterrag1098/K9/blob/86b594d9eea1ab61a0766af530acea205a163090/src/main/java/com/tterrag/k9/util/TypeBindingPersistentMap.java#L42

Confirm that this is still a breaking bug with 1.18.12. I have a class delegating to Guava `ImmutableList` and am getting complaints that it `does not override abstract method get(int) in java.util.List`.

I too experienced this problem delegating to a `SortedSet<MyClass>`. When I moved from Lombok version 1.18.10 to 1.18.14, it started building correctly from the maven command line, but it continued to fail with the usual errors in IntelliJ. It looks like folks are working on it, but it needs a bit more love. The lombok plugin appears to work correctly as it's not flagging a missing explicit implementation, but the IJ compiler is still not handling the generated methods correctly.

To work around this, I excluded all the members of Set (base class to SortedSet) and implemented explicit overrides for these. It
sucks, but it's still less verbose than implementing pass-through overrides for all of the methods of Set and SortedSet. If your base class only has a few methods, this could be a solution for you.

title: Can support kotlin?
body:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/12063612/27983564-4cac9e88-63f2-11e7-9a58-69e0827acfe0.png)
@Slf4j  ....@Data

nodes.body: https://github.com/MicroUtils/kotlin-logging ?

"Kotlin support" can mean two different things:

* Make lombok annotations in kotlin source files work. This is not and probably never will happen.
* When using `kotlinc`to compile both `kt` and `java` files, make lombok annos in the java files work.

That second one we'd fix if we can. For that see issue #2428

This sounds like the first, so, wontfix.
Hi @rzwitserloot  I wonder why this annotation `@slf4j` will probably never work in Kotlin files? It's really helpful for logging.

@zhangxueyii Consider the way lombok works: it joins in with the javac on an intimate level, does annotation processing in a special way and modifies the bytecode. The annotation processing is doing more than the official public api ever intended and offers. So lombok needs to find some special ways to do it, using protected apis, etc.
Thus for your request lombok would have to do the same thing with kotlinc, which is a different beast.

title: Using old code in new release, java2html from 2006....
body:
Please do not use old unmainted code in current projects. It makes it a nightmare for others to package. Even maven only provides binaries for de.java2html and not sources. The sources from upstream are a total mess.

Thus far having packaged hundreds of Java packages. Lombok is the absolute worst java package I have come across. It depends on a ridiculous amount of Eclipse, some 70+ packages. Not to mention bootstrap with lombok.patcher. Lombok seriously needs major work!!!

Now for a patch release, it seems 3 new dependencies are adding, java2html, freemarker, and another com.petebevin.markdown. Really should NOT be adding new deps on a patch release. Much less ancient ones like java2html. Seems there are some newer java2html on maven. Why de.java2html was used is beyond me. It has not been touched since 2006...

Lombok is making me hate Java. Please stop making a mess of this stuff... I am not surprised at all by the number of open bugs....

nodes.body:
Also  com.petebevin.markdown is the old namespace, per the release notes on 0.4
"Package name has been changed from com.petebevin.markdown to org.markdownj. The com.petebevin.markdown has been deprecated and will be removed in MarkdownJ 0.5."

The 0.4 package supports both namespaces, but for some reason Lombok went with com.petebevin vs org.markdownj. Which will break when 0.5 comes out. Likely better off to start with org.markdownj, and not require any changes when 0.5 comes out and com.petebevin is no more.

I am not a developer of lombok, just a common user looking around, but... can you contextualize what you are doing?

BTW, lombok is not intended to be added as a runtime dependency to anything at all - it is intended to be used solely as a compile-time-only dependency used in annotation processing. Including lombok in the classpath of an end-user application is just wrong. Having lombok as a runtime dependency is as bad and wrong as having the javadoc tool as a runtime dependency.

I don't have an authoritative word here, but I think that one of the main reasons why lombok is not very modularized is because since it should not be a runtime dependency, it is more valuable as a single-jar download of a tool that just works (regardless of the fact that it is bloated) instead of something that has careful projected dependencies that could be upgraded independently.

Lombok is something special because it is a tool that somewhats abuses both ECJ and javac by invading their private internal APIs and messing with on-memory compiler ASTs to do its black magic. Also, it needs to integrate with Netbeans, Eclipse, IntelliJ, etc, and this adds a lot of bloat. So, I'm not surprised that it needs many things from Eclipse.

About markdownj specifically, I have no clue on that.
I am packaging this stuff on Gentoo, [link](https://github.com/Obsidian-StudiosInc/os-xtoo/tree/master/dev-java/lombok).
Java2html, freemarker and markdown are not in lombok.jar. They are in the build script to generate the website and the installer.

"Lombok is making me hate Java. Please stop making a mess of this stuff... I am not surprised at all by the number of open bugs...." 

Be nice or go away

Please code and package software in a manner that is nice to others. Any attitude is a result of frustration after spending hours to package lombok and related. Just to have to spend additional time on a patch release due to other changes. I [packaged hundreds of java packages](https://github.com/Obsidian-StudiosInc/os-xtoo/). Any lack of niceness is a result of not being nice or friendly to others in how the package is coded, and/or built.

I am not using the build script. I do a straight javac via a Gentoo eclass bash function. You can see some in the [ebuild for lombok](https://github.com/Obsidian-StudiosInc/os-xtoo/blob/master/dev-java/lombok/lombok-9999.ebuild). It finds actual usage in code, thus having to add packages as compile time dependencies. DEPEND is build time, and RDEPEND is runtime. CP_DEPEND is for classpath. Anything that is in both is needed both at compile an runtime. Build time stuff would only be added to DEPEND and not RDEPEND. Things like javacc, etc. Used to generate code but not build time dependencies.

I cannot recall the issue # but FYI that patch came from another issue I opened where I was nice, as was response etc. Thus I tend to conduct myself based on the situation. I was not happy to have to package additional things for lombok. I only had to package some 70+ eclipse packages as dependencies of lombok....

FYI there are a few packages ~10 out of hundreds that really make me dislike java. Thus I do not make that statement lightly. Please do not take it personally as more feedback. It is not my mission, but it would be nice to see more Java packages be friendlier and built in a more consistent manner. Doing C coding and switching between say autotools, cmake, and meson. It is much more pleasant than dealing with say ant, maven, gradle. Mostly when it comes to things like dependencies etc. Java downloads other things tend to build. Thus many in java care less about packaging or others building the software. They just say use the jar and be happy. Status quo, but it can be improved.

Sorry for any harshness.

I understand where you're coming from. No hard feelings, and thanks for all the work you put into this!

First of all, right now our main focus is on jdk9 support. So it will take some time to improve things.

I think you are refering to https://github.com/Obsidian-StudiosInc/os-xtoo/commit/dc0aa4cfc834ac598810a7db59ddcac5a8a0dbfc#diff-a58af25837303da01a5e9d698ac3ded5

In https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/master/buildScripts/ivy.xml we currently make no difference between:
- the dependencies we need to create the jar file
- the dependencies to create the website and documentation
- the dependencies we need to publish everything

I guess we could make those distinctions. Would that help you?

Also, we already use some stub files to compile against the different ecj/eclipse versions. We could probably do the same for more of the eclipse code, but that will take some time. We would probably write some more code to extract those from the existing jars. This is something we considered before, but never got to do it.

What is the purpose of your packaging? Will it only be used for compiling other code using javac? In that case, it would be possible to remove the whole eclipse part as well as the installer, which is a Swing GUI and uses some packaged windows dll files.

The reason we put it all in one repository and eventually in one jar is because for most users, that's exactly what they want: one thing that's small and can do it all.
Oh, I forgot about the ecj-compiler. So not all "eclipse" code can be omitted, if you also want to support ecj.
https://github.com/rzwitserloot/com.zwitserloot.stubber

Yes that patch came from you referenced commit. We had a conversation there. I thought the patch came from you specifically. My main gripe was it seemed new dependencies were added in a patch release. Not sure why that was, I just was like "What?". I just packaged a bunch of stuff for lombok and now it needs more... If it was a minor or major version change, that would make a bit more sense. I would expect such changes. On patch release, x.x.N usually do not see such major changes. I surely would have noticed if it was needed to build as it ended up being with the latest release.

Thus I guess the solution to my issue/gripe is more in versioning. The distinctions is not so much necessary as I do not even pay attention to say pom.xml or build.gradles for depdencies. I care more about what the compiler needs. The rest comes later if its missing something for running or otherwise.

I guess a further gripe would be avoid adding new dependencies, code from other projects. That may not be practical always. If a project does have to be used, a current one. There are many ancient java packages still in use. Sources are hard to come by, and repos are in questionable states, etc. Many do not care as they just grab the ancient jar from maven or gradle. I would prefer if a package does add another as a new dependency. Its a current package, in good condition, actively developed, etc.

The stub file and other is a larger Java issue. Not blaming you all for the eclipse dependency chain. Not sure it can be avoided as this stuff even Lombok is a dependency of other stuff. So even with stubs I likely need the packages for actual usage in other stuff, Spring, etc. My goal is packaging other stuff, and the nature of Java. I end up packaging a lot of dependencies for any end goal package. Like Jenkins from source, needs Spring. Spring from source in its dependency chain needs Lombok, and many other things. I would blame Spring more than other stuff. it seems to depend on just about every Java package written indirectly :)

Not sure anything can be done to actually reduce lombok dependencies in my case. Not really so much the gripe as when they are added. Which comes back to versioning :) Something so small, can make such a difference. Also not adding old packages as new dependencies. Use new projects. 

The stubs and reducing deps bring other aspects. USE flags on gentoo control build options, including/excluding. There was talk of using stubs like pre-processor IF DEFINE in C/C++ to not have to have all dependencies present to build stuff. Though would need to be there for runtime. Some packages get around this by deleting files based on a USE flag, So say USE="-ecj" emerge lombok, as an example. That would require either stubs and/or deleting stuff that needed ecj, to avoid having ecj packaged and present on classpath, etc. That just ends up creating more work. Sometimes easier just to package the dependency, and based on other packages usage. Parts cannot be made optional it may need it all. I avoid the USE flag thing mostly for now and build packages as a whole, and all their dependencies...

I know I am a very abnormal Java user and packager. Gentoo is abnormal for most, much less building Java from source. I upset many doing things abnormally not even attitude or words. Some what why I do not worry about mine. If its just going to upset others with what I am doing, not saying. Run into various stuff as a result and the reception varies. Though the things I come across usually can benefit all. Java has some strange idioms. I am not trying to improve the world, but maybe a package at a time :)

If I can parse this feature request correctly, it is effectively not so much 'please update this dependency to something more recent', but more:

__Please do not change or add dependencies for minor version updates.__

Did I understand that correctly?

If so: This feature request is understood, and is __hereby denied__; as @rspilker tried to explain, absolutely nobody takes any notice of us updating certain kinds of deps, in any way or form, _except_ your unique use case. Handicapping ourselves like that serves the purposes of gentoo and not much else, and it seriously hampers our ability to produce updates.

If you can explain what you are trying to do, exactly, we can try to work out a good solution together. Please try not to use terms like 'CP_DEPEND'; you get really angry with the project lombok maintainers about not respecting the needs of your community, and yet you seem intent on treading on ours with disdain by using terms that aren't going to be familiar to java programmers that haven't tried to package for gentoo or another linux distro. Not everyone on earth is a gentoo maintainer; we have no idea what you are talking about, and your tone and attitude is making it very hard for me to work up the spirit to try to investigate.

Example of a thing I can try to help you with: "I am trying to write a script that turns the files in your github repo in a working lombok.jar, and this script cannot rely at all on any binary or internet download of any kind, it can only rely on binaries produced via a gentoo script (and such scripts themselves hold to the same rule: They can only pull in other gentoo scripts, and build from source, that's it)." I have no idea if that's what you're trying to do, I'm just guessing. I hope the idea of what I'm looking for is clear.

To be clear, its two fold
1. Please do not add new dependencies to a patch release, consider doing a minor or major release. That way it is less of a surprise to others.
2. Please do not add old projects as new dependencies. When adding a new dependency, ideally check to see if it is an active project, etc. Old code and projects need that no one is furthering need not be used any more.

Regarding 1;
I am not sure why versioning would hamper ability to produce updates. This came as part of a version/tag, just a patch version. Which typically reflects no major or minor changes, just bugs fixed etc.

Regarding 2;
At times to lots of focus say on Java releases. Java 9 etc. While projects continue to use very old code that is not being updated to use new Java features. It starts to create a mess. Not sure what the point is for current projects to use old code. Long time dependency is one thing, but new is strange.

I was explaining what I was doing, and even some details thus mentioning CP_DEPEND. @rspilker had said the dependencies were not compile/build time, but other. I was saying that per my experience in building, and showing the technical details of how with some explanation of variables, not just opinion. The dependencies were needed to compile, build time dependencies. Sorry for any confusion of new terms. It is just a bash variable. I am not sure why what would be hard to understand. Shell variables are normal in any OS or env. Java relies on them, JAVA_HOME, etc.

In simple terms, this is packaging Lombok for Gentoo, as a dependency of other stuff, I believe Spring. Gentoo being a from source distribution, packages build from source. Not using pre-built binaries. Only in some rare cases where things bootstrap themselves. Ideally it would be great if less things bootstrapped. From a packaging and building from source perspective it is not friendly. If you recall past issue opened on lombok.patcher and lombok [circular dependencies](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok.patcher/issues/2).

I had already spent considerable time to package a very large amount of dependencies for Lombok. More than I have seen for many packages, given it required a substantial portion of Eclipse. It was quite frustrating to on a patch release see new dependencies that required more time. Thus the tone.

The lombok circular dependency thing is something we'll reconsider at some point (it's on our list of things to do; just not particularly high on it).

I understand the source of your frustration. Doesn't change the fact that your 2 requests are both denied. I understand entirely that it's frustrating for you, but you're the only one who benefits with us granting these requests, and while you evidently can't see how it hampers development, I don't think it's worth the time to explain. It just does.

Thanks for the consideration on the circular dependency issue. Though that I already worked around and is not an issue like the one raised and closed.

@rzwitserloot I some what expected the denial thus the tone and attitude. If you cared such things would not be done in the first place. Though at least the issue has been raised for the record. Though I rather a more honest we I rather not. If your concerned about tone.

If versioning effects your development. Not sure what to say, but versions are very cheap in git. This was a version release to begin with. If minor or major vs patch messes up your development.... That sounds very strange and likely not justifiable technically, beyond personal preference.

As for continuing to use old code. Clearly you do not care about the Java eco system. Nor weak links for Lombok. java2html was never even updated for Java 1.5. It is that old. Added to Lombok in the same year Java 9 is to be released. Most projects are looking forward. if Lombok wants to live in the past, using projects of yester year that is surely logical. But almost no one supports 1.5, much less 1.4... Even vendors have moved on. Oracle will not support 1.5, nor IBM or Redhat.

When coming across such, almost knowing it will fall on deaf ears not to be changed. Tone is more justified in my opinion. This just creates a mess in the Java eco system.

title: @Delegate is not working for method with different generic overloads

nodes.body: Still being an issue ...
Can you post a code example which we can all (try to) compile?

[demo.zip](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/files/1345945/demo.zip)

Building the project with maven results in the following error:

com.example.lombok.overloading.demo.client.EventRepositoryDelegee is not abstract and does not override abstract method delete(java.lang.Long) in com.example.lombok.overloading.demo.third.party.AbstractEntityRepository

If I use your `Comp` and use `Integer` as the replacement for `ID` then the error is `The method get(Integer) is ambiguous for the type Base` (as it should), which is different from what you have.  Otherwise there's no problem.

Your Maven example, as I said, gives no error for me and the error you are reporting for it is different than the error you are reporting for this one, which indicates that you're doing something different. You need to create a simple example like I did which produces the same error to be used for comparison.

Also have a look at the [Delegate](https://projectlombok.org/features/experimental/Delegate) page which talks about problems with generics.

I'm wondering why `mvn clean install` is not generating the mentioned error on your machine. So lets change my demo.zip in the following way:

- I removed the spring-data dependency
- I tried to reproduce the same interface-hierarchy as spring-data does

The new [demo2.zip](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/files/1347055/demo2.zip) is producing the mentioned error just as I pointed out:

`/demo/src/main/java/com/example/lombok/overloading/demo/client/EventRepositoryDelegee.java:[9,8] com.example.lombok.overloading.demo.client.EventRepositoryDelegee is not abstract and does not override abstract method findOne(java.lang.Long) in com.example.lombok.overloading.demo.third.party.two.ExpectedEntityRepository`

I'm afraid `@Delegate` is not able to analyze the interface-hierarchy of the third.party.one-package

I created a [CompactDemo.zip](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/files/1347359/CompactDemo.zip) based on your demo. I removed completely the Spring dependencies (you still had them) and minimized the amount of code needed to produce the error. Please verify that you're getting the same error after a clean install.

If you do, then you'll notice that the error comes from having a generic interface bridging the method, `interface EntityRepository<T>`. If you either remove the `<T>` or add the method `void findOne(Long id);` to `EntityRepository` you should get a successful compilation. This is a bug because the generic parameter is meaningless yet changes the behavior.

title: @NonNull parameters on constructors are validated only after the base constructor call

nodes.body:
Wow! I was thinking about using a constructor with a unique number of arguments, but this won't work either as there could be
```
 public Descendant(Object... args) {....}
```
and the generated constructor takes precedence when it applies.

---

Whenever there's a parameter in the super call, you can use a helper method like
```
private <T> T returnFirstAndCheckAllOthers(T result, @NonNull Object a, @NonNull Object b) {
    Objects.requireNonNull(a, "a")
    Objects.requireNonNull(b, "b")
    return result;
}
```
and pass the first argument through it.

This solves the `super(useA ? a : b)` problem. It doesn't help with `super(a.trim() + b)`, but this case is easy. It doesn't help with parameterless `super()` calls, but they at least don't produce any warnings, so this may be alright. 

---

Anyway, it looks far too complicated.

> If we turn it into:
```
super(returnFirstAndCheckAllOthers(f1(a, b), a, b), f2(a, b));
```
... then we blew it. It must be the very first thing evaluated, so use
```
super(f1(returnFirstAndCheckAllOthers(a, a, b), n), f2(a, b));
```
instead.

The rule is simply "put it in the very first possible position". It relies in the function argument evaluation order, though only because of `f2`.

- closure - this probably breaks when enough generics come in
- `ignoreAllButLast` - I like it better than my method. It's the C comma operator.
- `.... && .... && .... ? .... : .....` - that's even better as it needs no synthetic method...
-  ... but `Objects.requireNonNull(a, "a") != null` would probably produce a warning
- ... so I'd suggest to use `Objects.requireNonNull(a, "a") == a` instead
- ... which may produce a warning because of not using `equals`
- ... so we either have *a helper method or a warning*

---

Now I see that you picked up a trivial problem, which can be solved with
```
super(f1(Objects.requireNonNull(a, "a"), Objects.requireNonNull(b, "b")), f2(a, b));
```
The helper function/expression is only needed when some argument won't get evaluated or gets evaluated too late or only conditionally. Something like
```
super(f1(a), f2(a==b ? c : b))
```
would need it.

`startGreatCatastrophe` - soon to come, anyway.

So, you assume automatic disambiguation of all constructor calls (that may become ambiguous after adding additional new private constructors) within the class (or within the outer class in case of nested classes).

Well, if it is technically not so hard (I don't know much about internals of lombok and interfaces it uses to analyse/alter the code) — then why not.

Of course this still will break some very weird cases with reflection (like `cs = MyClass.class.getContructors(); cs[cs.length()-3].newInstance(args);`) — but I think it's ok to break them.

I again ran into this. I'm afraid, the general case are rather unsolvable, as the funny solutions we elaborated above are far too complicated. However, two things could be done, covering most cases:

- (optional) Whenever there's an always-executed dereference and #1197 gets used, the argument occurrence could be enclosed by the check.
- Whenever it could easily determined that the check surely comes too late, omit it.

I already see that it indirectly comes from § 8.8 “Capitalization of inferred names”. It says:
> Thus when we extract a property or event name from the middle of an existing Java name, we
normally convert the first character to lower case. However to support the occasional use of all
upper-case names, we check if the first two characters of the name are both upper case and if

@grimly The obvious ones: 1. They (can't be overridden but they) still can override a method. 2. They are methods (my rule is: no non-private non-constant fields).

@grimly, do you mean: over the public fields?

Well:

 1. **Consistent (unbroken) API**.

    Right now you have properties `getX`/`setX` and `getY`/`setY` backed directly into the fields `x` and `y`. Then you add calculated `getPhi`/`setPhi` and `getRho`/`setRho` properties.  2. Don't forget that nobody forces you to use both `lombok.Getter` and `lombok.Setter` at once. You can use trivial (lombok-generated) getter with more complex setter (e.g. `this.value = value; repaint()`). Or a trivial (lombok-generated) getter with more complex getter (e.g. `return this.value != null ? this.value : parent.value`). Or only trivial getter with no setter; or trivial getter with other ways to set (like `T getValue()` + `void setValue(T value, String changeReason)`).

@rspilker, sorry, maybe I ask something stupid, but why don't you consider "I want to have sub-classes, but they are not allowed to override my getter/setter" to be an actual use case? (What do you mean by actual use case then?)

Can you describe a common, real world (non-hypothetical) scenario where the class in not final, but the getters and setter must be final, and that that's the best solution for the problem.

In my experience, lots of code bases are favoring composition over inheritance. Most data classes don't have sub-classes. And if they do, there is no requirement that the getters/setters need to be final. I mean, that invariants are fundamentally broken.

@rspilker, for me "I want to have sub-classes, but they are not allowed to override my getter/setter" is a real-world every-day (every day when I use Java) scenario.

> In my experience, lots of code bases are favoring composition over inheritance.

Exactly. That's why I tend to have things `final` by default. Usually I make the whole class `final` (therefore making all members implicitly final).

But in some cases we allow class to be inherited. In that cases usually _specific_ methods are allowed to be overridden but not _all_ methods. I.e. in such classes I by default mark all methods as `final` and then unmark those of them that are allowed to be overridden by design.

I.e. almost **every** class that I allow to be inherited has at least some final methods (though for most of the classes I forbid inheritance at all). And if such (non-final) class has some trivial getter and/or setter methods, they're most certainly final — because they're usually not the part of the stuff that is by design allowed to be overridden.

Maybe it matters that I use Java not for my work but for my hobby projects. Never-the-less for me it's a usual thing: I make everything final by default and then consciously "unfinalize" some small parts. Getters and setters almost never get "unfinallized". (If I were a Lombok designer, I'd made getter and setters final **by default**, but I understand that now it might be too incompatible change.)
Consider abstract base classes (for e.g. database objects => my use-case) as a real-world scenario.

We also had that use case (database mapping classes for JCR). JCR also has a (very special) notion of inheritance. Thus, it becomes even more important to design the inheritance in Java well, especially as we allow plugins with customer-specific database sub-classes (i.e. code that we do not control).

Joshua Bloch also says "Design for inheritance or else prohibit it" (Effective Java). Getter and setters are a typical example where you do not want any subclass to mess around with. Imagine a subclass overriding the getter for the unique ID.

Agreed. Whenever possible, all methods should be either abstract or final.

"because I want to have sub-classes, but they are not allowed to override my getter/setter" it's an actual use-case. Just because you don't think so doesn't make it less important.

I agree that a `final` getter that simply returns the property seems useless. And I agree with the concept of composition over inheritance.
But this doesn't mean that inheritance is useless or should not be used.
So many times I start writing some classes and then I realize that all those classes share something that is better expressed with inheritance and not composition.
In those cases, I refactor my classes extracting a base abstract one, and at that moment I often realized that those commons behaviours must not be overridden. So I need to add the final keyword on base class methods.
And sometimes those base class methods are just simple getters... And all is good, because the important thing is that this method, regarding its complexity, it's something that subclasses should not be able to override, so I want to enforce this behaviour.

The final keyword in simple getter often appears in my value objects. Those value object often have a value and I want to be sure that value object subclasses don't return whatever they want. I want they initialize the value calling `super(value)`, maybe adding some validation logic, but I don't want they change what the value object return as the value. So I need the final keyword in my getter method.

You can argue that I can simply declare my field `public final` and all works fine.
Not at all. I want to be open to change how the value is provided through the getter in my base class, so to avoid a "huge" refactor in my codebase I always use a getter method instead of letting access the raw property.

Everything would be better if Java had properties like Kotlin, and getters and setters for those properties.
But Java doesn't have class properties, so I need the final keyword in my getter

> In my experience, lots of code bases are favoring composition over inheritance. Most data classes don't have sub-classes. And if they do, there is no requirement that the getters/setters need to be final. I mean, that invariants are fundamentally broken.

Mockito will mock all methods of an object if they're not final.
So I have a custom mock class which e.g. counts something and I'm incrementing a counter, I say `@Getter long x;` but at runtime I get `org.mockito.exceptions.verification.NoInteractionsWanted`, why? because the non-final getX() was mocked. I google and end up here.

Surely, adding a single optional parameter to `@Getter` and `@Setter`, one that's already being used in other parts of Lombok, couldn't be _that_ complicated! Could it? Plenty of people have given actual real-world use cases for this feature request, so there's not a lot of weight in the claim that it wouldn't be useful. And honestly it's kind of silly to develop annotations for generating Java getters and setters, but arbitrarily decide not to make them feature complete with Java's method declaration syntax, just because you think that keyword isn't important enough.

We asked for a use case and so far nothing that convinced us has been stated, except for the mockito one which isn't good enough. Hence, it's not low hanging fruit.

>  Surely, adding a single optional parameter to @Getter and @Setter, one that's already being used in other parts of Lombok, couldn't be that complicated!

It's trivial. The PR would take us, what, 2 hours?

And that mindset of yours ("just add everything that seems easy when a few folks ask for it!") means that 5 years from now, you type `@Getter(` and ask your IDE about what parameters there are, and you get a list of 50 parameters. Also, our test code which should optimally also test combinations of features, will consist of the combinatory explosion which has ballooned to 15 million different combinations.

We've maintained this project for 12 years. We believe that our hesitance at introducing features 'just cuz it seems easy' plaus a significant role in this.

Thus, whilst 'this is really easy to add' certainly helps, it's not, by any means, the most important consideration.

__We need use cases__.

We need use cases. I'll bat down a bunch of stuff stated as use cases in this issue which either aren't use cases or aren't convincing.

@canemacchina wrote:

No, it's not an actual use case. Nobody sets out to say: "I wish to fasten this plate to this other plate by drilling holes through both and using a screw and bolt getup". That's completely pointless. Someone sets out to build a table, and as part of making the table, they run into the issue of needing to fasten two metal plates together. We need to hear about the table. If we have no experience with tables, we may even need to hear about the concept of 'serving dinner to big groups'. We'll keep asking for more details until we can fill in the rest of the 'chain' so to speak, and the above is so close to the 'how' and so far removed from the 'why', it is completely useless. We don't use everything you use, so we may come across as a bit dense. It's partly because we very well might be (case in point: Neither roel nor I use spring or mockito, coincidentally). And partly because we want everybody to understand why a feature is adding to `lombok.*`. If we're adding this feature solely to satisfy, say, spring autowired, it should be in `lombok.extern.spring` - that's the place for features that cannot be understood without first understanding spring.

WHY do you need to make subclasses that 'cannot override the getter'? If you simply intend to prevent overriding because you're aware that _in general_ that is not a good idea, we're right there with you. But java is what it is, the solution is not to pepper `final` on every method you ever write. Or at least, we do not agree with that as a solution, and the vast majority of the community is on 'our' side on this: Just open random java projects on github and you'll find very few that have marked all but a handful of methods/classes as `final`. The solution lies elsewhere: A java programmer is supposed to know that you can't _just_ start overriding random bits and bobs without at least trying to understand what you're doing, and overriding a lombok-generated getter/setter is real easy to understand. Hence, __I just want to make them `final`!__ is not a use-case, or if it is for you, then it holds absolutely no convincing power at all for us. Go to the next level: _WHY_ do you want it to be `final`?

@marcioggs wrote:

> This would be useful on Spring applications to autowire a field on an abstract class.

See, this is helping. A little bit: Now 'overwriting' the setter breaks auto-wiring and I can see how that may be non-obvious enough that the one doing the overriding just misses this. But this isn't even remotely close to good enough.

This is good work though: Link to reputable tutorials (I consider baeldung reputable, I'd think most would) helps. Links to the web-hosted source control of major projects engaging in a certain style helps. To convince us something is universal boilerplate, you need to hit both beats in that sentence: The boilerplate part tends to be easy enough to show, the universal part - therein lies the rub.

We may not use the frameworks you use daily. Even if we do, many lombok users won't. The feature needs to make sense either without mentioning those frameworks at all, or by mentioning such a varied batch of different frameworks where this comes up that it's effectively universal.

@haelix888 wrote:

> Mockito will mock all methods of an object if they're not final.

You bet. That counts and is helping push this request towards feasibility. I think I want more. I don't like mockito, but I'm pretty sure the java community has embraced it with gusto, but the problem here isn't motivating me, roel, or anyone else to write the PR (that is the easy part). Hence, the only thing that matters is community understanding.

@rzwitserloot I think someone also mentioned abstract classes when used with DI frameworks and whatnot, or just when proving things for external usage and the like.

TBH, I understand that these might not be soooooo compelling use-cases, but I see there is already other things of the same sort on Lombok (makeFinal in FieldDefaults for example) which are arguably more useful, but may end up not so useful of you can override the getters or something.

So I think we _could_ consider this a low-hanging fruit by that token?

I'm only following this issue because I once thought I needed something like that, so I guess people _are_ running into use-cases?

(This other person's attitude is totally not acceptable, but I decided to address your other points regarding not considering adding this feature).

I can provide a PR for this if it makes it easier to justify adding it? (I never bothered to make it happen after I moved in from the project where I needed it, but I can find some time this weekend or the next, I think)

@rzwitserloot got your points. 

As for the code sample, I would assume the field-level one has precendence over the class-level one, IIRC. I think I've done that sort of thing before and it's what I remember seeing when I did #2513.

Yes, field-level annotations have precedence, I think that's what almost everybody would assume, but do they act like annotations and thus, `@Getter` with nothing else 'overwrites' access to `PUBLIC`, or do they act more like language features, and there's a difference between not mentioning it (meaning: Do something sane, a good default - not neccessarily `PUBLIC`). It's not about what lombok currently does. It's about the simple point that it's hopelessly confusing.

I would optimally want to rewrite `AccessLevel` to include some sort of `INHERIT` or `CHAINING` or whatever option, and rewrite the default to that, defined as: "Inherit from parent type, if the parent type doesn't mention it, PUBLIC" - now confusion has been eliminated. But I'm not sure if that's entirely backwards compatible.

Nice to see some "progress" for this feature request. :)

I must admint I don't understand the confusion.
Field-level annotations have precedence. That's it. And it is what I would expect.
And why is this discussion suddenly about access level?

I get your point with "50 parameters" for the @Getter/@Setter annotations, but I think it is a bit exaggerated.
Keeping the API intuitive is not always an easy job. We all know that.
But at the point where intuition ends, the documentation will provide clarification I dare say.
And there's also the IDE.
"Eclipse" for instance shows the details of all methods (incl. the Lombok generated ones) in the class outline view.
So there's no need for guessing what will happen: The IDE (incl. "Intellij IDEA" and many others) will tell you right away.

I still think support for the "final" keyword in the byte code for getters/setters generated by Lombok would be a great addition.
It is a language feature and people like me tend to use such things. ;)

In my case I use final methods (incl. getters/setters) in abstract classes in order to point out that those methods are not safe/destined for overriding. Even in non-abstract classes this approach is useful.
Inheritance in Java is tricky sometimes and I think it is good practice to design classes with inheritance in mind.
The "final" keyword is very helpful in this context.

Thanks for your patience and keep being "cautious" regarding change requests.
I think you're handling these things very well!

Cheers!
-Ferdinand-

@rzwitserloot 

> You bet. That counts and is helping push this request towards feasibility. I think I want more. I don't like mockito, but I'm pretty sure the java community has embraced it with gusto

Happy to see some action here and also that my "use case" with Mockito is deemed the most material so far (albeit not reaching critical mass).

FWIW I though I might add that final also has (almost surely) an bearing on performance also and Getters being so widespread and conveniently generated with Lombok, this fact is not without significance.

Please consider (benefits/downsides) `@Accessors` as a home for `makeFinal`. 

If it's part of `@Accessors`, I think a config key would actually make sense, because than it's a style for "all your DTO's" or something like that.

@o-pikozh Yes, and someone else in this thread indicated they clearly expect that to be `PUBLIC`, and thus you see why this is a blocking issue (which can be solved, but, explains why I'm mentioning it, and why I'm slightly miffed at the cavalcade of 'why have you not added this already it is so simple!'). I'm liking @rspilker 's idea of shifting this to `@Accessors`, that makes this issue entirely moot.
The result there would be a non-final getter, according to the documentation. Just commenting on the fact it could be confusing the same way adding it to Getter would.

From the [documentation](https://projectlombok.org/features/experimental/Accessors):

> `@Accessors` currently does not 'cascade' from field `@Accessors` annotation to the class-level `@Accessors` annotation, but it does 'cascade' to lombok.config. Changing this is not difficult but backwards incompatible. It's not likely to break much existing code, but this needs to be decided on before the feature can move out of experimental status.
Have at it: https://projectlombok.org/download-edge

title: Make @Singular create mutable collections
body:
For mutable collections (the java.util ones supported by Singular), let `@Singular` create mutable collections instead of wrapping them in `unmodifiable*` or using `empty*` or `singleton*`.
It could be an option disabled by default, but accessible like this `@Singluar(mutable = true)`.
It feels to me that being forced to go from mutable to immutable just by adding a convenience `@Singular` to a field is counterintuitive.

nodes.body: Or we can have the current behavior of creating immutable collections applied when the class is also marked as `@Value`, but have mutable collections otherwise a default.

> 
> 
> Or we can have the current behavior of creating immutable collections applied when the class is also marked as `@Value`, but have mutable collections otherwise a default.

I REALLY like the first suggestion of adding an optional (mutable = true) parameter to the Singular annotation. But changing default behavior in a widely used library is not something I would ever encourage.
Any update on this please! I believe this is crucial feature that Lombok team should consider.

Thank You guys for letting me know that im not the only one that wish to have this kind of feature with Lombok. 
Creating mutable collection at the moment results in bad looking code. 
I spend hours on trying to figure it out how to do this better with Lombok and found this thread.

We are in dire need of this feature right now. I understand the advantages of immutable collections in certain scenarios, but the practical advantages of mutable collections are often more important in real world projects.

There are a ton of complications if these things become mutable. We'd have to explain all this, add a sizable maintenance burden, which makes this feature fall under [overgrowth of annotation parameters](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/wiki/LOMBOK-CONCEPT:-What-does-it-take-to-become-a-lombok-feature%3F#user-content-overgrowth-of-annotation-parameters).

Sorry folks. We're not going to do this, and would not accept a PR.

Thank you rzwitserloot for your reply.
I understand that I don't get all the implications of adding this feature.
Good luck continuing work on this beautiful project.

Cheers

@Laures wrote:
> so instead i fell back on Lombok.Default and added the Singular-Convenience Methods myself

We reserve the right to change anything related to $ fields in minor point releases. In other words, don't do this.

The most direct route to a fix seems to be to introduce a feature whereby you can have lombok inject an all-args constructor as normal, but allow you to write a 'mutator' method; its argument(s) take the place of where lombok would have ordinarily put the parameter, and its return value takes the place. Then you can add a mutator to the all-args constructor so that you can wrap it in your own whatever-list-you-please, without the burden of having to write out a parameter for all the fields, write all the `this.x = x;` assignments, and maintain all that when you add/remove/change fields.

Sort of, except now you don't get the benefits of all the smart stuff lombok does under the hood for singular, and this breaks some rules (for example, our `builder()` guarantees that you can call `build()` more than once without all hell breaking loose. With your example, all hell would break loose.

I get the need for something like this, but there are a billion-and-one requirements and most of them get into hairy questions that don't come up except in exotic scenarios. Which means it _seems_ like an easy feature, but isn't.

The point stands: This isn't happening anytime soon; we don't run into this often but the proposals so far seem to be written by folks who don't seem to be on the same page as we are as far as problems are concerned. That leaves us at an impasse, and that's why the issue remains closed.

A more thorough proposal for the mutator idea, plus some documentation updates for `@Singular` to explain how you can use a mutator to create your own mutable list variant, seems like the easy answer.

@Setter doesn't properly copy @Nullable with ElementType.TYPE_USE
body:
It seems that internal Lombok logic for `@Setter` generation doesn't copy (to the generated setter argument) `@Nullable` annotation that only has `@Target({ ElementType.TYPE_USE })`

Looks like Lombok is explicitly looking for `@Target({ElementType.PARAMETER})` on the `@Nullable` annotation when deciding whether to copy the annotation.

Since `@Target({ ElementType.TYPE_USE })` is perfectly valid for using on method arguments it looks like a Lombok bug.

nodes.body:
Can you give example code including the fully qualified annotations? And what you expected from lombok. And if you use `javac` or Eclipse?

Lombok does not inspect the annotation; we copy the annotation solely on the name.

I'll try to make examples when I have more time, but it doesn't look to me that Lombok copies annotation solely based on name. Or potentially maybe Lombok tries to copy annotation but the underlying code generation library fails?

Basically what I did -- I compiled code under Eclipse using Lombok 1.16.18. When I discovered that it wasn't worked properly, I tried to decompile the resulting class files.

From those I concluded that Lombok does not copy Nullable annotation with only `@Target({ ElementType.TYPE_USE })` when using `@Setter` (i.e. the annotation doesn't appear in decompiled code and Eclipse behaves like there's no annotation).

Once I've added `@Target({ElementType.PARAMETER})` all became well -- annotation appears in decompiled code and Eclipse behaves as if annotation is present on setter's parameter.
I suspect that the eclipse compiler attached the annotation to the type of the field, and not to the field itself, and we only copy the annotations on the field.

[lombok-nullable.zip](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/files/1350801/lombok-nullable.zip)

Attaching zip archive with Eclipse project (using Version: Oxygen Release (4.7.0) Build id: 20170620-1800)

Look into decompiled2 folder -- that's where I've put decompilation results from the generated class files. As you can see -- getter is always annotated with `@Nullable`, but setter argument is only `@Nullable` when we have `ElementType.PARAMETER` target.

So clearly Lombok 'sees' the annotation. It just doesn't 'put' it into setter argument -- which looks like a bug to me.

nodes.body:
As you can read in [the documentation](https://projectlombok.org/features/EqualsAndHashCode#supported-configuration-keys) in the section "Supported configuration keys" it is possible to put the following line in a `lombok.config` file:
```
lombok.equalsAndHashCode.callSuper=skip
```

I would recommend to put this `lombok.config` file in the directory containing the code where you are sure that that's the right behavior.

If you want it in your whole project, you can put it in the root of all your source code.

title: Generate static field name
body:
JPA Metamodel Generator generates Metamodel (e.g. SingularAttribute) for each Entity field.
But sometimes you just want to use a field name in string. More often you want to use it not on a class which is not Entity (DTO for example).

That is why I’d suggest ```@GenerateFieldName``` annotation where one has possibility to create static access to the variable name. For example:


```
@GenerateFieldName
private Integer myVariable;

…
assertEquals(MyClass.FIELD_MY_VARIABLE, "myVariable")
```

It could be used anywhere where you need to bind some value to specific field using reflection or beanutils

title: custom NonNull annotation
body:
Allow lombok.config configuration of a fully qualified class name for the ``@NonNull`` annotation.

The reason is that #1384 has been rejected, but the need is still there.
IntelliJ has very nice nullability checks, but I can't use it for types (e.g. I can't declare ``List<@NonNull String>``).

So now I am torn between 2 options:
- use Lombok and have bad IDE support, but good runtime checks
- use a different annotation for ``@NonNull`` and have good IDE support, but no runtime checks

Since ``@NonNull`` doesn't have any properties, it should be possible to configure which annotation to use in Lombok, and those of us that are not stuck with an End-Of-Life product (JDK 6 or 7) can still use modern IDE support.

As a side note, this is only an issue if one is forced to use Java.
Kotlin has something much better: compile-time errors for nullability mistakes.

title: No getter method generated from private static final String with Data annotated to a class

nodes.body:
You're right. This sounds like a documentation bug. AFAIK `@Data` is supposed to work like

*`@ToString`, `@EqualsAndHashCode`, `@Getter`, `@Setter` and `@RequiredArgsConstructor` on the whole class*

This makes sense, as etters for static fields hardly ever make sense. Usually, classes have a few private static fields which should stay really private and auto-generating etters for them would make `@Data` harder to use.
I don't think `private static` fields in classes *should stay really private*, I think a `@Getter` method for them is usually necessary. Don't you think so?

@cinqs Me? Sure.

As a `static` field means global state, it's better to avoid it, unless it's a constant (but then you usually just make it `public static final`). If you need static non-constants, then it's better to keep them private. Etters make it slightly better by providing some control.

Singletons are evil, but considered to be better than statics. Dependency injection is considered to be the ultimate good.

For anything global, I use Guice with `@Singleton`, so I get a proper object with non-static fields, which gets injected where needed. This works nicely with Lombok: https://softwareengineering.stackexchange.com/a/256177/14167

I can't recall when I recently used any etters with static fields. I'm not saying, it's *never* needed, but it should be used very rarely. Therefore, I consider `@Data` ignoring statics right.
ok, then, I will add `@Getter` myself. And you fix the documentation declaration.

title: Eclipse 'report problems as you type' reports non-existing nullability problems.
body:
I've originally filled the bug with Eclipse: https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=525381
However Stephan Herrmann says it's not an Eclipse problem but instead is a Lombok problem: 'It looks like the lombok Eclipse plug-in succeeds in propagating the @Nullable annotation from the field in one case and fails to do so in another case.'

-------

Using Lombok ( https://projectlombok.org/ ) for getter/setter generation + enabling Null-analysis in Eclipse works correctly (there are no warnings/errors in the project) but 'Report problems as you type' Java editor option incorrectly highlights editor code as having problems.

Reproduction steps:
- Take clean Eclipse Oxygen J2EE (eclipse-jee-oxygen-R-win32-x86_64.zip)
- Run it to create a workspace
- Exit
- Install Lombok (1.16.18) for this Eclipse by running lombok.jar; you can take the jar from the attached Eclipse project zip from lib folder; if you don't want to run the jar, you can modify eclipse.ini directly, add: -javaagent:lombok.jar (and copy jar to wherever that .ini is)
- Run Eclipse and import attached Java project into workspace; possibly you'll need to clean & rebuild it, not sure.
- Observe that there are no compilation problems in the project (no markers in package explorer, nothing in Problems view)
- Open ThingyUser.java and observe null-related warning and 'dead code' warnings displayed in the editor (there's still nothing in Problems view)


The 'Problems' view in this case is correct -- there's no actual problem with the code -- generated getters & setters are properly annotated with Nullable and therefore there should be no warnings or errors. However the 'Report problems as you type' functionality doesn't appear to 'understand' this.

Note that @Nullable being used is non-standard one -- it has an additional ElementType.PARAMETER target because Lombok does seem to require it for proper Setter generation.

[generated-code-bug-demo.zip](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/files/1398737/generated-code-bug-demo.zip)

![problem-screenshot](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/106305/31775712-be16532a-b4bf-11e7-8c14-12c788cce455.png)

title: @RequiredArgsConstructor does not respect @NonNull fields in superclass

nodes.body: <strike>`int` is a primitive and can never be null.</strike> (Example use case was updated.)
@wrprice Corrected. :)

@Maaartinus That's why I declared the superclass as abstract--the child class has to initialize the field instead of a constructor in the parent.

That's a good point about lombok working in the compile stage. I imagine there's a (super ugly) way to inspect the code to determine if it has a superclass, but it would probably be too hacky and  fragile to be worth it.

[EDIT: the solution in the comment below is less horrible (and much easier) than this one.]
It's also quite ugly and redundant, but how about adding a `check` parameter to `@NonNull`--something like `NonNull(check=Parent.class)`? Although I would admit that would be so embarrassingly ugly I wouldn't even document it.
@wrprice exactly. See my other bug. :)
@wrprice as @Maaartinus pointed out, if Lombok could look for parent constructors, it could also (and should) look for the fields directly. The issue is it can't easily.

Maybe a slightly less horrible solution would be to add an `include` parameter to `@RequiredArgsConstructor`, like (citing the above example) `@RequiredArgsConstructor(include="someProperty", includeType = Integer.class)`? No javadocs though, but they're not there anyway. :)

@wrprice yep, the child couldn't use a no-arg constructor (well, it _could_) because it needs to initialize `someProperty`. But that's beside the point of this issue, since we're trying to create a constructor in the first place.

> That's why I declared the superclass as abstract--the child class has to initialize the field instead of a constructor in the parent.

@alvint But that's impossible in Java. The field is private, game over.

Even if it wasn't, that's a very strange idea to let subclasses do the initialization.

> I imagine there's a (super ugly) way to inspect the code to determine if it has a superclass, but it would probably be too hacky and fragile to be worth it.

There indeed is such a thing, it's called resolution and and it's indeed too fragile.

> It's also quite ugly and redundant, but how about adding a check parameter to @NonNull

AFAICT no chance. Implementing new Lombok features is orders of magnitude more difficult than a similar thing in an annotation processor. The maintenance is even worse as Lombok can't use a proper stable API.

Therefore a feature doing something strange has no chance. A feature requiring resolution has no chance either. This one is both.

---

> Maybe a slightly less horrible solution would be to add an include parameter to @RequiredArgsConstructor, like (citing the above example) RequiredArgsConstructor(include="someProperty", includeType = Integer.class)?

This would work for a single field only.

There's a similar proposal for specifying the super-constructor to be called, but don't keep your fingers crossed. There are tons of feature requests and hardly any progress recently. The authors concentrate on stability and Java 9 compatibility.
@Maaartinus yep, i left out the multiple fields stuff for simplicity of expressing the concept. I figured they'd automatically add it.
@Maaartinus crap, the field should not be private. Edited. Thanks for catching that.

For all generated constructors, we currently cannot use any information from the super type, since that would require resolution. This also goes for builders. Without manually adding that information to each subclass, I do not see this working anytime soon. And adding information about the parent class is also a horrible solution. So we're kinda stuck here. I'm closing this issue, not because I think it isn't important, but because I don't see how we can solve it. Sorry.

 ```java
final LombokBuilder<Dog> lombokBuilder = LombokBuilder.<Dog>builder().animal(new Dog()).build();
```

I don't think that this is a lombok problem.

If we're going to add something, it will be in a way that allows getters to make a safecopy of the field or wrap it in something unmodifiable. This is not a collections-only concern.

title: delombok: generated Javadoc for getters and setters should be put on @param and @return

nodes.body:
It is possible to define @returns and @param on the fields javadoc, lombok will move it:

> NEW in lombok v1.12.0: javadoc on the field will now be copied to generated getters and setters. Normally, all text is copied, and @return is moved to the getter, whilst @param lines are moved to the setter. Moved means: Deleted from the field's javadoc. It is also possible to define unique text for each getter/setter. To do that, you create a 'section' named GETTER and/or SETTER. A section is a line in your javadoc containing 2 or more dashes, then the text 'GETTER' or 'SETTER', followed by 2 or more dashes, and nothing else on the line. If you use sections, @return and @param stripping for that section is no longer done (move the @return or @param line into the section).

However, if these tags are absent, I would agree that copying the fields javadoc as default is nicer than an empty javadoc.

With the newer JDKs (I think this started with JDK 11, but I'm not sure), javadoc compilation by default lints very strictly. You'll be seeing this a lot: `warning: no @return` and with the default settings, the Javadoc Maven Plugin will fail when used on delomboked sources that don't manually specify all `@param` and `@return` parameters. So it would be great if delombok by default produced code that passes the new linting.

While that's not the case, and you don't want to add "water is wet" twice to every field Javadoc, the commonly suggested fix is to just turn of the linting of the Javadoc altogether. This can be done with `<additionalOptions>-Xdoclint:none</additionalOptions>` in the Javadoc Maven Plugin.

If you're on Java 8 source, javadoc compilation will still fail with `javadoc: error - The code being documented uses modules but the packages defined in https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/ are in the unnamed module`. Instead of turning off doclint, you can fix both problems by declaring the correct Java version for the javadoc plugin:

```
<plugin>
	<groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
	<artifactId>maven-javadoc-plugin</artifactId>
	<configuration>
		<source>1.8</source>
	</configuration>
</plugin>

```

title: @Builder.Default: error: non-static type variable T cannot be referenced from a static context

nodes.body: I can reproduce the problem.

Java main() method cannot access a non-static member of its class. That means, public static void main(String[] args) is a static method. Instance variables (variables defined in the class but not marked as static keyword) cannot be accessed from a static method without referencing an instance of the class. An attempt to use the variables and methods of the class which do not have the static modifier without creating an instance of the class is caught by the Java compiler at compile time and flagged as an error: Cannot Be Referenced From a [Static Context](http://net-informations.com/java/err/static.htm) . To solve your problem, you need to create an instance of your class and then you can access the methods and variables of the class that have not been declared with the static modifier .

Static methods are useful if you have only one instance where you're going to use the method, and you don't need multiple copies (objects). Non-static methods are used if you're going to use your method to create multiple copies.
