title: Setter (kind of) for List, Maps with lazy create

nodes.body:
Lazy initialization, as well as the concrete type of created List (Map, Set, etc.), has behavioral and/or threading implications that probably shouldn't be left up to Lombok annotations to solve and then hide the details.  It also means that Lombok would need to potentially address any place where the lazy field is dereferenced to check for `null`, and substitute an empty collection instead?

Is the map allocation really something you've profiled and _need_ to optimize to be lazy?  Even then you might be better served by writing a reusable [forwarder][fwd] or [proxy][prox] to handle the lazy initialization aspects; that would encapsulate and take care of making the map init/use lazy, but it still costs you some GC pressure with an eagerly-allocated wrapper object on the heap.

[fwd]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forwarding_(object-oriented_programming)
[prox]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proxy_pattern

We were looking into a number of techniques since I started this ticket. What we realized is that what we are really missing is... an easy way to extend Lombok. Yes, I agree, this is tricky. Like most things about Lombok features. It has consequences all over the places as only that most obvious patterns will not have those. 

For now, what we did was to write our own annotation that will address our need. I think it would be sufficient addressing mine and many other requests by providing a good extension point. I am happy creating internal tools that address our needs but now it's actually not simple...

title: Eclipse save actions with `@EqualsAndHashCode` without fields add misplaced `final`

nodes.body:
What I wrote in this comment, was mostly wrong, so I rewrote it from scratch. 

Eclipse obviously tries to add `final` to the local variable in the `hashCode` implementation, which leads to adding it in front of `@EqualsAndHashCode`. This obviously doesn't make the variable final, so it happens again and again.

I mistakenly placed `@EqualsAndHashCode(onlyExplicitlyIncluded=true)` on the enclosing class, while `@EqualsAndHashCode.Include` were correctly placed on fields of the nested class, where they did nothing. This caused my confusion. It should produce a warning, but otherwise, it did what it should.
Is there any way I can help with this further?

Probably not. Lombok must work on 1.6 so you can't use lambdas.

I don't understand why you've made this complicated lambda. Isn't it just.. `if (members.isEmpty()) resultDecl.modifiers |= Modifier.FINAL`?
Fixed in that commit, will be in the next version. Didn't bother mentioning it on the changelog, this change doesn't seem to warrant that.

> Probably not. Lombok must work on 1.6 so you can't use lambdas.

Didn't have that in mind at that moment. Sorry.

> I don't understand why you've made this complicated lambda. Isn't it just.. `if (members.isEmpty()) resultDecl.modifiers |= Modifier.FINAL`?

That `members.isEmpty()` catches most cases, but there might be a case inside the `for` in which no more statement is added. In that case the variable should be final, too. Though I'm not sure if token can get `!= null` or if the types dimension can be less than zero.

	at java.base/java.lang.ClassLoader.loadClass(ClassLoader.java:499)
	at java.base/java.lang.Class.forName0(Native Method)
	at java.base/java.lang.Class.forName(Class.java:291)
	at lombok.javac.JavacTreeMaker$SchroedingerType.getFieldCached(JavacTreeMaker.java:156)
	at lombok.javac.JavacTreeMaker$TypeTag.typeTag(JavacTreeMaker.java:245)
	at lombok.javac.Javac.<clinit>(Javac.java:155)
	... 49 more
```

The reason is that the lombok library auto-registers a Java annotation processor. 

Fortunately, there is a workaround for project A, which is to disable annotation processing under Java 10:

```
    <profile>
      <id>lombok-fix</id>
      <activation>
        <jdk>[10,)</jdk>
      </activation>
      <build>
        <pluginManagement>
          <plugins>
            <plugin>
              <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
              <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
              <version>3.7.0</version>
              <configuration>
                <!-- Disable annotation processors to avoid build failing on Java 10 with lombok -->
                <compilerArgument combine.children="append">-proc:none</compilerArgument>
              </configuration>
            </plugin>
          </plugins>
        </pluginManagement>
      </build>
    </profile>
```

This works as long as project A does not need to make use of annotation processors at all. If it needs annotation processors, it might be possible to list the requires processors explicitly: https://maven.apache.org/plugins/maven-compiler-plugin/compile-mojo.html#annotationProcessors

nodes.body:
AFAIK, lombok is solely an annotation processor tool and should not be used as a runtime dependency to anything that is not another annotation processor tool (and even if this is the case, this is questionable). Many projects that violated this rule already caused many problems downstream elsewhere.

This hints that your Project B is incorrectly configured, because it should not let its dependency in lombok leak out of its build proccess. This could be achieved by something like that (sorry if I get some detail wrong):

```xml
<properties>
    <lombok.version>1.16.20</lombok.version>
</properties>

<pluginManagement>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>3.7.0</version>
            <configuration>
                <annotationProcessorPaths>
                    <!-- Lombok should be used as an annotation processor. -->
                    <annotationProcessorPath>
                        <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
                        <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
                        <version>${lombok.version}</version>
                    </annotationProcessorPath>
                </annotationProcessorPaths>
            </configuration>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</pluginManagement>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
        <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
        <version>${lombok.version}</version>
        <optional>true</optional> <!-- Do not let it leak out as a transitive dependency! -->
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

If you aren't allowed to change B's `pom.xml` file, you may try to exclude it from A:

```xml
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>some.group.id</groupId>
        <artifactId>projectb</artifactId>
        <version>${projectb.version}</version>
        <exclusions>
            <exclusion>
                <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
                <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
            </exclusion>
        </exclusions>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

Also, note that if A does uses lombok directly (independently of B), it should also not allow it to leak out of its build proccess, just as I showed in the first snippet above.

The snippets above probably would still need a lot of hammering to cope with all that module craziness that Java 9 added, but this should have nothing to do with this issue.
@victorwss thanks. I have opened an issue with the project through which I acquired the transitive dependency on lombok. Let's see what they say.

@victorwss thanks for the clarification, this was definitely our bad. We will implement the proposed fix for our release this week and update. I would say in general you can close this. I will update here if we have any problems.
@agibsonccc @victorwss thanks! Closing the issue.

title: Not work on Android Studio 3.1
Suggestion - an @Exclude annotation
body:
One of the common problems I face is the simplicity of adding, removing and - in general - managing what should be covered by Lombok and what not. The obvious answer is _everything_, but life is never that simple. 

On the level of using `@Data`, `@ToString` and other annotations on the class level... things can be complicated. Sure, I can go one level lower and add `@Getter` and `@Setter` annotations to each class, use `exclude` on `@ToString`, etc. - but does it make Lombok so useful at this point? Still, the answer is *yes*, but... Yes, but. It doesn't make life so much easier.

As with `@NonNull` annotation, my suggestion is to introduce an optional `@Exclude` or honoring some other annotation here. A simple one that would be used by all class-level processing and will skip this specific property from adding to the resulting code. So no more getter and setter for the specific property, no inclusion in hash code and `ToString`, etc. That would make my code more and more often way more readable...

That's why I wrote "_in hash code and ToString, *etc*._". In this case, `@AllArgsConstructor` is tricky, but I think it also should be included. We're talking here about fields that are processed, used internally but still require a private or package level access. 

Let me give you an example to picture why I do believe it's a good idea.

I have a Hibernate mapping. In one of the entity I have and `@Id` field for which I do not want any access to since it is generated by a very specific, custom made generator. It is a requirement that we have fulfilled, regardless of the fact whether it is a good or a bad idea. In this case, in the API of that entity, we do not want people to even know about it. A getter would be acceptable, but a setter - never. This entity has 26 properties - again, not our choice, just the way it is. Yes, we can introduce `@Getter` and `@Setter` on the level of each field as we need them, sure. But this doesn't make the code easier to read, makes it messy actually. It is much nice just to have a `@Data` annotation; it makes it uber-clean. But `@Data` doesn't even allow us to filter out a property from `toString()` method. So we are forced to use `@ToString` with a filter, `@EqualsAndHashCode,` `@Getter` and `@Setter` on class level. At this point, the convenience `@Data` is no longer a convenience...

I am all for a clean API of Lombok. But I am also for a clean code of my projects. I do not want some dramatic changes, but I do believe that either `@Exclude` annotation or extension of `@Data` and/or `@Getter` and `@Setter` to include more complex scenarios when used on type-level would be beneficial and seems like a fairly simple extension of this amazing tool...

Right.

One thing that helps break down tables with way too many columns if you
have an annotation based hibernate mapping is creating objects tagged with
```@Embeddable``` and embedding those in the bigger class that describes
the entire table.
( I suspect that's also possible with XML based mappings, just haven't used
that in a while).

That at least should help you break down that class into somewhat smaller
easier to compose parts.

I know that's probably not the answer you want to hear, but classes with 26
fields are not very maintainable to begin with ;-)

As for a ```@LombokExclude``` annotation .. I'd sooner have the exclude
property that is present for various other annotations extended to class
level getter/setter annotations.
At least that way things are consistent. Besides, I have no idea how that
annotation would interact with the existing exclude fields on
```@ToString``` etc .. that sounds like complexity we don't really need
right now.

We do use `@Embeddable` but not always it makes things easier. Actually, we use a hell lot of different techniques to make our code readable, Lombok among them. project is to simply start writing the code.

title: @Builder should copy field annotations to builder methods (where appropriate)

nodes.body: What to do if annotation has target = FIELD?
If the annotation is not applicable, it is not applicable.

Lombok can't detect it as it runs on an early stage of compilation. IMHO such a feature needs to be configured in lombok.config, listing all annotations which should be copied and where. That's not very nice, but it's very practical as it needs to be done just once per annotation class (rather than its occurrence).

Fixed in latest edge, thanks to @wmdietl :)

title: Add option to super-call in builder constructor
body:
Add a new attribute to `@Builder`, determining if there will be a super call in the builder constructor.

My use case:

* There is a class `Message`, containins an attribute `type`.
* There are sub-classes like `LoginMessage`, that have attributes like `username`.
* Both `Message` and `LoginMessage extends Message` are annotated with `@Getter`, `@Setter` and `@Builder`, thus `LoginMessage` provides `getType()`
* When built with `LoginMessageBuilder`, `getType` will always return null for a LoginMessage
* I am setting the type in the constructor of `Message`, but that constructor is not called upon `#build()`

nodes.body:
I think that you either misunderstood some thing or failed to explain it correctly.
The constructor of the superclass must be called by the constructor of the subclass, the builder can't do anything about that. Also, if `LoginMessage` provides `getType()`, why it is stored in `Message` instead of `LoginMessage`? What does the `getType()` of the `Message` actually means?

Can you provide a code of what you want to write as lombok-spiced code and what you expected to be the equivalente delomboked code?

As I wrote an example, I just recognized that the error came from something else. I got NullPointerExceptions due to bad architecture, fixed the architecture and got another NullPointer, but it wasn't from the `_type`.
It works, and it should have worked before, I think the error was somewhere else.
Thank you, you are a good rubber duck 😄

It's called implicitly actually, and I should have known this from the beginning.

title: Feature request: @Cleanup on fields using java.lang.ref.Cleaner
body:
[`Object.finalize()` is deprecated starting with Java 9](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/9/docs/api/java/lang/Object.html#finalize--). The new [`java.lang.ref.Cleaner`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/9/docs/api/java/lang/ref/Cleaner.html) is a great way to implement cleanup work that one would traditionally put in a `finalize` method. However, it takes a lot of boilerplate to write a cleaner. I think it would be great to have `@Cleanup` work on fields where it would generate code utilizing a `Cleaner`. As a fallback for compiling code for older java versions, it could generate a `finalize` method. However, this may prove tricky to do for non-final fields because a Cleaner may not hold a reference to the object it is affiliated with:
Note that the cleaning action must not refer to the object being registered. If so, the object will not become phantom reachable and the cleaning action will not be invoked automatically.
— https://docs.oracle.com/javase/9/docs/api/java/lang/ref/Cleaner.html

nodes.body: @Maaartinus Right now I'm working with an API (wrapped native library) that expects one to call close() to clean up native resources. While it _shouldn't_ happen that a close() is forgotten, I'm using `Cleaner`s to ensure that anything that might have been leaked gets cleaned up when its corresponding object gets collected.

@xnrand OK, so you have to write many `Cleaner`s, right? The problem is that there are so many feature coming in and that implementing (and maintaining!) anything with Lombok is way harder than using standard annotation processing (as the latter is fully supported, while Lombok works in gray areas). So only the most wanted features get a chance (I'm not a project author, but that's what one of them wrote).

I wonder if the cleaners can be generated using annotation processing or reflection?

The official way to ensure close is called on opened resources is the
try-with resources statement.
https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/essential/exceptions/tryResourceClose.html

If you don't have control over the call sites you have a different problem
though.

You suggest `@Cleanup` on a field. I assume that would mean that if a value is assigned to the field and this object is eligible for garbage collection, we ensure the field is explicitly "closed", whatever that might mean. 

There are some pretty big gotchas here:
- Where would we get the cleaner instance from. We shouldn't create one for each class, since that spawns a whole thread.
- The cleanup code executed must be in a static context (not referencing the outer object). But we need the value of the field. Lombok can obviously generate code. In this case, we would need to generate a class, containing the reference to the resource and the cleanup code in the `run` method. 
- We would need to create a field containing an instance of that class, and a (private) getter to give the containing class access to the resource. We probably should re-use the original field, and change the type.

Although I do see the opportunity to reduce a lot of boiler-plate, I don't think this is used common enough to warrant our time.

title: Feature request:  @Builder to use setters rather than @AllArgsConstructor
body:
The `@AllArgsConstructor` is a bit controversial. It makes an ugly API,  it causes issues with Jackson, sometimes Hibernate and JAXB, the way it is used it makes the .class file a bit larger just for a single purpose, JVM needs to check for potential super constructors...

It would be nice if the builder class could (optionally) directly call setters on a newly created object, and then simply return that object on `build()`.

What would be the point of having a builder then, right? Two reasons:

1) Getting rid of a constructor with parameters,

2) The setters could be (package) private. `Foo.Builder` could access them, but setters would not be visible outside. This would allow package (or inner static) classes to alter the object, but from the outside, the class would be "unmodifiable".

As a bonus, a builder class implemented this way would be faster create smaller .class file.

nodes.body:
So you propose to replace the implicit allargsconstructor with implicit
setters then. ;)
What about classes that do not need setters?

Frankly, this is very much a matter of taste and preferences. I for one
hate setters for a whole bunch of reasons. If it was possibly to get rid of
them entirely, I would.
Your list of problems with the allargsconstructor does not really convince
me, either.
- Jackson works fine with it. Works fine with builders, too.
- Generated setters would make that object even bigger (one method per
field, not just one method)
- The ugly API isn't even directly visible
- The JVM always needs to check for super constructors, also for the no
args constructor the builder still needs to call (and generate).

Conversely, making objects only partially immutable like that makes a whole
host of optimisations harder. Having fields final, not having setters,
gives the JVM guarantees your version won't be able to give.

So no, not an improvement.

title: @UtilityClass compile error

nodes.body:
I was skeptical of this and made a test intending to refute this bug. However, for my surprise, I just confirmed it.

I have a somewhat large project that uses some classes with `@UtilityClass`. Using `import static mypackage.SomeUtilityClass.*;` works nice for me. However, if I use `import static mypackage.SomeUtilityClass.someStaticMethod;`, then javac spits a lot of compile-time errors.

**EDIT**: Seems that `@UtilityClass` won't be applied anywhere if any member
of any `@UtilityClass`-annotated class are imported staticly anywhere else without using `*`. I.E. a single bad orange wastes the entire basket.

Oh, this is a big sorry for the javac compiler for you.

For some reason, non-star static imports are evaluated before the annotation processor gives lombok a chance, meaning that an error occurs, and the annotation processors will not be triggered at all.

This is a known bug, and not something we can change easily in lombok.
@rspilker So, you consider this to be a javac bug instead?

title: instanceof in equals()
body:
The `instanceof` expressions should not take place in `equals()` method.
You should use this.getClass().equals(that.getClass()); instead. (or even ==)
The `instanceof` approach results in a bug:

When B extends A and we have objects `A a` and `B b`:
a.equals(b) returns true 
b.equals(a) returns false

As you can see this behavior breaks one of the equals() principles: symmetry

That's because a.equals(b) checks instanceof A for b and b is acutally an A. So it's true.
After that the rest of equals body checks only the fields present in A class.
Backwards: a instanceof B returns false, which is obvious.

nodes.body:
**Did you test it? How?**

Lombok does it exactly right: It allows instances of different subclasses to be equal if you wish and to never be equal if you wish. The symmetry is maintained when you use it right.

That's why `canEqual` is needed, see [this lengthy paper](https://www.artima.com/lejava/articles/equality.html).

I guess, this should be documented better as at the moment, I can't find an explanation there. But note that the doc is already pretty long.

title: User should be able to set lock property for `@Synchronized` to be transient (in entity class)
body:
When using `@Synchronized` in entity class generated lock property is not marked as transient (hence, it requires not needed field in database).

Current fix would be to have custom lock property within the class (marked with `@Transient`), and use `@Synchronized("<custom_lock_name>")`, but it would be nice to have something like `@Synchronized(onLock_=@Transient)`.

nodes.body: I can't think of any reason to ever try to serialize the lock. So, I think that always adding the `transient` modifier (if it is not `static`) would be the ideal solution.

Also, initially I think that being able to add annotations to the lock is an overkill. On a second thought however, it might be useful to instruct frameworks and other tools to ignore those fields (e.g. Jackson's `@JsonIgnore`). But, on a third thought, this seems to be such a rare and particular corner-case that it would probably be better to be manually coded instead of relying on lombok for that.

Further, instances of JPA entities are not designed to be thread-safe and should not be shared among multiple threads or multiple `EntityManager`s. If you are sharing JPA entities between multiple threads and requiring synchronization on them, you are probably doing something wrong, and this have nothing to do with using lombok.

Right, right. Didn't remember that while thinking of simple multitreading safety.

I leave you this issue in case anyone would prefer using `onLock_` for other annotations on lock property (like the one you've already mentioned - `@JsonIgnore`).

We currently generate an `Object[]` to be able to serialize it. The problem is that otherwise we would also have to generate deserialization code, otherwise you would get a NullPointerExecption.

The workaround is that you provide a field yourself: `@Synchronized("lock")`.

title: Custom maven repository for lombok edge releases
body:
I'm aware that publishing lombok versions to maven central is a very complicated, boring and laborious process that can't be done by nobody else other that the project owners (@rzwitserloot and @rspilker), and this is something that inhibit releasing too many edge versions as official versions.

So, I'm proposing a simple workaround. Create a maven repository hosted at projectlombok.org and upload whichever edge versions generated to there. Since you'll have the full control of the repository, this should make it much easier to publish whichever artifacts you want to whenever you want to.

Also, this solves another issue with edge releases. The edge release that I download today may be different that the edge release that my neighbour downloads tomorrow, and if we work on a project that uses lombok, this might affect its stability and its build reproducibility. By giving a unique version string to each edge version ever published (even if it is something simple like appending the date/time of its generation or something more laborious as using full semantic versioning), this issue would also be solved. Also, this simplifies the live of people who uses maven or gradle.

Finally, uploads to maven central would still be reserved to glorified non-edge releases.

nodes.body:
Yes, we were already thinking along these lines.

Can someone tell us exactly what files we should host for a SNAPSHOT repository, and how we can have multiple SNAPSHOT releases wit hthe same version number, build on different days?

I suggest forgetting about releasing as SNAPSHOTs.

Let's say that you release a new edge today. Then you would name it as lombok-1.16.21.20180517. If you release another one tomorrow, call it lombok-1.16.21.20180518. There are other ways to do that, since you can put whichever number versions that you want.

SNAPSHOT versions are not intended to ever be released. Their purpose is to give some version string for the thing that you are coding right now, which is specially useful when you are coding many different modules at the same time and they have some dependency relationship between them.

Distributing versions tagged as SNAPSHOT in maven repositories is a big no-no. They shouldn't ever leave the local repository in your .m2 folder.

BTW, since you are using ant and uses a pom.xml solely to be able to distribute lombok in maven repositories, I don't think that you will ever need to see or care about SNAPSHOTs, just forget them altogether.

Looking at [your pom.xml](http://central.maven.org/maven2/org/projectlombok/lombok/1.16.20/lombok-1.16.20.pom), it looks fine (except for the googlecode issues link being very outdated, but it is not used for anything other than documenting it for people who look inside the pom.xml searching for this data, i.e. nobody).

To release a new version in your own repository, I think that you will only need to publish those files:

* `http://projectlombok.org/mavenrepo/org/projectlombok/lombok/<your-version-string>/lombok-<your-version-string>.jar`

* `http://projectlombok.org/mavenrepo/org/projectlombok/lombok/<your-version-string>/lombok-<your-version-string>-pom` (edit the file contents to match the version string, of course).

* `http://projectlombok.org/mavenrepo/org/projectlombok/lombok/<your-version-string>/lombok-<your-version-string>-javadoc.jar` (optional, but ant can do it easily).

* `http://projectlombok.org/mavenrepo/org/projectlombok/lombok/<your-version-string>/lombok-<your-version-string>-sources.jar` (optional, but ant can do it easily).

* A bunch of `.asc`, `.md5`, `.sha1`, `.asc.md5` and `.asc.sha1` files. I think that they are also optional.

I.E. Just follow the structure already given [here](http://central.maven.org/maven2/org/projectlombok/lombok/1.16.20/).

For publishing them, you can just manually copy the files to the corresponding virtual folder on the site. For lombok, it ends being much more easier doing this manually than trying to make a crazy maven plugin work with that.
If the ant build can be used to install the lombok.jar to the local maven repository (`~/.m2/repository`), https://jitpack.io/ might be an option.

I want to cite something I saw [here](https://timboudreau.com/blog/maven/read):

> Maven has plenty of warts - I learned the hard way *never* to actually use `-SNAPSHOT` in my project versions, because it's the magic "download the internet" keyword that convinces Maven to delete perfectly good JARs and try to download them again - great fun on an airplane or through the great firewall of China - I think that one misfeature causes most of the agony and loathing of Maven out there.

Here is a workaround that I use myself. Every day a release is built and published to bintray from the latest head of this repo.
https://github.com/iherasymenko/lombok-publisher
This pull request #1780 might be some of use here.

We're going to do an edge release very soon using jitpack. The edge release page should then contain a link to the right jitpack page. I've just tested using https://jitpack.io/#org.projectlombok/lombok/master-SNAPSHOT and that worked.

title: Feature Request: Google Flogger

nodes.body:
I didn't realize that was the reasoning behind the log annotations. I thought it was to reduce boilerplate.

Are you certain the stack trace call is expensive? I ask because everything else in Flogger is highly optimized, and the main two operations are a single, cached reflective Class.forName() call, and a Throwable.getStackTrace() call, which should be quicker than the expensive Thread.getStackTrace.

I would _definitely_ use it if it were added to Lombok, as I have used it in other projects. I think other users might enjoy it, too. :)

> Are you certain the stack trace call is expensive?

I can't speak for him, but I'm sure, it's *relatively* expensive. It'd very bad for performance when done for every log line, but it hardly matters when done once per class. I guess, it can (and will) be optimized using JEP 259, but I'd bet, hardly anybody will notice.

title: Installation for Eclipse in system directory
body: Hi, I am quite struggling with installing `lombok` to my Eclipse running on Ubuntu 18. Even when running the installer as `root`, it still complains that it cannot write to `/snap/eclipse/12` directory, because of missing permissions. Could someone point me to the correct procedure of installation to a system directory?

nodes.body:
Hi, maybe you need to change the permissions of  directory (/ snap / eclipse), try running this command on the linux terminal :
sudo chmod 777 -R /snap/eclipse

I don't think so. The root just doesn't care about the standard file modifiers, the access is always granted. There may be other kind of permissions missing or a different problem producing a wrong error message, I can't tell. Concerning writing to the directory, I'd try `echo > /snap/eclipse/12/foobarbaz` as root, maybe the reason becomes clear.

@Smedzlatko Maybe temporarily granting the whole subtree to yourself (`chown -R smedzlatko /snap/eclipse`), installing Lombok and then changing back might work.
You can "install" lombok by hand, modifying `eclipse.ini`. To get the instructions, launch `lombok.jar` and click on the link "Show me what this installer will do to my IDE installation".
I am having this issue as well, is the only current option to install it by hand? (running lombok-1.16.22.jar)

Just to give a little more perspective, the way to get a nice, current version of eclipse on ubuntu is to install it with snap (https://snapcraft.io/).  
Snaps are self-contained and read-only squashfs volumes that ubuntu mounts (squashfs is always read-only, so you can't get around that with chmod) using the snap command.  Its especially appealing for eclipse because of how difficult java is to version, and that java versions don't line up with ubuntu releases.

So the problem isn't "we need to install it by hand."  It's that *we can't install it in a read-only partition*.

As I see it, I think we have four options:
1. We could use overlayfs to add a layer on top that is writeable in order to modify eclipse.ini.
2. Add an argument to eclipse startup so that it uses a different eclipse.ini.
3. Install eclipse manually (and then KEEP installing it manually every time we need an upgrade).
4. Figure out how to make lombok work the same way that all the rest of the eclipse plugins do - where it doesn't need to write to eclipse.ini to work.

I don't really like any of the options except the last one; they all seem like kludges.  Unfortunately, I don't know how to do the last one (or if it's possible).

Hi,
Try [this link](https://askubuntu.com/questions/1051926/how-to-make-eclipse-installed-via-snap-use-a-differerent-configuration-when-star/1051927#1051927). I used it to copy my eclipse.ini and add -javaagent:lombok.jar. It's working.

> Hi,
> Try [this link](https://askubuntu.com/questions/1051926/how-to-make-eclipse-installed-via-snap-use-a-differerent-configuration-when-star/1051927#1051927). I used it to copy my eclipse.ini and add -javaagent:lombok.jar. It's working.

Yep, That works. Thanks

title: 1.16.22 - constructor ... already defined in class

nodes.body:
See the changelog - was hit by this as well:
> FEATURE: Private no-args constructor for @Data and @Value to enable deserialization frameworks (like Jackson) to operate out-of-the-box. Use lombok.noArgsConstructor.extraPrivate = false to disable this behavior.

Anyhow, I wonder why this isn't reflected in the release changelog that this breaks with `@NoArgsConstructor` already being defined. (If it is intended after all). If it is, I wonder why the release version is just a patch increase.

And because the new feature adds a private no-args constructor I wonder how we can change the visibility modifier of the constructor? Shouldn't the one coming from @NoArgsConstructor have precedence over the one from `@Data`?

@dreis2211 

> Anyhow, I wonder why this isn't reflected in the release changelog that this breaks with `@NoArgsConstructor` already being defined. (If it is intended after all).

I'd bet, this is a bug. The only sensible behavior is the explicit annotation taking precedence, i.e., `@Value` implying a weak `@NoArgsConstructor(access=PRIVATE)` which gets discarded in case an explicit `@NoArgsConstructor` is present.

> And because the new feature adds a private no-args constructor I wonder how we can change the visibility modifier of the constructor?

IMHO, these two rules make sense:

- explicit wins over implicit
- higher visibility wins (as each annotation adds a feature, combining them means getting the higher visibility as with a `public` thing you can do everything what you can do with a `private` one)

In this case both rules agree that there should be a `public` constructor.

I somehow hope this is a bug. This being intended would be "suboptimal" ;)

> explicit wins over implicit

We basically agree what we would expect in terms of precedence. 👍

Sidenote: When I see somebody using `@Data` I'm always wondering if they're aware, that `@Data` is using deep equals and if they're aware of consequences... 
I think this should be really emphasized in documentation!
Came in this morning to the same error. We use AllArgs and NoArgs in most of our POJOs. Things are borked now :(
Yes, this is a bug. Sorry. Will see how soon we can make a new release.
Btw, if there're class inheritance, none of `@Data, @NoArgsConstructor, @AllArgsConstructor` should be annotated on subclass.

title: Improve @FieldNameConstants functionality
body:
`@FieldNameConstants` is realy great, but it generates names like this: 
`private Date date;` becames `public static final String DATE = "date";`, 
which causes generated names to mix with other static fields. 
Moreover it is not alway clear if "DATE" is field name, or some date for example.

My suggestion is to prepend `FIELD_` prefix to all generated names, so: `private String date;` will become `public static final String FIELD_DATE = "date";`

That way generated names are nicely groupped and we immediatelly know what it represent.

nodes.body: Yup. Added in commit b8e85f5dc7044e9a4bd43c41786bdda2a38f50ac and will be in 1.18.0 to be released soon. It's a bit more involved; you can config prefix and suffix via both the annotation itself and `lombok.config`

title: extraPrivate=true from 1.16.22 breaks Jackson creator detection

nodes.body:
Seconding this one.
Having working lombok annotated code break in subtle ways that are
undetectable by the compiler is not acceptable, imho.
Famous example of other projects' policy here:
https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/235335/why-is-there-a-linux-kernel-policy-to-never-break-user-space

The alternative that could be done in this example would be to define the
default values with the field declarations (```private ImmutableList<
Endpoint> endpoints = ImmutableList.of())```).
That *should* work, if lombok doesn't mess with it. But see above.

Aside from that:
I don't think a no args constructor makes sense if there are other
constructors available - like the requiredargs constructor implied by Data
and Value annotations.

I've been waging a silent war on no args constructors in old projects,
replacing them (and setters) with actual constructors and JsonCreator /
JsonPojoBuilder annotations for a while now. The whole "instantiate with a
no constructor, then call a ton of setters"  pattern needs to die imho, for
a bunch of reasons. This quiet adding back of a no args constructor stands
in the way of that.

All in all: Please don't.


On Wed, May 30, 2018 at 2:28 AM, Bogdan Calmac <notifications@github.com>
wrote:

> to a vanilla @Value + @Builder is overriding the all-args constructor so
> that I initialize the fields to a default value irrespective of how the
> object is built: through the all-args constructor (Jackson deserialization)

"Don't only practice your art, but force your way into it's secrets, for it
and knowledge can raise men to the divine."
     -- Ludwig von Beethoven

@bcalmac You say that `extraPrivate=true` breaks Jackson, but is't it what it should happen if there is an empty constructor and your visibility is set to any?
I mean why would you create an empty constructor for a Value object? And why are you setting `extraPrivate` to `true`??
I have a similar case, and it's fine, so maybe you should first (if you have all you dtos/value objects armed like this one) set Jackson visibility to 
```java
        objectMapper
                .setVisibility(PropertyAccessor.FIELD, JsonAutoDetect.Visibility.PUBLIC_ONLY)
                .setVisibility(PropertyAccessor.GETTER, JsonAutoDetect.Visibility.PUBLIC_ONLY)
                .setVisibility(PropertyAccessor.IS_GETTER, JsonAutoDetect.Visibility.PUBLIC_ONLY)
                .setVisibility(PropertyAccessor.SETTER, JsonAutoDetect.Visibility.PUBLIC_ONLY)
                .setVisibility(PropertyAccessor.CREATOR, JsonAutoDetect.Visibility.PUBLIC_ONLY)
```
or just 
```java
        objectMapper
                .setVisibility(PropertyAccessor.SETTER, JsonAutoDetect.Visibility.PUBLIC_ONLY)
                .setVisibility(PropertyAccessor.CREATOR, JsonAutoDetect.Visibility.PUBLIC_ONLY)
```
since the others are defaults,,
so that regardless if there is private no arg ctor - Jackson will not see it.
(The advantages are obvious, since less reflection is used, etc.)

Also, consider that a no-args constructor even violates the definition of immutable / value objects. Immutable objects are supposed to be fully initialized at construction time.

Also, the Lombok [documentation](https://projectlombok.org/features/Value) states the following (and I think it makes total sense):

> Also, any explicit constructor, no matter the arguments list, implies lombok will not generate a constructor. If you do want lombok to generate the all-args constructor, add AllArgsConstructor to the class. You can mark any constructor or method with @lombok.experimental.Tolerate to hide them from lombok.

@bcalmac 

> extraPrivate=true is not my choice. The functionality was added in 1.16.22 and is enabled by default.

Yes, I know. I mean, yes there is that new setting and whether it is enabled by default or manually by developer, all you need to do to neutralize relevant effects is, well, to turn it OFF. I understand that you might not turn it ON, but why don't just turn it OFF now?
It works perfectly.

> I thought some more about this since yesterday and I'm even more concerned. In the Jackson world, 2 constructors instead of one means more ambiguity for deserialization. I was looking through the documentation yesterday and I couldn't even find a place that details the rules for resolving the ambiguity (that is, which constructor will be used). From unit tests, it looks like it prefers the no-args constructor.

Yes, sure no-arg. 
There is no ambiguity. It chooses explicit `@JsonCreator` if there is first or no-arg as a second priority.
Just put `lombok.noArgsConstructor.extraPrivate = false`  and there will be no difference with using `1.16.20`

I know I can get the code to work. I just wanted to raise a flag about what seems to me a dubious feature that's enabled by default, and can easily break your code if you just casually upgrade Lombok. I can very well be wrong, I haven't seen a description of this feature other than _"to enable deserialization frameworks (like Jackson) to operate out-of-the-box"_. For me it was already working out of the box, without any Jackson annotations.

@soberich Do you usually perform a regression test of third-party libraries used in your projects when making a minor version upgrade? That would be the only way to catch breaking changes like this one.

@soberich All right, fair enough. Are you familiar with the reasoning behind adding the extra no-args constructor? Can you explain or point me to the relevant info?

There may be something to it, but adding a no-args constructor to an immutable class is inconceivable (from my outsider perspective).

> There may be something to it, but adding a no-args constructor to an immutable class is inconceivable (from my outsider perspective).

The reasoning is very simple: A dumb deserializer first creates an empty instance using the no-args constructor and then it sets the fields using reflection (ignoring `private` and hacking away `final`). Apart from `Unsafe` hacks, it's the only way how to create an object without understanding how to use a different constructor.

The no-args constructor is the traditional way as before `@ConstructorProperties`, there was no way how to find out what the constructor arguments mean. It used to be the only way and it had to be used also for immutables. Even the [JLS][] accounts for it.

[JLS]: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se7/html/jls-17.html#jls-17.5.3

OK, so there are some cases when serialization needs to be hacked with a private no-args constructor. This still doesn’t justify having the hack as the default behavior. 

As of today, Jackson can successfully deserialize a Value based either on ConstructorProperties or parameters-module. 

The way it is, developers need to explicitly opt out of a hack needed only for old code instead of just enabling it when needed. Does that make sense?

Also consider that this hack is originally intended for Jackson. How can we evaluate the impact of this breaking change on other libraries and frameworks that do similar introspection? An extra constructor out of the blue is a big deal.

The order matters? Wow, did not know that..

I did take a look into Lombok's code a while back, though, so I thought it could work. I tested and it did lol

I'll try to address all things mentioned.

First, regarding (semantic) versioning, we underestimated the impact of this change. We thought adding a private no-args constructor would NOT break any backwards compatibility.

The reason we added this feature was that since java9 `@ConstructorProperties` moved to the module `java.desktop`, which is not added by default. This let us change the our code generation to switch from opt-out to opt-in.

We got a lot of feedback that that version broke a lot of projects, for instance #1563. So we looked for an alternative.

Another reason to add this feature is to create a stepping stone to allow default values for fields created via the constructor AND via a builder.

Regarding the order of the annotations, I didn't expect that the order would matter, but it does make sense now. Also, we obviously didn't have enough test cases for the interactions between annotations.
We're going to release 1.18.0 very soon. This will be a breaking change, in the way that we're going to change the opt-out into an opt-in.

@rspilker, thank you for chiming in. Isn't jackson-module-parameter-names an adequate alternative to `@ConstructorProperties`? 

From what I understand, this is a Jackson / Java 9 issue, I wouldn't expect Lombok to automatically fix it for me. Different projects would probably what to go with different solutions. IMHO Lombok should stay true to what a `@Value` is, and that does not include a no-args constructor. By getting in the middle of this, Lombok stops being a helper for generating boilerplate code and starts prescribing how objects should be designed.

Now, if this feature is here to stay, how would you reconcile it with the statement below? It's a guarantee that once you step in by defining a constructor, Lombok gets out of the way.

> Also, any **explicit constructor**, no matter the arguments list, implies **lombok will not generate a constructor**. If you do want lombok to generate the all-args constructor, add AllArgsConstructor to the class. You can mark any constructor or method with @lombok.experimental.Tolerate to hide them from lombok.
@rspilker I've just seen you previous message. Changing this to an opt-in is completely satisfying to me.

Hello,

> @rspilker, thank you for chiming in. Isn't jackson-module-parameter-names an adequate alternative to @ConstructorProperties?

It is, unless you have a class with one constructor parameter. In that case jackson would fail (it would detect it as a delegating creator instead of a property one) unless you have `@JsonCreator` or `@ConstructorProperties`. See https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-databind/issues/1498 for details.
Correct. I do have some of those cases and use `@JsonCreator`. This also means that I need to define  an explicit constructor so I can attach the annotation.

title: Missing static import makes unrelated classes fail to compile

nodes.body:
Yes, this is a known bug, and not something we can fix.

The problem is that javac tries to resolve static imports during parsing, so before annotation processors get the chance to run. And if an error occurs during parsing the annotation processors are not run at all.

Please register a bug at Oracle/OpenJDK.
This also means that we cannot give a better error message.

In our project we have Lombok in use. One colleague had extreme performance problems. After typeing 2 characters, we had to wait several seconds. After taking several threaddumps, I realized how to fix his computer.

### 1. Disable Lombok Configuration
There is a configuration possibility, which I have seen in [LombokConfiguration](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/7e94041dbc177476020969b00d3411020418f903/src/core/lombok/core/LombokConfiguration.java). If you do not have a **lombok.config** file, then you can disable eclipse from searching of it. Just define _-Dlombok.disableConfig=true_ as JVM argument, and its gone. Eclipse will not look for the config on every key press.

**One recommendation could be for the lombok developer:** it would be good to cache all lombok.config files in the memory. Then you would just need to subscribe somehow to get notified about new lombok.config files or about updates to them. This way the config would not be searched on every key press.

title: overload setter Feature Proposal
body:
I think `lombok.javac.handlers.JavacHandlerUtil.methodExists` should check the type of param.

Now I need to write an overload set method to cast some type into the original type of a field, then I have to write that method and the original setter method as well.

eg: `String egField`  I need to write `public void setEgField(int egField)` which will cast `int` to `String` and I also want the `public void setEgField(String egField)`

Does this make sense?

nodes.body:
> I think `lombok.javac.handlers.JavacHandlerUtil.methodExists` should check the type of param.

I'm afraid this isn't done as it'd be too complicated due to generics and [resolution](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/wiki/LOMBOK-CONCEPT:-Resolution).

> Now I need to write an overload set method to cast some type into the original type of a field, then I have to write that method and the original setter method as well.

No, you don't. Just mark your method with `@lombok.Tolerate`. Your case is exactly the motivation behind this annotation.
@Maaartinus thank you

title: @setter    java.lang.String  trim()

nodes.body:
That's where more specific cases should be handled by yourself.

Myself I would prefer to use or just allow an empty string instead or even an optional of String. Why not even use the Option class from Vavr.

I hope you see my point. You have so much opinions in the java community it would be difficult or impossible to please everyone.
Believe or not this is a common case, would be great have the option of trim the string in the @Data or @Setter.

If this is a "common case" is more an individual point of perspective imo.
Personally I can't remember to have seen this before.

And this would only work for String arguments.
Therefore I would suggest more a specialized annotation like @StringSetter which could handle more string specific behaviour.
@StringSetter(trim=true, convertion=uppercase|lowercase|none, maxLength=positiveNumber|unset)

- trim: trim a non null string (like you suggested)
- convertion: nonNullValue.toUpperCase(), nonNullValue.toLowerCase()
- maxLength: cut after the specified length or leave it as it is if not specified

The @StringSetter option sounds amazing. About my point of view, you not always have the option to edit or optimize your data sources, and when the DB admin define the data as fixed char instead or varchar, and other similar cases, you need to do the setters at hand with the boilerplate code, or use reflections and the performance impoverishment of that. Your option make my life a lot easier.
May be having property for Setter (and @Data) like  `lombok.setter.trimString`, default false will support as is, activated true as needed
Hi, is this ticket lost?
Ping...
That's not what null is for, this request is silly, it's not boilerplate. Will never happen. I apologize for not having closed it earlier.

The request is not silly. May be, it is not boilerplate, but it is a practical need in business applications which deal with user input, and the typical boilerplate code is the ideal place to handle it.
I'd be willing to explore contributing this enhancement if the project team was open to accepting a pull request.

I don't think adding this proposition is a good idea, because:

1. Having an annotation parameter just for the case that it is present on method with a `String` parameter can be confusing. What do you do when it's `true` on a non-`String`? Error out? Ignore it? Furthermore, it clutters your auto-completion.
2. A special `@StringSetter` seems even more ridiculous to me. Where do we go from there? `@StringGetter`? `@IntegerSetter(maxValue=10, minValue=0)`? Even if we can agree that this will never happen, another annotation that does nearly the same than another annotation is a huge maintenance burden: You have to think about all those possible interdependencies (e.g. with `@Data`) and also unit-test them.
3. What do you do with constructors? Should they also automatically trim once there is such special setter? What about `@(Super)Builder`?
4. Last but (at least to me) most important: I barely see such a pattern in my daily coding life. I would even consider it bad practice in many cases, because you should _always_ sanitize (user) input as early as possible. Sanitizing in a data or value class is in most cases one step too late. If your data class happens to be the first step of your input pipeline (maybe because you are using a deserialization framework like Jackson), you should still make the sanitation explicit, because in such a case that's definitely not boilerplate.
Ideally, the uninitialized field is set to the default value needed. It can be in the Class definition level or a validation layer.

I found out that whenever an old system application insert/update data to SQLServer DB, it added spaces to fill the digit of characters if data type is char. E.g., column data type is char(8) and the value is only 4 digit characters, it will add 4 spaces at the end. In new application, those Tables with data type char(d) are mapped as String in Entity classes. The idea of trimming a String field if it's not null is helpful in cases like this.

title: @FieldNameConstants should work on interfaces with getters/setters
body:
Our model classes often implement an interface consisting of getters and setters. We implement them multiple times for different architectures using lombok's `@Getter` feature.
The `@FieldNameConstants` annotation would be useful for us, but because our project structure is such that the interfaces are compiled seperately from the implementations as a "common" package, together with common business logic, we can't use it. It would be great if it was possible to add `@FieldNameConstants` to interfaces, such that for each `getPropOne()` and `setPropTwo()`, constants `FIELD_PROP_ONE` and `FIELD_PROP_ONE` respectively are generated and be accessed without knowledge of the actual implementation of the model class.

`git bisect` told me it's this commit: https://github.com/metasfresh/metasfresh/commit/c2a98c26ea78e7036876404d2c2b94335ce7304f (which i suspected..the problem is that i did a lot of stuff in there :blush: )

@metas-ts 
> which i suspected..the problem is that i did a lot of stuff in there

That's a problem. Commits should be small... but no matter how hard I try, sometimes, I get a bunch of meaningless commits I have to either spend a one more day on or simply squash into one nice commit. I always squash them, but keep the history in a backup branch privately, in case I need it for a case like yours.

As your current problem is that Lombok does nothing at all, it might help to create a trivial file for testing it. Anyway, I guess, the problem is caused some `pom.xml` and you may be able to reproduce the problem by picking one of them into a previous commit. Just guessing, good luck!

The problem in this case is a static import. The problems with this is that if you refer to a type that will be generated by an annotation processor, javac is going to freak out.

For some reason, javac tries to resolve static imports too early in the process. This causes an error, IIRC already during parsing. And if an error exists in that phase, the annotation processors are not triggered at all. None of them. So lombok does not get a chance to generate the code, or give a better error message.

Please file a bug report at Oracle, we cannot fix this.

I found ... not a solution but rather a hack ... to get this running with Maven and JDK 9 / 10.

So first you have to add the annotation processor path, as already mentioned before:

```
<annotationProcessorPaths>
   <path>
     <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
     <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
     <version>${lombok.version}</version>
   </path>
</annotationProcessorPaths> 
```

Now I also get the _"/lombok/dummy/ForceNewRound0 ... file should be on source path"_ error.

To fix this, I analyzed which parameters Maven passes to javac and reproduced the compilation process by directly calling javac.

I first found out that it works if you remove the "-sourcepath" parameter. However, that should not and cannot be done with Maven.

After another day of experiments, I found out that it also works if you add "/" (I assume that's where the _/lombok/dummy/ForceNewRound0.java_ file is written to) to the sourcepath.

And that can be done with Maven ... although it's kind of hacky:

You need to add to the _maven-compiler-plugin_ the following compiler arguments:

```
<compilerArgs>
	<arg>-sourcepath</arg>
	<arg>${project.basedir}/src/main/java${path.separator}${project.basedir}/target/generated-sources/annotations${path.separator}/</arg>
</compilerArgs>
```

This doesn't really replace the "-sourcepath" compiler argument, but it adds a second "-sourcepath", which overwrites the first one.

As I said, this is not a clean solution, but it works and maybe it's a starting point to find a real solution.

Unfortunately my previous hack breaks the build in IntelliJ IDEA with javac when the project contains tests:

Here's a way to get the hack running in Maven, IntelliJ and Eclipse: 

I define the sourcepath in a separate Maven profile "update-sourcepath-for-lombok", so it's ignored by IntelliJ:

```
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.8.0</version>

      <configuration>
        <annotationProcessorPaths>
          <path>
            <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
            <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
            <version>${lombok.version}</version>
          </path>
        </annotationProcessorPaths>
      </configuration>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>

<profiles>
  <profile>
    <id>update-sourcepath-for-lombok</id>
    <build>
      <plugins>
        <plugin>
          <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>

          <configuration>
            <compilerArgs>
              <arg>-sourcepath</arg>
              <arg>${project.basedir}/src/main/java${path.separator}${project.basedir}/target/generated-sources/annotations${path.separator}/</arg>
            </compilerArgs>
          </configuration>
        </plugin>
      </plugins>
    </build>
  </profile>
</profiles>
```

And when running Maven on the command line, I activate that profile:

```
mvn -Pupdate-sourcepath-for-lombok clean package
```

nodes.body:
I now notice the delomboked code did not generate correctly.

my expectation is that if the builder is supplied a value, it uses that value, else it executes the statement provided to default to calculate the default.

goal being I pass in an entity,  and all of the effective values are pre calculated, but the builder can override the precalc ones.

As @Maaartinus already said, initializer expressions for fields should be possible to be evaluated in a static context. You could see the constructor as a static method. You could refer to other already initialized fields, but then those must be evaluable in a static context.

We could try and make an effort to allow for referencing previously initialized fields. But that's a lot of work. 

But referring to uninitialized fields would never work. Theoretically we could reorder initialization order, but that would be so unexpected, that we're not going to consider that.

title: Lombok does not reflect refactoring changes to other classes in Eclipse
body:
Hello

For more details here:

* [STS does not apply expected refactoring with Lombok](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ide/issues/288)

If I have an entity class with `@Data` I can confirm the getter/setters and other (toString etc) are generated. I can use that POJO in peace in other classes. But if for example I have the `name` field and later is refactored to `firstName` the getter/setter are **only** reflected in the same class, but not in other classes.

nodes.body:
This seems like a fundamental impossibility. If you refactor the field, then Lombok re-generates the getters and setters and to the rest of the world, it was a delete-then-add action (the old methods disappeared and then new ones appeared). You would have to do some really fancy and complicated tricks to anticipate what the new ones will be called, hook into Eclipse's refactoring engine, apply the refactor, then allow the methods to change.

Likewise, Eclipse can't refactor the methods themselves because it's generated. If Eclipse could refactor them, then a workaround would be to rename the methods via the outline view then rename the fields to match.

Not a member of the Lombok team, but I would rate this as "there are bigger fish to fry".
The issue has been addressed and is [covered by a test](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/blob/master/test/eclipse/src/lombok/eclipse/refactoring/RenameTest.java)

title: Allow defining exception type on @NonNull

title: AllArgsConstructor should mark constructor parameters with same annotations that are used for fields

nodes.body: Problem is that an annotation may be valid for fields, but not for method parameters. So such a behavior must definitively be made "opt-in" individually for each field/parameter/annotation via the `@*ArgsConstructor` annotations. This would probably make the syntax quite ugly.

@janrieke Sure, with `@*ArgsConstructor`, it'd be pretty ugly. With configuration, it'd fine.

The main use case are binding annotations (Spring `@Qualifier` and Guice `@Named`) and they can and should always be copied. I can't imagine, why someone would like to control it on a class level. So with a line in config.lombok, it'd done.

I've never seen any other annotation with a simple name `Qualifier` or `Named`, so
```
lombok.constructor.copyToArgument=com.google.guice.Named
```
or just
```
lombok.constructor.copyToArgument=Named
```
should be no problem, even if Lombok can't determine the FQN.

Hey @janrieke , @Maaartinus!
Any progress on this issue? 
Or at least maybe some guidelines how to implement it? 
Thanks :)
Did not test it, but this should work in 1.18.4 using the config option `lombok.copyableAnnotations`.

Thanks @janrieke , it does work!
I assume this ticket might be closed then.

title: Issue with constructor generation in 1.16.22

nodes.body:
This is probably related to this [change](https://projectlombok.org/changelog):

> FEATURE: Private no-args constructor for @Data and @Value to enable deserialization frameworks (like Jackson) to operate out-of-the-box. Use lombok.noArgsConstructor.extraPrivate = false to disable this behavior.

This was no good idea and was fixed in 1.18. Moreover, it looks like there was a bug leading to generating 
`@NoArgsConstructor` twice.

Either install 1.18 or follow the above advice.
@Maaartinus thanks, upgrading fixed it.

body:

According to the docs, `@Value` generates an AllArgsConstructor, and in case of conflicts, a compile error rather than silently dropping the constructor... But that doesn't seem to be the case here. This was also an issue on 1.16.20.

```

nodes.body: My bad, sorry!

@TheRealMarnes I'm not sure if you remember this, but perhaps you could explain what was the error, which apparently you've found and closed the issue because of it?

It seems that I've got a similar issue with the `@Value` annotation - the All Args Constructor doesn't get generated in case when a custom constructor is present in the class.

Oh yeah, so now I've also read the documentation of `@Value` a little bit further: https://projectlombok.org/features/Value

For anyone facing this problem as well - the documentation states:

> In practice, `@Value` is shorthand for: `final @ToString @EqualsAndHashCode @AllArgsConstructor @FieldDefaults(makeFinal = true, level = AccessLevel.PRIVATE) @Getter`, **except that explicitly including an implementation of any of the relevant methods simply means that part won't be generated and no warning will be emitted**. For example, if you write your own toString, no error occurs, and lombok will not generate a toString. Also, **any explicit constructor, no matter the arguments list, implies lombok will not generate a constructor.**

So basically, IMO the Javadoc is a little bit misleading, as it states:

```
Equivalent to {@code @Getter @FieldDefaults(makeFinal=true, level=AccessLevel.PRIVATE) @AllArgsConstructor @ToString @EqualsAndHashCode}.
```

In the next line, a URL to the complete documentation is provided, nevertheless a small notice, that there're some exceptions, would be nice.

Yeah I just researched this again and found the same "small print":

> Also, _any_ explicit constructor, no matter the arguments list, implies lombok will not generate a constructor. If you do want lombok to generate the all-args constructor, add `@AllArgsConstructor` to the class.

I agree the documentation is misleading when it says that an annotation is equivalent to a combination of other annotations. Constructors in particular often give me different behavior between using the individual annotations and the composed ones.

My experience using lombok on 2 projects has led me to use `@Data` and `@Value` only on absolutely "dumb" pojos that do not and should not contain any logic whatsoever. As soon as a class gets any more "smart" than just a DTO bean, I use the individual annotations to avoid confusing behavior and to improve clarity (reading a list like `@Getter @EqualsAndHashCode @ToString` is easier than remembering what exactly the composed annotations add up to).

I used `@Value` with `@NoArgsConstructor(force = true, access = AccessLevel.PRIVATE)`  so `AllArgsConstructor` was not made at all. Finally I found the reason on this issue. I think that lines should be inserted to lombok docs. 

Belows are the documentation when i hover mouse over `@Value`. It said nothing about those exception cases.

```text
Generates a lot of code which fits with a class that is a representation of an immutable entity.
Equivalent to @Getter @FieldDefaults(makeFinal=true, level=AccessLevel.PRIVATE) @AllArgsConstructor @ToString @EqualsAndHashCode.
Complete documentation is found at the project lombok features page for @Value.
```
I have just been bitten by this too, after going off the Javadoc which states its equivalence to @AllArgsConstructor. +1 for at least highlighting in the Javadoc that it is _not_ fully equivalent.

@roeniss We can't stick every detail into the hover-over javadoc. The full documentation is at `https://projectlombok.org/features/NameOfFeatureHere` - (or possibly `/features/experimental/NameHere`, for experimental features), the javadoc merely gives you enough for all but the complex cases.

title: New Feature: Support for Vavr collections in @Singular builders

nodes.body:
We have similar need over lombok'Builder + vavr's Option while we build JPA Entity with DDD Entity(Aggregation Root)'s stateData. 

In this case, stateData has Option values(field or getter), and JPA Entity has non-empty field with default values. So we need to jump between Option.none() with default value and their types.

such as:

StateData => JPA Entity
sd -> 
    JPAEntity.builder()
   .fieldX(sd.optionValue.getOrElse(defaultValue))
   .build()

JPA Entity => StateData
en ->
   StateData.builder()
   .optionProp( en.getterX == defaultValue ? option.none(), option.some(en.getterX) )
   .build()

it's quite verbose, maybe it is fake requirement, or we need a concise expressive solution.

Vavr is _very much_ dancing to a completely different tune from the rest of the OpenJDK world, and every new java release means vavr is off on its own little planet a little more. Almost everything it does is either something OpenJDK is going to add at some point, or more likely, OpenJDK adds something different that caters to the same problemset.

As a result, I don't use VAVR at all. As far as I know, @rspilker doesn't either.

Thus, we can't possibly agree to this. We've been maintaining lombok for 12 years and intend to maintain it for at least another 12. We can't do that if we have no idea what a feature is even supposed to do.

The stuff I see so far strongly indicates this feature is multiple ballparks removed from being clear, concise, and easily understood even by a non-VAVR user, thus, odds that we'd accept any PR on this is abysmally low.

There is no clear plan, and if someone comes up with one, we have no way to judge if it is fitting for VAVR's needs. It would take some sort of community effort, for example, get the VAVR team itself on board, if they tell us that some 'this is what you write with lombok, and this is what it would delombok too' is the right way to go, that'd be pretty convincing, then we would be able to maintain the feature going forward. Without that - I have no real way to tell and as I think VAVR is just wrong as a point of principle, I don't want to delve into it enough to be capable of determining if any feature proposal fits the bill.

Hence, without that signoff from the core vavr maintenance team itself, I don't see a way forward.

title: Add @IteratorEquivalent annotation to provide methods with various iterable components.

nodes.body: The reason for it is speed and shortness. In my opinion, it's not bad practise right to have it as there are some cases when the develpoer is to pass varargs, for example, this is a standart situation when there are always *n* elements and they are simply passed as varargs and the method simply iterates over them using forEach-Array which is then transformed to for-i. However there may be a dynamic number of elements (for example they are filtered in some way before method invocation) so it's an `Iterable` object and it may be better to use forEach-Iterable for it transformed to while-Iterator by the compiler rather then first transforming it to Array (and if it's not `Collection` but other `Iterable` implementation there may not be `toArray(T[])` method, for example).

Collections and Java 8 Streams kick the pants off both Arrays and Iterables
imho.
I don't really think people should be using either, except in some specific
(rare!) cases.

Apart from that: Is it still boilerplate if it's only a handy thing that
you *might* use rather than something you really need? Are you going to
apply this pattern all over the place? Are you going to use several
variants of this on each class all the time? Adding these methods is going
to have a non-zero cost in terms of class size and therefore are you sure
you really need all that?

I think having unused code is a bad practice.

@JarvisCraft I'm pretty sure, you're doing it wrong. You let your API explode for probably non-measurable low-level premature optimization. Sure, it's nice when you can pass all of the following

- `Player`
- `Player...` (or `Player[]`)
- `Iterable<Player>`
- `Iterator<Player>`
- `Spliterator<Player>` (added by me)
- `Stream<Player>` (added by me / @randakar)

but you have 6 methods instead of one. You can apply this idea to two or three arguments and get 36 or 216 methods. That's just the opposite of a good API.

Ideally, there should be just the scalar method. Sometimes, it's convenient to use it with varargs, other times it gets called a lot with a collection (or alike), so adding such a method or maybe two should be considered. But doing so makes the API bigger and you should always think twice before doing it.

Adding multiple such methods doesn't carry its weight. I prefer to use `Collection` everywhere, as it covers most cases and conversions like `Arrays.asList(T...)` are simple and cheap. I considered to use `Iterable`, but it's not needed often enough. I can't recall when I used an `Iterator` or an array recently, it may be months ago. YMMV but code gets cleaner if you *make some choice and stick with it*.

- `ignoreNull` - see Guava comments on fail-fast `null`-unfriendly code
- `inline` - probably a pessimization as JVM inlines itself, but it can't handle long methods well
- `compress` - I can't really imagine generating such a code and hoping it never goes wrong

title: Feature request: apply @Cleanup to fields

nodes.body: @SergiusSidorov That might work, but `close()` should still be added to the finalizer just in case. And it may sometimes need to be `AutoCloseable` instead of `Closeable`. (The only difference between the two interfaces is that `Closeable.close()` can't throw checked exceptions other than `IOException`.)
Having a finalizer does have severe impact on the garbage collector.

@Pr0methean  a finalizer method can bring a big problem for performance. 
The general advice is do not use a finalizer if it's possible. There is [the good article](https://plumbr.io/blog/garbage-collection/debugging-to-understand-finalizer) about it.
Then how about a parameter, so that there's only a finalizer if it's `@Cleanup(finalize = true)`?
Imho lombok should not provide incentives to use things generally considered as bad practice. So let the class implement `Closeable`, or implement things manually.

title: Internal java compiler error on JDK 10 when log annotation on interface
body:
Incorrectly annotate an interface with a logging annotation such as `@Log` or `@Slf4j`.

For example:
```java
@Slf4j 
interface Test {}
```

Attempt to compile on JDK10. Observe the very cryptic:
`Error:java: Compilation failed: internal java compiler error`

Attempt to compile on JDK8. Observe the readable error:
`Error:(3, 1) java: @Log is legal only on classes and enums.`

I realize it's an incorrect usage but the JDK10 error message is extremely difficult to debug as it gives no indication of where the problem occurred and requires significant effort to track down. I spent a ton of time tracking this down for another engineer on our team where if the correct error message was shown the problem would have been immediately obvious to them.

title: @Accessors() generate fluent accessors by default if lombok.accessors.fluent is true
body:
`@Accessors()` doesn't respect the default value of its `fluent` parameter when it conflicts with `lombok.accessors.fluent`.

This means that if your project's default is to use fluent accessors, but you want to use get/set for e.g. legacy public code, you need to specify `@Accessors(fluent = false)` even tho you'll get a warning that it's redundant with the default value.

nodes.body:
The standard meaning of annotations is that omitting an argument is equivalent to using it's default value. This is necessary as there's no way of distinguishing these two cases via annotation processing or reflection.

However, this is pretty impractical and Lombok tries to be smarter about it. I guess, empty `@Accessors` is a no-op, rather than an equivalent of `@Accessors(fluent=false, chain=false, prefix={})` and that's a good thing (at least in general, as it allows to override a single setting without specifying all others).

The question is where the warning comes from. I can see none in my Eclipse. Can you switch it off?

Yes, I don't think it's a bug, just that it's a bit confusing when adding the annotation.

I'm using Android Studio 3.1, based on some IntelliJ IDEA build from a few months ago, and it's really good at graying out whatever is unnecessary/redundant. In this case it's flagging `fluent = false`, since the annotation's code indeed shows that `false` is the default value for `fluent`.

I only opened the issue because it might possible to fix Lombok so that the default values are indeed default at compile time, e.g. by not hard-coding `false` but using some static property instead? I haven't looked into it…

> I only opened the issue because it might possible to fix Lombok so that the default values are indeed default at compile time, e.g. by not hard-coding false but using some static property instead? I haven't looked into it…

I'm rather sure, it's impossible. Annotations are very rigid and they have to work from the class file alone. The default must be a compile-time constant or even a literal (I don't know).

Lombok does some useful magic allowing to "partially override" an annotation. Idea produces a useful warning here. It's just that this warning doesn't apply, because of the magic.

I guess, Lombok can't fix it. Maybe the Lombok-Idea-plugin can. For sure, Idea could automatically exempt all `lombok.**` annotations.
@Maaartinus: Created mplushnikov/lombok-intellij-plugin#495

title: @EqualsAndHashCode should allow skipping the hashCode method
body:
I am working on a project where we are required to have a coverage of at least 80%.
One problem we have is that we are using @EqualsAndHashCode because we need to have the equals method, but we don't use hashCode. 
Because of this multiple times we don't reach the limit for the coverage.
In the Javadoc for the java.lang.Object#equals method we have this description:

"Note that it is generally necessary to override the {@code hashCode} method whenever this method is overridden"

This means hashCode is not really always necessary. On the other hand if we are using hashCode then we should have equals.

nodes.body:
> This means hashCode is not really always necessary.

Not really... when you override `equals`, but not `hashCode`,
- you break the contract: Equal objects *must* have the same hash code.
- one year later, someone uses your object as a key in a `HashMap` and nothing works

That's no good idea. The proper solution for your coverage problem is to configure the coverage tool to ignore Lombok-generated methods. [Configure Lombok to add an annotation][g] and use it.

[g]:
https://projectlombok.org/api/lombok/ConfigurationKeys.html#ADD_LOMBOK_GENERATED_ANNOTATIONS

Actually, ignoring the method is a cop out too, I think. That way you can
never be sure you have covered everything that needs covering.

Best way: Use http://jqno.nl/equalsverifier/ on it. And ToStringVerifier on
the tostring method. I've written a (really) small library for data / value
annotated objects that basically calls those things in sequence, dealing
with odd cases like jacoco fields and the like. Unit test for each
individual class is really really small - one line of actual code for
standard value objects - and you get good coverage for it in return.
