I agree with @randakar and @Maaartinus that adding this would be a bad idea. Allowing lombok users breaking the equals-hashcode contract (let it be on purpose or by accident) will contradict almost everything lombok aims for.
If you need a special-purpose solution, then implement it. And if you don't want to write lengthy equals implementations, use EqualsBuilder from Apache Commons or similar helpers.

From the Javadoc: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/10/docs/api/java/lang/Object.html#hashCode()

> It is not required that if two objects are unequal according to the equals(java.lang.Object) method, then calling the hashCode method on each of the two objects must produce distinct integer results. However, the programmer should be aware that producing distinct integer results for unequal objects may improve the performance of hash tables.

For JPA entities I would like to let equals be generated by lombok but hashCode just be "return 31". This way, I can guarantee that hash codes never change when entities are persisted.

Details here (Chapter: Using a Generated Primary Key):
https://thoughts-on-java.org/ultimate-guide-to-implementing-equals-and-hashcode-with-hibernate 

--> maybe add an option to @EqualsAndHashCode to use a constant for hashCode?

> hashCode just be "return 31"

'cause 42 is too common, right? ;) But seriously, this would break a contract, too, namely that of all `Hash*` classes, as they're supposed to be `O(1)` and you'd make them `O(n)`. IOW, you'd get a serious slowdown pretty everywhere.

Some people claim that equality of entities should be content based, i.e., include everything but the `id`. Other claim that nothing but the `id` (and the class) should be used. I followed the latter and added `assert id != 0` to both `equals` and `hashCode` (which were trivial to write manually). This way, my IDs never change when it matters (as I test with assertion on).

I obviously can't use transient entities as hash keys, but that's an acceptable price.

If only `42` was a prime...
I agree that you decrease the performance of `Hash*` classes. That's why I would make this option opt-in. Currently I am not sure if it is save to use Lombok-generated `equals` and `hashCode` with JPA/Hibernate. 
And I think you also cannot put transient entities into a `*HashSet`, which seem quite a restriction.
When you write your `equals` and `hashCode` yourself, there is obviously no issue to discuss here.

> If only 42 was a prime...

It'd be enough when it wasn't even. As all used hash tables (I've ever seen) in Java use power of two sizes, all you need is co-primality to two, i.e., an odd number. Primality itself is irrelevant, 33 about as good as 31 and a bigger number would be somewhat better.

> Currently I am not sure if it is save to use Lombok-generated equals and hashCode with JPA/Hibernate.

Nothing is save with mutable keys. Anyway, you have to choose whether you want to use the ID or the "business keys" in your `equals` (IMHO using both would be crazy).

> And I think you also cannot put transient entities into a *HashSet, which seem quite a restriction.

When there are multiple transient entities, then I use a mapping like from `itemNo` to `item`, so there's no problem. There's pretty always a simple workaround. The persistent entities are more common.

Note that with a constant `hashCode`, you could use a `HashSet` only as efficiently as `List`, and that'd be a problem with hundreds or thousands of entities.
Did you test having a hand-written hashcode, annotated with `@Tolerate`, and `@EqualsAndHashcode` on the type?
@rspilker Does it work? Should it? Given https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/pull/52#issuecomment-72106077, I'd say no.

While I agree with all of you on both the usefulness and the necessity of generating both equals and hashCode at the same time, and ensuring uniformity across all test cases, I have to agree with @ccronemberger too.
The lombok frameworks main purpose is to add syntax in a configurable way. This should be consistent in itself too, and features should be as general as possible (even if we don't see the usefulness, or would decide against using it). To be adaptable to different project requirements is the reason lombok has as many users as it does.

The purpose of Lombok is to kill boilerplate. Being adaptable is a side
effect ;)

title: @Builder.Default fails for init expressions using super or this

nodes.body:
This is by design and cannot be fixed. To wit:

The way Builder.Default works is that the builder 'gathers' all the required fields, and once its done that, invokes the all-args constructor. During the 'gather' phase, we don't have an instance.

The only way to fix it is to generate a combinatorial explosion of constructors, to generate a constructor with a boolean for EVERY field in addition to the field value, or to have a sentinel 'I have no value, go with the default' option so that the constructor itself chooses whether to invoke the 'produce default value for this field' method; that's the only way we can make those methods non-static.

All possible options to address this cause more harm than this problem, therefore, they're all a bad idea.

In other words, your concern is valid but addressing it breaks more stuff.

title: @Slf4j why not support @Inherited ?

nodes.body:
It's a bit difficult to guess what you are referring to, without any explanation or use case.
But what I think you want is that any subclass of a class that has an `@Slf4j` annotation also automatically gets the `log` declaration generated.

First con is that not every subclass will actually use the logger. Then lombok would generate unused code.
Second con is technical: At the time lombok steps in and generates code, resolution did not take place, yet. I.e., the type hierachy has not been established by the compiler, and thus lombok cannot resolve superclasses. And that means that lombok annotations cannot be inherited from superclasses.
I think @janrieke covered it well. Feel free to re-file another issue with more details if you meant something else, @liujinjin777

title: Feature request: @ToString allows skipping null-value fields
body:
It would be nice if I could skip null-valued fields in the generated toString(), e.g. with

```
@ToString(excludeNulls = true)
class MyClass { ... }
```

As Optionals are not supported by lombok, I may have one or more fields that are nullable in my DTO, and which do not need to be set during construction.

This is a nice-to-have; it's not the end of the world to need to copy the generated toString and add in my null-exclusion logic, nor indeed to see "fieldName=null" in the toString output, as I only use it for logging. If it's not an easy win, don't worry about it :grin:

nodes.body: I could work on it, let's see if someone confirms me.

@chriswilty This issue is a duplicate of quite a few -- IMHO erroneously -- closed issues, as stated [in this comment](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/1297#issuecomment-283407301).

@mohasaid The idea has been discussed since ages and implementing it without helper methods is [said to be a lot of work](https://groups.google.com/d/msg/project-lombok/9on7mFH3z34/Y9HvIJxn0JAJ). And it's getting more complicated as new features get added, like using methods rather than fields only.

It'd make sense to add `skipNulls` as an option to the nested annotation `@ToString.Include`, too.

Anyway, you'd better await an OK by the project owners.

---

PS: There are related feature requests like skipping empty fields, but it's unclear what "empty" means in general. For a field like `private SomeType amIEmpty`, it's unclear, how to test it. `SomeType` could be a  descendant of `Collection` to be tested with `amIEmpty.isEmpty()` (or `amIEmpty.size() == 0`) or an implementation of `CharSequence` to be tested with `amIEmpty.length() == 0`. Actually, it could be both. 

The only good news is that it can't be an array. This can of worms should probable be left closed.

@Maaartinus Thanks for the input, and the link to #1297, which I'd managed to miss.

I feel that issue has exploded a bit with all the "oh, and how about if it did this..." issues linked. In contrast, the concept of nulls being a special case is already part of lombok (`@NonNull` and the `@-ArgsConstructor`s) which is why I felt it would be a natural addition.

I deliberately didn't include a request for `@ToString.(In|Ex)clude` because I foresaw that it could be a springboard for all sorts of other requests to expand the functionality of those, however, for the sake of completion and consistency it might make sense to augment those also. I'm not sure that it makes sense to have `skipNulls` as an option to `@ToString.Include` as skipping is an exclusion; probably something like `@ToString.Include(onlyNonNull = true)`.

Anyhow, as stated it's not a big problem to need to write my own toString, so I won't be upset if this issue is closed also :)

@chriswilty 

> I'm not sure that it makes sense to have `skipNulls` as an option to `@ToString.Include`

My only problem with this is that it mayn't be very useful. Quite often, you want to include (or exclude) some fields, quite often you want to exclude all nulls, and probably only rarely you want to include some field unconditionally and others only when not null.

> as skipping is an exclusion; probably something like `@ToString.Include(onlyNonNull = true)`.

IMHO the name should be the same as `@Whatever.Include` is (a sort of) the per-field variant of `@Whatever`. It just has double duty: Ensure that the field gets considered AND optionally override options. While some options make no sense in one place (e.g., `callSuper` or `rank`), others do. Don't let English grammar details take over logic (see SQL or Javabeans for where it leads to).

I'd read `@*.Include(skipNull = true)` like "include this field, but skip it if null". It's still an inclusion, it's just conditional. ;) More importantly: It's an override for the equally-named option on the master annotation.

IMHO `@*.Exclude` should never get any options. In this case, conditional exclusion is tempting, but conditional exclusion is the same thing as conditional inclusion, just with the inverse condition. This would lead to needless ambiguities.

Any progress on this? And by "this" I mean allowing something like @ToString(excludeNulls = true) at the top level (class level), not something on each individual field. I am working on a project and we are using lombok, except the @ToString for this very reason, because it would pollute the logs by listing null fields. So as it is (without the capability to skip null fields), the @ToString is useless to us.

telling an open source dev 'this needs a higher priority' is a great way to cause demotivation. Not fair to the great contributors we do have, but, @remigiusv – you need to work on your manners. I don't work for you! If I could write this feature such that it wouldn't work for just you, I'd do it. Fortunately, open source doesn't work that way, but, cripes. Way to be a downer.

Not a high priority right now. The problem with adding 'just this feature' without considering the greater scope is that if we DO eventually get around to rethinking how to make ToString more configurable, perhaps we then realize that we have to deprecate this feature, or we now have two ways to accomplish the same thing which is a needless raising of learning curve and opening the door to style debates.

+1 for this feature, I can see some cases it is undesired but for all DTO (in particular in microservice erea) it is really a code and time saver to be able to skip nulls (and lombok is literally about it right?).

What about other default values? Like `0`, `0.0`, `false`, `'\0'`? What about the empty string? Or even skipping every value that has the same value as the field initializer expression, or even take constructors into account?

What makes `null` so special that it deserves explicit and special handling?

@rspilker the fact it can be not initialized - which is not true for primitives. For example in a DTO, adding a "integer" (functionally) you can choose to make it appearing or not by using Integer or int so a natural toString implementation would be enabled to follow that. That said if you go the @ToString.SkipIfEquals("...") path I'm more than happy with it too while null can have a "on class" toggle (=  good default) since it is still the most common in most application (even if I agree some only use primitive but it is not mainstream at all). Finally, empty string and initializer cases don't make sense for me since it is about representing the values. Only specifity is: do you keep nulls or not in the reprensentation.

I guess we can take inspiration from most common JSON setups there, generally null are ignored and you can force them to be shown. All other settings are rarely used (for "tostring" case) so I guess only supporting null is a huge step forward and that if can be refined for primitives later if needed but i'm not sure primitive really pollute the output as much as strings/objects in practise.

> What about other default values? Like `0`, `0.0`, `false`, `'\0'`? What about the empty string? Or even skipping every value that has the same value as the field initializer expression, or even take constructors into account?
> 
> What makes `null` so special that it deserves explicit and special handling?

what you listed are value and null is absence of value

Didn't we recently have in some issue the idea of having a configurable toString-implementation? I think someone was asking for JSon-output (or even xml?) ...

If we could specify something e.g. like: "toString.defaultImpl=my.special.package.MyPrettyFormatter.objectToWhateverILike", and have the an option for individual @ToString-annotations to override the default everyone could simply plug in their own make-me-happy-toString-implementation to their likings without bothering the lombok-team any further about individual preferences ...

sometimes i need other value if the field is null.. if user.email is null, i could have user.name and user.surname :) what about user.somefield with @ToString(converter=MyValueToStringConverter.class) (with Object Referenz)

@aleksej-turko-dgn That's not a good idea. We _already_ support such a mechanism, via annotating a method with `@ToString.Include` which has the same name as your field (or, just specify the field name in the `@Include` argument) where you can write this logic. The problem with your approach is that for your idea, there are 50 other slightly exotic situations, thus, it turns the annotation parameters into a really crappy Domain Specific Language (crappy because annotation params are _very_ limited indeed).

@dstango Maybe. There are a ton of requests for more customization of toString's outputs, but so many of them strike me as 'well, if lombok grows enough warts to cater to them all, the sheer amount of crud you have to shove into annotation parameters to configure it all / the additional code you need to write in 'converters' and the like feel like they add up to just as much code as just writing the toString yourself).

There's:

* Skip `null`
* Have alternate toString converters
* Deal with loops in collections
* unpack Optional
* star out passwords and other sensitive info (this seems security-wise boneheaded in the extreme, but, it's a common request!)
* skip _empty_ things, with never any particularly good definition of how one determines whether an object can be empty and if so, how to figure it out. Reflectively call `isEmpty()` on it? Resolve the type and check if it has a visible `isEmpty()`? But that's structural typing.

The problem is, some of those seem veto-ably silly to me, some seem great but I do not see a route as to how to deliver it without breaking rules (such as the `isEmpty()` thing - we aren't going to go with structural typing. Java isn't a structurally typed language. And there isn't an `Emptyable` annotation like there's an `AutoClosable` either) - which leaves a few that are useful and are doable, such as this, but just ignoring the other stuff for now and delivering the simplest thing that could work on the few things that are possible just feels like being in a hole and digging even deeper: Without considering the wide range of effects, any changes we make now just cramps our style or forces us to break compatibility later if ever we do find neat ways to deliver on as much as is requested in a decent way.

So far our general point is: These are mildly useful things for debugging purposes primarily, not things that should be expertly crafted to look juuuust right. In other words, if you:

* Emit `toString()` output to users
* Document in your API that the output of `toString()` is formatted in some specific fashion so that programmatic access can parse the output.
* Emit `toString()` output to log files that don't exist as a debugging aid afterthought but are security-reviewed and transferred from contained environments to larger ones for long periods of time, or are used for audit trails

Then our advice is _not to use `@ToString` at all_. (Also, our advice is _not to use `toString()` for these purposes!) - and the toString() docs agree with us, at least on the first 2 items in that list.

__All__ these requests have in common that they are either distant nice-to-haves for the 'use for casual debugging' purpose, or even that it has no effect on that usecase at all and it's _solely_ to cater to the above 3 items. So, so far, the easy solution is: ToString just isn't meant for that. We cater only to the 'nicer debugging output' thing.

We aren't opposed to making `@ToString` do more. But we __are__ opposed to one-off fire-and-forget actions. We want something that feels particularly well-thought-through.

A few ground rules to keep in mind:

* If you want to modify how a limited subset of fields act, e.g. "I want to mask out a password" or "I want this _particular_ field to be skipped if it is empty / null / whatever", we _already support this_: Make a method that returns the output you want, and use `@ToString.Include`. The one update I am interested in is a way to state that if this returns `null` that this means you want to skip the entire field somehow: If you really want to print `null`, well, you're in a method, return `"null"` then - but do we just introduce this change? Do we add a parameter to the annotation? (oof, we consider the cost of adding a parameter as high: It's the only way to prevent a situation where lombok annotations have 50 parameters, we think 'it is flexible but the parameter list is endless and you need a manual to know what the heck to configure, not to mention the combinatory explosion of what lombok would have to test to cover all uses' is worse than 'it is simple but doesn't quite cater to everything under the sun').

* If you want to modify how _all_ fields with a given property (e.g. of some type) act, we'd be interested in that, but it can't turn into some sort of framework and remember that lombok cannot add dependencies (there can be no `LombokToStringSystem.registerRenderer(Thingie.class, thingie -> "THINGIE: " + thingie)` style thing, that's runtime, lombok does not exist at runtime).


This issue remains in that weird in-between space where it's a decent enough proposal but we see no way to design a way to deliver on it, except things that feel incomplete.

@rzwitserloot you summarize all sorts of requests that have been made, and I agree Lombok shouldn't grow a `@ToString`-annotation-with-a-multitude-of-parameters-to-rule-them-all.

Yet: where's the trouble in providing a config property that could override Lombok's default implementation easily by referencing a static method that would do whatever a user requests. If the implementation is sub-optimal to whatever security-, nullability-, Optional-, emtpy-, or other concerns that's not the responsibility of Lombok, but the user's. Sounds right to me: more freedom for the user comes with more responsibility ...
Thus: all the valid points you mention become trade-offs to be dealt with by the user.

Of could one could do a simple `toString()`-implementation for every single class, that calls that exact static method mentioned. Thus one would replace `@ToString` with an individual toString()-method. No big deal.

Yet it becomes really handy if I use `@Data`, that has an implicit `@ToString`. It keeps the code nice, clean, concise. And if that uses the configured static `@ToString`-method we can keep the class clutter-free ...

Just my 2 ct ...

@rzwitserloot thanks for your quick response, and: yes, you got me right and your example fits. (I thought I had sketched it already in my earlier message, but that was not fleshed out -- sorry.)

And yes: the way I see a realization is mostly via reflection. If you want e.g. some json you can use gson or whatever library you like to produce some serialization. This is something happening all the time in real world projects, and I don't see what's speaking against it, and I can't imagine reflection going away as it's so widely used.
You might say 'performance is worse', but we're talking primarily about a debug output here, so that doesn't count.

You're saying reflection is getting more and more complicated. I'm not sure what you're exactly referring to -- maybe the stricter encapsulation of internal classes, and consequences of applying the module system more strictly? I'd argue: these things don't really matter, as the classes I annotate with `@ToString` are in my own code, so I have full access to them, and should be able to use reflection on them. But maybe you have something else in mind.

Anyhow: it might be an option to have several overloaded static `toString()`-methods with different types to handle different cases. While that might be useful sometimes (e.g. for certain child classes from common parent classes that should be handled in a similar way), a degenerated variant would be to have such a static `toString()`-method for every class with the `@ToString`-annotation, which would be an implementation from the category: "how to write unmaintainable code".

Regarding the pony etc.: I have no strong desire for this feature (I'm usually happy with the current implementation), but I saw so many different feature requests around `@ToString`-special-features, that I thought: "why not provide some extension point, that opens a practical way to handle such situations, while at the same time frees you and the Lombok team from putting any energy into such specific request like "please hide my password fields", "convert null to an empty string", "leave out field if vale == null", "produce json/xml/yaml/..."

But if the most obvious implementation idea for such a `toString()`-implementation is reflection, and you don't want to provide a way that often would result in reflection usage -- then I don't have any idea how to realize it. If you want to force reflection-less `toString()`-implementations, then you'd either have to provide a multitude of annotation-parameters (meh...), or come up with a lomboqueske template-language to generate highly flexible source code for each individual `toString()`-implementation (I guess that's out of scope for Lombok, and would be a maintenance burden anyhow) ...

So: sorry, not more than another 2 ct from my side -- I'm out of magical ideas, if reflection in the user's implementation is out of the question ...

May I point back to feature request https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/1752?
If a user could iterate at runtime over all fields and get their values, she or he could easly exclude null values or hide passwords based on the specific field or even based on the type.

Think it does not make much sense to plug a custom "converter"/mapper cause at the end it means the user should just override the underlying tostring method.
Handling null (or not) makes sense cause it is generic but agree other cases can be too much.

> If you want e.g. some json you can use gson or whatever library you like to produce some serialization.

Well, there we go. From a java design perspective, having your `toString()` emit JSON is something I would instaflag as a knockout bug. That's not what it is for. If you want to write some java code that does do that, more power to you. Far be it from me to complain about hackery and using things for purposes it wasn't really intended to :) - but where I draw the line is: You can't then call that 'boilerplate'. And if it's not boilerplate, lombok has no business catering for the use case.

If we add this feature and it requires reflection to use it, the next thing that is going to happen is about 50 bugs a day filed about WTF that's about. Gathering up all the requests and takes on what folks expect a 'ToString is now more flexible' feature would look like, that caters to a tiny slice of them and annoys the other slices.

No can do.

@Tobias4git wrote:

> If a user could iterate at runtime over all fields and get their values

Just write `toString()` if you want to do that. I'm going to have to yell at you too. I will summarize your comment:

* JUST do this easy thing!
* Absolutely no code to indicate what it actually looks like.
* 'easy thing' isn't easy and I have no idea what you think it should look like.

You're wasting everybody's time.

New rule: If you propose a way forward, either it includes code that shows how to write it with lombok and what lombok delomboks that to, or I delete it.

@Tobias4git Ah now your comment makes a lot more sense :)

I've had to shoot down #3328 unfortunately. The same problem it has (namely, you have to write loads of unchecked casts (as in, casts that are just wrong if you fatfinger it _and_ are rather error prone, not that you get the warning)) - applies to trying to use that fix here, too. Well, not specifically _here_ - but string  concat is pretty much the one and only place in all of java where just shoving objects in is fine. _Other than_ toString, letting `@FieldNameConstants` have a `getValue()` methods is useless unless you accept tons of unchecked casts. Hence, why we're not doing #3328.
Not even in the same ballpark as something I'd find acceptable. I'm not sure how I can explain why that is so very much not at all what we are looking for though :(

@dstango Ah, actual code as part of a proposal. That's great! Thank you.

As a feature request this is vetoed. The problem is something I already mentioned earlier in this issue: The only obvious implementations possible for such a thing (given that it will have to accept a `Map<String, Object>` is to go on a reflection spree. Or possibly on a a pattern matching spree.

Even if that is acceptable (it isn't), all implementations I can think of will just casually `.toString()` all the things _except_ those specific types that this 'explicit toString implementation' actually cares about. Which sounds simple and obvious _but is incorrect_ in that you now lose lombok's smarts about e.g. what to do with arrays.

"Slap all fields together into some flavour of `java.util.Map` and pass it to a single static do-it-all method" is a dead end, I think.

title: Using Entity.id only on equals() lead to unexpected behavior when id = null

nodes.body:
I'm afraid, your `equals` is completely broken as it compares two entities with different non-null `id`s as equal. In the following I'm assuming, you've mean `return this$id == other$id;` instead of `return true;`.

> Note the `if (this$id == null || other$id == null ) return false;`
instead smth like `if (this$id == null && other$id != null) return false` which is now produced

What currently gets produced is the equivalent of `Objects.equal(this$id, other$id)`, i.e., just null-safe equals. That's surely correct, albeit problematic with JPA. This line

> `if (this$id == null || other$id == null ) return false;`

solves the problem, but without also following what Vlad wrote about `hashCode`, it can lead to other problems, when the entity gets assigned an `id`. So the only good solution for JPA is your above `equals` and a constant `hashCode`... you're testing a single field... you need no Lombok for this, right?

What I mean:
- There's no perfect solution for JPA. (*)
- JPA changes the `id` and using a mutable field for EqHC is broken by design.
- Using business fields for EqHC is even more broken.
- **Your preferred solution needs no Lombok.**

FWIW, I'm using manually written EqHC which throws when called with `id` being `null`.
- This feels rather wrong, but it's fail-fast.
- Entities whose identity may change shouldn't be used as keys and this way I ensure it.
- It's quite possible that this may be problematic with bigger projects, for me it works well.

---

(*) Except maybe assigning a unique id already in the constructor.

nodes.body:
I guess, this happens because of occurrences of the field name in the generated code. The generated code claims to be written where the annotation stays. During refactoring, Eclipse replaces all occurrences of the old field name by the new name using this information, without bothering to check the original code.

This happens to `@EqualsAndHashCode` as well and seems to cause #1628, too.

No idea, if Lombok can solve it, but Eclipse surely could.

It also happens with `@Data`.

title: Performance improvements
body:
I played around a bit with jprofiler and identified some hotspot methods that can easily be optimized.
I've created several PRs for each optimization:

#1760 #1761 #1762 #1763 #1764 #1765 #1766 #1768 

All in all the performance gain is not much, it's about 5% (except #1766 - if you using a non-lombok project - and #1768 ) - so decide if it is worth to have the minor changes in the code base.

As far as I see, the critical paths are the traverse/traverseChildren methods. The AST tree is traversed several times (one time for each handler-priority)
I do not yet understand each detail of lombok, but is it really neccessary to traverse the same tree several times for each priority. Wouldn't it be better to traverse the tree one time, gather all data of used annotations and do the whole work afterwards?

nodes.body: Thanks to the commets of @randakar, I reflected all the changes and made one PR #1771 that really improves performance (not only 5%) by mainly reducing method invocations. I only adopted the most important changes
I think I've incorporated the relevant pull requests.

title: New features for @FieldNameConstants

nodes.body:
That's a good news! Maybe it'd make sense to name it `@FieldNameEnum` instead, as `prefix` and `suffix` are rather useless with an `enum` (the old `@FieldNameConstants` could stay untouched for some time).

The only usage problem, I can see, is that `pkg.FieldnameTest.Fields.test.name()` is not a compile-time constant, so there's no string usable in annotations like e.g., [Hibernate's uniqueConstraints](https://docs.jboss.org/ejb3/app-server/HibernateAnnotations/reference/en/html_single/#d0e189) (though here, the "logical" column names get used which may differ from the field names, so I should have chosen a different example).

@rzwitserloot Above, you wrote `pkg.FieldnameTest.Fields.test`, which violates the conventions, though I could imagine myself wanting to violate them, too. I guess, by default, it should behave like before ("same name as the field it represents, except with all uppercase letters, with underscores in front of the uppercase letters in the original field")?

- configuration (maybe `lombok.fieldNameEnum.uppercased`)?
- member `final String pkg.FieldnameTest.Fields.TEST.fieldName = "test"`?

Implementation is now on master branch: 3d432c38d0cfeb36b8e7402eca56faaafcf7bac7

along with the docs: 0038b48eeacac0389980902e65b4976dd5605c69

Because the feature is in experimental I decided (for now, we can revisit this decision prior to releasing v1.18.4) to just remove the old way entirely and replace it with this new way.

You can now choose whether you want an enum or an inner type with psf String constants; by default you get the string constants, you have to explicitly choose to go with enum instead. Only configurable aspect right now is the name of the inner type.

I can see adding 'uppercased' as an option via lombok.config, but piling it into the annotation itself feels like a bridge too far (too many finicky settings, and it's purely a style thing; I don't think any framework demands that these are capitalized).

title: "@Slf4j" annotation ignored in Groovy class [Lombok v1.18.0]

nodes.body: groovy does not support or have lombok. What it does have, is lombok-inspired annotations. So, yeah, what you're trying to do probably should work, but we can't fix it; lombok is not actually included in groovy.

title: Wrong Getters & Setters generated

nodes.body: Your example code is wrong. I'm assuming now that you have both `@Getter` and `@Setter` on the class. I just check that code with lombok 1.18.0 and it works as expected. So there is definitely no setter method like yours generated. The only "problem" is that because of the "is" in `isFormula`, the setters for both fields would have the same name and signature, and therefore lombok only generates the first one (for `isFormula`). This is not a bug. You have to change the names, or use `lombok.getter.noIsPrefix = true` (which also affects the generation of setters).

title: Code coverage on @NonNull

nodes.body:
No; lombok is a compile-time only dependency, so there's no place we can stick this $$$nonNull$$$ method that's still in existence at runtime. We'd have to generate it.

Applying DRY to code generation is a silly argument. As with all programming maxims and rules of thumb, you can apply it badly. Try to think of what the maxim is actually trying to prevent and then use that insight. For example, DRY is primarily about saving yourself from having to fix the same bug, or apply the same change request, in multiple places (or worse, forgetting about a few places and creating an inconsistent experience, and/or bugs). None of this applies to code generation.

The coverage tools thing is quite a relevant remark but I don't have a real solution to it; we can generate a private method to do it in _each_ class that has `@NonNull` annotations in it, but those aren't entirely invisible (they show up in autocomplete dialogs and the like), and that makes the cure worse than the disease.

opinion/rant follows:

A code coverage tool which marks `if (x == null) throw new NullPointerException();` as a problem because the line isn't covered, is indicative of why code coverage is a silly thing to chase. Don't use code coverage tools in this way! It makes you _remove_ defensive code, and/or screw up your APIs to make it possible to create inconsistent state just so you can at least test that your code does something deterministic and testable when you create inconsistent situations. In other words, code coverage tools deployed in the mode you seem to be deploying it, makes your code worse: Your APIs become worse, and your code becomes more brittle. It's lose/lose.

Another issue is the value of coverage: Unless you get a straight up 100%, the percentage value is useless. In most projects, only 5 to 20% of all lines of code are the real meat and potatoes: The tricky code, the business logic, the complicated algorithm. The rest sets stuff up, reads parameters or settings, configures, passes stuff on, etcetera.

So, let's say you score 90% code coverage.

What does that mean? If the 10% not covered is a bunch of exotic boilerplate or defensive code, you've effectively got perfect coverage. But if the 10% not covered is the meat and potato code, you've basically covered nothing of import whatsoever.

In other words, 90% code coverage is a meaningless statistic. It says nothing. But that 90% code coverage number is giving everyone a false sense of achievement.

Said even more simply: Dump your code coverage tools because they are bad, they make you write bad code, and they mislead you about the quality of your code.

There is one good reason to use a code coverage tool: "Line for line": Looking at some line of code, run a bunch of tests and/or a real run whilst you manually press some buttons, and then ask a code coverage tool which test or tests covered the exact line you're looking at. That's a fine tool and a nice aid for figuring out complicated issues. Note that lombok's nullcheck being impossible to trigger is no problem whatsoever when code coverage tools are deployed in this fashion.

But that's it; the moment anybody starts mentioning the word 'percent' or 'full code coverage', my disdain for said code shop grows.

end rant.

I like this rant a lot.

It's accurate. Percentage coverage is a piss poot metric. Unit tests that
only cover the happy path, ditto. You want to cover the corner cases and
those won't be covered if you only test the easy stuff.

I disagree that having full coverage is necessarily a bad sign though.
Given that you want some kind yard stick  for "good enough" that is not
entirely subjective, it may be better than nothing or some meaningless
percentage of partial coverage.

I don't think unit tests should ever be the whole story or some kind of
holy grail though. Higher level tests tend to be more reliable indicators
of "stuff being broken" than unit tests. Those still have coverage, of
course, but code that can not be reached from there probably should not be
covered..

Having said that, IDEs like IntelliJ (with the JetBrains `@NotNull` annotation) generate code that is very similar to the one I proposed when you build through the IDE (which is one thing I don't like about it, since you don't get the same build from your machine or from running gradle/maven on your CI box).

I imagine that the Lombok plugin would be able to take care of not showing the method (but I've never written an IDE plugin, so it might not be possible). Also, I think that this only applies to _this_ class, as the method should be private.

-----

As for your opinion/rant - I pretty much agree with everything! Code coverage is a rather meaningless number which can be easily manipulated. 

> Said even more simply: Dump your code coverage tools because they are bad, they make you write bad code, and they mislead you about the quality of your code.

This one, not so much: Running a code coverage tool, **and analysing its results** can lead you to find meaningful things that you're not testing (perhaps for a good reason, or perhaps by simple forgetfulness) such as branches or error conditions that might be part of the _meat and potatoes_, or at least the _gravy_ :wink:.

I think Lombok is a great tool, and I think if we can make it play nicer with some other concerns, that are important to _some_ people, it can become an ever better tool.

Thanks for taking the time to thoughtfully respond to this issue.

title: Restarting Eclipse or switching workspaces injects Lombok a second time
body:
Restarting Eclipse or switching workspaces injects Lombok a second time.  I'm not sure if this causes issues in practice, but it seems problematic.

To reproduce:

1. Start eclipse
2. Select Help → About Eclipse
3. Note that "Lombok v1.18.0 "Envious Ferret" is installed. https://projectlombok.org/" is at the bottom.
4. Select File → Restart (or File → Switch Workspace)
5. Once Eclipse has opened again, select Help → About Eclipse
6. Note that the "Lombok v1.18.0 "Envious Ferret" is installed. https://projectlombok.org/" text is repeated twice.
7. Further restarts or workspace switches each add the text an additional time.  Fully closing eclipse and starting it again does clear it, though.

Eclipse version: Photon Release (4.8.0) (there's a lot of other eclipse info, but I'm not sure exactly what of it is useful and some of it contains somewhat personal information; if there's something else about the version that is needed let me know).

nodes.body: Oh nice.
New in Photon
Lombok wasn't really being loaded twice, just, the code that updates the eclipse about text was being called again. That code is now smarter about not re-applying the change.

We have a bunch of these bug reports. The problem is, there are 3 completely different ways we can fix it:

[1] per issue, adopt contention-free syntax, accept that sometimes it does not exist.

Example: Take the option **Use 'this' qualifier for field access** – if there is no way to configure eclipse to do the opposite, i.e. **Remove unnecessary 'this' qualifiers** or even **remove unnecessary qualifiers** or even **remove unnecessary code**, we can just generate it that way, which has no impact whatsoever on any existing users and now solves this specific variant of the 'overlapping text edits' bug.

If there is an opposite setting (i.e. there is a way to make eclipse use save actions to add a node, as well as one to remove it if it is explicitly present), then this solution is impossible.

[2] per issue, pinpoint patch a fix.

This is quite complicated: Hunt around for the save action's analysis code and patch in an explicit check there to notice it's generated code and skip it. Sometimes this means checking the flag (We do set a flag), sometimes it means skipping any node at a certain position. That last one is not always possible; setting position to 0 or -1 causes other issues. The flag isn't always there either. This is a lot of work and it is hard to be sure that any given fix is going to work on all the many many eclipse versions in active use.

[3] Fix this whole range of issues once and for all.

If we're going to spend a lot of time anyway (as per [2]), why not find a more holistic solution and patch into eclipse a more solid knowledge of the notion of generated AST nodes, fixing them ALL in one fell swoop.

[4] Add formatting config.

I'm loathe to add this to lombok.config; whilst it has benefits for delombok which can also use it, how many people are really going to spend time telling lombok precisely how they prefer to format their code? If there was some standard way to do it I might be interested, but asking users to configure their preferred style in their linter, and then to do it again in their IDE, and then to do it a third time in lombok.config? I don't think we should go down this road.

But what we CAN do, perhaps, is check eclipse's save actions and style config and follow it: Update the eclipse variant of our handler for `@EqualsAndHashCode` and have it actively check the current save action settings and generate according to its preferences.

This also sounds relatively convoluted, but maybe it's not too difficult (a lot depends on whether we have the right objects available to us from which we can navigate to the save action settings. These things tend NOT to be global static variables, and there's the OSGi/equinox module system to consider, which all makes it hard to actually know this stuff).


I'm not sure which of these 4 roads to walk down. I think it's [3], which makes this a big project and not in scope for the next release.

@vyemialyanchyk  I'm not opposed to the feature... actually, I had such an idea myself, but for every use case, I found a different solution, which was at least equally good.

> Proceeding with example, why do you think 1 assertion for 1 property there?

Do I?

You wanted to copy *all* properties of `Aa` and I copied the reference to the *whole* `Aa` object instead. There's nothing like "1 assertion for 1 property" in what I added.

---

I'm not part of the team, just a fan. The reason for Lombok providing relatively few features is that it has a much higher implementation overhead than any library. Writing a code generator or a reflective solution would be a matter of a few minutes. Doing the same with Lombok may take hours and there may be many more of maintenance.

This feature sounds rather harmless w.r.t. to the implementation... it might be a nice extension to `@Data`. It'd surely need a much better name (`copy` and `assign` are out of question; I'd propose `copyFrom` or `overwriteBy`) and some use case, where it can be easily replaced by something existing.

Well, as one of the two dictators as far as feature requests are concerned:

I understand what you're asking for, it may from time to time by useful, but not often enough to be worth the mental load of having this be something we'd need to list on the feature page and such.

title: How to run (de)lombok with big classpath?
body:
I'm developing a gradle plugin which contains a task for running delombok.

I currenty invoke delombok using a command like this:
(one argument per line for better readability)
```bash
/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/jdk1.8.0_171.jdk/Contents/Home/bin/java
-Dfile.encoding=UTF-8
-Djava.io.tmpdir=/Volumes/Daten/git/gradle-plugins-test/lombok/build/tmp/delombok
-Duser.country=DE
-Duser.language=de
-Duser.variant
-cp /Users/larsgrefer/.gradle/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/org.projectlombok/lombok/1.18.0/c4647d46f0742746ac07ce4abeeee9b2fb18d147/lombok-1.18.0.jar
lombok.launch.Main
delombok
--format=pretty
--target=/Volumes/Daten/git/gradle-plugins-test/lombok/build/delombok/main
--classpath=/Users/larsgrefer/.gradle/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/org.slf4j/slf4j-api/1.8.0-beta2/ba136e771a794f77ab41fa879706e5cbd5b20f39/slf4j-api-1.8.0-beta2.jar:/Users/larsgrefer/.gradle/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/org.projectlombok/lombok/1.18.0/c4647d46f0742746ac07ce4abeeee9b2fb18d147/lombok-1.18.0.jar
/Volumes/Daten/git/gradle-plugins-test/lombok/src/main/java
```

On big project this command can exceed 32767 characters which causes errors on windows: https://blogs.msdn.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20031210-00/?p=41553

## What I've tried so far:

### Classpath Manifest
A common and well known workaround for such problems when invoking java applications with a long classpath, is to create a single jar which contains the actual classpath in its `MANIFEST.MF`.
Unfortunately this does'nt work for delombok's `--classpath`-option

### Calling `lombok.launch.Main.main()` directly
Since the gradle task from which I want to run delombok is a java process itself, i've tried to directly invoke lomboks `main()`-method. Unfortunately this isn't an option too, because lombok internally calls `System.exit()`.

## Possible solutions

### Support argfiles
Other java tools like `javac`, `javadoc` and `ajc` allow you to put all your command line arguments into an file, which can be passed to the process instead of the actual arguments: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/tools/windows/javac.html#BHCCFGCD

### Provide an API
It would be great to have a java API to invoke (de)lombok directly without the need of creating an additional java process

nodes.body: As far as I can see, we only call `System.exit()` if something goes wrong, or if you pass the help parameter.
`lombok.core.Main#main(String[] args)` calls `System.exit()` in every case
@rzwitserloot is going to implement the `@filename` syntax soon. In the meantime, we we will only call System.exit if the return code is not zero.

Since Java 9 the `java` command natively supports `@argument files`, ~so implementing this in lombok would only be necessary for java 8.~

A nicer option would be a java API for invoking lombok, so I don't have to start an additional process
I just experimented with the native `@file`-support in Java 9+. Unfortunately this seems not to work for the actual application arguments but only for the arguments directly read by the JVM
delombok specifically now supports `@args.txt`. Check it out in edge: https://projectlombok.org/download-edge

title: Make Getters and Setters on Date (or other mutable objects) set/return new copy.

nodes.body:
Date being mutable like that is a bug. That class should be treated as
deprecated, and replaced with ZonedDateTime or LocalDateTime instances
wherever possible.
This is not a lombok problem, imho.


On Wed, Aug 1, 2018 at 11:47 AM, Ivica <notifications@github.com> wrote:

> Let's consider the following class:
>
> @Getter
> @Setter
> public class SomeClassWithDates {
>     private Date start;
>     private Date end;
> }
>
> This will result in normal getters and setters. Then somewhere else in the
> code:
>
> SomeClassWithDates obj = new SomeClassWithDates();
> Date now = new Date();
> obj.setStart(now);
> .....
> now.setYear(...);
> //now the obj.getStart() will be also modified
>
> Proper implementation will be instead of returning get and set directly on
> the object, call new Date on the passed argument in the setter:
>
> public void setStart(Date date) {
>    this.start = new Date(date.getTime());
> }
>
> public Date getStart() {
>    return new Date(this.start.getTime());
> }
>
> My best guess is that this should at least work for Java Classes like Date
> (since it needs to know which constructor to call and with which data), but
> maybe some other annotation can be added. An idea will be also to have an
> argument in @getter <https://github.com/getter> and @setter
> <https://github.com/setter> for example:
> @Setter(new = true)
> And possible a method reference to the constructor:
> @Setter(new = true, with = Date::getTime)
>
> I am not sure if there was already an issue similar to this one. What do
> you guys think?
>
> —
> You are receiving this because you are subscribed to this thread.
> Reply to this email directly, view it on GitHub
> <https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/1799>, or mute the thread
> <https://github.com/notifications/unsubscribe-auth/AAKCRZIo0K7Ngn0cSZItksEEOCCBHaf_ks5uMXlEgaJpZM4VqL2q>
> .
>



-- 
"Don't only practice your art, but force your way into it's secrets, for it
and knowledge can raise men to the divine."
     -- Ludwig von Beethoven

Ok, let's suppose that your field, getter and setter is `StringBuilder`. This means that it is inherently mutable. Making a copy of it before returning will probably not work as intended.

Maybe something like `@Getter(makeCopy = "clone")` could do it? The copy would be created by calling the `clone()` method (after checking out for `null`s) and casting the result into the same return type of the getter. If `clone()` method is not available or declares to throws the nasty `CloneNotSupportedException`, just allow javac complain with a compile error.

Alternatively you could add `@Getter(makeCopy = "yourOwnCopyMethod")` and it would call `value.yourOwnCopyMethod`.

If you can't modify the target class and it does not provide a method for cloning/copying, maybe a `@Getter(makeCopy = "yourOwnCopyMethod", staticCopy = true)` to make it call a static `yourOwnCopyMethod(value);` method instead?

Fair, Lombok could do something like that.

There is of course the Clonable interface as well. Classes implementing
that should be easy to support - but if won't cover Date, let alone byte
arrays.

I'm thinking the generic version, where you hook a Transformer into setters
and getters sounds interesting. It will have limitations - don't think we
should try to change the method signature with that, for instance - but I
can see uses for this.

Nonetheless, I have doubts. I often see cases where people write code that
calls the same getter multiple times for no good reason. Getters are
supposed to be cheap, if they start involving deep clones of potentially
complex objects, they won't be.


Op za 15 sep. 2018 05:40 schreef Maaartinus <notifications@github.com>:

> This is not a lombok problem, imho.
>
> @randakar <https://github.com/randakar> Right, but there could be a
> Lombok solution. I surely agree that Date is obsolete and shouldn't be
> user anymore, but there are things like byte[] having no replacement.
> ------------------------------
>
> If clone() method is not available or declares to throws the nasty
> CloneNotSupportedException
>
> @victorwss <https://github.com/victorwss> org.bouncycastle is full of
> Cloneable classes declaring for whatever stupid reason to throw. In
> org.apache.http and quite a few more packages, there's more of it.
>
> So it'd be better to catch and wrap.... but this would fail for methods
> not declared to throw. I doubt if Lombok can tell which is which without
> resolution so maybe a dirty hack like
>
> try {
>     if (Boolean.FALSE.booleanValue()) throw new CloneNotSupportedException();
>     return (MyFieldType) myField.clone();
> } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) {
>      throw new RuntimeException(e);
> }
>
> or an additional argument like wrapCloneNotSupportedException=boolean may
> be needed. Or just catch (Exception e), which is considered dirty for
> reason I find mostly wrong.
> ------------------------------
>
> I'd personally be happy with something like @Getter(cloner=MyCloner.class),
> where it'd be the user's responsibility to write *their own* cloner class
> and ensuring it has a matching *static* method for everything it gets
> used for. Writing the class should be pretty trivial
>
> public class MyCloner {
>     public static Date clone(Date input) {
>         return (Date) input.clone();
>     }
>     public static byte[] clone(byte[] input) {
>         return input.clone();
>     }
>     // overload with all needed variants
> }
>
> It's hacky, but very simple and practical. It could lead to compile-time
> errors, but this is no big deal. Actually, it's no deal at all, as you'd
> get a message like "The method clone(....) in the type MyCloner is not
> applicable for the arguments (byte[])".
>
> The annotation would accept *any* class and Lombok would just handle null
> and otherwise do a trivial static method call, relying on overload
> resolution. For Lombok itself, there's no way to enforce that a proper
> class gets used. This sounds worrying, but it's no different from what
> happens when writing a plain java statement.
>
> It handles deep cloning, cloning with bells and whistles and cloning with
> whatever, simply by using @Getter(cloner=MyDeepCloner.class) (sure, the
> user has to implement it, but that's a matter of minutes for simple cases
> and some googling otherwise; anyway, not something, Lombok could perfectly
> solve itself).
>
> Actually, I'd call it transform instead, as it could be used also like
> @Setter(transform=MyNotEmptyStringChecker.class), partially solving a
> different issue.
>
> —

>

Back to my own issue, I agree with your first response that, having a mutable objects in such a cases is deviant. Although Lombok indeed can do something about it (already explained by others above), I think the focus should be not supporting non-standard/buggy approaches. Users should seek for what might be the real problem, because having a mutable object could lead to many other issues. 

In the current cases (the one that I explained in the beginning), custom implementation will be better approach in my opinion now, in cases where immutable object cannot be provided.
What about the cases of `List` and `Map` that suffer the same issue? (And it also impacts the `@AllArgsConstructor` as well)

title: Add option to define a prefix for @Builder methods

nodes.body:
'with' is, by convention of course, something you use to indicate you get a clone with 1 updated value. Builder does not clone, and we don't want to create the impression that builder is something it isn't.

There's no use for this 'prefix' idea, _except_ for withX.

I know this is probably not what you want to hear, but, you'll have to make the case to your team that your convention sucks.

@rzwitserloot, I am curious to understand why 'with' indicates a clone. The common convention to use 'with' for builder methods is, by convention, read as "creating a builder with value x and with value y", implying that the builder object stores/contains these values. 

https://en.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/with uses terms like 'accompanied', 'having', or 'possessing'. None that indicate cloning.

@rzwitserloot The problem is not when "my" convention sucks, it is when a convention has been adopted by many in the industry, thus making lombok integration hard with common/complimentary/legacy software that could increase its adoption. Case in point, I think lombok+jackson is a pretty killer combination for writing minimal code, and both mostly support better patterns than public, no-arg constructors and universal setters. The inability to specify what the resulting builder setter method prefix (or lack thereof) will be makes this integration with jackson a pain, and also seems an arbitrary line to draw in lombok configurability. It is already quite flexible, but then you hit "the thing" that makes adopting it for your team/company/application/integration problematic, and it seems like many feature requests or pull requests in this area over the years have been declined on mostly semantic grounds.

You could simply add `@JsonPOJOBuilder(withPrefix = "")` to the builder class. One could argue for a parameter `onBuilder` for `@Builder` (similar to the `onConstructor` parameter for `@*ArgsConstructor`) to avoid manually writing the builder class definition. But even without it, I would never say that "it's a pain".

I just did a quick google-based comparison. Although there seems to be a slight prevalence for the "set prefix" convention, there are also many examples of "no prefix". The least number of examples seem to use the "with prefix".
Making it configurable seems to be no big deal at first glance; however, such a feature has to be supported and maintained for the rest of lombok's lifetime, and for both `@Builder` and `@SuperBuilder`. Lombok is not a project backed by a large company or a larger number of maintainers, so adding such a feature must be well-considered. It just seems not worth it right now.

Thanks @janrieke, I completely appreciate your last point about maintainability, the longest phase of most features. In my particular example with jackson, your suggestion is exactly what we have done, and requires per class cruft we can mostly otherwise remove with lombok. Thought I'd add a plug in case another submission like https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/pull/1066 comes up.

I am a bit confused. Lombok team is against having builder methods with a prefix, e.g. set?
For instance, `Foo.builder().setName("Ondra").build()` - that's something you don't want to support?

I find it pretty weird that the convention is said to be without prefixes if the API itself has examples with a prefix like Locale and Calendar Builder:

https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/api/java/util/Locale.Builder.html
https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/Calendar.Builder.html

Right. But there's a bigger case for allowing prefixes, specifically `set`:
Refactoring (replacing constructor with a builder and vice versa) is much easier when the methods have the same names. I have done this on around 120 classes and believe me - it would make a big difference. Esp. for the PR reviewers :)

I agree with @Sam-Kruglov! Adding a prefix option to the Builder annotation is definitely cleaner than having to add empty boilerplate code just to add Jackson's JsonPojoBuilder annotation to the generated builder. 

That leaves the naming convention of the builder methods to the developer, which is the lesser of two evils IMO.

Just another one here that would have liked to add a prefix onto builder methods.
We have a massive amount of builders using the 'with' prefix. We would be so glad to replace them with Lombok-generated ones. But the builders are invoked from groovy tests and being unable to specify a prefix means we would have to rename every single method on the builders to align the groovy tests before we can replace them with `@Builder`. This is going to be more work than what my company can afford at the moment, I'm afraid. Also it would force us to change test-code when it was not strictly necessary which is added risk and cost to the equation.

We would also like to combine Jackson and Lombok `@Value` classes. It's not that bad to add the `@JsonPOJOBuilder` annotation on the `Builder`, but it's also not that clean and straightforward.

title: default case in switch statements
body:
as its a bad behaviour not to cover the default case in a switch statement, but mostly or at least sometimes you dont want to handle it and just throw a runtime that tells this case can/should not happen its boilerplate that coud be covered by lombok that just throws the mentioned runtime exception.

thx for the nice tool

nodes.body:
@Maaartinus The annotation could be put in the method, constructor or in the class and then, lombok would be able to check all the `switch` blocks therein.

However, @punkratz312, I'm against this feature because:

1. This is not really very common. Partly, because the `switch` statement is a bad smell per se. If you are using `switch` statements, you are probably doing something wrong.

2. The amount of boilerplate code that it saves is minimal (`default: throw new AssertionError("bad switch value");`), and it is plausible that the annotation boilerplate ends being heavier than the amount of code it avoids. If there is a bunch of `switch`es in your class and you intend to lombokize all of them away with a single annotation, then see item 1 above.

3. This is something that is better handled by static analysis tools like [spotbugs](https://github.com/spotbugs/spotbugs). Though it won't reduce any boilerplate code, it'll warn you if you just forgot to write the `default` case in the `switch` statement.

The only feasible way forward, given that annotating statements is [A] hard and [B] is probably MORE boilerplate, in the end, then the oneliner `default: throw new AssertionError("Missing case");` you're trying to avoid here, is the following:

A (probably lombok.config-powered) completely automatic, blanket application where lombok will, silently and without ANY annotation to indicate this magic is happening, add such defaults to EVERY switch statement you care to compile with javac/ecj whilst lombok so happens to be on the classpath.

Which does solve the dilemma quite well: The whole point is to be a lint-like catchall, designed explicitly to help you out when you forget.
The downside is rather obvious though: That' some voodoo magic. We're basically saying: With lombok on the classpath, java's switch statement is _different_, if you want uncovered cases to no-op their way through a switch statement, you gotta end with `default:` and then close your block.

I can see the case for a 'rewrite java to be more stringent', a kind of `"use strict";` from javascript, but then for java.

But that's a much bigger deal than this simple issue, and if the _only_ thing that you get is this switch behaviour I don't think it's worth it.

So, we need to [A] decide that this is a direction lombok should take, and [B] make a longer list of things we can automatically 'strict-ify'.

That just feels like the job for a different tool. Let's not go there for now.

title: lombok.config files are not taken into account for Gradle cache
body:
How to reproduce:

1. Take any Java project
1. Add a `lombok.config` file to the root of the project. Contents:  `lombok.anyConstructor.addConstructorProperties=false`
1. Compile the project: `gradle compileJava` 
1. Repeat the command. Since the compiled artifacts are cached, the second invocation should take significantly shorter, maybe even 0s.
1. Change the `lombok.config`: `lombok.anyConstructor.addConstructorProperties=true`
1. Re-invoke the compile command. It takes 0s.

Gradle thinks everything is up to date since Lombok processor does not declare the config file as an input.

nodes.body:
gradle gives you 4 options:

* You can not set anything in which case your mere presence completely disables incremental compilation.
* You can say you are an isolated AP (this is what lombok does and is _mostly_ correct), in which case incremental compilation works fine.
* You can say you're an aggregating AP. Not relevant here; lombok isn't.
* You can say you're dynamic, and then answer at runtime... but you have to answer pretty much immediately before you get to know what files you are supposed to process.

Therefore, gradle makes it impossible for us to interact and say that something changed in a way that requires a rebuild.

We can't fix this problem; gradle needs to expand on their API first, then we may be able to do something. Please file with gradle.

title: @Log / @Slf4j on interface - better error notification
body:
Today I've spend a couple of hours with this error message in my gradle build:

```
:some-project:compileJava FAILED

FAILURE: Build failed with an exception.

* What went wrong:
Execution failed for task ':some-project:compileJava'.
> Compilation failed; see the compiler error output for details.
```

Adding any sort of --info or JVM compiler flags didn't give me any more information other than the fact that the javac process exited with a unsuccessful return code and with no message.

After isolating the code that caused the error I found that this was the source of the problem

```
@Slf4j
public interface SomeInterface {
    // ...
```

It was kind of obvious once I understood this - you cannot add a 'private log` field to an interface.

But I think we should try to provide a better error message. Maybe the pre-procesor should throw an exception if one tries to do this?

nodes.body: Lombok raises an error in this case, and both Maven and Eclipse use that error to print a meaningful error message: `@Log is legal only on classes and enums.` So this is either an issue in Gradle itself or in your Gradle configuration.

That `@Data` problem (not calling `super`) seems to be a different problem unrelated to `@SuperBuilder`. I'm getting the warning even without the `@SuperBuilder` annotation. Can you also confirm that, @kingraser?

EDIT: The warning is intentional, see the lombok documentation on [`@EqualsAndHashCode`](https://projectlombok.org/features/EqualsAndHashCode). So you have to explicitly add `@EqualsAndHashCode(callSuper=true)` to your subclasses even though they already have the annotation implicitly via `@Data`.

title: Improving @Wither implementation and making SpotBugs happy with it.

nodes.body:
Just add this line to `lombok.config`
```
lombok.extern.findbugs.addSuppressFBWarnings=true
```
It's not the default as it leads to warnings for those not using FB/SB.

> This approach also have the advantage that it avoids that `exampleInstance.withElement1("X").withElement1("X")` creates a new instance twice.

Actually, it doesn't as `"X" == "X"` because of all string literals being interned. But I see what you mean, but the choice of `==` over `equals` was intentional. It avoids copying in some cases using a trivial fast test, while `equals` can be arbitrarily expensive.

I guess, I proposed once an option of `@Wither` covering cases 1-3, but nobody seemed to care. I guess, case 4 makes sense, too, and there should probably be an option making it to default. However, the possible gain is rather limited and nobody was willing to implement it. I'm also rather happy with how it works now...

I would not go for a list of sane types, Resolution is already tricky, and we would never be able to expand the list if newer types are released.

There could be a list specified in `lombok.config` but that is also not so nice, and the resolution problem would still exist.

No solutions yet, just sharing my thoughts.
[Why we closed this issue](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/wiki/ISSUES:-Why-we-close-issues-without-a-lot-of-explanation.)

title: @Cleanup does not function for variables declared in for-each loops.
body:
One cannot annotate a variable declared and assigned to within the header of a for-each loop with `@Cleanup`, as the library does not recognize the variable as being initialized.

I would expect the following to work:

`for (@Cleanup var someObj : container) ...`

nodes.body:
It's hard to imagine what you'd expect as the intended behavior for this. The most likely is that lombok should add the cleanup code at the end of the `for` loop (because it is the end of the variable's scope). However, this will alter the contents of the `container`, breaking any use of its contents after the loop. This is dangerous.
Besides, although `@Cleanup` is attached to the variable, its _meaning_ is primarily connected the instance, because the instance has to be cleaned. The variable just carries the annotation. And in your case, the instance is constructed somewhere else...

So the only reasonable extension to ease your case I see is to allow cleaning up collections. Then you could add the annotation on the definition of `container`, and lombok could loop through the collection at the end of its scope. However, I don't know if that is implementable, and I doubt that there is a larger need for it.

In this situation, we have a really weird setup where `close` is overloaded to finalize an object, and trigger an update of the parent container (without changing its structure - it just replaces a container element), and the containers are lists. So, closing the object basically finishes the pending operations, but doesn't alter the container.

I actually wouldn't expect a `close` to ever alter the container that the object is contained by - it should alter the object, but I would imagine the container would generally maintain the same reference to the now-closed object, as Java doesn't have any concept of things like RAII. Even in, say, C++, you could `delete` the object, but unless the object's destructor (the closest analog to 'close' here) altered the container it was in, the container's state wouldn't change (unless it was something hash- or data-based like a hash/unordered map or a binary tree, in which case the container would be made invalid).

I could also envision someone passing a list of input streams and looping over it, wanting to close them as they finished.

I also have a problem with this coding style, although I can understand that it sometimes makes sense.

In general, we are talking about an ownership problem. Who is responsible for closing a resource. Typically, it is the code that created it.

In the Enhanced For-loop, the ownership of 'things to close' should typically not transfer to the loop.

I think the best we can do now is generate an error if you use `@Cleanup` on a loop variable.

The current behavior for enhanced for-loop is: `ERROR: @Cleanup variable declarations need to be initialized.`
For the old-style for-loop it is: `ERROR @Cleanup is legal only on a local variable declaration inside a block.`

I do agree that the error message for enhanced for-loop could be better, but at least your code won't compile, so there is no problem of accidentally leaving resources open.

title: Suggestion: Type Inference.
body:
I have a suggestion for a feature. 

I was trying to implement something that would be simple using C++ templates, but is effectively impossible with generics, as generic wildcards cannot be used as full types.

I tried to get around this using the (deprecated) @Delegate, both in a method-local class and in an anonymous class, hoping that I could expand the interfaces of `T`  to the new class in order to support rudimentary metaprogramming and type inference. This did not work, as @Delegate cannot used in methods with arguments (presumably to prevent the user from passing Arg.class to the annotations type list).

If something like this could be supported, it would make Java far more powerful and easier to use, and would gain some of the compile-time dynamicism that C++ has had since CFront.

Effectively, I would like some way to expand a generic wildcard into a meaningful type.

nodes.body:
About delegates, use `@lombok.experimental.Delegate`. And please, format your post adequately to avoid pinging random unrelated people.

Further, without you providing some code, it is very hard to figure out what exactly you trying to do and if it is feasible.

However, I should note that Java is not C++, that Java's generics are very different than C++ templates despite the syntax similarity and that lombok do not have the purpose of cpluspluszing Java.
I have no idea what this would precisely look like, but I sounds like something that just doesn't mesh with what generics are.

title: Overloading a Builder's method for mass-adding to a Singular field removed the default convenience methods

nodes.body:
I would have expected and error saying `Manually adding a method that @Singular @Builder would generate is not supported. If you want to manually manage the builder aspect for this field/parameter, don't use @Singular.`

As far as I can see from the code, it only looks at the method names. One of the reasons is that it is very hard for us to see if you've created an overload or a replacement method. The latter will not really work since we have an (on purpose) undocumented internal representation that is optimized for further processing.
@rspilker I see the error you mentioned. However, overloads should be supported with `@Tolerate`. This is a typical use case for it, but it seems to be ignored, so I'd suggest to reopen.
[@Tolerate](https://projectlombok.org/api/index.html?lombok/experimental/Tolerate.html) is still experimental for now, But that would be a good way to mitigate this issue.

I have encountered this exact issue. Currently I work around it by using a different name for the method I write that takes a different the of arguments from the method that lombok generates, but  being able to overload the lombok method would create a cleaner interface. IMHO, I concur with the suggestion that explicitly annotating the manually created method with [@Tolerate](https://projectlombok.org/api/index.html?lombok/experimental/Tolerate.html) would be a good compromise.
I remark that this issue is a duplicate of the older (albeit less well documented and commented on) https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/1498

title: lombok.var conflicts with auto import in IDEA
body:
I have a Java 10 lombok (1.18.2) project in IDEA (2018.2.3) with the lombok plugin (latest) enabled.

IDEA is configured with `Editor | General | Auto Import | Add unambiguous imports on the fly` enabled.

With this configuration, if I type `for (var x`, what happens is that after I type the space before `x` it does an auto import check.  I'm not sure exactly what's going on at this point; it doesn't actually add an import for `lombok.var`, but in the process of whatever lookup it's doing, the space I typed is removed, so I end up with `for (varx` instead.  It's pretty frustrating, because it repeats if I backspace and try again so some cursor gymnastics are needed to type the correct thing.

I realized that I can prevent this by adding "lombok.var" to the `Exclude from import and completion` section, so there is a reasonable workaround.

I guess `lombok.var` is a feature for pre-Java 10 projects.  It's an unusual identifier. title: Delombok does not support -p arg for javac >= 9
body:
Hi, 

thanks a lot for this project! It has helped the java community a lot. I don't want to go back to not using it anymore! 

When using Delombok with Java 9 or 10 on a project that has a module-info.java file, the build will fail.

I found this via the lombok-maven-plugin. It turns out that this happens because when delombok starts javac, it does not put itself into the modules path. As a result, javac will refuse to compile: 

* the _module-info.java_ itself
* and all classes using Lombok annotations

The fix - as pointed out on lombok's website - is to add lombok to the _module path_ via the `-p` arg. However, currently Delombok does not handle that behaviour on it's own, neither does it expose the `-p` arg via it's api, which would allow the lombok-maven-plugin to work with java 9 and module-info.java 

Thanks again for the great project!

nodes.body: docs also updated but that'll only go live when we push a stable release. lombok now adds itself as module, and you can now pass --module-path to delombok. Give it a spin in edge: https://projectlombok.org/download-edge

title: Feature Request: option to update source code with generated methods.
body:
Would be great if there was an option to make lombok, on each compile, actually save the generated methods in the source code. I prefer being able to read the methods that exist for a certain class, but I hate writing the boilerplate. there are generators that help with this, but I forget to run them. 

It would be great if lombok could be configured to generate boilerplate according to annotations(as it already does), but then actually update the source code with that boilerplate.

This would mitigate the one common argument I hear against using lombok.

nodes.body:
Disclaimer: Not a member of the lombok team, just an interested observer.

That being said:

This sounds sensible .. but it really isn't.
- Generated code is not going to be readable. It was never meant to be.

- If there is some kind of bug in that generated code, how are you going to
know, and how are you ever going to update?
Once it's generated, changing it becomes your problem, whereas if it is
done on the fly you can keep your source current with the latest lombok.

- If it's customised in some manner, whomever reads it later is not going
to know unless it is very well documented (in the source code itself).

- If you are going to do this the next logical step would be to also put
the generated code for jackson annotations, spring annotations, hibernate
annotations, and mockito annotations inside the class itself. Ditto for
generated proxies. And while we're at it, we probably should get rid of the
concept of interfaces altogether and just put implementations everywhere...
see where this is going?

Examining the generated code is easily possible using delombok or any other
decompiler. Feel free to do so, but making it the preferred form for
modifications .. that way lies insanity.

Also this way if you want to change some behaviour in a generated method, you'd just have to remove the said annotation and lombok would not overwrite it .

about readabillity of generated methods, I'm sure that could be mitigated. (this request just doubled in size though...)

At least now people cant complain that your code wont compile unless you have a compilator plugin (which is a valid concern, methinks) 

about the "logical next steps" you talk about, I disagree that they are logical next steps at all, and even if they were, it wouldn't be an argument against this particular step :)

@andersmartini This might be somewhat useful, however:

- Would you expect a compiler to mess with your sources?
- What if you have unsaved changes in your editor?
- For this to be useful, you'd need a plugin for *your* IDE, otherwise you can just add a few lines to your gradle/maven/whatever build file calling delombok.
- The generated code may be long, so it's easy to miss the `@Generated` annotation and edit it by mistake.
- Lombok uses the annotation processor API and there's no support for overwriting the sources there.

Most people don't want to read the generated code. Personally, I'm happy, it's not there. I'd be even more happy, if there was an option to hide it from the outline (or gray it out).
