title: Lombok put annotation on builder method parameter instead method itself

nodes.body:
It's intended, because annotations like `@NonNull` can only be placed on the parameter, not on the method. Lombok cannot automatically determine which annotations to put on the parameter and which on the method. Thus, it puts them all on the parameter, which is the safer choice.

In this case, this does not work with Jackson, but I don't know a good way to solve it. I'm not a lombok maintainer, but to me it seems that adding more config options will push the complexity of this feature too much towards incomprehensibility.

So my suggestion is to request a feature with Jackson so that `@JsonProperty` is also recognized if present on the method's parameter. This may seem a bit far-fetched, but remember that the annotation has a similar effect if present on a constructor's parameter.

That's why you have to explicitly switch on copying for your annotation, because lombok cannot know if the annotation is also for `ElementType.PARAMETER`. However, for annotations that are for `ElementType.FIELD`, it is more likely they are also for `ElementType.PARAMETER` than `ElementType.METHOD`.

But of course that's not safe, it's just more likely to be valid. If we want to be able to support all cases, lombok would need separate config options `annotationsCopyableToParameter` and `annotationsCopyableToMethod`. Furthermore, we'd need to be able to configure that for builders differently (because builders may have different semantics for their parameters/methods/variables). But that's what I meant with increased complexity.

Well, yes... covering all possibilities might be unfeasible. Reasonable defaults are also good, but I believe that for cases like this there must be some sort of escape hatch. Global configuration is way too general to handle this. Maybe additional annotation(s) that control where other annotations should be copied would be a better approach (at least more granular). 
My main issue with current behavior is that I have to repeat JsonProperty annotation at both field and builder method/field level which is boilerplate and error prone approach.

@AngryGami 

> Global configuration is way too general to handle this.

Are you sure? My idea would be to allow to configure exactly where an annotation should go, but only globally. This makes it much more complicated than the current state ("copy to where it makes sense most of the time"), but still very simple when compared to your proposal.

It's also much less verbose, as you don't need to repeat the information for every field. Are there case when you want e.g., `@JsonProperty` to be handled differently than in your last example?

I don't have any usecases where JsonProperty should go not to a method but I assume someone might have. My proposal is not a replacement for global configuration, but merely an escape hatch for situations when someone want to override behavior that in all other cases is fine. Situation with NotNull annotation above is an example where you might want that. Verbosity could be mitigated by making @CopyToBuilderAs annotation attachable at class level and therefore work for all fields in the class.

title: Feature Request: @Patcher -- generate a TPatcher and "Patch<T>" class

nodes.body:
> Having the @Patcher annotation applied to a class should generate a class called FooPatcher

This sentence shows that this is not the job for Lombok. Lombok manipulates existing files and does not create new ones; standard annotation processors do. Luckily, writing an AP is orders of magnitude simpler than extending Lombok.

You could also use reflection, which is even simpler. It's ugly as it's a manual step and it requires the code to compile before it can be processed, but that's what I'm using a lot currently and it works pretty well.

Infact, AFAIK applying `@Builder` works in a similar manner.

BTW, I am not suggesting that any new files be generated, but that 2 types be generated, similar to how the Builder class is generated by the use of the `@Builder` annotation.

Please see the code around the following line of code.

https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/4126bc277286279c38fa2df785b56eae88b606af/src/core/lombok/javac/handlers/HandleBuilder.java#L113

OK, I see that you want the generated `Patcher` to be an inner class just like the `Builder`. You've looked into the source code and don't you think that it's damn complicated? The Lombok's way(*) is only usable for the very most important features, which are also simple enough, so that they can be implemented in a way satisfying the majority of users (while patching seems to have many possible options).

I really don't think, your `Patcher` crosses the bar, but I'm not in charge of this project. I'm just saying that it looks rather complicated. It's also not perfectly clear to me, what it should exactly do. For this, something like ["With Lombok" and "Vanilla Java"](https://projectlombok.org/features/GetterSetter) would be needed.

---

(*) The Lombok's way is necessary for enhancing existing code on-the-fly and is much more complicated than using AP or reflection. Recently, I wrote a code generator for comparing my entities field-by-field, generating and applying a "binary patch", and some other features. All in all some 400 lines of trivial code, half as much as the class you linked (note that there's an eclipse implementation, too).

I have no doubt that it is complicated, as indeed most of what's been done in Lombok is. In fact, to handle this properly, another class which implements `Converter<S, T>` would also be needed. Yes, I did realize that Eclipse has it's own implementation as well, although the reasons are a bit unclear to me.

I am not sure whether other people would be interested in a `@Patcher` annotation, which will allow only changes to an object to be captured by an object. That's why I raised this feature request to see if it generates any interest! :)

Thank you for engaging with me, and taking the time to respond. I really appreciate it.

> Yes, I did realize that Eclipse has it's own implementation as well, although the reasons are a bit unclear to me.

Eclipse has its own Java compiler, and Lombok is manipulating the abstract syntax tree (AST) generated by the compiler - thus each compiler has it's own version/type of AST - that's the reason.

title: Working with Lombok without any IDE plugin
body:
Is it possible to work with Lombok without any IDE plugin? As we can do it with [Immutables](https://immutables.github.io/), for example? 
It's a [pain](https://github.com/mplushnikov/lombok-intellij-plugin/issues/513) to be dependent on third-party plugins (

nodes.body:
Of course you can. Just ensure `lombok.jar` is on the classpath when invoking `javac`. Maven or Gradle will do that for you if you add Lombok as dependency. But you can also do it completely manual.
However, if you use IntelliJ, you will still get error markers, and its internal compiler will not work. That means you have to invoke Maven/Gradle each time you make a change, and things like hot code replace won't work.

I have Lombok dependency in Maven pom.xml like the follows (it's generated with Spring starter):

```xml
    <dependencies>
        ...
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
            <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
            <optional>true</optional>
        </dependency>
        ...
    </dependencies>
```

Then I compile the project I can see compiled classes in the `target/classes/` folder with Lombok code. But I can't see any generated source files in the `target/generated-sources` folder (as other code generators do, for example, Immutables or MapStruct). So then I turn off the Lombock plugin in IntelliJ IDEA I get error markers in the code. So is it possible to make Lombok generate such source code?

Lombok is not a code generator; it does not generate new source files. Instead, it makes its changes directly during compilation of a single Java source file, so Lombok only affects the compiled class files.

You can use `delombok` to get what would be the Java code for what Lombok generates, and work with that (i.e., throw away your original source files). However, you loose all Lombok annotations and, thus, the brevity of them.

Thank you for clarification. )
It would be great if code generation was implemented - we wouldn't depend on third-party plug-ins...
That is conceptionally impossible, because Lombok's annotations modify the source file they are in. You cannot achieve this functionality with a classic code generator that generates new files.

@Cepr0 What you want is plain impossible. You want to write `@Getter` in your IDE and to get it now. In the same class, in your IDE. You don't want a generated read-only code somewhere, which your IDE could simply reload; you want you IDE to see changes in the file you're just editing.

In Eclipse and Netbeans, all you need is `lombok.jar` installed in the IDE. It's not third party, it's the only file this project produces. For intellij idea, you indeed need a third party plugin.

nodes.body: Could it be that it's the raw types?
I have also seen this with non-generic types (String, MyClass) I think I have seen it with generic types that are properly constrained (Set<String>, List<? extends Number>)
I am getting this issue with Java 11 and `val` from Lombok.
Another suggestion: Does this only happen when compiling test code? We've had some other reports about bugs that could only be reproduced when compiling tests.

Having the same issue when using `val` randomly in different places of the exact class (sometimes it is NPE, sometimes StackOverflow). Above is a PR with this error and attempts to fix it (Travis shows full error-logs there).

I'm having this issue with openjdk 12/lombok 1.18.12
And it is random also, pretty annoying.

-vmargs

You will need to rename /Applications/Eclipse JEE.app to /Applications/Eclipse.app for the current version of lombok (1.18.4) to install into Eclipse properly.

/rob

title: Lombok with Jackson Deserializer from camelCase

nodes.body:
Are you sure this would work? I would expect Jackson to ignore that annotation on internal private fields of the builder class. At least it would be a bit surprising to me. But even if it works in Jackson, there is no easy way for Lombok to determine which annotation to put on the fields. For example, `@NonNull`-like annotations should not be put on the fields, because it's perfectly legit for such fields to be `null` during the lifetime of a builder instance.
So I would say the same as in #1961: That should be changed in Jackson.

I would have hoped that `lombok.copyableAnnotations+=com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty
` would allow me to force Lombok to copy certain annotations.
Also looking at https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/1634, what if you have, annotations like `@JsonSerialize` and `@JsonDeserialize` should be copied to the fields.
Just for clarification: You want the annotation to be copied to the field, right? Because currently it _is_ copied to the method's parameter, but Jackson does not recognise this.

I just verified that (surprisingly) it works if the internal private field of the builder has the `@JsonProperty` annotation, but the method has not. That's kind of weird, because only the public API of the builder (and not the implementation details of the builder) should be relevant to Jackson. On the other hand, Jackson is known for doing weird stuff. ;)

However, as stated above, IMO Lombok should not blindly copy all `copyableAnnotations` to the fields of the builder, because annotations like `@NonNull` (which are copyable by default) are semantically wrong there.

yes, the real issue is that 'copy that annotation where relevant' is insufficient information. With builder, there are at least 5 places we can copy it to:

* The internal field in the builder that is used to track the property (which it should NEVER be copied to; that is basically an internal implementation detail and often doesn't even exist; for example, if you have an `@Singular Map`, there are 2 fields to 3 fields in the builder to track the status for that: 2 lists and a boolean. Surely any annotation that needs to be copied, should definitely not be copied to any of those 3!)
* The parameter of the 'setter' method in the builder.
* The entire method of the 'setter' method in the builder.
* For `@Singular`: The parameter of the singular variant.
* For `@Singular`: The method of the singular variant.

We could blow copyableAnnotations apart into 5 things, but, copyableAnnotations is by design used by more lombok features which come with their own 'actually this could apply to multiple locations', so unless we're all okay with like 10+ copyableAnnotations config keys (and to be clear, we are not), this is one of those 'this is impossible' feature requests.

What we can attempt to do is hardcode well known commonly used annotations, which is inelegant but them's the breaks.

I'll look into hardcoding special behaviour for `@JsonProperty`.

title: [FEATURE] User defined annotations and handlers via SPI
body:
There's been several issues related to this, but I have only seen feature requests asking lombok to support custom/meta-annotations. In that sense, this is related to #557, among others, but approaches it differently.

I recently came across an article, [Implementing a Custom Lombok Annotation](https://www.baeldung.com/lombok-custom-annotation), where the author takes advantage of the fact that lombok's annotation handlers are loaded via [ServiceLoader](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/37434ba0cba68ea232efea0824d3f71e5e287dc2/src/core/lombok/javac/HandlerLibrary.java#L177) to inject their own annotation handler.

Lombok's documentation makes no mention of this, so I am sceptical (as I always am of baeldung, but the title was intriguing). Is this kind of custom extension, in any way, supported by lombok? If not, is it something you would consider supporting? I do envision pain for some users (IDE plugins, lombok may not play nice, eg #1359), but I'd like to hear your thoughts. If nothing else, this seems like a good way to solve #557, which was last updated as not possible.

> This feature would require resolution in a very early stage of processing. Currently that is not possible. 
>
> — <cite>rspilker</cite>

It (naively) seems this approach solves the problem by delegating logic to the author of the custom annotation, rather than lombok dealing with the general case.

title: [BUG] "val" not able to infer lambda expressions types with Java 8 and Eclipse 4.10
body:
**Describe the bug**
I don´t know exactly if that's is a bug or a feature indeed, but when you try to do the next code at Eclipse:

val function = value -> "Hello world";

Compiler complaints with the next message: 

"val is not allowed with lambda expressions" and "Cannot convert from String to Class<? extends annotation>"

I guess that message is happening because the compiler is unable to infer the "value" parameter at the lambda expression, but even if you provide it:

val function = (Integer value) -> "Hello world";

You get the same error.

**To Reproduce**
Use:

val function = value -> "Hello world";

or

val function = (Integer value) -> "Hello world";

**Expected behavior**

The compiler should be able to infer the type of val for the given function or functional interface.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - 1.18.4
 - Java 1.8.0_192, eclipse 4.10

nodes.body:
This is just how java works; java11's own 'var' can't do it either. Lambdas work like this:

FIRST, check where and how the entire thing is intended to be used, so, forget about the lambda, check the outer context (look from the lambda node in the AST __outwards__), which usually is either 'this is a parameter to a method' or 'this is the initializing expression for a variable', then check what type is needed, and armed what that info, try to figure out what kind of FunctionalInterface the lambda is trying to masquerade as.

With `val`, by definition there's no 'outward' type info.

Said differently: with `val function = (String a, String b) -> -1;` what value would you like lombok to infer? `BiFunction<String, String, Integer>`? Why not `Comparator<String>`? What you want is not possible and is not how java works.
Very good answer and clear, I was thinking about the Scala system to infer lambda parameters, but what you said makes sense, Thanks
谢谢老板,你的回答对我很有帮助,我想知道 val到底在什么情况下使用呢?

Ah, well, you cannot "set" the plural, only add the elements from the collection provided.

So this is not a bug, it is a feature. Calling it with `null` means, don't add anything. There will be no exception.

@randakar, it seems that you are asking if a field inside a @Builder  annotated class which field is annotated with both @Singular and @VarArgs would have a var-args-style method generated along with it.

That would definitely be a useful extension of this idea, imo. But I think that perhaps it should be part of a separate feature request, once @VarArgs support is stable? What do you think?

@kalexmills Disclaimer: I'm not a project owner, just a big fan of it.

I'm a bit skeptical about it being implemented anytime soon. I'm sure, it is a useful feature, but maybe not useful enough, given the high overhead for implementing and maintaining Lombok features.... With varargs and generics, more problems than usual are to be expected.

Some generalizations:
- It should work with any number of arguments as long as the last one is a `Collection`.
- It should work with `List` and `Iterable`, too.
- With some minor modifications, it could work with `Set`. Probably not worth it.

It should accept a `name` argument for cases not covered by your "All" suffix removal.

We would prefer to always generate the same code, which basically means right now that it still needs to be java6 compatible.

Although I understand your request, I think we should not implement it:

- Generics and arrays don't work well together. If I have to choose between var-args or generics, I choose generics.
- In my experience, there is hardly a good case for both collections and var-args in APIs. 
- The overhead in the calling code is `List.of(a, b, c)`. Still overhead, but not too bad
- If there are a lot of calls, the manually added method that contains your implementations is also possible and simple, and probably worth to have in you source code. It's only three lines, more that a single annotation, but given that I expect them to be sparse, better than adding the mental load of `@Varargs` to all our users.

While I agree with @Maaartinus that having both `Foo build()` and `FooBuilder build(arg)` in the same builder doing completely different things makes for _deplorably bad_ API, there is a fine line between the notion of 'lombok should not accidentally generate crappy code' and 'lombok should attempt to eliminate lunacy'.

title: [FEATURE] VarArgs variants for @Builder

nodes.body:
You do realise that the entire point of the builder pattern is to make sure
people do not accidentally call .things() with the arguments in the wrong
order by having each field declared explicitly?
Because this is basically taking it a step backwards.

On Sat, Jan 12, 2019 at 5:52 PM K. Alex Mills <notifications@github.com>
wrote:

> *Describe the feature*
> Add an extra add method generated by @Singular, which accepts a varargs
> parameters -- thereby creating a nice(r) API which can also operate like
> List::of.
>

> @Singular
>

>

> Delombokified:
>
> class Builder {
>
> /* all the methods currently added by Singular */
>
>
>
>   public void things(Type... types) {
>
>     this.things(List.of(types));
>
>   }
>
> }
>
>
> *Describe the target audience*
> Anyone currently using @Singular may find that the additional flexibility
> afforded by being able to replace
> builder().thing(a).thing(b).thing(c).thing(d). by
> builder().things(a,b,c,d) is quite nice.
>
> *Additional context*
> This idea was tangentially mentioned in #1279
> <https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/1279>, but this feature
> request only targets @Singular.
>
> In #1568 <https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/1568> a question
> was raised as to whether method chaining current builder methods was
> better. The additional method calls suggested in that issue could be
> considered as extra boilerplate required by Lombok (which is boilerplate
> Lombok creates? 🤔)
>

"Don't only practice your art, but force your way into it's secrets, for it
and knowledge can raise men to the divine."
     -- Ludwig von Beethoven

@randakar, I'm not sure that I follow. My proposal is only to remove the need for separate calls to `Collection::add`. It seems to me that there are three cases to consider, but please correct me if I am wrong.

Case 1) The collection annotated by `@Singular` is an ordered collection. In this case, we compare two usage patterns: `builder().thing(a).thing(b).thing(c)`, which results in a series of invocations `list.add(a); list.add(b); list.add(c);`, as compared to `builder.things(a,b,c)` which would result in the invocation `list.addAll(List.of(a,b,c))`. The resulting state is the same in both cases. 

I don't see how it's any easier or harder to get the order of arguments wrong in either one of these cases.

Case 2) The collection annotated by `@Singular` is an unordered collection like a `Set`. In this case, the order in which the operations occur won't affect the result.

Case 3) The collection annotated by `@Singular` is a `Map`. VarArgs do not help us in this case. This proposal was not intended to include maps.

If you'll pardon my straw-man, the only way I can understand your response is if the underlying implementations of the `List` or `Set` interfaces used produce side-effects along with calls to `add`. This can't be right, though, because it seems to me to be a strange use-case to want to support.

Ah. Never mind, I was mixing up a few things there.

Thanks for explaining the proposal with a Lomboked and a Delomboked example!

__TL;DR:__ We're rejecting this proposal.

There are a few problems with this. In random order:

* This is a backwards incompatible change. `builder.things(null)` currently resolves to `builder::things(Collection<? extends Type> things)`. By introducing `builder::things(Type... things)`, now the users have to add a cast to `Collection<? extends Type>`.
* We cannot use `List.of` in our generated code, due to compatibility with older java versions. 
* The use-case is not so big. Instead of `builder().thing(a).thing(b).thing(c).thing(d)`, you can already write `builder().things(List.of(a,b,c,d))`
* We don't think it is worth making this an opt-in, because that clutters our API and code

This doesn't address the other three points (so it should still be rejected on the merits of those), but the `List.of` bullet point goes away if you replace it with `Collections.unmodifiableList(Arrays.asList(things))`.

title: [BUG] @NonNull on primitives arrays does not compile in Eclipse (Java 7)
body:
Using Lombok 1.18.4, the following code :
```java
  public void foo(@NonNull byte[] data) {
    // ...
  }
```
compiles with Java 7's javac, but not inside Eclipse. This occurs only for arrays of primitives: (`@NonNull String[] data` works), and this problem does not occurs with Lombok 1.18.2.

To be clear, my goal is to guarantee that `data` won't be null.

I have opened this [Eclipse ticket](https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=543304). The answers I got makes me perplex :
* the proposed syntax `byte @NonNull [] data` won't compile in Java 7, so I can't use it
* It seems that this problem is triggered by the introduction of `ElementType.TYPE_USE` in the annotation.

Eclipse guys seems to say that TYPE_USE is incorrectly used in Lombok annotation, see in particular [this comment](https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=543304#c6) and [this one](https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=543304#c11).

This could be related to this commit: https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/commit/d7873f2d21564e8e7f22409fe03681d7dd4c8c1e

nodes.body:
Okay, well, eclipse/Stephen Habermann misanalysed. Lombok is (mostly) fine here.

I've dumped a very detailed analysis of this over on the eclipse bug (the ticket you opened), because this is something eclipse needs to fix, we can't help without causing more pain than we solve.

There is one thing where lombok can be considered to be wrong. Given this code: `void foo(@NonNull String[] arg)`, then:

 in java 1.6/1.7 TYPE_USE should be ignored entirely; this is an annotation on the parameter and that is that. Therefore lombok should generate a nullcheck in the method. Lombok does just that. Note, javac also interprets things this way, whether you use javac1.7, or supply `-source 1.7 -target 1.7` to javac 1.8, 9, 10, or 11. You can confirm this by checking the class file with the `javap -v` command.

in java 1.8+, the annotation can be interpreted to be on the entire parameter, as well as on the `String` part of `String[]`. The spec states that both interpretations are to be treated as correct simultaneously. This weird state of affairs means that this one annotation counts twice. This is in fact precisely what both javac and ecj in 1.8+ mode do: This one annotation is visible twice in 2 different locations when inspecting the produced classfile with `javap -v`. There is only one obvious interpretation of this dual state of affairs: Both the array, as well as each element inside of it, is to be considered as 'should never be null'. Lombok has no support for doing nullchecks in array _elements_, and therefore should only do what lombok does support, which is: Generate a nullcheck on the array. Fortunately this means the behaviour of lombok does not change even though the interpretation of the annotation did, between java7 and java8.

As far as eclipse is concerned, as I advised in the eclipse ticket, on j1.7- compliance mode they should not complain. With j1.8+ compliance mode it is feasible to state that `@NonNull byte[]` is a nullity issue because you can't mark `byte` as `@NonNull`, in which case you can (because you're in 1.8+ compliance mode) turn that into `byte @NonNull []` instead, at which point eclipse will stop complaining.

This leads us into the one bug that lombok does suffer from right now: If you type this: `void test(String @lombok.NonNull arg)`, lombok generates no null check, and it really should.

I'll address that and then close this issue. If eclipse elects to do the wrong thing here and disregard this bug report there's really nothing we can do about it unfortunately.
We're still working on it.
@rzwitserloot See also #1999, which is probably related.

2 hours of research in the JLS, typed half an essay with the fine folks over at eclipse about the intricacies of non-null annotations (the sheer complexity of that topic continues to boggle the mind), 10 hours of coding, including adding a new type of annotation handling which meant I had to teach 10 year old code, and all for a bug that's so obscure we've decided not to list it in the changelog.

Nevertheless, that was an awesome ride and I learned a lot. Glad it's done, and thanks for reporting it!
What a lot of work for a so small problem! Anyway, thanks for the time spent on this and for your analysis.

title: [BUG] Warning: java: @Builder.Default requires @Builder or @SuperBuilder on the class for it to mean anything.

nodes.body:
This isn't a lombok bug, or, if it is, we're not going to fix it because it is an extreme cornercase.

The only way this happens if:

[1] You've got a star import on lombok, and

[2] You override the generated builder name to be 'Builder' _AND_ you make that class by hand, which... coincidentally, is _exactly_ the name of lombok's annotation.

So, that `@Builder` annotation? Lombok thinks it is a reference to the inner class, therefore that annotation is clearly not a reference to `lombok.Builder`, therefore, there is no `@lombok.Builder`, therefore, warning.

We could dive into the precise java rules about what the `Builder` in your snippet is referring to (is it `lombok.Builder`, or is it `TestPojo.Builder`?), but let's not.

The fix is easy enough: Either don't pick precisely `Builder` as your builderclassname, or, don't star-import.

Performance: replace toArray(new T[size]) with toArray(new T[0])

- the instance should/must also implement `equals` and `hashCode` using the fields marked with `@Id`, and
- it makes sense for the instance's `equals` and `hashCode` methods to use the same or similar code as `PK`.

Specifically, both `PK` and `SystemUser` should produce identical hash codes for the same IDs (really this is just "nice to have").

Also, regardless of whether to produce similar hash codes, since `@IdClassAnnotation` implies that the class is an entity, and that implies even more boilerplate (at least the entity needs `equals` and `hashCode` as mentioned above), It may be simpler for the end user that instead of  `@IdClassAnnotation` just have a more general `@LombokEntity` annotation. This would automatically add `equals` and `hashCode` to the entity based on any `@Id` annotations, and if more than one `@Id` is present, create `PK`.

Also, if A and B are `SystemUsers`, and if A != B, and if either `subsystem` or `username` is null in either entity, then `A.equals(B)` and `B.equals(A)` should return `false`, since we're imposing additional restrictions on equality.

More generally, if any component of a primary key is null, then the whole primary key must be considered null for the purposes of equality. And an entity instance with a null primary key must be considered not equal to another instance of the same entity class with a null primary key.

I agree that generating `equals` and `hashCode` using the primary key is the right thing, but AFAIK most people use an "all-args-equals" instead. So this feature should be IMHO optional. Maybe there should be `@LombokEntity` with both features optional.

One tiny simplification: `SystemUser.hashCode` can delegate to `SystemUser.PK.hashCode`.

I'm unsure about the `null` treatment. For `equals`, this sounds good, but no matter how you define `hashCode`, it will most probably change when persisted. I myself let both method throw on nulls; that's probably too bold and incorrect, but so far it worked well.
`hashCode` is fine as is; the additional restrictions only apply to `equals`. Using a delegate for `equals` and `hasCode` seems to me a good idea, if the entity contains a composite key.

Yeah, @rspilker misunderstood your question.

What you want to do is impossible. There is no way to get the referenced class as a j.l.Class instance at 'annotation processing time', because that class is probably not loaded.

Therefore, you cannot have a class literal.

What you CAN get, is a raw string reference to it, and then take it from there. It might get a tad complicated to turn, say, 'String.class' into 'oh, that is referring to java.lang.String'.

To do that, don't turn it into an instance, but use the other methods that AnnotationValues has. For example, `getRawExpressions` (that would return the string "String.class") or `getActualExpressions` (it'll return a list of eclipse internal AST node representing it. You can't easily get from there to `java.lang.String` either).

If you have good ideas as to how to make dealing with these things easier, we're all ears.

NB: This is extremely hard to fix, probably impossible; javac bombs out without even initializing annotation processors. It is technically more or less allowed to do this, even though it is not consistent with how javac otherwise operates, which makes it pretty much pointless to attempt to file a bug with openjdk to fix this on their end.

Also, this is an error of the kind that stops annotation processors from running. That means if this error occurs, lombok doesn't run at all, and thus you tend to get a blast of errors. That's also not something we can fix.

[JEP 216](http://openjdk.java.net/jeps/216) seems relevant, but this bug existed before JEP216 was delivered, and still exists afterwards. All it really means is that this import stuff is complex. It already felt near impossible to get this fixed at the openjdk side, and with convoluted JEPs muddying the waters, even more so.

As this seems to be hardly fixable for javac, while it's working for Eclipse and IntelliJ:
Is it possible to add a warning/error [Edit: inside Eclipse and IntelliJ] to the static import statement in case it is based upon a @UtilityClass annotated class and the element being import is not marked as static?

That way people might not be confused at the time they see such problems.

Unfortunately, we don't have [resolution](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/wiki/LOMBOK-CONCEPT:-Resolution), and even if we had, we wouldn't necessarily know what code was generated by which lombok construct, possibly leading to false positives.

Sorry to repeat myself from [a closed duplicate issue][1], but I really do believe that if this can't be fixed (which, I believe you that it can't), then the annotation should be deprecated. If it's possible to require the `static` keyword, then that's a better option than full deprecation. But the current situation -- that it's pretty easy to get into a position where everything just breaks, with error messages that are very hard to break down -- is a bad one. A build tool needs to be more rock solid than this.

[1]: https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/884#issuecomment-447160900

There is no single lombok annotation that causes this. For instance, it also affects `@Builder`, and you cannot mark `@Builder` as deprecated, because it's a non-experimental feature that is crucial to the majority of lombok users.

I think @Maaartinus hit the nail on the head. `@UtilityClass` basically does two things: a private constructor and marking members as static. The first one of those, lombok already has an annotation for; and the second one is (a) easy without lombok and (b) unsolvably broken with lombok.

In addition, statically importing a `builder()` method is rare -- if I've ever done it, I can't remember. Statically importing members of a utility class happens all the time (guava Preconditions, JUnit asserts, etc.), and is basically the use case that static import was designed for. If it doesn't work with lombok utility classes, then imho they're more trouble than they're worth.

> In addition, statically importing a `builder()` method is rare -- if I've ever done it, I can't remember. 

Where this bug hits me, is when you define a custom builderMethodName.
So, i'd like to replace "Car.builder().brand("BMW").build();" with "car().brand("BMW").build()".
You'd want to import Car.car but because of this issue you'll have to use Car.car(), which makes the custom builder method name useless for my usecase.

I feel like this should be better documented if it really is unsolvable. Warnings in the javadoc of annotations which generate methods or some sort of “Frequent Problems” section on the website. Since no errors appear in an IDE, perhaps the IDE plugins could generate an error if you statically import such a method? No clue if that is possible though.
EDIT: it is documented in the small print of the `@UtilityClass` annotation, but not on the `@Getter` page. (I was having this same issue with `@Getter`s.)
There is an issue in the lombok-intellij plugin (mplushnikov/lombok-intellij-plugin#291) with the suggestion to add an enhancement.

I'll share my experience in case it helps anyone else. This issue puzzled me because I was able to statically import lombok-generated constructors in a project, but not in another one. It turned out to be that, in the project that was working, I was using static import only in test code, while in the project that failed I was using static import both in prod and test code. I guess, for the former, prod code was fully compiled first, so by the time test code was compiled the static constructor was built and ready to be statically imported. I hope this saves some head-scratching for someone else.

Whilst I won't dispute that the form `List.of()` may be generally more common than `list()` (I don't have data to base the dispute on), I'd say that, at least in certain circles, the second form is definitely more popular. Coming from a Scala shop, the first form feels quite alien to me; but I appreciate this is personal opinion.

I guess what I'm trying to say is that, if there was a way to support the second case easily, I'd very much support it.

I won't get into that discussion as there are examples for both ways, such as `Stream.of(...)` and `Arrays.asList(...)`.

Though, in https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/2044#issuecomment-464907315 I suggested a workaround to simplify handling these kind of problems:
> As this seems to be hardly fixable for javac, while it's working for Eclipse and IntelliJ:
> Is it possible to add a warning/error [Edit: inside Eclipse and IntelliJ] to the static import statement in case it is based upon a @UtilityClass annotated class and the element being import is not marked as static?
> 
> That way people might not be confused at the time they see such problems.

Is that feasible?
Thanks for explaining this in that much detail @rzwitserloot. It finally makes sense to me. I agree with you, # 3 (updating the documentation) could be a good short-term solution for this.
It was already documented in the fine print. But, updated status to negative. I don't think this feature is getting out of experimental as long as this problem persists.

title: [FEATURE] Allow use of @Builder with only a toBuilder() method and no @Builder.Default warnings
body:
## Current Functionality
Lombok's `@Builder` annotation always adds a `builder()` method to the annotated class, which can be used to easily create instances with specific values using a fluent interface.

This annotation was later extended with a `toBuilder` parameter which causes Lombok to also generate a `toBuilder()` method. This method returns a builder based on the object's current attribute values. A practical usage of this that we use extensively in our entities is to very easily provide a shallow-clone for objects by annotating the class with `@Builder(toBuilder = true)` and calling `toBuilder().build()` to get a shallow-cloned instance.

A separate `@CopyConstructor` annotation [has previously been denied](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/908#issuecomment-430001916) with the reasoning that the above pattern is entirely sufficient for performing shallow clones (which is indeed the case).

## Our Use Case
We'd like to continue using `toBuilder` like this to shallow-clone objects; however, the fact that Lombok warns on every single "missing" `@Builder.Default` annotation is quite annoying. `@Builder.Default` does not make a lot of sense in combination with `toBuilder`, as the latter method already copies over the contents of all fields regardless of their initializer.

Imagine the following field in an entity class:
```java
private Set<UserEntity> affectedUsers = new HashSet<>();
```
When the class is annotated with `@Builder`, Lombok will produce a warning for the above field stating that it will not be initialized when not explicitly set in a builder call like:
```java
MainEntity.builder().affectedUsers(...).build()
```

This makes sense with standard builder classes, however on classes that are _only_ used with `toBuilder` to provide easy cloning, warnings on such fields do not make sense, since `toBuilder()` simply copies over all values from the existing instance anyway, including the already initialized field in the example.

## Proposal
Therefore I'd like to propose a parameter `onlyToBuilder` or something similar for the `@Builder` annotation, which
- leads to no `builder()` method being added and
- no warning being produced for fields with default initializers but no `@Builder.Default` annotation.

This would allow us to continue using `toBuilder()` to easily perform shallow clones, but _not_
1. add an unused `builder()` method and
2. spam the compile output with `Builder.Default` warnings.

nodes.body:
That feels far too exotic; it breaks the 'it's a parameter party!' rule (which is: If accepting all feature requests of similar exoticness as this one, does the lombok annotation end up having many tens of parameters? Then deny the feature request).

However, I do see the painpoint, I just don't know how to address it without making the annotation grow a few too many parameters.

What about this:

We make it legal to write `@Builder(builderMethodName = "")`, and we interpret this to mean: Don't make that method at all.

Additionally, if we don't make a builder() method, either because of the above setting, or because you already wrote one yourself, we skip the step where we emit those missing `@Default` annotation warnings?
Liked your idea (+ my tweak) so much, added. Will be in next release.

nodes.body:
The 'value' of this proposal is real (dummy classes are a thing), but low, because we're not saving a whole lot of boilerplate with this feature.

The problems are considerable:

2. Is DUMMY the right name? Or EMPTY? Or SENTINEL? Or configurable?

3. What about generics?

4. Generally, if serialization is involved, the DUMMY should deserialize such that all DUMMYs are reference-equal to each other. Making this happen is non-trivial.

title: [FEATURE]  @SelfLift

nodes.body:
Cool feature, but, no can do.

[A] this requires resolution, which is really [difficult](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/wiki/LOMBOK-CONCEPT:-Resolution).

[B] self-types are in general a missing java feature, and this hack of generating casts is a lot more complex then it sounds. Now imagine generics are involved, for example.

[C] generally this is solved by way of generics, see for example how enums are defined, or Comparable. (`Comparable<E extends Comparable<E>>`). This has various disadvantages compared to a true self-type, but nevertheless it's what is common today.

But mostly the resolution thing.

title: [FEATURE] @StepBuilder
body:
Please consider supporting the "Step Builder" pattern.

See:

- http://www.svlada.com/step-builder-pattern/
- http://rdafbn.blogspot.com/2012/07/step-builder-pattern_28.html

I'll copy the pros/cons listed in the first article, since I think they do a good job summarizing the pattern:

> Pros
> 
> 1. User guidance for your API through object creation process step by step.
> 2. API User can call builder's build() method once the object is in the consistent state.
> 3. Reduced opportunity for creation of inconsistent object instances.
> 4. Sequencing initialization of mandatory fields.
> 5. Fluent API.
> 6. No need for providing validate() method for field validation.
> 
> Cons
> 
> 1. Low readability of code needed to implement the pattern itself.
> 2. No eclipse plugin to help with code generation. (On the other hand, there are plenty of code generators for Builder pattern generator).

The cons can mostly be solved by Lombok itself.

nodes.body: Although this sounds like a nice idea at first glance, there are a few other cons. As this feature request already came up several times, there is a wiki page with the reasons why the maintainers think it is not a good idea to add it to lombok: https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/wiki/FEATURE-IDEA:-%22Mandatory%22-fields-with-@Builder

> > 3. Your autocomplete dialogs and outline views in your IDE get infected with a massive list of weird stuff.

> Why does it get infected? It won't get infected if you require the steps to be declared in specific order and there's no combinatorial explosion.

I think this refers to the interfaces for the steps. Those must obviously be public, and this will make them appear in autocompletion dialogs for types.

I'm not a maintainer, but I contributed `@SuperBuilder`. And let me say that this was a hell of a work that took more than 10 full working days overall and more than a year from start to its first release (although admitted that I wasn't a lombok expert before). In comparison, a step builder looks to me as at least equally complex, probably more (just think of all generics possibilities!).
So even if there would be a chance to convince the maintainers that this is a good idea, someone else would have to implement it. The maintainers have their hands full with other stuff: bug reports, adaptation to new Java versions, and -- no offense -- adding more useful features.

I understand it might be a non-trivial amount of work to implement.  The goal of this issue is only to, as you said, convince the maintainers that it is a good idea.  Prioritization can be addressed separately.

I do think the cure is worse than the disease. I also explained at length in that wiki article what the real cure should be. At risk of sounding arrogant: This is not something we're ever going to implement.

title: [FEATURE] Allow @Value classes not to be final
body:
Using the `@Value` annotation currently creates a value object with a `final` class. Effectively, the `final` modifier's only purpose is to prevent subclassing of that type which is an honorable goal and probably okay in most of the cases. In combination with `staticConstructor` it's actually not even needed as the constructor generated is turned private anyway and all the user ends up with is a public static factory method anyway.

### Why would I want a value object not to be final?

As indicated there are use cases that require subclassing of the types. #892 describes one where user code would do this. However, frameworks might want to create short lived proxies for those types to allow e.g. the application of a method reference for sole invocation recording purposes. E.g. in Spring Data we'd like to provide [a `Sort` abstraction](https://jira.spring.io/browse/DATACMNS-1450) that's supposed to allow the following:

```java
Sort.sort(Person.class).by(Person::getName).asc();
```

We already have infrastructure in place that creates a proxy for the given type, takes the method reference, executes it on the proxy and in the method interceptor find out about the method that was invoked, the reference invokes to build up the sort expression. This requires a type that we can create a proxy of in the first place.

The code that's generated by `@Value` creates a type that's effectively immutable anyway as it doesn't expose any means to change state of an instance. So while it's perfectly fine to resort to making that type `final` by default, it would be cool if the user could opt out of that for convenience reasons

nodes.body: Hmm, doesn't `@NonFinal` on the class do exactly this, or am I missing a point here?

In fact it does. It just didn't cross my radar as it's in the experimental package and closely aligned with `@FieldDefaults`, which sort of created the impression it was usable with fields not with types.

I'd be fine with the documentation being updated to mention this more prominently. A boolean flag right within `@Value` would still be slightly nicer, I guess.
In fact, the javadoc isn't really clear at this point. This should be improved, together with the website documentation on `@Value`.

> The code that's generated by @Value creates a type that's effectively immutable anyway as it doesn't expose any means to change state of an instance.

Yes, but you can add new fields and setters for them in the subclass . So if you want a really immutable class, it must be final. That said, I agree with you.
I welcome a suggestion on how to improve the documentation.
Raised a tiny PR for this https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/pull/2111
PR integrated :)

title: [FEATURE] @TemplateValue @ParseTemplate

nodes.body:
> where they have the $ syntax in front of a string, but I'm not sure if that's possible.

I'm afraid, it's not as Lombok comes after the parser. When the parsing fails, there's no Lombok there.

---

> ofcourse an import would have to be added

Currently, Lombok is not needed at runtime and I'm rather sure, the authors want this to stay as is.

But that's no problem here, as an implementation like
```
final String result = "Hello " + uniqueTemplateValuesMap.get("name") + ...
```
would be only slightly more complicated (I know, it was just an example).

Avoiding the map should also be possible, as everything is known at compile time. This would reduce the runtime-overhead to exactly zero.

---

I'm afraid that `@TemplateValue` may make this feature much less usable. As the only advantage of `@ParseTemplate` is a shorter (and more readable) syntax, requiring writing more is counterproductive.

On the one hand, it feels more error-proof, OTOH it's a pain. Lombok could actually show a compile-time error when it sees something like `"Hello {name} {lstName}..."` (note the typo).

---

I guess, Lombok could do it, but I'm not sure, if it fits and whether it's useful enough. There were proposals about adding multi-line and raw strings long time ago, which are now definitely abandoned as it'll come in Java. I have no idea, how big the implementation overhead would be.

What will come in Java exactly? And also, something I forgot to mention, this would be extra useful if that would be possible for string coming out of configuration / language files (which might be a bit harder to do when using your example implementation change).

Obviously, I'm not fully sure what can and cannot be done, but if possible to reduce the need to write more, only using `@ParseTemplate` which would then search for variables inside the method or fields inside the class.
(Also, when using a decent enough editor, the write overhead is not that bad)

I really do hope that Java, at some point, makes a way that allows for easier String interpolation (now there is String.format, I know, but I feel like it's much easier to read & understand when actually typing the variable names).
As explained, we can't do it, unfortunately.

title: [FEATURE] More transparent jar naming when installing into IDE
body:
**Describe the feature**
I would like to put forward the suggestion of naming the artifact `lombok-$version.jar` instead of simply `lombok.jar`. If there are reasons for distributing it with the opaque name as the download, then I would suggest to at least rename the file that is copied into the IDE directory. Every now and then, I wonder which Lombok version my IDE has installed, and looking at a file named simply `lombok.jar` is not helpful, and does not follow the typical artifact naming conventions.

My suggestion is thus to rename the artifact, at least the one in the IDE directory, to something like `lombok-1.8.16.jar` as part of the installation process. This will then allow me to see at a glance which library version my IDE is using, and in case of issues or debugging allow me to trivially change the versions by adjusting the `eclipse.ini` file or the IDEA equivalent.

**Describe the target audience**
Everyone who has multiple projects or workspaces working with multiple Lombok versions who wants to see at a glance which version their IDE is running.

nodes.body:
I understand your request, and do see the benefits.

Some things you can do already:

- I just want to point out that `java -jar lombok.jar --version` shows you the version number. And in a running eclipse you can see the version number in the Help - About Eclipse dialog.
- If you want to, after installing TOPdesk, you are free to rename the jar file and modify your `eclipse.ini` file. Or not use the installer, copy the jar to a directory of your choice and modify the ini file as approriate. 

The current setup replaces `lombok.jar` if it already exists. If we would use a jar file name based on the version, should we just remove all `lombok-xxx.jar` files? Or should we just leave them?

Since it is already possibly to do this manually, I'm closing the issue.

title: [FEATURE] @Singular support for LinkedHashMap
body:
**Describe the feature**
Add support for LinkedHashMap for the `@Singular` annotation. 
If you look at the list of supported types it is not in there:
[https://projectlombok.org/features/Builder#singular](https://projectlombok.org/features/Builder#singular)

Currently the BuildSingularMaps generates a LinkedHashMap under the hood so this should be easy to add support for:
[https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/master/test/transform/resource/after-delombok/BuilderSingularMaps.java#L168
](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/master/test/transform/resource/after-delombok/BuilderSingularMaps.java#L168
)
**Describe the target audience**
Anyone who uses objects that need to preserve key order.

**Additional context**
We need LinkedHashMaps in our client interfaces so that our clients will respect JSON ordering. We are using lombok annotate pojos but we current we cannot apply the @Singular annotation to a LinkedHashMap type. Map will not suffice in this case for us.

nodes.body:
I'm afraid, it can't work as (for more than two elements) `@Builder` generates an unmodifiable Map wrapping a `LinkedHashMap`. The resulting map is not a subclass of `LinkedHashMap`. The good news is that key order gets preserved, the bad news is that you can't modify the map and can't declare it as anything but one of the three interfaces listed in the doc.

> we cannot apply the `@Singular` annotation to a LinkedHashMap type

Indeed, you can't, but you can have a `@Singular private final Map<K, V> map;` and trust the builder to honor your order.

Disclaimer: I'm not a project maintainer. I also may be wrong, now and ever.

Lombok could provide itself with its own `unmodifiableLinkedHashMap` call to make this work.

We're using JAX-RS interfaces along with Jersey's `WebResourceFactory` and MicroProfile Rest Client to get POJOs filled up with JSON from the wire such that our POJOs honor the JSON-ordering of keys.
@derekm Lombok is a compile-time-only dependency. There are a few useful things which could be done if it was present at runtime, but as it stands, it can have no own classes at all.

As @Maaartinus already said, we already preserve insertion order.

We're not planning to add new types. Possibly it is possible for you to switch to Guava types?

Regarding "We're not planning to add new types": I didn't mean that we're not willing to support more existing Collection types. I meant, like @Maaartinus write, Lombok is a compile-time dependency, and we're not willing to change that any time soon. If there is a _popular_, existing library that has an UnmodifiableLinkedHashMap, we're willing to add it to the supported Collection types.

I was assuming Lombok could inject at compile-time its own subclasses as needed.

I'm not very familiar with the proprietary compiler extensions that Lombok is hooking into, but maybe the way I imagine Lombok injecting its own internal classes is not possible.

Unfortunately, it is only since Java EE 7/8 and MicroProfile that LinkedHashMap is becoming a common and preferred "interface", invalidating all kinds of static analysis tools and former best practice around always using the Map interface.

If it is impossible for Lombok to inject its own implementations, we may have to take this argument to a library like Guava who is stuck in the now-worst-practice mode of "always use a Map!"

title: [FEATURE] Ability to suppress run-time null checks of @Getter and @Setter

nodes.body:
Short term work-around: You can create your own annotation, and teach IntelliJ to treat is like a NotNull. Since lombok does not know your annotation, we will not generate a null-check.

We are considering a long term solution.

The list of built-in non-null annotations is not modifiable from the configuration system. They are hard-coded.

Regarding the _syntax_ of the configuration system, the way to make remove individual entries from a list is:
```
lombok.copyableAnnotations -= my.Annotation
```
To remove all of them use:
```
clear lombok.copyableAnnotations
```

I think we now have a solution for you.

**Describe the feature**

A version of the lombok jar without Windows software.

The OWASP dependency check detects the two `.dll` files in the lombok installer.

- `lombok/installer/WindowsDriveInfo-i386.dll`
- `lombok/installer/WindowsDriveInfo-x86_64.dll`

title: Constants generated with @FieldNameConstants are in lower camel case
body:
**Short description**
`@FieldNameConstants` generates an inner type with string constants in a lower camel case.  Doesn't depend on `asEnum()` is true or false.

We understand that `@FieldNameConstants` is an experimental feature, but we are also widely using it within a lot of our projects. It is sad that in the last Lombok versions it was refactored in a way to use a lower camel case as an only possible solution to name the constants.

I have seen other issues that are connected with this one. (Or issues that are dedicated to the same question). And I understand why you want to keep the current solution as a default one. But it is definitely not clear why you are against to make an option to let developers choose the code style they want.

**Expected behavior**
A lot of developers are using following code styles as primary ones. And it's amiss, that new lombok updates break them.

According to [Google's java style guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html#s5.2.4-constant-names) :

> Constant names use CONSTANT_CASE: all uppercase letters, with each word separated from the next by a single underscore.

[Oracle's java language specification](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se8/html/jls-6.html#jls-6.2) says:

>Constant names normally have no lowercase letters ...

May we expect that you will add an option to let us choose between naming styles? Maybe as an additional parameter in the annotation. It would be great to make developers choose the way they want to follow.

**Target audience**
Possibly every developer that has been using lombok's `@FieldNameConstants` feature alongside `uppercase constants` code style.

nodes.body:
Isn't this kind of a ridiculous concern? Slavish adherence to a style guide seems like a bad idea to me.

However, if a significant chunk of lombok users share this to me ununderstandable concern, and it's easy for us to add, eh, well. We aim to please, I guess :)

working on it. It'll be a config key option only and not the default. Because if we make it the default, then someone is gonna name a variable, say, `DVDPlayer` and then complains that we turned that into constant `D_V_D_PLAYER`.

Can we get something like this? https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/3477

Alternatively, something like
```java
@FieldNameConstant(value = "dvd_player")
String DVDPlayer;
```

so at least we can specify the name to use for a few odd fields...

title: @AllArgsConstructor Is Dangerous!
body:
## The Problem
@AllArgsConstructor seemingly generates the order of constructor arguments based on the position of fields within the actual source file. If one has two fields with the same type, the seemingly innocuous change of switching the declaration order will produce compile-able, but buggy code as the constructor arg order is now changed.

## The Solution
Generate arg order using something more predictable, such as alphabetical ordering; or better yet, deprecate @AllArgsConstructor :)

nodes.body:
This is a matter of perception and preference. Once you know the order of
the fields changes the order of the constructor arguments it's actually
quite useful to be able to reorder the arguments as you wish.

If you want to create your objects in a way that does not depend on the
order of the fields, use `@Builder`

I think it's implemented this way on purpose. It is reasonable to let the parameter order follow the order of field declarations.
Using any other order has exactly the same drawback: For instance, if the annotation would use alphabetical ordering, renaming a field could similarly create a compatible constructor.
Deprecating is also clearly not an option, as so many developers rely on this feature. If you feel this annotation is too dangerous, then simply switch it off in your project by `lombok.allArgsConstructor.flagUsage = error`.

There's no easy answer on this topic, but I'm in the camp that this feature is dangerous. This essentially shifts compile time errors into runtime bugs. I avoided scripting languages like NodeJs, PHP, Ruby on Rails because I don't want runtime headaches. I'm an experienced developer, so personally, this feature is not dangerous to me. It's in consideration to an ecosystem that includes millions of junior developers as well as enterprises that already struggle enough with code quality. This annotation is simply a loaded gun..

> This is a matter of perception and preference. Once you know the order of the fields changes the order of the constructor arguments it's actually quite useful to be able to reorder the arguments as you wish. If you want to create your objects in a way that does not depend on the order of the fields, use `@Builder`
> […](#)

Hi, as a junior developer, I've been struggling with the @AllArgsConstructor and @Builder problem. I know that using @AllArgsConstructor may cause issues with reordering arguments or fields. While reading through the official @Builder documentation, I came across this part "If a class is annotated, then a package-private constructor is generated with all fields as arguments (as if @AllArgsConstructor(access = AccessLevel.PACKAGE) is present on the class)." 
This led me to believe that @AllArgsConstructor is automatically created when I use the @Builder annotation. That's why I've been avoiding using @Builder and trying to manually write down the builder pattern...
However, if @Builder is not concerned with ordering issues, I'm ready to use it. Can you explain how @Builder avoids dependency on the order of the fields even though it works as if @AllArgsConstructor is present on the class?
I would really appreciate it if you could help me get rid of this question that's been lingering in my mind for days!
Thanks!

ˋ@Builderˋ needs some constructor with all arguments internally to actually create the resulting object. Yet - as the builder is generated together with the constructor any changes in the parameter order of the fields and thus the constructor are automatically considered and respected. So the generated builder is always in sync with the constructor.
You can use `@SuperBuilder` if you don't want the all-args constructor.

title: [BUG] Inconsistency with toBuilder() with/without @Singular

nodes.body: @fpeter8 FYI

> I mean the whole concept of toBuilder() is to create a completely new instance like we would with builder() without the need to copy over every property manually.

This would require deep cloning and that's sort of impossible to implement (in an efficient and generally useful way).

The difference between fields with and without `@Singular` ist that
```
@Singular MyShinyListNobodyHasEverHeartAbout<String> list3;
```
would not compile as the annotation requires a collection/map it knows. This makes the depth-1 cloning possible as all implementations are known.

Actually, not impossible - at least with limitations. Known collections can be deep copied easily. If an object has the lombok toBuilder() method, then it could be called recursively, so deep copy is still an option.

BUT that is not my point here. I can even accept that this does no deep-copy whatsoever, because supporting everything is borderline impossible, and requires something like mapstruct. BUT if that is the concept here, then `@Singular` shouldn't break that.

Hmm, currently, we use `@Singular` to add behavior as well as a trigger to signal we're dealing with one of the known collection types/ The field not annotated with `@Singular` are treated as `Object`.

One could argue that IF the type of the field is one of the types supported by `@Singular`, we can give it also special treatment.

However, adding `@Singular` now also checks if it is one of the supported types. If it's not, you get an error. This make it possible for us to support other collection types in the future.

But if we give unannotated fields also special treament, adding a new supported collection types would change existing code, making it a (potential) breaking change.

Is there a good reason to not just add a singular annotation?
Closed due to no feedback from reporter

Sorry for the delay.  

Anyway your suggestion is that we should add a @Singular annotation to _every_ collection we have in our code? IMO it would be viable if there would be a way to configure this at lombok.config. If it requires actually writing it out constantly, then it's not a viable option for any project. Devs are lazy. They will forget it.
Or maybe the @Builder should have a value like alwaysSingular or copyCollections, and that should be configurable at the lombok.config.

You can't use both annotations together.

2 options:
Please add a parameter to @Getter(getStatic=true)
OR
Please add a parameter to @Log(getter=true)

title: [BUG] Wrong parameter names passed to another annotation processor
body:
**Describe the bug**

Related issue: https://github.com/micronaut-projects/micronaut-core/issues/1566

This class:

```java
@Introspected
@Value
public class Payload {
  private final String id;
}
```

leads to different parameter names:

```java
// id
Payload.class.getConstructors()[0].getParameters()[0].getName();

// arg0
BeanIntrospection.getIntrospection(Payload.class).getConstructorArguments()[0].getName();
```

The actual class has the correct name (`id`).

The `micronaut` team believes `lombok` is not properly passing parameter names to the other annotation processor.
Thus their generated class (`BeanIntrospection.getIntrospection(Payload.class)`) seems to see auto-generated names (`arg0`, `arg1`).

**To Reproduce**

1. `git clone https://github.com/achaphiv/micronaut-introspection-issue`
2. `./gradlew test -i` or `./mvnw test`

**Expected behavior**

`./gradlew test -i` or `./mvnw test` passes.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version: 1.18.6
 - Platform: javac 1.8.0_202 (mac) & javac 1.8.0_191 (linux)

Note that my test project *works* in `eclipse`.
It only fails via `javac` with either `maven` or `gradle`.

**Additional context**

https://github.com/achaphiv/micronaut-introspection-issue

nodes.body:
First of all, I'm trying to find out where the problem might be.

I created the following code:
```java
@lombok.Value
public class Payload {
	private final String id;
	
	public static void main(String... args) throws Exception {
		System.out.println(Payload.class.getDeclaredMethod("main", String[].class).getParameters()[0].getName());
		System.out.println(Payload.class.getConstructors()[0].getParameters()[0].getName());
	}
}
```

If I compile it using `javac -cp lombok.jar Payload.java` and run it, the output, as expected, is:
```
arg0
arg0
```

If I compile it using `javac -cp lombok.jar -parameters Payload.java` and run it, the output, as expected, is:
```
args
id
```

If I execute `javap -v Payload` on the latter, as expected I get:
```
...
  public Payload(java.lang.String);
    descriptor: (Ljava/lang/String;)V
    flags: (0x0001) ACC_PUBLIC
    Code:
      stack=2, locals=2, args_size=2
         0: aload_0
         1: invokespecial #12                 // Method java/lang/Object."<init>":()V
         4: aload_0
         5: aload_1
         6: putfield      #13                 // Field id:Ljava/lang/String;
         9: return
      LineNumberTable:
        line 1: 0
    MethodParameters:
      Name                           Flags
      id                             final
...
```

So far, everything behaves as expected. Possibly the problem occurs when multiple annotation processors are active on the same code base in the same round.

We do have some code to collaborate with MapStruct, that might be reusable here, where collaborating annotation processors can pick up changes, possibly in a next round.

In general, developers at Oracle think that relying on the names of parameters is not necessarily a good idea, because it's not explicitly clear that renaming a parameter becomes a breaking change, since it is now part of your public API.

The suggestion is to annotate the parameters instead. Lombok will copy those parameters if you put them on a field, if you teach lombok that they're copyable annotation, by specifying that in `lombok.config`.

Since figuring out what's the problem here is a lot of time, and this is the first time we've encountered this problem, I'm closing this issue.

nodes.body: Just FYI, you can make that `between` method a line shorter: `return scheduledFor(scheduleTimeFactory.scheduleBetween(from, to));` :)

It's not a matter of documentation. It is a matter of making a distinction between 'feel free to mess with these' and 'hands off / don't mess with these unless you _really_ know what you are doing', and then documenting how you can recognize the 'dont touch those' fields. Which kinda takes care of itself if we chuck a $ in there, because the (hopefully?) universally agreed upon java-ese for 'no touchy'.

Any field marked with `@Singular` or indeed `@Builder.Default` has custom behaviour associated with it, and should result in the fields used for these to be hands-off!-ized with a dollar. `@Singular` already does this for maps. It should also do so for sets and lists. Any field protected by `@Builder.Default` already generated a dollarized `$set` boolean field, but should also dollarize the value field, presumably by appending `$value` to it.

If we apply this change it's gonna mess with all existing code that touches these fields directly, which is backwards incompatible, but the odds are increased that such code is doing the wrong thing already. Which makes the breaking change warranted.

I'm positively inclined to dollarizing ALL fields involved in special treatment, be it singular, or default.

The upcoming release doesn't have any breaking changes yet. Let's push this forward to 1.18.10.

Good point @rzwitserloot. I imagine the perfect solution to make such mistakes impossible altogether would be to wrap the fields of the builder in a bean and use setters. That would make the delomboked code unreadable or at least overcomplicated. That's why I suggested just to put some documentation on this. I can agree that dollarizing the value field is a better idea and should solve the problem.

Just bumped into this breaking change. I thought you are supposed to increase major version for those, not patch version, or are you not following semver?
Also, IDEA plugin doesn't see those $value and $set fields

Would it be possible to set the default value of the field in the Builder to the same value as what's defined for the field annotated with `Builder.Default`? Instead of having a marker to check if it was set or not.

I find that it's super easy to fall into the trap when you add custom variants in the generated builder.
And there are no good ways around it. The only one would be to use a different name for the custom method, but that's not always great from an API perspective.

Another issue that makes it hard to have builder customizations+default values is because Lombok doesn't generate the different setters in the builder if there is a custom variant with the same name. If this was taking in consideration the full signature then people could delegate to the generated version in most situations.

Even if they are not of the same type, this doesn't necessarily prevent you from doing the defaulting in a different way that plays more nicely with custom code.

One problem is that you seem to do the defaulting in the generated build method, perhaps you could instead do it at initialization time.

Thanks for the pointer to `@Tolerate`, it does help with some of these problems.

This has caused an incompatibility issue with Jackson.  Jackson's BeanDeserializer looks for the $set version of the property at [this line](https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-databind/blob/2.11/src/main/java/com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/deser/BeanDeserializer.java#L368), doesn't find it and so doesn't override the default.
My apologies ^^^ - turns out the test had a bug and the upgrade merely highlighted that bug.  Nothing to see here, move along.

Thinking on it, there is a magic unicorn, but I'm not sure we want it: Instead of detecting if you fail to invoke `$set = true`, what if we... generated it for you? This is trickier than it seems like, e.g. we'd have to turn:

`for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) if (i == 5) x = 10;`

into:
`for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) if (i == 5) {x = 10; x$set = true;}`

and we'd have to flag as error something like:

`for (x = 0; x <10; x++) { /* error - you can't set x in one of the 3 'for' components */)`

as well as:


`while (x = 0 != 10) /* error, can't use the assignment as expression */`

but we could theoretically do all that.

Hey thanks for giving this a second thought :)

Regarding the side effect use case, this feels somewhat unnatural to me. I'd expect it to have similar semantics as default values for attributes in Java, which does run that code anyway even if you provide a different value through the constructor or some other mean. I wonder in practice how common are either use cases. I can definitely say that the issue I mention occurred in the project I'm working on several times, to my self and colleagues of mine. And is not related to some technical aspect in our code base, but mostly just about how we imagine this API would work.

From an outside perspective the different options sound quite complex, I really would just imagine something that sets the default value "statically" which stays close to std Java and keep generating the setter if there isn't another one with the same signature.

That said, I've been using the Tolerate workaround so far and delegated to the generated setter which does the job, so I'm fine with that :) Thank you!

title: [FEATURE] Add @Object (and @ServiceObject) to complement @Data/@Value

nodes.body:
Adding `@Slf4j` automatically is annoying; it always injects the field and thus will result in 'unused private variable' warnings unless you actually log something. I can see a feature where we inject the field automatically the moment you actually try to use it (it'll be an error to try to type 'log' and it won't show up in autocomplete dialogs, until you finish the log statement, at which point it will appear. That is its own problem (you might want autocomplete on .warning() and the like, which you probably won't get, not for the first time you use it), and the performance impact of having to scan every file you touch for usage of variables named `log` might be rather heavy.

The combination of these things sounds a lot like `@Data`. I guess here you want automatic private + no automatic getters? Is that worth adding a name and the associated learning curve?

Ad Slf4j: I already pictured this to be a problem. I just wanted to point out that this combination of annotations is very heavily used by me and stands for one exact thing: a "Service Object". Maybe my requirement could be expanded to "combine lombok annotations into a custom one" - which is probably even more difficult to solve (don't know the architecture behind it)

Ad Object: Does it really? I tried to demonstrate that is exactly the **opposite** of `@Data` and wanted to point out that the lombok **perfectly** supports datastructures or struct-like objects but not objects in the OO-sense. 

I thougt it was worth adding because of the sheer amount of annotations required for such a behaviour (which was probably the motivation for `@Data` and `@Value`) and because you have a defined and exact name for the outcome (which would be `@Object` as opposed to `@Data`). 

Various resources could be linked to here. I picked one random from the top of my search results: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/23406307/whats-the-difference-between-objects-and-data-structures

It sounds too exotic for me (as in, if we allow this, there are about 10 other combos we should add, and clearly having 12 different esoteric combinations each with a different name all in the lombok.* package is bad), so, we're not adding this. If we ever do composable annotations (#2294) you can make this yourself, however.

title: [BUG]  Lombok generates only one @Getter and @Setter for a field name

nodes.body:
@vadym-l 
> I don't quite understand this irrational behavior

I guess, the reason is the javabeanscrap insanity: With their rules, there's no one-to-one correspondence between field and getter names. So the names could collide. I don't recall the rules anymore, so I can't give you an example.

Moreover, there are people using their own rules and defining getters manually, when they dislike the name lombok would generate. So when lombok sees `getName`, it doesn't generate `getNaMe`.

Sure, it could be smarter when it sees that the first getter was actually generated by lombok itself. But this is more complicated, would break backwards compatibility, would need a precise specification, updating documentation, maintenance.... and seriously, *how often do you need it?*

> If this change as complex as you describe

I wouldn't say, it's complex. If it was code generation using reflection or plain annotation processing, I'd vote for finding the best solution. But lombok has to deal with undocumented compiler internals and that adds more than an order of magnitude overhead. And it has many users with many wishes, a few contributors and only two maintainers (I'm not a team member).

> by providing an additional attribute "getterName"

... which saves you a single line (or two or zero, depending on your formatting style) in a very rare case of name clash due to different casing. At least, I hope, it's a rare case in your code. :rofl: 

> Or by providing an additional attribute "caseSensitive" on the class level

I guess, `lombok.config` would be the best place, but many similar proposals were shot down because fulfilling all peoples' wishes would cause an explosion of options (just read through all the `@ToString` proposals). These options love to interact in unforeseen ways causing unexpected bugs and maintenance costs. There are quite a few options I'd personally love to see in lombok, but I gave up on most of them. Lombok as is saves me maybe half a megabyte of boilerplate (more than Java 8 features do) and much more is hardly achievable (at least not without a medium-sized company backing it).

Sorry, although I understand that there is a use-case for it, due to the reasons @Maaartinus mentioned, we're not going to add support for multiple fields that have the same case-insensitive name.

It's not common enough to warrant extra time on it.
Duplicate of #2693

    find delomboked -name *.java |xargs javadoc
