title: Support @Delegate on multiple fields of same type, such as List

nodes.body:
I'm not sure it's that convenient.

Let's say you had the option to do that. That'd mean, here, you'd get:

    clearElements()
    listIteratorElements()
    iteratorElements()


that's great, but then...

    addElements(Element e) // huh, only a single element??
    addAllElements(Coll..) // Weird
    setElements(int, E) // this sets a single element, weird name.

You could use just singular `Element` as suffix, but then the first list is a bit odd. `clearElement` sure sounds like 'delete one element', not 'clear the entire list of elements'. You could go with a prefix:

    elementsAdd
    elementsAddAll
    elementsClear

and that's a sight better to be sure, but it's in the minority for how methods are commonly named. Clear blue sky? I'd expect the method to add an element be named `addElement` and not `elementAdd`.

Conclusion: This is a LOT harder to do right than it looks.

I agree with all of the above. 

In all, I just wanted two things:
1. Not calling `getElementts()`.
2. Not checking `getElements()` returning null.

Probably not worth it. It just struck me to be able to `@Delegate` one field, but not two.

The fix for having `getElements()` return null is partly just kicking the can down the road, and partly irrelevant because there are better solutions.

## Kicking the can

Lets say elements IS null, what does `container.elementsAdd()` do then? Silently do nothing? That is appealing at first thought, but with some longer thought, that is in all sorts of ways the wrong way to go about it. You end up with: In absence of explicit information about what to do.. throw an NPE. Yeah okay we get to add a nice message but that's not much of a win over `.getElements().add()` which would also throw one, AND java will soon make NPEs like this have a nicer message anyway.

## Wrong place to do it

null does not mean, and never has meant, 'empty'. It means 'no value'. If, for some concept, 'no value' and 'empty' are dangerously close to being interpreted as semantically equivalent, or there really is no sense in having 'no value' there, and any border cases are best solved by having the empty value be the standin, then __DO NOT EVER USE NULL HERE__. The fix is to find the place where this field or variable ends up being null, or where some API call returns null, and fix it, so that it's empty list instead. This doesn't necessarily involve an if. For example, upgrade `map.get(key)` to `map.getOrDefault(key, "")`.

The feature thus awaits a really good use case to warrant further efforts in solving the naming issue. Until then let's just close it.

title: [FEATURE] SwallowException

nodes.body:
In general my gut reaction to 'swallow exceptions' is that people write code that does this far too often (for example, the majority of java programmers incorrectly go out of their way to ignore any `IOException` that falls out of an inputstream/reader's `close` method). I am very hesitant, in that I would be really sad if people incorrectly think the best way to deal with exceptions they don't wanna deal with is to start tossing `@SwallowException` on everything (I'd much rather they toss `@SneakyThrows` on there!)

But, in fairness to your proposal, the scenario DOES come up.

The point is: The cost is high; not just maintenance (which is not too bad; this has a lot of overlap with `@SneakyThrows` which is already a supported feature), but mostly in footprint: By supporting the feature we tacitly somewhat approve of it, and a casual glance at the lombok featurelist might cause someone who is really looking for `@SneakyThrows`, to find this instead, and apply the wrong thing.

We have to balance that 'cost' with the 'value' in catering to this boilerplate. Which then leads to the question: How often do you want to swallow an exception? Often enough to warrant a lombok annotation to do it?

I have my doubts that this gets over the 'sufficient value compared to the cost' bar.

Any insights on this would be welcome!

> How often do you want to swallow an exception?

The right question is "How often do you *should* swallow an exception?". And the answer is "about never". Unfortunately, (mostly due to the checked exception nonsense and partly due to ill-advised examples in books), swallowing exceptions is the most common and most deadly Java sin.

While "swallow and log" is much better and the use case of the OP is fine, I'm afraid that supporting this would lead to even more beginners spending days with code running seamlessly but doing nothing useful due to swallowed exceptions.

In fact, I'd go so far as to say that if you swallow-and-log it just has GOT to be wrong. There ARE use-cases: Imagine a web request handler runs into a 'client hung up' connection error. That's a classic case of just swallow-and-ignore, or, if you want to log this, then the logging really ought to be quite custom, including IPs and the precise request; none of these things would occur if you use this feature proposal with the `@Log` thing going on.

In other words, I bet anytime you think of swallowing exceptions, one of these things is going on, 50%+ of the time:

* You really shouldn't, it's jumping to the wrong solution. It'd be better to fix APIs to let you throw things, and to add proper handlers at entrypoint invokers to not blow up the world. I _really_ dislike catering to crap APIs with lombok. Feels far too much like tacit approval.
* You want to swallow, but log the event, and the proper way to log it is sufficiently customized that lombok couldn't automatically generate it. In other words, not boilerplate, and lombok really can't help you here.

The remaining 50% is probably almost universally 'I want to swallow exceptions and completely ignore them', and I think I'm being generous when I say that it's as high as 50%; I bet the above 2 'fail cases' are the (vast?) majority.

I'm going to put the kaibosh on this. Feel free to comment further if I'm missing a useful case.

title: [FEATURE] need for @Builder.Default ?

nodes.body:
@nimo23 
> So maybe lombok can make that automatically by watching for the new-operator instead of the need to watch for `@Builder.Default`.

That's pure magic. You'd react to `new`, but there are things like static factory methods (Guava provides tons of them) which are used in place of a constructor (e.g., `Lists.newArrayList()` or `ImmutableList.of("a", "b")`). There are tons of other ways how to create a new object. So this would be a very strange criterion.

The problem is not with the `new` operator, but with field initialization in general. In a `@Builder`-annotated class, this line
```
private List<User> users = new ArrayList<>();
```
actually defines two fields: one in your class and one in the builder. Yet there's a single initializing expression. The questions are: Should it be used in the builder, in the generated constructor(s), in manually written constructors?

*I could imagine using it in the builder unconditionally.* Lombok is conservative by requiring an annotation. Your approach might do what's wanted most of the time and sometimes, lead to very bad surprises.
It's more more complicated than you think, @nimo23. What you want just isn't even remotely possible.

title: [FEATURE] Configurable default AccessLevel for generated constructors
body:
### As is
The annotations to generate constructors by default have `AccessLevel.PUBLIC`

### Desired
Allow to set another default AccessLevel for constructors in `lombok.config`

### Why
I would like to make the generated constructors private by default. That is very handy when using mainly static factory methods.

nodes.body:
If you let lombok make these static factory methods (using `@AllArgsConstructor(staticName = "of")` for example), then private is the default.

And if you're in the habit of always writing a custom one, I don't think it's a good idea to squirrel away the notion that the generated constructor is always private in a setting. I think the notion 'every single last class file I ever write, or at least almost all of them, will always have an explicitly written static constructor' is _very_ exotic style, and beyond what we should be supporting.

We need to think of the principle of least surprise. `@AllArgsConstructor` generating a private constructor because of a setting in `lombok.config` is in my opinion beyond what is reasonable to expect casual readers of code to think of.

So, no can do :(

title: [BUG] Lombok compatibility for java14
body:
Java 14 adds new features; in particular, the pattern style instanceof (example: `if (x instanceof String y)`), which means the AST structure for `JCInstanceOf` has changed. This needs to be reflected; annotation-relevant stuff is unlikely to occur here, so mostly our pretty printer needs to be able to handle it, and we need to double-check that the TreeMaker still has the old-style method; if not, `@EqualsAndHashCode` does generate `instanceof` code at least, and would need an update.

TODO:

* Update prettyprinter for `JCInstanceOf` and possibly add a printer for `JCPattern`.
* Add a test file, to run only at 14+, just to doublecheck that the prettyprinter gets new-style patterns right.
* Wait for ECJ's response to this new feature.

First of all, the issue started to appear because our Java analyzer switched to use ecj as a frontend. My understanding is that Lombok EclipsePatcher is patching "our" classes at the same time as "regular" Eclipse compiler.

> Is org.sonar.classloader.ParentFirstStrategy open source?

> Almost looks like sonar is using its own classloader architecture, which is a bit superfluous (eclipse is built on OSGi and already has this)

Our analyzers are not Eclipse/OSGi bundles, and they are used in non OSGi environments (like IntelliJ, SonarQube server, ...). Our SonarLint Eclipse plugin is obviously an OSGi component, and internally we are creating custom isolated classloaders to dynamically load each analyzers.

Do you have a suggestion of what we could to restore the compatibility?

I'd stick with your model, because the JDT plugin's ECJ may not be the version your code is written for.

But, lombok does not know that; it patches all 'ECJ-esque' classes that the VM process is attempting to load. There is some advantage to lombokizing sonar's ECJ, in that it would in theory make sonar more aware of lombok's additions, but that's a sizable can of worms that perhaps we shouldn't get into. Given that things seemed to be doing allright before your update to using ECJ, perhaps the easiest course of action, at least for now, is to ensure that lombok does not lombokize sonar's ECJ.

When we apply the patches, we know which classloader is responsible as we're trying to patch it.

Normally in eclipse land, that's generally an instance of `org.eclipse.osgi.internal.loader.EquinoxClassLoader` (for all eclipse plugins), or `org.eclipse.equinox.launcher.Main$StartupClassLoader` (that's what eclipse boots with).

I'm pretty sure that, if I were to install sonarlint into my eclipse, I'd find that it's an instance of `.org.sonar.classloader._something_`. We can detect that, and not patch it.

title: [BUG] Bad return type in lambda expression

nodes.body:
This is a java type resolution issue and not a lombok bug. You're asking too much of java's type resolution here (the fact that SuperBuilder makes a whole bunch of generics juuuust to hack a 'self type' into java is convoluting matters considerably, but the point of SuperBuilder is that the concept (a builder that is properly chainable even in a hierarchy of types) __requires__ these generics.

So, not a java bug, not a lombok bug, but an unfortunate array of circumstance that has as end result that type resolution doesn't work in places where you might have expected that it would. Short of java introducing some new language feature (such as a self type) there is nothing lombok can do to alleviate this.

title: [BUG] @Builder on class level: Cannot make a static reference to the non-static

nodes.body:
This is intentional behaviour; lombok is working as intended.

In java, you CAN do what you're trying to pull here, but it causes all sorts of wonky behaviour and is explicitly called out in many style guides as 'things not to do'. When java creates objects, there are 2 separate 'tracks' of code that need to be run _for each layer in the hierarchy_ (so for your class, and your parent's class, and your parent's parent, all the way to j.l.Object). If you put in one of these tracks any code that has instance scope, you've got yourself a tricky chicken-and-egg problem where final fields hold values you never assigned to them, to name one 'Whaaaa????' thing that happens then.

And you're doing that here.

Perhaps your explicit impl of hashCode does not use any instance state, but that's bizarre; for example, lombok's own hashCode would look at your own tmpId as part of the hashCode to generate. Not only would 'tmpId' be null, which is probably fine, but any other field, even one with a default or an explicit value associated to it with the builder is also blank. The hashcode so generated is likely a constant value for all objects created regardless of what values you set and _CLEARLY_ not what you wanted.

Java regretfully allows this crazy broken stuff that you shouldn't be doing, but that doesn't mean lombok is going to. That expression is static context.

You're going to have to find another way.

title: [BUG] Stack overflow in val handler
body:
**Describe the bug**
Attempting to use val can cause a stack overflow within Lombok in certain cases.

In the miminal example below, the issue is an interface with a recursive generic type.  The problem only arises in this specific case -- many minor changes to the code will bypass it (e.g. changing the method parameter to a raw `Thing`, or giving it a concrete type such as `Thing<Integer>`, or changing the interface type to `<T extends Comparable<T>>` or `<T extends Comparable<?>>` will all cause the code to compile successfully).

**To Reproduce**

    import lombok.val;
    
    public class Example {
        public void run(Thing<?> thing) {
            val x = thing;
        }
    }
    
    interface Thing<T extends Comparable<? super T>> {}

**Expected behavior**
Lombok infers the type of `x` as `Thing<?>`, or emits an informative error if it is unable to handle this case by design.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version 1.18.12 (and all the earlier versions I tried, back to 1.12.2)
 - Platform: javac 1.8.0_211 and javac 11.0.4-ojdkbuild

The stack trace I get (for javac 11, Lombok 1.18.12) is:

title: [BUG] Non-deterministic bytecode generation in certain environments
body:
**Describe the bug**
When using certain combination of annotations lombok may produce different bytecode for exactly same source and environment on subsequent compilations. This prevents me from making reproducible build.

**To Reproduce**
[bug-example.zip](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/files/4193162/bug-example.zip)
This is sample project should demonstrate problem. Just run `build-until-sha-different.sh` (assuming you have bash/diff/sha1sum/maven). It will iterate building this same project several times until subsequent builds produce class files that is not exactly byte-to-byte equal.
I've used some classes from guava library, but doubt this is hard requirement, though this problem is very sensible to some unknown factors so I'll describe my environment in more details below. Problem is not reproducible without lombok annotations so I assume this happens because of lobmok.


**Expected behavior**
Should get exactly same bytecode each time if nothing had changed in source or environment.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
lobok version is latest release:
```
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
            <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
            <version>1.18.12</version>
            <scope>provided</scope>
        </dependency>
```
This is happening in docker container based on `alpine:3.11` with java and maven installed:
```
# java -version
openjdk version "1.8.0_242"
OpenJDK Runtime Environment (IcedTea 3.15.0) (Alpine 8.242.08-r0)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.242-b08, mixed mode)
```
```
# mvn -version
Apache Maven 3.6.3 (cecedd343002696d0abb50b32b541b8a6ba2883f)
Maven home: /usr/share/java/maven-3
Java version: 1.8.0_242, vendor: IcedTea, runtime: /usr/lib/jvm/java-1.8-openjdk/jre
Default locale: en_US, platform encoding: UTF-8
OS name: "linux", version: "4.15.0-1050-kvm", arch: "amd64", family: "unix"
```

**Additional context**
Here are example of such files produced:
[1_SimpleBug.class](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/files/4193242/1_SimpleBug.zip)
[2_SimpleBug.class](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/files/4193243/2_SimpleBug.zip)
These are plain class files I just give them `zip` extension so github accept them.
And here how they different:
```
# cmp -lb 1_SimpleBug.class 2_SimpleBug.class
4053  66 6     65 5
```
I.e. somewhere in byte 4053 (actually 4052 since 0-based) files have different bytes. I've track down which section of class file this bytes are related to and found that these are verification_type_info field in Stack map frame structure with tag Object_variable_info and byte that is different is a pointer to constants pool entry.
So one file points to 35 entry and another to 36 and here what constant pools for these two files contains (generated with `javap -v` command):
```
1_SimpleBug.class
   #35 = Utf8               supSetStringParameter10
   #36 = Utf8               Lcom/google/common/base/Supplier;

2_SimpleBug.class
   #35 = Utf8               supSetStringParameter10
   #36 = Utf8               Lcom/google/common/base/Supplier;
```
They are identical, so why these pointers suddenly different?
So it looks like lombok, during bytecode generation, had shifted these values somehow.

Disclaimer: I'm not a project owner.

This problem is very sensitive to some unknown factors in the environment and code structure. E.g. I also cannot reproduce it on same version of jdk (1.8.0_242 though AdobtJDK build) on my windows machine. It not reproducing every build (need to run build several times). I cannot reproduce it without NonNull annotation on even one of the parameters. I cannot reproduce it with delombok. I can't even reproduce it without guava Supplier class as type of the parameters. Only combination of linux + jdk build version (alpine uses musl so jdk is slightly different) + docker + certain structure of the code + lombok Builder and NonNull annotations making this issue to appear. So maybe this is not even lombok problem but jdk/compiler problem... I'm not 100% sure. I don't think docker is actually makes any difference though, it is just a convenient way of creation exact environment I need. I can give my docker setup that I've used:
This opens shell in container (1):
```
# docker run -it alpine:3.11 /bin/ash
/ # apk add openjdk8 maven
```
in another bash copy bug-example project into container:
```
# docker cp bug-example 339a7bda:/root/
```
switch back to (1):
```
/ # cd ~/bug-example
/ # ./build-until-sha-different.sh
```
Even for me this not always work. I.e. sometimes it does produce exact same bytecode. Though with my real code it happens 100% of the time but I can't put it here it is too big and have way too many dependencies.

Here is docker image that have everything baked-in:
https://drive.google.com/uc?id=1i04_dVL0Rp5rxXCMuHaS4LYREkZjAAW1&export=download
You can try to reproduce it yourself with:
```
# docker load -i bugexample.img
# docker run -w /root/bug-example --name bugtest bugexample /bin/ash build-until-sha-different.sh
```

I find it plausible that lombok is (part of) the problem here, and welcome any PR that fixes it, but, given these 3 facts:

* There is a high likelyhood that there's either absolutely nothing we can do about it (javac issue), or that the fix would be man-months of work (if it's because the nodes we generate have the same position, and that javac, ordinarily generating elements based on file position, then goes by some secondary sorting order; one which is non-deterministic per VM, such as system identityhashcode – we can fix that, by pretty much rewriting how lombok works. Not really feasible to do for something like this).

* Non-deterministic code gen usually does not matter; you'd have to care about deterministic bytecode and most java users do not. We'd love to cater to those that do, of course, but, the # of people who are suffering even if this bug occurs is naturally low.

* And that, as @AngryGami 's (excellent!) reporting seems to indicate, the bug requires some fairly exotic scenarios to even show up in the first place.

Throw those aspects into a blender and I'm afraid this has extremely low priority. We'll get around to fixing it probably sometimes before the year 3854.
:) "nondeterministing" was a word :), but thank you 👍

All of this was for nothing. Maven was main culprit. First time I ran my build it downloads lots of stuff that maven require (apart from my project dependencies) and then start compilation in same jvm. Second time build runs there is no need to download so compilation starts immediately. I don't know exactly why but first invocation of compiler is somehow affected by state of the jvm and this cause it to produce slightly different bytecode.

Solution was to add <fork>true<fork> to my pom.xml file and build now is totally reproducible... though takes ~2x more time :)

title: [FEATURE] Alternative semi keyword `const` working exactly like `val`
body:
<s>The lombok functionalities `var` and `val` are realized as stub `@interface`, to stay within java syntax. Since both types are named similar, they are easiely confused. An `@interface const` could be realized, to be used alternatively to `val`, and be handled by the same mechanism that handles `val`-replacement today. Both could even coexist, to be backwards compatible. No special configuration is neccessary, but thinkable, for someone wanting to deprecate `val` in their code base.</s>

const is already a keyword, though never implemented. Therefore this is probably not possible to implement, which is most likely why it was done with 'val' in the first place.

nodes.body:
I wish we'd have thought of that. But as you say, it's a keyword. It is unlikely but plausible that it passes the syntactic validity stage and that usually means that lombok gets to run (at which point we can fix everything), but even if javac works like that (i.e. it invokes lombok before generating error statements and ending the compilation process), I think it's too finnicky to rely on it to continue to do this.

Also, if I could go back in time, _maybe_ const'd be better, but now that the val feature has been out for a few years, the cost of the change makes the cost/benefit analysis no longer work out.

I like the idea though :)

> I presume this won't address reference loops.

I'd bet, it won't. It's very hard to create immutable objects with loops as you need an object reference before the object gets created. It's doable, and there's a lengthy discussion in some Lombok issue, how this could be done, but it's damn complicated. Add inheritance and generics to the mix and enjoy....

Anyway, immutable reference loops would need a new sort-of-constructor creating all participants at once, not something as simple as a better wither.

I like the idea, and it's indeed shorter. However, I'm not sure it's easier to comprehend for people not used to the new idiom.

I just though (only a few minutes, so this is neither very elaborated nor well-thought-out) about how such a feature could be designed when
a) we have to stick to the Java syntax, but
b) do not have to care much about how this could be implemented, because we could fix the whole `with` call chain once lombok runs. So here's my idea:

`movie = movie.withDirector().withDob().withYear(1999);`

The actual implementations of that (no-args) methods do nothing, they are just there to allow code completion and the correct return type of the last call. I'm quite sure you could achieve this using an inner helper class with a type parameter that is bound to the type of the first instance, `Movie` in this case. 

When compiling, lombok could detect calls to those empty methods and replace them by the actual invocations, here:
`movie.withDirector(movie.getDirector().withDob(movie.getDirector().getDob().withYear(1999)));`

Sounds too weird? ;)

@janrieke 
> I'm quite sure you could achieve this using an inner helper class

I guess, you'd need an inner class per field, but it could work. As the class is just imaginary, this doesn't matter much, but I'm not sure whether it helps understanding. Your syntax is nicer and shorter than the lambdas, but it's more magical and possibly not that flexible. It's
```
movie.withDirector().withDob().withYear(1999);
```
instead of
```
movie.withDirectorBy(d -> d.withDobBy(b -> b.withYear(1999)));
```
i.e., despite saving not many characters, you get a much simpler expression.

> Sounds too weird? ;)

No, but I'm afraid, not doable.... your expression can occur in any class, and then you know nothing about `Movie` having `withDirector()` generated by Lombok. There may be no such method (and you should error out) or there may be a manually written method doing something completely different (and then you shouldn't touch it at all).

For this, we'd need something clearly indicating it's Lombok's stuff like
```
lombok.with().movie.withDirector().withDob().withYear(1999);
```
but without the arg-less methods actually existing, autocomplete wouldn't work and it's all rather ugly.

---

I'm trying to get inspiration from [immerjs](https://immerjs.github.io/immer/docs/introduction), [immutable-js](https://immutable-js.github.io/immutable-js/) and other JS libraries, where this feature is called "deep updates". However, it seems to be too far (JS is way more flexible and the libraries try to provide much more).

I've chosen the following functional interfaces:

[obvious choices]

* long -> [`LongUnaryOperator`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/util/function/LongUnaryOperator.html)
* int -> [`IntUnaryOperator`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/util/function/IntUnaryOperator.html)
* double -> [`DoubleUnaryOperator`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/util/function/DoubleUnaryOperator.html)
* object -> [`Function<? super T, ? extends T>`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/util/function/Function.html) - so not `UnaryOperator` because, hey, if you want to transform a field of type `Number` using a function that takes in any `Object` and returns an `Integer`, that should work.

not so obvious:
* boolean -> [`UnaryOperator<Boolean>`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/util/function/UnaryOperator.html) – there is no `BooleanOperator`; going with the usual function seems odd here, as lowercase-b-boolean really isn't an object, so allowing a function that transforms any object into a boolean is weird, and clashes with what we do for other primitives. However, going with an `IntUnaryOperator`, 'casting' the boolean to a 1 or 0 value and 'casting' the response back seems to assign arbitrary truthy and falsy aspects to 0 and 1, which isn't idiomatic java so that doesn't feel right either.
* char, short, byte, float -> [`IntUnaryOperator`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/util/function/IntUnaryOperator.html) (and for the float, `DoubleUnaryOperator`), which means your transformer is handed an int and not a char/short/byte/float, and whatever you return is then cast to char/short/byte/float to make it fit. Especially with char that isn't necessarily fantastic API, but I'm not sure offering a `Function<? super Character, Character>` is a better choice. These primitive types don't have an _XUnaryOperator_ functional interface variant, and lombok does not want to add runtime dependencies, so I'm a bit stuck having to think of java.* functional interfaces that work well for these.

Are there compelling arguments to be consistent and use `Function<? super X, ? extends X>` for all of them, X being either the type of the field directly, or if primitive, the wrapper equivalent? If we do this (and we already do something like this with booleans), is it okay that if you return `null`, you just get a plain jane NPE, not specifically adorned by lombok with a clear message (though that is coming to JDK15 if memory serves, we'd get it automatically then).
@rspilker what's left is the docs. I'm leaving that, plus reviewing the work, to you.

I can't wait for this feature! 😃

As to types of "not so obvious" functional interfaces:
- I don't think it matters that much (as long as Lombok doesn't become a runtime dependency) because I'm under an impression that this feature won't be used too often for `char` (let alone `short` or `byte`)
- certainly, choosing `IntUnaryOperator` for `char` aligns with the approach of JDK 8 (although I don't like how easy it becomes to confuse a character with a code point then)
- if *I* had to decide, I guess my *slight* preference would be to neglect performance and just have `UnaryOperator<Character>`, `UnaryOperator<Byte>`, etc. (especially knowing that work on Value Types for Java is in progress under Project Valhalla)

> if *I* had to decide, I guess my slight preference would be to neglect performance and just have `UnaryOperator<Character>`, `UnaryOperator<Byte>`, etc. (especially knowing that work on Value Types for Java is in progress under Project Valhalla).

This makes sense.... and one day we may get `UnaryOperator<byte>`, too. The future will probably render all current choices ridiculous, including all the special function interfaces like `LongUnaryOperator` (which then may or may not be declared as `extends UnaryOperator<long>`).

I wonder whether it's possible to account for the future in Lombok. Maybe there could be a configuration key, which currently would give you a single choice, namely doing what's described above. Anyone who gets a method dependent on any of the non-obvious choices would also get a warning, pointing to the doc describing the current state and recommending to add the configuration to silence the warning. The advantage is that the default could be changed in the future without breaking anyone (little gain for not much work). I'm afraid my explanation wasn't very good....

title: Support builderClassName in @SuperBuilder
body:
**Describe the feature**
The `@Builder` annotation supports the `builderClassName` parameter. I would be nice it `@SuperBuilder` did as well.

**Additional context**
I did check the latest version of Lombok and didn't see the parameter in there. However, it does appear that this option is supported through the config file, as shown in [HandleSuperBuilder.java](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/39c2903c885f52cb99e36f0a0c896bcca2bc794f/src/core/lombok/javac/handlers/HandleSuperBuilder.java#L185).

nodes.body:
There is a reason why there is no such parameter:
1. There are two builder classes. So either the parameter must affect both, or we need two parameters, making it even more complex.
2. SuperBuilders in subclasses rely on the builder class name of the superclass. There is no way to detect a differing builder class name in the superclass, so we'd need another parameter to specify that.

So all in all this is too complex both for users and for us to maintain.

That being said, could you describe your usecase? Maybe we could find another solution.
PS: Allowing setting this via config is kind of a compromise: It will change the names consistently, so unless you use SuperBuilder across project borders it will just work.

It'd have to be one heck of a use-case, given the complexities as @janrieke stated. I'm pre-closing this, but feel free to answer with novel solutions or dire use cases and we can always re-evaluate :)

To elaborate though, my use case is I want some of my models to be extendable (hence `@SuperBuilder`), but I also want them to work nicely with Jackson. As you know, this requires me to define the builder class manually, which is very ugly for classes with `@SuperBuilder`. I have opened a feature request with the Jackson team (https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-future-ideas/issues/47) for a change to make this easier. It's probably better solved over there.

I'm also aware of the recent `setterPrefix` parameter on `@Builder`, which would be nice to have on `@SuperBuilder`. I see you have a discussion going for that at https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/2154.

Furthermore, we are working on a Lombok annotation that automatically inserts all necessary Jackson annotations into the generated code to make `@(Super)Builder` work in Jackson (and without having to use Jackson's defaults like the "with" prefix).

`@Jacksonized @(Super)Builder` will be in the next release. It will insert all necessary Jackson annotations to make Jackson use the generated builder when deserializing. No need for manual modifications to the generated builder code any more.

nodes.body: I do foresee some issues; presumably if you have one of these you have more, and you'd want to know if an object is 'locked' (as in, all the set-only-once fields have in fact all been set exactly once at this point, making it effectively immutable now.)

1.yes, grammar @Setter(onlyOnce = true) sonds acceptable.
2.I didn't consider about thread safety because this function shall be invoked only once in normal situations.
And IMO people add this Annotation, they will be careful about the property is somehow "final", and shall NEVER set them twice in there code.
And that Anntation also reminds others who try to maintain/read the codes this property is somehow "final",  thus help them understand the codes better.
But since it will be invoked only once in normal situation, it sounds also no performance harm to sync it, so yes your code solution are better.

3.
> I do foresee some issues; presumably if you have one of these you have more, and you'd want to know if an object is 'locked' (as in, all the set-only-once fields have in fact all been set exactly once at this point, making it effectively immutable now.)

I actually don't care about this. For me myself, I do not need this, the reason is stated in section 2.
But it is no harm to add such a function IMO.

I also see more merits in making it an option of `@Setter`, also because we need to copy some of the annotations.

The value field also needs to become `volatile`.

One big difference with actual final field is that those can be cached/inlined after the constructor has completed. That's why I am not a fan of using the word 'final' for this.

In most cases I've observed, refactoring the code to use true final fields was a better solution.

Note: we would also have this for static variables, where it is a much more common idiom.

> And IMO people add this Annotation, they will be careful about the property is somehow "final", and shall NEVER set them twice in there code.

This makes no sense. If nobody would ever do this wrong, there'd be no point to this feature.
Catering to accidents is the whole point. If we're going to cater to that, we should do it for as many cases as can reasonably be covered.

Whether a feature is a good idea or not, is a cost/benefit analysis.

You may not need the 'locked' aspect, but others do. If the feature does not cater to it, the 'benefit' side goes down. And this feature is already likely not crossing the bar.

Between the performance issues and the 'locked' aspect, this feature is clearly going to end up on the wrong side; either it's too 'costly' (too complicated), or doesn't have enough 'benefit' (does not cater properly to enough use cases).

title: [FEATURE] Improve builder to allow to build from super class object

nodes.body:
_Preliminary remark_: I'm not a lombok team member, but I contributed the `@SuperBuilder` feature.

So you have a cat, want to do some surgery and make a dog out of it, but it should keep its name, right?
I think it is theoretically possible with `@SuperBuilder`. However, I see two major problems:
1. How do we configure this feature? I mean, why should it be only the direct superclass that can be converted? Any superclass is legitimate if you consider this feature legitimate. Furthermore, as we cannot resolve types when lombok runs, we need that information in the annotations of both superclass and subclass, and it must be consistent. This will be beyond any comprehensibility, and I foresee hundreds of bug reports where people simply do not understand the configuration.
2. I do not think this is a very common use case. On the other hand, it would require a lot of work to implement such a feature and to maintain it. The cost/benefit ratio seems very high.

But -- good news -- I am pretty sure you can do it manually by using the `toBuilder` feature and customizing the builder classes of both superclass and subclass. You'll probably need at least one new method in each of them that is similar to the generated `protected B $fillValuesFrom(C instance)` method. Have a look at the `delombok` output to get a starting point.

If you can't get it to work, feel free to submit a question to StackOverflow, tag it with "lombok" and I'll have a look at it.

Actualy I've a Pet and I want to build a Dog from it.
As in my real code Pet is completly legit, I just want to be able to build the dog builder object from the pet object with the existing pet fields already set in my dog builder, so I just have to complete it with Dog specific fields and avoid unneeded manual copy of each pet field.
Technically it makes no difference if you have a pet or any subclass of it as starting point. Also the solution I proposed stays the same.

I do not doubt this could be a legitimate use case. I think it's just too complex to implement in Lombok considering the crazy generics stuff `@SuperBuilder` already generates right now. And it probably requires incomprehensible configuration via annotation params.

Together with the fact that it can be implemented manually by customizing the (abstract) builder class, I'd vote for 'no', but as I wrote I'm not a Lombok team member.

I may have found a solution (I'm not yet fully convinced that there will be no problems with it, e.g. generics on the superclass?). It requires some modifications on how we generate the internal toBuilder methods, but as those are marked with a "$" it should be clear that anyone who messes around with those might get broken code on a lombok update.

Here's my solution (for `Child extends Parent`):

* `protected B $fillValuesFrom(final C instance)` will become `protected B $fillValuesFrom(final Parent instance)`. This implies that builder subclasses do not override that method anymore, but simply overload it.
  * A nice side-effect of this is that we can get rid of the static helper method `$fillValuesFromInstanceIntoBuilder`, because we can integrate it into `$fillValuesFrom`.
* Add a new method to the `Child` class:
```
public static Child.ChildBuilder<?, ?> toBuilder(Parent instance) {
	return new Child.ChildBuilderImpl().$fillValuesFrom(instance);
}
```
This `$fillValuesFrom` method call will resolve to `ParentBuilder::$fillValuesFrom` at compile-time.

With this, we do not need any more information when generating the superclass' builder. It is sufficient to add something like `@SuperBuilder(withSupertypeToBuilder = {Parent.class})` to the subclass.

What with how complex it is and how it's not going to work well for certain cases (generics on parent), and requires some fairly convoluted args, I'm not so sure this is a worthwhile addition to lombok.

If you're (@janrieke) excited about this addition by all means, I'll trust your judgement, but I'm tempted to write this one off as too hairy to dance around lack of resolution to deliver on it.

I'm not too excited, but what I like is that this approach would actually simplify the current `toBuilder()` code even without the new feature.

So when I find the time for it, I think I'd first make the simplifications and thoroughly test that. Then it would be simple for users to manually customize the builder to add this. I'm also not convinced whether we should add this feature due to the type param issue.
I'll leave this open and on low-prio for a while. For future self / other curators of the buglist: If this has no further traffic for a few months, feel free to presume it can be closed.
What's the status of this issue?

No progress in the meantime.
From my point of view, the path should be changing `$fillValuesFrom` as drafted above. From there on, users can implement this feature on their own by customizing their superbuilders.
I vote against a fully-automatic support for this feature in Lombok due to the described generics issues.

I could help reviewing PRs on this, but I don't have the time to implement it on my own at the moment.
And of course the final decision is on the Lombok maintainers, not on me.

@ahaverdings That `$` should be screaming at you: What? No! Don't!.

That it doesn't annoys me, but, them's the breaks. This is sufficiently complicated with nowhere near enough intent by contributors and maintainers to wade into the already extremely complicated Builder/SuperBuilder mechanism that I'm just going to close this; seems better than to keep an issue open for a decade.

For those who want to take the risk that it might break without notice with a new Lombok version, you can take a look at [my answer at StackOverflow to a similar question](https://stackoverflow.com/a/66817135).

Soo is there any actual way to do this? It would be super helpful for the project I'm working on.
But I can't risk using an API that might break with an update.

The pure-lombok customization approach (see link in my previous comment) works and will most likely also work in future releases, as there are no plans to modify how `@SuperBuilder` works. However, there is no guarantee.

I don't see a solution where this feature could be natively supported by Lombok, as there are unsolved problems e.g. regarding type parameters.

if that's not enough for you, you can still go with the MapStruct approach.

title: [BUG] lombok.addNullAnnotations treats the custom annotation name in lowercase
body:
**Describe the bug**
```
lombok.addNullAnnotations=CUSTOM:javax.validation.constraints.NotNull
```
When setting addNullAnnotations like above in lombok.config, ```javax.validation.constraints.NotNull``` is evaluated as ```javax.validation.constraints.notnull``` (lower case even for annotation class name". Therefore compile error is occurred due to no class found.

**To Reproduce**
1. put following in lombok.config
```
lombok.addNullAnnotations=CUSTOM:javax.validation.constraints.NotNull
```
2. Then create following code in your project.
```
import lombok.Builder;

import javax.validation.constraints.NotNull;

@Builder
public class Test {
    @NotNull
      Integer a;
}
```
3. Then compile.. it ends up with following error message
```
Error:(7, 1) java: cannot find symbol
  symbol:   class notnull
  location: package javax.validation.constraints
```

**Expected behavior**
 javax.validation.constraints.NotNull is recognized.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version : 1.18.12
 - Platform : all platforms

**Additional context**
https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/master/src/core/lombok/core/configuration/NullAnnotationLibrary.java#L128-L133

It's because the nonNullAnnotation and nonNullAnnotation is extracted from  ci variable which is converted to lower case.

nodes.body:
I clearly don't 'get' the validations package; how the heck would anyone want to annotate an element to state 'this MUST be null'? What I thought I did understand about it is that it is about validation and not about assertion – you can have an object where a field marked with `@Validation.NotNull` holds a `null` value and that is just fine; that merely means if you were to ask: "hey, is this object valid like this?" – the answer is 'no'. A user can submit a form which doesn't fit the rules. That's still reality - that is the proper representation of what they submitted. The point is not to throw exceptions or get wavy underlines in IDEs, the point of the annotation is to generate a human readable error message.

Which would strongly suggest making lombok generate it in such places is inappropriate. Am I misunderstanding how it works? I have no problem adding this annotation to our list of built in supported stuff, _IF_ it makes sense. I thought it didn't make sense.

Separate from that, the lower-case thing? yeah, bug. Thanks for spotting it, and the PR to fix it, I'll merge it soon :)

What if the field is non-final, and there is a setter. Is it still deterministic? I don't know what CF's definition is, but it should warn here; maybe another thread, in between your first invocation of `getField()` and the second one, set the field to null. We could generate Pure in a few cases, but not very many. We intentionally elected to generate only `@SideEffectFree` and not `@Pure` because that, at least, is a guarantee we can actually make.

The ones where we can generate `@Pure` aren't particularly interesting; the only nice one is on generated getters for final fields, which is still worth considering.

Second point, on the topic of CF integration: Where's my promised `@ReturnsReceiver`, `@NotCalledMethods`, and `@CalledMethods` at? :)

We designed the CF feature because Michael showed us these annotations, but as far as I can tell, they still haven't showed up in CF v3.2.

I've fixed lombok to no longer generate them until you set checkerframework to '4.0', and they are no longer generated if you set it to 'true' either, as a temporary bandaid, but I was left with the impression team CF would be adding these!

The above does as follows:

* canEqual is now Pure instead of SEF.
* getters are Pure instead of SEF... but only if the field is final.
* The private self() methods in superbuilder are Pure instead of SEF.
* ReturnsReceiver and CalledMethods and NotCalledMethods are now bound to v4.0 and not v3.0 (set `checkerframework = 4.0` to get em; `checkerframework = true` now is equivalent to `checkerframework = 3.2` which no longer generates those.

That sounds right to me, but if I messed that up, let me know by replying (I track closed issues).

Current edge release has the feature: https://projectlombok.org/download-edge

(Not listed in the changelog; not important enough for an entry I think).

title: [FEATURE] @NoArgsConstructor initialize empty collections
body:
**Describe the feature**
`@NoArgsConstructor` annotation could be somehow configured to initialize collection fields to the correct empty collection.

Currently, it initializes them to `null`. Using `@Singular` annotation on the collection field does not change the behaviour.

Maybe I am missing something, but I cannot find references regarding this anywhere, sorry for the confusion in case.

**Describe the target audience**
Everyone wanting to mix the convenience of the annotation with the safety of initializing collections to the correct empty collection at object creation time.

**Additional context**
Currently only workaround seems to be implementing the no arg constructor ourselves.

nodes.body:
The problem with trying to silently initialize fields to a sentinel/blank value is threefold:

1. null is just as much a sentinel as empty. It's not obvious that _everybody_ would want and assume that they get empties vs. nulls.
2. It is not backwards compatible.
3. How do we know what an appropriate empty type is? What if you have, say, a guava `ImmutableList`? We can't look at the inside of that class def, and even if we could, there is no convention or interface to identify 'call this static method'. I guess we could call just `new FOO();` for a field defined as `FOO x`, whatever `FOO` might be, but that's in fact the wrong thing to do in many cases: `List<String> x = new List<String>();` does not compile.

The only real solution is either that you specify the expression to generate a blank, which defeats the point (that's more boilerplate than we replace!), or that we build in a giant library of type to known blank expressions, which is a lot of work and then means that anybody reading code has to guess if we included the 'blank expression mapping'.

We can solve a lot of these issues by introducing an annotation: Now the first 2 problems are solved, and at least for the third, if we don't know how to do it we can just generate a warning.

That's a plausible road to go here, but `@Singular` doesn't really fit the role. That's for builder, and 'initialize this to a blank value' makes no sense either.

No, the right annotation must be: `@NonNull`, I think. However, we already do this; if you enforce a no-args-constructor when nonnull fields are involved, we.. still make them null, because, hey, you asked, and that actually meshes with the use case (initializing objects which then get immediately filled, for example via setters, by some framework, such as JPA/Hibernate).

I'll discuss with @rspilker if we want to change (and in that sense, break backwards compatibility); we have a minor break release (1.20) planned. If this misses the boat you're in a for a long wait.

Hello and thank you for the fast reply.

I understand your points, and was actually more investigating whether this was an already available functionality  that I somehow could not use properly, or simply a missing feature, which you confirmed to be the case (thanks).

As for your comments:

1. true, the difference being that `null` might lead more easily to `NullPointerException`, while an empty collection is usually handled more gracefully in the application code.

2. also true, but as you noted in your point 3, you would not be able to provide a default for every collection anyway, therefore you would need to receive some input, maybe via some arguments provided to the annotation, making it backwards-safe (no arguments provided means the old behaviour persists)

3. I agree with your analysis, and am currently handling the case by implementing the empty constructor myself; however as you stated, although difficult, it might not be impossible if the developer himself provides the necessary empty constructor. In terms of clutter this approach might be as much as actually writing the method directly (although nobody does it anymore, that's why we love lombok ;) )

Anyway, I am not in dire need of such a feature, so from my side I wouldn't want to rush it since the workaround is not painful or difficult to use.

Thank you again and have a nice day

Probably deprecate it, yeah. Maybe wait a version of 2, because otherwise people with a 'split' codebase (half of the devs on some codebase are on lombok 1.18.10, the others on 1.20) would be forced to either check something in that doesn't work at all for half the users, or to check in something that gens deprecation warnings for half the users.

So, about a year in, then we deprecate the old. Maybe one day we remove it entirely.

Messing with `@Builder.Default` should be done together with issue #2340 .

I was just coming to look for this exact issue! What is the status of this feature?

I'd also like to throw an idea in that we could simply add it as an option to the `@NoArgsConstructor` (e.g. something like `setCollections=EMPTY_LIST` then the default is `setCollections=NULL`  where `EMPTY_LIST` and `NULL` are enums to be imported). 

Having the `@Default` option at the top level is also pretty great, since it could apply to `@NoArgsConstructor` and `@RequiredArgsConstructor`
Actually nullableParams should be default and this should be enabled by default on all fields when using `@Value`, otherwise it's too much annotating.

@mwisnicki `@lombok.Default int number = 3;` means: If you pass `0`, then it turns into 3.

I find that highly surprising behaviour. In other words, a really bad idea. Treating `null` as a placeholder for 'actually I want the default' is pushing it but at least debatable. "Upgrading" `int` fields into `Integer` parameter types is also something that's solidly in the 'veto' camp. It's just too weird, and clashes with how the java community tends to do this stuff today (which is: With overrides).

title: [FEATURE] Super Builder should optionally have a public *BuilderImpl
body: Could the Super Builder have a configurable access to *BuilderImpl so that it can be be used outside the class. Like in Generics.

nodes.body:
Could you further elaborate on your use case? Because typically you should not need the Impl, apart from when you want to instantiate the builder (which you'd typically do just by calling `builder()`).

Adding another parameter to `@SuperBuilder` might not sound like a big deal, but it increases the maintenance burden for us. Furthermore, it may confuse users, because most people simply use this annotation without knowing about the large amount of generics-loaded code with two different classes that is generated by Lombok. And this is absolutely legitimate, and we thus hide as much implementation details as possible.

I will have to get back with an example for you but basically the I have a hierarchy of classes, we will call them transformers, that construct the lombok genereated classes with their builders.  Each transformer of the hierarchy maps to a specific lombok generated classes and passes its builder to parent transformers before filling out the fields that are defined by that class (and not inherited).  
You may need to see an example before you understand my use case fully.

I think I may actually be able to do what I want.  The generics in my example and implementation are across three types of class (controllers, transformers and the generated lombok builders with generics) where each is defined as a hierarchy.  In my first attempt I may have defined the generics wrong or too tightly, but I believe I have resolved that issue.

[lambok-super-builders-example.zip](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/files/4313070/lambok-super-builders-example.zip)

Regardless I am forced to use wildcard generics which I find ugly and confusing and try to minimize the usage of them.  I recently contributed a fix to another project that generates inheritable builders as well, https://github.com/joelittlejohn/jsonschema2pojo/pull/1101, and have a later suggestion to improve it some more with https://github.com/joelittlejohn/jsonschema2pojo/issues/1104.  If you look at the later pull request you can see this project has choose to take the approach that the inner method end in Base, as most people will not use this builder and leave the one consumers use as to match the name of the class.  

We made the base/inheritable builder as abstract so no one could use it directly and exposed the "generic resolved" version for ease of use.  In the jsonschema2pojo's version of an inner class builder you don't have the awkward builder as having a generic of itself being exposed to the user.  
**The only time they are exposed to the generics is if they need to extend the class or generically use the class in ways I described above.**

Regardless I do like your helper builder constructor method.

We cannot use `*BuilderImpl` as return type, because that would cause the methods of subtype builders not to be callable, because they extend the abstract `*Builder`, not the `*BuilderImpl`. I'm almost 100% sure that there is no way to change this, because I spend several weeks to get all this to work in a type-safe manner without any type casts.

Back to the original feature request: an access modifier for the impl. From my point of view, as your use case does not require this feature, the only argument that remains is "it doesn't look good". Considering that a) this is a matter of taste, and b) such a use case seems quite rare, I vote for "no".

But I'm not a lombok team member, I just contributed the `@SuperBuilder` feature. So the decision is not up to me.

Regardless maybe someone can combine the work from both projects to make a more user friendly version based on both of these implementations.  I personally like the jsonschema2pojo method. One thing is also the method that actual returns the builder should be renamed to end in builder because that is what it returns.

If I understand it correctly, jsonschema2pojo is a regular Java tool that generates code. It can do things an annotation processor like Lombok can't. Especially it can gather information on the class hierarchy and the content of every class in it. That is not possible for Lombok, which can only see the current single compilation unit.
That makes it impossible for Lombok to generate builders like jsonschema2pojo.
Fair enough. Yes it generates Java code based on json-schema spec (with extension) with the sun code model library. I suppose it might have more information about parent classes.
I will close this for now.

Leaving it open as it is still a problem.

@rzwitserloot I understand you don't feel compelled to invest time into STS specific issue. 

However, the question is whether this problem is 'STS specific' though. The truth is that I don't know. But if I were to take a wild guess, I would assume that its probably not. STS is just Eclipse with some additional plugins. So the chances are that if its a problem for STS it is a problem for any Eclipse installation with the same version of JDT. 

The way to verify this and know for sure would be to try whether similar problem arises when using a plain Eclipse with Lombok. I'm not sure I can try it (well I can, but TBH I don't know if I know enough to actally be able to reproduce the problem at all).

I.m.o @bismoy2013 who is the one actually experiencing the problem would be the best placed to try whether the problem is STS specific or generally also a problem with a vanilla Eclipse + Lombok setup. I do sense his patience is wearing very thin.

Anyhow, if we can get some clear evidence that the problem is indeed STS specific, it would go a long way in convincingin me or someone else on STS team to invest the time to try and debug it.

As it is though we do not feel like it is our responsibility to debug Lombok, a tool that we do not officially support nor recommend, and do not include with our STS distribution builds. Users can of course install it on their own initiative. and far be it from us to stop them. However we do not feel responsible for problems it may cause (and their have been many instances that I can recall were Lombok did cause problems, which also part of the reason we don't really like to endorse or recommend it to our users).

@kdvolder you'll be happy to know that millions of eclipses with lombok are out there, every day. Either they're all just accepting the slowness (an extraordinary claim), or nobody is running into this (which makes it either STS specific, or it's not STS specific but nevertheless extremely exotic). It also strongly suggests just faffing about, clicking random buttons, hoping the slowdown occurs is not going to be a fruitful bug hunting exercise either. And that's the only real plan I have here (though, given that it is highly likely STS related, as so far nobody's reported eclipse slowdowns), I'd do that with an STS install and not an eclipse install.

We now have a single plausible report that lombok + some specific STS version has slowdowns, but no real formula to reproduce it. If neither team STS nor lombok currently wants to spend resources on this one, the next step is to wait for more reports, and more detailed reports.

If I or anybody else created the impression that you have a _responsibility_ to reproduce and fix this, I apologize – you certainly do not :)  open source licenses are rather explicit in disavowing merchantability and responsibility for pretty much everything.

However, users gonna user, and I'm pretty sure that the % of all lombok users that uses STS is much, much lower than the % of all STS users that uses lombok. Thus: You do not owe an explanation to lombok's maintainers. But you might owe one to STS's users.

Lombok's core maintainers are 2 people who get paid enough to work at minimum wage for a few hours a week max on lombok. I'm pretty sure team STS has more resources than that, so from a perspective of 'who has the most resources to throw at this problem', I don't feel obligated. We _must_ triage our time to work on what's most important to the community and this just isn't making the cut; not without more details on how to reproduce this.

title: [FEATURE] Default lombok.addJavaxGeneratedAnnotation to true if java.xml.ws.annotation present
body:
**Before submitting**
:+1: 

**Describe the feature**
In #985, the default value of `lombok.addJavaxGeneratedAnnotation` was changed from `true` to `false` for Java 9 support.

As a next step, this issue requests that `lombok.addJavaxGeneratedAnnotation` default to `true` if the target version of Java is <= 9 or if the `java.xml.ws.annotation` module is present (javac was invoked with `--add-modules=java.xml.ws.annotation`).

**Describe the target audience**
By setting the default `lombok.addJavaxGeneratedAnnotation` configuration more appropriately, developers will get more expected results. For example, test coverage tools currently don't realize that lombok generated code is generated because it's missing the `@Generated` annotation, so any project that uses those tools must manually set `lombok.addJavaxGeneratedAnnotation=true`. Since lombok is all about things just working and making development simpler, it should automatically set this configuration when it makes sense to do so.

title: [FEATURE] Default lombok.nonNull.exceptionType to JDK when targetting Java >= 9
body:
**Before submitting**
:+1: 

**Describe the feature**
Currently, the default value of the configuration setting `lombok.nonNull.exceptionType` is `NullPointerException`

This issue proposed that when targeting Java >= 9, the default value of `lombok.nonNull.exceptionType` be `JDK`

**Describe the target audience**
The current default, `NullPointerException`, generates `if` statements which results in lots of branches. Code coverage tools, such as JaCoCo, see these branches and will require tests for each one in order for the code to be considered covered.

 `JDK` doesn't generate any branches. Therefore, code coverage tools "just work" the way developers expect.

Instead of requiring all developers to realize this situation, it would be better to have lombok automatically use the best default configuration based on the version of java targeted.

**Describe the bug**
I want to create annotation processor collaborated with lombok. In JDK 8, constructor parameter names of target class is different from the actual. They are `arg0`, `arg1` and so on. In JDK9+, it is properly recognized.

**To Reproduce**
Create a class with lombok constructor annotation like the following.
```java
@Data
public class SomeData {
    private final int id;
    private final String name;
}
```

Create annotation processor newly. In the first round, put the class into a list named `deferredElements` in order to attempt this process after lombok processing.

In the second round, pick the class from the list and check the parameter names from the generated constructor.

**Expected behavior**
Parameter names should be recognized properly even with JDK8.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version : 1.18.12
 - Platform : Gradle 6.0.1, Azul JDK 8.0.242, 9.0.7 and 11.0.6

**Additional context**
Full example is in [my repo](https://github.com/itanoss/example-annotation-processor-with-lombok).
you can see via `./gradlew assemble`.

Under JDK8:
```
$ ./gradlew clean assemble
...
Note: Constructors: [SomeValue(int,java.lang.String)]
Note: Parameter names: [arg0, arg1]
Note: Constructors: [SomeData(int,java.lang.String)]
Note: Parameter names: [arg0, arg1]
```

Under JDK9, 10 and 11:
```
$ ./gradlew clean assemble
...
Note: Constructors: [SomeValue(int,java.lang.String)]
Note: Parameter names: [id, name]
Note: Constructors: [SomeData(int,java.lang.String)]
Note: Parameter names: [id, name]
```

title: [FEATURE] Option to @With to drop the 'with' prefix
body:
Our shop very much embraces functional/immutable programming. Our immutable fluent interfaces don't have a `with` prefix; everything is expected to be immutable by default.

`final Thing newThing = oldThing.foo(foovalue).bar(barvalue);`

The `with` adds noise. In fact, mutable things are expected to have `set` prefixes because the noise stands out.

I notice that `@Builder` defaults to prefix-less fluent chains. We'd like to have some equivalent way of making `@Value @With` behave similarly. Maybe `@With(prefix="")` or `@With(prefix=false)`?

nodes.body: Seconding this. Software written with immutability in mind doesn't need to specially mark "withers".

title: [BUG] @JsonDeserialize not copied to the proper place?

nodes.body:
I had a similar issue with `@JacksonXmlProperty`, and created PR #2416 for it. It seems there are some more annotations that need to be put in that list...

* `@JacksonXmlProperty` is the XML counterpart to `@JsonProperty`. It allows XML-specific settings, e.g., setting the namespace. Copying it to the builder's setter will allow using a builder to deserialize XML when there are @JacksonXmlPropertys present. See also FasterXML/jackson-dataformat-xml#384.
* `@JsonIgnore`: If this annotation is present on either the field, the setter, or the getter, the property is completely ignored both on serialization and deserialization. However, as this annotation currently is not copied to the builder setter method, the property will _not_ be ignored when using a builder. That is inconsistent, thus lombok should copy that to the builder setter, too.
* `@JsonManagedReference`: Don't work within a builder, Jackson complains: `back reference type (model.Container) not compatible with managed type (model.Container$ContainerBuilder)`. Whether it could work depends on the order the instances are created: If the "inner" instance is created first, it could work. Not the other way round. The Jackson docs suggest it does not work, because that annotation also may not be put on a constructor parameter.
* `@JsonBackReference`: Also does not work, although the Jackson docs suggest that it should, because the "outer"/container object is already created at that time, so it should be possible to set that as the back reference. The error also looks like this is a bug: `Problem deserializing property 'back' (expected type: [simple type, class Container]; actual type: 'Container'), problem: object is not an instance of declaring class (through reference chain: Container["forward"])`. I created FasterXML/jackson-databind#2686 for this.
* `@JacksonInject`: Also works only if copied to the builder setter method. Thus, lombok should copy that, too.
I checked all annotations that look reasonable to me (see updated post above). Did I forget one?
I did: `@JsonAnySetter`, but that is a special case, because it also needs `@Singular` to work.
Hmm, what about `@JsonAlias` and `@JsonView`? I think that should be copied, too.
All merge requests have been fulfilled. Can someone verify the [edge release](https://projectlombok.org/download-edge)?
Works as expected.

Correction: Does not work for `@JsonDeserialize`. That's on me, I made a copy-and-paste mistake, and now the package name is wrong. :(
I'll file another PR.
There are a few more annotations I forgot. Updated PR.

title: [FEATURE] make builder class and methods also private if constructor is private

nodes.body:
Disclaimer: I'm not a Lombok team member, so just an opinion here.

Sometimes you want the builder to be the only way of instantiating your class, together with customizing the fields of the builder. In this case, you would do exactly that: define a private constructor and put `@Builder` on it.
So there is a use case for the current behavior, too.
It's difficult to decide which use case is the more common one.

However, changing Lombok's behavior here would be a breaking change. Furthermore you can use `@Builder(access = AccessLevel.PACKAGE)` to set the access level. So although your request sounds reasonable, I think it's better to stick with the current behavior.
Agree with Jan. There is a valid use-case for the current behaviour, and a way to change it, so there is no sense in breaking backwards compatibility

title: [BUG] Add support for the kotlin incremental compiler
body:
**Describe the bug**
The annotationprocessor entrypoint checks the actual runtime type of the ProcessingEnv and will immediately abort on modern versions of kotlinc, which is relevant as it's the default choice for the most recent android dev kit. The actual type of the processingEnv is:

https://github.com/JetBrains/kotlin/blob/master/plugins/kapt3/kapt3-base/src/org/jetbrains/kotlin/kapt3/base/incremental/incrementalProcessors.kt#L75

which is just a wrapper around the usual javac one probably (that class is a wrapper, I haven't yet investigated what it wraps, but presumably, standard javac), overriding only the filer, and the source of the filer is in that link as well. Shouldn't be too difficult to adjust the bits of lombok that need access to the AST to 'unwrap' the wrapper.

See also: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/project-lombok/xwnsiaRK3fM

nodes.body: I'm at this point not sure if the above problem description (that is: That we need to add a type of processingEnv) is still relevant, given that [the lombok plugin for kotlinc](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/lombok.html) exists. I'm closing this as duplicate of #1169.

I have a different similar large project with codemining turned on but without lombok and it doesn't suffer from this kind of delays. The only way to be sure is to simply delombok everything up front and
comparing it with the lombok version.

Thing is, to some extend a slowdown is to be expected.
1) lombok needs to do work when compiling. Codemining compiles everything,
possibly multiple times in parallel.
2) because lombok makes your code more compact you effectively have more
code on screen at any given time, so codemining has to do more work.

The question is whether this really is due to a bug in lombok or because
codemining is doing crazy things that get worse due to the circumstances
above.

nodes.body:
Sounds like a straightforward variant of

On Sat, Apr 18, 2020, 09:28 TreffnonX <notifications@github.com> wrote:

> Java does not have a generic placeholder to represent the actual current
> class, as opposed to the declaring class of any field, method, and thelike.
> This would be tremendously helpful e.g. with methods that are supposed to
> return the object which's method is called, similar to a builder-pattern:
>
> MySubclass myObject= ...;
> myObject.refresh().doSomethingElse();
>
> While the above will work, if doSomething is defined on or above the same
> type as refresh, this is - more often than not - not the case, especially
> if MySubclass is derived from a type declaring many standard functions for
> it's derivates. Assuming that refresh returns the called upon instance,
> it could be the same type as myObject, assuming at the time of
> invokation, I knew that type.
>
> To achieve this, and handle similar issues, a placeholder annotation type
> could be introduced, similar to the var and val types, which is then
> replaced in the declaring class (and all compilation units marked with a
> certain annotation). Consider the following example:
>
> @...public class MySupertype {
>     // will become signature:
>     // public MySupertype refresh();
>     public THIS refresh() {
>         //...
>         return this;
>     }
> }
>
> @Redeclarepublic class MySubtype  extends MySupertype {
>     // will redeclare all fields and methods with 'THIS':
>     // public MySubtype refresh() {
>     //     return super.refresh();
>     // }
>     // this implicitly declares the refresh method again, with the more specific return type of this class.
> }
>
> In this example, both MySupertype and MySubtype declare a refresh method,
> but with different return types. The only issue I see is that the
> compilation units are separate. However, since MyDerivedType is a subtype
> of MyHibernateType it should theoretically be possible to leave some
> trace in the supertype, which could then be used in the subtype to save the
> day.
>
> —

Except... you do it the `@SuperBuilder` way: Create a static inner class `ThisTypeHelper` (with fancy type params), which you could use as return type. That class provides a `get()` method, which has the correct return type (with the help of the type params).
I've not tested this, so I'm not sure that this really works. Similar to `@SuperBuilder`, you'd need it on every class in the hierarchy, and you'd have to call the `get()` method instead of just using the returned value. The `@ActualThisType` (or whatever it's called) annotation could replace relevant occurrences of `THIS` and `this` with the correct statement (e.g. `return this` in a method with return type `THIS` becomes `return ThisTypeHelper.for(this);`)
Don't know if that's worth it...

Well, if anyone has the expertise to implement something like that it's you

Thank you for trying though, it seemed simpler when I thought about it. But I understand that - more often than not - the restraints lombok must function under prevent such things. Hopefully, one day there will be a solution to this, but for now it seems we have to stick with the verbose redeclaraton.
Let's wait what the Lombok maintainers say. Maybe they have another idea.

There is [a possible solution](https://www.sitepoint.com/self-types-with-javas-generics/) that works without those type params:
* Rename the annotated class (e.g. `AbstractMySupertype`), make it abstract, and add the `<THIS extends A<THIS>>` type param and use it as return type.
  * Subclasses inherit from this abstract type (and will also be processed according to these steps).
* Create a public concrete implementation `MySupertype` without a type parameter.
* Create an interface with the orginal inheritance, so that `instanceof` on the concrete classes still works as expected.

However, there is a technical problem: lombok does not generate new compilation units, it just modifies existing ones. As the JLS does not allow more than one `public` class in a compilation unit, all other have to be package-private. So if you want to inherit from such a class across package borders, that won't work. That's a show-stopper IMO.

So users of the annotated class should only work with the interface? Then you need the type params on the interface, otherwise you won't have the actual return type. And then the problem with the unnecessary `<?>` remains. Or did I get you wrong?

How recent? At which version does it stop working?



On Mon, Nov 30, 2020, 17:37 Manuel Ryan <notifications@github.com> wrote:

> I'm also experiencing this error with the following code on lombok 1.18.12:
>
> @Value@Builder(toBuilder = true)public class MyClass {
>

>
>         @NotNull
> 	@Builder.Default
> 	private final List<@Valid MyObject> listOfValidObjects = Collections.emptyList();

I tested with jdk 11 (LTS) and I don't have the error. With jdk 15 (latest non-lts) I have the error. Seems to be related to annotations inside the method signature definition (in my case @Valid), if I remove the @Valid I don't have the error, even with jdk 15.

I hope this helps.

I'm not sure if this one is a lombok issue or not but I analyzed what happens and at least the generated internal structures are different. The regular java if condition gets translated to an AST like this on `JCIf -> JCParens -> JCBinary`, the EqualsAndHashCode if conditions to `JCIf -> JCBinary`. 
You can see that lombok doesn't add JCParens, thats most likely why jsweet fails to parse the the result properly. 

So I think there are two possible solutions: lombok generates the same structure than javac or jsweet learns that not every if condition is wrapped into a JCParens. Given that the `toString()` implementation of `JCIf` prints the lombok code properly I think this one have to be fixed in jsweet.
