title: [FEATURE] Configuration Option for @ToString to print in JSON format
body:
**Describe the feature**
The ability to configure the `@ToString` to output in JSON format as opposed to the default "class name, along with each field, in order, separated by commas."

Ideally, you could configure this setting on both a class level (via @ToString and @Data) annotations and on a global level (via lombok.config).

Local Examples:
```
@ToString(format = ToStringFormat.JSON)
public class POJO {

}
```

```
@Data(format = ToStringFormat.JSON)
public class POJO {

}
```

Global Example:

`lombok.config`
```
lombok.toStringFormat = JSON
```

**Describe the target audience**
JSON is a popular format for REST API.  I constantly find myself logging a POJO in json format so I can easily debug requests.  
It would be nice to do something like:
```
log.debug("POJO:  {}", pojo.toString()); //pojo.toString() prints in JSON format
```

As opposed to something like this:

```
log.debug("POJO:  {}", new Gson().toJson(pojo));
```

**Additional context**
Obviously, this is just a nice to have feature.  I only want it because of debugging and logging, but if I had to guess, there's probably some other devs out there that would like Lombok ToString to print in JSON format (and possibly other formats) for various reasons.  It would be nice to have some out of the box configuration options for the ToString method in general.

nodes.body:
The problem is that Lombok can't do it. It could change the format of the output, so it looks JSON-like, but when it delegates to another `.toString()`, things can break. I'm afraid, it can't do any better than generating
```
public String toString() {return new Gson().toJson(this));}
```
and that's something the user can do themselves in a much more flexible way.

Moreover, JSON lacks the information about the class, which is sometimes important for debugging.

The best solution that follows SOLID principals and Functional Programming would be to use Lombok `@ExtensionMethods` and create a` public static <T> String toJson(T source)` and implement it using a JSON formatter of your choice

This will then allow your code to look like: `String json = myobj.toJson();`

hi.
If we have a general config that we can say that **all toStrings are generated in json format**, then there will be no more inconsistencies.
Need to do this because we want to use tools like **logstash** and their json parser.
What is the opinion of the Lombok team in this regard?
No, that's still insufficient: `toString()` for classes like maps or sets does not work, as well as all classes without `@ToString`. There is simply no way to do this.

Apache's [ReflectionToStringBuilder](https://commons.apache.org/proper/commons-lang/apidocs/org/apache/commons/lang3/builder/ReflectionToStringBuilder.html) can do JSON format using [ToStringStyle.JSON_STYLE](https://commons.apache.org/proper/commons-lang/apidocs/org/apache/commons/lang3/builder/ToStringStyle.html#JSON_STYLE) and it is fantastic.

Yes, it does have some limitations and you can create non-parseable JSON if an included object is using a different ToStringStyle, but that is on the developer and is not the fault of the library. It may not create the most robust JSON, but I've never had it not work for debugging purposes.

It would be wonderful if I could simply tell Lombok to use Apache's class. As it is, I just never use Lombok's toString() except for the most basic program

If it would be feasible I'd prefer a generic config like

```
toString=new Gson().toJson(this));
```

... or whatever command a developer might prefer, instead of making lombok hard-coded dependent on whichever specific other library.

This would give maximum customisation while keeping lombok's effort and maintenance burden at a minimum.

Prerequisite: lombok's annotation processing can do such a thing easily.

I'm completely fine with "If it delegates to another toString that isn't JSON, then it breaks". This is the way Apache Common's JSON Reflection JSON toString() works and it's still very useful. This tradeoff is good for when speed is most important.

The other two options: Delegate to an JSON-P implementation or Google Gson would completely correct, however this would be at the cost of speed since both rely on reflection. 

Each use case will value speed vs correctness, and I'd assume let to the user make that decision. Thank you gentlemen!

It may be fine for you, but it will obviously create huge expectations that can never be fulfilled by Lombok due to technical reasons already explained here.

You won't have to answer the incoming pile of bug reports and feature requests. The Lombok team has to.

And don't just use performance as an argument again and again without plausible measurements. I doubt that a runtime-optimized Jackson serialization is much slower than a native implementation.

This is really important, the JSON format is more versatile. In fact, it is very simple to achieve this. There is no need to use libraries such as Gosn and Jackson. Lombok only needs to replace = with: (replace with {,) with } when outputting toString. This seems very simple, why doesn't lombok do this?
Or lombok provides a way for users to configure the output symbols of attributes in toString. The output symbols of objects can be configured by users themselves using =, (,) or: ,{,}.
Because it is _not_ simple, as explained above. Use a JSON library, because lombok will not implement it.

nodes.body:
Can confirm that it doesn't work using Java 14. It works without any problems using Java 8. 

During debugging I noticed that the value set in the `if` path of this snippet
https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/d54b360af9bdd66885badb80007d6839ea9d48f8/src/core/lombok/javac/handlers/HandleVal.java#L118-L122
breaks type resoultion which leads to this error. Simply using the `else` path works. I'm quite sure that this stuff is there for a reason and simply removing it will break other things...

Yes, the problem is that later java versions do more "target typing"

In short, this using target typing, binding of the types of parameters or return types depends on the type of the variable it is assigned to. 

Since the older compilers didn't care, we could just use `java.lang.Object`.

For the newer compilers, we use a non-existing type. The compiler should be able to handle that, since types could be created by an annotation processor in a later stage.

Possibly, the fix here is to make those non-existing types unique by adding a suffix (counter or random string).

The target typing problem would only be visible when using expression that depend on that. That would explain why in some code compiler using the 'else' route.

The type resolution for this example works properly, `val` gets replaced by `final java.lang.String` later in this handler. The created structure is exactly the same as the structure generated using `final java.lang.String` directly. The dummy type is not present anymore but gets set during the regular attribution stage. I guess that there is some kind of cache that gets polluted during type resolution, most likely one of the fields defined in `Context` but thats really hard to debug.

title: [BUG] @With - IllegalArgumentException: Not a parameterized type!
Allow noIsPrefix for getters on a per-getter basis

nodes.body:
IMHO there are just three usable options:

- You have to be javabeans compatible. Then you're partially out of luck as the crap is incompatible with itself (for fields named like `uShaped`), but in general, it works out of the box.
- You want to be consequent and always use "get" and "set" prefix. Then put `lombok.getter.noIsPrefix = true` in `lombok.config`.
- You want to use the fields name as for the getter and setter (like in a builder). Then use `lombok.accessors.fluent = true`.

So you'd actually be replacing 4 or 5 lines with a single parameter, which is definitely worth it for the readability if not the time saved. And people who don't want to use it can just ignore it. They don't have to see it in their code unless they're using it.

> you open your eyes

Crap on ideas all you want. But don't make it personal, please. Tone down your comments, this isn't the first time you've come across as abrasive (and that's coming from me, which presumably says something). The point is to be constructive, insinuating that other participants in this issue are lazy or incapable of drawing out ideas to their logical conclusion is decidedly not constructive.

> And people who don't want to use it can just ignore it.

IDE autocomplete dialogs will show it. This line of arguing is not going to change the status of this issue.

>  and see the rest of the required boilerplate

Exactly. Which is why this feature is dead in the water. The maintenance burden is significant, and that the linkage is weird: Changing the getter name doesn't just change the getter lombok generates, but also the equals and hashcode, with/builder 'deconstructors', and who knows what else.

The right place for messing with names is `@Accessors`. Which was never intended to mainly be used on a specific field, so it's not a light feature request if that is to carry the burden of picking the entire accessor name for a single field. However, `@Accessors`'s technical implementation in lombok already 'cascades': Check the field, and if it is not there, check the class, and if that's not there, check the config. That should mesh well with having it carry the job of what you're trying to accomplish with this feature request.

__To be crystal clear: This is __never__ going to be added to `@Getter` unless it is a complete reimagining of what `@Accessors` currently does.__

I am inclined to agree with OP that it would be a useful feature to enable the naming of specific fields' accessors to be coerced using annotations. Trying to figure out how to do that has led me here, after all.

I do find it surprising that Lombok hasn't adopted an approach similar to that used by libraries such as Jackson, whereby pretty much every globally configurable option can be overridden using annotations both at the class and the field level, as appropriate.

nodes.body: `val` is a sizable maintenance headache. I'm wondering if its smarter to just replace it with `final var` and retire the idea that it works on java8. I assume lots of you are using `val` together with java8, right?
For me,yes. when use java 17,usually use the effective fInally of java, it may ok to only use val for java 8.

@rzwitserloot
Yes, we're on Java 8. I know I'm comfortable with using `final var` over `val`. `final var` also translates to later versions of Java better than `val` does. Just to clarify are you suggesting dropping `val` entirely in a future release or just for certain Java versions?

Well, `var` was introduced in java 10; you can't use it on 8.

I'm thinking we should detect you're on 10+ and then translate `val` to `final var`. This is ever so very very slightly different from `val`, specifically:

* `val` allows multiple statements; var does not, e.g. `lombok.val x = 5, y = 10;` is legal, `var x = 5, y = 10` isn't.
* `var` will dutifully turn itself into unexpressible types. For example, `var x = new Object() { void foo() {}}; x.foo();` actually works, even though there's nothing you can replace `var` with that makes that work. Similar things happen if you use a ternary op such as `var x = a ? b : c` where b and c share multiple unrelated types (e.g. `Collection & Serializable` - `x` is then all of those types even though `Collection & Serializable x = null;` isn't legal java. `val` can't do those things currently nor are we planning to.

It's very minor. But annoying, in that if we change how  `val` works, it's not _just_ cosmetic / implementation detail. It can in theory break existing usages of `val` or even change behaviour, though that's a really exotic situation if that ends up changing behaviour.

Possibly it'll simply be gated by a setting. `lombok.val.toVar = true` or whatever in `lombok.config`. But then we're really throwing in the towel: The only real point to such a thing is: "We know it causes less problems". I use val a lot myself on eclipse and I fairly aggressively remove it when I see it (replace it with `var`) - because eclipse gets confused a lot more with `val` than it does with `var`. Not when your code is fine, but when you start having syntax errors, eclipse can make sense of what remains less well. Replacing it with `var`, all those issues would go away.

I don't foresee ever just deleting `val` from lombok outright. But I can see a world where we always translate it to `final var`, i.e. if you're on Java 8 it just won't work. It's one of a few reasons I truly severely dislike the line OpenJDK takes on what they think backwards compatibility means - the fact that so many folks are still on JDK8 for plausible reasons is exactly what I said was going to happen when jigsaw was introduced the way it was. Maybe a bit of a cassandra complex thing going on. But it really takes the wind out of the sails for my motivation to work on keeping `val` working properly the way it is set up now (which is a lot of work, it's all very tricky to make it work right).

Point is, so far we've taken the approach of thinking java8 will start being relegated to very low percentages faster than the maintenance burden overwhelms us - so, once java8 hits <5% numbers, just replace the functionality outright with `final var` and be done with it. But, the adoption rate of java8 is holding very steady. So I'm now reconsidering - I no longer think that's right.

That leaves the alternatives:

* Spend the effort.
* Just drop-in replace `final var` automatically on JDK10+. With an opt-out via lombok.config.
* Keep its current behaviour, don't spend the effort, but do add an opt-in to replace it with `final var`.

I'm leaning to the third option, but, __it would mean that `val` without opting in gets `experimental` level bugfix treatment__ - i.e. we aim to fix em but with less focus and time pressure. I think that's pragmatically speaking already how we treat it, because of the above reasons. So please don't advocate against it just because you think it'll motivate us to keep it functioning better than we do now.
@rzwitserloot We added this replacement some time ago in #2928.

Some how it also works use `val`, I just don't know what happened.
Summary:
1. version `1.18.24` both `lombok.var` and `lombok.val` not effect when the code block contains `INTERFACE.super.CALL()`
2. version `1.18.26` and `1.18.28` both effect.
@colonelpopcorn which version you are using?

(I forgot we already did this, Rawi01 reminded us in a comments 2 up from here) that on lombok 1.18.22 and java 10+, we already replace it with `final var`.  So, just.. shift to jdk17, and all will be well.

title: [FEATURE] "simple" @PostBuild annotation
body:
**Description**
The idea is to have a basic, simple, ability to validate (or post-process) an object created by a builder *without polluting lombok* `@Builder` with non-building problems ; to do so : 
- have the possibility to annotate _one_ instance no-arg-and-no-checked-throw method (of the class decorated with a builder) with a `@PostBuild`
Example:
```
@Builder
public MyClass {
    private String someField;
    
    @PostBuild
    private void validation() {
        // do stuff here
    }
}
```
- in the _lomboked_ version, that method would be called by the `.build()` _after_ creating the object, but _before_ returning it (instead of creation-return currently done)

**Precisions/Rationale/Benefits**
- separation of concerns: this avoids polluting `@Builder` with validation or other problems - the logic here is strictly build-related - "callback after object is built" (no need to support `@Validators` or `@WhateverChecker` by the builder, the validation logic is totally on developper-side in the annotated method ; and the method could be used for other things - eg. filling missing values, etc.)
- more expressiveness: the approah presented allow for more elaborate validation because at the time of callback, all fields are already set (eg. check of coherency between multiple interdependent fields)
- the restriction to only one instance no-arg-and-no-checked-throw seems reasonable
  - the method to call back should not have arguments
  - the method to call back should not have checked exceptions (otherwise this would pollute the signature of the `.build()` method)
  - one callback post build is enough, no need for more than one
  - only instance method will have access to the value of instance fields
- maintenability of post-processing code:
  - if an unchecked exception is raised from the `@PostBuild` annotated method, the stack would be "clean" (readable, leads directly to existing - as opposed to generated - code)
  - validation (the annotated method) is easy to debug (it's a normal method in normal code)
- minimal impact : the approach is totally compatible with current functioning of `@Builder` (eg. works if the constructor is generated by lombok or provided by the developper, etc.)

**Background**
- There is a recurring (but diverse) need for some checks of values of built object, eg.
[java - How to run code after constructor in a Lombok builder - Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/37968696/how-to-run-code-after-constructor-in-a-lombok-builder)
or [#674](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/674) that has a more ambitious scope.
or [java - Lombok builder to check non null and not empty - Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/44855981/lombok-builder-to-check-non-null-and-not-empty)
- the idea is somehow close to the [@After](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/wiki/FEATURE-IDEA:-@After) idea, but different (here we have a build-lifecycle callback)
- currently, the less "hacky" way to achieve a somehow similar result is to have an explicit all args constructor (which has to be manually updated every time the object fields change); at the end of the constructor do some validation of all fields.

**Stupid-proofing**
To detect invalid usage at compile-time :
- if a `@PostBuild` annotated method is not valid (not instance/no-arg/no throw...) : there is a compilation error
- if more than one method is `@PostBuild` annotated in a `@Builder`decorated class : compilation error
- if `@PostBuild` is used on a non-`@Builder`decorated class: compilation error

nodes.body:
Is this feature still open?
Can I take a look as a new contributor?

If I have not missed anything important the `@PostGeneratedConstructor` feature can be used for this one. The PR (https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/pull/2522) is there, it just needs to be merged. To be honest I have not tried if it works together with `@Builder`.

As far as I understand @PostGeneratedConstructor, you simply annotate the method to call, and it will be called from any generated constructor.

My proposal had several simplifying constraints (eg. no checked exceptions, etc.), but most importantly the behavior is guaranteed and does _not change upon subsequent modification of non-lombok related code_ (the same way @Builder tolerates auto generated constructors or developper-provided ones without changing the behavior of the code and without hidden side-effect).

With a PostGeneratedConstructor or a #1207 approach you have one real-life case of silent chnange in behavior : a class has initially only one generated all args + PostGeneratedConstructor (or #1207) _then_, later, a custom constructor is added by another developper : no warning, no error, but at runtime the validation (or method to call) is called or not depending on which constructor is called ; aka a subtle regression, that can comme up very late in testing or worse, after delivery of product.

This predictability and stability of behavior is (one of the reasons) why I framed my description as I did ; the Builder annotation is one of those cases where Lombok _can guarantee_ that the validation will always be called, whatever the type of constructor used by lombok.
Other Lombok annotations have this same nice quality of "behavior stability" against modification of code that is non-lombok related (+ edit/compil time warning in IDE if something is off, eg. you manually overwrite an auto-gen getter/setter)

To transpose that to your approach : I don't know if there's a nice way to at least add compile/edit time warnings to @PostGeneratedConstructor, so that the situation underlined above can be made apparent to the developpers.
Eg. something like
- if at least a @PostGeneratedConstructor is present in a class C and calls someMethod()
- and C also contains at least one non-generated constructors that do *not* call directly someMethod()
- then some warning is raised at compile/edit time

If I'm not clear, I apologize, do not hesitate to ask for clarifications.

The idea of `@PostGeneratedConstructor` is to handle the most common cases that right now can only be handled by replacing the generated constructor. The provided example is one of these cases where the annotation would solve the problem. 

You are right that a custom constructor might behave different but thats actually the reason why `Generated` is part of the annotation name. Lombok cannot know if you want to call the annotated method or not, what it does is throwing an error if there is no generated constructor at all. 

I think that in most `@Builder` related cases the annotation should work. If you use the default constructor generated by `@Builder` everything should be fine. If you add a custom constructor later on, lombok will show a compilation error. 

It is also possible to override the `build()` method so it can not be guranteed that it calls `@PostBuild`

>  It is also possible to override the build() method so it can not be guranteed that it calls @PostBuild.

Well, TIL, damn.

> Lombok cannot know if you want to call the annotated method or not, 

It was more the following, _the annotation being the marker_ of the "intent", ex.:
- say, a class is annotated with `@PostGeneratedConstructor`
- the class already has some generated constructor (say AllArgs)
- some time later (may be years) a new dev (not necessarilly aware of the effect of the annotation) manually adds a custom constructor

Then you have 3 cases:
- the custom constructor delegates to the all args -> the post processing will be done, no problem
- the custom constructor does not delegate to the all args, but explicitelly calls the post processing -> the post processing will be done, no problem
- the custom constructor, does none of the above -> *problem*, no post processing, this is where I imagined a warning could exist (eg. "Your constructor does not invoque the [post processing X] but all synthetic constructors do.")

But, if its not technically possible, that settles it, then.

`@PostGeneratedConstructor` it is.

I still think that `@PostConstructor` cover most of the usecases. Field level validation/transformation before object creation is the only thing that is not possible this way. Did I miss something?

I also think that it is pretty easy to understand that a methode annotated with `@PostConstructor` gets called after the object creation. With a proper name (e.g. `validate`) almost everyone should be able to understand what the method does.

Oh, interesting. Uh.. yeah that works. Oof that's ugly. But it works. Should we... go for that? Presumably the number of times you add `@PostConstructor` whilst also having your own constructors is not all that common. It will pile that cruft into your code (and might trigger linter tools), and will pile that cruft into your delomboked code as well, which is a bit of a downside.
@rzwitserloot Thats what my PR does if it detects a `return`. In all other cases it adds the method calls to the end.
Ah, there's a PR, 🤦 - that's why all this sounds so familiar.

> Having any method named 'unsafe' anywhere seems crazy to me.

Fair enough. 

There are two things that need to be done: build and validate. If the expectation is that the `build()` method will return a validated object, then it needs to validate before it returns. That's why I suggested breaking it into two pieces: 

1. A private method that does what the build method does today (just constructs an object). Call it what you want, but it has to be different than the public method. 
2. A public method that calls the private method, validates the result, and then returns it.  

I don't see any fundamental problem with the approach and it works pretty well for me already. Currently, however, there is no way to make the build method private, which means I'm left with an extra public method on my builder class that isn't supposed to be called. Having the option to set `buildMethodAccess = AccessLevel.PRIVATE` seemed like a low risk, backward compatible change that would allow for a clean pattern for inserting build validation logic. Maybe I'm missing something here. 

If Lombok implements the @PostBuild feature, sure -- no need for an extra method if you want to just add the call to the PostBuild method at the end of the build method. Not an approach I can apply today, though.

As for @PostConstructor ... it sounds like a nice feature, but it also sounds a _lot_ more complex than the original @PostBuild request. What will Lombok guarantee?

e.g. 

* what if one constructor calls another -- how many times will the validation method be called? Remember that constructors can call other constructors and change state afterward. 
  * what if the validation method has a side-effect, such as logging metrics?
  * what if validation is expensive or requires a call to an external system?
* Lombok will not be able to prevent other classes from getting references to instances that haven't had their @PostConstructor method invoked. Will that be the expectation of the average developer?

Guarantees about some sort of @PostBuild annotation seem more manageable. e.g. "If the class annotated with @ Builder has a method annotated with @PostBuild, the auto-generated build method will guarantee the PostBuild method is called exactly once before returning the new instance to the caller".

I agree with phiferd on this.

There is a large population of Lombok users today who are really struggling
to properly implement the builder pattern when there is anything beyond the
most simple of cases, and I think it is a very good idea to put the focus
on solving those problems - especially if the solution is simple and not
controversial.

Having buildMethodAccess = AccessLevel.PRIVATE added to @Builder would be
more than sufficient, and seems like it would be simple to implement,
forwards and backwards compatible, and very low risk.

Our code has so many places where we are having to hand-write build() when
Lombok could absolutely be doing it for us - if we could just make
the generated method private.  Adding a field to our builder classes
requires changes in multiple places.  If the order of the fields change
(and therefore the order of the fields in the constructor changes) it's an
even bigger nightmare. We are making design tradeoffs between "do we take
the risk of things silently breaking when we add or adjust fields? or do we
try to do code review to prevent anyone from calling the wrong build()
method?".  As an architect, these are not tradeoffs that I am happy having
to make.

FWIW - I believe that the buildMethodAccess idea was proposed in October
2017  (https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/1489 ).


A @PostBuild (or @PreBuild) annotation would be a little cleaner as it
would mean we wouldn't have to actually declare the builder class.  But the
real need is to make the build() method private so we can add our own
public method that validates/transforms then delegates to the private
Lombok generated build() method.


Long and short:  @PostBuild (and similar) are nice-to-haves.  Controlling
access level of the build method is a game changer that will make @Builder
actually usable for tons of cases where it is not being helpful today.

The lombok configuration system caches the file content and only reads it again if the last modified timestamp changes. title: [FEATURE] @Creator annotations to get instances of an annotated inner class.

nodes.body:
While this one is technically possible I do not understand why such a method is required if a simple constructor call (`box.new Jack()`) would be sufficient. To be honest I do not use non-static nested classes that often.

Disclaimer: I'm not a project owner.

The point is, `createJackInABox` is overloadable, while`box.new Jack()` will always and ever return an instance of exactly `Jack`.
What if `Jack` is abstract to begin with? In my example. this would generate an abstract method, that I could call and I would get a more specific instance of something extending `Jack` during runtime. This feature would specifically be helpful for certain factory-patterns where the outer class delivers a specific instance, but can be overloaded, so that a more specific classes instance is returned.
But I am beginning to believe that my use case might be more specific than I first anticipated, and I am not so sure anymore this belongs in lombok.

title: [FEATURE] @Builder on an interface method
body:
# Use case:

I have this method defined in class `DbConnection`:
```
    @Builder(builderClassName = "MultiInsertBuilder", builderMethodName = "insertMultiple", buildMethodName = "insert")
    int insertMultipleValues(
            @Nullable Table table,
            @Singular Collection<? extends List<?>> values,
            Boolean ignoreDuplicates, /* ignore by default */
            Integer batchSize /* default 1000 */
    ) {...}
```

Now I have to extract an interface because there are different implementations for Oracle and Postgres.

Simply adding the annotation on a method in an interface leads to:
> error: non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context

# Implementation

There are a couple things that need to change in comparison to a builder on a method in a `class` or `enum`:

* the method returning a new builder instance must be marked as `default`.
* the class of the builder is static (that is how interfaces work), therefore it must capture the instance of the outer interface explicitly; instead of calling `DbConnection.this.insertMultipleValues(...)`, it should create:
```
        private final DbConnection $that;

        MultiInsertBuilder(DbConnection $that) {
            this.$that = $that;
        }
```
and change the call to: `return $that.insertMultiValue(...)`

# Concerns

* This only works in Java 8+ since it relies on default methods. I don't think it harms not to support older versions. For older versions:
  * the builder method can simply be not generated (not forward-compatible solution), 
  * alternatively this use of Builder will cause an error (forward-compatible solution).
Or we may decide never to generate the builder method but that despite being forward-compatible would be limiting to many users.
* How the field should be called? `$that`, `$enclosing`, `$outer`?

# Builder Support

I also found that `@Builder` is allowed on enum's constructor, which causes a compile error:
> error: enum types may not be instantiated

It is not entirely related to this feature request, but can probably be fixed at the same time. I assume that we want to report an error to the user in such situation.

|  | type | method | constructor | 
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| class | Works | Works | Works |
| enum | Error | Works | Bug |
| interface | Error | Proposition | N/A |

nodes.body:
Ok, I started implementing it; it does not look hard; verbose but doable.

So far I only have one question: `com.sun.tools.javac.code.Flags` does not contain constant for `DEFAULT` because it was not a modifier in Java 6 (`net.java.openjdk.custom-javac6.jar`). How should I handle this?

---

I was fooled by error messages from Intellij plugin instead of Lombok itself. Actually the table should look like this (proposed improvement is highlighted):

|  | type | constructor | method | static method |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| class | Works | Works | Works | Works |
| enum | error: enum types may not be instantiated | error: enum types may not be instantiated | Works | Works |
| interface | error: $typename is abstract; cannot be instantiated | N/A | **error: non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context** | Works |
| annotation interface | error: modifier static not allowed here | N/A | error: non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context | N/A |

Just a hint: Before you invest too much time on a pull request, you should wait for some feedback from the maintainers. There may be reasons why this does not work (and should not work). One could be that this is not a real builder pattern any more, but a kind of method-argument collector.

I would simply not generate the `builder()` method. If you are on java8+, you could still add it manually to the interface or to the implementing class, as it's quite trivial.

title: [FEATURE] Add support for class fields metadata similar to Kotlin reflection
body:
In Kotlin to get a field metadata is very simple
```
class A(val p: Int)
val prop = A::p
```
Most usual use case is to get the field name `A::p.name`. This is also similar to C# `nameof`.
It will be very useful for mapping in persistence entities, in json mapping, in validation.

I propose to add a new annotation `@ReflectionMetadata` which will create a new field in the class
```
@ReflectionMetadata
class Point {
    private Integer x;
    private Integer y;

    public static final $PointReflectionMetadata $meta; // this will be generated
```
So, it will be possible
```
Point::$meta.x.name
```

nodes.body: This is already covered by https://projectlombok.org/features/experimental/FieldNameConstants

The following example reproduces the issue. Make sure to be on the edge-SNAPSHOT or latest master. Versions lower or equal to 1.18.12 will lead you to #2359.

```java
@SuperBuilder
public class ClassA<T> { }
```
```java

```

title: [BUG] lombok.NonNull handled differently from checkerframework.NonNull

nodes.body:
I agree that this behaviour is a little bit confusing. In general lombok only modifies/creates stuff that is annotated and  `checkerNonNull` is actually a normal method that works without lombok.

I think there are multiple solutions:
- Use [Accessors](https://projectlombok.org/features/experimental/Accessors) (this might work only in this example)
- Use both annotations at the same time
- Remove the generated `null` check for non-lombok `@NonNull` annotations. This will most likely break some stuff.
- Modify lombok to also add `null` checks for [all the other annotations](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/7dfbe4323c15cbd88983380b27a250d2a381d148/src/core/lombok/core/handlers/HandlerUtil.java#L82). This might be even more confusing as it modifies classes without a single lombok annotation.
- Modify lombok to add `@NonNull` checker framework annotation if its own `@NonNull` annotation is present. Thats something thats already there for some other handlers.
- Use meta annotations (#557)

Disclaimer: I'm not a project owner.

So far, our reasoning was: 
- If a field is annotated with any NonNull, the intention is 100% clear. We can add null-checks to constructors and setters.
- If we would insert null-checks for external NonNull annotations, we're not 100% certain that that's what expected.

Currently, if you've configured you're using the checker framework in `lombok.config`, we generate a lot of checker framework annotations to help with static analysis. I'm not sure if the `org.checkerframework.checker.nullness.qual.NonNull` is one of them, but we could.

title: [FEATURE] Type-safe builder

nodes.body:
I know this one as `Step builder pattern`. 
The implementation should be quite simple, it requires no fancy additional stuff and it removes a bunch of boilerplate code so this one seems to be a good candidate for a lombok feature. The only problem is that it creates a bunch of additional interfaces and that might slow down compilation. 
One thing that should be considered is how this one gets enabled. Possible soloutions: `@Builder(required = true)`, `@StepBuilder`, `@Builder(steps = true)`, `@Builder.Steps`, ...

Disclaimer: I'm not a project owner.

title: Contradictory Builder documentation regarding access level of @AllArgsConstructor
body:
There is an inconsistency between the website documentation and the Javadoc documentation with regards to the access level of the generated constructor.  One claims that it is package access level; the other that it is private.

### Javadoc
https://projectlombok.org/api/lombok/Builder.html
> If a class is annotated, then a private constructor is generated with all fields as arguments (as if `@AllArgsConstructor(access = AccessLevel.PRIVATE)` is present on the class), and it is as if this constructor has been annotated with `@Builder` instead.

### Website
https://projectlombok.org/features/Builder
> Finally, applying `@Builder `to a class is as if you added `@AllArgsConstructor(access = AccessLevel.PACKAGE)` to the class and applied the `@Builder` annotation to this all-args-constructor.

## Expected behavior
The two sources of documentation should be consistent with each other, and match whatever Lombok is actually doing.

## Version info:
 - Lombok version: 1.18.12
 - Platform: N/A

nodes.body: This is already fixed: https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/pull/2515

> This is already fixed: #2515

Thanks. I did some searching before creating the issue, but I clearly missed that one.

title: Lombokify/Delombokify should convert/deconvert constructor calls to invoke builder
body:
**Before submitting**

I have not found a pre-existing request for this feature

**Describe the feature**

When Lombok is introduced into a project, I have found it commonplace to find places where the builder pattern should have been used but wasn't done perhaps due to someone not bother to coding the builder (or not knowing that most IDEs can generate it).

Accordingly, it would be nice if there was a way for Lombokify to take and not very-well self-documenting long constructor call like:

      new Member("david", "blickstein", null, "1600 Pennsylvania Ave",  null,  null,    3,   "", new Date(),  0, 0, 4, null, null)

And turn it into an invocation of a Lombok builder.     Or perhaps an IDE plugin.

nodes.body:
Lombok itself does not offer such refactoring operations.

When you speak of "lombokify", I think you are referring to a feature of the IntelliJ Lombok plugin. That is a separate project: https://github.com/mplushnikov/lombok-intellij-plugin

title: [FEATURE] Composition builder

nodes.body:
After reading https://jonasg.io/posts/object-mother/ under:

> But what if your test requires a specific field in one of the nested custom objects to be in a particular state? [...]

I wondered if lombok had this functionality.

Sadly this does not seem to be the case, and it would definitely help in having a maintainable test architecture. Is there any update on this?

I don't see the upside. For starters, you're asking for months of work in a simple feature. "Any update on this?" is a bit.. I dunno. Comes across as rude and entitled, but perhaps I'm reading too much into it.

At any rate, denied. This is silly - what possible gain is here? Why is this:

```
.phone()
.type(PhoneType.HOME)
.number("1234-5678")
.continueUser()
```

superior to?

```
.phone(Phone.builder()
  .type(PhoneType.HOME)
  .number("1234-5678")
  .build())
```

I'm quite sure it isn't which makes this request pointless. I'll keep an eye out. This issue is closed either way - even if there's some sense to this idea, it's far too large to just keep on the books as 'something we will get around to' - it'll need a PR with a full implementation, tests, docs, the works - and that's _only_ if someone can convince us there is a point to this. Quite a steep hill to climb, so closing it.

I definitely didn't want to come off as rude :-) Sorry if it came across that way! I'm aware the time of an OSS maintainer is valuable and it is often a thankless job. I'd also hate to imply that I'm demanding for this to be implemented!

 Thank you for taking the time to reply @rzwitserloot !

title: [FEATURE] Allow Lombok annotations to fail silently
body:
**feature description**
Add a property to lombok.config "failSilently" (boolean, default: false). False will produce the current behaviour while setting it to true just ignores failing annotations completely. No build errors/warnings are produced.

**target audience**
Users of code-generation (like openapi-generator) would still be able to use their tool in combination with lombok.

**examples that should not fail anymore**:
* Adding `@AllArgConstructor` `@NoArgConstructor` to a no-property class (openapi: allOf with no extra properties)
* Adding `@AllArgConstructor` to an interface (openapi: oneOf with discriminator)

nodes.body:
Honestly I do not understand why you need that, most likely because I have no idea what openapi-generator does. Can you give an example? In general it sounds like a bad idea to silently throw away errors, especially if that gets used project wide.

Disclaimer: I'm not a project owner.

openapi generator generates java code from an openapi specification file. You can create inheritance structures. It also allows to specify annotations which it simply applies to every type it generates. There are certain kinds of specs that produce either empty classes or simple interfaces. This prevents lombok annotation usage because when the generated java code compiles, it will fail.

By failing silently it allows one to use lombok in combination with those generated classes. You could use two different lombok configs. One in project root, the other in generated client root.

I have not thought about a second config only for the generated code, that seems to be okayish. A flag like this should be possible, if I have not missed anything it should be quite easy. I still think that it would be the best soloution to update the generator to only generate valid code.

The problem with that would be, that Lombok would have to become a first class citizen of openapi generator since there is no way for the generator to know, that a Lombok type annotation has more validation other than those that Java provides out of the box (ie Retention and Target).

Thanks for the confirmation, that this is indeed possible! And thanks for your time!

Regarding adding the same annotation to an interface, I would consider that a problem with the code generator.

Also, this sounds like a very specific problem (AllArgs and NoArgs when there are no fields), and a very broad suggested solution. I can imagine that we can NOT generate a warning in this specific scenario.

IIRC, Lombok does not error in this case. We emit a warning. In generated code, I would accept warnings.

Note that javac goes out of its way to allow you to have generics on each 'element' in a dotted type name, even though in common java you just never encounter generics anywhere except on the final element. This makes the code of javac considerably more convoluted, and ecj has this as well, which is a very light indication that in this particular instance, ecj's got it wrong, and this IS proper java syntax after all.

title: [FEATURE]

nodes.body:
As Joshua Bloch says in his book "Effective Java", "Consider alternatives
to Java serialization."

This kind of nonsensical stuff is one the reasons why.

The maintainers have repeatedly stated they are trying to prevent a massive
growth in the number of parameters the lombok annotations take. That means
that features like this have a really high bar to clear, one of which is
that this has to be a common code pattern. Which may be true for your
project, but without serialization this problem goes away and serialization
in general is on it's way out.

At least in it's current form. The java language designers have stated they intend to redesign it. (https://adtmag.com/articles/2018/05/30/java-serialization.aspx?m=1)

Reading that stack overflow post one of the ways to counter this is to
implement default readObject() and writeObject() methods that call the ones
on the superclass. This sounds like a way forward. That can be a new
annotation, meaning people not using serialization aren't affected by it
and the maintenance burden for parameters on getter/setter/accessor isn't
increased.

Could this work for you?

title: [FEATURE] Allow @Log4j2 (and probably its cousins) on interfaces
body:
Since Java 8 allows static variables in interfaces, couldn't the `Log4j2` annotation apply there as well as classes?
I think this may be literally a one word change, plus a comma.

nodes.body: Hovewer both static fields and static inner classes in interfaces cannot be private.
I don't think it is common enough to have a public logger in an interface. Also, accessing the logger when implementing multiple interfaces with log fields would also be interesting.

@rspilker — I just ran across some code in the wild (that otherwise uses the Lombok logging annotations) that creates a static logger on an interface for use within its own default methods.  So this feature could be used within an interface without accessing the logger externally to the interface.

But the point about it being non-private still applies.

Making em public feels really ugly, though. The handicapped nature of default methods (you can't have constants at all unless you make them public, and you can't have private static inner classes either) means I usually just make a package private class in the same package with the meat and potatoes and then farm the work out to this from the default method. That also solves the logging issue.

title: [Question] Would it be possible for lombok not to use javac internal APIs, but to generate "real" code when processing annotations?
body:
It is "well known" that Lombok uses javac internal APIs.
My question is:
It is (now?) possible to generate code using annotation processors to generated code (i.e. using java poet) so the code is compiled "as-is" without the usage of internal apis. Would it be feasible to write Lombok so this is done? If yes, is it planned? Is there a reason not to do so?

nodes.body: Lombok actually is an annotation processor. Unfortunately it is not possible to modify an existing class using the standard api, thats why lombok uses the internal API.
Thanks a lot!

nodes.body:
As lombok is a compile-time-only dependency, there should be no runtime differences on different machines, even with differing java versions (which you do not seem to have). Once the class file was generated, lombok simply does not exist any more from the viewpoint of the JVM executing the class file. So I doubt that this is a lombok issue.

My guess is that there is something wrong with your classpath. For instance, you may accidently have a conflicting class `ManageReportDto` somewhere else in your classpath, causing the classloader on your deployment system to load another class file than locally.

another old dependency with ManageReportDto was there in my classpath. That has caused the problem.

title: Variables with similar names - "Cannot find Symbol" for getter method

nodes.body: I can confirm that lombok only generates one getter if there are two fields sharing the same name with different upper and lower case characters. It's quite funny that `@EqualsAndHashCode` and `@ToString` still try to use these methods. Seems to be a bug.

I think the root cause is here. It's because lombok checks getter names without case sensitivity.
https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/blob/8943b49dfed95228e324422435a77597a95943c0/src/core/lombok/javac/handlers/HandleGetter.java#L203
I'm curious why...

And also it shouldn't work for the eclipse compiler because it also has the same check...

It was introduced here:
https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/commit/89d60fcebbd86c971b9b564c7bd68903978c0649
@rzwitserloot Is it some kind of feature?

Original issue: https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/148, https://groups.google.com/g/javaposse/c/4AzRsqJdzKM

It seems like the reason for this behaviour is to handle cases where someone wants to add a method like `getURL` by hand and not generate a lomobk method. As that could also solved using `@Getter(AccessLevel.NONE)` I think that lombok should switch back to case sensitv method name comparision.

title: [FEATURE] Create a @Constants annotation, which marks all fields as public static final.
body:
Many applications need at least one file of constants. These classes often contain exclusively `public static final` fields, and possibly `protected` or `private` members.

This feature request is for an annotation called `@Constants`, which is like a combination of `@UtilityClass` and `@FieldDefaults(level = AccessLevel.PUBLIC, makeStatic = true, makeFinal = true)`, the latter of which does not yet exist with a `makeStatic` argument.

This will save a large vertical column of field access modifiers from these lists of constant values.

nodes.body:
The trouble with that type of class is that this is actually not a
engineering practice I would recommend.

See
https://softwareengineering.stackexchange.com/questions/290006/good-practice-to-hold-constants-in-their-own-file
for example.

title: [BUG] Breaking change in 1.18.4 but only patch part of version updated
body: The last version 1.18.4 includes a breaking change: https://projectlombok.org/changelog - but only the patch version was updated. It broke our nightly builds since we have a + on the patch version. Do you not follow https://semver.org/ and can this be expected again?

nodes.body: One of the maintainers wrote a statement about semver [here](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/2115#issuecomment-583779474), I think you can expect it to happen again.

There are only two ways to correctly use semver:
- Keep the major version number at 0. According to semver, this means all versions are experimental and there are no guarantees regarding backwards compatibility.
- Always increment the major version number. There are no guarantees regarding backwards compatibility.

Even a bugfix is an observable change in behavior that potentially breaks some other person's build. Given the amount of users we have, this has happened for nearly all bugfixes in the past.

We do increment the minor version number if we expect a bigger impact. You could say we do loose semver.

title: Declare `@Synchronized` lock fields as `Object[]` instead of `Object`
body:
**Describe the feature**
Instead of declaring the lock fields (`$lock`, `$LOCK`, and `readLock`) as `Object`, they should be declared as `Object[]`.

Declaring a lock object field as type `Object` is a uniquely poor choice, because it is the one and only datatype in Java that could be either an array or a non-array object. Implementations such as OpenJ9 use a different offset for the lock word depending on whether or not the object is an array. That means if (and only if) your field is declared as an `Object`, the jit-generated code must contain a branching sequence that tests whether the object is an array.

For any other field type, this extra code is not needed.

**Describe the target audience**
Users of `@Synchronized` on OpenJ9 and any other JVM using different lock word offsets for arrays versus non-arrays.

nodes.body:
I never thought about something like this and I only found [this](https://blog.openj9.org/2019/04/02/lock-nursery/). I might have missed something but I think that OpenJ9 uses lock words for `j.l.Object` and completly excludes arrays. If I assume that the lock word stuff is faster than regular locks an array implementation will be slower than the current one.
Can you provide more details why you think that an array is faster?
I agree with @Rawi01 that possibly a better fix would be to replace the Object[] with something else that is an Object, Serializable and small. Something like `new Integer(0)`.

title: Lombok does not play nice with Error Prone
body:
Running Error Prone on classes with Lombok annotations (e.g. `@Data`, `@Slf4j`) crashes compilation.

Here is an example:
https://github.com/google/error-prone/issues/1700

nodes.body:
There are two problems here: Lombok does not update the end position table and Error Prone does not skip the generated code. The first one can be fixed but that unfortunately only replaces the exception with an warning/error (at least in some cases). To also remove that one Error Prone has to skip generated code. There is a command-line flag `-XepDisableWarningsInGeneratedCode` for that which can be used together with `lombok.addJavaxGeneratedAnnotation = true` but that will only work if you use Java <= 8 or if you add `javax.annotation.Generated` to your classpath. 

A possible solution is to add `javax.annotation.Generated` for Java <= 8 and `javax.annotation.processing.Generated` for Java 9+.

@Rawi01 Adding Java `@Generated` annotation will not help, since it has `@Retention(SOURCE)`.
In any case, the issue is that currently build crashes with exceptions instead of producing Error Prone messages. I understand from your comment that this is something that can/should be fixed in Lombok.

This has to be fixed by error-prone, perhaps try to file a feature request there / search for an existing one to subscribe to. There is nothing we can do, short of extensive hackery of error-prone's internals (well beyond what's reasonable / possible on our side). They need to add the ability to mark some annotation as indicating: "Skip this method, entirely", and then you can tell lombok to generate this annotation.

If such a facility already exists - can you reply to this issue with some more details about how to configure it (or, alternatively, perhaps there is e.g. `@com.google.errorprone.Skip`, and lombok can generate that annotation - then reply with the docs on this feature); we could add a page on the website that explains how to set this up, that sounds like a fine addition.

Lombok can (and should) add new fields/methods/types to the end position table (`Javac.storeEnd`). 

@sergeykad Why should `@Retention(SOURCE)` be a problem for a compiler plugin like Error Prone? If it is useless the flag would not exist.

> Lombok can (and should) add new fields/methods/types to the end position table (Javac.storeEnd).

Probably, but it won't fix the errorprone situation; at best, combining errorprone+lombok without errorprone having facilities to ignore generated methods results in errorprone raising a ton of irrelevant flags on lombok code (irrelevant, in that none of them are bugs or leaks or otherwise problematic).

About `javax.annotation.Generated`: It is a dumb and useless annotation. Partly because of that idiotic retentionlevel (source-level linting tooling can use it, but there's plenty of class-level linting tools around, they can't use this, not to mention other class-level tools that could use 'this code is generated' information), but mostly because during jigsaw this annotation got effectively backwards broken, so the few people and tools that generated it (like lombok) had to break backwards compatibility too and stop generating it.

I hate this annotation. It is beyond clear that the shepherds of it (oracle/openjdk) cannot be trusted with it. I strongly advocate that all libraries involved stop using it. The only reason lombok can be coerced into generating it at all is because we used to, and we wanted to give an easy upgrade path to those users of lombok who have integrated it into their projects and now cannot easily back out of its use.

Thus: We support it, whilst advocating in no uncertain terms that this annotation is bad and should never be used.

As a followup, that does mean life is so much harder for communicating the notion of 'generated'. I don't like that errorprone doesn't have a skip annotation, but in their defense, had they 'joined the bandwagon' and built in support for `javax.annotation.Generated` then errorprone+lombok still wouldn't actually work out of the box, and potentially they'd be in the same boat (where Generated causes issues when upgrading from 8 to a jigsaw-supporting JDK with broken Generated). Thus, it is understandable, perhaps, that errorprone has no such annotation nor support for it. Nevertheless, they're going to have to build it or lombok+errorprone is never going to be a nice experience.

title: [FEATURE] spring-boot main annotation (e.g. @SpringBootMain)

nodes.body:
It is really useful to replace 3 (or 4 with annotation suppressing coverage tool which you can add there manually even now) lines of code with 1 line once in an application? There are also scenarios which require doing stuff before calling `run` (setting up `MDC` for example), in which cases the annotation will not be useful.

From my experience, the main class of Spring Boot applications often exists only to have the main method, so the presence of the main method does not pollute it. The main method is also not a place where people would make mistakes.

Some project generators already generate the main class with the main method for you, so you actually need to manually replace the method with the annotation. The generators will not switch to using Lombok for just one annotation as there are people who don't want to use Lombok. Setting up Lombok is another place where things can go wrong for newbies who would then blame Spring for being hard/tricky to use.

Lombok is a tool which is very hard to maintain, it is not as easy as adding a template with desired expansion, which by the way you can do in your IDE.

We can go a bit further: why not having an annotation (for example in `package-info.java`) for generating the whole main class? This would actually be much easier as regular annotation processors are designed to produce new class files (instead of modifying existing ones which Lombok does).

Just my two cents. I am not a Lombok maintainer, I am a user and I have contributed once, so I am knowledgeable of its internals.

Reinier and I really do not care about the code coverage problem. I don't even see the problem? Is the main method not executed? Talk to the developer of your code coverage tool on how to configure it to not report this main method.

Also, we're talking about replacing 3 lines of boilerplate by one annotation. In the whole project. That's not enough to warrant the extra maintenance burden.

title: [FEATURE] extend @Setter to optionally add a boolean condition

nodes.body:
> `user.setName(StringUtils.isNotBlank(name), name);`

This seems much harder to read than:

> `if (StringUtils.isNotBlank(name)) user.setName(name);`

I assume the source of this request is misguided style guide hokey pokey, where the above would not pass linter tools and needs to be a 3 liner. As the doctor said when the patient came in and says: Doc, it hurts when I press here!

Stop doing that.

I mean it - style guides, linter tools, code quality checkers - these are tools. If you find you write this code so often you want lombok assistance, maybe they need to be revisited at your org. I would not generally multiline such an interaction, and the fact that you'd be willing to one-liner it if lombok made this method suggests that the fundamental notion of doing 'two' things (writing a condition that needs checking, and writing an expression along with a set method to send it to) on a single line if only lombok made you a single method to do it suggests that as a fundamental principle you're okay with it too. Tools need to be used, until they are no longer fit for the purpose you picked them up for, then they need to be abandoned or changed.

I know that me trying to explain to the java community that mandatory braces is overzealous is probably Old Man Yelling At Cloud levels of futile. However, even if I get past my 'geez, we are working around silly style maxims now?' hangup on this feature request, there's still two further considerable problems:

1. For human eyeballs, it's rather hard to 'parse' `.setAge(age != null && age > 0, age);` Will people immediately clue in that this code sets if the condition is true and is a no-op if not? It's not idiomatic, right? I have never seen this commonly used.
2. I find it morally objectionable to help somebody, if what they want help with, is dig their own grave. The problem with this mindset is that it's the 'silently do nothing on unexpected input' mindset. In my experience, this mindset is extremely detrimental to code quality. So, in general, if this really is idiomatic, I hate it. If someone calls `.setAge(-1)`, then either age needs to become -1, or an exception should occur. "Silently do nothing, leave age what it was" is bad code style; it means that if you have a bug that leads to age being -1, then nothing happens, which means finding that bug is going to be a wild goose chase. That's bad. Exceptions are nice: They point at the problem. However, it is unclear with such a `@ConditionSetter` idea what lombok is doing if the condition fails. Exception? Silently do nothing?

Between it not being idiomatic and being confusing, this stands no chance - closed.

title: [FEATURE] Create object from builder object, instead of all arg constructor

nodes.body:
Lombok already accomplishes the stated goal ('prevent all ways of constructing the object except via the builder') by making that all args constructor `private`. We can debate if this strategy is a better way to accomplish the goal than the one lombok has chosen, but at this point your feature request gets the considerable additional burden of being so much better that it warrants a sizable backwards compatibility break, which it stands no chance in hades of getting over.

Perhaps your intent is instead that even code within the same source file needs to forced into going via the builder. Yup, your solution would accomplish this, whereas lombok's current impl doesn't do that. But I don't think that's worthy enough to complicate matters by making e.g. a setting or a parameter on the builder.

Note that `@SuperBuilder` works exactly like this. I don't advise using features just because by total coincidence their implementation details currently lines up with what you need, but, stick a `@SuperBuilder` on there and you'll get this, I think.

title: [BUG] Lombok and MapStruct no longer work on JDK 1.8

title: [BUG]
body:
**Describe the bug**
@Builder results in name shadowing

**To Reproduce**
Using eclipse set name shadowing to be Error instead of Warning or Info.
The @Builder will get a red flag

**Expected behavior**
There shouldn't be any name shadowing happening.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - 1.18.16
 - Java 14
 - Eclipse 2020-09

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here.

nodes.body:
The solution: don't set it to Error. We do add @SuppressWarnings, but we cannot suppress Errors.

The errors are the result of an inner type having the same field names as the enclosing type.

But since the inner type is static, Eclipse is in our opinion wrong about the shadowing.

Additional comment: Eclipse already has a relaxed setting where the parameters of constructors or setters are allowed to be the same as the fields, where that _IS_ actual shadowing. 

I think that the Builder patterns, `@With` and `@WithBy` would benefit from the same treatment.

Also, I wouldn't mind if we could somehow tell Eclipse what code is generated, and have different treatment inside generated code.

title: [BUG] static import of @UtilityClass method causes annotation processing to fail
body:
**Describe the bug**
If you perform a static import of one of the methods from a class annotated with @UtilityClass from within the same project, i.e. not via a dependency, annotation processing completely fails, and you get compilation errors for other unrelated classes that use lombok annotations.

**To Reproduce**
As described above, simply create a class annotated with @UtilityClass and do a static import of one of its methods from another class. Also add some other code with lombok annotations. You should get spurious compilation errors. This only occurs when running maven build commands and not from the IDE.

**Expected behavior**
The static import should be handled without issue.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok 1.18.16
 - javac, both 1.8.0_152 and 11.0.8

**Additional context**
The effect is as though lombok annotations are not being processed at all, and for a long time I thought this was the case, only to narrow it down to this.

nodes.body:
Duplicate of https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/2044

Not really possible to fix, unfortunately. Javac tries to resolve imports
before lombok has run, at which point the methods haven't been generated
yet.

title: [FEATURE] "Mandatory" fields with @Builder
body:
**Before submitting**
I want to inform that I've read wiki page titled **FEATURE IDEA: "Mandatory" fields with @Builder**, 
https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/wiki/FEATURE-IDEA:-%22Mandatory%22-fields-with-@Builder
but after reading this lecture I've got an amazing idea - details below.

**Feature description**
Assuming we have Lombok annotated class

`@Builder(builderClassName = "Builder")`
`@Data`
`public class Person {`
`    @NonNull    private String firstName;`
`    @NonNull    private String lastName;`
`    private String email;`
`}`

Why can't you implement this highly desirable feature of separating required attributes from optional ones following examplary code listing? Note and() method. It could be named more specifically, like optional() or something.

`new Person.Builder().firstName("name").lastName("surname").and().email("email@domain.com").build()`

By now Lombok offers @NonNull annotation which throws exception when annotated fields is not set by builder. 

**Target audience**

**Additional context**
Checkout my project 
https://github.com/jrobertgardzinski/builder-pattern
You'll find there:

- 4 implementations, where the most interesting of them are: PersonWithNestedBuilderAsAnonymousClass.java and PersonWithNestedBuilder.java. I tried hard to make IDE hints not making developer confused about overwhelming methods choices.

nodes.body:
> but after reading this lecture I've got an amazing idea - details below.

That sounds promising!

> By now Lombok offers @nonnull annotation which throws exception when annotated fields is not set by builder.

Twisting `@NonNull` into similar but alternate meanings (in this case, 'mandatory') is probably not a good plan. What if I call `.firstName(null)`?

I've looked at your example, and I see nothing that would prevent this code:

```
Person.builder().and().email("a@b.com").build();
```

or this:

```
Person.builder().firstName("name").and().email("a@b.com").build();
```

and in general I don't see how an `and()` method is going to either prevent us having to make a billion types, or how this is superior to having editors be aware of the notion of mandatory methods as outlined in that wiki article.

I'll give you some time to respond, but it sounds like this isn't going to work :(

You may also be interested in "staged builders" feature of Immutables. https://immutables.github.io/immutable.html#staged-builder

It does seem that this problem should be solvable at compile-time with no runtime penalty, but at least it's better than nothing.

title: [BUG] Installation via jar problematic on Mac Sierra and later
body:
The documentation for Eclipse states "Double-click lombok.jar". On a Mac with macOS "Sierra" or later, the Apple Gatekeeper will block this action as the jar is unsigned.

Please include at least one workaround in the documentation, such as using `java -jar ~/Downloads/lombok.jar` from terminal.

Otherwise, please consider signing the jar with an inexpensive certificate such as Comodo (you could use Patreon to raise the money for that).

nodes.body:
Not sure if signing using such a certificate would solve the problem.

We are migrating to using the Eclipse plug-in system P2 to install Lombok into your Eclipse.

It's not so much about the cost, it's about the maintenance burden of figuring this stuff out. From my limited understanding of what gatekeeper is, signing it with a comodo cert, or the concept of 'a signed jar' has no effect whatsoever on what gatekeeper would do.

I'm going to give it a week or two for somebody to explain to how to fix this problem, and if nothing is forthcoming, this issue will be closed with no action. title: [BUG] Can't get Lombok working in eclipse (anymore)
body:
I have the most annoying situation that Lombok all of a sudden seized working in Eclipse 2020-09! And I have no clue as to why. :-(

About 2 weeks ago (when I installed Lombok for a new project into my Eclipse setup) I first faced the issue that v1.18.4 was not working and stalled Eclipse's startup. I then googled and found out that this was a known issue and I then first reverted to v1.18.12 (which worked) and a few days later - once it had become available - I upgraded to v1.18.6 which also worked fine!

About a week later I suddenly get compile errors re. all log(), toString() and misc. setters and getters that Lombok is supposed to create. It is as if Lombok suddenly got de-installed or deactivated. But of course its .jar is still sitting next to the eclipse.exe and the -javaagent entry in eclipse.ini is also still present and correctly points to the .jar.

I then tried reinstalling it (using the meanwhile available v1.18.8, then 1.18.6 again and finally reverting to v1.18.2, but with NONE of these versions Lombok "returned" to action inside eclipse. Building with Maven on the command line always worked fine. 
It is only inside Eclipse that all the Lombok-generated methods are flagged as missing. 

Any idea anyone what could cause this and how to fix?

nodes.body:
I finally found out what's going wrong here: 
I had also enabled the AspectJ "nature" for that project in Eclipse (as I had intended to write a few aspects).

And that - as I had to learn - doesn't go together well with Lombok. Obviously the AspectJ builder overwrote the results of the Lombok compiler and hence all the Lombok-generated stuff was missing.

Disabling/removing the AspectJ nature from the project brought things back to normal.

So - next will be to find out if and if so, how, the two can be made to co-exist.

nodes.body:
@david-g-williams What does NonNull have to do with it? Lombok should absolutely not be making stuff up out of whole cloth - if the field `TypA typeA` is annotated with a non-null marker, then lombok will silently copy it for you. And if not, it won't, and it shouldn't. Thus, this sounds like all you want is a combination of `@RequiredArgsConstructor` and the private/final field defaults.

It sounds like you should be using `@Value`. I don't see why this is so incredibly common, it warrants a boilerplate buster for the boilerplate buster.

title: [BUG] lombok.config files aren't read in when compiling with sbt 1.4
body:
**Describe the bug**
Since about sbt 1.4, there's an incremental compilation thing happening with sbt which is causing the `sourcefile` field of javac's CompilationUnits to report a virtualized URI, which lombok cannot turn into a file path, thus causing lombok to just give up on trying to find the directory to start the chain of looking for `lombok.config` files.

**To Reproduce**
Compile 'Hello, World!' in a java file with sbt while you have a `lombok.config` file present; lombok will completely ignore that config file.

**Additional context**
The URI reported by sbt is something like `vf://tmp/$%7BBASE%7D/src/main/java/example/Main.java`

See also [Pull Request 2643](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/pull/2643)

title: [BUG] @Getter and @Setter don't follow JavaBean naming convention

nodes.body:
This is a duplicate, and the maintainers have already stated they are not
going to address this.
See https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/issues/1661 for background.





On Wed, Nov 18, 2020 at 9:34 PM Giacomo Baso <notifications@github.com>
wrote:

> Suppose I have a field named oDo. For this field, lombok generates
> methods getODo and setODo. I didn't question it at first, because it felt
> the natural capitalization, however it's not actually compliant with JavaBean
> naming convention
> <https://download.oracle.com/otndocs/jcp/7224-javabeans-1.01-fr-spec-oth-JSpec/>
> .
>
> According to 8.8: Capitalization of inferred names
>
> to support the occasional use of all upper-case names, we check if the
> first two characters of the name are both upper case and if so leave it
> alone.
>
> the getter getODo actually corresponds to a field name ODo. It follows
> that the correct getter name for oDo is getoDo. Indeed, this is the
> getter name generated by Eclipse, VS Code and I suppose other IDEs.
>
> More importantly, it's the name used by Jackson to serialize fields,
> therefore a class like:
>
> @Value@Builder@Jacksonizedclass Foo {
> 	@JsonProperty("do")
> 	private String oDo;
> }
>
> results in a duplicate serialization:
>
> {
> 	"do": "<value>",
> 	"odo": "<value>"
> }
>
> Interestingly, @Data doesn't suffer from this problem because
> @JsonProperty is copied onto the setter, making Jackson switch to that
> getter/setter pair for serialization/deserialization.
>
> See also:
> https://stackoverflow.com/questions/26224938/getters-setters-when-first-word-has-second-letter-capitalized
>
> Using jackson 1.18.16
>
> —

nodes.body: Seems to be similar to #2131
Well, sounds like a more or less self  contained test case so somebody can profile this properly. Thanks, @mschaaf

a simplified flamegraph of the slowed down compilation:
[flames.svg.gz](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/files/5747844/flames.svg.gz)

a raw flamegraph of the slowed down compilation:
[flames.svg.gz](https://github.com/rzwitserloot/lombok/files/5747850/flames.svg.gz)

There are millions of InapplicableMethodExceptions and FunctionDescriptorLookupError exceptions thrown during resolution:

a stacktrace for  `FunctionDescriptorLookupError`
```
com.sun.tools.javac.code.Types$DescriptorCache.findDescriptorInternal(Symbol$TypeSymbol, Scope$CompoundScope) Types.java:735
com.sun.tools.javac.comp.Attr.attribStat(JCTree, Env) Attr.java:724
lombok.javac.JavacResolution.attrib(JCTree, Env) JavacResolution.java:235
lombok.javac.JavacResolution.memberEnterAndAttribute(JCTree, Env, Context) JavacResolution.java:203
lombok.javac.JavacResolution.resolveMethodMember(JavacNode) JavacResolution.java:151
lombok.javac.handlers.HandleVal.visitLocal(JavacNode, JCTree$JCVariableDecl) HandleVal.java:133 3367800
lombok.javac.JavacNode.traverse(JavacASTVisitor) JavacNode.java:120
...
```

millions? Oof. `val` is a tricky beast. This is a bug and we should fix it, but it feels like it's not an easy fix.

Is your team on jdk11+? I wonder if we should detect java version and define `val` behaviour as just turning itself into `final var` if the host platform AND the `-source` option (which I think we can figure out, though that'll require some extra code to the framework layer) allow it (so, JDK10+).

One problem is that `final var` and `lombok.val` are almost, but not quite, equivalent:

* `var` allows you to have unwritable types, such as LUBs (`var x = list.get(0);` where `list` boils down to `List<Foobar & Serializable>` - is legal, and makes `x` be of type `Foobar & Serializable`, even though you can't actually write that in a java file. All methods of both Foobar and Serializable are invokable. An even easier test; `var x = new Object() { void foo() {} }; x.foo();` is legal, but there's nothing you can write for `var`, other than `var`, to make that work. `val x = new Object() { void foo() {} }; x.foo();` does not work, because according to the rules of `val`, the best 'writable' type is Object, which has no foo method.
* However, this is legal: `lombok.val x = 10, y = "Hello";` whereas `var` disallows that comma entirely. Actually, it looks like `val` is broken in this regard in current 'master' branch, so I guess nobody cares about it (I haven't seen any issue report on this fly by). That kinda proves this is not as important as it sounds.

The primary issue is that you write code that works if compiled on JDK11 with `-source 10` or higher, and breaks if you don't, but not with an error that states: "Hey, you are using a feature that is not supported at this source level".

That's a cost, but probably worth paying; even if we make `val` a lot faster, it remains a bit of a hairy, resolution-based feature, and replacing it with `var` is much simpler. Unfortunately, this may not be as simple as I'm making it out to be, because `javac` "unrolls" a var quite early in the process last I checked, it's possible lombok runs 'too late'. But, before I investigate if we can do that... good idea, or no? If it can be done at all it's probably a much, much faster path to avoiding the performance drain than endeavouring to fix the problem properly.

We are now at java 15 and at the time of reporting, we were on java 11.

And yes millions I profiled with Yourkit and during that it shows a total of 6 million with 3 of each exception and was still profiling.

> We are now at java 15 and at the time of reporting, we were on java 11.

I think I can conclude from this you'd prefer the much quicker fix of turning `val` into `final var`? (potentially quicker - not 100% sure we can do this, but if we can, it'll probably be easy to implement)

Yes, I prefer a quick fix because it would allow us to continue without making an exception in our code for `val` until it is fixed.
I can test Lombok versions with a potential fix if necessary.
