title: [BUG] Eclipse 2021-06 Cleanup "Remove variable assignment before return" removes @EqualsAndHashCode
body:
**Describe the bug**
When activating the new Eclipse 2021-06 Cleanup option "Remove variable assignment before return" `@EqualsAndHashCode` annotations are removed when executing the cleanup.

**To Reproduce**
* Use Eclipse version 2021-06
* Create some small Java class, probably with one or more fields, but not necessarily.
* Add the `@EqualsAndHashCode` annotation to that class.
* Make sure everything is syntactically correct.
* Activate the Cleanup option "Remove variable assignment before return"
(can be found in the project properties > Java Code Style > Clean Up > Edit > tab "Unneccessary Code")
* Execute the Cleanup function

**Expected behavior**
The annotation is not removed.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok 1.18.20
 - Eclipse 2021-06 (4.20.0)

**Additional context**
I used delombok to have a look at why this might occur and noticed, the generated `hashCode` method ends the following way:

```java
result = result * PRIME + ($previousCheckpoint == null ? 43 : $previousCheckpoint.hashCode());
return result;
```

That's exactly what that cleanup function tries to change to:

```java
return result * PRIME + ($previousCheckpoint == null ? 43 : $previousCheckpoint.hashCode());
```

While there are some more issues open regarding such kind of influence of Eclipse on the Lombok annotations and it seems, there's no easy or known way to avoid Eclipse removing/updating the generated code, this might be fixable by changing Lombok to generate code as in the second code example instead of the first to make sure, Eclipse does not touch it.

nodes.body:
I just took a look at the Eclipse related handling code and found the return statement generation at https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/blob/master/src/core/lombok/eclipse/handlers/HandleEqualsAndHashCode.java#L48

My notices:
1. Placing the `return` statement in the last result calculation line would require a change to `createResultCalculation`.
Such a change might make that method less readable and probably require good comments in code.
2. In case `cacheHashCode` is `true`, this problem should not appear from what I expect. (I didn't test it!)
3. A workround could be used to trick-out Eclipse: Prior the `return` statement there could be some noop statement to make sure, Eclipse does not try to optimize the code.
Well, I'm definitely not a fan of that.

I just looked at the Lombok implementation for this or that. Though, if you're fine with either way (or probably some additional one), I could try to create a Pull Request or at least a first suggestion.

Thanks for reporting this issue, I have checked some of the new Eclipse cleanups but it seems like I missed this one. We usually try to hide generated code for the cleanups to avoid conflicts like this one, see [EclipsePatcher.java#L209](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/blob/master/src/eclipseAgent/lombok/eclipse/agent/EclipsePatcher.java#L209). I will check why it doesn't handle this cleanup tomorrow morning.
It works for me, can you share an example class? I activated only this cleanup, is there another one active in your setup?

I just created a new and clean project for testing and just a single dummy class.

I'll hand that over to you whenever I'm back home today.

Thanks for your support @Rawi01, I just had one more look at my configuration and noticed, that I missed to update the Lombok version of my Eclipse installation. After upgrading from 1.18.18 to 1.18.20, the problem's gone.

title: [FEATURE] Delegate to JDK-provided methods like Long.hashCode(long) in generated hashCode()

nodes.body:
Problem is those methods exist since 1.8, but (at least up to now) Lombok also supports Java 1.7 and 1.6.
And if Lombok's hash calculation doesn't create more collisions than Java's, why should it be changed? There is no need for the hash value to be consistent with `Long`. 
Code reuse isn't important if it's generated code.

:+1: I agree; `hashCode()` and `equals()` method sizes can easily become really big and nasty for `@Data/@Value` classes that contain more than few fields.

Similar functionality can be enabled in `lombok.config` for `@NonNull` - if configured, `@NonNull` is implemented with `Objects.requireNonNull()`, reducing bytecode size in effect.

So I would vote for configurable behaviour of this implementation If maintainers decide to act upon this feature request. New implementation should use `Objects.hash()` or `Objects.hashCode()` for `hashCode()` and `Objects.equals(a, b)` for `equals()`.

title: [FEATURE] Call setter method to assign value in @Builder

nodes.body:
Hello guys.
I'm also wondering if there is any chance for the feature proposed by @joutvhu to be implemented. 
I've seen different alternatives to make the builder call the setters in `Foo`, including:

1. create your own constructor annotated with  `@Builder`.
2. [create](https://www.baeldung.com/lombok-builder-custom-setter) a `public static` inner class inside the `Foo` class, then implement just the parts of the builder you want to perform some custom validation.
3. [override](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/42379899/use-custom-setter-in-lomboks-builder) the `protected Foo(final Foo.UserBuilder<?, ?> b)` inside your `Foo` class.

The issue with all these alternatives is that we need to write boilerplate code, which we are looking to avoid by using Lombok.

Since the builder uses the all-args constructor (generated with `@AllArgsConstructor` or written by the developer), it would be great if we have something such as `@AllArgsConstructor(callSetters=true)` and `@Builder(callSetters=true)` (since we aren't required to include to first annotation to use `@Builder`).

The `@ToString` annotation even has a similar behaviour, where it calls the available getters, which is enabled by default. If you don't want that, you can use `@ToString(doNotUseGetters = true)`.

There was a discussion about this in #783, which was closed without providing more insights about it.
@rzwitserloot might you shed some light here?

/cc @BernardCarvalho

title: [BUG] Lombok makes Eclipse very slow
body:
**Describe the bug**
When Lombok is installed in Eclipse, it makes its operations extremely slow.

**To Reproduce**
1. I used a completely new Eclipse installation from https://download.eclipse.org/eclipse/downloads/drops4/R-4.20-202106111600/ and downloaded eclipse-SDK-4.20-win32-x86_64.zip just to be sure, but It happens also on existing installations.
2. In Eclipse's .ini file, I added:
    ```
    --illegal-access=warn
    --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED
    ```
    as a fix for getting Lombok to work.
3. I installed Lombok from the updated site https://projectlombok.org/p2. The "About" section says "Lombok v1.18.20 "Envious Ferret" is installed. https://projectlombok.org/".
4. Import the minimal project [LombokTest.zip](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/files/6783686/LombokTest.zip) (it's a cut down version of a big project, so it has some leftovers, but it doesn't matter). You might notice that building it is very slow despite it having only 1 source file. Sometimes building is fast, probably because of the incremental compiler.
5. Open the only source file, `com.test.lombok.Descriptions.java`, go to one of the fields and try to inline it by pressing `alt+shift+i`, the operation will take a lot of time just to bring up the dialog. Sometimes it's fast, probably because of caching. In such a case, if I restart Eclipse and try inlining again, the problem comes back.
6. Uninstall Lombok and restart. The inline operation will complete instantly. (In the "About" section there is still "Lombok v1.18.20 "Envious Ferret" is installed. https://projectlombok.org/", although Lombok was removed from the installation details. This is probably a separate bug.)

**Expected behavior**
Build and inline operations should be fast.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - 1.8.20
 - Eclipse Version: 2021-06 (4.20) Build id: I20210611-1600
 - Java 16

**Additional context**
Could be related to #2489

nodes.body: I also notice a massive slow down using your example class but this is an eclipse problem, it also happens without lombok. According to the profiler the slow down happens during type interference (as in https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=512156). It seems to work if you replace `Map.ofEntries` with `Map.<String, String>ofEntries`.
Interesting, I could not reproduce it without Lombok, but I will take your word for it and report it at Eclipse's bug tracker.
If you have additional info, maybe it's best to post it there.

JDK 17 release is just around the corner and it would be very convenient to have at least a lombok snapshot to start working on the migration.

nodes.body:
Thanks for the reminder, release date for Java 17 is 2021-09-14.

So far I have identified these tasks:
- [ ] Support new switch expressions
- [ ] Support sealed classes
- [ ] Update ASM to 9.1+

I already started to fix the first switch expression related thing (https://github.com/Rawi01/lombok/tree/jdk-17).

An edge release is out with this patch applied. Give it a whirl if you like :)

https://projectlombok.org/download-edge

The edge release works well on a large project that uses most of Lombok's features. We had trouble with the @Singular annotation and slow val performance. Both are fixed as I verified on OpenJDK 11 and 17GA. We are keen to upgrade and hope that a new release can be cut soon.

Hi,
I confirm that everything is now working fine with JDK 17 🎉
Weeeellll, time for us to start getting a new release out the door Real Soon Now. @Rawi01 deserves all the credit for making it work. @clemstoquart gracias for checking the edge build!

nodes.body:
Lombok doesn't even use Gradle by itself. I use Gradle 7.2 with Lombok in my projects and they are clear of all deprecation issues. I think that this is really a problem in your build script. By the way, a common mistake is to put Lombok in the classpath or in the modulepath, which triggers a warning and could create some nasty problems, and I strongly suspect that this is your case. I configure Lombok in Gradle with this:

```
annotationProcessor(group: "org.projectlombok", name: "lombok", version: versionLombok)
compileOnlyApi(group: "org.projectlombok", name: "lombok", version: versionLombok)
testAnnotationProcessor(group: "org.projectlombok", name: "lombok", version: versionLombok)
testCompileOnly(group: "org.projectlombok", name: "lombok", version: versionLombok)
```

Where `versionLombok` is set to `"1.18.20"`.

@rspilker and @rzwitserloot - I recommend closing this issue. However, since configuring Lombok to work with Gradle isn't exactly trivial, maybe a help page or documentation somewhere about that might help.

@victorwss I assume you aren't happy with the current documentation as found on our [gradle setup page](https://projectlombok.org/setup/gradle) right?

The fix would presumably be to make that site better. Possibly to add a feature to lombok that it detects any misconfigured gradle builds, or at least common anti-patterns, and spits out a warning or error that points at that site, but that's quite a bit more work.

A PR with an update that page would be welcome!

As per your advice I'll close this issue. If you want to contribute the specific failings of that page but don't want to send a PR or do the legwork of writing it all in readable english, feel free to open a new bug report with notes as to what needs fixing :)

title: [BUG] Jacksonized generating empty json

nodes.body:
A `@Jacksonized @Builder` is only used for deserialization.

You are serializing, so there is something else wrong with your code (which probably has nothing to do with Lombok). I can't check what it is, because your example does not compile (you use different classes in the test and the code above).
Sorry I copied the wrong classes

I reviewed this and found that there is no problem and the behavior is exactly as expected.

Removing the `lombok` annotations still gave the same result.

Doing a check on the default configuration of the Jackson Object Mapper (what is included and ignored during serialization):
```
Visibility
  - getter: PUBLIC_ONLY
  - isGetter: PUBLIC_ONLY
  - setter: ANY
  - creator: ANY
  - field: PUBLIC_ONLY
```

This has not changed in a long time.  Possible solutions (tested):

1. Add the `@Getter` annotation to the Pojo being serialized
2. Configure the `ObjectMapper` with `objectMapper.setVisibility(PropertyAccessor.FIELD, JsonAutoDetect.Visibility.ANY);`
3. Configure the pojo with an additional Jackson annotation: `@JsonAutoDetect(fieldVisibility = Visibility.ANY)`

title: Publish Certificate Fingerprint used on Eclipse Update Site
body:
The [Lombok Eclipse Installation Page](https://projectlombok.org/setup/eclipse) says:
> WARNING: This plugin installer is currently unsigned, and we have given up on figuring out how to fix that; if team eclipse or somebody else can help us out, we're all ears!

However there seems to be some kind of signature after all. Eclipse just doesn't trust it. It asks me whether to trust the certificate?

**Describe the feature**

I don't have a solution for this, but maybe a **workaround**. Publishing the expected certificate fingerprint on the Lombok website would give Eclipse users more confidence. The SHA1 fingerprint that I currently observe is this one:
```
16:27:76:2E:E4:80:AE:37:B9:35:26:86:6D:88:2D:1D:1C:6D:9C:49
```
Eclipse displays it in the *Thumbprint* field of the *Details* view. It does not print all those colons though. To get that representation you can export the certificate and run the following command on it:
```
openssl x509 -in ProjectLombok.der -inform DER -noout -fingerprint -sha1
```

**Describe the target audience**

Probably not many, since there are so many other ways to install Lombok. Just thought I'd try the Eclipse way this time. I'm hoping that Eclipse will keep me updated with new versions.

**Additional context**

The Lombok Eclipse Update Site and the Lombok Website run on the same domain and use the same server certificate. So checking a certificate fingerprint published on the website is somewhat redundant.

In any case, publishing the certificate fingerprint only makes sense, if the private key that belongs to that certificate is being kept confidential. I have not investigated that. And someone would have to update the website, if the private key or the certificate ever change.

title: [BUG] Bad Checker Framework annotation NotCalledMethods
body:
When setting `checkerframework = 4.0`, lombok generates `org.checkerframework.checker.calledmethods.qual.NotCalledMethods` on the setter methods of `@Builder`/`@SuperBuilder`.
However, this annotation does not exist. It's still located in the old package: `org.checkerframework.checker.builder.qual.NotCalledMethods`

This results in a compile error.

**To Reproduce**

Compile 

    @lombok.Builder
    public class BuilderTest {
        String name;
    }

with lombok.config:

    lombok.addNullAnnotations = checkerframework
    checkerframework = 4.0


**Expected behavior**
Generate the correct annotation.

A better solutions would be (from my point of view) generating no annotation at all. If the Checker Framework will support this annotation eventually, lombok could start generating it again (with the help of the version check). However, I doubt the usefulness of such an annotation: Why should it be a misuse of the builder pattern to call a builder setter method twice? For instance, you could fill in some default values into a new builder and pass it to other methods to possibly overwrite those default. And when using `toBuilder()`, you will have no choice but calling a setter twice, because all methods must be marked as "called" on the return type of `toBuilder()` to avoid Checker Framework complaining about uncalled methods.

Furthermore, the minimum version for `@CalledMethods` (and `@This`) should be reduced, as it is already supported by Checker Framework 3.16.0 (maybe earlier).

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version: 1.18.20
 - Checker Framework version: 3.16.0
 - Platform: javac 11.0.12

title: Question about a comment

nodes.body: Since Java 9 using `setAccessible` generates a warning if you try to access fields/methods of an non-exported class. As lombok needs to read/write java compiler classes it hides this warning by directly setting the field using `Unsafe`. Since Java 12 the used `override` field is internal and lombok uses a fake class to find the actual offset of the field. `setAccessible` still works properly if you access classes that allow you to do that.

title: [BUG] @Builder problem with classes consisting of one field and ObjectMapper
body:
**Describe the bug**
Hi. I noticed that classes consisting of one field have problem with JSON De-serialization via `com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper` - the default json tool embedded in Spring Boot -  when they're annotated with `@Builder`. 

**To Reproduce**
- Create a new Spring Project
- Create a class with `@Builder` annotation (`MyClass.java`)
- Try to convert a json to the class using `ObjectMapper` 

```java

@Builder
@Data
class MyClass{
    private Integer id;
}
```

```java

String jsonStr = "{\"id\":1}";
ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
mapper.reader().readValue(jsonStr, MyClass.class);
```

**Expected behavior**
You'll face an exception like this:
`JSON parse error: Cannot construct instance of <the_class>(although at least one Creator exists): cannot deserialize from Object value (no delegate- or property-based Creator); nested exception is com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.exc.MismatchedInputException: Cannot construct instance of <the_class> (although at least one Creator exists): cannot deserialize from Object value (no delegate- or property-based Creator)
 at [Source: (PushbackInputStream); line: 2, column: 2]`

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - 1.8.20
 - Java 11 - IntelliJ

**Additional context**
Once you add another field to the class or remove the `@Builder` there will be no problem in parsing.

nodes.body: You can add a `@NoArgsConstructor` or try one of the solutions at https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51464720/lombok-1-18-0-and-jackson-2-9-6-not-working-together/51465038#51465038

I found an explanation by ivansenic [here]( https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/1563#issuecomment-363460962). But this still does not explain to me why adding a second field to the object also works... What am I overlooking? Do you have an idea, @janrieke?

@BinaryBrain01 @yasharzb It sounds like you should stick a [`@Jacksonized`](https://projectlombok.org/features/experimental/Jacksonized) on there, maybe that'll help? I don't have much experience with combining lombok and jackson's object mapper, I'm afraid.

Thanks for your response, @rzwitserloot, but the issue was actually already resolved for me (by removing the `@Builder`). I was just curious why adding a second field to the object also resolves it. Because when I look at the explanation of the cause of the issue, I don't understand why that would help too.

@BinaryBrain01 I don't see how ivensenic's explanation says anything about a difference between having 1 field or two fields.

* The basic issue is that jackson needs to know which constructor to call __and__ what each of its arguments mean, or it cannot work.
* Because the no-args constructor has, well, no args, jackson just knows what to do when it is there. In that sense, the no-args is 'special': That one works out of the box, any arguments and it needs _something_ to tell it how it works. This can be a `@ConstructorProperties`, for example.
* `@Builder` implies `@AllArgsConstructor`, which means `@Builder` modifies your constructors: Without `@Builder`, you have a no-args constructor. With `@Builder`, you don't.

The fix is usually to add a `@ConstructorProperties`. You can ask lombok to add it, but as the linked issue explains, oracle broke this annotation, and now you need to add `requires java.desktop;` if you compile with JDK9+. This sucks, and it's oracle's fault. They broke backwards compatibility on that one unfortunately. I think `@Jacksonized` adds it.

Assuming it's related to that, thus, this issue isn't something we can address (Oracle isn't going to undo their mess, as that would be even worse now).

My apologies for abusing this platform to satisfy my curiosity! I agree that this bug can be closed.

It is just that I experienced something similar to the original post by yasharzb, where we had an `@Builder` on an object with a single field and then it would not get deserialized. 
To resolve it, we could either remove the `@Builder` (which ties to the explanation that you would then get the no-args constructor which works for Jackson), _or_ we could add a second (dummy) field to the object, and that worked too. 
For the latter, we would still have _no_ no-args constructor; the `@Builder` would still modify the constructors, which, according to the explanations, should be compensated by e.g. adding `@ConstructorProperties`. However, we did not need to do that... And I still do not get why...

P.S. What would be the appropriate platform to continue this discussion?

> My apologies for abusing this platform to satisfy my curiosity!

Entitled behaviour annoys me (example: comments with just "+1" in it, especially after I write out why something is quite tricky). Curiosity is welcome, you have nothing to apologize for!

You can continue the conversion here, but I'm not sure how many folks you'd reach in a closed bug. Did you look at `@Jacksonized`? If you're using a class with jackson, and you don't do exotic stuff, and you annotate it with `@Jacksonized`, and it doesn't do the expected thing, that's definitely a bug then. The `@Jacksonized` annotation was contributed by @janrieke who, I think, uses jackson (and lombok) on a daily basis. Hence why I'm not quite as familiar as I ought to be as core maintainer about what it does.

If there is a difference between 1 and 2, especially if it works fine with 2 but doesn't work with 1, that does sound like _something_ is not right on the lombok side, there might still be a bug here.

If you have the time, perhaps investigate a tad; I'd be interested in:

* Does `@Jacksonized` fix the problem?
* For code that works fine with 2 fields, but breaks with 1, what is the meaningful difference between the delomboked output of the working (2 fields) case vs the 1 field case, other than the obvious (namely: 1 field less, one 'setter' less in the builder, etc). For example, if one case generates `@ConstructorProperties` and the other doesn't, then that's extremely relevant. You can delombok with for example `java -jar delombok -p TheSourceFile.java`. (`java -jar delombok --help` for more - it's a bit like javac, except instead of class files it emits source files that compile with stock, lombok-less `javac`).

I also don't have an explanation right now, but I'll look into it. I'm quite busy ATM so I don't know when.

`@Jacksonized` will probably fix it, but only because Jackson will use the builder in that case. The question is: Why does a 2-args constructor work, but a 1-arg does not?

I still bet this is either a Jackson bug or some Jackson magic, but not a Lombok issue.

title: Generate builders with solicitor pattern
body:
Currently builders present the same options to the developer even if required fields have already been filled in.

For example, if there two fields, foo and bar, then there are fluent setters for foo and bar, and both of those are always visible.

Using the "solicitor" pattern, instead of returning the same builder after every setter call, a solicitor object that wraps the builder is returned, and the solicitor presents only the next field or fields to be set (one field if there is only one choice, multiple fields if more than one choice makes sense at that phase of evaluation).

The last solicitor object offers optional fields, and also offers build() as one of the available calls.

If the object being built offers a tree of possible paths, then branching logic can be included in the solicitors that returns a new solicitor based on the most-recent selection.

Combined with auto-complete in an IDE like IntelliJ or Eclipse, this approach yields a much better authoring experience for developers than a "flat" builder like lombok currently generates.

Lombok could generate solicitor-based builders. It would require annotating the order in which to prompt, and indicating which fields are optional, and some way to indicate branching logic when there is a tree of paths. But the reward would be best-in-class builders.

Creating solicitor-based builders manually is a pain. It would be a boon to get them automatically.

title: [FEATURE] @Setter may ignore null argument
body:
I propose an option for setters to ignore null inputs without throwing an exception.
`@Setter(nullPolicy="ignore")`

It often happens that DB entities need to be updated from sparsely populated DTOs, leading to lots of code fragments like
`if (dto.getA()!=null) {entity.setA(dto.getA();}`

It would be preferable to just `entity.setA(dto.getA())`; or `entity.setIfNotNullA(dto.getA());`

Such an option could be for all non-final members at the class level or for individual fields. Conversely, fields could be marked as `@NullPolicy("throw")` to overwrite the class-level annotation.

nodes.body:
You should probably prefer `Optional.ofNullable(dto.getA()).ifPresent(entity::setA)`, but setters can accept null values just fine, so why "ignore" unless you have some field that you don't want to override? (in that case, a direct setter doesn't make sense without some extra logic). 

If you don't want to allow them, then add `@Nonnull` annotations (lombok or javax) to the fields in the entity class

title: [FEATURE] A way to create custom constructors (where the field(s) to include are explicitly indicated)
body:
## Background and description

Lombok currently offers 3 'flavours' of constructor generation, all of which pre-define which fields are intended (in that they are named `NoArgsConstructor`, `AllArgsConstructor`, and `RequiredArgsConstructor`, which are words that describe which fields are to be included inherently). One of these features is wound up with `@Builder` (which implies `@AllArgsConstructor` under most scenarios).

There are multiple feature requests for more fine grained control of which fields are to be included, generally in the vein of 'how can I mark a field that lombok thinks is required as not actually required, or vice versa', or 'how can I exclude a field from `@Builder`?'.

These feature requests do not make sense, it's like asking 'how do I add a corner to a circle'. Nevertheless, the underlying requirement is a use case we'd like to cater to, so we need some sort of 4th flavour of constructor: Based on a custom list.

One annoyance is that java allows multiple constructors in a class, so it's not really right to talk about __the__ custom constructor; one can merely talk about __a__ custom constructor. This does not mesh well with annotations, and doesn't mesh well with the most obvious approach (which is to mark each field you want included explicitly, but how do you indicate that some field should be included for custom constructor 1, and not custom constructor 2?)

## Simple proposal - single `@CustomConstructor`

We ditch the use case of multiple custom constructors, relegating that to the 'that is no longer boilerplate; lombok cannot help you out anymore' dustbin. In this case, all we really need is [A] a `@CustomConstructor` annotation  (valid on types) and [B] a `@CustomConstructor.Include` and `@CustomConstructor.Exclude` annotation (valid on fields).

Obvious downside is that you can only have 1 custom constructor.

It is a compiler error if you have include/exclude annotations and no `@CustomConstructor` on the class. It is a compiler error if you have `@CustomConstructor` on a class and zero include/exclude annotations (because, does that mean 'I want no fields' or does that mean 'I want all of them').

## Denied alternative: Omit `@CustomConstructor` itself (only have Incl/Excl)

It seems like the `@CustomConstructor` annotation itself doesn't really need to exist; a single Include or Exclude annotation is enough. However, that complicates matters a bit for `@Builder` and co, and I don't think it helps readability of the end result, nor does it help discoverability of the `@CustomConstructor` feature. Unless I've missed something (in which case feel free to comment), I'm denying this alternative.

## Denied alternative: Stringly typed multiple custom constructors

We _could_ introduce the concept of the 'constructor name'. Then you could do something like:

```
@CustomConstructor({"a", "foo"})
public class Example {
    @CustomConstructor.Include("a")
    private int includedInAButNotInFoo;
}
```

but this seems really hard to use, easily fatfingered, lacks IDE support (auto-complete on those constructor names is not going to happen, obviously), and even causes confusion when you want to define one constructor by way of inclusion (only these fields), and the other by way of exclusion (all fields except the ones marked for exclusion).

Making this feature way more complicated in the name of what to me seems like a really exotic usecase (multiple constructors required, all of which are field-based and none of which fall under the notion of 'all', 'none', or 'required'), doesn't sound like a good plan. Unless there's a common pattern/very commonly used library out there that more or less requires at least 2 custom constructors that I'm not aware of (in which case, comment and name them), this isn't going to happen (especially not for a first take on this idea; we can always add it later without breaking backwards compatibility if we must).

### What about final fields?

What do we do with non-included `final` fields? Just init them to 0/false/null? Allow a mechanism to specify the default (this is incredibly complicated, so before you chime in: YEAH! It makes this feature about 10x more complicated, I'd like to hear a clear proposal on how. Any comments with a simple 'yes, important!', even if it goes with a personal story on how much you need it, are not particularly desired, I don't think anybody would argue defaults aren't useful). This defaulting question also extends to NoArgsConstructor to some extent.

* Just use a single default annotation doesn't work - java's annotation system doesn't allow e.g. `@Default(System.currentTimemillis())` at all (only compile time constants need apply). Even if we restrict defaults to only CTCs, you'd need one annotation for each type (`@DefaultInt`, `@DefaultBoolean`, etc).
* Allowing the field initializer to serve (the way builder works: `@Default private int field = 5;`, implying that only for those constructors that do not include `field`, set it to `5`) is also complicated: What if that expression has side-effects or resolves to a mutable entity. Does that mean it's resolved once for the entire class and that value is assigned as default, or is the expression resolved every time? We also have to 'mess' with your hand written code and move that initializing expression around, which makes this feature very complex and significantly increases maintenance burden. We'd also have to answer some questions about having 2 separate defaulting mechanisms - this really doesn't sound like a workable idea unless we unify `@Builder.Default` and this `@Default` first, but how do we do that, preferably maintaining backwards compatibility?

I will assume that this feature will be implemented separated (as in, we'll ship without defaulting support now; we can always add it later).

Status of this feature request: Gather feedback and use cases first, before making a decision.

body:
**Describe the bug**
The lombok Eclipse installer escapes @ characters in the javaagent path to lombok.jar in eclipse.ini, then Eclipse fails to start with an alert window containing "JVM terminated. Exit code=1" followed by the content of eclipse.ini.

**To Reproduce**

- Make a new Eclipse installation with a path containing @ character
- Make a lombok installation on it.
- Start Eclipse

**Expected behavior**
Eclipse starts.

**Version info:**
 - Lombok version: 1.18.20
 - Eclipse 2021-03 (4.19)
 - Ubuntu 20.04
 - OpenJDK 16 as Eclipse runtime (installed through Ubuntu apt repositories)

nodes.body:
It sounds like you actually intended to say that lombok does _not_ escape `@` characters, but that it should start doing so. I don't know how one should properly escape it; can you fix your `eclipse.ini` file so that it works and then show us what lombok's installer should be generating?

Parked: This issue will be closed without action if no feedback by 2021-09-30.

Thank you for your reply.

The installer _do_ escape @ characters which, I presume, prevents the JVM to access the agent.

Failing eclipse.ini: 
`-javaagent:/home/strat\@domain.local/dev/eclipse/lombok.jar`

Working eclipse.ini:
`-javaagent:/home/strat@domain.local/dev/eclipse/lombok.jar`

Interesting. A leading `@` is interpreted by `java` as 'actually, the remainder of this cmdlinearg is a path; open it as a text file and process the contents thereof as command line arguments' which is presumably why we escape it. Evidently, either [A] that processing does not 'work' in eclipse, or [B] that only kicks in when the `@` is the first character in an arg, not when it appears halfway through.

I think we can presumably leave the usecase of 'my filename _starts_ with an @ symbol' as unaddressed and simply cease escaping it. Alternatively, the entire idea of escaping anything in these simply does not work, and if lombok believes that a path will not 'work' in the provided form in the `eclipse.ini` file, then it should just error instead, or we figure out what the correct way is to escape, say, a forward slash in a name.

I'm still somewhat surprised; `\@` in linux shells is simply `@`.

At any rate, I've also tested shoving a `:` as well as a space inside a path name, and then simply leaving it unescaped works.

The issue was already reported to the JDK as well, as [mentioned](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/2940#issuecomment-905506692) in #2940: https://bugs.openjdk.java.net/browse/JDK-8272981

title: [BUG] @Getter didn't copy javadoc on the field in inner class.
Allow field name specification for @Log (and friends)
body:
It would be nice to have the logging annotations allow for the logging field name to be configured, something like:

```java
@Slf4j(name="LOGGER")
```

to generate something like:

```java
private static final Logger LOGGER = LoggerFactory.getLogger(YourClass.class);
```

I have some co-workers who are very adamant that a static field should be in all caps. It would also be helpful in situations where you may have more than one logger in a class.

nodes.body: You can change the field name by setting the `lombok.log.fieldName` config key in your [lombok.config](https://projectlombok.org/features/configuration).
That would work if you want ALL of them named the same thing. The approach I am suggesting would allow it to be configured on a per-use basis.

That's right, but why do you want to use different names in the same project/module? Are multiple loggers in the same class something you use often and do you think that this is still boilerplate? To be honest I have never seen that in one of my projects.

> That would work if you want ALL of them named the same thing. The approach I am suggesting would allow it to be configured on a per-use basis.

We made an intentional choice - that only the most exotic usecases would possibly by interested in configuring the name of the logger field on a per-class basis. We don't cater to those use-cases, because that road inevitably leads to the same place: 50+ options on each and every annotation we have, and a combinatorial explosion that is not testable. Not an acceptable situation, and surely you'd agree with that, if you think through what lombok would look like if you go down this rabbit hole.

The solution is painful but, IMO, the only right move: Grow up. It's ridiculous to do the styleguide fighting by way of who gets to a source file first. Have a conversation about it, pick a style, and try to be diplomatic about it. Give and take.

If you want some arguments, well, lombok does not default to `LOGGER`, that's one. Pretty sure all the tutorials of all the popular log frameworks don't do it. Go look trough the source code of popular libraries that use loggers. I bet they don't do it. There is a significant upside to following conventions even if you disagree. The camp that wants `LOGGER` therefore has to make a particularly strong case, as they'll effectively be arguing that they are right, and the vast majority of the java community are wrong. Possible, but, extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.

Here's another: Just about every doc out there says that all-caps is for 'constants'. "anything that is `static final`", that is one definition for "constant". But surely `static final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();` doesn't count, right? You can add and remove stuff from that list at will, it's not immutable at all. Is that 'constant'? Clearly no. Loggers? That's... a slightly harder case to make, but it mostly doesn't swim, walk, or sound like a constant to me.

A third is that log statements are less important to code flow and should probably not be particularly 'screamy', which all-caps var names tend to be. Then again, perhaps the pro-`LOGGER` camp thinks they should be _more_ screamy. Then it's a valid point that has boiled down to something quite esoteric and personal (do you want your log statements with extra screamy or not?)

I think that takes the wind out of the sails of most of the common arguments in favour of all-caps `LOGGER`, and gives you an additional 'common conventions dictate' bonus reason to then win the argument.

But, it's just some name. If the other folks on the team are considerably more invested in seeing it in all caps, then I suggest you let it go and give in. Add the key to the proejct-global `lombok.config`, and refactor all existing code. Shouldn't be too difficult; a basic search-and-replace should be able to take care of it, and lack of compilation errors on a full build will confirm.

But if this turns into a situation where a chunk of the dev team takes the 'THIS.. IS... SPARTAAAAAA!!!!!' route on every mostly meaningless style 'debate', do yourself a favour: That's unprofessional and infantile, and no good will come of enabling such behaviour. Pick the fight (not for the name of the logger, but on the notion that the team ought to be capable of holding a low-drama and short debate and then pick a side, and if it can't, the team is dysfunctional and needs to treat as critical that it needs to learn it, and learn it now). If that's not on the table, I'd get out of there. Find another team to work with. Programming is hard enough as is.

title: [BUG] @EqualsAndHashCode should always compare class type in "equals"
body:
When annotating classes with ```@EqualsAndHashCode``` (or ```@Data```), Lombok generates the "equals" and "hashCode" methods.
However, the equals only compares the class properties and not the class types as well. This is a bug.

Why is this important? Because I have an abstract generic class, like "Identifiable", which contains only the field "long id", and the class is annotated with ```@EqualsAndHashCode```. Then I make subclasses from it. Yes, I can add ```@EqualsAndHashCode(includeSuper=true)``` on these subclasses, and this means overhead, because not just the ID, but the other fields will be compared as well. And if there are cyclical references, like class A containing a List<B>, while B having a reference back to A, "hashCode" will cause a stack overflow. So the most correct way is to only add ```@EqualsAndHashCode``` on the generic abstract class.

If I would ever only process subclasses of the same type, it would work properly. But if I have some "Set" or "Map", like ```Map<Long, ? extends Identifiable>```, Lombok will only compare ID, and not the class type, saying that object of class A equals object of type B, if both have the same ID.

Please fix this. For now, I had to remove Lombok annotations and implement my own "hashCode" and "equals" methods.

nodes.body:
Lombok already does this right, and has for a decade or so, see the `canEqual` method (check the [feature page on EqualsAndHashCode](https://projectlombok.org/features/EqualsAndHashCode)). You can write your own `canEqual` and change the behaviour, for example by adding a simple `return getClass() == other.getClass();` check.

The behaviour of lombok in regards to how it deals with sub/superclassing is intentional, we considered all this.

If something is unclear, perhaps the documentation needs an update, but I did a quick read and it seems clear enough as is. Feel free to suggest updates, though :)

One workaround (that would also confirm a thing or two as to what's going on, so do please report back) is that you run eclipse, itself, on JDK8. That doesn't mean you're limited to developing for JDK8 and lower in eclipse. Eclipse itself is a java application and thus needs to run on some JDK. It'll run on many JDKs and as it brings its own compilers and such to the table, the JDK you run eclipse on is effectively irrelevant for what you can do with said eclipse.

Thus, install a JDK8, make sure your eclipse boots off of that. I think you can configure it during the OOMPH install, but, the `eclipse.ini` file contains a path to the JDK that will be used, so you can just edit that.

I'm confident this problem will disappear if you config it to use a JDK8. I'm pretty sure it'll go away on any JDK up to at least 14, but perhaps a 15 or 16 is problematic. Hence, can you report back? Should help with reproduction and from there, a fix.
This is a duplicate of #2810 and already fixed in the [current edge version](https://projectlombok.org/download-edge)

title: The Java new keyword should be optional.
body:
**Describe the feature**
The Java new keyword is used to create an instance of the class. In other words, it instantiates a class by allocating memory for a new object and returning a reference to that memory. We can also use the new keyword to create the array object.

Creating class objects is an activity that repeats many times, even in small projects, so 
as programmer I would like to omit the **new** keyword every time I instantiate a given class. 

**Describe the target audience**
All programmers who have had contact with the Kotlin programming language, They will quickly see the benefits of this simple change.

title: [SEMANTICS] `@NonNull` is currently allowed on classes; it does nothing. Warn for this.
body:
Lombok updated `@NonNull`'s targets to include `TYPE_USE`, as `@NonNull` has documentary purpose as well.

However, that also means you can annotate types themselves with it. This is legal right now:

```
@NonNull class Test {}
```

This, naturally, has absolutely no effect on lombok. However, one might erroneously think that this is a defaulting hint (that it would e.g. generate null checks in setters or even generate null checks for every non-primitive parameter in methods in the annotated class). That is a reasonable assumption to make.

This seems to me like mostly a design mistake in what `TYPE_USE` means, but that's surely not getting fixed as it'd break backwards compatibility in java itself.

To avoid the confusion, lombok should generate a warning that cannot be ignored. This would even be backwards compatible. I can't imagine a useful documentary purpose (what does `@NonNull` _on a class itself_ mean, semantically? Nothing but confusing answers there). Alternatively, just generate an error. This wouldn't be backwards compatible, but then who would have annotated classes with `@NonNull`, other than folks who thought that would have some effect, in which case generating an error now is only a good thing: We're informing them that their code was buggy.

See [issue 1619](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/1619) for more context.

nodes.body:
It would be nice if `@NonNull` on classes could mean that you could never assign null to a reference of this type by default. Would be great for instance for something similar to the `Optional<T>` type, since you want to use `Optional.empty()` in the absence of a value, not `null`.

This capability could be a nice substitute for the missing feature that a lot of other languages have. For instance, if `@NonNull` isn't inheritable, you could create a class `MyObject`, annotated with `@NonNull` and then create a subclass `MaybeMyObject` or `NullableMyObject` (Or just `MyObject`, but in a `nullable` subpackage) without the annotation. This would act like `MyObject` vs `?MyObject` in PHP to indicate nullability of a type.

title: [FEATURE] Generate JSF component properties

nodes.body:
Seems like we eliminate a ton of easily messed up boilerplate in trade for a low maintenance burden. Sounds like a good idea.

As for the name:

* `@lombok.extern.faces.JsfComponentProperties`
* `@lombok.extern.jsf.JSFComponentProperties`

Or some other combination sounds right. I'm guessing the first one is the better option (fits the `DvdPlayer` style conventions of writing acronyms in java's CamelCase format, and you import from package `javax.faces`, I think, so presumably `faces` is more natural than `jsf` on this one. But, you're clearly more familiar with the domain :)

Some questions:

* Is it to be expected that these properties can have generics, e.g. `public List<String> getProperty1() { .. return (List<String>) getStateHelper()....`? If it is, how do we deal with the ugly-cast, do we also add the `@SuppressWarnings`? Given that it's all runtime glue, the generics do nothing, I assume. Should we leave the warning (but then, how would one get rid of it? `@SuppressWarnings` on the field? `@lombok.extern.faces.JsfComponentProperties.SuppressUnchecked` on the field?
* Are lowercase enum names the common pattern? It matches what `@FieldNameConstants` does, so that'd be nice if it is :)
* If the initializing expression contains side-effects and/or isn't stable, what would you expect? Let's say its `long property5 = System.currentTimeMillis()` - would you expect the `get` command, when the statehelper doesn't have anything (so the default kicks in) to return the time as it is was when the class was loaded, or would you expect the get command to execute the expression (thus, that `getProperty5()` returns the same thing `System.currentTimeMillis()` would.
* Which spec controls the translation from property name to accessor name (`fCell` to `getFCell()` or does JSF expect `getfCell()`)? See issue #2693 - if JSF explicitly fails unless we generate `getfCell()`, or something in the chain fails no matter which way we go, we should probably make an exception here and generate what JSF needs even if it isn't compatible with with lombok's `@Getter` would do (or if happiness is impossible with a field named `fCell`, we should error out on the field and explain the problem).
* I assume `getStateHelper()` is coming from [`javax.faces.component.UIComponent`](https://github.com/jboss/jboss-jsf-api_spec/blob/cb33d215acbab847f2db5cdf2c6fe4d99c0a01c3/src/main/java/javax/faces/component/UIComponent.java) -  Looks like any usage of this feature would necessarily require that you extend _something_. What should we do if the outer class doesn't extend anything - should we just silently add `extends UIComponent`, or should we error out?
* Should we also generate something for `getFamily()` and that constructor that invokes `setRendererType`?
* How big is the problem here that in your example (`SelectOneMenuBase`), lombok can make on `getTitle` and `setTitle` for you, but isn't going to be able to figure out that it should stick an `@Override` on these?
* I assume [this](https://github.com/jboss/jboss-jsf-api_spec/blob/master/src/main/java/javax/faces/component/html/HtmlSelectOneMenu.java) is the source of HtmlSelectOneMenu. That very file, even though somebody checked it into github, has `// *** GENERATED CODE - DO NOT EDIT ***` at the top of it, so somebody out there already wrote some code gen system for this problem already. Is whatever made this commonly used (in which case the need for this feature goes down, or at least the focus on marketing this feature goes up), or is it something internal (in which case the fact that JBoss saw the need to write a code generator for this stuff only highlights that lombok should add this feature)?
* That code (HtmlSelectOneMenu as above) calls `handleAttribute` in addition to `getStateHelper().put`, which I assume is some internal JBoss thing and not relevant for this code generation. But it does open the question: If you want additional behaviour to e.g. a set method, do we just say: Hey, then write the whole thing yourself; feel free to use the `PropertyKeys.propName` enum value we made for yo uthough. Or do we say: No problem, we'll inject that put line for you / you can tag some method as 'please run this method, supplying the enum and the property, as part of a `set` call? e.g. that this JBoss code could be replaced with:

```
@lombok.extern.faces.JsfComponentProperties.SetterHelper
public setAccesskeyHelper(PropertyKeys key, String accesskey) {
    handleAttribute(key.name(), accessKey);
}
```

Where lombok figures out what to do, per argument (you can have up to one argument of type PropertyKeys, and up to one argument of the key type, with any name and in any order).

* Let's say someone tags a top-level class with `@JsfComponentProperties`, I assume the best idea there is to just error out and refer to the feature page on projectlombok.org in the error message showing how to use it. Or should we just spell it out (make an inner class and annotate it. The fields of that class are turned into properties, the initializers on those fields are considered the default-generating expression). I guess there's no nice way to just make this feature 'tag your top level with `@JsfComponent`, and we'll take care of the rest. Seems a bit crass to scan for an inner class whose name matches the pattern `xKeys`. Then again, tagging in _inner class_ with an annotation which then results in lombok generating a ton of stuff in its enclosing class is also slightly weird. As this is an `extern` feature, weirdness is fine (We presume that the user knows the library and its associated patterns well, for `extern` features).

I think satisfactory answers are available for all these questions, and armed with those, the feature seems good to go!

Is there really a convention to use CamelCase for acronyms? What about `URLConnection`?

`faces` is most likely the better name, there is already is a set of `@Faces...` annotations so I think `@lombok.extern.faces.FacesComponentProperties` is a better name.

- Yes, generics are possible. I think we can add a `@SuppressWarning` as soon as we detect the generic.
- Yes, lowercase is common in this case.
- Great question, I never used something else than a constant value. To keep it simple I would simply copy the initializer to the method parameter, if the user needs something else it is still possible to implement a custom getter.
- IIRC it is getfName because it uses `java.beans.Introspector.decapitalize`
- Adding the extends seems to be a little bit to much magic especially because we add the annotation to the inner class and not to the component itself. An error is fine I guess.
- I think we should keep the first version as simple as possible.
- As `@Override` is only a marker I think we can simply ignore that.
- Interesing, there also was a code generator in mojarra (JSF implementation) some time ago (https://github.com/eclipse-ee4j/mojarra/commit/a4bac4a260a7823e7ee0823e2326d06ef802da6b). I also checked a bunch of other projects and found two related issues (https://github.com/primefaces/maven-jsf-plugin/issues/4, https://github.com/jakartaee/faces/issues/1193).
- As mentioned above I think we should allow the user to implement custom methods.

> Is there really a convention to use CamelCase for acronyms?

Yes, adopted by amongst others Oracle/team OpenJDK and google.

> What about `URLConnection`?

Predates the convention. Same for `URL` and `URI`.

See:

* [Google Style Guide on this topic](https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html#s5.3-camel-case)
* I think 'Effective Java', but I don't have a copy of the book handy. Links I found on the web suggest page 237.
* For a real spin, think of `HttpURLConnection` which mixes conventions. It partly has to (`HTTPURLConnection` looks real bizarre), but it also serves as a nice objective example: `DVDPlayer` is not just subjectively the wrong choice (as in, 'it is not (any longer) the official convention). It is in fact __objectively__ the wrong choice. No style guide needed. Auto-complete systems based on first-letter-of-each-camelcased-word, such as most IDE's 'open type' dialogs, also don't really know what to do with `DVDPlayer` (it's not found if you type `DP`), whereas `DvdPlayer` is handled just fine.
* [O'Reilly java pocket guide](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/java-8-pocket/9781491901083/ch01.html) on naming conventions (section 'Acronyms', explicitly says `GpsVersion`, not `GPSVersion`).

> `lombok.extern.faces.FacesComponentProperties`

Works for me!

> Yes, generics are possible. I think we can add a @SuppressWarning as soon as we detect the generic.

Yup, let's just flat out generate it if needed and not make it configurable. I don't foresee any point in wanting to e.g. not generate it. `@SuppressWarnings` is a bit of a mess (the actual keys you can pass to it are severely underspecced, which has resulted in various tools interpreting `@SW` annotations in different ways, and generally means we have to usually add `"all"` to the pile, but, one way or another, we just need to figure out what `@SuppressWarnings` line works for the maximal amount of common environments and generate it. But, yes, only if we detect generics.

> Great question, I never used something else than a constant value.

My primary concern is that users of this feature will make an assumption about how it works and will consider their assumption so obvious that they'd be highly surprised if it worked differently than what they think it does. Except, there are non-trivial amounts of programmers with that idea making different assumptions. I'm not sure there's any solution there other than to just accept that some folks will get confused and a little angry that 'lombok made such a dumb choice', and all we get to do is pick which group gets angry. One way out is to only allow literally constant literals, and not even refs to constants (because we need resolution to know), but that feels needlessly restrictive.

Copying the initializer though... not so sure we can do that. Expressions can contain almost all syntax nodes, as `new Object() { whatever you want here }.foo();` is a legal expression. Copying _all that_ is impossible. We can _move_ it, though. With some minor risk (we're moving nodes and therefore changing contexts, which may break stuff), but there are other places we already do this. We mostly operate on the assumption nobody would be silly enough to actually make that the default. I guess the call is: Just.. do something, whatever. Some folks won't like it, but the vast majority of the team its a constant value and its a moot point.

> IIRC it is getfName because it uses `java.beans.Introspector.decapitalize`

Okay, let's do exactly that and not make it configurable.

> Adding the extends seems to be a little bit to much magic

Okay, that means the feature will error out and link to the docs if you put the annotation on a top-level typedef.

title: [DOCS] Improve documentation for @ToString
body:
Similar to #2870, which I also raised, I have an answer on Stack Overflow related to `@ToString` which I noticed has 9000 views. It seems to be the case that people are under the impression that it may be possible to change the format of the string generated by `@ToString`. 

Since people are obviously searching for this a lot, I think it would be worth making it clearer in the documentation that this is not possible.

Current

> Any class definition may be annotated with `@ToString` to let lombok generate an implementation of the `toString()` method. By default, it'll print your class name, along with each field, in order, separated by commas. 

Suggested change

> Annotating a class with `@ToString` will cause lombok to generate an implementation of the `toString()` method. There is configuration to specify whether field names should be included but otherwise the format is fixed: the class name followed by parentheses containing fields separated by commas, e.g. `MyClass(foo=123, bar=234)`.

nodes.body:
Could do. But we have some open issues on allowing you some flexibility. The problem is, the amount of use cases are staggering and it quickly spins out of control into something that takes 5 pages of manual and involves inventing a regex-like templating engine. All that just for some toString stuff. So we keep holding off.

Maybe you're right, and we should just update the docs now. We can always change it again if we do come up with a simple yet flexible solution.

Yeah, could get complex. FWIW, I've always been perfectly happy with the format lombok spits out, and supporting a more specific set of use-cases seems beyond the scope of the problems lombok usually sets out to solve. Obviously if there's an elegant solution which increases flexibility without ballooning in complexity then everyone's happy.

I forgot to include the StackOverflow post in question. It's here: [How to change the output of the method generated by Lombok's @ToString?](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/50379937/how-to-change-the-output-of-the-method-generated-by-lomboks-tostring/ )

title: [BUG] @Log fails on nested enums
body:
**Describe the bug**
Compilation fails when the annotation @Log is set on a nested enum.

**To Reproduce**
Here is an example:
```java
class Example {

  @Log
  enum Status  { OK, KO }
}
```
The following error appears during compilation:  
`@Log is not supported on non-static nested classes.`

**Expected behavior**
Should compile without error.
Was working fine in 1.18.20

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok 1.18.22
 - all platforms

**Additional context**
Addind the keyword `static` to the enum seems to workaround the problem.

nodes.body: Context for implementers: Lombok demands `static` on inner classes here because lombok wants to make a static field, and in java that isn't legal (or wasn't for most of its lifetime) in non-static inners. Apparently the idea is that such static fields should be placed in the outer class instead. However, enums are by definition `static` - they do not hold a reference to an instance of the enclosing class. You can put `private static final` fields in them and you've always been able to do that. Thus, lombok should just shut up and do it, its overly zealous here. It should consider `enum` type defs as inherently static.
@rzwitserloot if this hasn't been worked on already, I would love to contribute.

@varkart Feel free! Should be as simple as removing two lines, or at least 'guarding' an existing `if (mods.static) { addTheError(); return; }` with checking if the type is NOT an enum first. Make sure to add your name to AUTHORS as well :) – no need to mess with the docs, we'll review and take care of that part.
@rzwitserloot  at your convenience could you plz review the PR and let me know if any additional changes are needed.

title: [BUG] Use of `@FieldNameConstants` generated `Fields` constants in MapStruct's `@Mappings` annotation breaks Java compilation when using several `@Mapping` annotations without wrapping them in a container `@Mappings` annotation
body:
**Describe the bug**
I have a class `MyClass` with a property `prop`; the class is annotated with `@FieldNameConstants`.
When I try to use the generated `Fields` class in MapStruct's mapping annotation, for example
```java 
@Mapping(target = MyClass.Fields.prop, ignore = true)
```
then Java's compiler can't find any of Lombok's generated builders anymore (and several, possibly all, other generated items, like loggers):
```
[ERROR] path/to/Another.class[line:pos] cannot find symbol
  symbol:   class AnotherBuilder
  location: class com.example.Another

```
(Note that the errors seem to occur for all classes using Lombok, not just the one with the `@FieldNameConstants` annotation.)

I ensured to use the setup as described in [MapStruct's reference guide](https://mapstruct.org/documentation/stable/reference/html/#_set_up), but with latest stable versions of the three dependencies 
```xml
    <lombok.version>1.18.22</lombok.version>
    <mapstruct.version>1.4.2.Final</mapstruct.version>
    <lombok-mapstruct-binding.version>0.2.0</lombok-mapstruct-binding.version>
```

I suspect it's down to how the preprocessors are chained, but rearranging the `path` elements in the pom.xml didn't yield any changes in the result.

**Expected behaviour**
Lombok generating the `Fields` class first, then MapStruct running and successfully using the constants, and the build passing. Changing MapStruct's annotation makes it all pass:
```java 
@Mapping(target = "prop", ignore = true)
```

nodes.body: @anno1985 Could you try something out? Replace lombok with v1.18.22 and give it another go. We changed a bunch of things with the mapstruct integration; if it works in 1.18.20 we know it's either an error in the setup documentation or a problem with one of the changes introduced in .22. (And rerun it a few times; I vaguely recall that the processor ordering boils down to hash ordering because some code somewhere first puts them all in a `java.util.HashMap`, and the hashcode depends on a system hashcode at some point, which boils down to memory position. In other words, the hash values are arbitrary and thus you end up with a bug that occurs randomly 50% of the time (if the ordering goes lombok then mapstruct, it all works. If it goes the other way, the build fails). So, run ~20 times in a row to be sure. Only if all 20 tries seem to work out, we can be reasonably sure it's not just down to getting lucky that many times in a row.
Using 1.18.20 doesn't work either - which I assumed is what you meant I give a go (as I was already using 1.18.22)...? :)
But just to be sure I also compiled 20 times with 1.18.22 - no luck there either

I have created a minimal project with just Lombok and MapStruct, and it compiles there without issues. So this is likely an issue with our project's setup. I'm going to try add a few other dependencies into the mix in order to figure out what is causing this.

Okay, so, I did some more digging. 

Given `MyClass#entityOnly` exists but `MyClassDto#entityOnly` doesn't,
And `MyClass` is annotated with `@FieldNameConstants`
When I use `@Mapping(target = "entityOnly", ignore = true)` on my mapper `MyClass toEntity(MyClassDto dto)` because I have set`unmappedTargetPolicy=error`
Then I get lots of compilation errors
 
But when I remove that `@Mapping` and the `unmappedTargetPolicy=error`
Then it compiles. 

Given `MyClass#prop` exists
And `MyClass#property` exists
When I use the following to map the two
```
    @Mapping(source = MyClass.Fields.prop, target="property")
    MyClassDto toDto(MyClass entity);

    @Mapping(source = "property", target = MyClass.Fields.prop)
    MyClass toEntity(MyClassDto dto);
``` 
Then it compiles as well.

So this is likely not a matter of order between MapStruct and Lombok (and/or OpenApi; the normal mappings work, after all, even when they reference the `Fields` class), but rather an issue with using `ignore=true` for a property that doesn't exist on `target` (to deal with compilation aborts because `unmappedTargetPolicy=error` is enabled).

Is this something you will look into, or should I open a ticket against the mapstruct project? 
(That is, who looks after `lombok-mapstruct-binding` - and is it related to that?)
I've opened a ticket on MapStruct's tracker as well; cf. above. It contains an example mapper to reproduce the issue.
@anno1985 yes, that was a typo, I meant: try with 1.18.20. Hmm, so doesn't work in either. Gracias for the reproduction recipe!

I've had a look at the example from @anno1985. And I do not think that it is related with MapStruct or Lombok, and I think that there is nothing that could be done by either annotation processor about this. 

The compile error we are getting is happening really early in the compilation, even before the annotation processors are run.

The errors I see are:

```
[ERROR] /~/lombok-mapstruct-issue/src/main/java/Mapper.java:[24,29] cannot find symbol
  symbol:   variable Fields
  location: class Entity
[ERROR] /~/lombok-mapstruct-issue/src/main/java/Mapper.java:[25,29] cannot find symbol
  symbol:   variable Fields
  location: class Entity
[ERROR] /~/oss/lombok-mapstruct-issue/src/main/java/Mapper.java:[24,5] expression not allowed as annotation value
```

When I add
```
<compilerArgs>
    <compilerArg>-XprintProcessorInfo</compilerArg>
    <compilerArg>-XprintRounds</compilerArg>
</compilerArgs>
```

to the maven-compiler configuration the processor information is not printed at all. Once I remove the `@Mapping` annotations then I can see

```
[INFO] Compiling 3 source files to /Users/filiphr/development/oss/lombok-mapstruct-issue/target/classes
Round 1:
	input files: {Entity, Dto, Mapper}
	annotations: [lombok.Getter, lombok.Setter, lombok.experimental.FieldNameConstants, lombok.NoArgsConstructor, org.mapstruct.Mapper]
	last round: false
Processor org.mapstruct.ap.MappingProcessor matches [org.mapstruct.Mapper] and returns false.
Processor lombok.launch.AnnotationProcessorHider$AnnotationProcessor matches [lombok.Setter, lombok.Getter, org.mapstruct.Mapper, lombok.experimental.FieldNameConstants, lombok.NoArgsConstructor] and returns false.
Processor lombok.launch.AnnotationProcessorHider$ClaimingProcessor matches [lombok.Setter, lombok.Getter, lombok.experimental.FieldNameConstants, lombok.NoArgsConstructor] and returns true.
Round 2:
	input files: {}
	annotations: []
	last round: false
Processor org.mapstruct.ap.MappingProcessor matches [] and returns false.
Processor lombok.launch.AnnotationProcessorHider$AnnotationProcessor matches [] and returns false.
Processor lombok.launch.AnnotationProcessorHider$ClaimingProcessor matches [] and returns true.
Round 3:
	input files: {}
	annotations: []
	last round: true
```

This makes me believe that the problem is in the fact that at the time of processing the files because they need to be used by the annotation processors the information is just not there and can never be there, since in order to be there one of the processors needs to run. In order to use the fields from Lombok you'll need to do 2 different compilation units. This is not like using classes, since classes have a special way of being marked in the annotation processors that they are not present. However, the `FieldNameConstants` are not like that.

In any case, MapStruct is quite type safe so you can use the strings in the `@Mapping` if something changes MapStruct will have a compile error anyways. If you use the MapStruct IntelliJ plugin you can have refactoring support as well.

@rzwitserloot I hope this analysis helps. If you have some ideas that we could don on the MapStruct side, please let me know. I am happy to help our joint users have a good experience with Lombok and MapStruct.

NB: this on its own will compile
```
@Mapping(target = Entity.Fields.entityProperty, source = "dtoProperty") 
Entity toEntity(Dto dto) 
```
provided `unmappedTargetPolicy` is set to `warn` - even though it uses `Fields`. Shouldn't that then fail as well? (Sorry for the brevity, I'm on my mobile.)

Thanks for having had another look! :)
@rzwitserloot maybe it's worth leaving a note re interoperability and available workaround on the feature's explanation page in the small print section?

@anno1985 Well, we have a 'fine print' section for esoterics like this.

title: [BUG] lombok.fieldDefaults.default* errors with records
body:
**Describe the bug**
When `lombok.config` is specified with `lombok.fieldDefaults.defaultPrivate = true` and/or `lombok.fieldDefaults.defaultFinal = true` compilation fails with the following: 

`error: @FieldDefaults is only supported on a class or an enum.`

**To Reproduce**

`lombok.config`:
```
lombok.fieldDefaults.defaultPrivate = true
lombok.fieldDefaults.defaultFinal = true
```

`Foo.java`:
```
public record Foo() {
}
```

**Expected behavior**

While the error is valid if `@FieldDefaults` were explicitly used for a record, the expectation is that Java records would be excluded as a candidate for `lombok.fieldDefaults.default*` instead of applying and erroring.

title: [BUG] @Builder and @RequiredArgsConstructor with a non-final field result in a compilation error

nodes.body:
This is documented and intentional; perhaps there's a bug in the intellij plugin as it should be flagging this as an error (but this plugin has a [separate issue tracker](https://github.com/mplushnikov/lombok-intellij-plugin)).

`@Builder` implies `@AllArgsConstructor` _unless_ an explicit constructor is written, in which case Builder will assume the programmer knows what they are doing and that the constructor builder will call will 'work out' and resolve to it.

`@RequiredArgsConstructor` counts as 'an explicit constructor', so Builder doesn't make one here. You can just add `@AllArgsConstructor` as well (have both that and `@RequiredArgsConstructor`) and all is well again.

title: [FEATURE] Set serialVersionUID in @StandardException
body: Rather annoyingly, javac lint insists on exceptions having a serialVersionUID. It'd be great if `@StandardException` added it.

nodes.body:
Lombok intentionally does not cater to idiotic linting rules, and that one is idiotic. (Specifically, the rule: "All things that are serializable must have a serialVersionUID" is extremely dubious. Applying this rule to things that are serializable by accident is downright stupidity).

It's a daily struggle; it's tempting, for convenience, to 'fix' it. But, here's the more crucial problem: Adding serialVersionUID here is either [A] just straight up making your code quite a bit worse (yes, this linting rule gives you incentive to make your code worse. I'm using the word 'stupidity' for good reason), or [B] makes it only slightly worse but writing it 'semi-properly' like this is actually really expensive, in the sense that it'll add whole new dependencies that lombok currently doesn't have; stuff we need to maintain indefinitely.

Given that we'd be doing all that just because of a boneheaded move in a linter tool, I'm vetoing it.

For clarity:

_Explanation of how it works: Whenever you serialize any object using java's baked in serialization mechanism, the 'serialVersionUID' of a class is written into the data as well. When deserializing, that class needs to be on the classpath, _AND_ it must have the same svUid. If it doesn't, deserializing throws. The svUid of any class is defined as [A] the value of the `static final long serialVersionUID` field if it is present, or if it is not, [B] the result of computing it, which is based on hashing all signature aspects of that class (extends, implements, the type and name of all the fields, the return type, name, and parameter types and names of all methods). If you want to see it, the `serialver` tool (in the `bin` dir of any JDK distro) will tell you._

The reason that it is boneheaded to complain about this is that the UID part of the serialization mechanism is what it is, and whilst it's not great, it is actually _better_ than what this linting rule is pushing you to. Specifically, this is the proper model of serial version UID management:

* Do not use java's baked in serialization mechanism, duh.

But, let's roll with it, and go for the distant second best option:

* All classes start out with the computed svUid. __Do not explicitly add one__.
* When you update your code and you are actually doing the silly move of using serialization to communicate between different versions of the same app, then by default any class is no longer compatible with a previous version of itself if any part of any signature changed.
* ... unless the author has _explicitly_ opted into writing a version update that IS compatible with older versions and has taken the time to write tests and document this behaviour. In this case they obviously have the older version (how else could they make the promise that you can deserialize something 'saved' with the old version using the new version, if you don't even have the old?) - so they run the `serialver` tool on the old version and __explicitly write this into their new version__.

The above is obviously (to me anyway) vastly superior to any other approach, _if_ (de)serializing between versions is even relevant (which it really shouldn't be). Thus, if you go with the rule of 'do not use serialization', then the linting rule should be disabled. If you go with the alternate best way to go about it, the linting rule should still be disabled: It is in fact RIGHT that all classes start off without any svUid initially, and it is literally impossible to know which svUid should be written if you deign to write one out explicitly.

## Seriously, generate it though!

Okay, let's ignore all that and say we add this feature. But what number shall we put in? There are 3 options.

### A constant value, such as `1L`

This just changes the conventions: Instead of defaulting to the behaviour of 'any signature update makes a class incompatible with a previous version of itself - to change that, add svUid', you've now changed that behaviour to 'any signature change, even adding a field, doesn't matter - that class is still serialization-compatible with any previous version of it - to change that, add svUid'.

That's silly, and the linter tool is wrong, and we won't make lombok worse (or rather, make lombok generate worse code) just because of some linter tool's bad choices.

### The actual svUid

This is superfluous, and therefore a DRY violation, and therefore silly: If you don't write the svUid field in, then the svUid of that class is then by definition the same thing we'd generate. We keep the saner default (any sig change means: incompatible), but we're now generating something that is literally completely pointless. It's like adding `import java.lang.*;` to all java files. Literally does nothing at all, as all java files do that already whether you write it or not.

In fact, a linting tool should probably flag down any code that is literally pointless as being superfluous. So we'd be writing code to satisfy an existing bad linting config, which should be flagged as bad code by hypothetical better linters. We're not going to do that.

But even if we change our mind, adding this functionality to lombok isn't exactly trivial: We'd have write a dummy value, let the compilation occur, and then get in there and 'fix' your class file to put in the proper svUid. Because this is a chicken-and-egg situation (how do you determine the serialver of a class if the `.class` file doesn't exist yet?). Alternatively, we write from scratch a tool that can determine the serialver based on an AST (a tree representation of a source file). This requires resolution and is man-months worth of work, obviously not worth it.

Thus, _IF_ I'm wrong and this is a good idea, surely it boils down to this option, except this option is a few orders of magnitude too much worse given the dubious benefits.

### What you want: The svUid of the previous version, _IF_ you are compatible with it

But this is of course impossible. Lombok has no idea what the java source file looked like in a previous version. We're not going to go `git` spelunking.

But I do see one option to help out a little bit: How do you turn this linter rule off? We should probably add that to the docs of `@StandardException`, perhaps in the small print.

Leaving this issue open for that feedback.

Wow, thanks for that detailed explanation. You should post it to a relevant Stackoverflow question.

javac is basically saying, "The serialver tool is wrong," which is an odd thing for tools in the same toolchain to be saying about one another. Actually, it probably is a bad decision to calculate SVUID from so many factors. Just using field names and types would have made more sense (which might be a reasonable lombok feature request). (To add to the rant: Why is it called a Unique ID? The whole point is that it need not be unique.) In any case, I don't use Java serialization, so I'll just disable the lint rule.

A brief note in the docs about the decision to not generate SVUID with a link to this issue or SO is a good idea.
