title: [FEATURE] @ToString whether can chose output type,like @ToString(type = "json")

nodes.body:
I can't accept this feature. For two reasons.

## toString is by spec unstructured; you're going against it here.

JSON is structured data. There is no point to JSON unless you intend for some software to read it back.

The problem is: `toString` is fundamentally undefined. As in, the docs explicitly mention that toString does not have a proscribed format, and explicitly mentions that you should not attempt to parse the output of it with anything except human eyeballs. It's for shunting into a log file as unstructured data, looking at in a debug session. That's about it.

Of course, there's a way to fix that: Just don't call it `toString()`; call it `toJson()` or whatnot. If you want, you can even make `toString()` just be `return toJson();`. But forcing a user of your class to invoke toString() for something other than 'unstructured data to shunt into a log file or show in a debugging session' is wrong, and this feature would __require__ a giant warning that explains this programming maxim. We don't make features like that.

## This is idiotically complicated

"Serialize a java class into JSON" is incredibly complicated. Jackson and GSON and co are not tiny libraries by any means. We'd have to either reproduce all that, or be a light wrapper around them, or put heavy restrictions on this feature and e.g. say that every field must be a primitive, a String, or a List/Array/Map where the component types are recursively one of these types. Which then strongly incentivizes folks to make a `Map<String, Map<Integer, List<Double>>` which is bad java.

This misses the mark. By miles: It's a high cost feature that incentivizes bad code.

title: [FEATURE] SuperBuilder with final fields regarding this keyword in super constructors

nodes.body:
The problem is not the `this` keyword.  The problem is that the constructor you implemented manually is not used when instantiating an object via `@SuperBuilder`.

For 'regular' initializations the solution is to move your expression to a field initializer and put `@Builder.Default` on it. However, as explained in #1749, you can't do that for expressions containing `this`.

Your only way out is to implement the  `@SuperBuilder` constructor manually. Use `delombok` to c&p it and change it according to your needs.

PS: Theoretically, the behavior of `@Builder.Default` could be changed for `@SuperBuilder`. In contrast to `@Builder`, `@SuperBuilder` performs the field initialization inside the constructor and not the builder. Thus, you could access `this` in there.
I think all we need to do is to remove the `static` from the `$default$xyz` initializer method. But there may be side effects I don't see.

title: [FEATURE] Re-Consider regarding alien NonNull annotations
body:
**Before submitting**

This has been already talked in #2757 

**Describe the feature**

It could be said as _sort of_ good things that lombok takes care of some `@No(n|t)Null`s but it could reach to an unexpected behavior.

But it's clear that every annotation defined within frameworks/libraries has it's own meaning and validation context along with specific verification stages. 
Adding a null-checking condition to generated setters may cause problems, and sometimes, takes time to debug. 

```java
@org.springframework.lang.NonNull // Shouldn't be Lombok's business
@javax.validation.constraints.NotNull
@lombok.NonNull // This should be the one that Lombok takes care.
String some;
```

Regardless of the documentation of any alien `@NonNull` annotation mandates,
Lombok should take care of the `@lombok.NonNull` and of it only.

title: [BUG] lombok config command should return a non-zero exit status if there's an error in the provided config file
body:
**Describe the bug**
When running `java -jar ~/.ivy2/cache/org.projectlombok/lombok/jars/lombok-1.18.20.jar config server/src/lombok.config` when there's an error in the config file (syntax, unknown key, etc.) the exit status is still 0, so the command can't be used from scripts to determine whether the developer has made an invalid change to the config file.

**To Reproduce**
Add a line like this to your lombok.config:

```
lombok.withdsf.flagUsage=ERROR
```

Note that `withdsf` is not a valid key

Run `java -jar ~/.ivy2/cache/org.projectlombok/lombok/jars/lombok-1.18.20.jar config server/src/lombok.config`

**Expected behavior**
The exit status should be > 0.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version
`1.18.20`

 - Platform (javac or eclipse, and if so, what is the output of `javac -version` / the version listed in the _about..._ dialog of eclipse.
```
openjdk version "11.0.9" 2020-10-20
OpenJDK Runtime Environment AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.9+11)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.9+11, mixed mode)
```

nodes.body: Good idea. What exit code do you suggest?
Currently, we do exit with 1 if there's a command line problem, like unsupported flags, or invalid keys or directories.

I think that any unique code would work well. 
Most tools use unique integers -- which would suggest using "2", or whatever the next free one is 


Some others use bitmasks, so that the exit code can indicate more than one condition in a single integer. In that case, the next bit would be '2' - allowing '3' to mean "command line problem" AND "config file problem". That said, this doesn't seem like a relevant approach in this particular situation.
Any suggestion on where to document the meanings of those exit codes?
@rspilker sorry, I missed that last comment - at the bottom of https://projectlombok.org/features/configuration in an "Exit Codes" section?

Reviewing that documentation: We don't really explain the notion that you can run `lombok.jar config` to 'debug' an existing conf file, at all. Re-opening issue, with the specific purpose of adding a whole section to the `/features/configuration` page to explain that, and that section should include the info about the error codes we return.

Duplicate of #1118

title: @Accessors(chain = true) doesn't generate overrides for methods in child classes
body:
**Describe the bug**
I have a parent class with a method `setDescription(@NonNull String description)`. Then I have its child. When I try to use `childVar.setDescription("Example")` it returns an instance of the parent class, which doesn't allow writing something like `return new ChildClass().setDescription()`. This also breaks a list of calls in fluent style, if I will call a method of one of the parent classes between child method calls - it returns parent instance and there is no chance to return to the child's context and call their methods.

**To Reproduce**
1. Create a parent class with one setterMethod(of something) and annotate the class with `@Accessors(chain = true)`
2. Create a child class
3. Create a method somewhere and a variable inside it with a type of *child* class
4. Try to assign the result of `new ChildClass().setterMethod(...)` to the variable

**Expected behavior**
the setterMethod(...) call on the child will return ChildClass, because it is called on a ChildClass instance and there are no type conversions inside


**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version: bundled with spring-boot-starter-parent 2.5.6
 - Platform javac 11.0.12 / IDEA Build #IU-212.5284.40

nodes.body:
That would require [resolution](https://github-wiki-see.page/m/projectlombok/lombok/wiki/LOMBOK-CONCEPT:-Resolution) which is extremely difficult. The amount of feature requests I could write up for when we have resolution is as long as my leg, see keeping them all open is not useful, and there's no worry we lose sight of stuff like this if ever we figure out a way to do resolution correctly. Hence, closed.

As an additional complication, there is just no way to do this without being __highly__ surprising, _or_ more annoying than you think it will be. There are only two options:

1. If you happen to have lombok on the classpath and you have a class X, which uses __no__ lombok annotations anywhere in it, but it so happens to `extends` a class that does, do you want lombok to then add all these pointless passthrough overrides _just_ to update the return type? This might have performance implications and breaks a golden rule: We don't want the compilation of classes without any lombok annotations to just change (or not) depending on whether lombok is loaded.
2. Alternatively, you need to either use some lombok or preferably, a specific special annotation _just_ for: "Please fix my fluent methods for me", which is annoying and easily forgotten.

Here's the simple conclusion: If you like both class hierarchies and fluent style, java isn't for you, and lombok has no readily implementation solution to address that. Java kinda needs a 'SELF' type, and this would be a fine argument to make to team OpenJDK to add it. I don't think lombok can be of any serious help.

In other words, even if resolution was a thing we could do, this is not a feature we could add lightly.
Duplicate of #1147

title: [BUG] Using @Builder.Default with Java 11 may lead to wrong generic type

nodes.body:
The problem is that there is a position based cache in `javac` that gets used for resolving some types. Lombok moves the initializer to a new method if you use `@Builder.Default` and sets the position to match the annotation position as it does for all generated nodes. Both of the arguments share the same position so the resolved type of the first one gets used for the second one too.

A possible workaround might be to not change the position of the initializer but there might be some unintended side effects.

**GOAL**
Reduce the length of toString() outputs by ignoring variables that are null.

**BENEFIT**
Greatly improves the readability of object outputs, especially on data beans that contain many null variables.

Thanks for your consideration!

title: eclipse highlighting issues with `@SneakyThrows` and `@Cleanup`
body:
I still get highlighting issues with `@SneakyThrows` and `@Cleanup` since they are mentioned on methods and variables, maybe that's the difference

_Originally posted by @rzwitserloot in https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/2950#issuecomment-929752026_

nodes.body: Can you provide a small example with instructions how I can reproduce it? In my short test everything seems to work as expected.

> Can you provide a small example with instructions how I can reproduce it? In my short test everything seems to work as expected.

Please find the `@SneakyThrows` in the project https://github.com/Ranger-118/lombok-demo.git and try to compare when comment it. I'm using VSCode which is same as Eclipse.

Thanks for this perfect example.

The problme is that lombok hides generated nodes for refactorings, cleanups and the highlighter. In most cases this works flawlessly but `@Cleanup` and `@SneakyThrows` create a wrapping `try` statement and because this one is generated all child elements get hidden. This also affects cleanups in eclipse that will simply not touch the body of such methods. The only real fix I know is to replace the generic hider with specific ones for all refactorings (thats how it was done some time ago) but thats a lot of work...
@Rawi01 I can understand the workload, not a lifeblood case anyway, you may fix it in proper time.
@Rawi01 Or maybe you could brief a bit more so that I do it myself?

Lombok marks all generated nodes (classes, methods, statements, etc.) as generated. This information is required to handle some cases for example the cleanup/save action part. If eclipse tries to perform some cleanup for the generated nodes it sometimes simply fails because there is no actual code that can be changed. To handle this lombok used some patches for a handcrafted list of save actions. Eclipse added a bunch of new save actions/cleanups in the latest versions and instead of adding them all by hand I replaced this list with a generic mechanism (https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/commit/ff8af6164dfffa0827d12a342da35fc89d37c504).

Eclipse uses the visitor pattern to traverse the AST and the new patch intercepts the `accept` method and simply returns if the node is generated and the visitor should not see the node and all of its children. This obviously also hides the generated `try ... catch` statement and its children. This was an unintended side effect of the new patch.

The fastest way to fix it is to revert the generic solution and add all new save actions to the list (started that some time ago https://github.com/Rawi01/lombok/commit/c8c46afd5ca1eb86ea9ffec5576cfd65269f6704). The downside of this is that we have to adjust the list everytime eclipse (or the language server implementation) changes.

A different approach might be to keep the current idea but not hide the children of a `try`. I tried that by removing the generated flag for the generated `try` but this leads to exceptions in some save actions...

To only fix the highlighting you can also remove the `SemanticTokensVisitor` in `PatchFixes#isBlockedVisitorAndGenerated` and add custom patches for this class.

body:

@EqualsAndHashCode is supposed to take into account lombok.addNullAnnotations configuration, however that doesn't work properly and results in 'org.eclipse.jdt.annotation.Nullable cannot be resolved to a type'

**To Reproduce**
Eclipse 2019-12 (4.14)
-javaagent:lombok-1.18.22.jar
Maven:
```
		<dependency>
			<groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
			<artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
			<version>1.18.22</version>
			<scope>provided</scope>
		</dependency>

			<artifactId>extra2-epl</artifactId>
			<version>2.7.0</version>
		</dependency>

```
lombok.config
`lombok.addNullAnnotations=none`
(or anything else really)

```
@NonNullByDefault
@EqualsAndHashCode 
public class LombokFail
{

}

```

-> **org.eclipse.jdt.annotation.Nullable cannot be resolved to a type**

Commenting out @NonNullByDefault fixes the issue

I assume the key moment here is that annotations I use include org.eclipse.jdt.annotation.NonNullByDefault but at the same time javax.annotation.Nonnull (instead of Eclipse's one) and some kind of detection/generation goes haywire inside.

**Expected behavior**
Correct annotations should be placed and code should generate properly.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
Eclipse 2019-12 (4.14)
-javaagent:lombok-1.18.22.jar

nodes.body:
Your problem is simply that solf has embedded it's own version of the NonNullByDefault annotation, without including the other Eclipse annotations. You need to declare the following dependency if you want to be able to resolve those annotations:

```
<dependency>
	<groupId>org.eclipse.jdt</groupId>
	<artifactId>org.eclipse.jdt.annotation</artifactId>
	<version>2.2.600</version>
</dependency>

```

@JohnPaulTaylorII thank you for proposing a solution!

However can you perhaps elaborate why
`lombok.addNullAnnotations=none`

would require Eclipse's annotations on classpath?

I would assume that, when Lombok sees NonNullByDefault, it assumes (and rightly so) that you have all the Eclipse annotations on the classpath, not just NonNullByDefault. I think the heart of the issue is that the referenced solf library includes a half implementation of the Eclipse annotations, which essentially means that Lombok can only provide half a solution, and the compiler will complain about the missing half.

I disagree that Lombok should assume anything.
There's configuration option 'lombok.addNullAnnotations' which is supposed to take care of resolving what annotations to use (including the option to use custom annotations).

I think it's a bug that Lombok 'decides' to use Eclipse's annotations disregarding the value of 'lombok.addNullAnnotations'

I believe what you're asking for is an impossible situation. You've specified the class as NonNullByDefault. This means that the argument to .equals(Object) is NonNull. However, this isn't true; .equals accepts null arguments. So Lombok _must_ mark the argument as nullable. The only correct annotation for this, since org.eclipse.jdt.annotation.NonNullByDefault was used, is org.eclipse.jdt.annotation.Nullable, so that is what Lombok must add to generate a correct .equals(Object) method. Otherwise, the method signature is incorrect and callers of .equals will be unable to compare to null.

It doesn't strike me as a bug that Lombok cannot respect a setting saying not to use null annotations when null annotations are already present in the code. Especially when the only valid solution is to make use of an annotation from the same source package. Again, the solf.nullanno package directly includes the code for one of the annotations from org.eclipse.jdt.annotation instead of correctly depending on the full (and very small) maven package.

I do not think I'm asking for impossible.
Generating non-null/nullable annotations on methods with no prototypes (e.g. equals/hashCode as opposed to getter/setter which are generated from fields) is an optional action; older versions of lombok simply never generated them.

If lombok does want to generate those annotations (which is a nice feature to have), it must respect the settings -- e.g. if it's 'none', it should be 'none'.

But other settings don't work either, e.g. I initially tried to use CUSTOM:classname in order to use annotations that I wanted, but it also was ignored and was failing. When I tested it more, it seems like this setting has no real effect despite what documentation says, so looks like a bug to me.

And solf.nullanno isn't doing anything 'incorrect'. The Eclipse's annotation there is different from default Eclipse's one (it has different settings for what is considered non-null by default) -- this is one of the reasons it doesn't depend on Eclipse's package.

Good work by everybody else who commented here – it is indeed intentional behaviour. The presence of NonNullByDefault means that `Nullable` must be added to e.g. `equals(@Nullable object other)`.

What you're asking is that lombok generates __broken code__. I get that it's confusing when you specifically asked lombok not to generate nullity annotations and it does so anyway, but it's intentional, correct, and will not be changed.

I cannot fathom why some project includes NonNullByDefault but not the others. The point is: Your setup and outlook is broken, and/ or that library is broken. Lombok isn't at fault here. It sounds like  you may have to file an issue at some other project for this.

title: [BUG] Changed AST tree even though no lombok used in file

nodes.body:
Lombok does not change the source, it only modifies the AST but only if there is a lombok annotation. I created an example that declares multiple variables, added a breakpoint in the first lombok method and noticed that eclipse already splitted it up into multiple `LocalDeclaration` nodes.

Have you checked that the problem goes away if you downgrade to an older lombok version? How do you get the source for a `TypeDeclaration`?

Vehement agreement with @Rawi01 here: That's an extraordinarily claim, given that lombok simply doesn't do anything until it sees lombok annotations. Lombok definitely isn't expanding LocalDeclaration/FieldDeclaration like this, ever. If you're observing it, either you're getting the run-around from eclipse and it's not actually lombok related somehow, or, lombok is calling 'getters' on the AST nodes and eclipse is doing it in those methods.

In that last case I'm pretty sure that if lombok hadn't 'caused it', something that is about to happen (firing off save actions, compiling the file, etc - something inevitable that is about to occur) would do it, so then there really is no issue here: Something is going to expand that node no matter what, lombok merely makes it happen a blink-of-an-eye earlier than without lombok. Doesn't sound like a thing we should attempt to 'fix'.

However, the one thing that makes me pause and think: Maybe we should look into this, is that _if_ this is caused by attribution (which is somewhat expensive), _and_ it occurs even in files with no lombok annotations in it, then that means lombok's mere presence causes more attribution than required, so if we can eliminate it, we speed up eclipse+lombok, and that's worthwhile.

Here are the next debug steps as I see it. It's quite a bit of work, perhaps - not sure when we have the time to do this. But if someone else cares to do this, muchos gracias, owe you a drink of your choice:

* First, and looking at @LukasBasiura here - I want to ascertain in which scenario(s) is whatever-it-is-that-causes-the-expansion __not__ inevitable anyway? As in, which scenarios exists where, if lombok wasn't there, we save the cost of that attribution. To be clear, if all that removing lombok would do is that you still get the same number of attribs, but they would merely occur a little bit later, there's no relevant performance gain to be had. So, what actions attrib only if lombok is loaded in eclipse? A great answer to this question would be something like: "Set 'auto-format on save' in save actions, make an edit in a file with `int a, b;` in it and no lombok annotations at all. Save the file: With lombok, that `int a, b;` is expanded, without it, it isn't." That one is a double whammy - not just a performance win, also an actual 'bug' of sorts; mere presence of lombok shouldn't change the behaviour of the auto-formatter.

* Assuming the above leads to a 'yes' answer., and not just 'only when you use this (fairly obscure) plugin': A reproducible case that comes up often enough that warrants spending the time, then - Write some code that, with the lightest of touches, finds a specific `int a, b;` node (say, it's always in the top level class, first FieldDecl object), and prints the current status (expanded or not). Preferably using only field reads, we want to avoid whatever it is we do that causes the expansion. Then, pepper the lombok transformation process with calls to it to figure out which exact line causes eclipse to perform the expansion. That look if we can avoid it, or if we can do a pre-scan to early-exit if no lombok is found. Could do with a debug breakpoint + a watch as well.

title: 关于lombok重写equals方法的疑问

nodes.body:
The test `(!(o instanceof TestLombok))` is to ensure that `o` is either an instance of the TestLombok class OR of a subclass. If that's not the case, the objects can never be equal.

If `o` is an instance of TestLombok or of a subclass, it is still uncertain if the class hierarchy fully supports the equals contract.

That's why we ask "other" is they "canEqual" us. And of you would call the reverse `a.equals(b)` to `b.equals(a)`, in all circumstances should that give you the same results.

And our default implementation of canEqual, which can be overwritten, is another instance-of check.

I hope this answers your question.

## Latest assesment

1. This vulnerability is only present in Log4j core binaries below version 2.16.0, and not in any other logging frameworks.
2. Lombok does not distribute any Log4j binaries, nor does it declare (transitive) dependencies on anything.
3. If you use any of the `extern` lombok features, like `@lombok.extern.log4j.Log4j`, lombok will generate code that will use those libraries, but you are responsible to have direct or transitive dependency on those libraries, otherwise the lombok generated code will not compile.
4. Similarly, you are responsible for having the binaries available in your runtime, otherwise the class initialization might fail.
5. In the lombok testing code, we used to have a version that contains this vulnerability, but since the tests don't process any user input (the tests are hardcoded) and the generated code isn't even executed, running the tests did not lead to an RCE on the machine executing the tests.

So, no, Lombok itself does not need any changes, and is not responsible for any security problems your product might have regarding these broken Log4j libraries.

### Mitigation
1. Please follow the guidelines provided in [the original CVE page](https://www.randori.com/blog/cve-2021-44228/) to find out if your product is affected. Alternatively, our partner [Tidelift has a great advisory](https://blog.tidelift.com/tidelift-advisory-log4shell-critical-vulnerability-what-you-need-to-know-and-do?utm_source=maven-org-projectlombok-lombok&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=enterprise)
2. Upgrade your Log4j dependencies to at least 2.16.0
3. If that's not possible on short notice, [here are some pointers on how to make an older installation secure](https://github.com/apache/logging-log4j2/pull/608#issuecomment-990305306)

### Feedback
If you do not agree with the current assessment, please add a comment to this issue. However, please make sure you've read the other comments, and make sure you understand the problem.

__The balancing act:__
- Don't waste our time by asking more questions that you could have figured out yourself
- Do speak up if you are convinced we missed something, or new information is available 

### Latest changes
- 2021-12-17 18:00 CET: Changed the recommended version from 2.15.0 to 2.16.0 
- 2021-12-12 01:14 CET: The dependency used in the tests has been updated. Before that, since it was only used in tests, no user input was possible and the generated code was not executed, Lombok was already secure. But now, even external tools that analyse our code can also see that. We hope that that reduces the number of questions on our mailing lists and issue tracker.

Does anyone have the same question?

title: [FEATURE] Method chaining

nodes.body:
@juriad 
If method with annotation in super class, it could be overriden with method, which invoke super and return current type.

Annotation could not be compared with another library, where it is implemented with retaining.

Breaking a chain could be an option in lombok.config.

> I recently came across Concurnas and its call-site double dot notation for returning the receiver. But that looks out-of-scope for Lombok.

Dart had the same syntax. In Lombok, we cannot add that, since we can only use valid java syntax. The best we could do is 

```java
foo.$.setX(x).$.setY(y);
```

In this example I used `$`, but that could be anything other valid java identifier.

I would love to add a call site solution, since it also would work for other existing void-returning methods. However, how would you opt-in for this in your source file. What I mean by that is that most lombok features are triggered by adding an annotation on your source code at some level, so anyone reading your code understands that there might be something going on.
I totally agree with @rzwitserloot, but in all fairness we could implement that lombok only processes `.$.` if you `import lombok.$;`.

title: [FEATURE] want a Class Attribute copy function
[FEATURE] replace Beanutil.copyproperties() function

nodes.body:
Other code-generating libraries can do this and do it better. Look at https://mapstruct.org/.

Lombok can't do this because the code requires the knowledge of the fields (and constructor and setters) of the target of the conversion - magic word - resolution.

It is also arguably the wrong place to do this in a data class because it mixes responsibilities - data class should hold data, not convert them. Once Lombok allows simple copying of properties of compatible types, there will come requests for adjusting the data types, using different constructors (mapping @Value), ignoring fields, deep copying of collections...

I am not a Lombok maintainer, but I expect this feature request to be closed for the aforementioned reasons.

title: Undocumented change in 1.18.22
body:
Hi, there appears to be an undocumented change to `@Builder` and the generated code that has affected our MapStruct `@AfterMapping` code generation. There is a known issue (which we have only just discovered) in MapStruct when using builders - see [here](https://github.com/mapstruct/mapstruct/issues/1862) - and after upgrading Lombok from 1.18.20 to 1.18.22 we are now triggering the documented behaviour. In earlier version of Lombok this is not the case, e.g. MpStruct is not detecting the builders and is generating code as expected.

Can someone confirm what may have changed which means MapStruct is now detecting the builder to be available where it previously could not?

Well, that is really strange, especially since we do not use maven to compile our code.

What's going on here?
Oh, you are compiling other code using maven and this is the jit compiler that kicks in and tries to optimize the bytecode

ok i am going to disable the jit compiler then.
Do you have another idea ?
Unfortunately not. The log is not a lot of help here.
Is it in j9 possible to only prevent the jit compiler from compiling classes that start with 'lombok'? If so, I think other users would be interested as well.

which kind of additional information you need ?
it's Java version: 11.0.13
I think the issue occurs when rewriting the classes for each lombok annotations there are used in each classes
What exact compiler? I see j9 in the classpath. Are you using the Oracle JDK? OpenJDK, Adoptium?

To be crystal clear here: Whatever JDK you're running this on is broken and you're filing the bug in the wrong place - it's on them, not on us. But, it'd be good to research if the worst case scenario is happening here, which would be:

* Start with a lombok user running `javac` on a J9-based OpenJDK (Javac itself is a java app and runs on some VM; the `javac` command line tool is just a wrapper that starts `java` (the VM) with the right arguments.
* Then, they use lombok for anything, and this crash immediately happens. Whether they use maven or gradle or straight up `javac` on its own, and probably even if lombok is on the classpath but you aren't using any lombok features (as the traces seem to indicate whatever is happening here, happens during lombok init).

__Next step for @Tonicku__:

We need to everything about your OpenJDK installation; the one installed at `/var/jenkins_home/tools/hudson.model.JDK/OpenJDK11`.

OpenJDK is __not a distribution__! - that is not an answer. OpenJDK is a source code repository. Somebody `git clone`d that repo, built it, and shipped it to you. Given that the vendor is IBM, I think we're looking at adoptium perhaps? I'm not sure. From your traces we're 99% sure that it's a J9 variant.

Example answer we need:

"I went to `https://developer.ibm.com/languages/java/semeru-runtimes/downloads/`, picked 'open edition', 'Java 11 (LTS)', 'Linux', and 'x64' from the dropdowns, and then downloaded the JDK variant of the v11.0.13.0 release, as an rpm, and installed it using redhat's rpm tool."

Given that it's not our bug, without this info I don't think we should spend any further time on this issue - parked, delete if no feedback 2021-02-01.

Let's first check if this is a problem with OpenJ9 in general or something more specific to your hardware, and then let's check if it's still an issue in semeru 17 (jdk-openj9 is called semeru these days, adoptopenjdk.net is obsolete – maybe your jenkins is out of date or possibly team jenkins hasn't gotten around to updating that GUI of that part of the installation process?) - and then file a bug with them if so.

Going on a redirection spree from adoptopenjdk, the downloads should be here: [https://developer.ibm.com/languages/java/semeru-runtimes/downloads](IBM OpenJDK Semeru download page).

I downloaded IBM semuru JDK-11.0.13+8 x64, fired up an AWS ec2 server on x64, installed it, and tried to compile a trivial java file using 1 lombok feature, just with `javac -cp lombok.jar ThatFile.java` and it worked fine. At this point I don't know what's going on but the worst case scenario (where javac-on-J9 straight up fails on all platforms if using lombok) has been disproven.

title: [BUG]fName field naming difference with jdk
body:
Hi, I found a field naming problem:
Field name like xXxxx(The first letter is lowercase, the second letter is uppercase).Our database was used many years ago, fields are named starting with "f", table names are starting with "t", and views are starting with "v" (this is the database naming convention at that time)
Lombok generated name is getXXxxx, and the norm for jdk, jackson, mybatis and most frameworks is getxXxxx.
In this case, json will not be able to parse the content, the persistence layer will not be able to assign values, and many other problems. Could you fix this kind of naming method? This will be helpful for development work .
thanks.

nodes.body:
I think you should use the [Accessors feature](https://projectlombok.org/features/experimental/Accessors).

If this is common in your whole codebase, in the upcoming version of lombok you can use `lombok.config` to fix this:

```Shell
lombok.accessors.capitalization = beanspec
```

In the meantime, we can offer to get rid of the letters 'f'and 'v' by using
```Shell
lombok.accessors.prefix += f
lombok.accessors.prefix += v
```

> 我认为您应该使用[访问器 功能](https://projectlombok.org/features/experimental/Accessors)。
> 
> 如果这在你的整个代码库中很常见，那么在即将推出的龙目岛版本中，你可以用它来解决这个问题：`lombok.config`
> 
> ```shell
> lombok.accessors.capitalization = beanspec
> ```
> 
> 同时，我们可以通过使用
> 
> ```shell
> lombok.accessors.prefix += f
> lombok.accessors.prefix += v
> ```

It would seem more correct to do:
```java

title: [BUG] @UtilityClass fails to make inner class static in Java 9+
body:
**Describe the bug**

When a class is annotated with `@UtilityClass`, and this class has an inner class, the inner class is also treated as `static` in Java 1.8, but is not treated as `static` in Java 9 and later. This causes compilation failure under Java 9+ for code that compiled correctly in Java 1.8.

**To Reproduce**

Save the following as `Outer.java`:

```java
import lombok.experimental.UtilityClass;

@UtilityClass
class Outer {

  Object buildInner() {
    return new Inner();
  }

  class Inner {}
}
```

Compile this file using `javac` from Java 1.8, and observe that compilation succeeds with no diagnostic output:

```text
% /path/to/java-1.8/bin/javac -cp lombok.jar Outer.java
```

Now compile this file using `javac` from Java 9 or later, and observe that compilation fails:

```text
% /path/to/java-9/bin/javac -cp lombok.jar Outer.java
Outer.java:7: error: non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context
    return new Inner();
           ^
1 error
```

**Expected behavior**

Java 9 and later compilers should have compiled this source file, producing no diagnostic output.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version: 1.18.22
 - Platform: `javac` 9

**Additional context**

The problem first arises with Java 9, but also occurs in Java 11, 14, and 17. (I haven't tested Java 10, 12, 13, 15, or 16.)

#2519 seems closely related, but was closed because it could not be reproduced. However, that earlier report mentioned nothing about different Java versions. In this new report, I find that the Java compiler version is critical: the problem only arises in Java 9 and later, not in Java 1.8.

nodes.body: Heh, yeah that's no doubt what happened with #2519. Nice find. No need to test on the non-LTS versions except the last for such things.
The generated code is fine but we also have to adjust the related compiler symbols, in this case we have to remove the enclosing type of the inner class.
I think the first release containing this fix is version [1.18.24](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/commit/ba0f12846d0d3b192db32e781d5d2555be837eee).

title: [BUG] Why can RequiredArgsConstructor generate null-check statement for spring NonNull

nodes.body: Yes, this is expected. Lombok contains a [list of know `NonNull` annotations](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/blob/36db0524e4d0f6bc6fa2440b0df2c425c4d130fc/src/core/lombok/core/handlers/HandlerUtil.java#L84) and generates the `null`-checks if it detects one of these annotations.

@xma08 Yes - as @Rawi01 said, we have a list of types we know specifically mean 'null is never okay here'.

3 points:

* There are many nonnull annotations that do _not_ mean that. For example, JPA/Hibernate's `@NotNull` means: When making the sql `CREATE TABLE` statement, add a non-null constraint. But instances of this class can have `null` here - that just means: "When inserting, let the DB engine generate the default here". JPA's NotNull is not in our list. It's possible we misjudged `org.springframework.lang.NonNull` (though, fixing that now would be backwards incompatible, oof, I hope not). If that's the problem, please post an explanation, with some proof (links to documentation and the like) – most of us don't use spring.
* This feature is specifically for the setter and the constructor. Lombok will generate nullchecks in any method you write if you use specifically `@lombok.NonNull` on the parameter. That feature (if `@NonNull` on a handwritten method or constructor, inject a nullcheck) requires specifically using `@lombok.NonNull`).

title: [BUG] @Builder does not copy @JsonTypeIdResolver from Jackson

nodes.body:
Yeah, it's enough to add it in there. The only question is: Is it appropriate to copy annotation `com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.annotation.JsonTypeIdResolver` __in all circumstances regardless of context__?

I think the answer is 'yes', and then it is indeed as simple as adding it.

Thank you for your support!

In the given circumstance when deserializing we land here: https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-databind/blob/2.14/src/main/java/com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/introspect/JacksonAnnotationIntrospector.java#L1493 Given that both annotations complement each other and that JsonTypeInfo is already in the whitelist in Lombok, `com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.annotation.JsonTypeIdResolver` should be treated equally. 

However the above solution has a mistake. It probably should be rather added to `COPY_TO_SETTER_ANNOTATIONS` instead of `BASE_COPYABLE_ANNOTATIONS` because the right place would be there: https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/blob/master/src/core/lombok/javac/handlers/HandleBuilder.java#L924 (also the other annotations are there).
Otherwise, with `BASE_COPYABLE_ANNOTATIONS` the annotation is attached to the parameter instead of the setter method of the builder.

I am not sure if the annotation should then also be added to `JACKSON_COPY_TO_BUILDER_ANNOTATIONS`.

Adding it to `JACKSON_COPY_TO_BUILDER_ANNOTATIONS` should not be necessary. I strongly suspect Jackson will perform type identification before it will determine in which way it should instantiate. So this annotation will probably have no effect on the builder class. However, I did not test it (and I don't know when I have time to do so).

Jackson cannot know the type beforehand so it has to discover the type while deserializing. That is the whole point of [TypeIdResolver](https://fasterxml.github.io/jackson-databind/javadoc/2.7/com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/jsontype/TypeIdResolver.html). JsonTypeInfo is the descriptor where to find the id (extracted from the parent's field in my case) and passes it to the TypeIdResolver to find the appropriate class. Currently, only the JsonTypeInfo is found, so Jackson has no idea what to do.

I have updated the JUnit test in https://github.com/Nithanim/lombok-jackson-builder-bug/tree/d07d2e82e812576ab1cc336bc89b3ce6fdf9e48b
`JACKSON_COPY_TO_BUILDER_ANNOTATIONS` means "copy these annotations from the class to the builder class". It does not affect copying annotations from fields to builder setter methods.

Oh, sorry! I now know what you mean (I think). My reasoning was, that the builder will be used for discovery instead of the annotated class. But you are probably right that that does not make any sense.

title: [PROMOTION] Promote `lombok.experimental.Accessors`
body:
Before we promote it:

* Currently, Accessors half-cascades: If you have an `@Accessors` on both a field and the class it is in, any properties not set at all on the field-level `@Accessors` does __not__ look at the class-level `@Accessors`, but __does__ look in `lombok.config`. Instead, it should cascade as one expects: From field-level `@Accessors`, to type-level `@Accessors`, to `lombok.config`. This is technically backwards incompatible, but for an _experimental_ feature, this break is well on the correct side of what's acceptable. We do not intend for the feature to cascade from inner type to encompassing type, though - that feels more like you want some accessors default to apply to an entire package, and that's what `lombok.config` is for.
* Edit the `website` dir; move docs to main, move entry in `experimental/index.html` to the promoted list. Explain the cascade feature.

title: [BUG] @Setter not processed when a setX(Y y) exists

nodes.body:
Wontfix - this is Intentional behaviour.

* Use `@Tolerate` on your explicit setter to tell lombok that you don't want it to consider this method.
* If you put `@Setter` on the field, you'd get a warning (telling you that Setter does nothing here). However, you don't get this (again intentional behaviour) when you put it on a class. I don't know how to avoid the confusion here, unfortunately.

The reason this is intentional and we won't be changing it: It's actually rather difficult to attempt to 'figure out' if we should make that setter or not. For two reasons:

* If you have a supertype, say, `setError(Object o)`, you probably don't want lombok to generate a setter as well. Or maybe you do - I bet if I interview 1000 java developers, about 500 of them will be adamant that there is a clear answer to this question, but they won't all agree. Hence, picking a side is highly likely the wrong answer. If you disagree, note that we can't write code for this case in the first place without involving [resolution](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/wiki/LOMBOK-CONCEPT:-Resolution). Which is not an option.
* If you use type bounds, then this gets even more complicated. Is `public <T extends String> void setError(T err)` reason for lombok not to generate it? I sure hope so, because if we do, that's a compiler error - those 2 signatures clash.
* Now I'm dipping into academics, but, `public void setError(String... x) {}` - if that exists, should lombok generate one or not? We could legally (it's not a signature clash), but it'd be rather confusing if we did.
* What if, specifically for booleans, there is `public void setSomeBool() {this.someBool = true;}` - I'm not so sure someone would expect lombok to also make `setSomeBool(boolean v)`. Less of a case, but it doesn't help.

The first 2 bullets on their own are enough, let alone all 4.

For all these reasons, __there is no right answer__, so we choose not to play: Existence of any method named `setFoo` regardless of arguments means we don't generate a setter. `@Tolerate` exists to work around this.

title: [FEATURE] Provide option to cache toString

nodes.body:
Given that `toString()` should only ever be used for logging and debugging, if toString is too slow for you, you're doing something very wrong. Lombok explicitly does not cater to eliminating boilerplate in crappy code. Which leaves the few times where caching toString would be non-crappy code. I'm sure that happens too, but only in extremely exotic circumstances... and lombok doesn't cater to those either, which is why this feature is being rejected.

A few further reasons to explain in some more detail:

The reason we don't cater to that is the insinuation. If lombok has that feature, then our users will see it - their IDE will tell them, hey, look, `@ToString()` has a cache option! I guess that means lombok thinks that it's often useful (we don't cater to exotic cases, that's our very motto, hence I can't fault a user when they assume a lombok feature implies its a somewhat common need).

Said differently, say you're Jane Q. average java coder and you see this. You then wonder: Huh. I wonder when I need this?

And there's no good answer. I bet a ton of folks start thinking: Oh, this is such a great idea, we should always cache this, for everything. This is horrible:

* We now have boilerplated lombok: Instead of writing `@ToString`, you have to write `@ToString(cacheStrategy = ToString.CacheStrategy.LAZY)`, which is much more complicated. Instead of writing `@Value`, you now have to write `@Value @ToString(cacheStrategy = ToString.CacheStrategy.LAZY)` which is ridiculous.
* It's just wrong. No, you should not as a rule be caching your toString except in _extremely exotic_ circumstances.

My guess is that you're simply misunderstanding what toString is for, and therefore using it wrong, and you're now asking for boilerplate busting on this wrong use. Here are a few simple guidelines for toString:

* If you spec what the `toString()` method returns, you're doing it wrong. The point of toString is to be unspecced, and therefore, you should never write code that relies on what it contains.
* Code that calls toString needs to treat it as information that is meaningless to computers. Only humans can read it. If you convey it to the user in an interface, a debug tool, or a log file, you're fine. If you parse it, send it as part of an API (Unless in a 'description' field or otherwise intended solely for human consumption), you're doing it wrong.

As a separate issue I can see that you want to write something like:

```java
log.trace("Sending {}", yourObj);
```

And that the above is in some tight loop. If you've enabled trace-level debugging, that statement, whether `yourObj.toString()` is cached or not, is going to _kill_ your performance. Logging is not free. However, if you have disabled trace, then the incessant calling of toString in the above code may still kill your performance even though the log statement is a no-op. However, caching toString is __not__ the answer. Logging frameworks have solved this problem. You can just pass a lambda that calculates the toString, and the log framework will simply not invoke it because it checked first and found out that `trace` level logging isn't enabled.

Feature rejected.

One question remains: Is this supposed to happen or should Lombok handle this more gracefully?

@rzwitserloot I prototyped (the code is horrible) a style preserving delombok version some time ago. It takes an AST snapshot, performs lombok transformations and compares the result with the snapshot. This comparision creates a list of text transformations (borrowed the idea from eclipse refactorings) that can be applied to the original source code. This approach limits the changes to code that were changed by lombok and preserves all the little format details.

Do you think it makes sense to extend the prototype any further?

@Rawi01 Wow, that's going much further than what I was thinking of.

There are 2 orthogonal issues here:

* Delombok needs to deal with code that has no lombok transforms in it. Does it copy it verbatim, or auto-format the entire source file (copy verbatim probably superior, but requires 'detecting' the difference somehow, and weaving generated and non-generated code in a way that at least doesn't look completely wrong).
* Delombok __must__ be capable of pretty-printing: Generated nodes can't look horrible. Specifically for this case: Delombok's current prettyprinting approach for long chains of method invokes is suboptimal. It's relevant: `toBuilder` generates code that is a (potentially) long chain of invokes. Currently the prettyprinter piles em all on a single line. It's not horrible in that the argument lists are extremely short (no lambdas, all 1 arg, all field or getter calls).

For this case, either point would work: If lombok preserves formatting in code with no lombok transforms in it, that'll solve @jpage4500's problems. If lombok's autoformatter is better, then presumably it would also solve it.

However, for lombok's future these are orthogonal points.

Considering them both separately:

## Delombok preserves better

That would certainly be awesome. But it does feel like a feature that will often fall off the radar during testing and changing lombok itself. Hence it feels like a bad idea if its maintenance intensive. It also sounds complicated (at least to me), but if you have a prototype that works and you think you can nail it down well, okay. That would absolutely be an improvement.

if it helps to simplify matters: For any node delombok can easily determine, I think:

* If it is non-generated.
* In which case, what its start position is,
* ... and if, in the original verbatim source, you can 'travel back' from that pos and see only whitespace until you hit a newline.
* ... and then conclude that the prettyprinter should newline first.

If lombok just adds that and nothing else that would already solve this specific case, no?

A thing or two depends on where exactly `startPos` resolves to. Given, say, a JCMethodInvocation node, is the startpos on the dot? If yes, this would work, unless someone has the style of:

```java
Stream.of(stuff).
  map(x -> foo()).
  filter(Foo::bar).
  toList();
```

(i.e: Dot at the end, then a newline. Versus: Newline, then `.filter` as first non-whitespace on the newline). I think that dot-at-the-end style is extremely rare and thus acceptable to just not support it properly. It's "just" pretty printing, not core functionality.

But if a more thorough preservation system is not much more difficult than merely preserving newlines, by all means.

## How _DO_ you pretty print chains of method invokes?

Lombok's `toBuilder` actually generates potentially long chains of method invokes. Hence why this part is on its own also somewhat relevant.

If delombok's prettyprinter does a better job of at least 'autoformatting' long chains of method invokes, whether they are written by the user or generated by lombok, then this issue becomes at least less problematic, if not irrelevant.

long chains of method invocations is a hairy problem. Clearly a chain of 20 invokes (say, stream API, they can really create some extremely long single statements with no braces in it) should never be auto-formatted as piled on a single line. However, we can't "just" print every 'chained' method invoke (a JCMethodInvocation where the receiver is itself a JCMethodInvocation node) on a newline:

```java
if (x.toLowerCase().equals("hello")) {
```

should clearly not be autoformatted to:

```java
if (x.toLowerCase()
  .equals("hello")) {

```

So how could an autoformatter figure out what to do?

* 'max line length' basis. Only if a single statement, if piled into a single line, would mean that line exceeds `MAX_LINE_LENGTH`, start looking for chains of invokes inside it. Find the longest chain and split it up. Now re-run analysis on each individual line, again preferring first to split up chains before applying any other line-splitting logic.
* Work on a max-chain basis: Find any chain of invokes that involves more than `MAX_CHAIN_LENGTH` invokes and split them up regardless of how long (in character count) that chain is.
* A heuristic points-based system: For any chain of invocations, each method in the chain gets 1 point. Each lambda anywhere in the chain (usually these things have lambdas as arguments, e.g. a `stream().map().filter().sort().collect` chain) adds another point. Any invoke with 3 or more params is half a point. Any chain that scores 4 or higher gets split up. This probably gets too complex to expose a config for, and is probably too complicated to try to 'auto-detect' (delombok autodetects if you seem to like tab or space indent and acts accordingly; trying to autodetect this seems beyond doable though). So, lombok would just ship with a hardcoded set of rules that produce passably readable code.

I checked eclipse and it has loads of settings for this; it seems to be focussed on preserving max line lengths. I don't like max line lengths, hence mine is set to 1000, and thus hitting auto-format in my eclipse will just pile everything into giant lines. (I never auto-format my code; if I ever get into that habit, my current settings are entirely inadequate).

delombok is not intended to be a full code formatter - if you have formatting needs then you should let delombok do its thing and then throw that result through your formatter. However, delombok _should_ produce output that your average java coder will at least not find gratingly unreadable. Based solely on that principle, piling a long chain of invokes on a single line is suboptimal - that's beyond what is reasonable as a bare bones autoformatting.

Also talked it over with `@rspilker`.  He doesn't like going off line length, and I don't either. We have big screens and about half of the really long lines in my source files would look worse if split, in that they aren't the core thing you should be looking at when trying to understand a method. It's almost always a long chain of method invokes that would be improved by splitting, specifically (not just 'anything that is really long'). A single method invoke in the chain could still be quite long and, at least in @rspilker and my personal preference for formatting, should _not_ be split up 'just because it is a long line'.

Keeping that in mind, that score system thing seems like it is both relatively easy to write and should produce passable output.

The 'problem' that this issue highlights requires either that we preserve better, _or_ that we pretty print nicer. Optimally lombok does both, though.

title: [FEATURE] Package Level, Inheritance, Custom Annotation support for @ExtensionMethod

nodes.body:
> And it helps people to discover features (methods) using OO paradigm.

That's a very tricky statement. The fact that you get to write e.g. `somePathObject.writeString("hello");` isn't OO at all, it's just simple syntax sugar to remap that to `Files.writeString(somePathObject, "hello")`  – it's not object oriented, you can't 'override it' in the normal sense. It just _looks_ like OO. It's already a tricky case that leads to confusion, it's a very bad idea to start throwing the very terminology at the concept that only deepens that confusion.

> If I import specific package, it will enable the extension method

That won't work - `import x.y.z;` is java-ese for __alias__. An import statement runs absolutely nothing in `x.y.z`, it doesn't even cause x.y.z to load. An import statement __disappears__ during compilation, it isn't in the resulting class file at all. An import statement in java does ONLY two things:

* Any usage of `z` on its own anywhere a type is expected, is understood to be `x.y.z`. It saves some typing, that is all.
* If `x.y.z` is not on the classpath when you compile the code, javac will emit an error even if you use `z` nowhere. It doesn't have to do this; the spec merely indicates it will (and it does). It's effectively a 'linting' rule, if you simply delete the block of code in `javac` that generates this error, nothing would break. Other than this linting rule that the java lang spec says must be applied.

Hence, it'd be weird if all of a sudden if lombok is involved, an import _does_ have actual side effects. So, no, we're not going to do that.

> If I inherit specific class, it will enable the extension method

Also no. For a different reason: We don't 'like' lombok voodoo. We want somebody looking at java source code that uses lombok features to have a reasonable chance of figuring out what's happening even if they aren't aware lombok exists. When you see:

```java
@Value class Foo {
  String x;
}
```

Then:

* That `@Value` is a _direct link_ to the functionality lombok is going to apply (it turns the class into a value class), in contast to e.g. `extends SomethingUtterlyUnrelated` - where `SomethingUtterlyUnrelated` would add extension functionality. That's not obvious.
* `Value` is a lombok type, you can CMD+click it in your IDE or just hover over it for lombok's javadoc which will tell you precisely what's happening and indicates precisely which library is doing the work here.

If you need to go check the javadoc of seemingly unrelated sources in order to figure out that lombok is somehow involved, that's not good. There is SOME argument to be made that annotations can be considered to be inheritable (some are, some aren't), but lombok isn't really an annotation processor. It is a boilerplate buster: It's just that most of its features are triggered by using annotations. Hence, we don't want to go down that rabbit hole, and lombok holds as general principle that _all_ of its annotations (except `@NonNull`, because why not) are 'private' implementation details and therefore by definition cannot be considered to be inherited.

> If I create custom annotation which has @ExtensionMethod annotation, it will enable extension methods where I use the custom annotation.

This is a concept we call meta-annotations. You make an annotation of your own which implies a whole boatload of lombok annotations. It's a way to boilerplate-bust the boilerplate buster: If you want to stick:

```java
@ExtensionMethod({a.class, b.class})
@Value
@ToString(includeFieldNames = true)
@Accessors(fluent = true)
...
```

On multiple classes, just write one annotation that implies all that and stick _that_ annotation on your classes instead. One of our lead contributors is currently working on this. In order to fight the voodoo magic aspects, we'll probably __require__ that this annotation's fully qualified name includes `lombok` or `Lombok`. Thus, `com.foo.myproject.LombokDbModel` or `com.foo.myproject.lombokmeta.DbModel` - but something so that there's a fair shot that someone reading that code will figure out what's happening sooner rather than later.

title: [PROJECTMGMT] Rename 'master' to 'main' branch
body:
We'd like to follow programming trends unless there's a good reason to deviate from them. Seems like the default name for the common deployment branch in git setups is to be 'main'; ours is currently 'master'.

I'd like to change this. But how does this impact others? Does this require manual actions by any and all forks and PRs in progress? Is [5 steps to change github default branch](https://stevenmortimer.com/5-steps-to-change-github-default-branch-from-master-to-main/) from Steven Mortimer a good guidebook? Are there pressing reasons not to change names?

This is, as far as I can tell, fairly low priority, so we'll wait a while for feedback.

title: [FEATURE] Multi-language website support
body:
**Feature description**
Enable  contributing translation into different languages of the Lombok website documentation.

**The target audience**
Translate contribution is  volunteering.
Consumer is everyone for whom English is not native.

nodes.body:
I'm not opposed; one problem is: How do we confirm that a translation is fit for purpose? I guess we can toss it through google translate to at least confirm it's not complete hogwash.

Thing is, __you can already do this__. Just.. send a PR, the website is in this github project. You'll also have to do the work of adding a little flag and all that. @rspilker is chief website wrangler. I'm sure he'll be willing to put in a little time to automate picking the right language based on the incoming Accept-Language header, but that's the only small detail you can't fix with a PR.
You can also use some tool to manage these translations (e.g [Weblate](https://weblate.org/)). It also helps to keep the translation up to date.

I have a few problems with this:
* As Reinier already mentioned, how can we verify the translation? Is it okay, or possibly misleading?
* My browser already offers to translate any page that is not in any of the languages I understand
* There are several online tools that can translate a web page
* Our HTML is already tagged `lang="EN"`. This should help translation tools

In my day job, I have a some experience with keeping documentation up-to-date across multiple languages. It is really hard.

So in my moderately expert opinion, we should not add translations.

title: [BUG] @Builder requires inner records to be explicitly static
body:
**Describe the bug**
An inner record with a builder reports "@Builder is not supported on non-static nested classes." despite `record` being implicitly static.

**To Reproduce**
Simple class that should reproduce it (reduced from my complex service)
```java
public record Outer(String hello) {

   @Builder
   public Outer {
   }
   
   public record Inner(String world) {
   
      @Builder
      public Inner {
      }
   }
}
```

Which results in:

```
[ERROR] Failed to execute goal org.apache.maven.plugins:maven-compiler-plugin:3.8.1:compile (default-compile) on project svc: Compilation failure:
[ERROR] /Users/rajat.murthi/Documents/Repos/svc/src/main/java/com/test/Outer.java:[9,9] @Builder is not supported on non-static nested classes.
```

**Expected behavior**
`@Builder` should work as expect as in outer records and normal static inner classes.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version: 1.8.22
 - Platform:
 
 java --version
openjdk 17.0.1 2021-10-19
OpenJDK Runtime Environment Temurin-17.0.1+12 (build 17.0.1+12)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM Temurin-17.0.1+12 (build 17.0.1+12, mixed mode, sharing)

**Additional context**
Adding the redundant `static` keyword to the inner class seems to fix the problem.

https://openjdk.java.net/jeps/395:

```text
A record class can declare nested types, including nested record classes. If a record class is itself nested, then it is implicitly static; this avoids an immediately enclosing instance which would silently add state to the record class.
```

nodes.body: We're currently looking into the whole is-this-thing-static code. I expect that that will address this issue as well.
I think lombok version 1.18.24 fixed this issue.
@irisindigo That's nice to hear :)

title: [BUG] Difference in equals() : "@Builder+@Getter+@EqualsAndHashCode" vs "@Builder+@Value"

nodes.body:
`@Value` makes the class final. You don't need the `canEqual()` in that case, because it is only relevant if there might be subclasses.

It's also documented here: https://projectlombok.org/features/EqualsAndHashCode

title: [FEATURE] Lombok Maven+ECJ bootstrap agent
body:
I have created (but not published) a small bootstrap agent to make using Lombok with Maven and the ECJ compiler easier. That combination currently requires either a non-portable build (as described on the setup/ecj page) or putting lombok.jar into source control with your project. The bootstrap agent allows you to contain the build in your pom.xml without embedding lombok.jar.

The project is located at https://github.com/JohnPaulTaylorII/lombok-maven-ecj-bootstrap.

Questions:
1. Is this worth including in the projectlombok space rather than mine? (I know it's fairly niche.)
2. If not, is it okay to publish this artifact using the org.projectlombok group, or would you prefer if I use a different one?
3. Would a PR updating the setup/ecj page to explain this alternative setup be accepted?

Thanks for your consideration.

nodes.body: I don't mind either the jar file directly in the projectlombok git repo or this solution; but how do we efficiently 'get it' there? We could fold it into lombok.jar and ask users to e.g. run `java -jar lombok.jar setupMavenBootstrapper` which unpacks this tiny jar and makes that `.mvn/jvm.config` file as well. Perhaps it even adds/fixes your pom.xml file. That sounds slightly nicer, perhaps?
I hadn't been able to come up with a very good distribution technique... However, that does sound like a pretty good solution. I can certainly work on that integration.

title: [FEATURE] Lombok Config Maven Plugin
body:
I have created a Maven plugin for generating a root level lombok.config file from configuration in the pom.xml. 

Use Case:
In many cases, such as an enterprise setting, it happens that there is a highly opinionated parent pom.xml file which many projects inherit from. This plugin allows Lombok base configuration to be one of those opinions. Projects can still override configuration easily, but developers don't have to remember to enable null annotations or rename the log file or whatever the shared opinions are.

The project is located at https://github.com/JohnPaulTaylorII/lombok-config-maven-plugin.

Questions:

1. Is this worth including in the projectlombok space rather than mine?
2. If not, is it okay to publish this artifact using the org.projectlombok group, or would you prefer if I use a different one?

Thanks for your consideration.

title: [FEATURE] Narrowing lombok.copyableAnnotations target
body:
# Problem
Right now, annotations in `lombok.copyableAnnotations` are copied to all eligible places generated by lombok. The problem is that some annotations does not make sense in all places.


## Example 
In spring one can configure lombok `Autowired` and `Value` annotations like this (to support `required=false` in generated constructor injection):
```
lombok.copyableAnnotations += org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired
```

The Problem is that `@Autowired` is then copied to getters and causes Spring runtime warnings:
> Autowired annotation should only be used on methods with parameters:


# Feature
Allow to specify `copyableAnnotations` per generated method/lombok annotation.

I would like to configure:
 "Copy annotation foo.Bar to getters" instead of "Copy annotation foo.Bar to every possible place"


# Proposal
To stick with current conventions, annotation specific config could be following:
```
lombok.getter.copyableAnnotations += foo.Bar
```

NOTE: I think `lombok.getter.copyableAnnotations` list should be merged with `lombok.copyableAnnotations` to not break current configs

nodes.body:
I've spoken about this before but can't find the issue. It's a combinatory explosion; I could come up with at least 15 different unique 'takes' on precisely where lombok should and should not copy annotations to, and under which conditions - half of which would also be hard to implement due to lack of resolution.

That's way too complicated - the tests and docs alone'd be a nightmare. So, that's just not a solution that actually solves the problem.

Instead I think the right move is to continue to expand on lombok's baked in support - whilst we can't ask a random lombokuser to consider precisely which of the 15+ different variants of copy behaviour they'd like, we _can_ ask the core developers of whatever library is fielding said annotation.

Unfortunately, we don't have _that_ either - we do have an easy way to add new annotations to lombok's baked in list of 'annotations that should by default be copied', but not (yet) a way to specify more specific copy behaviour. A real problem there is veracity: Someone is going to send a PR adding some annotation we don't know about along with an exact specification of the required copy behaviour. But how do we know it is correct? We don't use it and this stuff is complicated; it may well take us many hours to figure out what the library even does and determine if the PR is correct.

We think there's a solution to that too: Only a project owner can send it. If they want to contribute a broken definition, they're ruining their own project's utility just as much as they're ruining lombok's with it. Also, any issues that come up about incorrect copy behaviour can be trivially closed with 'well, the project maintainers who wrote that annotation thinks this is how to do it, so go file a ticket with those folks. And please explain to them we will also be sending them the angry hordes because a fix to the copy behaviour is backwards incompatible'.

But that does mean I bet it'll be used a lot less - not every project maintainer would presumably be interested or motivated to write such contributions.

Point is: We think it's the right way forward, but it's low priority. That means a PR that updates lombok to let you easily add PRs that match annotation type names to copy behaviour would be accepted, but note that we'll document that only project maintainers get to submit PRs. And it also means we're likely never going to get around to it ourselves.

As written in https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/3166#issuecomment-1091090969 i think also it makes no sense on some types of Annotations.
Especially the Annotation javax.validation.constraints.NotNull makes no sense from my point of view.

Is it possible to disable the whole feature or can we remove the Annotation javax.validation.constraints.NotNull ?

@el-dot i think with lombok.getter.copyableAnnotations you can define additional Annotations to copy.
We want to exclude the javax.validation.constraints.NotNull or to disable the whole feature.
@c-koell Maybe something like `lombok.getter.copyableAnnotations = []` would work? (Not sure and have no time to check this, but adding elements by `+=` suggests that `=` may override the list)
After a short look at the code i think it is not possible to clear the hardcoded list of annotations :-(

@el-dot your suggestion is denied; it boils down to having lombok actively act incorrectly (copying annotations whose semantics do not imply that copying them is correct), and then handwave the problem away by saying 'eh, it does not matter, users can look up how to fix lombok on their own by adding to the 'negative' copyable list'.

No.

There are only two available options:

* You, @c-koell and everybody else using this annotation is misunderstanding their purpose is abusing them. That's on you.
* The inclusion of this annotation on the list is incorrect and it should be kicked. That's backwards incompatible, so that's a big deal, but, if it shouldn't be on there, it shouldn't be on there.

I'm mystified as to what, exactly, a third option would look like.

Regardless of which of the above 2 explains this, 'just let users remove the annotation from the copy list' is incorrect.

@rzwitserloot 

> Regardless of which of the above 2 explains this, 'just let users remove the annotation from the copy list' is incorrect

It's not about is it correct, but should I be able turn off lombok parts which I don't want.

I don't believe lombok, as boilerplate generation library, should be generating code I don't want it to (for any reason).

@bkoziak As I said in issue #3166, in the scenario where `javax.validation`'s `@NotNull` is on a field and lombok makes getters and setters for it, it fairly clear from various documentation that it should either be on the field, or be on the getter/setter and not both. However, it is not at all clear to me that the only correct answer is: "It should remain on the field only". It feels more correct that the right answer is: Move it to the getter/setter, delete it from the field.

Given that the validation project cannot be bothered to fix this on their end (how hard is it to see this and just.. not double-validate? You're proposing we bend over backwards to attempt to write smarter code that tries to figure out what's going wrong, when they can trivially do so), my patience for trying to fix this is really, really low. Why don't you go bother this silly validation project that decides to apply the exact same validation rule twice in a row because they couldn't be bothered to realize that the semantic definition of the annotation they decided to use is nowhere near as mechanically clearly defined to warrant dogged insistence on doing a silly thing (namely, same validation twice in a row)?

> It's not about is it correct, but should I be able turn off lombok parts which I don't want.

That's not how lombok works. Specifically, we don't want to give you a twiddling knob for every imaginable thing, as that would result in an untestable, extremely hard to document combinatory explosion of options, and a needlessly steep learning curve, or, 999 twiddly bits that are all documented as: "This knob exists solely to work around bizarre (wrong) takes on semantic meanings and buggy / badly designed libraries", and that seems overly hostile.

@rzwitserloot I get your point and in general agree. What I don't understand is why @NotNull was added to the list. Up until 1.18.24 this annotation was not copied to accessors automatically what didn't cause any issues (I'm aware of) but now it is and it clearly is troublesome for many people (validation is quite common thing). Wouldn't be better just to keep status quo until behavior of the hibernate validator library (and probably others) allow to safely copy it? What's the point of adding a change that instead of improving breaks stuff?
Issue closed - further discussion about specifically validation.NonNull copying in issue #3180. An opt-out mechanism is not going to happen, which is what this issue is asking for as a solution.

title: [FEATURE] Add a feature for limiting @SuperBuilder for alien ancestors

nodes.body:
I don't think that's a good idea, and it's technically nearly impossible:

- Lombok cannot access the superclass. Thus, it does not know which constructor to call. If there is no default constructor, Lombok cannot know which arguments to supply.
- Without knowledge of the superclass, Lombok also cannot generate builder setter methods. What use does a builder have if there are fields missing in it?

So from my POV I'd say no. You can also do it manually, which is better in this case in my opinion: https://stackoverflow.com/a/61763012/10026074
Given that it's technically almost impossible and not anywhere close to a marquee feature, I'm just going to close this.

It's gonna be an issue.

I hopped for some sort of solution who could do an update automatically eachtime the ParentClass changed.

That's technically impossible for any annotation processor, not only lombok.
Your only way out with lombok is to convince the authors of that library to also use lombok and put a `@SuperBuilder` on their class.

I'm not aware of any tool that fits your use-case of automatically generating a builder for a class from a library during compilation.

If its impossible, why does it work when i dont use 'toBuilder' ?
Also, i agree lombok shouldnt be able to access the private field, BUT it should be able to use the setter instead.

Well, we agree that it would be nice if Lombok could do that, but it's simply not possible at the moment.

The problem is that annotation processors only have access to the compilation unit that is currently compiled. Any other compilation unit (e.g. the superclass) can not be accessed. Thus, Lombok simply cannot see the setters from the superclass.

Your one working example does compile because you manually provided the information how to set the field in the superclass by adding a constructor that has that field as parameter. For `toBuilder` you also have to provide the reverse mapping manually via `@ObtainVia`. That's what @Rawi01 is referring to.
