title: [FEATURE] @Singleton or @Instance annotation

nodes.body:
The preferred idiom for singletons in Java is to use `enum`. This automatically ensures singularity and is inherently thread-safe.
One disadvantage is that you cannot lazily load it (because enums are always initialized on classload).

However, the "classic" way is unsafe due to reflection: Even if you make the constructor `private`, you can create new instances by making the constructor accessible and calling it.

I'm not a Lombok team member, but I'd vote against an annotation that generates a "classic" singleton implementation. One the other hand, an enum-based implementation is only one line of boilerplate (the `INSTANCE` line), making it not very useful as a Lombok annotation.

You may still mess with that by making the private `INSTANCE` accessible and setting it to `null`. Even `final` won't help. But, well, that's really evil... 

But yes, I didn't think of the `extends` issue. That's at least a use case (don't know how frequent).

If Lombok would implement such an annotation, it must at least do the following:
- Make the class `static final`.
- Add the `INSTANCE` and the getter.
- Add a private constructor ensuring single instantiation, or alter the existing constructor to ensure this.
- Error out when there is more than one constructor.

PS: Your lazy getter (and constructor) check isn't thread-safe, but that can be fixed with double-checked locking.
yessss, that would work the same way but it requires more code than just `@Singleton` annotation

I'm not sure it's worth it. I'm pretty sure @rspilker and I discussed it a number of times and never considered it on the right side of the bang for the buck divide.

These are the use cases I'm aware of for it:

* You have a specific implementation of a general type, and this specific implementation is a singleton; either because they always are and the only reason we can't just use `@UtilityClass` is because there's a type hierarchy and `static` doesn't "do" hierarchy, or because the concept doesn't proscribe singleton-ness, but this take on it does. __The `enum` hack does not work here__, unless the type you want to have a singleton implementation for is an interface.
* Some combination of exotic factors just leads naturally to a situation where singleton is a good idea. By definition ignorable - not boilerplate.
* Misguided non-cases. Abuse of the pattern is rampant and is going to considerably mess up any attempts at studying use cases and dealing with feature requests:
    * A way to introduce global state. Most likely the author really wanted a dependency injection framework, or just wants to pass an instance around and needs to rethink their code flow design to avoid whatever made them go: "Oh no I do not want every third method in the entire project to grow a list of 18 arguments!" - or, in very rare cases, global state is warranted, but this is such a minefield that it feels immoral to even suggest that this is common enough to warrant a lombok feature. I think users of lombok should be able to intuit that anything lombok offers a feature for is boilerplate, and therefore acceptable in your average java project. Global state is not something I want lombok to 'peddle'. Hence, this is a non-case. It's a negative case, even: Rampant abuse of this pattern makes me want to veto `@Singleton`.
    * Singletons where it should just be utility methods. If it is right to introduce a global, unconfigurable single implementation as the only imaginable one - then why not just make a bunch of static methods? `java.lang.Math` does not have a singleton, and `Math.max` is a static method. Many usages of singleton out there should just be all-static methods instead, and `@UtilityClass` already exists to cater to this crowd. It's another negative use case: Singletons that should have just been utility classes is common, and merely suggesting this code style error is acceptable by introducing `@Singleton`, in addition to confusing matters by having both `@UtilityClass` and `@Singleton`, makes me want to veto `@Singleton`.
    * Singletons for things where alternate implementations really do exist - this is what dependency injection frameworks are all about. One impl of the twitter API for production use, but another for the testing infrastructure, that sort of thing. One way to get around dep injection frameworks is to have global state instead (the twitter API has a global 'go into test mode' flag or field and the test code `@Before`'s itself into test mode first, for example). I don't think this is right, and we shouldn't enable such bad code.
    * It could be `@UtilityClass` but the author wants to future-proof for the day that it cannot be. Author is wrong; making a singleton doesn't future-proof anything, as the vast majority of calls will just be of the form `SingletonType.getInstance().doThing()` which is equally useless to `SingletonType.doStaticThing()` as far as 'refactor it to an actual object you need to create and initialize first' purposes are concerned. Author is misguided and should just apply YAGNI and use `@UtilityClass`, or author correctly identified that future proofing is warranted, but should be adding a bunch of arguments, or rethinking the architecture somewhat to elevate this state to fields, or should possibly be using an injection framework instead and configuring it as singleton for now.
    * It could be `@UtilityClass` but author doesn't like the style or is misguided by the notion that 'static is bad' and hilariously thinks a singleton is the way out - in other words, fails to understand the underlying principle is 'global state is bad', or is letting style preferences beat objective, falsifiable damage to the quality of your codebase, either way, utterly misguided principle that makes them _think_ they want `@Singleton`, but, they really don't.


@janrieke 's `enum` suggestion is right out - he says that this is 'the preferred idiom'. I hope not, because if that is true, then the majority of the java ecosystem are misguided in this regard. The `enum` hack doesn't work for precisely the one time when singletons are definitely the right answer (when you need a specific impl of some class - enums cannot `extend` anything), and it is dirtying up your API: That a type is an enum is not and cannot be an implementation detail! You can't 'hide' enumness from an enum, it's right there, it will be `instanceof Enum`, the type hierarchy shows it to you, etcetera. A singleton has no relationship whatsoever to the concept of `enum`s, and the fact that your singleton does implement it is therefore merely accidental exposure of implementation details which is _bad_. Thus, doubly bad, thus, wrong. Given that it's so pervasive that someone whose programming skills I rate quite highly has been entrapped by this wildly wrong idea is making me want to write `@Singleton`, so this balances the scales out somewhat :)

There are two aspects that make writing singletons complicated:

* Laziness - the need to create the singleton object only when it is truly needed and not at any point before then. But this is __highly misguided__ and I think I ran into a scenario where laziness truly was needed __once__ in a very long programming career, compared to literally hundreds of blogposts, tutorials, book chapters, and questions about wanting singletons in a way that clearly indicates they (think they) need it. The java classloader system is __already lazy__ - a class is not loaded (and hence, not initialized, and hence, that singleton object is never made) until the class is used someplace. The time difference between when a class is initialized vs. when it is used is too small to matter, and the odds that the class must be loaded, but no instance is ever actually needed, is so tiny, that it's not worth writing code for. Especially considering that the vast majority of singletons out there in live java code and notably including the proposal here calls a no-args constructor which costs nothing. Worrying about laziness for this is __completely incorrect__. One of those mass delusion situations. You're nuts if you think you need this! Of course, if we ever do make a `@Singleton` and you write an actual constructor (or an initializing expression on an instance of course), we'll just leave it alone, and you can stick your pricey code in there, no problem. At any rate, if you want laziness and it's warranted (rare), then ensuring the initialization only ever occurs once in a thread safe fashion can be a little bit complicated.
* Serialization. In order to ensure only one instance exists even when you use java's own serialization mechanism can be a little bit tricky. Not overly so - we can trivially generate the right stuff here. It's unfortunate that we cannot _detect_ whether you need it, and given that java's own serialization in general is a big mistake, I'd have been great if we simply do not generate unless needed. We can generate it if you `extends` nothing (or literally `j.l.Object`, and `implements` nothing. But if you extends or implements anything, you might be serializable and therefore we have to generate the read/write replacement code. Yich: That code might trigger linter tools, doesn't do anything at all if you aren't serializing, and needlessly clutters up your private API (autocomplete dialogs within the class itself, for example). Also, the number of times the OpenJDK team is talking about serialization in a negative light + their prepensity to break stuff recently means I'm foreseeing unfortunate situations where we have to bend over backwards because OpenJDK messed with stuff.


----------------

There are solutions to all of these concerns:

* Have a `serialization` or whatnot parameter on the annotation. If it is unset:
    * If the `@Singleton` class doesn't extend anything and doesn't implement anything (or extends `j.l.Object`), don't generate it.
    * If the `@Singleton` class is declared to `implements` Serializable, generate it.
    * Otherwise, error out and demand that it is explicitly set to something.
* Have a wiki page that explains why you are highly likely to not need lazy singletons.
* Possibly add to the docs some notes on when singletons are likely not really what you want, couched in terms of 'this is not what `@Singleton` is for'.

But add all those caveats and is it even worth it?

The recommendation to use `enum` comes from Joshua Bloch's _Effective Java_. One reason (among others) is the serialization issue you describe. Using `enum`, you simply don't have to worry about it, as `enum` serialization is handled by the JVM itself.

However, I never ever in my professional career had to manually implement a singleton. Whenever something like a singleton was necessary, I used a DI framework for it. So I'm also not convinced that an annotation for it is worth it (although that's obviously heavily based upon personal experience).

> The recommendation to use enum comes from Joshua Bloch's Effective Java.

Appeal to authority is still a logical fallacy. But let's not throw Joshua under the bus here: If you have to __handroll__ the serialization replacement code, it's such a drag that I completely understand looking for a way out and wanting it so badly that you're willing to accept some damage to your API - that you start considering that damage the lesser evil.

With lombok providing the feature, that reasoning is now moot and the API damage is no longer acceptable. Joshua may well agree with this sentiment - hence, the power that appeal to authority arguments do hold when we're specifically talking about code style is severely limited here.

I'd be on this like white on rice if there was a fairly easy way to use the baked in serialization+singleton-ness of java's `enum` feature without exposing the fact that you actually have an `enum` outside the package, but I don't think that's possible.

> Appeal to authority is still a logical fallacy

I don't think this is an appeal to authority, but rather an explanation of where did the `enum` thing come from. 
It truly is the "preferred idiom" (preferred as in statistics) by the virtue of a lot of people reading Effective Java and following its advice, as Joshua had a very convincing explanation of why `enums` should be preferred, including security, I think.
And not only that, but it's also short to write - how can anyone resist that.

If we try to speak about `enum` breaking the semantics, making the class `instanceof Enum`. 
Well, Lombok is also creating a mess of classes, where 50% of it is often implemented via annotations out of sight and another 50% being implemented by hand, because the default getters/setters are too basic, or because custom ones are needed, with custom invariants, or different types compared to the field.
By out of sight, I mean, when you document your fields, and you simply don't see any of those `@Data`, `@Getter`, `@Setter` on top of the class.
Or having the field plainly written out as `private final String x`, but `public String getX()` being implied. 
E.g. when you create a class, and all of it is marked as private, but it's actually all basic public getters/setters, with null checks at best.
Everything can be misused. And there are always trade-offs to consider.

About enums not being able to extend classes. Any time I needed something like this, I actually used interfaces. 
And that was very rare. I mean, needing singletons is rare.

Which is to say, so-o-o rare, that I don't see why would anybody want an annotation so much for something like this. Is it going to save what... 2 lines of code across of a 100k lines of code project? 

And if that annotation is parameterized to have parameters for the `getInstance` method name, maybe field name, whether the field is public, whether it's an eager singleton, or held in the static holder class, then the whole annotation becomes just as long, as implementing the said singleton by hand.
And that's not counting the effort from you and rspilker to implement, test and document it all.
I would also refrain from using the annotation, if that lazy initialization code is not using the double-check-lock-pattern. If such lazy init is introduced at all.

> Well, Lombok is also creating a mess of classes, where 50% of it is often implemented via annotations out of sight

That's an oxymoron (an argument that disproves itself, and is therefore trivially incorrect) - The whole point is - it is __out of sight__, an implementation detail. The problem with using `enum` to make singletons is that it's __in sight__. You can see it. It messes with your type hierarchies. You can't hide it.

> y out of sight, I mean, when you document your fields, and you simply don't see any of those @Data, @Getter, @Setter on top of the class.

That's __a good thing__, you're saying it like it's a bad thing. You document the what and perhaps the why. You never document the how, because that's an implementation detail. If you had been able to tell the difference between a hand-written setter and a lombok-generated one, that would be __really bad__, because it removes a large part of the very point of lombok: You can just have lombok generate that stuff for you, and if later you decide: Oh, wait a second, I need to do all sorts of non-boilerplate in there, you can just... do that. Without any user of your library being the wiser. It's entirely backwards compatible. __That is good__, not bad.

tl;dr: 
Ah, I see. 
We were just speaking about two different things.
Your concern for `enum` was focused around the type system and byte code, from what I understand.
My concern is focused on the effect on the source code semantics from developer perspective.

Full:

> The problem with using enum to make singletons is that it's in sight. You can see it. It messes with your type hierarchies. You can't hide it.

Yes, yes. The type hierarchy is messed up. This "type system perspective" we actually agree on.
I don't think anything was disproved though, because I was speaking about something else.
I was speaking about source code, not byte code.

As a developer, I don't care much, that using `enum` messes up my type hierarchy, because I never had a problem with it.
I use "interfaces" for polymorphism, and composition for code reuse. Inheriting implementation is my last resort, so I didn't have any need to extend an `enum` from other classes.

But I do care that when I see the keyword `enum`, I expect an enumeration of values.
Because that's what the keyword says.
Yet in case of `enum` singletons it's just one value instead of an enumeration, and not a mere value, but actually a fully fledged class.
This irks me. But it's a trade-off I can accept, because the benefits outweigh it for me.

> That's a good thing, you're saying it like it's a bad thing. 

Yes, from byte code perspective Lombok is doing a good job. When you use Lombok annotated classes from outside, they look just as if they were written by hand. It would be bad, if you'd require some special syntax to call Lombok accessors.

> Oh, wait a second, I need to do all sorts of non-boilerplate in there, you can just... do that

Yes, it is good, that you can trivially replace lombok generated code with hand-written code.

The bad thing I was talking about, was about what the source code of the class looks like, when you do that.
Or even when you don't do it.
Like, when I have a field marked `private`, but it's actually a public property. And this fact is out of my sight - my human sight - because the annotation is somewhere out of my screen space due to javadocs and what not.
(why would I mention javadocs in my previous message, if not for this perspective?)
Where as in something like C# or Kotlin, there's no such congitive dissonance, because the field LOOKS public (it doesn't say private anywhere).

And even if you don't have javadocs, sometimes you require additional invariants, or some normalization logic in getters and or setters, or withers, or builders.
And my eyes start glazing, because I now have to violently jump around the file to understand the classes intended semantics vs what the code says.
The "public interface" of the class becomes a blurry mess.
Where as in vanilla java, you have the private implementation details (fields) on one side, and all of its public API below. 

I do love me some `@EqualsAndHashCode` / `@ToString` though.
That thing is truly boring most of the time.
And absolutely trivial DTO classes, which can be annotated with some `@Data` and be done with it.

And the reason why I'm not as concerned about the type system, is because, uh... 
When I want to use some class, I don't see its public interface like a compiler does.
I open that class's file, and inspect its source code. And when Lombok is misused/overused, then I have to repeat the job of Lombok, by piecing together all of the annotations and hand rolled code in my head, just to understand what the code would've been without the annotations.

Maybe, someday somebody will develop an IDE plugin that shows some kind of preview of the resulting class :) .

To wrap it all back into my original message about enums, and likening it to Lombok.
If somebody is willing to accept Lombok regardless of how it affects source code readability, then he's likely to accept what the `enum` singleton does to the source code readability as well.
Be it because he accepts the trade-off, or because he simply doesn't care.

Update: 
> Maybe, someday somebody will develop an IDE plugin that shows some kind of preview of the resulting class :) . 

Actually, there's one. I haven't thought about using it this way, but Intellij's "structure" view shows the preview I was thinking about.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4677693/171580495-bdbaedcf-fc6d-4d7b-88fc-979ebbed1eeb.png)

Discussed it with @rspilker and we're not doing this. By a very large margin we think the use cases are rather disjunct, and very rare - not worth the maintenance burden. Just use `@UtilityClass` - in those rare cases you really need this, it probably isn't boiler plate. I know every patterns book and whatnot has a chapter on Singleton, but that's a red herring. You rarely need em, and if you think you need them a lot, you're probably doing it wrong.

> Just use `@UtilityClass`

I noticed you mentioned somewhere, that `@UtilityClass` is moving out of experimental soon. 
Is that true?
Curious, because the feature page says it won't move out, because of the non-star static import issue.

title: [BUG] Data class with same character field (with different upper-lower-case) missing Getter and Setter

title: [BUG] Lombok fails silently on static import of a getter

nodes.body:
This is a known bug in javac in regards to annotation processors and non-star static imports. We've looked into it before and there's nothing we can do - lombok isn't even executed. The only 'fix' is to rewrite the entire core launch pipeline of lombok into being a compiler plugin instead. That will probably work but we aren't even sure.

This is one of those 'closed as wontfix with regrets' tickets: Yeah, this is a bug, absolutely. It'sj ust that we cannot fix it - the party that can is wrong but says this isn't a bug, last time I checked.

I see. That's an unfortunate situation. It might make sense to put up some sort of a "known issues" page for this and potential similar issues, as it is quite hard to track down. Either way, thank you for your explanation, it's good to know what to look out for.

title: [FEATURE] @Record
body:
Java 17 records are half-baked (see below). And they're only 17+. Lombok's Data is a similar, better solution, but it differs enough in its behavior from records as to be unnecessarily confusing and incomplete.

The problems I've found with Java 17 records:

  - *Main problem:* Javadoc is weird and/or broken and/or not standardized and/or asinine (totally ruins records!)
  - bad syntax, especially for multi-line declarations. Eg, comma on last component is illegal
  - toString ignores arrays

Problems with `@Data`:

  - Adding a constructor deletes the autogenerated "canonical" one (need to use Tolerate)
  - fields aren't private+final by default
  - non-static nested classes are permitted
  - non-final fields are permitted (not sure if it's good or bad)
  - accessors aren't fluent (ok, I know you want this configured at project level, but it would help to just match Records)

nodes.body: Maybe, @Value is more similar analog for Java 14+ records, then @Data for comparing?..

> Java 17 records are half-baked (see below).

As co-author of lombok's `@Data` and `@Value` there's not much point in chiming in here with an Amen! Preach it! - I might be a _tad_ biased. But, let's just say, no argument from me on this :)

NB: Just as I was regretting the choice to even introduce 'fluent' (that is, just `.name()`, not `.getName()`), given that the java community has clearly standardized on `getX()`, and whilst wordy, it actually helps in IDEs: If you want a property, the shortcut key is effectively `.geCTRL+SPACE` which shows you specifically all getters and nothing else, which is nice. Aaaaaannnnnnnd the openjdk team throws out the backwards incompatible bombshell of going 'fluent' for their `record`s, making the best API in the entire JDK (`java.time`) look outdated now. Oof.

> Main problem: Javadoc is weird and/or broken and/or not standardized and/or asinine (totally ruins records!)

Huh. Didn't know that. But that does sound like something that might be fixed in the future; I rather doubt the current status of the notion of backwards compatibility amongst the OpenJDK team (which is really low - they break stuff all the time now) would mean they'd hesitate to clean up javadoc. Nobody ever promised javadoc gen to be super stable.

> bad syntax, especially for multi-line declarations. Eg, comma on last component is illegal

This matches the notion that method invocation argument lists can't have trailing commas either. But, speaking of which, __that could change__, I know quite a bit (lombok, ya know) about the parser architecture and syntactic definition of java / `javac`, and this could be added without much hassle. I've planned to advocate for this when the time is right. Still, sure, yes. It's annoying right now, and somewhat of a weird oversight this wasn't added. I'm not quite sure how `@Data` and co fix this, though.

> Problems with `@Data`:

Data fundamentally has nothing to do with records at all. You're comparing guns and grandmas.

`@Value` - that's lombok's equivalent. So let's evaluate your list of 5 issues in light of `@Value` and not `@Data`, which is explicitly designed for mutable objects (whereas record enforcing immutability). `@Value` is designed for immutables (it does not quite enforce, you can use `@NonFinal`, for example). I'll also shuffle your bullets around to be in the most convenient order for explanations.

> fields aren't private+final by default

* They are, with `@Value`. The class itself is also made `final` (similar to how `record` is final).
* Unlike records, if you know what you're doing and really want to opt out of this, you _can_, with `@NonFinal`, and you can of course just explicitly shove a `protected` or what not (or even `@PackagePrivate`). We want to steer programmers in the right direction, and we don't want to build features which do not appear to be useful except for highly dubious code. However, that leaves plenty of room for flexibility: We allow you to make non-final fields, non-final classes, and non-private fields _if_ you explicitly opt for these things. By design.

> non-static nested classes are permitted

I do not understand why records don't permit them. What confused hoops has the OpenJDK team jumped through? Perhaps the simplest one: Hey, we can always choose to make that legal later on in a point release; we cannot choose to make it __illegal__, that'd be backwards incompatible, so lets err on the side of caution. However, it is just _weird_, especially if you consider `record` just a convenient shortcut to make an immutable class and get a boatload of boilerplate pre-generated for you (including the ability to deconstruct in java18's new pattern features, though I think the idea is that non-records can specify deconstruction recipes in a later java release, so still pre-fill boilerplate, really). You really need to consider `record` as quite fundamentally a very different concept in order to justify the choice.

Point is, lombok clearly chose the interpretation that a `@Value` class is just a class, with a whole bunch of convenience generated for you. So why in the blazes would we deny this?

There's nothing fundamentally incompatible with allowing non-static inner classes here. In contrast to e.g. defaulting them the class itself to be non-`final` - a non-`final` class that SEEMS immutable (all fields are `final`, and, why not, are all of immutable types themselves) doesn't really act like it if anyone can just subclass and add mutable state. You can't make that kind of argument for the presence of non-static inners: How does the existence of non-static inners make the record (or `@Value class`) any less immutable or value-like or record-like?

> non-final fields are permitted (not sure if it's good or bad)

As explained earlier, by design. You have to explicitly opt in - if you just write `String foo;` it'll be made `final`, you'd have to write `@NonFinal String foo;`.

> accessors aren't fluent

Yes, by design. OpenJDK messed this up. See `LocalDate` and friends, and ~75% of the java ecosystem, which has non-fluent getters. When in rome, act like romans. Which is why its weird that the Roman Senate chose to act like a bunch of barbarians from Gaul on this choice!

> Adding a constructor deletes the autogenerated "canonical" one (need to use Tolerate)

The trickiest one here. But, this is really the only bullet that is left standing to some extent, and it's a dubious one at that. It's not worth introducing `@Record` _just_ to effectively mean `@Value @AllArgsConstructor`, surely you'd agree.

Thus, denied - because the good news is, this basically exists already, it's just called `@Value`, not `@Record`.

NB: Once the JDK grows the ability for classes to specify deconstruction recipes we will be adding that to `@Value`, probably out of the box. I doubt it'll be backwards incompatible outside of ridiculously contrived cases. Let's hope so!

> Adding a constructor deletes the autogenerated "canonical" one (need to use Tolerate)

Sorry, didn't see @Value. But hopefully the javadoc comment was useful to you. (It shows how bad the current crop of JDK devs are that they don't even think about documentation.)

Off-topic, but my view is that getters/setters make sense for mutable state, but final fields should just be public. In any case, the JDK has plenty of fluent properties. These have been trendy since NIO in Java 1.4.

Nonstatic-by-default local classes are annoying. They're unnecessary 99% of the time. The extra reference just makes work for the GC and JIT. Makes sense that a simple bag of data would be static.

Anyway, it's always pleasant to talk to you)

title: [FEATURE] @Jacksonized counterpart for users of JSON-B
body:
**Requested feature:**
The `@Jacksonized` annotation is great for deserializing JSON to immutable DTOs. It would be great if an equivalent for users of JSON-B could be added to Lombok as well.

**Target audience:**
Users of plain Java EE/Jakarta EE.

nodes.body:
This probably only has a chance to be integrated if somebody volunteers to implement it. I have no idea what's required to be generated in order to make things work.

`@Jacksonized` is quite simple because it reuses an existing builder and just puts some additional annotations on it. JSON-B doesn't seem to support builders, so an annotation for it has to do much more than `@Jacksonized`. Which means: That's probably not an easy task.

@thowebar As janrieke said, your feature request assumes we know what you intend to do. We don't - so this feature request is a gigantic undertaking: We'd have to read in what JSON-B and all that means, how many folks use it, if they all use it in roughly the same way (or at least 95%+ do), and precisely what we should generate. And _then_ we have to write the feature.

I can't guarantee we accept PRs here (because we can't go on the word of a single feature requester that they did all that work and did it correctly), but showing precisely what you want lombok to generate would be a good start.

Thus, awaiting a contribution, in the form of 2 snippets of code (or more, if more are required to cover all relevant use cases):

* 'this is what I want my code to look like, with lombok annotations and where relevant lombok.config settings'
* This is the vanilla (lombok-less) java code that should be generated for it.

If that doesn't show up by 2022-07-10, we'll close this issue.

body:

To avoid restarting eclipse.jdt.ls, I tried to make use of the _agentmain_ to load the lombok agent to eclipse.jdt.ls using the Java Attach API. However, the lombok agent threw an UnsupportedOperationException "class is already loaded and cannot be modified".

Questions:

1. Whether lombok can work properly by using the _agentmain_ to load the lombok agent to eclipse.jdt.ls without restarting eclipse.jdt.ls?
2. Are there other ways to dynamically load lombok into eclipse.jdt.ls without restarting eclipse.jdt.ls?

Thanks for your consideration.

nodes.body: `agentment`? Never heard of it. Is that a typo?

> `agentment`? Never heard of it. Is that a typo?


> `agentment`? Never heard of it. Is that a typo?

I'm sorry, it should be `agentmain`.
@rzwitserloot any thoughts?
I'm sure both are possible, but these questions are not appropriate here - they sound like questions you should be asking team `eclipse.jdt.ls`, not us.

@rzwitserloot Thank you for providing comments. I'm looking for new ways to dynamically load lombok into Eclipse JDT platform. After some investigation, I have some findings but also some questions I want to get clarified. Appreciate a lot If you could provide some insights.



1. AFAIK, most third party Java tools contribute to JDT capabilities through OSGI bundle. I'm wondering the reason behind why lombok team choose to inject lombok.jar as a Java agent instead of OSGI bundle?



2. In addition, Eclipse JDT provides APT to support annotation processor, do you think is it possible to load lombok.jar as annotation processor of JDT-APT?



Thank you for the great lombok project.

Lombok hooks into the compiler to modify the AST and also changes some internal methods to hide the AST modifications. Without that eclipse would try to modify the source code of the generated nodes which is impossible because it is not there. To add these hooks lombok changes some of the classes using a javaagent, a normal plugin cannot do that.

I think it is possible to run lombok as anotation processor but this will still require most of the patches. Splitting it up will lead to new problems where the annotation processor and agent use different versions.

>  I'm wondering the reason behind why lombok team choose to inject lombok.jar as a Java agent instead of OSGI bundle?

OSGi bundles work by hooking into an extension point. The requisite extension points do not exist (or didn't last time we checked), hence, agent was the only way. We can, of course, be an OSGi module that then live-loads itself as an agent, this has been possible since java8 if memory serves. We do such a thing if you want: You can load lombok into eclipse as an eclipse plugin (this _just_ means we do the agent stuff from our module init instead of at VM boot).

> In addition, Eclipse JDT provides APT to support annotation processor, do you think is it possible to load lombok.jar as annotation processor of JDT-APT?

It is not. Lombok does things that APs can't normally do, unless the AP offers more features than the spec provides for. Eclipse's AP impl doesn't provide what we need (and one shouldn't expect it to, we need rather a lot).

title: [FEATURE] (Super)Builder chaining

nodes.body:
It's a somewhat interesting idea, but I'm closing this. Way too many smelly things, not nearly enough upside. I can think of rather a lot of reasons this is not a good idea for lombok. A select few highlights (this is by no means complete):

* Why are you bringing `@SuperBuilder` into this? Don't you just mean `@Builder`? Why do you have a builder on a class that also has mutable fields? None of this feels very well thought through. 
* Lombok doesn't know. Given the file `A.java`, and a field `B b`, how does lombok know that B, itself, has a `@Builder` annotation on it? [Lombok cannot just go and check](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/wiki/LOMBOK-CONCEPT:-Resolution), so you'd have to specify it. Even if lombok could know, I'm not sure it's a good idea to assume folks would _always_ want this functionality. Even if you think it's a fair assumption to make, changing that now would be backwards incompatible.
* Thus you can't do this without an annotation or something similar on the field/param. That's potentially acceptable but is complicating matters: How would users of lombok know this feature existed?
* We'd need to generate a duplicate, which really should be in `B`, _or_ we generate an entire B-builder inside A. Either way you've now tightly entangled 2 classes which is bad.

That's just a small selection.

To address these points:
> Why are you bringing `@SuperBuilder` into this? Don't you just mean `@Builder`? 

I mean both. In our case we have an hierarchy structure of classes because of which we are using the `@SuperBuilder` annotation. Previously we had another `Builder` framework generated through xjc, but since we're moving from jaxb-generated model to a manually written model we still want to keep much of the usage the same. One of the things in there was the builder chaining suggested here. For the example I've changed it now to `@Builder`, but I would expect `@SuperBuilder` to have the same functionality.

> Why do you have a builder on a class that also has mutable fields?

Because in our data model, we read from xml. Possible we change a few fields and write back to xml. We also generate the information, that is mostly done through builders and as immutable as possible. But for this `Issue` that is not related, so I've edited it out of the original post.

> Lombok doesn't know. Given the file A.java, and a field B b, how does lombok know that B, itself, has a `@Builder` annotation on it? [Lombok cannot just go and check](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/wiki/LOMBOK-CONCEPT:-Resolution), so you'd have to specify it. Even if lombok could know, I'm not sure it's a good idea to assume folks would always want this functionality. Even if you think it's a fair assumption to make, changing that now would be backwards incompatible.

I'm a little bit familiar with APT processing, but wasn't familiar with the fact that because lombok chains in way earlier than other processors they have access to less information than other processors. With other processors I can request information about other `Type`'s and check if an annotation is present on that type, if for lombok this is not possible then indeed it would make this impossible. If this is indeed the case for lombok than it is indeed a valid reason to close this issue. 
However, I assume that the `@SuperBuilder` knows if the parent also has the `@SuperBuilder` annotation. Couldn't the same method be used to determine whether or not a class is annotated with an `@Builder` or `@SuperBuilder` annotation? 

> Thus you can't do this without an annotation or something similar on the field/param. That's potentially acceptable but is complicating matters: How would users of lombok know this feature existed?

This is basically a continuation of the previous point. The field/param shouldn't get an additional annotation. If that is required to make this work then it wouldn't be acceptable (imho).

> We'd need to generate a duplicate, which really should be in B, or we generate an entire B-builder inside A. Either way you've now tightly entangled 2 classes which is bad.

Again a continuation of a previous point. You do not want to generate a duplicate/entire B-builder inside A. You want to reference the other builder that will be/has been created during the processing of that class. The entanglement doesn't change at all, `A` knows that `B` exists. `A.Builder` knows that `B.Builder` exists. The dependency between the classes and the builders are the same.

Just took a closer look at how this is done in `@SuperBuilder` and it seems to be a documented requirement that all superclasses also have the `@SuperBuilder` annotation. Removing it at one superclass will cause no lombok specific error to be thrown, but only default compiler errors.

After seeing this the builder chaining idea is currently not possible within lombok itself.

I am not sure if supporting pre-JDK19 and JDK19-and-after variants of `switch` AST at the same time is feasible, so maybe the handlers for `lombok.Singular` should be refactored to use a sequence of "plain" `if` blocks to be more future-proof with regard to changes to `switch` statement in future JDK releases.

title: [BUG] Endless loop while compile

nodes.body:
This also fails if you try to call the extension method by hand because the method is ambiguous. The loop happens because lombok is unable to find a matching method, it simply picks the first method that has the same name and a matching first parameter. 
For eclipse it also checks the argument types and add an error message if it does not match. It does not try to find a better match. In `javac` this will usually work as long as both extension methods are in the same class because it runs before the compiler resolves the methods. If the right method is in a different class it will still fail.
This is part of the latest [edge release](https://projectlombok.org/download-edge), all feedback is welcome.

> Can you please try to describe your problem again in different words and why you think this is a lombok bug?

In this Java class, the type of the element "result" is "int", and the output value of a new object is turned into "string", which is obviously wrong. This problem exists not only in Lombok, but also in spring

> Can you please try to describe your problem again in different words and why you think this is a lombok bug?

This is obviously caused by the toString () method, in which the getResult () method is called. I think we should directly take the value of "result". Whether result=2 or the type of result becomes string, it is against the common sense of Java, which is unacceptable.

You can configure lombok to not use getters: `@ToString(doNotUseGetters = true)` or `lombok.toString.doNotUseGetters = true` in your `lombok.config` if you want to change this beaviour in more than one class.

title: [FEATURE] @ToString.Obfuscate to protect sensitive data but allow us to query for it in logs
body:
**Description**
Talking about security, in specific data leakage, one of the more painful area are log messages.
We need log messages, we need to track user behavior in our system as well as troubleshoot issues, and we need information so we can query these logs for it, but for security reasons, we should not log sensitive data on them.
One of the best ways to deal with this juxtaposition is obfuscation, and here is the feature opportunity for project Lombok.

I would like to have a ToString.Obfuscate which by default hash (sha1) the content of the field and then Base64 encodes the result, before printing it with the toString() method, in this way the data will be searchable and we could use it, for example, to track a user email through our system and check it's behavior but would render useless for an attacker.

btw, having a project-wide configuration key for the salt of the SHA1would be the following step or configurable hash and encode algorithms

**Target audience**
Every single java project that uses Lombok, because removing the boilerplate to make your application more secure will result in a general security improvement of java projects.

**Additional context**
Attenuates the risk of "Unintended Data Leakage" as exposed by OWASP:  https://owasp.org/www-project-mobile-top-10/2014-risks/m4-unintended-data-leakage
It could impact also the risk of "Insufficient Logging and monitor failure" since we could log more things without fear of disclosing sensitive information.

nodes.body: I have been thinking on the same lines. Something to use like @ToString.Obfuscate(override="REDACTED"), or even if Exclude provided a parameter for obfuscation. There's value in knowing whether the field was originally got a value, was empty or null, which I'm not sure Exclude currently has the semantics for.

title: Primitive Pseudo Generics
body:
**Describe the feature**
A kind of pseudo generic for primitive classes. So, one can write a Vec3<Primitive> class, and then use this notation to make variants of it for bytes, shorts, ints, longs, floats, doubles, etc. As opposed to simply writing Vec3b, Vec3s, Vec3i, Vec3l, Vec3f, and Vec3d. Same principle can be applied to other Vecs, Matrices, and any other class you might wan to write a copy of for several different primitives.

**Describe the target audience**
People doing math, physics, and graphics, mainly - but I'm sure lots of other programmers will be able to find a use for it.

**Additional context**
This would be far superior to simply coping a class and doing "find, replace: Primitive 1 -> Primitive2", which is the current easiest method.

nodes.body: Oh, for bonus points, find a way to allow specifying vecs of arbitrary length? This one is probably too specific and an absolutely unreasonable pain to write, but, it'd be neat to be able to demand a Vec42l with the same ease one gets a Vec3i.
This sounds to me more like a use case for a regular annotation processor, because you are generating _new_ classes. Lombok focuses on modifying existing classes.
Not entirely true! @Builder creates new classes, I'm pretty sure. So, there is precedent.

Of course you could do it with lombok and generate all of those as inner classes.

But I don't think you want that, for several reasons:
- You have to convince the core team that such a feature is worth the maintenance burden.
- You probably have to implement it yourself (the core team members are quite busy with other things). You have to write handlers for `javac` and eclipse.
- You have to wait for the IntelliJ people to add it to their plugin.

This will take years. For example, `@SuperBuilder` took more than 4 years until it reliably worked with all IDEs.

If you want such a feature, write your own annotation processor. It's significantly easier than adding it to Lombok, and it will work with common IDEs out of the box.

**Version:**

`lombok-1.18.24.jar` retrieved from https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/org.projectlombok/lombok/1.18.24

**Describe the bug**

* As described [here on StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/56596416/lombok-constructor-is-undefined/) in 2019 (and experienced by myself earlier today with the latest `sts-4.15.3.RELEASE` for Linux), using Lombok decorators such as `@Data`, `@NoArgsConstructor`, `@AllArgsConstructor` doesn't seem to produce the expected effect, and results in compilation errors and a `Constructor ... is undefined` error message during runtime.

**Hacky solution:**

* There is [a solution](http://codeomitted.com/setup-lombok-with-stseclipse-based-ide/) (which works) which consists in copying a Lombok JAR or its symbolic link to the STS installation directory, and putting a special mention about that JAR in the `SpringToolSuite4.ini` file, also located in the STS installation directory: `-javaagent:lombok.jar`.

nodes.body: That's not a hack, that's exactly what the Lombok installer would do. So is the actual problem that the Lombok installer does not work with current STS versions?

I didn't use the Lombok installer, just —like I said— retrieved the information about the dependency from https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/org.projectlombok/lombok/1.18.24. 

Then, at runtime, I got the error message in console. But unfortunately no guidance from Lombok about what I could do — although it would be nice it there was guidance. You know, the same kind of message Spring Cloud dependencies show sometimes in console, when the problem seems to be well-known, and the fix easy to explain.

Lombok is not a regular annotation processor. To do its work, it has to hook into the eclipse compiler. It cannot do that just by being on the classpath when compiling. Thus, you need to install Lombok to your IDE, as described [here](https://projectlombok.org/setup/eclipse).
Without that plugin, eclipse simply does not know about Lombok. Therefore, its compiler cannot know what went wrong or give you an advice how to solve it.

```XML
<setupTask
	xsi:type="setup.p2:P2Task"
	label="lombok-site">
	<requirement
		name="org.projectlombok.feature.feature.group"
		versionRange="[1.18.24,1.18.24]" />
	<repository
		url="http://projectlombok.org/p2/"/>
	<description>Project Lombok</description>
</setupTask>
```

and follow through the normal installation process clicking Next and Finish buttons as needed.

When the process gets to the Lombok feature, it will generate an error and fail to install Eclipse. In simple install mode, clicking the log link in the error message or in advanced mode a stack trace featuring the example above will be displayed due to the inability to verify the Lombok package signature with the built-in certificate authorities.

The installation _should_ succeed and produce a running installation of the Eclipse IDE that includes the Lombok feature.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version: 1.18.24 "Envious Ferret"
 - Platform:
    - javac version: 11.0.15
    - Eclipse Installer: 1.18.0 Build 4828 ([2020-09](https://www.eclipse.org/downloads/download.php?file=/oomph/epp/2020-09/R/eclipse-inst-linux64.tar.gz))
       - This is the last version of the installer that will run on Java 8, though 11 was used here,
    - Eclipse:
       - Version: 2022-06 (4.24.0)
          - This is the last version that will work on Java 11,
       - Build id: 20220609-1112
    - OS: CentOS Linux release 7.8.2003

When installed manually by a user, the Project Lombok feature can be installed, but requires the user to accept the certificate in a separate dialog.

If the requirement includes attributes to indicate that it is optional and non-greedy, then the installer will successfully add the Lombok site to Eclipse, but NOT install the feature. Then the user can manually install it without having to add the site to Eclipse. This is marginally better than forcing the user to install it entirely manually.

```xml
<!-- Signing errors prevent fully automated install. Optional, non-greedy, adds site, but still requires manual install -->
<setupTask
	xsi:type="setup.p2:P2Task"
	label="lombok-site">
	<requirement
		name="org.projectlombok.feature.feature.group"
		optional="true"
		greedy="false"
		versionRange="[1.18.24,1.18.24]" />
	<repository
		url="http://projectlombok.org/p2/"/>
	<description>Project Lombok</description>
</setupTask>
```

For users stuck with Java 8, this may still be a problem, but the work-around in the description may help a little bit.

title: [FEATURE] Make the *BuilderImpl and its constructor package-private

nodes.body: I must admit I don't really understand the use case/problem. Is it just that there is some additional logic in the setter? Then you already have a problem without your `builderOf`: If someone sets `some` via builder, the setter will also not be called. So you probably have to fix that (either by duplicating the setter logic in the builder or by customizing the constructor such that it includes the setter logic). Then your problem with `builderOf` also goes away.

I guess customizing `@SuperBuilder`'s constructor is your only reasonable choice. I will not vote for relaxing the visibility modifiers on the `...BuilderImpl` class, because
- this doesn't fix your underlying problem, and
- could lead to bugs if someone messes around with that internal classes (which would be visible where they should not be).

Historical reasons I guess, the message of the commit that added theses lines:
```
Rewritten @Cleanup's new null analysis prevention to not use
Lombok.preventNullAnalysis but go with Collections.singletonList(expr).get(0)
instead; while this does create a pointless object, it doesn't cause a clash
when eclipse has lombok 0.10 installed but the project uses 0.9, which doesn't
have preventNullAnalysis. Eventually, once 0.9 is long forgotten, this can be reverted.
```

I think `@Cleanup` is a great feature and must not be abandoned, but improved!

The bad thing is: if a "close" method throws an exception, it completely replaces the original exception from the body. 
Better:
Swallow the exception from `close`
Event better
Java 7 Suppressed exceptions

nodes.body:
Thanks for the really detailed bug reports. 

As far as I know you can use `suppressBaseMethods = false` to not override implemented methods but there might be something else that is broken. `@ExtensionMethod` is way more complex than other annotations and it seems like it is not used that much. I fixed everything I need for my own project but I'm sure that I missed a bunch of cases (e.g. the wrong warning about uninitialized variables).

Wow, cool! Where does that option come from? 😮 Setting it to `false` fixed ALL of the problems described here, even the weird ones. 👍 

I wonder why is something like that not the default? And not documented. And why is it an option anyway.

I can think of no use case, where I would want the current default. And apparently I'm not the only one. Someone just wrote in the discussion group, that he prepends a Δ symbol to all of his extension methods, so they don't clash with existing methods.

I have changed the default to `false` in my patched library, and that fixed all the problem related to name clashes in my code base, and I don't even have to specify this everywhere. Yay! I'm happy. 😄 


Regarding the original bug report, I added some more of these "weird" failure cases, where some seemingly unrelated stuff does not compile anymore:
- https://github.com/marc-guenther/lombok-problems/blob/fbea946cd423c78d84f6fb7e0b617cf515e868c9/prob/lems/ProblemWithOverloadedMethod.java#L84

This one I find particularly interesting. An `s == null` fails:
```
.filter(s -> s == something)
             ^
             s cannot be resolved or is not a field
```

where as `s.equals(something)` succeeds:
```
.filter(s -> s.equals(something))
```

I also attached a version of all the failure cases with the `suppressBaseMethods=false` setting, and they all succeed.

Interesting. It had never occurred to me to use extensions methods to overwrite existing methods ;-)... So far I always wanted to add new methods that were formerly missing to my classes.

Regarding "surprising", I on the other hand found it rather surprising that my classes do not compile anymore, just because I added `@ExtensionMethod` annotation to it, without changing anything else. But the case you describe, although rare, also would be very hard to track down when it happens. Very unfortunate.

I don't really have a solution to this conflict, I must think about this some more. At the moment, I am very happy with setting `suppressBaseMethods = false` everywhere. The `true` case has too many bugs to be useable for me.

In the mean time, can we add this parameter to the documentation? Is the website available in Github anywhere? I couldn't find it, or I would have created a PR for it.

title: [BUG] lombok update from 1.18.12 to 1.18.20 change  jackson format

nodes.body: Probably because Lombok started copying `@JsonFormat` to the getter. Before (without the annotation on the getter), Jackson does not see this annotation anywhere in the actual class `ChildVO`. Now Lombok copies it to the getter in `BaseVO`, and Jackson recognizes it because the setter is visible in the `ChildVO` class, and the annotation is inheritable.

title: [FEATURE] Add Ant support for noCopy, onlyChanged, etc.
body:
**Describe the feature**
The Delombok Ant task supports setting the classpath, source path, verbosity, encoding, etc. However, several features have been added to the Delombok class that are not currently supported in the Ant Task. These include noCopy and onlyChanged.

I recently followed the instructions [here](https://projectlombok.org/features/delombok) and was able to get the Delombok task running in my current Ant project. However, I also wanted to add support for only running Delombok on changed files. Unfortunately, since the onlyChanged feature is not supported in the Ant task, I can't do that.

**Describe the target audience**
Users who have Ant projects and want to use the new features Delombok features with the Delombok Ant task. This is especially useful for creating Javadocs.

**Additional context**
I'm willing to implement support for this if you're open to accepting a pull request.

title: [BUG] Should @Jacksonized add @JsonProperty to fluent methods?

nodes.body: Possibly related: https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/3265

That's not a bug, that's a new feature. `@Jacksonized` only affects `@(Super)Builder`. Thus, it is only relevant to deserialization.

We can talk about extending it to `@Accessors`, but I'm quite sure that would mean more than just adding `@JsonProperty`.

I'm aware that `@Jacksonized` is only there for Builders but arguably a user is reasonable in expecting it to work correctly for Serialisation too which is why I labelled it "BUG".

`@JsonProperty("fieldname")` on the getter seems to solve the problem for me.

nodes.body: Thanks for reporting this issue. The error is caused by an optimization that terminates further processing when no unhandled annotation is left. This kicks in right after `@Setter` gets handled and ends the processing. I am still trying to find the best solution for this.
To qualify the issue, I have only been able to reproduce it in the Eclipse IDE, it does not happen on Intellij

I'm not sure we should even support this. The current state of affairs is certainly problematic, but if writing it would result in an error explicitly spelling out you can't stick lombok annotations in `onMethod`, I'd find that acceptable. And, of course, the  behaviour should be consistent between eclipse, javac, and intellij.

nodes.body: I'm unable to reproduce this issue. Can you please double check that updating lombok does not fix this problem? Since 1.18.22 lombok replaces `val` with the native `final var` (if available) so this error should no longer happen or at least there should be a different error message.

Thanks for your reply @Rawi01. Probably you have not been able to reproduce the problem because we removed all the conflicting `val` usages from the project in order to allow compilation. This happened in this PR: https://github.com/pravega/pravega/pull/6947. Most likely, you have tried to compile the project with the fix in already, so it worked for you.

To reproduce the problem, just go to the commit before that PR, and you will be able to reproduce. That is, once cloned the project, just type: `git reset --hard a3eea57b337abc9a25e725e6a6b36e6f8bd90050`. This is the commit id prior to the fix, so if you try to compile the project with this commit (or any commit before that), you will be able to reproduce the original issue.

**Describe the bug**
I have recently upgraded my project's Java from 16 to 19. Now, compiling throws an error at a class that has @SneakyThrows - particularly at line 63. Here's my deduction process:
1) I've been getting an empty error ("X:63" with no elaboration); I've changed that line, then outright deleted it, and it still was happening.
2) I cleared the class to only have about 50 lines, then it started throwing an error at the 63rd line of another class.
3) I decided to comment out all the Lombok annotations in both classes and it compiled successfully.
4) I slowly uncommented all the annotations and it compiled successfully, with the exception of @SneakyThrows - in fact, the only 2 classes that had SneakyThrows were the classes that it would throw compile errors at.
As such I've come to a conclusion that something is wrong with the SneakyThrows interpretation, and, for some reason, it's all good in Java 16.

@marc-guenther, integration with other libraries and frameworks is always cool. There is key difference! Documentaion says about NonNull annotation designed specifially for lombok purposes, but i don't use it! Why lombok NonNull is ever exists if lombok generate cheks for every pattern matching annotaion? Thats kinda strange..
I'm not sure; presumably because not everyone wants to ship with a runtime dependency on Lombok-specific annotations?
@prdoyle Lombok should never be a runtime dependency

@trokhinas wrote:

> It seems like Lombok intepret any NotNull annotation for generating null checks or it is a bug?

Not 'any'. A certain well-known list of annotations that strongly imply a direct correlation between "the value is `null`" and "a bug has occurred; that should never happen; this state is nonsensical and semantically meaningless."

Specifically, for `@RequiredArgsConstructor` and lombok generating a 'setter' (a thing that takes in a param and assigns it to a field, so, setters, withers, and constructors), lombok works like that. We try to maintain this list and you can use `lombok.config` to modify it.

In contrast, if you want lombok to generate a nullcheck for a parameter in a method, specifically only `lombok.NonNull` will do.

This behaviour might be confusing but it is what it is. It has advantages. It's not simple to determine what behaviour would be best, which means the status quo wins, because the status quo gets 'does not break existing stuff' for free.

> In the lombok changelog, the latest entry states that 'BUGFIX: Turns out treating https://github.com/NotNull as an annotation that indicates lombok should generate nullcheck guards causes all sorts of problems.'

That's old news. The 'problems' that this entry refers to, is that not every annotation named `@NotNull` or `@NonNull` __actually__ implies what I wrote before (that if the field turns out to hold `null` at any point in time after construction has completed, that this implies "a bug has occurred; that should never happen; this state is nonsensical and semantically meaningless.").

A trivial example is JPA (hibernate)'s `@NotNull` annotation. That merely means: "When generating a `CREATE TABLE` SQL statement, include the proper SQL to add a NOT NULL constraint to the column representing this field". There __IS__ a semantically valid interpretation of an instance of that class holding a `null` value: This object is representing a row-to-be (it hasn't been `save()`d yet, and would fail if you try); it is not in an SQL-valid state yet but that's fine, as it's a tool to create a row, and the tool hasn't reached that phase yet. In other words, the lifecycle of this object can be in an invalid state, that its purpose. The semantic explanation is simply 'row not finished yet'.

Another example is validation frameworks - the semantic explanation for a `@some.validation.framework.NotNull` marked field being `null` is obvious: It represents input from an external system or from a user. Sure, that input isn't valid. But the semantic meaning is clear: Instances of this class represent what a user entered into a form. `null` means the user didn't pick a value for, say, an HTML `<select>`, or whatever. The semantic meaning is clear - and the validation framework will ensure that the business process being modelled will not advance beyond this phase.

This is in sharp contrast to e.g. intellij's `@NotNull` which has the aim of ensuring that the object is never `null` to begin with.

If this explanation is unclear, then that's a sad state of affairs but it is what it is, you will not convince us to move our opinion without being familiar with this nuance.

@marc-guenther wrote:

> Also I'm confused now. Apparently org.jetbrains.annotations.NotNull and javax.validation.constraints.NotNull are treated differently by Lombok?

See the above paragraph. Yes, they are treated differently. Yes, that is intentional. Yes, this behaviour is correct (as in, you want it to work this way. If you think it shouldn't, you either don't understand what validation frameworks do, or I don't).

@trokhinas wrote:

> test purposes

When you write `public void foo(String name) {}`, do you write a unit test to double check that if you pass an inputstream to the `foo` method that some failure occurs?

Of course you don't - you can't compile that. You trust the 'basis' - in this case, the combination of `javac` and the JVM class verifier ensuring that this contigency case __cannot__ occur.

Hence, 'test purposes' doesn't appear to make much sense here. It __cannot__ be `null` - unless you yourself write explicit code that sets it to `null`, e.g. with a direct field write (because lombok's generated constructors and setters won't let you do that).

You don't test for impossibilities. If you disagree with that sentiment and you feel that it is necessary, I don't really know what to tell you. Work on your imagination, perhaps? It is not possible to test for impossibilities; there are far too many (an infinite universe of them, in fact). Hence, if you think you are testing for everything including those, no, you aren't. That's not an ideal you should be chasing.

Lombok is opinionated in the sense that lombok aims to only include __boilerplate busting__ - a combination of something that comes up a lot + takes a lot of effort to write without lombok.

A crucial aspect of that is _comes up a lot_. It's hard to come up with a use case for this (and 'testing purposes', as outlined above, doesn't cut it). It doesn't matter that you cook up some exotic scenario where it's useful: We do not cater to exotic scenarios.

@trokhinas wrote:

> Why lombok NonNull is ever exists if lombok generate cheks for every pattern matching annotaion? Thats kinda strange..

For two reasons:

* `@lombok.NonNull` is the only annotation that will generate a null-check on arbitrary parameters. (in contrast to lombok-generated setters/withers/constructors, where any nullity annotation that strongly implies 'should not ever be null' does that).
* To avoid having to pull in another dependency. The JDK core libs don't have a nonnull annotation.

The title of this issue is 'undocumented'. It isn't.

@rzwitserloot - thank you for taking the time to write this comment. It is very clear.

The trump card here is this:

> you can use `lombok.config` to modify it.

So, when all is said and done, people can set the desired project-specific behaviour. I think that means we're really just arguing over documentation at this point. 😄

@rzwitserloot in addittion to prdoyle's answer:

Would it make sense, if I update PR #3525, so that the users can opt-in with a config-key? 

I totally understand, that the PR is a bit dangerous, as it will really break things when other non-nulls were used in a "wrong" way (wrong = depends on the developer's perspective) 

Regardless if the PR will be merged or not, I would like that the documentation should be more clear in this point. For example:


Important: Various NonNull annotations on fields are recognized only by lombok generated code (setters and constructors.) 

Null checks in self written functions and constructors are only generated for lombok.NonNull annotations. This has historic reasons and will not be changed. (OR This can be changed with config key X....) 




Roland

title: [FEATURE] Logger annotation for Temporal
body:
[temporal.io](https://temporal.io/) is a workflow-based orchestrator for microservices.

An usual workflow calls a series of activities, each of which can be implemented by a different microservices. The activities are unit of work, that can timeout, be retried, or be compensated if the workflow ultimately fails.

To provide resilience, a worklow must be *replayable*, meaning there are no side-effects except inside activities. For this reason Temporal uses a wrapper `ReplayAwareLogger` around loggers, and logger must always be defined using this wrapper in workflow classes:

```java
org.slf4j.Logger io.temporal.workflow.Workflow.getLogger(TYPE)
```

It would be useful if lombok could add a dedicated `@TemporalLog` annotation for temporal-wrapped loggers, as mentioned in the [documentation](https://projectlombok.org/features/log):

>  Please contact us if there is a public, open source, somewhat commonly used logging framework that we don't yet have an explicit annotation for. The primary purpose of @CustomLog is to support your in-house, private logging frameworks.

title: Simplify the use of extension methods

nodes.body: This is similar to https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/922

> This is similar to #922

Similar, yes. But couldn't this approach alleviate the performance problems inherent to the request in #922 ? Annotating the extensions class would effectively limit the search scope, no?

> Similar, yes. But couldn't this approach alleviate the performance problems inherent to the request in #922 ? Annotating the extensions class would effectively limit the search scope, no?

I'd guess the opposite: The project would need to be scanned for ```@ExtensionClass``` annotations first, before any further compilation steps could be done ...

Given these weird problems described in #3261 (and some others I haven't even reported yet, which cause NPE in the compiler), I wouldn't want extension methods to be applied to my entire project all at once. Too much stuff that can go wrong. Extension methods unfortunately are not very stable.

I have defined a shortcut in Eclipse called `ext`, which resolves to `@ExtensionMethod(LombokExtensions.class)`. It's very quick and easy that way to enable my extension methods on a specific class. But then, I only have one class where I define my static methods, so that might not be feasible for others.

> > Similar, yes. But couldn't this approach alleviate the performance problems inherent to the request in #922 ? Annotating the extensions class would effectively limit the search scope, no?
> 
> I'd guess the opposite: The project would need to be scanned for `@ExtensionClass` annotations first, before any further compilation steps could be done ...

Maybe we can use config to limit the scanning scope and improve the efficiency, such as restricting the package in which the extension method resides by project configuration(a global lombok.config).

I'd propose to go forward with the discussion in #922: as the configuration system allows to have config-files for individual subdirectories (https://projectlombok.org/features/configuration), that would be a great approach to place @ExtensionMethod-Definitions that are valid for many classes. 
BTW: Did anyone ever try to put @ExtensionMethod into `package-info.java`? That wouldn't populate to sub-packages, but might be helpful anyhow in some cases ...

I've been on a project recently where the team, although familiar with Lombok and making extensive use of it, nobody knew about `@ExtensionMethod` and I got some sideways looks about it during PR reviews. I had to explain what it does and why (IMO) it sometimes makes code read better. To do that, I explained that I first encountered the concept when I took a 4-5 year side trip into C# Land. Even after explaining it to some pretty good developers, there was still uncertainty about it - they had trouble accepting _that much_ magic from Lombok.

I tell that story to explain why I'm not thrilled about using config files for this. A developer who has not encountered `@ExtensionMethod` before, if there is no annotation to signal its usage, is likely to be hella confused about it. It's subtle and many Java developers probably haven't encountered the idea before. Hide it in a config file and you're just making that potential confusion more likely.

tl;dr  Java code should be in .java with the rest of the code (including annotations), not hidden away in a config file that most developers aren't even going to know to look for.

@erizzo: While I can totally relate to getting suspicious looks (I do, too), but that's not an argument against a config-file-possibility! If your team doesn't agree to use such an option in a config file, then simply don't do it. You can already configure lombok to reject the `@ExtensionMethod`-annotation ... 
The annotation `@ExtensionClass` proposed above would suffer from quite the same problem, btw: you wouldn't see it in the class in which you're using it.


I understand you colleagues perception that `@ExtensionMethod` is kind of (too much) magic, but I find it soooo handy to just press "." to pop up content assist and get offered appropriate extension methods alongside regular instance methods. :-) I also like to use extension methods as an intermediate step, if I don't have a certain method in a class from a company internal dependency, and experiment with the exact details how I would that method and it's signature to look. Extension methods allow my experiments to stay local in my application, and when it's mature enough I can promote it as a contribution to the common library.

And I confess I like to use it to bypass the stream() / collect() dance for simple filter or map situations.

Also adding some useful methods to the final String class comes in quite handy ...

At first encounter I thought lombok were all about `@Data` and it's siblings, but my view has expanded to include `@ExtensionMethod` now :-P.

@dstango I want to clarify that I'm not arguing against using `@ExtensionMethod`, just the idea of putting it in the config file. You're right that I and my teams can simply not use that; I just want to point out why it might not be a good idea in general.

title: [BUG] Cannot find symbol errors when migrating to Spring Boot 3 due to @ConstrutorBinding changes
body:
**Describe the bug**
Lombok breaks silently if annotation without ElementType.TYPE is used on a type.
This results in "cannot find symbol" on every usage of lombok-generated symbols. 
It's very hard to find the cause when hit with this bug.

**To Reproduce**

Spring Boot 3 dropped `ElementType.TYPE` from `@ContructorBinding`:
https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/commit/44b88cc88c2e848154a98ae17c03b1cd6c8f5830#diff-b777c5786f45759cb351f1d367175439ee177f65a14bc6677886c1cf93e6e582

It's easy to hit this bug when migrating Spring Boot 2.x codebase that has code like

```java
@Data
@ContructorBinding
@ConfigurationProperties("foo")
class Foo {
  int bar;
}
```

To fix, `@ConstructorBinding` should be replaced with `@RequiredArgsConstructor(onConstructor_={@ConstructorBinding})` or removed altogether.

**Expected behavior**
Lombok should fail fast and log root cause of the problem.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version: 1.8.24
 - Platform: azul-jdk 17.0.5

nodes.body: I actually faced this issue too, using lombok 1.8.26, Java 17 and Spring Boot 3.0.4. Lombok just wouldn't work and the compiler just complained "cannot find symbol".

OpenJDK Runtime Environment Zulu17.40+19-CA (build 17.0.6+10-LTS)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM Zulu17.40+19-CA (build 17.0.6+10-LTS, mixed mode, sharing)

Lombok: `1.18.26`
Spring Boot: `3.0.4`

This is a `javac` problem. For some reason the compiler does not call annotation processors like lombok if unrecoverable errors occour. One of these errors are annotations on the wrong element. A different example is a static import for non-existing methods (see #2044).

As an annotation processor lombok can not handle these cases but it is possible for a compiler plugin. I created a PoC yesterday to test if that works and it looks good so far. As this is also useful for other annotation processors I might publish it as standalone plugin too.
Let me know if you need some beta testers. I'll try getting a few of my colleagues on board then.

nodes.body:
There is this:
`@Builder(toBuilder=true)`

and that allows you to:

`var newFoo = oldFoo.toBuilder().build();`

I've covered that specific case in my initial post and explained why it doesn't suit our needs @dave-duetto . I need to control which java Class is instantiated, NOT allowing subclasses. If I do new Parent(sonInstance), I want the son properties to be lost (que the fastest way is to directly instantiate Parent, instead of using a builder. The child class may have created a toBuilder itself, and ruin the mechanism for me. The only way to control the instance type beyond any doubt is a copy constructor. Keep in mind that the goal is to reduce the overall knoweldge of the project in order to be productive. What if a guy whos new just copies a class with the toBuilder to create another instance? I've seen pretty incredibly crazy stuff that comes from copy-pasting without knowing / caring much, this feature intents to reduce que impact of that

I think it's already implementable with minimal customizations to `@SuperBuilder`. But before I outline the approach, let me first say that your example isn't really convincing to me.

My primary issue with it that you are using inheritance, but `InternalData` is not really related to `DataForFront` in terms of inheritance. They just happen to share a few fields, but serve a different purpose: `DataForFront` is a DTO that crosses the application border, and `InternalData` is used for internal processing and will never cross the application border.
To illustrate, imagine you decide to add a new API version, with a different data format. So you design a new `DataForFront2`. So what are the inheritance relations now between `DataForFront`, `DataForFront2`, and `InternalData`? This does not work any more.

So what you really want is a _mapping_ (or potentially multiple mappings in case of several API versions) between `DataForFront` and `InternalData`. (Tip: Have a look at [MapStruct](https://mapstruct.org/).)

But for cases where you really need to "convert" an instance to a supertype instance, you can do the following:
* Add `@SuperBuilder(toBuilder=true)` to all classes in the hierarchy.
* Follow the idea of [this StackOverflow answer](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/66783284/can-i-use-the-lombok-builder-passing-the-parent-class-as-parameter/66817135#66817135), but instead of adding a `toBuilder(Parent p)` method to the child class, add it to the parent. You also don't need the `$fillValuesFromParent` method. So it's just this:
```
    public static DataForFrontBuilder<?, ?> toBuilder(DataForFront p) {
        return new DataForFrontBuilderImpl().$fillValuesFrom(p);
    }
```

Disclaimer, as also mentioned on StackOverflow: Note the $ prefix on the methods. This basically says: I'm an implementation detail; don't use me unless you know what you are doing, I might break on the next Lombok version without further notice (which, however, is unlikely, `@SuperBuilder` has been quite stable for a while).

You mixed up two different thinks. `lombok.addNullAnnotations` set the annotations that get used for generated code. If you want to copy annotations that are not in the internal base list you have to use `lombok.copyableAnnotations`.

Apart from that, I agree that Jakarta annotations should be directly supported.

That config property will solve my issue, thanks for your swift reply! But it would be nice if this is an automatic one since many frameworks (spring-boot 3 for example) switched to Jakarta.

```
lombok.copyableAnnotations+=jakarta.annotation.Nonnull
lombok.copyableAnnotations+=jakarta.annotation.Nullable
```
