body:
I use the @Builder annotation in my project; when I try to get the Builder object using the new SomePojo.SomePojoBuilder() method, access is restricted
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/124959879/219829288-c47d08e2-cb9a-4096-8829-7ea8edd10402.png)
By decompiling the class file, you can see that the Builder internal class modifier in the compiled class file is public static. Usually, in Java, an internal class modified by public static can be accessed externally;
used @Builder class
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/124959879/219829478-1124e172-f258-46ab-963a-d7ae0a926f84.png)
unused @Builder class
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/124959879/219829438-de52b85a-e57b-488d-a3b1-4ea60ccf75ca.png)
Since the compiled class file has the internal class modified as public static, why can't I get the builder by new in my code? Instead, you have to call the static method builder() to get the builder.

This is my own hand-written Builder, which can be instantiated by way of new;
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/124959879/219829412-dde26b5b-8a63-4803-97d6-a34589814177.png)

Is this a bug or is it by design?

nodes.body:
It's by design. There are two idioms for builder creation, and at least at the time of introduction of the `@Builder` annotation in Lombok, there was no clear preference in the Java community.
So Lombok chose one (and IMO its the better one, because it's shorter and more readable especially when there are type parameters like with `@SuperBuilder`). And as there should not be two syntactical ways for the same task, Lombok does not support the other idiom.
BTW: You can still customize your builder and manually implement a public constructor (it's just empty), and suppress the generation of the `builder()` method by `@Builder(builderMethodName="")`.

title: [BUG] @NonNull on a primitive array field on a record isn't working

nodes.body:
It works as expected if you annotated the method parameter and not the array type e.g. `@NonNull byte[] bytes`.

It seems odd to me that it works at all (e.g. for normal methods) but there's probably a good reason I can't figure out.

IMO the meaning should be:
- `String @NonNull [] strings`: the array must not be `null`, but its elements can be `null`.
- `@NonNull String [] strings`: the array may be `null`, but if it's not, its elements must not be `null`.
- `@NonNull String @NonNull [] strings`: neither the array nor elements may be `null`.

For primitives, the second case is obviously irrelevant. So I think Lombok is wrong here.

**But:** That is only true if it's a type annotation and not a parameter annotation. Lombok's `@NonNull` is both, so it's impossible to distinguish. However Lombok should at least support the type annotation case 1.
Available on [edge](https://projectlombok.org/download-edge).

title: [FEATURE] customizing the @Builder to allow easy creation of the Test Data Builder pattern

nodes.body: Groovy's `@Builder` doesn't create a real builder, it is more like Lombok's `@Accessors(chained=true)`. Another way to go could be `@With`.

Yes, but I think `@Accessors(chained=true)` would be more similar to Groovy's `@Builder`.

It's not as powerful as Lombok's `@Builder`, e.g. it's missing a `@Singular` feature.
However, I must admit I don't really see the problem with Lombok's current builder implementation. For me, the additional `builder()`/`build()` methods add _clarity_, because they follow the well-established builder idiom, and not the Groovy style (which is not really common).

I want to have Test Data Builder no common builder - that's a difference.
In my tests I want to get rid off some technical concepts - one of them is the builder method.

Try to change your perspective for a while and try to treat your some tests like live documentation.
So in my tests I want to have business language, and try to hide some technical implementation details.

From business perspective:
```java
thereIs(anOrder().withAmount(eur(40)))
```
vs.

```java
thereIs(anOrder().withAmount(eur(40)).build())
```

A builder without `build()` method is impossible because you need some trigger to create the actual object. The only way you can drop the method is using `@Accessors(chain = true, prefix = "with")` or `@With(er)`. The former will modify the object you passed and the later will create a new object after each method call.

You can combine `@With` with an object mother to handle the default values and you are done. There is no need to use `@Builder` if you don't want to create a builder.

You only need a object mother if you want to add default values for your objects in your tests. You can also add your test data as default values in your class but I would not design it like that.

title: [BUG] extension method clashes with existing method on different class (javac only)
body:
**Describe the bug**
I defined an extension method `Optional.stream()` (yea, I'm stuck with Java 8). This has the same signature as the already existing `Collection.stream()`, which should be perfectly fine.

Unfortunately it isn't. Now the already existing `Collection.stream()` doesn't work anymore. And I never even used this new extension method.

The problem only happens, when `Collection.stream()` is called inside of a Lambda that is passed to yet another extension method (`flattenTree()`):
```java
list.stream().flattenTree(p -> p.kids().stream()).collect(Collectors.toList());
                                              ^
```
Here the first `stream()` is irrelevant. The second `.stream()` shows the error, it is called on the `List` returned by `p.kids()`.

But for some reason, Lombok wants `p.kids()` to return an `Optional` in order to call `.stream()` on it:

Output of _javac_ (Eclipse is fine):
```shell
javac -cp lombok-1.18.26.jar prob/lems/ProblemWithJavacButNotEclipse3.java
prob/lems/ProblemWithJavacButNotEclipse3.java:56: error: method stream in class Extensions cannot be applied to given types;
        list.stream().flattenTree(p -> p.kids().stream()).collect(Collectors.toList());
                                                      ^
  required: Optional<T>
  found: List<Person>
  reason: cannot infer type-variable(s) T
    (argument mismatch; List<Person> cannot be converted to Optional<T>)
  where T is a type-variable:
    T extends Object declared in method <T>stream(Optional<T>)
```


It works when the lambda is passed to a normal non-extension method (`flatMap`):
```java
list.stream().flatMap(p -> p.kids().stream()).collect(Collectors.toList());
```

It also works when the inner .stream() is called on something whose type is known:
```java
list.stream().flattenTree(p -> Collections.<Person>emptyList().stream()).collect(Collectors.toList());
```

So specifying the type of the `p` parameter also fixes the problem:
```java
list.stream().flattenTree((Person p) -> p.kids().stream()).collect(Collectors.toList());
```

**To Reproduce**

See here for an example project:
- https://github.com/marc-guenther/lombok-problems
Type `make problem3` to trigger.

The relevant section of the code:
- https://github.com/marc-guenther/lombok-problems/blob/9b971e2b86b208ec6d9deb65b3e0ad3630ce0c59/prob/lems/ProblemWithJavacButNotEclipse3.java#L53-L62

**Expected behavior**
Two things:
- javac and Eclipse should show the same behaviour
- The example should compile of course

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
- Lombok version: 1.18.24
- Platform: javac 1.8.0_282, Eclipse 2019-03 (4.11.0)

**Additional context**
Contrary to #3334, the `suppressBaseMethods` option did not make any difference here. I have it set to `false` by default, but even setting it to `true` did not change anything.

**Describe the bug**

I have a parent class, and a child class that extends it.
I want to make constructors that calls 'super()' and I have so many questions, because there's nothing in the doc about it :/

- Does @ NoArgsConstructor calls super?
- Does @ RequiredArgsConstuctor calls super?

nodes.body:
In Java a constructor always have to call a constructor of the parent class. If you do not specify one it calls `super()`.

There is no special magic in Lombok for constructor annotations so they always call the no-args parent constructor.

title: [BUG] @SuperBuilder does not compile when child class defines different buildMethodName than parent class

nodes.body:
Lombok cannot look into the parent class to find out what its build method name is. In addition, allowing different build method names would be confusing and thus will likely result in bugs. So even if it was technically possible, I don't see a reason why Lombok should allow it.

Maybe you could point out the use case of having different build method names.

We stumbled accross it, as we wanted to have clear separation between lombok generated code and custom (manual) lombok code. As such we named the build method in a child "initBuild" and then made a custom implementation of build() doing our custom stuff and call initBuild(). However that also causes the problem of having both, build() and initBuild() methods public, which is not desirable. 

Clearly this is not a real use case but cosmetics. If we would keep to go down this route a simple workaround is to put in a manual 
````java
public abstract C initBuild();
````
into the parent - OR - do not change build method names, but override them directly.

I suggest to put a note into the documentation. There is a section about not changing the Builder class name within the hierarchy. The same should apply to the buildMethodName then as an advise.
````
lombok.builder.className = [a java identifier with an optional star to indicate where the return type name goes] (default: *Builder)
This is the name of the generated builder class; any star in the name is replaced with the relevant return type. Note that the parent class must also have the same setting (the entire type hierarchy annoated with @SuperBuilder needs the same setting).
````

Cheers
Brian

Actually, together if this verifies [Issue 3418](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/3418) there is no way to provide a manual implementation of the build method in the abstract Builder and providing an implementation of build() in the BuilderImpl class has the problem, that Builder member variables are not accessible. 
The only chance would be to instantiate the object using new Child(this) and then use class getters to retrieve the actual member values.

For the use case of validating the set of member variables before actually "building" the object, this seems wrong.

What am I missing?
Thanks

Cheers
Brian

**Expected behavior**

title: [FEATURE] @ToString as JSON format
body: Hi, I've been thinking. Is it possible to generate @ToString as JSON format? If so, I'm happy to try to implement it and submit a pull request.

nodes.body: Duplicate of https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/1297

AFAIK, Lombok is not included with JSON libraries, therefore cannot guarantee valid, parsable JSON output without extra effort.

This is a one-liner with most libraries, such as Jackson. 

```java
String asJson = mapper.writeValueAsString(value);
```

This is really important, the JSON format is more versatile. In fact, it is very simple to achieve this. There is no need to use libraries such as Gosn and Jackson. Lombok only needs to replace = with: (replace with {,) with } when outputting toString. This seems very simple, why doesn't lombok do this?
Or lombok provides a way for users to configure the output symbols of attributes in toString. The output symbols of objects can be configured by users themselves using =, (,) or: ,{,}.
It is _not_ simple. Take the time to read the discussion in the linked issue and other duplicates of that issue.

> only needs to replace = with: (replace with {,) with }

title: Allow @AllArgsContructor and @With to skip transient fields
body: Transient fields are meant to be, well, transient. When creating a new instance or invoking a wither, it seems natural to ignore transient fields, like serialization/deserialization would do. Could be controlled via a flag.

title: [BUG] @Singular race conditions for maps

nodes.body:
I found no concurrency garantee for `@Singular` in [it's own documentation](https://projectlombok.org/features/Builder#singular). Futhermore, that garantee may slow down sequential execution because of unnecessary synchronization. 

I suggest to create `[FEATURE]` request for adding boolean parameter `async` for `@Singular` annotation, which will provide concistency in case of parallel execution when set to `true`.

title: [BUG] Autocomplete for `val` variables stops working "randomly" in Eclipse
body:
**Describe the bug**

In Eclipse 4.27+ with Lombok 1.18.27+, recognizing the type of `val`-defined variables and then also logically autocomplete of their members stops working "randomly" (described below). The code _compiles_ fine, Eclipse shows no compilation errors, yet it shows that the given variable defined via `val` is a plain `Object`. And sometimes it is even "stuck in the middle": the type is displayed correctly, yet autocomplete lists only `Object` members.

It is basically the same problem as described at redhat-developer/vscode-java/issues/2983 ([this](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/34871211/223144302-7d4426ae-8d21-486a-8392-08111979b1a7.png)) with the following differences:

* It happens in Eclipse.
* It happens even after upgrading Lombok to 1.18.27 (edge release) or 1.18.28 (upgraded because of the support for `lombok.config` - see #3332).
* It happens seemingly _randomly_.

No errors seen in Eclipse logs which could point to the problem.

**To Reproduce**

It seems like the problem can be reproduced on this minimal example Java code:

```java
import lombok.val;

public class LombokExample {

    protected String breakVal = "anything";

    public void main(String[] args) {
        val num = String.valueOf(args.length);
        // num wrongly shown as Object if breakVal field is initiated within its declaration
        System.out.println(num.charAt(0));
    }
}
```

Steps to reproduce:

0. Close all editors in Eclipse. (purely optional - one can just leave either A, or B from step 2 focused)
1. Restart Eclipse.
2. As the first editor open:
    A: the class above (or seemingly any class which doesn't use `val`) - breaks!
    B: a class which uses `val`, but doesn't use any field initializers - doesn't break!

Note that when the functionality breaks, it breaks _globally_ - i.e. it affects editing of Java classes from completely unrelated projects. Until another Eclipse restart.

**Expected behavior**

Eclipse should recognize and show proper `val` variable type _all the time_.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**

 - Lombok version: 1.18.27 and 1.18.28 (and with Lombok 1.28.24, it gets even worse: `Object` is _always_ shown for a `val` variable)
 - Platform: Windows 10, javac 11.0.18, Eclipse 2023-03 (4.27.0) and 2023-06 (4.28.0) (both "Eclipse IDE for Enterprise Java and Web Developers")

**Workaround**

As described above, it looks like the issue can be avoided by always firstly opening a class (`*.java`) with `val` but without any field initializers when (re)starting Eclipse.

A few versions ago the eclipse compiler was moved into its own OSGi module which makes it impossible to read the eclipse classes. Instead of rewriting everything I added the classloader of the core module to the compiler module classloader (#3347). This worked in some cases but it turns out that the initialization order in eclipse is different if there is an open file or not. I fixed that too (#3411). The whole prepend stuff happens after the first parse but if the class contains some features (e.g. `val`) some lombok classes get loaded before the parse ends and these classes are unable to find the eclipse stuff. Thats what causes this issue. I fixed that by prepending the classloader after the parser class gets initialized.

title: [FEATURE] Do not privatize constructor when using staticName on @All/@No/RequiredArgsConstructor
body:
Currently when staticName is used and the programmer wants to create a static constructor plan constructor that is generated along side it is set to PRIVATE access. This actually makes evolution of old codebases harder, since it's not possible (with just Lombok) to refactor code/tests in a 2/3-step process.

0. Class have only "new" constructor (@AllArgsConstructor) - this doesn't facilitate mocking construction at all in modern mock frameworks. We want to move away from such a code, but not in 1-step process.
1. Use @AllArgsConstructor(staticName = "of") - both constructors are available and developer can now write **new** tests using new static constructor without **at the same time** refactoring old tests/production code.
2. Steadily move tests/production code to use static constructor - until 100% of code uses static constructor.
3. PRIVATE'ize basic "new" constructor.
4. ... Profit?!

It would be good to be able to do just that.

title: [BUG] extensions method with long/double argument causes JNI error when run in Eclipse
body:
**Describe the bug**
An extension method with a `long` or `double` parameter, which is called with an `int`, causes an JNI error during runtime when loading the class.

Definition of the extension method with a `long` argument:
```java
public static <T> void hello(String that, long n) {
    // nothing here
}
```

Calling it with an `int`:
```java
public void someMethod() {
    "".hello(1);
}
```

This compiles, but when run in Eclipse, produces the JNI error below.

Calling with a `long` instead (eg. changing the `1` to a `1l`) fixes the problem.

**To Reproduce**

See here for an example project:

- https://github.com/marc-guenther/lombok-problems

The problem can be seen in the [JNIProblem.java](https://github.com/marc-guenther/lombok-problems/blob/7aafa1e7489ec89c4eaee4e801ee9564c2aa3eed/prob/lems/JNIProblem.java#L35-L46) class.

When launching the class in Eclipse, it will fail like this:
```
Error: A JNI error has occurred, please check your installation and try again
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack
Exception Details:
  Location:
    prob/lems/JNIProblem.someMethod()V @3: invokestatic
  Reason:
    Type integer (current frame, stack[1]) is not assignable to long_2nd
  Current Frame:
    bci: @3
    flags: { }
    locals: { 'prob/lems/JNIProblem' }
    stack: { 'java/lang/String', integer }
  Bytecode:
    0x0000000: 120f 08b8 0011 120f 1400 17b8 0011 b1  

	at java.lang.Class.getDeclaredMethods0(Native Method)
	at java.lang.Class.privateGetDeclaredMethods(Class.java:2701)
	at java.lang.Class.privateGetMethodRecursive(Class.java:3048)
	at java.lang.Class.getMethod0(Class.java:3018)
	at java.lang.Class.getMethod(Class.java:1784)
	at sun.launcher.LauncherHelper.validateMainClass(LauncherHelper.java:650)
	at sun.launcher.LauncherHelper.checkAndLoadMain(LauncherHelper.java:632)
```

With `javac`/`java` it works just fine:
```
$ make jni_problem
javac -cp lombok-1.18.28.jar prob/lems/JNIProblem.java
java -cp lombok-1.18.28.jar:. 'prob.lems.JNIProblem'
works in javac but not with Eclipse
```

**Expected behavior**
No JNI error :)

**Version info:**
 - Lombok version: 1.18.28
 - Eclipse: 2022-03 (4.23.0)

**Workaround**

Define both versions of the extension method (`int` and `long)`, and let one call the other.

When I tried this, it still wouldn't work. Turns out, Eclipse does not recompile my calling class, when the extension method class changes.

After a Clean Build everything worked fine.

nodes.body: Thanks for the detailed bug report. IIRC we already have some special handling for casts but it seems to be incomplete or incompatible with recent eclipse versions.
I can confirm that this fixes the problem. Thanks a lot! Always nice to fix a bug by removing "magic" from the code :)

title: [BUG] javax Nonnull on Record Fails to Create Null-Check
body:
**Describe the bug**
Using `javax.annotation.Nonnull` annotation on a Record's field does not generate a null-check.

```java
public record JavaxRecord(@Nonnull String shouldNotBeNull) { }
```

**To Reproduce**
Attached is [JavaxNonnullRecordExample.java.txt](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/files/12177141/JavaxNonnullRecordExample.java.txt) which shows that using the JavaX Nonnull fails to generate null-checks, but lombok's own NonNull _does_ generate null-checks. Note that since this requires the JavaX Nonnull annotation a jar will be needed for that (https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/com.google.code.findbugs/jsr305/3.0.2)

```
$ javac -cp lombok-1.18.28.jar:jsr305-3.0.2.jar JavaxNonnullRecordExample.java

$ java -cp lombok-1.18.28.jar:jsr305-3.0.2.jar:. JavaxNonnullRecordExample
JavaxRecord: FAILURE: Using Builder: A NPE should have been thrown
JavaxRecord: FAILURE: Using CTOR: A NPE should have been thrown
LombokRecord: SUCCESS: Using Builder: A NPE was thrown
LombokRecord: SUCCESS: Using CTOR: A NPE was thrown
```

**Expected behavior**
Annotating a field in a Record with "@Nonnull" from javax will generate a null-check.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version: 1.18.28
 - Platform: javac 20.0.1

nodes.body:
This happens because the generated builder uses the existing constructor if present. A record always has this constructor and lombok does not modify that one. If you add the lombok `@NonNull` lombok generates/modifies the record constructor and it works as expected.

I agree that this is a little bit confusing.

title: [FEATURE] Named null setter / clear function

nodes.body: Have you thought about how it should handle collections? Simply applying `null` is easy but I would not expect that behaviour for a `List` or some third party collection library.

> Have you thought about how it should handle collections? Simply applying `null` is easy but I would not expect that behaviour for a `List` or some third party collection library.

@Rawi01 not something I had considered, but I agree that the term clearing implies that a collection would be cleared down and i think that makes sense in that scenario. alternatively - there could be a configurable "clear" value specified in the annotation, that when an item is cleared down, it's value is assigned.

Unfortunately we have to deny this request.

The problem is a fundamental misunderstanding of what `null` is for. Or, rather, that the java community _itself_ is hopelessly confused about what `null` _actually_ means.

Going by the JLS and only by the JLS, `null`'s semantic meaning is:

* An uninitialized non-final field, or
* A 'slot' in a non-primitive array that hasn't been set yet.

You'll find no further philosophical waxing about what it is supposed to mean than that.

Contrast to SQL which is far more clear about it: `NULL` in SQLese means UNKNOWN, and therefore, it is entirely justified and logical that `NULL` in SQLese is infectuous. Even `x = TRUE` in SQL has 3 possible values (namely, `TRUE`, `FALSE`, and `NULL` - and even `NULL = NULL` doesn't evaluate to `TRUE` - it evaluates to `NULL`). This is sensible, eventhough this is the butt of many, many jokes about SQL, if you keep in mind what null actually means. if I ask you: I have the name of a person in my mind. I'm not going to tell you what it is and there is no other way for you to know what it is. Then someone asks you: Is Reinier thinking of "Jordan", you cant answer 'TRUE', and you can't answer 'FALSE'. you do not know. You can only answer "I don't know" - and `NULL` is the value in SQL-ese that conveys this.

If you apply the SQLese understanding of java, then you have a really, really big problem here: "Clear the value" __isn't necessarily the same semantic idea__ as 'unknown'. The JLS meaning of `null` is essentially useless ("the field is not set" is semantically meaningless; that is an implementation detail). The java community meaning of `null` is a total mess. If I search all github projects for `if (x == null || x.isEmpty())` I get half a billion results which is __utterly bizarre__ because that is hopelessly confused (i.e. really bad) code. If 'null' and 'empty' mean the same thing why is the state of this object in such a state? Why isn't x simply 'the empty string'? It can't be 'for performance reasons', because the JVM has an empty string ref floating around already.

To show you how much this semantic notion kills this idea, you tell me:

Given: `String name;` - if I ask "The name has been cleared - so, what is its value?" at a java conference or some such, I bet I get a nice even split: Half of the folks I ask will absolutely insist that must mean `name.equals("")`, and the other half will be thoroughly convinced that this must mean `name == null`.

So, we introduce a style war (should one call `.setName(null)` or `.clearName()`? It's bad to introduce 2 ways of doing things when they are pretty much equally easy to write and read and neither has a clear advantage or disadvantage), _and_ introduce loads of confusion. Whereas `.setName(null)` at least isn't confusing: If I ask that at a big conference, everybody will correctly surmise this code must mean `name == null` is true, and `name.equals("")` is false / throws.

Also, whilst the SQL 'null means unknown' is not particularly popular in java, it is "correct", in that the behaviour that nulls have fits that model best: If I ask a nullref a question (I call a method on it), an exception occurs. That's a totally sensible thing to do if the reference implies "I do not know what this value is". i.e. given `String x = null;`, the notion that `x.length()` should probably return `0` fits the mental model that `null` is semantically equivalent to the empty string. However, this model is broken, in that java itself doesn't work that way, as `x.length()` would throw an NPE. The mental model of 'null means: unknown' fits java's actual behaviour far better: Ask questions about the nature of the unknown value, and exceptions occur.

Hopefully that context fully covers why the answer is: No, and any PRs that add this feature will be closed without comment other than linking to this issue.

NB: Just to rub it in in case you are thinking about making a passionate defense of the idea, if the field is a list, should we [A] `list = null;`, [B] `list.clear();`, or [C] `list = new ArrayList<>();`? Going back to my hypothetical conference, I think we might have hit the sweetspot and score a nice 33%/33%/33% split amongst respondents. To be clear, unless the respondent score is 95% or more going one way, we deny the feature. This __epically__ fails to cross the bar, and its gets even worse once you consider how little boilerplate this saves.

body:
**Describe the bug**
Trying to test an application with both ASM and lombok fails.

"Potential easy solution" (TM): Rename the lombok shaded ASM package, so other software does not fail.


**To Reproduce**
Trying to use ASM and lombok at the same time will fail when running Tests (using IntelliJ or Maven).

As far as i can see everything is as described by https://projectlombok.org/setup/maven.
Note that running the main Method works, however running jUnit will fail.

I created a [minimal reproduceable example](https://github.com/BjoernAkAManf/mre-lombok-asm/blob/master/.github/workflows/maven.yml).

The error basically says that ASM is used by both lombok and ASM.
java.lang.LayerInstantiationException: Package org.objectweb.asm in both module lombok and module org.objectweb.asm


**Expected behavior**
Testing works out of the box and the Project compiles.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version  1.18.28
 - Platform maven 3.9.2 and IntelliJ IntelliJ IDEA 2023.2 (Ultimate Edition) Build #IU-232.8660.185, built on July 26, 2023 

**Additional context**
See #2549 and #2973 

PS: Thanks for the great software! I love using lombok, but it's quite a shame the issue above occurs. The previous listed issues boil down to:

1. Use explicit Annotation Processor (i specified them)
2. Require static lombok (i do)
3. No minimal example provided (see above)
4. User Error (I don't see how i'm doing something wrong, and i don't think JUnit / Maven is doing something explicitely wrong. Especially given, that lombok can be quite helpful generating Test Data Classes, where records do not suffice.

I'd be willing to give a try implementing reshading, but understanding the code base has been quite hard for me in the past.
So any pointer, if that change would be welcome, would be appreciated.

The git repository is only 8 or so files long each (i'd assume less than 10 mb each) and might be cloned shallow.

So as far as can see it's more or less git clone && mwnw verify to reproduce. I do not see where this reaches a file size of more than 1 GB let alone 5.

Anything else i can help you with? I could probably create a shell example with hard coded jars as well, would that be more helpful?

I'm suprised that this error occurs at runtime because lombok should not be at the classpath at that point. It is a compile time only dependency and the fix only affects the compilation steps. Can you try to exclude it for the surefire tests?
@BjoernAkAManf No need for shell scripts. Sounds like your example repo here will do fine as test case. Reopening.

**EDIT: Our conclusions in this comment are wrong - see next comment for explanation of what's really going on here!**


Cloned the project.

* Yes, it fails.
* Doing actual tests, it just isn't us. I think surefire perhaps ships with lombok somehow? i.e. an older version?
* mvn (the surefire plugin, rather) starts surefire with an `@` file for the args, and it deletes that file instantly. __It is just not possible to debug this stuff, and that's on surefire, not on us__. Thus, we're throwing in the towel: We're not fixing it, maybe surefire can fix it for you / can at least make the debug process less onerous. All that's needed for us to proceed is that we can actually _see what it is doing_, so we can check what modules it is actually throwing to shove on the module path, which is currently not possible no matter how many `-X` or `-e` args you provide to maven.
* If you use the `<configuration>` property in the surefire section of your pom file with: `<useModulePath>false</useModulePath>`, all works well again. That should be a convenient workaround until you can tell surefire to fix this / fix their launch procedure so there's a way to tell it not to use `@` files, or echo them to the command line on an `-X` / `-e` run, or to NOT delete the args file instantly after using it.

It's the dejavu ticket that bounces between closed and reopened.

Sooo, what's the programmer's version of treppenwitz? Where you toss in the towel, close the tabs and the relevant editors, and go do something else, and at that exact moment you go: Oh waaaaait a second?

Anyway, that.

Conclusion: Team OpenJDK is... ugh. They make bizarro and dangerous choices a lot.

The wait a second moment is this: The JVM figures out this split package thing _really quickly_ - like, we tell surefire to freeze on boot so we can maybe see that `@` file or connect to it and check some things and we never even get that far. We ask the JVM to print every class as it loads it, and it never prints anything relevant (zero lombok classes, for example). So, clearly then, it opens those modules and realizes there's a split package situation before it possibly could which is.. well, not possible.

Unless....

The java runtime just opens the jar __and scans directories__. If it sees 2 directories that match it immediately goes: Oh, oh! Split packages, abort abort. Which is silly. Maybe wait until something is loaded from there?

At any rate, __that's it__, that's why it still fails. It doesn't matter that we never load anything in the namespace, or that the concept of 'a package name' is a notion that exists only on the 'other side' of the classloader line (not on the 'go find the sources' line, it's on the `defineClass` / returns from `getResource` side of the line), so OpenJDK jumps the gun and this is a bug on their end. Which I'm sure they're neither going to spec nor fix, but, fortunately, we can fix it easily.

We've now updated our shadowloader to work off of a subdir instead. I cannot reiterate how disappointingly bad this is from how the JDK loads modules. Just to confirm, adding a 0-length file to the jars with path `org/objectweb/asm/oh-dear.txt` is enough to get surefire plugin to asplode again. Proving that this is it.

Fix will make it in time for the imminent 1.18.30 release. It'll be closed, for the last time, in an hour or two while I go clean up the commits and write a note in the changelog for it.

While I agree mostly with the sentiment, i think the requirement, that module directories are reserved to the actual module, so that classes and resources of a package only exist in their own Jar. It is not as intuitive as it should be. Especially with that error.

However, I'm glad the issue is fixed. I'll update the Repository as fixed once i get around to it. =)

> Sooo, what's the programmer's version of treppenwitz? Where you toss in the towel, close the tabs and the relevant editors, and go do something else, and at that exact moment you go: Oh waaaaait a second?

It's a new term (apparently circa 2009), but maybe ["shower thought"](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/shower_thought)?

body:
**Describe the bug**

When running Error Prone 2.21.0 on a project using Lombok, generated synthetic nodes with overlapping source offsets are causing a crash in Error Prone's NotJavadoc check.

**To Reproduce**

To repro, check out this branch:

title: [FEATURE REQUEST] Extending @FieldNameConstants
body:
Dear team:

@FieldNameConstants is a very helpful feature for our project and without which it would have been a nightmare for us using hard coded field names in all our Spark SQL Queries. 

However, is there a way we can extend @FieldNameConstans annotation to return snake case names ('field_name') instead of actual class member names? We need this kind of functionality in order to persist our domain entities using JDBC providers and Apache Spark in PostgreSQL.  

The main reason for such a feature is to address object naming conventions in some RDBMS and ORMs when database is created, the default behavior is to  convert class field names as per standard naming convention that database follows.  
This is resulting in some inconsistent styling issues in code. For example, if we stick to the naming convention like most databases would follow (e.g. snake case  'field_name'),  then this creates some awkward function names with getters & setters  (e.g 'is_enabled' => 'getIs_Enabled()'

Would it be possible to provide extended functionality to @FieldNameConstants.  A couple of ways could be:

	1. Accepting a regular expression pattern as a value for the annotation like 'uppercase'. i.e:
		@FieldNameConstants(namePattern="<someRegExPattern").  
	This patten should be applied to all field names that are being returned when we use:
		 <ClassName>.Fields.<FieldName>
	2. Providing a second object 'DbFields' in addition to 'Fields': 
	          @FieldNameConstants(DbFieldsWithCase='camelCase')
	3. Providing at least some pre-defined cases similar to 'uppercase'. Like, camelCase, PascalCase , snake_Case etc 
	        
This feature would be far more powerful than "nameof()" keyword provided in .Net and can eliminate a whole class of errors that would creep in because of hard coded field names.  Also, performance overhead can be justified as it's a compile time effort. 

Thanks in advance,

title: [FEATURE] Inversion of control for @ExtensionMethod

nodes.body: This is probably related to https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/922 and https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/3316

Most similar to #3316 indeed. I'm not really in favor of using a config file for this like in #922. The import of the method should be enough and it should obey the same encapsulation (and module-based strong encapsulation) rules as other methods.

A possible problem of the 'static import only' approach is a change of the semantics of the import: by simply adding the import you propose some there's also a usage implied, not only a name resolution.

Setting philosophical aspects aside, the practical implication is that you'll run into trouble with all sorts of auto-format-tools / organize import functions: they will not detect any usage of the said static method and probably remove the import, unless they know about such a lombok feature.

A lot of IDEs already support the concept of extension methods for other languages. You might be able to hook into that. 

For instance, IntelliJ IDEA supports extension methods for Kotlin. It even colors the methods differently to signal to the user that this is an extension method, to avoid confusion. The Lombok plugin would probably be able to mark the method as an extension method in a similar way, with similar syntax highlighting.

title: [FEATURE] @Builder add nullBehavior as a parameter
body: This would allow the updating of an existing object using the toBuilder() method to determine what behavior should occur if a field is going to be set to null in the builder.  This would help reduce boilerplate for the merging of objects in cases where the updating object can have null values that should not replace existing values.

nodes.body:
While I understand your feature request technically, I don't get the use case behind it. If you don't want `null` values to be set, why don't you simply add a check before? Or is it a library you are using that's missing this feature?

I'm asking because I see a problem with your request: The notion of `null` differs between developers. It could be, for example, "unset", "not yet set", "invalid", just a reference value (that's how the JLS defines it) or something in between or a mixture. If lombok would load semantics on this value beyond what's obvious, that'd be a safe way of making lombok users producing bugs. Especially if you cannot tell _at the call site_  that there is something special with the method.

Just guessing what the use case might be:

Consider a REST PATCH request: you'll might get a Json body with only some fields provided. The corresponding POJO might then contain only these provided fields filled with values, while the others are set to null. 
If you then get some object from your persistence store and want to change only the non-null tfields from the POJO, this might be the intended use case.

Anyhow: I'd rather say that sounds more like a mapping frameworks job than lombok's ... E.g. as elaborated here for model mapper: https://stackoverflow.com/q/49153100

This isn't solving some major issue or anything.  I noticed that with the Singular annotation, you can do `@Singular(nullBehavior = NullCollectionBehavior.IGNORE)` which will prevent a Collection from being set to null in the builder and thought that it could be useful to have that as a settable default for all builder fields.  It could reduce a lot of boilerplate null checks, especially in functions or methods with are handling mapping.

title: [FEATURE] Expand @ExtensionMethod target to PACKAGE and make it a repeatable annotation
body:
**Describe the feature**

Currently `@ExtensionMethod` can only be applied to Types: `@Target(TYPE)`. 
It would be beneficial if that would be expanded to `@Target(TYPE, PACKAGE)`, because thus it would be possible to add the annotation to a `package-info.java` file and thus have it available in all classes of the package. 

To avoid conflict with more `@ExtensionMethod` annotations in individual classes, it probably would be advisable to make it a repeatable annotation. This could be beneficial in individual use, too, as one could more easily add/remove lines with Extension-classes.

**Describe the target audience**

Everyone who loves to use `@ExtensionMethod` often and has some class(es) sitting around that are often used, and become automatically available for all classes of the package. 

If you're trying to be really clever you could combine it with something like https://github.com/bohnman/package-info-maven-plugin, which would allow `package-info.java`-templates that might even be available project wide automatically.

**Additional context**

This feature request is similar to https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/issues/922 -- in fact it proposes an alternative way to the proposed `lombok.config` solution. If an `lombok.config` solution would be implemented, this feature request would be obsolete. 
This proposal is thus an idea to circumvent any current issues that block going forward with a `lombok.config` solution, as it *might* be easier to implement (not sure about that, just guessing).

nodes.body:
Was there any blocker for the `lombok.config` version besides the potential performance impact? As you can also scope `lombok.config` to a package the performance should be identical. 

The advantage of `package-info.java` is that it is java code and you can use all IDE features out of the box. I'm not sure how easy it is to resolve the `package-info.java` annotations but it should be possible.

I like the repeatable annotation idea.

I don't know about blockers -- only remember @rzwitserloot saying ExtensionMethod needs a lot of love, and mentioning a general note to a long list of caveats. 

If the performance impact in compilation is 10%-20% I guess it's only if the lombok.config actually uses the feature, right? So I'd say the responsibility is with the user to decide on the trade-off. Don't know about your experience but my builds usually spend minimal time in compilation, but most of their time in resolving dependencies, running tests, building deployables, etc...
And I guess if such a feature is implemented there might be room for optimization, if the feature is well liked. 

Anyhow: the expected direct IDE support is an interesting aspect of the package-info way. Though IDEs require some assistance by e. g. a plugin for lombok anyhow...

He only mentioned one explicit case and that one works.

I rebased and reworked my old config based prototype and pushed it (https://github.com/Rawi01/lombok/tree/globalExtensionMethod). I only measured an increase in complation time of 2% (have to do that again on a quiet system).
If you want to run some benchmarks you can use the CI build artifact or build it yourself.

I accidentally compared my branch with the latest release, which did not yet include other performance improvements, which skews the results. In a real comparison, I was again able to measure a slowdown of 12 %. As the feature gets only enabled if the config key is set and can be limited to packages I think that is not too bad.

title: [FEATURE] Support jsr305 @Nonnegative and @RegEx
body:
Dear Project Lombok maintainers,

I am writing to request the addition of support for famous [JSR-305 annotations](https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/com.google.code.findbugs/jsr305/), 
specifically ```@Nonnegative``` and ```@RegEx```.

The JSR-305 annotations are widely accepted and used by many developers due to their robust null-safety capabilities. They provide significant benefits such as better readability, more informative error messages, and reduced code complexity [dzone.com](https://dzone.com/articles/when-to-use-jsr-305-for-nullability-in-java).

The ```@Nonnegative``` annotation can help enforce that a numerical value should never be negative, while the ```@RegEx``` annotation can be used to document that a particular method or field should represent a regular expression. These annotations can help prevent bugs related to incorrect values and improve code quality.

Current configuration options in Lombok include the capability to add nullability annotations, such as @NonNull, to methods and constructors [baeldung.com](https://www.baeldung.com/lombok-configuration-system). However, the lack of support for ```@Nonnegative``` and ```@RegEx``` in Lombok means that developers have to manually check conditions in their code, which can be tedious and error-prone.

It's important to note that other frameworks, such as Spring Boot, have started supporting JSR-305 annotations, which demonstrates their growing adoption in the Java community [github.com](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/issues/24647).

Adding support for ```@Nonnegative``` and ```@RegEx``` in Lombok would not only increase the library's functionality but also align it with the evolving best practices in Java development.

I understand that adding new features requires careful consideration and effort, but I believe that the benefits to the Java community would be substantial.

Thank you for considering this request.

title: [FEATURE] Proposal: Introduction of @Lock Annotation for Better JDK 21 Virtual Thread Support

nodes.body:
Let's flesh it out a bit. What does `@Lock` generate if the relevant field isn't already there. How precisely does it open the lock and how precisely does it close it. Is it necessarily j.u.c.ReentrantLock, or is it configurable? If configurable, in the annotation, or in lombok.config? What about R/W locks?

And, definitely, a bit of a treatise as to _why_. This is personal lack of experience. I never bother with locks, I always just use `synchronized`. If I need the power of R/W lock behaviour I'll use a juc lock (where a 'read' lock does not block out other attempts to acquire read blocks, but a 'write' block locks out all other writes _and_ reads, and open reads block out attempts to acquire writes) - but if I just need the basic lock that presumably this proposal will end up making for you, I don't get it.

Which isn't a showstopper in any way. Just a gap in my knowledge. But if I have to write the docs or at least sign off I have to understand how `synchronized` asplodes virtual threads but j.u.c. locks don't.

The main issue with `synchronized` and virtual threads is that it will pin the virtual thread to its carrier thread. To avoid this you can use another j.u.c and `ReentrantLock` seems to be a good fit for the same behavior as `syncrhonized` block.
This is a duplicate of #610 and @PimvanderLoos created PR #2859 some time ago.

So that's heading towards the simplest possible option. No way to configure which lock, for example.

Alright. Doesn't sound particularly complicated. I need to put a little bit of thought into the name of the var we create (do we use the same name as we do for `@Synchronized`, which would imply using both in one class will clash), and more generally should we just disallow mixing `@Synchronized` and `@Lock` in the same class. I'm tempted to jus disallow that, it'd be quite crazy to want to do it.

And if we go that far... is this just a matter of adding a config key `lombok.synchronized.useJucLocks = true`? I'm pretty sure that's going way too far, and `@Synchronized` generating juc locks is a naming mismatch (a casual reader sees `@Synchronized` and assumes `synchronized (x){` instead of `new ReentrantLock`, that seems like a logical assumption, so it'd be bad if that assumption is wrong - that's why I think that's going too far).

So far I'm at:

* lombok checks if you mix `@Synchronized` and `@Lock` in one class and if so, does not make any code modification whatsoever, and generates a compiler error.
* Otherwise, lombok checks if a field named `$LOCK` / `$lock` - that's the same name `@Synchronized` uses. I have a slight preference for not clashing names, but then.. what in the blazes should we call this field if not `$lock`? (`$LOCK` for `@Lock` on static methods, `$lock` for instance methods). If this field exists, that's used. Lombok will silently assume it's properly typed and generates calls to `.lock()` and `.unlock()`; if not properly typed, lombok still does that, so you'd get a 'no such method' compiler error on the `@Lock` annotation. If the field does not exist, lombok generates it. It'll be `private final`, it'll be of type `Lock`, and its initializing expression will be `new java.util.concurrent.ReentrantLock();`
* Alternatively if the annotation is of the form `@Lock("varName")`, lombok will not generate a field in any case and proceed assuming `varName` exists and is typed `Lock` or better. Lombok doesn't check this and just generates calls to `.lock()` and `.unlock()`.
* Specifically, it generates: Add `$lock.lock();` at the top, and wrap the method content in `try { CONTENT } finally { $lock.unlock(); }`.
* `lockInterruptibly()` is not available (Unless we really wanna mess with `@Lock(interruptable = true)`, I'm not sure we should until someone explains why its important). There is no particular need to deliver on this for the first version, as we can always add it (but _removing_ it, that'd be a breaking change, hence, if we're on the fence, "do not add it yet" wins from "add it now").

Anything I've missed?

Next step is cross checking how close @Pimvanderloos 's PR is to this idea.

title: [FEATURE] Getters and Setters for Embedded fields

nodes.body:
The problem is [resolution](https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/wiki/LOMBOK-CONCEPT:-Resolution): We know that your `personId` field is of type `com.foo.PersonId`.

__But we do not know anything about _that_ type__. We don't _know_ it has a `getName()` method. To know that, the AST first needs to be resolved: The JVM isn't like C - you don't have to order your compilation process and work with header files. (C compilers are 1- or 2-pass: If some code calls `String.toLowerCase()` before the compiler has processed the `String.java` file the compiler bombs then and there stating that doesn't exist). Java instead works in phases: First it parses __everything__, then builds up a simplified list of what everything has __totally ignoring actual source code__, and only then does it parse statements and the like. To avoid the C issue of needing to manage your passes.

But that puts lombok in a bind: If we wait until everything is resolved, well, then we're too late - we can't then add a method - the compiler has probably already errored out on someone calling a getter that we haven't made yet. In other words, we have to add the methods we generate __before__ the 'process actual statements' phase, or we're too late. However, until that phase is reached we don't know about the content of `PersonId` yet. Hence, this cannot be implemented easily.

One easy solution is rounds - the ability to tell the compiler to start the whole process anew. This is harder than it looks, and is a severe time penalty (that makes compiling take a lot longer). We do it for a select few lombok features, but it's a high maintenance burden and a high performance cost. There are other even hackier solutions (mostly involving trying to go in passes ourselves). For any lombok feature that doesn't affect signatures but only affects method content it's easier.

We do apply it for `@ExtensionMethod`, but we treat that as being in `experimental` - it is less stable and we are less sure about continued support for it simply because we foresee potential serious trouble if `javac`'s internals change a lot.

Hence, request, unfortunately, vetoed. We simply do not know how to deliver it in a way that the cost (in terms of maintenance burden, stability, and compile time it'll take) is worth the gain. Once we do, this and quite a few other common requests are top of the list.

title: [FEATURE] Remove additional compilation rounds
body:
**Describe the feature**
Lombok always initiates multiple rounds of annotation processing, ensuring that all handlers requiring resolution are processed within their dedicated rounds. This was a requirement in the past due to the fact that added methods and fields were not consistently added to type mirrors. However, a significant improvement was introduced in issue #2718, which not only enabled the support of other annotation processors in the same round but also paved the way for accomplishing all tasks within a single round.

Eliminating these rounds has the dual benefit of decreasing compilation time and streamlining the incorporation of other annotation processors that can execute after Lombok and access all the generated content.

**Describe the target audience**
Everyone

**Additional context**
I successfully implemented a proof of concept (https://github.com/Rawi01/lombok/tree/remove-additional-rounds) and it resulted in a 15% reduction in compilation time for my sample project.

nodes.body:
The whole 'patch up the type mirrors' trick also feels like a doorway to run all of lombok post-resolution just like ExtensionMethod and company do. Opens up doors such as automatically creating constructors that call the superconstructor and the like.

I wonder how we should go about releasing this; I foresee issues that our tests won't catch. A really long edge-release period? Lombok v1.20 while we also release lombok v1.18 for a year or so (maintain em both) to ensure 1.20 (with this PoC applied) is indeed stable?

Adding it to the next milestone more in the sense of 'we should consider it', not so much "this will definitely be in the next release".

I also suspect that there may be certain issues that our tests are not capturing. One particular concern I have in mind is the potential presence of extension methods on a type generated by a different annotation processor. At the moment this works in most cases because we delay the transformation to later rounds.

@Rawi01 Lombok does not portend to be compatible with other lomboks (i.e. other code-modifying compiler plugins, whether they launch via the AP loader mechanism or any other way). And vanilla APs cannot modify existing code, only add new code. So, we're now down to a really exotic case, where you `@ExtensionMethods` in a class that doesn't exist at first, but is generated by another AP.

Presumably we can make that work too - just..  ignore the issue of 'oh hey that class doesn't exist at all', and return false (not completed the actions required for this annotation yet), as another round _will_ happen and then it'll be well. So, I'm doubly not worried:

* Other than academic cases it won't come up.
* But if we want to support those, that probably already works right now.

I'd consider `@Delegate`ing an AP-produced type to be mostly in the same boat: Exotic.

As in, if we can significantly speed up lombok at the cost of breaking that, I think we should break it. (Even better would be that we speed up lombok _and_ continue to support this, of course).

title: [BUG] boolean @Getter conflicts with explicit getter
body:
**Describe the bug**
I found some code that had a private boolean field:

```java
private boolean property;
```

It had an _explicit_ getter method:

```java
public boolean getProperty() {
    return property;
}
```

I wanted to replace this getter with a Lombok `@Getter`, which would result in a `isProperty()` method, but leaving the `getProperty()` as a `@Deprecated` method.

During compiling the following message is logged:

```
Not generating isProperty(): A method with that name already exists (getProperty)
```

Funny thing is that if I would rename the getter to something else it would work, for example `whateverProperty()`. There seems to be some conflict between the "get" and "is" prefix for getters for boolean fields.

**Expected behavior**

The error message is not correct: there is not a method with that name. The functionality should be changed so this is just allowed, or the error message should be more clear. My preference: I would like to be able to keep (as `@Deprecated`) an _explicit_ getter method on a boolean field and have the `@Getter` generated.

**Version info (please complete the following information):**
 - Lombok version 1.18.30
 - Platform openjdk 
  11.0.17 2022-10-18
OpenJDK Runtime Environment Temurin-11.0.17+8 (build 11.0.17+8)         
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM Temurin-11.0.17+8 (build 11.0.17+8, mixed mode)

nodes.body: I agree that we could optimize the error message a little bit but at least it already prints the name of the conflicting method. To fix your problem you can add `@Tolerate` to your explicit getter.
It's intended behaviour. Leaving the issue open solely for improving the error message we produce here.

Multiline errors? I'd have to check what that looks like in eclipse and intellij. item 2 also feels superfluous.

I'm not sure if that was your intention, @nell-shark but I think it's fine to special case it here. There are 2 options:

1. The method that already exists has a name that matches exactly. In other words, you have `getFoo()` and lombok would generate `getFoo()`. In which case the error message can remain simple: `Not generating %s(): A method with that name already exists`, as it does now.
2. The method that already exists has a name that doesn't match. It's got different casing, or it's got an `is`/`get` discrepancy going on. (Going by memory, lombok does ignore same-letters-different-casing situations, primarily due to beanspec weirdness in regards to fields that start with 2 or more capital letters. `int xAxis` turns into `getXAxis()` according to some beanspecs and `getxAxis()` in others): Then a longer error message that is more specific about 'the other name'. Specifically in this case, I guess we can mention `@Tolerate` on a second line if multiline errors look acceptable on all relevant platforms.

title: [FEATURE] Consider reviewing equals() implementation for better performance
body:
There is an [episode of JEP Café](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kuzjX_efuDs) (very well explained, kudos @JosePaumard) that compares the performance of several implementations for `equals()`. Obviously different implementations excel in different use cases, but it does seem that most of the times the instance check (which I believe you do at the very beggining of your implementation, according to [the docs](https://projectlombok.org/features/EqualsAndHashCode)) is actually a performance hit on predictive branching.

I would say that people should look for an implementation that better fits their particular needs, but given that Lombok is a generic solution I think it would make sense to go with the implementation that performs better in most cases.

Assuming Lombok is aware of the target language level when generating the source code (which I assume it does), it could also potentially take advantage of pattern matching for instanceof, for Java 14 or higher.

nodes.body:
I always have mixed feelings about micro optimizations like this :)

We can easily remove the first line but I'm not convinced that this is a performance improvement in most cases. The benchmark is limited to a single java runtime on a single CPU architecture but branch prediction is really different on different CPUs. I do not have the ressources (time, hardware, etc) to measure on all these systems. Lombok also uses the `canEqual` method for non-final classes which might change the results.

Hi @Rawi01 . Thank you for the insight. I understand your concerns. The main reason for me opening this ticket was to raise the discussion and hopefully  gather few people with knowledge debating it. I also thought this is not common knowledge (at least it wasn't for me), so was also to raise awareness to it.

title: [FEATURE] Add internString boolean flag on @Setter Annotation to reuse JVM string pool if you want

nodes.body:
I get your use case, but I have concerns about integrating it into Lombok.

Lombok primarily is a "boilerplate buster". That means its features aim at avoiding writing common patterns over and over again. However, interning Strings is not something you expect to find in your daily routine work as a Java coder. If you really need it, you typically need it only on a single setter. As this also has an impact on memory footprint/GC, that is IMO something you should code manually and not hide behind an annotation. 
Last but not least adding a annotation parameter only for a special type may be confusing and clutters the auto-completion.

Disclaimer: I'm not a Lombok team member, just contributor.
I agree that the situations where you want to intern are rare enough to not warrant it as part of the annotation (and should be a "hands on" decision), but I like the idea

public class Reproducer<T> {

    }
}

Ok guys just to add some context here, from my code sluething. 

The main driver is those first 3 lines we saw before:

https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/blob/d6ee06c534e6f51c0c7a4ebed8636eff5dd91893/src/core/lombok/eclipse/handlers/EclipseHandlerUtil.java#L1333-L1338

If we change this as @snjeza  has done, it is extremely likely that the code will compile and run. However, it appears that the overrides that Lombok is attempting to add will not function. 

Lombok is attempting to introspect all calls to `org.eclipse.jdt.internal.compiler.ast.TypeDeclaration` and it's `printBody` method. When introspecting this, it attempts to discover any calls to a `AbstractMethodDeclaration` object's `print(int, stringbuffer)` calls. And then replace it with a call to lombok's `printMethod` instead. 

https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/blob/d6ee06c534e6f51c0c7a4ebed8636eff5dd91893/src/eclipseAgent/lombok/eclipse/agent/EclipsePatcher.java#L989-L995

Lombok's `printMethod` lives in `PatchFixesHider$Javadoc` and simply calls another Lombok version of it:

https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/blob/d6ee06c534e6f51c0c7a4ebed8636eff5dd91893/src/eclipseAgent/lombok/launch/PatchFixesHider.java#L432-L444

From there, it redirects to Lombok's `PatchJavadoc` class and it's `printMethod` implementation, to ultimately override the version in JDT. 

https://github.com/projectlombok/lombok/blob/d6ee06c534e6f51c0c7a4ebed8636eff5dd91893/src/eclipseAgent/lombok/eclipse/agent/PatchJavadoc.java#L68-L80

Basically,  `PatchJavadoc` has a version of `printMethod` that is intended to override `AbstractMethodDeclaration.print(etc)`  implementation. 

Simply put, using only the 3 line fix above will let it compile and run, but will likely not allow Lombok's override behavior to take effect, unless we add similar replacements for each step along this chain.

body:
**Describe the bug**
When making the variable name like 'aName,' 'A,' 'Name,' it creates an issue and is unable to set the variable value. In other cases, like when the variable name is 'user,' 'userName,' 'u,' it will work fine.

**To Reproduce**
1.Make an entity User(id,uName,city).
2.Add a controller for Post request and post data in request body.
3.Receive data direct in User object from request(@RequestBody User user).
4. Now Print or return the same data to see different results.

nodes.body: I understand your explanation. but can you make it clear weather this happens all the time or alternatively, What I am trying to understand is does it happen with a specific type of naming or only a specific name?

> **Describe the bug** When making the variable name like 'aName,' 'A,' 'Name,' it creates an issue and is unable to set the variable value. In other cases, like when the variable name is 'user,' 'userName,' 'u,' it will work fine.
> 
> **To Reproduce** 1.Make an entity User(id,uName,city). 2.Add a controller for Post request and post data in request body. 3.Receive data direct in User object from request(@requestbody User user). 4. Now Print or return the same data to see different results. 5. Expected you receive some of names as null.
> 
> **Version info (please complete the following information):**
> 
> * Lombok version = 1.18.30
> * Platform (Intellij IDEA)
>   **Additional context**
>   Trial code : https://github.com/insane51/lombok-bug.git

Hi,
  The bug actually is that when you have a uppercase right after single lowercase letter in name, the getter and setter is generated as follows  : 
  parameter name : uName
  getter : getUName()
  setter : setUName()

but the compiler is not recognising this as default getter and setter 
what the compiler actually recognises is 
getter : getuName()
setter : setuName()

and this are the getter and setter that u normally get if you use a Ide getter and setter generator. hence we have to consider this as a special case and generate appropriate getter and setter according to compiler recognition standards.
Use [lombok.accessors.capitalization = beanspec](https://projectlombok.org/features/GetterSetter#supported-configuration-keys) in your lombok.config (available since lombok v1.18.24).

nodes.body:
That's a limitation of the type inference capabilities of `javac`, it cannot guess the type parameter just by the later method call.
You need to add a type hint like this:

```
PageableListDefinitionDto.<User>createBuilder()
      .setResultList(list)
      .create();
```

title: [FEATURE] @Immutable for fields
body:
It would be nice to have an extension that makes fields immutable. Basically generating a setter-method for a private field that contains the code to only set the field once. 

Why am I thinking about it?
In many cases I am not using `static final` fields because I want to write unit-tests that surround these fields with Mockito.spies to write assertions that the objects are called at the right moments with the correct params. For this reason I am normally making these fields immutable instead of static final.

nodes.body: Can you add some more details why you need this and a normal constructor is not sufficient? I also don't get why you mentioned `static final` fields (constants).

Use case denied. This isn't common enough.

If you want to change our minds, a few notes:

* Internet 'polls' are irrelevant. It doesn't matter if you find 500 people to chime in that they'd love this feature. It's a biased sample, and we do not submit to that kind of peer pressure. If it seems like you're starting a bit of a brigade, we'll double down on vetoing it just to make doubly sure bad behaviour isn't rewarded.
* We need clear use cases that indicate our opinion that this isn't common enough, is misguided. Which is _not_ a matter of 'well, I found 500 people with bizarre setups where this might be useful'. It needs to be something one might write into a 'book of patterns', or something listed directly in the main tutorial of some very commonly used library, for example.
* We don't like mockito much; usually good code design obviates the need for it. Lombok has a rule that features that have no obvious use other than something that is usually bad code style - are vetoed. Because that feature's existence is tacit approval for the bad code style (given that there's no other obvious use for the feature), and we don't wanna do that. I point this out simply to save you time: I doubt examples of how this mockito-based use case is common, will make us reconsider.

title: [FEATURE] Lombok 1.18.30 still accesses JDK internal APIs
body:
We're trying to upgrade our maven project to Java 17. In the `pom.xml` file, we have set the latest lombok version dependency as shown below:
```
<dependency>
       <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
       <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
       <version>1.18.30</version>
</dependency>
```
We can build and compile our project using Java 17 successfully. However, when we use `jdeps` to analyze the dependency, we noticed that lombok code still uses some JDK internal APIs, see below:
```
lombok.javac.apt                -> com.sun.tools.javac.processing            JDK removed internal API
lombok.javac.apt                -> com.sun.tools.javac.util                   JDK removed internal API
lombok.launch                   -> sun.misc                                JDK removed internal API
```
Could lombok code make an enhancement to upgrade the dependencies that do not use these encapsulated JDK internal APIs? Thank you.

nodes.body: No, we cannot remove the references because thats how lombok works but you can do that by setting the scope of the dependency to `provided` or mark the dependency as optional. [(Documentation)](https://projectlombok.org/setup/maven)

@tudousitang wrote:

> Could lombok code make an enhancement to upgrade the dependencies that do not use these encapsulated JDK internal APIs? Thank you.

You're misreading the report from your tools. It's not that lombok depends on some library that then depends on javac internals. Lombok _itself_ depends on them. No, we can't replace it with something else; if we could, we would, but despite asking, the OpenJDK team hasn't provided anything we can use. As Rawi said, your tool shouldn't be mentioning this (it's an optional dependency - at runtime lombok isn't used at all. If it compiles, you're good to go).

Shipping lombok as a thing maven understands as a compiler (where lombok-the-compiler is just a very thin wrapper that launches javac-the-compiler straight from your JDK installation, passing the appropriate `--add-opens` is in progress.

title: [FEATURE] new parameter for Setter to return old value.

nodes.body:
> This is one of commons code I have seen in many projects

I have never seen this.

> Please add parameter for generating setters to have a way to return previous value

No. Not boilerplate, and would be wildly confusing as the signature does not indicate what's happening; if a `setX` method returns anything but `void`, the go-to answer generally is that it `return this;` at the end, for chaining purposes, which lombok already supports. The feature would be confusing. "Is confusing!" is not a death warrant for a feature request, but it significantly elevates the bar that has to be crossed; it has to add a ton of value.

This doesn't. Not even close. PRs would be denied, and I doubt there'd be a point to convincing us otherwise. Note that popularity contests do not work (there is no point finding 100 people to chime in here. That's not a statistically relevant amount of java coders, that's not how we determine such things). Find objective, falsifiable cases. Such as popular (as per objective measures such as how often it shows up in other deps, web search results, github stars and the like) libraries that strongly lean towards _you_ writing setters this way, or major tutorials/books that espouse this kind of thing. I doubt they exist.

Hi,
Same feature is used on Atomic Object with getAndSet method. I do not say it has to be setter, it could be getAndSet. 
I came with this feature request as there is no easy way to create own custom annotations, where I would be fine with it.

@jan-pesta the method is _literally_ called `getAndSet` to avoid all doubt. You could write a feature request for `@GetAndSetter`, which would produce for a field `String foo;` a method:

```
public String getAndSetFoo(String newVal) { String oldVal = this.foo; this.foo = newVal; return oldVal; }
```

Except:

1. This is not an acceptable name. `@GetterAndSetter` is _extremely_ confusing as I bet most people would incorrectly assume that means: Generate both a getter and a setter. Not "Generate a single method - a getAndSetter, which is neither a getter nor a setter but a weird amalgamation of it".
2. Not boilerplate.

We'd love for lombok to gain some features to make it relatively easy to add stuff to it on a plugin basis, but the effort required to get lombok there is epic. (years of work, I think). We don't have the resources to go quite that far I'm afraid :(

title: [FEATURE] Builder static default / empty constant

nodes.body: You can add `@Getter` to your static variable but the name of the generated getter is probably not what you want and that doesn't solve your consistency problem.

Yes that is where a functionality either with Builder or another annotation would be nice.

I can use getter when defining constant like `instance` which can give me `getInstance` which is fine.
But I think it is by choice if somone wants to keep their constants as UPPER _CASE or lower, my probelm is when we have builder why to even bother about creating the constant ourselves, when we can simply assign Class.builder().build()

@anuragagarwal561994 I'm not sure what you're suggesting. Generally a feature request, or even an attempt to start a debate on a feature request, should probably include at least an attempt at 'this is what it looks like with lombok' vs 'this is what lombok would make of it, i.e. the output of delombok'.

A serious issue is, well, you said it: Consistently. There does not appear to be a community consensus on this. Specifically, most builderized types don't have a 'default', and even if they do, there is no consistent naming scheme.

I'm not sure a consistent naming scheme is even a good idea. Take `java.lang.String`, for example. If we're going to have a default value at all, the right answer is __obviously__ `empty` or `blank`, and `getDefault` is __obviously__ a bad idea. Obvious in that it _is_ a subjective question (it's about which name is less confusing and more 'readable', all human concepts - subjective. Opinion, taste, and all that) - but as far as subjective questions go, this one has very clear answers and I'd bet a lot of money if I go around a java conference and ask whether one would think such a thing would be called 'empty' or 'default', 90%+ would say 'empty', and many will comment on how 'default' seems like a very bad choice indeed.

Also, there's `.of()` which is beginning to be a bit of a community consensus, as the standardized name of static methods that act like constructors. However, any such thing that accepts a list of arguments (e.g. via varargs), then ends up having `.of()` to be __the__ canonical way to make an empty ('default') object. This is already the case in __extremely__ commonly used code today:

```
List<String> list = List.of();
```

So, here, `of()` is the default, and I think that's a correct take here. __It would be a mistake if `java.util.List` also had an `getDefault()` method or a `DEFAULT` field with an unmodifiable empty list__.

And hence, your feature request would be a mistake.

Closed - but feel free to attempt to make a convincing argument as to why it's a good idea. Closed issues can be re-opened.

@rzwitserloot sure I think that is fair to say that the information above is incomplete, may be because it is my first time writing an issue in the lombok project. I will try to check other feature requests and try to come up with a descrptive argument before I would open this issue again.

title: [FEATURE] lombok.config: define once onConstructor, onMethod, and rule them all
body:
**Describe the feature**
I would like to propose a new attribute in `lombok.config` file to add default `onConstructor`/`onMethod` annotations for constructors, getters, and setters.

Example usage

```
lombok.requiredArgsConstructor.onConstructor += com.acme.annotation.MyAnnotation(param = "value")
```

**Target business scenario**
In my Spring Boot projects, I'm keen to constructor injection and I use it as most as possible
Especially in JUnit 5 tests, you can't use `@RequiredArgsConstructor` without setting `onConstructor_ = @Autowired`, otherwise JUnit won't load the test.

At least in my test directory, where my `lombok.config` should be placed, I would like a convention-over-configuration for annotating **all** `@RequiredArgsConstructor` with Spring's `@Autowired`

Note that this is inspired to the existing `copyableAnnotations`

Thank you for your time looking at this

title: [FEATURE] @EqualsAndHashCode(markFinal = true)
body:
**Describe the feature**
The `@EqualsAndHashCode` annotation is potentially very useful. When using [EqualsVerifier](http://www.jqno.nl/equalsverifier/) though (in default/strict mode), it will point out that the `equals(Object)` and `hashCode()` methods are not marked as `final`.

It would be great if we could have a boolean attribute on the `@EqualsAndHashCode` annotation for marking the generated methods as `final`. E.g. `markFinal`, with default value being `false` to maintain existing behavior.

For example:

```java
@EqualsAndHashCode(markFinal = true)
public class MyTree {
  // ...
}
```

**Describe the target audience**
Programmers that want to have optimal implementations of `equals(Object)` and `hashCode()` methods, and use [EqualsVerifier](http://www.jqno.nl/equalsverifier/) to validate that.

**Additional context**
—

nodes.body:
Hey @znerd,

As the [documentation of the given error message](https://jqno.nl/equalsverifier/errormessages/subclass-equals-is-not-final/) already suggests, you could make the whole class final. Therefore my question here would be: can you give an example where you need the class to remain non-final but disallow the subclasses to change equals and hashCode?

On the side note: the same documentation points to withRedefinedSubclass which would enable you to explicitly specify the subclass while using EqualsVerifier.

title: [BUG] SneakyThrows leaves traces to lombok in the class files

**Describe the bug**

title: [BUG] Fix getter annotation for Boolean class field definition
body:
@Getter annotation for a field of class Boolean should have **is** prefix instead of **get**, just like the primitive type.

To reproduce, from how I find out: Create an interface and an implementation class. In the interface create a method that returns Boolean (eg. Boolean isValid()), have a field in the implementation class called (eg. valid) and annotate the class or field with @Getter, the compiler will complain about the fact that the class did not implemented all the interface methods, and will create a getter getValid(), instead of isValid().

Suggestion: to have the same implementation for Boolean class, just like in the primitive boolean.

 - Lombok version: 1.18.28

title: [FEATURE] Kotlin style properties in Java?
body:
Hi,

Am curious if it's feasible to develop a Lombok annotation to provide Kotlin-style properties in Java. That is, the dev would normally use the property's name to access it instead of getter/setter methods. But if the dev defines a custom getter/setter method then it will be called while the property is still accessed by its name.

See https://kotlinlang.org/docs/properties.html#getters-and-setters for more info how it's done in Kotlin.

Would be nice to have Kotlin-like properties in Java as they make code clearer and easier to read, removing mundane function calls when really there's no need for them.

Regards,

title: [BUG]  @ExtensionMethod replacing bug in Stream#map

nodes.body: This is not a bug, the output is identical if you use the static method without lombok (`Stream.of("content1", "content2", "content3").map(Extensions.of(title)::setContent).collect(Collectors.toList());`). This is a method reference that is bound to the result of `title.of()`.
